etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English abandounen, from Old French abandoner, formed from à (Old French “at, to”) + bandon (Old French “jurisdiction, control”), from Late Latin bannum (“proclamation”), bannus (Latin), bandum (Latin), from Frankish *ban, *bann (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to proclaim, command”) (whence ban (English)), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”). See also ban (English), banal (English).

Displaced forleten (Middle English “to abandon”), from forlǣtan (Old English), anforlǣtan (Old English); see forlet (English); and forleven (Middle English “to leave behind, abandon”), from forlǣfan (Old English); see forleave (English).

Compare typologically abdicate (English), отказа́ться (Russian) (akin to приказа́ть (Russian), сказа́ть (Russian), указа́ть (Russian)).

etymologies.text: First attested in the 1300s. From Middle English abilite (“suitability, aptitude, ability”), from Old French ablete (“ableté”), from Latin habilitās (“aptness, ability”), from habilis (Latin “apt, fit, skillful, able”); equivalent to able + ity (English).

etymologies.text:
Preposition and adverb from Middle English aboute, abouten (Middle English), from Old English abūtan, onbūtan (Old English), from on + būtan (Old English) (compare modern but (English), bout (English)), itself from be + ūtan (Old English); equivalent to on + be + out (English) or on + but (English). Cognate with abûta (Old Frisian “outside; except”). Not related to bout (English “period of time”)

Adjective from Middle English about.

From Middle English above, aboven (Middle English), abuven (Middle English), from Old English ābufan, onbufan (Old English), from on (Old English “on”) + bufan (Old English “over”), (akin to ofan (Icelandic “from above”), bōven (Middle Dutch), bova (Old Frisian), bobene (Middle High German)) from bī (Old English “by”) + ufan (Old English “over”); also cognate with oven (Danish), boven (Dutch), oben (German), ovan (Swedish), oban (Old Saxon “oƀan”), obana (Old High German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested in 1557. From Middle French absurde, from Latin absurdus (“incongruous, dissonant, out of tune”), from ab (Latin “away from, out”) + surdus (Latin “silent, deaf, dull-sounding”). Compare surd (English).

etymologies.text: From Middle English abusen, then from either Old French abus (“improper use”), or from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (Latin “make improper use of, consume, abuse”), from ab (Latin “away”) + ūtor (Latin “to use”). The word accent (Old English) had been borrowed into Old English already, but was lost and reborrowed in Middle English. Displaced native swēġ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English aken, and ache (Middle English), from Old English acan (from Proto-West Germanic *akan, from Proto-Germanic *akaną (“to ache”)) and æċe (Old English) (from Proto-West Germanic *aki, from Proto-Germanic *akiz), traditionally explained as from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂égos.

Cognate with eeke (Saterland Frisian), ääke (Saterland Frisian “to ache, fester”), aken (Low German), achen (Low German), äken (Low German “to hurt, ache”), Eek (Low German (Germany) “inflammation”), akelig (North Frisian), æklig (North Frisian “terrible, miserable, sharp, intense”), aaklik (Western Frisian “nasty, horrible, dismal, dreary”), akelig (Dutch “nasty, horrible”).

The verb was originally strong, conjugating for tense like take (e.g. I ake, I oke, I have aken), but gradually became weak during Middle English; the noun was originally pronounced as as spelled (compare breach (English), from break (English)). Historically the verb was spelled ake, and the noun ache (even after the form started to become common for the noun; compare again break (English) which is now also a noun). The verb came to be spelled like the noun when lexicographer Samuel Johnson mistakenly assumed that it derived from ἄχος (Ancient Greek “pain”) due to the similarity in form and meaning of the two words.

* Late Latin *accapāre, the of *accapō (Late Latin “to finish”), from Latin ad- + *capum (Latin) (from caput (Latin “head”); see further above) + -ō (Latin).

* acabar (Catalan)
* achevare (Late Latin), acheviare (Late Latin “to acknowledge feudal liability; to complete, end”)
* acabar (pro) (modern acabar (Occitan))
* acabar (Portuguese)
* acabar (Spanish)

etymologies.text: From Middle English ajusten, borrowed from Middle French adjuster, or Old French —, from Latin ad (“to, up to, towards”) + iustus (Latin “correct, proper, exact”); Equivalent to . Probably influenced in sense by Old French ajouster (cf. modern ajouter (French)), from Vulgar Latin *adiuxtāre, from Latin iuxta. The Middle English originally meant "to correct, remedy" in the late 14th century, and was reborrowed from Middle French in the early 17th century. According to another view on the etymology, the word was actually derived from Old French ajouster (Old French) and then supposedly later influenced by folk etymology from Latin iustus (Latin); if so, it is a .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English affect, from Latin affectus, adfectus (Latin “a state of mind or body produced by some (external) influence, especially sympathy or love”), from afficere (Latin “to act upon, influence”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English after, from Old English æfter, from Proto-West Germanic *aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“further behind, further away”), from *h₂epo (Proto-Indo-European “off, away”).

Cognate with efter (Scots “after”), efter (North Frisian “after, behind”), after (Western Frisian), achter (Western Frisian), efter (Western Frisian “behind; after”), achter (Low German / Dutch “behind”), after- (German “after-”), efter (Danish / Swedish “after”), etter (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “after”), eftir (Faroese / Icelandic “after”).

The Irish usage to indicate recent completion of an activity is a calque of the Irish collocation Táim tar éis... (Irish “I have just...”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Formed from Middle English ayenes, agenes (Middle English), againes (Middle English “in opposition to”), a southern variant of agen (Middle English), or directly from again (English), either way with adverbial genitive singular ending -es (English); the parasitic -t (English) was added circa 1350, probably by confusion with the superlative ending -est (English). .

Cognate with juun (Saterland Frisian “against”), tsjin (Western Frisian “against”), tegen (Dutch “against”), gegen (Low German (Germany) “against”), gegen (German “against”), gegn (Icelandic “against”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English age, Old French eage (“aage, eage, edage”), from an assumed Vulgar Latin *aetāticum, derived from Latin aetas (“aetātem”), itself derived from aevum (Latin “lifetime”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force”). Compare âge (French). Displaced native ieldu (Old English).

The verb is from Middle English agen, from the noun. Originally found mostly as a participial adjective, probably an adjective in -ed (Middle English), derived from the noun, reanalyzed to create a verb; perhaps modeled on such pairs as senēscō (Latin) (seneō (Latin); verb) / senex (Latin) and vieillir (Middle French) / vieil (Middle French). Also compare se aagier (Old French), eogier (Old French “become of age”).

etymologies.text: From air + line (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English alarme, alarom (Middle English), borrowed from Middle French alarme, itself from Old Italian — all'arme! (Italian “to arms!, to the weapons!”), ultimately from Latin arma (“arms, weapons”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested 1891, from alcohol + ic (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The adjective comes from a conflation of several different terms:
* Middle English alich, alych (Middle English), alyke (Middle English), a Late Middle English development from earlier anlich (Middle English), anlyke (Middle English), from Old English onlīċ, anlīċ (Old English). Compare ähnlich (German).
* The borrowed Old Norse — cognate of the same word, álíkr (Old Norse), ultimately yielding similar Late Middle English forms.
* Middle English ylich, ylych (Middle English), ilich (Middle English), ylik (Middle English), ylike (Middle English), ȝelic (Middle English), from Old English ġelīċ (“like; alike; similar; equal”), from Proto-West Germanic *galīk, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz (“alike, similar”). Cognate with elyke (Scots), alyke (Scots “like, alike”), gliek (Saterland Frisian “like, alike”), lyk (Western Frisian), gelyk (Western Frisian “like, alike”), gelijk (Dutch “like, alike”), liek (Low German (Germany)), gliek (Low German (Germany) “like, alike”), gleich (German “equal, like”), lig (Danish “alike”), lik (Swedish “like, similar”), lik (Norwegian “like, alike”), líkur (Icelandic “alike, like, similar”). Equivalent to a-#Etymology 3 + like (English). Compare also allyk (Western Frisian “all the same, alike”).

Similarly, the adverb also comes from a conflation of several different terms:
* Middle English aliche, alyche (Middle English), alyke (Middle English), a Late Middle English development from earlier anliche (Middle English), anlyke (Middle English), from Old English onlīċe, anlīċe (Old English).
* Additionally Middle English oliche, olike (Middle English), ultimately from the Old Norse — cognate of the same word, álíka (Old Norse).
* Middle English yliche, ylyche (Middle English), iliche (Middle English), ylike (Middle English), ȝelice (Middle English), from Old English ġelīċe (“alike, similarly”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English alyve, alive (Middle English), alife (Middle English), olive (Middle English), olife (Middle English), on live (Middle English), on life (Middle English), from Old English on līfe (“alive”), from on (Old English “on, in”) + līfe (Old English), dative singular of līf (Old English “life”). In this sense, replaced cwic (Old English) (whence quick (English)). Equivalent to a- + life (English). Compare in leven (Dutch “alive”), am Leben (German “alive”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English all, from Old English eall, from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz, of uncertain origin but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“all”).

Cognate with a (Scots), a' (Scots), aa (Scots), aal (Scots), aw (Scots “all”), aal (Yola), al (Yola), all (Yola), aul (Yola “all”), aal (North Frisian), aale (North Frisian), ale (North Frisian), ali (North Frisian), åle (North Frisian “all”), al (Saterland Frisian “already”), aal (Saterland Frisian “all”), alle (Western Frisian “all”), al (Dutch “all”), all (de,lb “all”), oły (Ripuarian), ołły (Ripuarian “all”), אַלע (Yiddish “all”), al (Danish “all”), allur (Faroese / Icelandic “all”), all (Norwegian Bokmål / Swedish “all”), aillj (Norwegian Nynorsk), all (Norwegian Nynorsk “all”), 𐌰𐌻𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “all”); also holl (Breton / Welsh “all”), oll (Cornish “all”), alig (Irish), eile (Irish), uile (Irish), uileag (Irish), uilig (Irish “all”), ooilley (Manx “all”), uile (Scottish Gaelic), uileag (Scottish Gaelic “all”), aliái (Lithuanian “every”), ողջ (Armenian “entire, whole”).

The dialectal sense “all gone” is a . The use in etc. also has equivalents in German (see alles (German)).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English all, from Old English eall, from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz, of uncertain origin but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“all”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English allowen, alowen (Middle English), a borrowing from Anglo-Norman allouer, alouer (Old French), from Medieval Latin allaudō (“allaudāre”), merged with alouer (Old French), from Medieval Latin allocō (“to assign”). (via allaudāre (Latin)) or allocate (English) (via allocāre (Latin)).

The similarity with alyfen (Middle English) (from ālīefan (Old English)) and erlauben (German), both from *uzlaubijaną (Proto-Germanic “to allow”), is coincidental.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from Old English andlang, from prefix and- (Old English) + lang (Old English “long”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English aloud, , equivalent to a + loud (English) or a + loude (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English alphabete, borrowed from Classical Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος, from ἄλφα (Ancient Greek) and βῆτα (Ancient Greek), the names of the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, Α (Ancient Greek) and Β (Ancient Greek), lowercase forms α (Ancient Greek) and β (Ancient Greek). The Greek names derived from aleph (English), the name of the Phoenician — letter 𐤀 (Phoenician “ox”) and beth (English), the name of the letter 𐤁 (Phoenician “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects, having developed from the Egyptian hieroglyphs (𓃾 (Egyptian)) and (𓉐 (Egyptian)). . Dipslaced native stæfrǣw (Old English) (literally "staff-row").

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From alphabēticus + -al (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English alredy (“fully; already”), equivalent to al-#Etymology_1 + ready (English). Cognate with alreeds (Western Frisian “already”), alreeds (Dutch “already”), alreeds (Afrikaans “already”), alreide (Middle Low German), alreids (Middle Low German) , allerede (Danish “already”), allaredan (Swedish “already”), allereie (Norwegian Nynorsk “already”). More at all (English), ready (English).

The use as an intensifier in American English is a Yiddish שוין, attested from 1903.

In Singapore English, the use of already as a marker of action completion and change of state is analogous to , and . Compare sudah (Malay “(su)dah”) and 咗 (Cantonese), .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare eallriht (Old English “all-right, just, exactly”) (from eall + riht (Old English)), equivalent to al-#Etymology_1 + right (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old French alterer (altérer (French)), from Medieval Latin alterō (“to make other”), from Latin alter (“the other”), from al- (Latin) (seen in alius (Latin “other”), alienus (Latin “of another”), etc.; see alias, alien, etc.) + compar. suffix -ter (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Probably from alter ego (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French alternatif, from Medieval Latin alternātīvus (“alternating”), from the participle stem of Latin alternō (“interchange, alternate”). . Compare alternate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: alternative + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English althagh, from Old English — compound of eall (Old English “all (emphatic)”) + þēah (Old English “though”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English altogeder, altogedere (Middle English), equivalent to al-#Etymology_1 + together (English). Cognate with awthegither (Scots “altogether”), alzegater (Middle High German “altogether”), altegaar (Dutch). Compare also ealġeador (Old English), eallġeador (Old English “altogether”), allegearre (Western Frisian “altogether”). More at together.

The noun sense was popularized in 's 1894 novel '.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First used in 1812 as an alternative form of aluminum which was coined in the same year. From alūmen + ium (English).
* For information on the origins of the two spellings, see the Wikipedia article.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English alweyes, alwayes (Middle English), alweys (Middle English), a variant of Middle English alwey, alway (Middle English “always”), from Old English ealneġ, ealne weġ (Old English “always, perpetually”), from ealne (Old English) + weġ (Old English), equivalent to alway + s (English). Cognate with always (Scots “always”), allerwegens (Low German “very often”). More at all (English), way (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From amaze + ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From amaze + ing (English), from Old English āmasian.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: amazing + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ambassadore, from Anglo-Norman ambassadeur, from Old Italian ambassadore, from pro ambaisador (“ambassador”), derivative of ambaissa (pro “service, mission, errand”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ambahtaz (“servant”), from Gaulish ambaxtos, from Proto-Celtic *ambaxtos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi-h₂eǵ- (“drive around”), from *h₂m̥bʰi- (Proto-Indo-European “around”) + *h₂eǵ- (Proto-Indo-European “to drive”).

Displaced native ǣrendraca (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ambicioun, from Old French ambition, from Latin ambitiō (“ambition, a striving for favor, literally 'a going around', especially of candidates for office in Rome soliciting votes”), from ambiō (Latin “to go around, solicit votes”). See ambient, issue. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ambitious, from Middle French ambitieus, from Latin ambitiosus, from ambitio (Latin); see ambition (English). Compare with ambitieux (French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The is derived from Middle English among, amang (Middle English), amange (Middle English), amonge (Middle English “in the presence of, amid, among; in, within; between; during”), from Old English amang, onġemang (Old English), from on (Old English “on, among, in”) (probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“on, onto”)) + ġemang (Old English “crowd; mixture”) (from ġe- (Old English) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“beside, by; near; with”)) + (from mængan (Old English), mengan (Old English “to mingle, mix”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *menk- (“to knead; to press”))). .

The is derived from Middle English among, amang (Middle English “accompanied by, along with, by the side of, in association with, together; all the while, continually; also, besides; at the same time; from time to time, occasionally; meanwhile; within”), from Old English onġemang: see further above.

* mank (Dutch), maank (Dutch “among”)
* mang (German “among”) (dialectal)
* mank (Low German (Germany)), manken (Low German (Germany) “among”)
* monk (Saterland Frisian), monken (Saterland Frisian “among”)
* mank (Western Frisian “among”)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From amongs + t + excrescent]] (English), from among + s (English). . Root among (English) from Old English ongemang, from on (Old English “in”) + gemang (Old English “assemblage, mingling”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English amounten (“to mount up to, come up to, signify”), from Old French amonter (“to amount to”), from amont (Old French), amunt (Old French “uphill, upward”), from the prepositional phrase a mont (Old French “toward or to a mountain or heap”), from Latin ad montem, from ad (Latin “to”) + montem (Latin), accusative of mons (Latin “mountain”).

chain.meaning: to mount up to, come up to, signify

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Late Middle English *amusen (“to mutter, be astonished, gaze meditatively on”), from Old French amuser (“to stupefy, waste time, be lost in thought”), from a- (Old French) + muser (Old French “to stare stupidly at, gape, wander, waste time, loiter, think carefully about, attend to”), of and obscure origin. Cognate with musa (Occitan “idle waiting”), musare (Italian “to gape idly about”). Possibly from Old French *mus (“snout”) from Vulgar Latin *mūsa (“snout”) — compare - (Medieval Latin) mūsum (Latin “muzzle, snout”) –, from Proto-Germanic *mū- (“muzzle, snout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mū- (“lips, muzzle”). Compare müs (North Frisian), mös (North Frisian “mouth”), Maul (German “muzzle, snout”).

Alternative etymology connects muser (Old French) and musa (Occitan) with *muoza (Frankish “careful attention, leisure, idleness”), from *mōtǭ (Proto-Germanic “leave, permission”), from *med- (Proto-Indo-European “to acquire, possess, control”).
This would make it a cognate of musen (Dutch “to leisure”), *muoza (Old High German “careful attention, leisure, idleness”) and muozōn (Old High German “to be idle, have leisure or opportunity”), Muße (German “leisure”). More at empty (English).

chain.meaning: to stupefy, waste time, be lost in thought

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: amuse + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French amusement, from amuser + -ment (Middle French). Morphologically amuse + ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις, from ἀναλύω (Ancient Greek “to unravel, investigate”), from ἀνα- (Ancient Greek “thoroughly”) + λύω (Ancient Greek “to loosen”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French analyste.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ancestre, auncestre (Middle English), ancessour (Middle English); the first forms from Old French ancestre (modern French ancêtre (French)), from the Latin — nominative antecessor (Latin “one who goes before”); the last form from Old French ancessor, from Latin antecessōrem (Latin), accusative of antecessor (Latin), from antecēdō + -tor (Latin), from ante + cēdō (Latin). See cede (English), and compare with .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English auncyen, from Old French ancien, from Vulgar Latin *anteānus, composed of Latin ante (“before”) + -ānus (Latin). The non-etymological excrescent /t/ is by analogy with the common ending -ent (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Corruption of ensign (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English and, an (Middle English), from Old English and, ond (Old English), end (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *andi, from Proto-Germanic *andi, *anþi (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énti (“facing opposite, near, in front of, before”). Cognate with an (Scots “and”), än (North Frisian “and”), un (Saterland Frisian “and”), en (Western Frisian “and”), en (Dutch), ende (Dutch “and”), und (German “and”), on (Low German (Germany)), un (Low German (Germany) “and”), an (lb “and”), an (Ripuarian), ana (Ripuarian “and”), און (Yiddish), אונ (Yiddish), אונד (Yiddish), אונ׳ (Yiddish “and”), end (Danish “still; ever; even”), enn (Faroese “still, yet”), en (Icelandic “and”), enn (Icelandic “still, yet”), enn (Norwegian Bokmål “and”), en (Norwegian Nynorsk), enn (Norwegian Nynorsk “and”), än (Swedish “still, yet”), edhe (Albanian “and”) (dialectal ênde, ênne (Albanian)), ende (Albanian “still, yet, therefore”), ante (Latin “opposite, in front of”), ἀντί (Ancient Greek “opposite, facing”). ("if").

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Middle English ande, from Old English anda (“grudge, enmity, malice, envy, hatred, anger, zeal, annoyance, vexation; zeal; injury, mischief; fear, horror”) and Old Norse andi (“breath, wind, spirit”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadô (“breath, anger, zeal”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁- (“to breathe, blow”).

Cognate with Ahnd, And (German “woe, grief”), ånde (Danish “breath”), anda, ande (Swedish “spirit, breath, wind, ingenuity, intellect”), andi (Icelandic “spirit”), ëndë (Albanian “pleasure, delight”), animus (Latin “spirit, soul”). Related to onde (English).

chain.meaning: grudge, enmity, malice, envy, hatred, anger, zeal, annoyance, vexation; zeal; injury, mischief; fear, horror

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Middle English anden, from Old English andian (“to be envious or jealous, envy”) and Old Norse anda (“to breathe”); both from Proto-Germanic *anadōną (“to breathe, sputter”). Cognate with ahnden (German “to avenge, punish”), ånde (Danish “to breathe”), andas (Swedish “to breathe”), anda (Icelandic “to breathe”). See above.

chain.meaning: to be envious or jealous, envy

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|Angels depicted in the , 13th century

From Middle English aungel, angel (Middle English), from Old English anġel, either a modification of enġel (Old English) after its etymon Latin angelus (through the intermediate of Proto-West Germanic *angil) or a reborrowing from the Latin, which is in turn from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (“messenger”); later reinforced by Anglo-Norman angele, angel (Old French), from the same Latin source. The religious sense of the Greek word first appeared in the Septuagint as a translation of the Hebrew word מַלְאָךְ (Hebrew “messenger”) or מַלְאַךְ יהוה (Hebrew “messenger of YHWH”). .

Use of the term in some churches to refer to a church official derives from interpreting the "angels" of the in Revelation as being bishops or ministers rather than angelic beings.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Clipping: Angelman

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English anger (“grief, pain, trouble, affliction, vexation, sorrow, wrath”), from Old Norse angr, ǫngr (Old Norse “affliction, sorrow”) (compare ang (Old Norse), ǫng (Old Norse “troubled”)), from Proto-Germanic *angazaz (“grief, sorrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enǵʰ- (“narrow, tied together”).

Cognate with anger (Danish “regret, remorse”), anger (Norwegian Bokmål “regret, remorse”), ånger (Swedish “regret”), angur (Icelandic “trouble”), ange (Old English), enge (Old English “narrow, close, straitened, constrained, confined, vexed, troubled, sorrowful, anxious, oppressive, severe, painful, cruel”), Angst (German “anxiety, anguish, fear”), angō (Latin “squeeze, choke, vex”), angor (Latin “strangulation; anguish, torment”) (whence the English doublet ), French angoisse, ang (Albanian “fear, anxiety, pain, nightmare”), 𐬄𐬰𐬀𐬵 (ae “strangulation; distress”), ἄγχω (Ancient Greek “to squeeze, strangle”), अंहस् (Sanskrit), अंहु (Sanskrit “anxiety, distress, affliction”). Also compare with anguish (English), anxious (English), quinsy (English), and perhaps to awe (English) and ugly (English). The word seems to have originally meant “to choke, squeeze”.

The verb is from Middle English angren, angeren (Middle English), from Old Norse angra. Compare with angra (Icelandic), angra (Norwegian Nynorsk), angre (Norwegian Bokmål), ångra (Swedish), angre (Danish).

chain.meaning: grief, pain, trouble, affliction, vexation, sorrow, wrath

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English angrily, equivalent to angry + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English animal, from Old French animal, from Latin animal, a nominal use of the adjective form animāle (Latin), neuter of animālis (Latin), from anima (Latin “breath, spirit”).

Displaced native deer (English) (outside puristic usage) in the general animal sense, from der,deor (Middle English “animal”), from dēor (Old English), related to Tier (German “animal”), dier (Dutch), dyr (Danish), djur (Swedish) etc. Displaced also rother#Noun (English “horned animal, esp. ox”), from rother ,reother (Middle English “a bovine”), from hrīþer,hrȳþer (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English animal, from Latin animālis, from either anima (Latin “breath, spirit”) or animus (Latin). Originally distinct from the noun, it became associated with attributive use of the noun and is now indistinguishable from it.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: , from animō (Latin), equivalent to animate + ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ankel, ancle (Middle English), ankyll (Middle English), from Old English ancol (compare anclēow (Old English “ankle”) > Modern anclef (English), ancliff (English), ancley (English)), from Proto-West Germanic *ankul, from Proto-Germanic *ankulaz (“ankle”); akin to ökkla (Icelandic), ökli (Icelandic), ankel (Danish / Swedish), enkel (Dutch), enklaauw (Dutch), Enkel (German), akka (Old Norse), anckel (Old Frisian), and perhaps encha (Old High German), ancha (Old High German “thigh, shin”), from the *ankijǭ (Proto-Germanic “ankle, joint”).

Compare with अङ्ग (Sanskrit “limb”), अङ्गुरि (Sanskrit “finger”), angulus (Latin). Compare haunch (English) and Greek prefix ἀγκυλο- (Ancient Greek “joint, crooked, bent”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English anniversary,annyversarie,annyverary,annyversarye,anyversarye, from Anglo-Norman aniversarie,anniversarie and Anglo-Norman / Old French / Middle French aniversaire,anniversaire (modern anniversaire (French)) and their etymon Classical Latin anniversārius (“yearly”), from annus (Latin “year”) + vertō (Latin “to turn”). The verb is from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French anoncier, from Latin annuntio (“annūntiāre”), from ad (Latin) + nūntiō (Latin “report, relate”), from nūntius (Latin “messenger, bearer of news”). See nuncio (English). . See also an-#Etymology_4.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French annoncement. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English anoyen, from Old French enoiier (“to bother, disturb”), from Late Latin inodio (“to make loathsome”), derived from Latin odium (“loathing, hatred”). Displaced native dreċċan (Old English), gremman (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English anoy, from Old French enui. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: annoy + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested around 1382 as Middle English annuel, from Late Latin annuālem, annuālis (Latin), related to Latin annālis, adjective form of annus (Latin “year”). Used to categorize plants since 1710.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: annual + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English answere, andsware (Middle English), from Old English andswaru (“answer”), from and- + swaru (Old English), (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- (“front, forehead”) and Old English swerian (“to swear”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer-), suggesting an original meaning of "a sworn statement rebutting a charge". The cognates suggest the existence of Proto-Germanic *andaswarō (“a reply to a question”). Cognate with ondser (Old Frisian “answer”), andswōr (Old Saxon “answer”), - (Danish) and ansvar (Swedish “liability, responsibility, answer”), andsvar (Icelandic “answer, response”). Compare also andwyrde (Old English “answer”) (cognate to antwoord (Dutch), Antwort (German)), andcwiss (Old English “reply”), Schwur (German “oath, vow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English answeren, andswaren (Middle English), answerien (Middle English), from Old English andswarian, answarien (Old English “to answer, to respond, to deny an allegation under oath”), from Proto-Germanic *andaswarōną, *andaswarjaną (Proto-Germanic “to answer, to give a response, to rebut”), from *anda + *swarjaną (Proto-Germanic), *swarōną (Proto-Germanic “to swear an oath, to answer, to respond”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- (“face, forehead”) and *swer- (Proto-Indo-European “to swear”). Cognate with ondswera (Old Frisian “to answer”), ansvare (Danish “to answer, account for”), ansvara (Swedish “to answer, account for”), andsvara (Icelandic “to answer, reply”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ampte, amte (Middle English), amete (Middle English), amote (Middle English), ante (Middle English), emete (Middle English), emot (Middle English), emotte (Middle English), empt (Middle English), empte (Middle English), from Old English ǣmete, ǣmette (Old English), ǣmytte (Old English), ǣmætte (Old English “ant”), from Proto-West Germanic *āmaitijā (“ant”), of , but probably from Proto-Germanic *ē- (“off, away”) + *maitaną (Proto-Germanic “to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂y- (“to cut”). See also emmet (English).

Cognate with emotee (Yola), emothee (Yola “ant”), eamel (Western Frisian), eamelder (Western Frisian), eameler (Western Frisian “ant”), Ameisse (Alemannic “ant”), Åmasn (Bavarian), Åmeisn (Bavarian “ant”), amasa (Cimbric “ant”), emt (Dutch “ant”), Ameise (German), Emse (German “ant”), Emk (Low German “ant”), ömys (Ripuarian “ant”), אַמייזע (Yiddish “ant”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French antique (“ancient, old”), from Latin antiquus (“former, earlier, ancient, old”), from ante (Latin “before”); see ante- (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin ānxietās, from ānxius (Latin “anxious, solicitous, distressed, troubled”), from angō (Latin “to distress, trouble”), akin to ἄγχω (Ancient Greek “to choke”). Equivalent to . See anger (English); angst (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin anxius, from angō (Latin “to cause pain, choke”); akin to ἄγχω (Ancient Greek “to choke”). See anger (English); angst (English). The suffix has been influenced by unrelated -ous.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: anxious + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English any, eny (Middle English), ony (Middle English), ani (Middle English), aniȝ (Middle English), eniȝ (Middle English), æniȝ (Middle English), from Old English ǣniġ (“any”), from Proto-West Germanic *ainīg, *ainag (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *ainagaz, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”), equivalent to one + -y (English).

Cognate with eenich (Saterland Frisian “some”), iennich (Western Frisian “only”), enig (Dutch “any, some”), enig (Afrikaans “any”), enig (Low German (Germany) “some”), einig (German “some”); via *óynos (Proto-Indo-European) cognate with ūllus (Latin “any”), ūnicus (Latin) (whence unico (Italian “unique”), unique (French “unique”)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ani-bodi,anybodi,eny body. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From any + how (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English eny on, ony one (Middle English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From any + way (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English apart, aparte (Middle English), a-part (Middle English), a part (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: apology + -ise

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French apologie, from Late Latin apologia, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (“a speech in defence”), from ἀπολογοῦμαι (Ancient Greek “I speak in my defense”), from ἀπόλογος (Ancient Greek “an account, story”), from ἀπό (Ancient Greek “from, off”) (see apo-) + λόγος (Ancient Greek “speech”). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From French apostrophe, or Latin apostrophus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (“accent of elision”), a noun use of an adjective from ἀποστρέφω (Ancient Greek “to turn away”), from ἀπό (Ancient Greek “away from”) + στρέφω (Ancient Greek “to turn”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Latin apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή, from ἀποστρέφω (Ancient Greek “to turn away”), from ἀπό (Ancient Greek) + στρέφω (Ancient Greek “to turn”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English apparaunt, aparaunt (Middle English), from Old French aparent, aparant (Old French), in turn from Latin appārēns (“appārēns, appārentis”), present participle of appāreō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: apparent + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English apel, appel (Middle English “formal accusation brought in court; a challenge to trial by combat; an appeal to a higher court or authority; plea (for mercy, protection, etc.); pealing (of bells)”), from Old French apel (“a call”) (modern appel (French “a call; an appeal”)), from apeler (Old French “to call; to call out”), from Latin appello#Etymology_2_2 (“appellāre”), alternative form adpello (Latin “adpellāre”), from ad- (Latin) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at; to”)) + pello (Latin “pellere”) + -o (Latin “-āre”), ultimately from *pelh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to approach”), from *pel- (Proto-Indo-European “to beat; to drive; to push”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English apelen, appelen (Middle English “to accuse; to make a formal charge before a court, etc., impeach; to challenge to trial by combat; to apply to a higher court or authority for review of a decision; to call upon for a decision, favour, help, etc.; to call by a name”), from Old French apeler (“to call; to call out”); see further at etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English apperen, aperen (Middle English), borrowed from Old French aparoir (apparoir (French)), from Latin appāreō (“to appear”), from ad (Latin “to”) + pāreō (Latin “to come forth, to become visible”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂s- (“*peh₂-s-”), s-present of *peh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “protect”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French apparence, from Latin apparentia, from appareo (Latin). Morphologically appear + ance (English). . Displaced native hīew (Old English “the way something looks or seems”) and ætīewednes (Old English “act of appearing or coming into view”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English applicacioun, borrowed from Old French aplicacion (application (French)), from Latin applicātiōnem, accusative singular of applicātiō (Latin “attachment; application, inclination”), from applicō (Latin “join to, attach; apply”). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: See applicant (English), ply (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: apple + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originated 1645–55; from Medieval Latin appreciātus (“valued or appraised”), later variant of Late Latin appretiātus (“appraised”), the perfect passive participle of appretiō (Latin) (see -ate), from ad- + pretium + -ō (Latin).

Cognate to apprécier (French). Latin root also origin of English , which has various Romance cognates; see also precious (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French appréciation. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English aprochen, borrowed from Old French aprochier (modern approcher (French)), from Late Latin appropio (“appropiāre”), a verb based on Latin prope (“near”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pro- (a variant of *per- (Proto-Indo-European “before, in front; first”)) + *-kʷe (Proto-Indo-European “suffix forming distributives from interrogatives”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English approche (“approach, arrival”), from approchen (Middle English), aprochen (Middle English “to come or go near, approach; to adjoin, be close by; to enter (someone’s) presence; to be or become involved; to reach (a certain state); to arrive; to befall, happen to; to become similar to, resemble; to be a match for (someone)”); see etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English appropriaten, from appropriat + -en (Middle English), borrowed from Latin appropriātus, perfect passive participle of appropriō (Latin “to make one's own”), from ad (Latin “to”) + propriō (Latin “to make one's own”), from proprius + -ō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English appropriat (“appropriated”), see -ate and Etymology 1 for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: appropriate + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: approve + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English aproven, appreoven (Middle English), appreven (Middle English), apreven (Middle English), borrowed from Old French aprover, approver (Old French), approuvir (Old French), appreuver (Old French “to approve”), from Latin approbō, from ad (Latin) + probō (Latin “to esteem as good, approve, prove”). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English approuen, approven (Middle English), from Old French aprouer; a- (Old French) + a form apparently derived from the pro, prod, in Latin prōsum (“be useful or profitable”). Compare with improve (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English approximat (“approximat(e)”), from Latin approximātus, the perfect passive participle of approximō (Latin) (see -ate), further from ad- (Latin “to, towards, at”) + proximō (Latin “to come near”). The noun was derived from the adjective through substantivization, see -ate. See also proximate (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English approximaten (“to bring, put close (to)”), from approximat + -en (Middle English), borrowed from Latin approximātus, see -ate and Etymology 1 for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: approximate + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French architecte, from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (“master builder”), from ἀρχι- (Ancient Greek “chief”) + τέκτων (Ancient Greek “builder”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French architecture, from Latin architectūra. Originally from architect (English), from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (“architect”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Learned borrowing from Latin ārea

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English arguen, from Old French arguer, from Latin arguere (“to declare, show, prove, make clear, reprove, accuse”), q.v. for more. Displaced native flītan (Old English) and reċċan (Old English).

chain.meaning: to declare, show, prove, make clear, reprove, accuse

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English argument, from Anglo-Norman — and Old French arguement, from Latin argumentum. The English word is analysable as argue + ment (English). .

Displaced native racu (Old English) and ġeflit (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The obsolete senses are derived from Middle English argumenten (“to argue, discuss; to consider, reflect”), from Old French argumenter (“to argue”), from Latin argūmentor (“argūmentārī”), from argūmentum (Latin “argument (for a position); evidence, proof; point, theme; thesis, topic; plot (in theatre)”) (see further at etymology 1) + -or (Latin) (the first-person singular present passive indicative of -ō (Latin)).

The current sense is derived from the noun.

chain.meaning: to argue, discuss; to consider, reflect
argument (for a position); evidence, proof; point, theme; thesis, topic; plot (in theatre)

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Affix: arm + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: arm + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English arounde (“around, arounde”), from a- (Middle English) (from Old English a- (“on, at”)) + Middle English round (“circle, round”) borrowed from French, equivalent to a + round (English). Cognate with aroond (Scots), aroon (Scots “around”). Displaced earlier umbe (Middle English), embe (Middle English “around”) (from ymbe (Old English “around”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English arengen, arrangen (Middle English “to draw up a battle line”), borrowed from Old French arengier, arangier (Old French “to put in a line, put in a row”), derived from reng (Old French), rang (Old French), ranc (Old French “line, row, rank”), from Frankish *hring (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *hringaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ-, a form of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French arrangement. Morphologically arrange + ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English arest and aresten (Middle English), from Old French areste and arester (Old French “to stay, stop”), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (Latin “to stop, remain behind, stay back”), from re- (Latin “back”) + stō (Latin “to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”), equivalent to ad- + rest (English). Compare arrêter (French “to stop”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English arivaile, arivaille (Middle English), arrival (Middle English), arryvaile (Middle English), arryvaylle (Middle English), aryvayle (Middle English), aryvaylle (Middle English), from Middle French arrivaille, from arriver (Middle French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English arrogaunt, from Old French arrogant, from Latin arrogāns, present active participle of arrogō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English arwe, from Old English earh (“arrow”) (oblique form ēarw-), from Proto-West Germanic *arhu (“arrow”), from Proto-Germanic *arhwō (“arrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érkʷo- (“bow, arrow”). Cognate with ørv (Faroese), ørvur (Faroese “arrow”), ör (Icelandic “arrow”), örvar (Icelandic “arrows”), 𐌰𐍂𐍈𐌰𐌶𐌽𐌰 (Gothic “dart”), - (Asturian) and arcu (roa-leo “bow”), - (Aragonese), - (Galician), - (Italian), - (Portuguese), and arco (Spanish “bow”), - (Catalan), - (French), and arc (Romanian “bow”), arcus (Latin “bow”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Representing pronunciation.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English article, from Old French article, from Latin articulus (“a joint, limb, member, part, division, the article in grammar, a point of time”), from Latin artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂értus (“that which is fit together; juncture, ordering”), from the root *h₂er- (Proto-Indo-European “to join, fit (together)”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Displaced native cræftlīċ (Old English), with the earliest attestation 1425.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: artificial + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French artistique, from artiste (French) + -ique (French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English as (“as, als(a), alswa”), from Old English eallswā (“just so; as”), thus representing a reduced form of . Compare a(l)s (Low German (Germany)), als (German), als (Dutch).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin as. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Affix: a + -s

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Shortening of as hell (English) or as fuck (English) or similar.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ashamed, aschamed (Middle English), from Old English āsċamod, past participle of Old English āsċamian (“to be ashamed”), equivalent to a + shame + ed (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English aside, asyde (Middle English), a-side (Middle English), oside (Middle English), from Middle English on side, from Old English on sīdan, equivalent to . Compare beside (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English asken, axen (Middle English), from Old English āscian, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to wish; request”). Cognate with aaskje (Saterland Frisian “to ask, demand, require”), easkje (Western Frisian “to ask, demand, require”), eisen (Dutch “to demand, require”), heischen (German “to ask, request, implore”), иска́ть (Russian), इच्छति (Sanskrit) (whence ईछना (Hindi).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English aske, arske (Middle English), ascre (Middle English), from Old English āþexe (“lizard, newt”), from Proto-West Germanic *agiþahsijā (“lizard”), a compound of *agiz (Proto-Germanic “snake, lizard”) + *þahsuz (Proto-Germanic “badger”). Cognate of Echse (German “lizard”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English aslepe, equivalent to a + sleep (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English aspect, from Latin aspectus (“look, sight; appearance”), from aspiciō (Latin “see; catch sight of; inspect”), from ad- (Latin “to, towards, at”) + speciō (Latin “look, look at, behold; observe”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: of German Aspirin, from acetylierte Spirsäure (German). The trade name Aspirin is a registered trademark in some countries, but has entered the English language in generic usage, as various German trademarks were nullified in the United States after World War I (see also heroin (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English assessen, from Old French assesser, from Medieval Latin assessare, originally the frequentative of Latin assessus, past participle of assideo (Latin “assidēre”), from ad (Latin “to, towards, at”) + sedeō (Latin “sit; settle down”). Cognate with asentar (Spanish “to settle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: assess + -ment

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English assisten, from Old French assister (“to assist, to attend”), from Latin assistō (“stand at, bestand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English assistance, from Middle French assistance, from Medieval Latin assistentia, from Latin assistō (“to stand at”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English assistent, from Middle French assistant, from assister (Middle French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Latin associātiō, from associō (Latin) (perhaps via French association). Morphologically associate + ion (English).
The Philippine sense is a Spanish gremio.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin assūmō (“accept, take”), from ad- (Latin “to, towards, at”) + sūmō (Latin “take up, assume”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French asseurer (Modern French assurer (French)), from Latin ad- + securus (Latin “secure”). Cognate with asegurar (Spanish). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: astonish + -ment

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English at, from Old English æt (“at, near, by, toward”), from Proto-West Germanic *at, from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, near, to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). Cognate with at (Scots “at”), äät (North Frisian), äit (North Frisian), et (North Frisian), it (North Frisian “at”), at (Danish “to”), åt (Swedish “for, toward”), åt (Norwegian “to”), at (Faroese “at, to, toward”), að (Icelandic “to, towards”), 𐌰𐍄 (Gothic “at”), ad (Latin “to, near”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English athlete, from Latin āthlēta (and probably also partly from Middle French athlete), from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής, from ἀθλέω (Ancient Greek “compete for a prize”), from ἆθλον (Ancient Greek “prize”) or ἆθλος (Ancient Greek “competition”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle French athletique and Latin āthlēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀθλητικός (“relating to an athlete”), from ἀθλητής (Ancient Greek “athlete”): equivalent to athlete + -ic (English). For more, see athlete (English).

The Super Mario sense is effectively a reborrowing of Japanese アスレチック (“obstacle course”), originally borrowed from English athletic; this sense was itself originally a clipping of the genericized wasei eigo trademark フィールドアスレチック (Japanese “Field Athletic”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From athletic (English): see -ics. Probably formed on the model of gymnastics (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French atmosphère, from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (“steam”) + σφαῖρα (Ancient Greek “sphere”); corresponding to atmo- + -sphere (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English attome, from Middle French athome, from Latin atomus (“smallest particle”), from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (“indivisible”), from ἀ- + τέμνω + -ος (Ancient Greek). Atoms are so named because they were historically thought up as to be the smallest unit of matter, and thus indivisible. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: atom + -ic

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English attachen, from Old French atachier, variant of estachier (Old French “bind”), derived from estache (Old French “stick”), from Frankish *stakkā, *stakō (Frankish “stick”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“pole, bar, stick, stake”). . More at stake (English), stack (English).

Displaced native þīedan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French attachement. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French attaque, derived from the verb attaquer (French), from Italian attaccare (“to join, attach”) (used in ), from Frankish *stakkijan (“to stick, stick to, attach”). . Displaced native onresen (Middle English), from onrǣsan (Old English “to attack”); and resinge (Middle English “an assault, attack”) (compare onrǣs (Old English “an attack”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Late 14th century, as Middle English attempten, from Old French atempter, from Latin attemptō (“to try, solicit”), from ad- (Latin “to”) + temptō (Latin); see tempt (English).
The noun is from the 1530s, the sense "an assault on somebody's life, assassination attempt" (French attentat) is from 1580. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English attenden, atenden (Middle English “to devote oneself (to a task, etc.); to pay attention to (something), to look after; to consider (something); to expect or look forward to (something); to intend to do (something); to help or serve (someone), attend upon; to take care of (something)”), from Old French atendre (“to await, wait for; to expect; to intend”), from Latin attendō (“attendere”), adtendō (Latin “to pay attention to, attend; to direct or turn toward”), from ad- (Latin “prefix meaning ‘to, towards’”) + tendō (Latin “to direct one’s course; to extend, stretch; to exert, strive”). .

chain.meaning: to await, wait for; to expect; to intend

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English attencioun, borrowed from Latin attentio (“attentio, attentionis”), from attendo (Latin “attendere”), past participle attentus (Latin “to attend, give heed to”); see attend. Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French attitude, from Italian attitudine (“attitude, aptness”), from Medieval Latin aptitūdō (“aptitude”) and actitūdō (Latin “acting, posture”), from Latin aptō and actitō (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , past participle of attrahere (Latin “to draw to, attract”), from ad (Latin “to”) + traho (Latin “trahere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English attraccioun, from Old French attraction, from Latin attractio from past participle of attrahō (Latin) (= ad (Latin) + trahō (Latin)), equivalent to attract + ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French attractif, from Late Latin attractīvus, equivalent to attract + -ive (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: , from Catalan albergínia, from Arabic باذنجان (“the aubergine”), from Classical Persian بَادِنْجَان, from بَاتِنْگَان (Classical Persian), from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (“the plant that cures the wind”), from dra —, ultimately from Proto-Dravidian *waẓVtV. Cognate with വഴുതനങ്ങ (ml), बैंगन (Hindi). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English audience, from Middle French audience, from Old French audience, from Latin audientia, from present participle audiēns (Latin “hearing”), from verb audiō (Latin “to hear”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English auctour, from Anglo-Norman autour, from Old French autor, from Latin auctor, from augeō (Latin “to increase, originate”). The , also found in autheur (Middle French), is unetymological as there is no in the original Latin spelling. The OED attributes the h to contamination by authentic (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English auctorite, autorite (Middle English “authority, book or quotation that settles an argument”), from Old French auctorité, from Latin — stem of auctōritās (Latin “invention, advice, opinion, influence, command”), from auctor (Latin “master, leader, author”). For the presence of the h, compare the etymology of author (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: New Latin automaticus, from Classical Latin automatum (“automaton”) + -icus (Latin), from Ancient Greek αὐτόματον, neuter of αὐτόματος (Ancient Greek “self-moving, moving of oneself, self-acting, spontaneous”), from αὐτός (Ancient Greek “self, myself”) + μέμαα (Ancient Greek “to wish eagerly, strive, yearn, desire”). The original pronunciation, apparently with stress on the second syllable, was after the ultimate Greek base.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: automatic + -ally

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From available + ity (English); attested since the early 1800s.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|Standard deviation chart with the average at the center

The oldest meaning in English is . Borrowed from Middle French avarie (“damage to ship or cargo”), from Old French avarie, from Old Italian avaria where it is first attested in the 12th century in the context of Mediterranean trade. From there most sources trace it to Arabic عَوَارِيَّة (“damaged goods”), from عَوَار (Arabic “fault, blemish, defect, flaw”), from عَوِرَ (Arabic “to lose an eye”), but the OED gives it a Romance derivation from Italian avere (“property, goods”) or the like.

The English suffix -age (English) was added in analogy to words like damage (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English average, from Medieval Latin averagium, from aver (Middle English “horse or other beast of burden, service required from the same”) from Old English eafor (“obligation to carry goods and convey messages for one's lord”) from aferian (Old English “to remove, take away”); + -age (English).

chain.meaning: horse or other beast of burden, service required from the same

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English avoiden, from Anglo-Norman avoider, Old French esvuidier (“to empty out”), from es- (Old French) + vuidier (Old French), from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre < Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately related to Latin vacuus. Displaced native forbūgan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English awake, a shortened form of awaken (Middle English “awakened, awake”), past participle of Middle English awaken (“to awaken”). See verb below. Compare woak (Saterland Frisian “awake”), waak (Low German (Germany) “awake”), wach (German “awake”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English awaken and awakien (Middle English), from Old English āwacan and āwacian (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English awarden, from Anglo-Norman awarder, from Medieval Latin —, from Latin ex (“out”) + Medieval Latin wardare, guardare (Latin “to observe, regard, guard”); see ward, guard, regard.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English aware,iwar,iware,ywar, from Old English ġewær (“aware”), from Proto-West Germanic *gawar, from *waraz (Proto-Germanic “aware, cautious”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from *wer- (Proto-Indo-European “to heed; watch out”). Cognate with gewaar (Dutch), gewahr (German “gewahr”), var (Danish), var (Swedish), varr (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English away, awey (Middle English), awei (Middle English), oway (Middle English), o wey (Middle English), on way (Middle English), from Old English āweġ, onweġ (Old English “away”), originally on weġ (Old English “on one's way; onward; on”), equivalent to a + way (English).

Cognate with awa (Scots), away (Scots “away”), aweg (Old Frisian), awei (Old Frisian “away”), wäch (Saterland Frisian), wääge (Saterland Frisian “away”), weg (Dutch “away”), weg (German “away”), væk (Danish “away”), i väg (Swedish “away; off; along”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: See aweigh (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English agheful, awfull (Middle English), auful (Middle English), aȝefull (Middle English), equivalent to awe + ful (English). Compare eġeful (Old English), eġefull (Old English “terrifying; awful”).

The sense is a from the original sense of .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From awk + ward (English). Compare aukeward (Middle English “in the wrong direction”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bak, from Old English bæc, from Proto-West Germanic *bak, from Proto-Germanic *baką, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to bend”). The adverb represents an aphetic form of aback (English).

Compare , from Old Saxon bak (Old Saxon), and , , and . Cognate with Bache (German “sow [adult female hog]”).

etymologies.text: Borrowed from French bac

etymologies.text: From back + ache (English).

etymologies.text: Deverbal: back up

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From backward + -s (English). See also -s (English “used in the formation of certain adverbs: backwards, downwards, inwards, etc.”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English bakwardis, bakwardis (Middle English), a variant of bakwarde (Middle English), bakward (Middle English “backward”). Equivalent to backward + -s (English). Compare bäkove (Saterland Frisian “backwards”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bacoun (“meat from the back and sides of a pig”), from Anglo-Norman — bacon (Old French), bacun (Old French “ham, flitch, strip of lard”), from Old Low Frankish *bakō (“ham, flitch”), from Proto-Germanic *bakô, *bakkô (Proto-Germanic “back”), an extension of *baką (Proto-Germanic), whence back (English), which see for more. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“back, buttocks; to vault, arch”).

Cognate with baco (Old Saxon “back”), bake (Dutch “ham, side of bacon”), bahho (Old High German “ham, side of bacon”), whence Bache (German “wild sow”), Bache (Alemannic “bacon”).

Extension of pig (English “police”).

chain.meaning: meat from the back and sides of a pig

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bad, badde (Middle English “wicked, evil, depraved”), of origin. Perhaps a shortening of Old English bæddel (“hermaphrodite”) (for loss of -el compare muche (Middle English) from myċel (Old English), and wenche (Middle English) from wenċel (Old English)), or at least related to it and/or to bædan (Old English “to defile”), compare pad (Old High German “hermaphrodite”).

Alternatively, perhaps a loan from Old Norse — into Middle English, compare bad (Norwegian “effort, trouble, fear”), East bad (Danish “damage, destruction, fight”), from the Proto-Germanic — noun *badą (Proto-Germanic), whence also *badōną (Proto-Germanic “to frighten”), undarbadōn (Old Saxon “to frighten”), bada (Norwegian Nynorsk “to weigh down, press”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰ- (“to bend, press, push, oppress”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English bad, from Old English bæd, first- and third-person singular indicative past tense of biddan (Old English “to ask”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English badge, bagge (Middle English), bage (Middle English), bagy (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman bage or Medieval Latin bagea, bagia (Latin “sign, emblem”), of origin. Possibly derived from Medieval Latin baga (“ring”), from Old Saxon bāg, bōg (Old Saxon “ring, ornament”), from Proto-Germanic *baugaz (“ring, bracelet, armband”); or possibly the Anglo-Norman word is derived from an earlier, unattested English word (compare bēag (Old English “ring, bracelet, collar, crown”). Cognate with bagie (Scots), badgie (Scots), bawgy (Scots “badge”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English badly, baddely (Middle English), baddeliche (Middle English), equivalent to bad + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English bagage, from Old French bagage, baguage (Old French), from bague (Old French “bundle, sack”), of gem —/gmq — origin, probably from the same ultimate source as baggi (Old Norse “pack, bundle”). Compare also bag (English). . The old meaning of "nasty woman" likely derives from the sense of "something awkward to be carried" (compare faggot (English “faggot”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English bakere, from Old English bæcere (“baker”), from Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz (“baker”), equivalent to bake + -er (English). Cognate with bakker (Dutch “baker”), Bäcker (German “baker”), baker (Norwegian Bokmål “baker”), bagare (Swedish “baker”), bakari (Icelandic “baker”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From bake + -ery (English). Replaced earlier bakehouse (English). Originally "place for making bread"; as "shop where baked goods are sold", it was believed by British travelers by 1832 to be an American-invented term.

Sense 4 is by analogy with cake (English “buttocks”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English balaunce, from Old French balance, from Late Latin *bilancia, from (accusative form of) Latin bilanx (“two-scaled”), from bi- (Latin) + lanx (Latin “plate, scale”).
Displaced the word — wǣġ (Old English) akin to Modern English: wey from *wāgu (Proto-West Germanic “scales; weight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Italian balcone (“balcony, floor-length window”), from balcone (Old Italian “scaffold”) from Lombardic *balk, *balko (Old High German “beam”), from Proto-Germanic *balkô (“beam”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, pile, prop”). Akin to balco (Old High German), balcho (Old High German “beam”), balca (Old English “beam, ridge”). More at balk (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English balled, ballid (Middle English), bald (Middle English “bald”), of origin. Probably formed from Middle English bal, balle (Middle English “ball, round object, knoll, head”). Compare bældet (Old Danish “bald”).

An alternate etymology relates it to bǣl (Old English “fire, flame; funeral pyre”), from Proto-Germanic *bēlą. Compare balë (Albanian “white spot on the forehead”) and ballë (Albanian “forehead”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French ballet, from Italian balletto (“short dance, ballet”), diminutive form of ballo (Italian “group dance”) (cognate with bal (Old French), whence ball (English)), from Late Latin ballō (“to dance”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English bannen (“to summon; to banish; to curse”), partly from Old English bannan (“to summon, command, proclaim, call out”), from Proto-West Germanic *bannan; and partly from Old Norse banna (“to prohibit; to curse”), both from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to proclaim, to order; to summon; to ban; to curse, forbid”), from Proto-Indo-European —, innovative nasal-infixed zero-grade athematic present of *bʰeh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to say”).

Cognate with bannen (Dutch “to ban, exile, discard”), bannen (German “to exile, to exorcise, captivate, excommunicate”), banna (Swedish “to ban, scold”), भन॑ति (Vedic Sanskrit), բան (Armenian) and perhaps banoj (Albanian “to reside, dwell”). See also banal (English), abandon (English).

chain.meaning: to summon; to banish; to curse
to summon, command, proclaim, call out

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Banburismus (English); coined by Alan Turing.

etymologies.text: From zls — (compare ban (Serbo-Croatian “bȃn”)), from *banъ (Proto-Slavic); see there for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English *bangen, from Old English *bangian or borrowed from Old Norse banga (“to pound, hammer”); both from Proto-Germanic *bangōną (“to beat, pound”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰen- (“to beat, hit, injure”).

Cognate with bang (Scots), bung (Scots “to strike, bang, hurl, thrash, offend”), banga (Icelandic “to pound, hammer”), bånga (gmq-osw) , banke (Danish “to beat”), bengel (Danish “club”), bangen (Low German), bangeln (Low German “to strike, beat”), bingel (Western Frisian), bongel (Western Frisian), bengel (Dutch “bell; rascal”), Bengel (German “club”), bungen (German “to throb, pulsate”).

In the sense of a fringe of hair, from bang off (English).

In the sense of abrupt left turn, from and associated risk of a crash.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|The is one of the first modern central banks (), established in 1694.

Middle English banke, from Middle French banque, from Italian banca (“counter, moneychanger's bench or table”), from Lombardic bank (“bench, counter”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench, counter”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to turn, curve, bend, bow”). .

For the bench-bank relation, compare typologically ла́вка (Russian), прила́вок (Russian).

etymologies.text:

From Middle English bank, banke (Middle English), from Old English *banca (“bench”) (attested in hōbanca (Old English “couch”) and Old English banc (“bank, hillock, embankment”), from Proto-West Germanic *bankō, from Proto-Germanic *bankô. Akin to bakki (Old Norse “elevation, hill”), bakke (Norwegian “slope, hill”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English bank, banke (Middle English), from Old French banc (“bench”), from Frankish *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”). Akin to benċ (Old English “bench”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Probably from French banc. Of gem — origin, and akin to English bench (English).

etymologies.text:
From Middle English barren, from Old French barrer, from Medieval Latin barrare (“to bar”), from the noun. Cognate to barrar (Occitan), barrar (Spanish), barrar (Portuguese).

Preposition properly imperative of the verb. Compare barring (English).

etymologies.text: Ancient Greek βάρος (“weight”), as a variant of earlier barye (English) and barad (English). First attested as by suggestion of in 1903, while was proposed by , who first published about it in 1906 as German Bar, see there for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4

etymologies.label: Etymology 5

etymologies.text: From mid-17th century. Borrowed from Spanish barbacoa, from Taíno barbakoa (“framework of sticks”), the raised wooden structure the natives used to either sleep on or cure meat. Originally . .

etymologies.text: From Middle English barbour, from Anglo-Norman barbour, from Old French barbeor, from barbe (Old French “beard”), from Latin barba.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bare, bar (Middle English), from Old English bær (“bare, naked, open”), from Proto-West Germanic *baʀ, from Proto-Germanic *bazaz (“bare, naked”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰosós, from *bʰos- (Proto-Indo-European “bare, barefoot”).

Cognate with bare (Scots), bair (Scots “bare”), bar (Saterland Frisian “bare”), baar (Western Frisian “bare”), bar (Dutch “bare”), bar (German “bare”), bar (Swedish “bare”), ber (Icelandic “bare”), basas (Lithuanian “barefoot, bare”), bosy (Polish “barefoot”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English baren, from Old English barian, from Proto-Germanic *bazōną (“to bare, make bare”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English baarly, bareliche (Middle English), barely (Middle English), barly (Middle English), from Old English bærlīċe, equivalent to . Compare bare (Danish “only, just”), bare (Norwegian “only, just”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bargaynen (“to bargain, make a pledge for sale”), from Old French bargaigner (“to bargain”), from Frankish *borganjan (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Germanic *burgijaną (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to protect, secure”). Akin to boragen (Old High German “boragēn”), borgen (Old High German “borgēn”) (borgen (German)), borgian (Old English “to borrow, lend, pledge”). More at borrow.

Compare barguigner (French) and barganhar (Portuguese).

chain.meaning: to bargain, make a pledge for sale

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English barken, berken (Middle English), borken (Middle English), from Old English beorcan (“to bark”), from the Proto-West Germanic *berkan (“to bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerg- (“to make a noise, growl, bark”), from *bʰer- (Proto-Indo-European “to drone, hum, buzz”).

Cognate with berkja (Icelandic “to bark, bluster”), barki (Icelandic “throat, windpipe”), dialectal burgeti (Lithuanian “to growl, grumble, grouch, quarrel”), brbljati (Serbo-Croatian “to murmur”). For the noun, compare beorc (Old English), bearce (Old English “barking”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English bark, from Old English barc (“bark”), from Old Norse bǫrkr (“tree bark”), from Proto-Germanic *barkuz, probably related to *birkijǭ (Proto-Germanic “birch”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵós (compare frāxinus (Latin “ash”), béržas (Lithuanian “birch”)), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵ- (Proto-Indo-European “to gleam; white”) (compare bright (English)); akin to bark (Danish), börkur (Icelandic), borke (Low German) and berk (Albanian “bast”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English barke (“boat”), from Middle French barque, from Late Latin barca, a regular syncope of Vulgar Latin —, from Classical Latin bāris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (“Egyptian boat”), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (“small boat”), from egx-dem br, from Egyptian bꜣjr (“transport ship”). .

etymologies.text: Affix: bar + -man

etymologies.text: From Middle English barrer, barrere (Middle English), barryȝer (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman barrere (compare barrière (French)), from barre (Old French “bar”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English base, bas (Middle English), baas (Middle English), from Old French base, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις. .

etymologies.text: From Middle English base, bas (Middle English), from Old French bas, from Late Latin bassus (“low”). Cognate with bajo (Spanish), basso (Italian) and base (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Probably a specific use of Etymology 1, above; perhaps also a development of the plural of bar (English).
