etymologies.text: From Middle English basyn, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum (“wide bowl”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis, derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (whence also come (English)). . Displaced native stapol (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English basket, from Anglo-Norman baschet, basket (Anglo-Norman), bascat (Anglo-Norman), from latin
bascauda. Displaced native mand (Old English).

One theory is that it derives from Late Latin bascauda (“kettle, table-vessel”), from cel-bry-pro — (in baskodenn (Breton)), from Proto-Celtic *baskis (“bundle, load”), from purported Proto-Indo-European —, but this is now widely viewed as a qfa-sub — word for phonetic reasons. Related to fascis (Latin “bundle, package, load”) (whence fasces (English)), bokshe (Albanian “bundle”), bac'h (Breton “bundle, load”), φάκελος (Ancient Greek) and βάσκιοι (Ancient Greek) (); see also faggot (English “(originally) bundle of sticks”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|upright|Mariana's fruit bat () ()

Variant of Middle English bakke, of gmq — origin (akin to aftenbakke (Danish) and nattbacka (Swedish), both now dialectal). Swedish also has nattblacka (Swedish), and Icelandic has leðurblaka (Icelandic), in which the second element is a derivative of blaka (Old Norse “to flap”), but it is unclear whether this word is also the source of bakke, backa, etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|A player swinging a baseball bat ()

From Middle English bat,batte, from Old English batt (“bat, club, cudgel”), probably of cel — origin, compare bath (obt “club, cudgel”) and modern bazh (Breton “swagger stick”), ultimately from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰh₂- (“to strike, beat, pierce”), similar to the Gaulish source of battuō (Latin “to beat, pound”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English baten (“batten”), baten (Middle English “to beat”), from Old French batre (“to beat”), from Late Latin batto (“battere”), from Latin battuo (“battuere”), of origin; perhaps of gem — or cel — origin. In modern English reinterpreted as a verbal derivative of Etymology 2. Compare batter (English), battery (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Possibly a variant of bate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French bât, from Old French bast, from Vulgar Latin *bastum, form of *bastare (Latin “*bastāre”), from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (“to lift, carry”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English batel, batell (Middle English), batelle (Middle English), batayle (Middle English), bataylle (Middle English), borrowed from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (Latin “fighting and fencing exercises”) from Latin battuō (“to strike, hit, beat, fight”), of origin. Possibly from a Gaulish — or Proto-Germanic — root from Proto-Indo-European *bʰedʰ- (“to stab, dig”), related to beado (Old English “battle”); or possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit, strike, beat”). . Displaced native ġefeoht (Old English), beadu (Old English “beado”), camp (Old English), and wīg (Old English “battle”), among others.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Early Modern English batell (English), probably from Middle English *batel (“flourishing”), from Old English *batol (“improving, tending to be good”), from batian (Old English “to get better, improve”) + -ol (Old English) (le).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From French baie, from Late Latin baia, probably ultimately from xib — or Basque badia. Partly displaced native byht (Old English), whence bight (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English baye, baie (Middle English), from Old English beġ (“berry”), as in beġbēam (Old English “berry-tree”), conflated with Old French baie, from Latin bāca (“berry”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from Old French beee (“baee, beee”), from the verb beer (Old French “gape open”), from Early Medieval Latin bato (“batāre”). Compare Modern baie (French). More at bevel (English), badinage (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From the root *bai (Old French), combined with aphetized form of abay (English); verbal form of baier (Old French), abaier (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
thumb
From Middle English bay, bai (Middle English), from Old French bai, from Latin badius (“reddish brown, chestnut”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bem, beem (Middle English), from Old English bēam (“tree, cross, gallows, column, pillar, wood, beam, splint, post, stock, rafter, piece of wood”), from Proto-West Germanic *baum, from Proto-Germanic *baumaz (“tree, beam, balk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow, appear”).

Cognate with Boom (North Frisian), buum (North Frisian “tree”), Boom (Saterland Frisian “tree”), beam (Western Frisian “tree”), pome (Cimbric), póom (Cimbric), puam (Cimbric “tree”), boom (Dutch “tree”), Boom (Low German (Germany) “tree”), Baum (German “tree”), Bam (lb “tree”), pa'm (mhn “tree”), baojm (Ripuarian “tree”), בוים (Yiddish “tree”), bom (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “beam”), baðmur (Icelandic “tree”), 𐌱𐌰𐌲𐌼𐍃 (Gothic “tree”), bimë (Albanian “a plant”). .

The original English meaning of beam ("tree") is preserved in some compound words such as quickbeam (English).

The verb is from Middle English bemen, from Old English bēamian (“to shine, to cast forth rays or beams of light”), from the noun.

thumb|Wooden beams at the ceiling of a room

chain.meaning: tree, cross, gallows, column, pillar, wood, beam, splint, post, stock, rafter, piece of wood

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bere, from Old English bera, from Proto-West Germanic *berō, from Proto-Germanic *berô (“bear”).

Cognate with beer (North Frisian “bear”), Boar (Saterland Frisian), Boare (Saterland Frisian “bear”), bear (Western Frisian “bear”), per (cim,mhn “bear”), beer (Dutch “bear”), Bär (German “bear”), Boor (Low German (Germany) “bear”), baer (Limburgish), Béër (Limburgish “bear”), Bier (lb “bear”), baor (Ripuarian), bar (Ripuarian “bear”), beir (Flemish “bear”), בער (Yiddish “bear”), bjørn (Danish / Faroese / Norwegian Bokmål “bear”), björn (Icelandic / Swedish “bear”), bjøinn (Norwegian Nynorsk), bjønn (Norwegian Nynorsk), bjørn (Norwegian Nynorsk “bear”), *𐌱𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌰 (Gothic “bear”).

This is generally taken to be from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH- (“shining, brown”) (compare , , bė́ras (Lithuanian “brown”)), related to brown (English), bruin (English), and beaver (English).

On this theory, the Germanic languages replaced the older name of the bear, *h₂ŕ̥tḱos (Proto-Indo-European), with the epithet "brown one", presumably due to taboo avoidance; compare медве́дь (Russian “bear”).

However, Ringe (2006:106) doubts the existence of a root *bʰer- meaning "brown" ("an actual PIE word of [the requisite] shape and meaning is not recoverable") and suggests that a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰwer- (“wild animal”) "should therefore perhaps be preferred", implying a Germanic merger of *ǵʰw and *gʷʰ (*gʷʰ may sometimes result in Germanic *b, perhaps e.g. in *bidjaną (Proto-Germanic), but it also seems to have given the g in gun (English) and the w in warm (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English beren (“carry, bring forth”), from Old English beran (“to carry, bear, bring”), from Proto-West Germanic *beran, from Proto-Germanic *beraną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti, from *bʰer- (Proto-Indo-European “to bear, carry”).

Akin to beran (Old High German “carry”), baren (Dutch), bære (Danish), bære (Norwegian Bokmål), bera (Norwegian Nynorsk), gebären (German), 𐌱𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌰𐌽 (Gothic), भरति (Sanskrit), ferō (Latin), and φέρω (Ancient Greek), bie (Albanian “to bring, to bear”), брать (Russian “to take”), بردن (Persian “to take, to carry”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English bere (“pillowcase”), of obscure origin, but compare hlēorbera (Old English “cheek-cover”). Possibly cognate to Low German büre, whence Bühre (German), which in turn has been compared to bure (French).

etymologies.text:

Cognate with boten (Dutch), botten (Dutch), butten (Dutch “to push, strike”), boßen (German “to thrash”), *𐌱𐌰𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to beat, strike”) (whence, probably, botar (Galician / Portuguese “to expel; to throw”)); also fūstis (Latin “club, cudgel, knobbed stick, staff”), *fūtō (Latin “to strike”), bahe (Albanian), hobe (Albanian “sling”), բութ (Armenian), բույթ (Armenian “thumb”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English bet, from Old English bēot. bet (Middle English) would regularly yield *beet; the modern form is influenced by the present stem and the past participle beaten (English), perhaps by analogy with the paradigm eat (English):eat (English “ate”):eaten (English). Pronunciations with (from bette (Middle English), alternative simple past of beten (Middle English)) are possibly analogous to read#Etymology 2 (English), led (Middle English), met (English), etc.

etymologies.text: From Middle English bewty, bewte (Middle English), beaute (Middle English), bealte (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman — and Old French beauté (early Old French spelling biauté (Old French)), from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fair”); see beau (English). In this sense, mostly displaced native fæġernes (Old English), whence Modern English fairness (English).

Cognate with been (Yola “bees”), bi (North Frisian “bee”), bij (Western Frisian “bee”), bij (Dutch), by (Dutch “bee”), Biene (German “bee”), Bé (Limburgish), bie (Limburgish “bee”), Bei (lb “bee”), byn (Ripuarian “bee”), bieë (Flemish “bee”), בין (Yiddish “bee”), bi (Danish / Swedish “bee”), býfluga (Faroese “bee”), bý (Icelandic), býfluga (Icelandic “bee”), bie (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “bee”); also beach (Irish), meach (Irish “bee”), beach (Scottish Gaelic “bee; beehive; wasp”), fūcus (Latin “bee”), bite (Latvian “bee”), bitė (Lithuanian “bee”), пчала́ (Belarusian “bee”), пчела́ (Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian “bee”), včála (Czech), včela (Czech “bee”), pszczoła (Polish “bee”), пчѐла (Serbo-Croatian), bčela (Serbo-Croatian), pčèla (Serbo-Croatian “bee”), včela (Slovak “bee”), čebela (Slovenian “bee”), бджола́ (Ukrainian “bee”), биндзӕ (Ossetic), бындз (Ossetic “fly”), وينه (Pashto “termite; white ant”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Possibly from dialectal bene (English), been (English), bean (English “help given by neighbours”), from Middle English been, bene (Middle English “neighbourly help, prayer, petition, request, extra service given by a tenant to his lord”), from Old English bēn (“prayer, request, petition, favour, compulsory service”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōni, from Proto-Germanic *bōniz (“prayer, request, supplication”).

Thus a variant of obsolete ben (English “prayer; petition”) and . Cognate with bøn (Danish “prayer”), ban (Dutch “curse”), Bann (German “ban”). More at ban (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bef (“beef, bef, beof”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman beof, Old French buef, boef (Old French “ox”) (modern bœuf (French)); from Latin bōs (“bovem”), from Proto-Italic *gʷōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws. .

Beef in the sense of “a grudge, argument” was originally an American slang expression:
* attested as a verb “to complain” in 1888: “He'll beef an' kick like a steer an' let on he won't never wear 'em.”— New York World, 13 May;
* attested as a noun “complaint, protest, grievance, sim.” in 1899: “He made a Horrible Beef because he couldn't get Loaf Sugar for his Coffee.”—Fables in Slang (1900) by George Ade, page 80.

As to the possible origin of this American usage, it has been suggested that it can be traced back to a British expression for “alarm”, first recorded in 1725: "BEEF 'to alarm, as To cry beef upon us; they have discover'd us, and are in Pursuit of us". The term "beef" in this context would be a Cockney rhyming slang of thief (English). However, the continuous use of a similar expression, including its assumed semantic shift to 'complaint' in the United States from the 1880s onwards, needs further clarification.

Cognate with befoar (Saterland Frisian “before”), bevör (Low German (Germany) “before”), bevor (German “before”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English beggen, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Old English —, syncopated forms of bedecian (Old English “to beg”), itself of origin. Possibly from Proto-West Germanic *bedukōn, a frequentative verb derived from Proto-West Germanic *bedu (“plea, petition, prayer”, whence bead (English)). Alternatively from Proto-West Germanic *bedagō (“petitioner, requester, beggar”), an agent noun from the same source. Compare bēdagi (North Frisian “to pray”), 𐌱𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌲𐍅𐌰 (Gothic “beggar”). All ultimately from the root of bid (English), which see for more. An alternative theory considers the verb a backformation from beggar (English) and derives the latter from Old French begart (“kind of lay brother”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: Middle English beggen, of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Proto-Turkic *bēg.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English behaven, bihabben (Middle English “to restrain, behave”), from Old English behabban (“to surround, embrace, hold, contain, hold back, withhold, restrain”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihabbjan, equivalent to be- + have (English). etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English behinde, behinden (Middle English), from Old English behindan (“on the back side of, behind”), from Proto-West Germanic *bihindan, *bihindini (Proto-West Germanic “on the back side of, in the rear of, behind”), from Proto-West Germanic *bi- + *hindō (Proto-West Germanic “the hind side, back part”), equivalent to . Compare bihindan (Old Saxon “behind”), behinter (Middle High German “behind; back”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bileve, from Old English lēafa, from Proto-West Germanic *laubu from Proto-Germanic *laubō. Compare Glaube (German “faith, belief”).

The replacement of final with is due to the analogy of noun-verb pairs with in the noun but in the verb, creating a pair belief (English) : believe (English) on the model of e.g. grief (English) : grieve (English) or proof (English) : prove (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Cognate with belle (Western Frisian), bel (Western Frisian “bell”), bel (Dutch “bell”), Belle (Low German), Bel (Low German “bell”), bjælde (Danish “bell”), bjølla (Faroese “bell”), bjalla (Icelandic “bell”), bjelle (Norwegian “bell”), bjällra (Swedish “bell”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English bellen, from Old English bellan (“to bellow; make a hollow noise; roar; bark; grunt”), from Proto-Germanic *bellaną (“to sound; roar; bark”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to sound; roar; bark”). Cognate with bell (Scots “to shout; speak loudly”), bellen (Dutch “to ring”), bellen (Low German (Germany) “to ring”), bellen (German “to bark”), böla (Swedish “to low; bellow; roar”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bench, benk (Middle English), bynk (Middle English), from Old English benċ (“bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz (“bench”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg-.

Cognate with benk (Scots), bink (Scots “bench”), bank (Western Frisian “bench”), bank (Dutch “bench”), Bank (German “bench”), bænk (Danish “bench”), bänk (Swedish “bench”), bekkur (Icelandic “bench”). .

etymologies.text: From Late Latin beneficiālis (“beneficial”), from Latin beneficium (“benefit, favor, kindness”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English benefytt, benefett (Middle English), alteration (due to bene- (Latin)) of benfet (Middle English), bienfet (Middle English), bienfait (Middle English “good or noble deed”), from Anglo-Norman benfet (“well-done”), Middle French bienfait, from Old French bienfet, bienfait (Old French “foredeal, favour”), from past participle of bienfaire (Old French “to do good, do well”), from bien (Old French “well”) + faire (Old French “to do”), modelled after benefactum (Latin “good deed”). More at benefactor (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English berie, from Old English berġe, from Proto-West Germanic *baʀi, from Proto-Germanic *bazją.

The slang sense "police car" may come from the lights on the vehicles' roofs.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English berȝe, berghe (Middle English), from Old English beorġe, dative form of beorg (Old English “mountain, hill, mound, barrow”), from Proto-West Germanic *berg, from Proto-Germanic *bergaz (“mountain, hill”). More at barrow (English).

Cognate with burrow (Scots “mound, tumulus, barrow”), Bārig (North Frisian), beerch (North Frisian), beeri (North Frisian), beerj (North Frisian), berag (North Frisian), berig (North Frisian), berri (North Frisian), bärj (North Frisian “mountain”), Bierich (Saterland Frisian), Bíerig (Saterland Frisian), Bäirch (Saterland Frisian “mountain”), berch (Western Frisian “mountain”), pèrge (Cimbric “mountain”), berg (Dutch “mountain”), Berg (German “mountain”), Barg (Low German (Germany) “mountain”), berg (Limburgish), Bärrech (Limburgish “hill, mountain”), Bierg (lb “mountain”), pèrg (mhn “mountain”), באַרג (Yiddish “mountain”), bjerg (Danish “mountain”), berg (Faroese), bjarg (Faroese “cliff”), bjørg (Faroese “cliffs”), berg (Icelandic / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “mountain”); also برگ (lrc “mountain”), brzeg (Polish “bank, shore”), бе́рег (Russian “bank, shore”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English betrayen, bitrayen (Middle English “to commit an act of treason against”), equivalent to be- + tray#Etymology_4 (English).

bi- (Middle English) is from Old English be- (“be-”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”), from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near, by”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi (“at, near”). Compare also traitor (English), treason (English), tradition (English). The modern sense is due to influence from or merger with bewray (English “to reveal, divulge”), which is similar in sound and meaning. The similarity with betrügen (German), bedriegen (Dutch), from *bidreugan (Proto-West Germanic “to betray, deceive”), is coincidental.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English betwene, from Old English betwēonum (“between, among”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”) + *twīhnaz (Proto-Germanic “two each”), corresponding to be + twain (English). Cognate with between (Scots “between”), atween (Scots “between”), 𐍄𐍅𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌽𐌰𐌹 (Gothic “two each”), betweoh (Old English “between”), twinn (Old English “double, twofold”). More at betwixt (English), twin (English).

More distantly related to διά (Ancient Greek “through, across, by, over”) whence dia- (English “through, across, between”).

For the meaning development also compare with хооронд (Mongolian “between”), connected with хоёр (Mongolian “two”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English biyonde, from Old English beġeondan, from be- + ġeond (Old English); related to yonder (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: One explanation for the form with is that was parsed to . An alternative explanation is that it was parsed to but since speakers are aware of a general ~ alternation (as in electric ~ electricity (English) etc.), the softened was restored to a default when the “ending” was dropped. Similar cases are merc (English) , spec (English) for mercenary (English), specify (English). It seems unlikely, however, that this process is purely phonological and not at least partially based on the spelling ⟨c⟩.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

Perhaps a back-formation of *bykere (Middle English “beekeeper”), from Old English bēocere (“beekeeper”); or from Old English *bȳc, a byform of būc (Old English “belly; vessel; container”). Compare also byke (Scots “beehive, anthill; home, dwelling”), bý (Old Norse “bee”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French bikini, named after the place name Bikini (French), from Bikini (English), the name of the atoll where the United States tested nuclear weapons in July 1946; it was reckoned that the bathing suit would cause as much excitement as a nuclear bomb. This name was originally from German Bikini, the colonial name of the atoll as part of , and this was derived from Marshallese Pikinni.

Compare Benne (German “wheelbarrow”) and benne (Middle Dutch “basket”), whence modern ben (Dutch) and as a borrowing, bin (Western Frisian) (both "wicker basket").

The Old Norse is from Proto-Germanic *burdiz (compare berde (Old Frisian), berd (Old Frisian)); ġebyrd (Old English) is from prefixed *gaburþiz (Proto-Germanic) (compare geboorte (Dutch), Geburt (German)), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰértis (“*bʰŕ̥tis”) (compare fors (Latin “luck”), brith (Old Irish)), from *bʰer- (Proto-Indo-European “to carry, bear”). More at bear (English).

Cognate with bled (Western Frisian), Blatt (German), blad (Danish / Dutch / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), blað (Faroese / Icelandic), bláth (Irish “flower”), blodyn (Welsh “flower”), pält (xto), pilta (txb “leaf”), fletë (Albanian “leaf”). etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English blame, borrowed from Old French blame, blasme (Old French), produced from the verb blasmer (Old French), which in turn is derived from Late Latin blastemo (“blastēmāre”), variant of blasphemo (Latin “blasphēmāre”), from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω. . Displaced native tǣling (Old English “blame”) and tǣlan (Old English “to blame”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English blamen, borrowed from Old French blasmer, from Late Latin blasphēmo (“to reproach, to revile”), from Ancient Greek βλασφημέω. Compare , a doublet. Overtook common use from the native wite (English “to blame, accuse, reproach, suspect”) (from Middle English wīten (Middle English), from Old English wītan (Middle English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English blank, blonc (Middle English), blaunc (Middle English), blaunche (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman — blonc (Old French), blaunc (Old French), blaunche (Old French), from Old French blanc, feminine blanche (Old French), from Frankish *blank (“gleaming, white, blinding”), from Proto-Germanic *blankaz (“white, bright, blinding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ- (“to shine”). Akin to blanch (Old High German “shining, bright, white”) (blank (German)), blanc (Old English “white, grey”), blanca (Old English “white steed”), blanco (Spanish). More at blink (English), blind (English), blanch (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bleden, from Old English blēdan (“to bleed”), from Proto-West Germanic *blōdijan, from Proto-Germanic *blōdijaną (“to bleed”), from *blōþą (Proto-Germanic “blood”).

Cognate with blede (Scots), bleid (Scots “to bleed”), bläide (Saterland Frisian “to bleed”), bliede (Western Frisian “to bleed”), bloeden (Dutch “to bleed”), blöden (Low German “to bleed”), bluten (German “to bleed”), bløde (Danish “to bleed”), blöda (Swedish “to bleed”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English blynd, from Old English blind, from Proto-West Germanic *blind, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz.

Cognate with blind (Danish / Dutch / German / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), blindur (Faroese / Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English blynken, blenken (Middle English), from Old English *blincan (suggested by causative verb blenċan (Old English “to deceive”); > blench (English)), from Proto-Germanic *blinkaną, a variant of *blīkaną (Proto-Germanic “to gleam, shine”).

Cognate with blinken (Dutch “to glitter, shine”), blinken (German “to flash, blink”), blinke (Danish “to flash, twinkle, wink, blink”), blinka (Swedish “to flash, blink, twinkle, wink, blink”). Related to blank (English), blick (English), blike (English), bleak (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English blok (“log, stump, solid piece”), from Old French bloc (“log, block”), from Middle Dutch blok (“treetrunk”), from Old Dutch *blok (“log”), from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką (“beam, log”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“thick plank, beam, pile, prop”). Cognate with blok (Old Frisian), blok (Old Saxon), bloh (Old High German), bloc (Old High German “block”), bolca (Old English “gangway of a ship, plank”), bǫlkr (Old Norse “divider, partition”). More at balk (English). See also bloc (English), bulk (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: , as if it means we blog. The Oxford English Dictionary says the shortened word was coined 23 May 1999 and references the "Jargon Watch" article in an issue of an online magazine which attributes the shortening to Peter Merholz. The form blog is now so much more common than weblog that some misspell the latter as webblog (English), as if from web + blog.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound: Blog

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: blog + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English blody, blodi (Middle English), from Old English blōdiġ, blōdeġ (Old English “bloody”), from Proto-West Germanic *blōdag, from Proto-Germanic *blōþagaz (“bloody”), equivalent to blood + -y (English). Cognate with bläidich (Saterland Frisian), blöidig (Saterland Frisian), blouderch (Saterland Frisian “bloody”), bloedich (Western Frisian “bloody”), bloedig (Dutch “bloody”), blödig (Low German (Germany) “bloody”), blutig (German “bloody”), blodig (Danish “bloody”), blodig (Swedish “bloody”), blóðigur (Faroese “bloody”), blóðugur (Icelandic “bloody”). See Wikipedia for thoughts on sense evolution.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English *blodien, *blodegen (Middle English) (attested as blodeke (Middle English), biblodgi (Middle English “bi-blodgi”)), from Old English blōdgian, blōdegian (Old English “to bloody, make bloody”), from Proto-West Germanic *blōdagōn (“to make bloody”), from Proto-Germanic *blōþagōną (“to make bloody”). Cognate with bluotigen (Middle High German “to make bloody”), blodga (Swedish “to make bloody”), blóðga (Icelandic “to bloody”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: bloody mary.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English blowen, from Old English blāwan (“to blow, breathe, inflate, sound”), from Proto-West Germanic *blāan, from Proto-Germanic *blēaną (“to blow”) (compare blähen (German)), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁- (“to swell, blow up”) (compare flō (Latin “to blow”) and բեղուն (Classical Armenian “fertile”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English blo, bloo (Middle English), from Old English blāw (“blue”), from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue, dark blue, grey, black”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlēw- (“yellow, blond, grey”). Cognate with flavus (Latin “yellow”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English blowe, blaw (Middle English), northern variant of blewe (Middle English “blēwe”), from Proto-Germanic *blewwaną (“to beat”) (compare blegði (Old Norse “wedge”), einbläuen (German), blouwen (Middle Dutch)). Related to block.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English blowen, from Old English blōwan, from Proto-Germanic *blōaną (compare bloeien (Dutch), blühen (German)), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (compare floreo (Latin “to bloom”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English blusshen, bluschen (Middle English), blusschen (Middle English), blisshen (Middle English), from Old English blysċan (“to be red; shine”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *blaskijaną, from *blasǭ (Proto-Germanic “burning candle; torch”) or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *bluskijaną, from *blusjǭ (Proto-Germanic “torch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-.

Cognate with blöschen (Middle Low German “to blush”). Compare also blysian (Old English “to burn; blaze”), blozen (Dutch “to blush”), blusse (Danish “to blush”), blys (Old Norse “torch”), blus (Danish “blaze”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English boord, boorde (Middle English), bord (Middle English), bourd (Middle English), burd (Middle English), from Old English bord, from Proto-West Germanic *bord, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board, plank; edge; table”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰers- (“tip, top”) + *-dʰeti (Proto-Indo-European) or *bʰerH- (Proto-Indo-European “to pierce; to strike”) + *-dʰeti (Proto-Indo-European). The senses "food" and "council" are by metonymy from the sense "table".

Cognate with buird (Scots “board; table”), borde (Yola “table”), boerd (Western Frisian “board”), bord (Dutch “dish, plate; board, plank; sign”), boord (Dutch “border, boundary; bank, shore”), Bord (German “shelf”), bord (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “plank; table”), buord (Elfdalian “table”), borð (Faroese / Icelandic “board, plank; table”), *𐌱𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌳 (Gothic “board, plank”) (whence 𐍆𐍉𐍄𐌿𐌱𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌳 (Gothic “footstool”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From backboard (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bosten, from bost (Middle English “boast, glory, noise, arrogance, presumption, pride, vanity”), probably of gmq — origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“inflated, swollen, puffed up, proud, arrogant, bad”).

Cognate with bost (Scots), boist (Scots “to threaten, brag, boast”), bost (Anglo-Norman “ostentation”) (from ). Related to baus (Norwegian “proud, bold, daring”), dialectal baustern (German “to swell”), böse (German “evil, bad, angry”), boos (Dutch “evil, wicked, angry”), boas (Western Frisian “bad, wicked, angry, shrewd, clever”). Compare also dialectal - (Norwegian) bausta (Norwegian Bokmål), busta (Norwegian Bokmål “to rush onward, make a noise”). Possible .

Compare typologically puffy (English), напы́щенный (Russian), наду́тый (Russian).

chain.meaning: boast, glory, noise, arrogance, presumption, pride, vanity

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English body, bodi (Middle English), bodiȝ (Middle English), from Old English bodiġ, bodeġ (Old English “body, trunk, chest, torso, height, stature”), from Proto-West Germanic *bodag (“body, trunk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be awake, observe”). Cognate with botah (Old High German “body, corpse, trunk, torso”) (whence Bottich (swg “body, torso”), Bottich (Bavarian “body, torso, carcass; lower part of a shirt or jacket”)). See also bodice (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bile, bule (Middle English “boil, tumor”), from Old English bȳl, bȳle (Old English “boil, swelling”), from Proto-Germanic *būlijō, *būlō (Proto-Germanic “boil”).

Akin to buil (Dutch “boil, swelling”), Beule (German “boil, hump”), beyla (Icelandic “swelling, hump”). The expected form is ; the rounding of the diphthong could be caused by the initial b- and/or by association with etymology 2.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English boillen, from Old French boillir (see bouillir (French)) from Latin bulliō (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (Latin “bubble”). Displaced native weallan (Old English) (intransitive) and wiellan (Old English) (transitive). More at wall, well.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: boil + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bold, bolde (Middle English), bald (Middle English), beald (Middle English), from Old English bald, beald (Old English “bold, brave, confident, strong, of good courage, presumptuous, impudent”), from Proto-West Germanic *balþ, from Proto-Germanic *balþaz (“strong, bold”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-, *bʰlē- (Proto-Indo-European “to bloat, swell, bubble”).

Cognate with boud (Dutch “bold, courageous, fearless”), balt (Middle High German “bold”) (whence bald (German “soon”)), båld (Swedish “bold, dauntless”). Perhaps related to Albanian ballë (Albanian “forehead”) and Old Prussian balo (Old Prussian “forehead”). Compare typologically Italian affrontare (Italian “to face, to deal with”), sfrontato (Italian “bold, daring, insolent”), both from Latin frons (Latin “forehead”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English bolden, balden (Middle English), from Old English baldian, bealdian (Old English), from Proto-Germanic *balþōną, related to *balþaz (Proto-Germanic) (see above). Cognate with irbaldōn (Old High German “to become bold, dare”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bold, from Old English bold, blod (Old English), bolt (Old English), botl (Old English “house, dwelling-place, mansion, hall, castle, temple”), from Proto-Germanic *budlą, *buþlą (Proto-Germanic “house, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to grow, wax, swell”) or *bʰuH- (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with bold (Old Frisian “house”) (whence bol (North Frisian), boel (North Frisian), bøl (North Frisian “house”)), bodel (North Frisian), budel (North Frisian “property, inheritance”), būdel (Middle Low German “property, real estate”). Related to build (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English boldely, boldeliche (Middle English), baldeliche (Middle English), from Old English bealdlīċe (“boldly, earnestly”), equivalent to bold + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French bombe, from Italian bomba, from Latin bombus (“a booming sound”), from Ancient Greek βόμβος (“booming, humming, buzzing”), of the sound itself. . Compare boom (English).

etymologies.text: Affix: bomb + -er

etymologies.text: A shortened form of bombproof (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English bond, a variant of band (Middle English), from Old English beand, bænd (Old English), bend (Old English “bond, chain, fetter (English), band, ribbon, ornament, chaplet (English), crown”), from Proto-Germanic *bandaz, *bandiz (Proto-Germanic “band, fetter”)، from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie; bond, band”). Cognate with band (Dutch), Band (German), band (Swedish). . Related to bind (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English bonden

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English bonde (“peasant, servant, bondman”), from Old English bōnda, būnda (Old English “householder, freeman, plebeian, husband”), perhaps from Old Norse bóndi (“husbandman, householder”), or a contraction of Old English būend (“dweller, inhabitant”), both from Proto-Germanic *būwandz (“dweller”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, grow, appear”). See also bower (English), boor (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bon, from Old English bān (“bone, tusk; the bone of a limb”), from Proto-Germanic *bainą (“bone”), from *bainaz (Proto-Germanic “straight”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyh₂- (“to hit, strike, beat”).

Cognate with bane (Scots), been (Scots), bean (Scots), bein (Scots), bain (Scots “bone”), bian (North Frisian), Biin (North Frisian), biinj (North Frisian “bone; leg”), bien (Western Frisian “bone”), been (Dutch “bone; leg”), Been (Low German (Germany)), Bein (Low German (Germany) “bone”), Bein (German “leg”), Gebein (German “bones”), ben (Swedish “bone; leg”), bein (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Icelandic “bone; leg”), benañ (Breton “to cut, hew”), perfinēs (Latin “break through, break into pieces, shatter”), 𐬠𐬫𐬈𐬥𐬙𐬈 (ae “they fight, hit”). Related also to beinn (Old Norse “straight, right, favourable, advantageous, convenient, friendly, fair, keen”) (whence bain (Middle English), bayne (Middle English), bayn (Middle English), beyn (Middle English “direct, prompt”), bein (Scots), bien (Scots “in good condition, pleasant, well-to-do, cosy, well-stocked, pleasant, keen”)), beinn (Icelandic “straight, direct, hospitable”), bein (Norwegian “straight, direct, easy to deal with”). See bain (English), bein (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English boote, bote (Middle English “shoe”), from Old French bote (“a high, thick shoe”). Of obscure origin, but probably related to Old French bot (“club-foot”), bot (Old French “fat, short, blunt”), from Old Frankish *butt, from Proto-Germanic *buttaz, *butaz (Proto-Germanic “cut off, short, numb, blunt”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewt-, *bʰewd- (Proto-Indo-European “to strike, push, shock”); if so, a . Compare butt (Old Norse “stump”), butt (Low German “blunt, plump”), bytt (Old English “small piece of land”), buttuc (Old English “end”). More at buttock (English) and debut (English).

etymologies.text:
From Middle English boote, bote (Middle English), bot (Middle English), from Old English bōt (“help, relief, advantage”), from Proto-West Germanic *bōtu, from Proto-Germanic *bōtō (“atonement, improvement”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰed- (“good”).

Akin to bót (Old Norse “bettering, remedy”) (bod (Danish)), 𐌱𐍉𐍄𐌰 (Gothic), Buße (German). (a borrowing from Middle English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Inherited from Middle English bordure, from Old French bordeure, of gem — origin, from Frankish *bord, equivalent to modern bord (French “a border”) + -er (French).

Akin to borte (Middle High German “border, trim”), Borte (German “ribbon, trimming”). . More at board (English).

Not cognate to beard (English), although inside Germanic there may have been influence between the senses of these two roots: see e.g. barð (Old Norse “edge”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Scots bauther, bather (Scots “to bother”). Origin . Perhaps related to pother (Scots “to make a stir or commotion, bustle”), also of unknown origin. Compare pother (English “to poke, prod”), variant of potter (English “to poke”). More at potter (English). Perhaps related to bodhaire (Irish “noise”), bodhraim (Irish “to deafen, annoy”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: Perhaps related to pother (Scots “to make a stir or commotion, bustle”), also of unknown origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English botme,botom, from Old English botm,bodan (“bottom, foundation; ground, abyss”), from Proto-West Germanic *butm, from Proto-Germanic *butmaz (“bottom; ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”).

Cognate with bothom (Yola), bottom (Yola “bottom”), Boudem (Saterland Frisian “floor; ground”), boaiem (Western Frisian “floor; ground”), bodem (Dutch), boom (Dutch), boôm (Dutch “bottom; ground, soil”), Boden (German “floor; ground; soil”), baom (Limburgish “bottom; ground, soil”), Buedem (lb “bottom; earth, soil”), bödum (Ripuarian “bottom; ground”), bund (Danish “bottom”), buottn (Elfdalian “bottom”), botnur (Faroese “bottom”), botn (Icelandic / Norwegian Nynorsk “bottom”), botn (Norwegian Bokmål), bunn (Norwegian Bokmål “bottom”), botten (Swedish “bottom”); also bonn (Irish / Scottish Gaelic “base, bottom; sole (of foot)”), fundus (Latin “bottom”) (whence , via - (French)), πυθμήν (Ancient Greek “bottom of a cup or jar; the bottom of the sea; butt of a tree”), buzë (Albanian “rocky chasm”), անդունդ (Armenian), անդունդք (Armenian “abyss, chasm”), bin (Kurmanji Kurdish “bottom”), بن (Persian “bottom”), बुध्न (Sanskrit “bottom”).

The noun sense is first attested in 1794; the verb sense is first attested in 1808. The term is first attested in 1882.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bounsen, bunsen (Middle English “to beat, thump”), cognate with bunce (Scots), bonce (Scots “to bounce”). Of origin. Perhaps , related to bump (English), or related to bonchen (Middle English “to pound, beat”) and bonken (Dutch “to bump”).

Compare bumzje (Saterland Frisian “to pound, bang, bounce”), bûnzje (Western Frisian “to throb, bounce, pulsate”), bonzen (Dutch “to thump, knock, throb, bounce”), bunsen (Low German (Germany)), bumsen (Low German (Germany) “to beat, bounce”), bumsen (German “to thud, bang, pound”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bowe, from Old English boga, Proto-West Germanic *bogō, from Proto-Germanic *bugô.

Cognate with Booge (Saterland Frisian “arch, bow, curve”), bôge (Western Frisian “arc, arch, bow”), boog (Dutch “arc, arch, bow”), Bogen (German “arc, arch, bow, curve”), Bou (lb “arc, arch, bow, curve”), böga (Ripuarian “arc, arch, bend, bow, curve”), בויגן (Yiddish “arc, arch, bow, curve”), bue (Danish “arc, arch, bow, curve”), bogi (Faroese / Icelandic “arch, bow, vault”), buga (gmq-jmk “bow”), bue (Norwegian Bokmål “arc, arch, bow”), boge (Norwegian Nynorsk “arc, arch, bow”), båge (Swedish “bow”), boga (gme-cgo “bow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bowen, buwen (Middle English), buȝen (Middle English), from Old English būgan, from Proto-West Germanic *beugan, from Proto-Germanic *beuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewgʰ- (“to bend”).

Cognate with boo (Scots), bou (Scots “to bend, bow”), buigen (Dutch “to bow”), biegen (German “to bow”), bugen (Low German “to bow”), béien (lb “to bow”), bue (Danish “to curve, arch”), buga (Swedish “to bow”), 𐌱𐌹𐌿𐌲𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to bend, bow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bowe, bowgh (Middle English), a borrowing from Middle Low German bôch and/or Middle Dutch boech, from Proto-Germanic *bōguz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵʰus (“arm”). .

Cognate with boeg (Dutch “bow”), Bug (German “bow, prow (of a ship); shoulder joint (of an animal)”), Buch (lb), Bou (lb “shoulder joint (of an animal)”), bov (Danish “bow”), bógur (Icelandic “bow”), baug (Norwegian Bokmål “bow”), - (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and bog (Swedish “bow; shoulder (of an animal)”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: See bough (English).

From Middle English branche, braunche (Middle English), bronche (Middle English), from Old French branche, branke (Old French), from Late Latin branca (“footprint”, later also “paw, claw”) (whence pranke (Middle High German), Pranke (German “paw”)), of origin.

Perhaps of cel — origin, from a hypothetical Gaulish *vranca, from Proto-Indo-European —. If so, then Indo-European cognates include rá (Old Norse), vró (Old Norse “angle, corner”), and possibly rankà (Lithuanian “hand”), рѫка (Church Slavonic “hand”), rangë (Albanian “yardwork”).

The verb is from Middle English braunchen, from the noun.

Cognate with brand (Scots), brân (Western Frisian “fire”), brand (Dutch), Brand (German), brand (Danish), brand (Swedish “blaze, fire”), brandur (Icelandic), brand (French) (< Germanic). More distantly cognate with *gorěti (Proto-Slavic “to burn”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English breken, from Old English brecan (“to break”), from Proto-West Germanic *brekan, from Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (“to break”). .

Cognates of Germanic origin include brek (Scots “to break”), brekke (Western Frisian “to break”), breken (Dutch “to break”), breken (Low German “to break”), brechen (German “to break”), broyer (French “to crush, grind”), 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌺𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to break, destroy”), brek (Norwegian “desire, yearning”).

Also cognate with brishtë (Albanian “fragile”), frangō (Latin “break, break up, shatter”), whence fracture (English) and other terms – fragile (English), frail (English), fraction (English), and fragment (English).

The modern pronunciation shows an irregular change of Early Modern English to in the standard language; contrast this with the development of other words such as speak (English) and wreak (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From the earlier (nautical) term brise (English), brize (English “breeze”), from Middle English brees (“wind”). Ultimate origin .

Variously supposed to derive from a gem — source like Briese (Saterland Frisian “breeze”), brys (Western Frisian “a cool wind”), bries (Dutch “breeze”), early brysen (Dutch “to blow cool and fresh”), or from brisa (Spanish “northeast wind”).

The earliest attestations are in brees (Middle English) (1460), brisa (Catalan), and brezza (Italian) (all in 15th century), with Spanish (1504) and briza (Portuguese) (16th century) following closely after. The aforementioned Dutch cognates and brise (French), however, are attested later than the term in English. The only internal hypothesis for any of those languages is a modification of bisa (pro “strong wind”), which is not widely accepted.

Compare also breshër (Albanian “hail”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

Cognate with brems (Dutch “horsefly, warblefly”), Bremse (German “gadfly, horsefly”), bremse (Danish “gadfly, horsefly”), broms (Swedish “gadfly, horsefly”). Related also to brimse (Middle English “gadfly”), brize (French “gadfly”), bremman (Old English “to rage, roar”), fremō (Latin “roar, snort, growl, grumble”). See also bream (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Late Middle English brik, bryke (Middle English), bricke (Middle English), from Middle Low German — and Middle Dutch bricke , ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *brekan (“to break”), whence also briche (Old French) and brique (French “brick”). Compare also Brickje (Low German (Germany) “small board, tray”). Related to break (English).

The social media slang sense derives from memes about building up one's feed “brick by brick”, analogizing bricks with reels that inform the algorithm.

The sense of a helpful, reliable person comes from Lycurgus referring to the army as the walls of Sparta, every man a brick.

The adjective is from Middle English bright, from Old English berht, beorht (Old English), bryht (Old English), byrht (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *berht, from Proto-Germanic *berhtaz (“bright”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerHǵ- (“to gleam, shine, whiten”).

The noun is derived from Middle English bright (“brightness, brilliance; daylight; light”), from bright (Middle English): see above.

Cognate with bricht (Scots “bright”), bjært (Danish “bright”), bjartur (Faroese / Icelandic “bright”), bjart (Norwegian Nynorsk “bright”), bjärt (Swedish “bright”), 𐌱𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌷𐍄𐍃 (Gothic “bright, clear; evident”); also berth (Welsh “beautiful, fair, fine”), bardhë (Albanian “white”), brėkšti (Lithuanian “to dawn”), brzeżdżyć (Polish “to dawn”), бре́зжить (Russian “to dawn”), برازیدن (Persian “to beautify; to befit”).

Cognate with brizz (Scots), brausen (German “to roar; boom; pound”), brosnian (Old English “to crumble, fall apart”), broos (Dutch “brittle”), Brosame (German “crumb”), dialectal brøysk (Norwegian “breakable”), frustum (Latin “bit, scrap”), бръснути (Church Slavonic “to rake”), breshër (Albanian “hail”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in this form around 1620 (referring to a “bedbug”), from earlier bugge (English “beetle”), from Middle English bugge (“scarecrow, hobgoblin”) which is traced alternatively to:
* a Celtic root found in bogill (Scots “goblin, bugbear”) and obsolete bwg (Welsh “ghost, hobgoblin”); compare Welsh bwgwl (Welsh “threat, fear”) and bocanách (mga “supernatural being”).
* Proto-Germanic *bugja- (“swollen up, thick”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bu- (Proto-Indo-European “to swell”); compare bugge (Norwegian “big man”), dialectal Low German Bögge (Low German “goblin, snot”).
* or to a word related to buck (English) and originally referring to a goat-shaped spectre.

For the “insect” meaning the assonance with Middle English budde (“beetle”), from Old English budda, from Proto-West Germanic *buʀdō, from Proto-Germanic *buzdô, from the same ultimate source as above, might have played a role. Compare Budde (Low German “louse, grub”), budda (Norwegian “newborn domestic animal”), budda (Icelandic “purse”). More at bud (English). But ultimately this convergence of meaning doesn't prove a conflation of the two terms; they might have existed in parallel since PIE times with similar meanings, even if unnoticed by literary sources.

The term is used to refer to technical errors and problems at least as early as the 19th century, predating the commonly known story of a moth being caught in a computer.

Perhaps a variant of *bunge (Middle English) (compare dialectal bung (English “heap, grape bunch”)), from Proto-Germanic *bunkō, *bunkô (Proto-Germanic), *bungǭ (Proto-Germanic “heap, crowd”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰenǵʰ-, *bʰénǵʰus (Proto-Indo-European “thick, dense, fat”). Cognates include Bunke (Saterland Frisian “bone”), bonke (Western Frisian “bone, lump, bump”), bonk (Dutch “lump, bone”), Bunk (Low German “bone”), Bunge (German “tuber”), bunke (Danish “heap, pile”), bunki (Faroese “heap, pile”); 𒉺𒀭𒆪𒍑 (Hittite “total, entire”), pkante (txb “volume, fatness”), búožė (Lithuanian “knob”), παχύς (Ancient Greek “thick”), बहु (Sanskrit “thick; much”)).

Alternatively, perhaps from a variant or diminutive of bump (English) (compare hump/hunch, lump/lunch, etc.); or from dialectal Old French bonge (“bundle”) (compare bongeau (French), bonjeau (French), bonjot (French)), from Flemish bondje, diminutive of Flemish bond (“bundle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
16th century, from Medieval Latin burglātor, byform of burgātor (Medieval Latin “burglar”), derived from burgō (Latin “to commit burglary”), from Late Latin burgus (“fortified town”), itself probably from Frankish *burg (“fortress”), from Proto-Germanic *burgz, *burgiją (Proto-Germanic “borough, watch-tower”).

The -l- in may have been inserted under influence from latro (Latin “thief”). The shortened English form may have arisen through confluence with Old French burgeor (“burglar”), itself from the same Latin source.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From New Latin burglaria. . Displaced native hūsbryċe (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From late Middle English burne, birne (Middle English), metathesis metathetic form of brinne (Middle English), brynne (Middle English), a variant of brennen (Middle English), from Old Norse brinna, brenna (Old Norse “to burn”), from Proto-Germanic *brinnaną (“to burn”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenw-, present stem from *bʰrewh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “to boil”). .

The late metathesis of East Midland brin- to birn- (and subsequently burn-) parallels the phonological development of bird (English) and dirt (English) from brid (Middle English) and drit (Middle English). As this metathetic form became the Chancery Standard, it displaced the semantic functions and weak conjugation paradigm of the native bærnan (Old English) (weak), alongside the surviving remnants of byrnan (Old English) (strong).

Cognate with prönnan (Cimbric “to burn”), barnen (Dutch), branden (Dutch “to burn”), brinnen (German “to burn”), brennen (lb “to burn”), brīn (Ripuarian “to burn”), ברענען (Yiddish “to burn”), brænde (Danish “to burn”), brenna (Faroese / Icelandic “to burn”), brenne (Norwegian Bokmål “to burn”), brenna (Norwegian Nynorsk), brenne (Norwegian Nynorsk “to burn”), brinna (Swedish “to burn”), 𐌱𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to burn”); also bros (Cornish “blazing, boiling”), bruth (Irish “heat; eruption; surf”), brwd (Welsh “eager, keen; passionate, zealous”), defrutum (Latin “grape must reduced by boiling”), πορφύρω (Ancient Greek “to boil, heave”), burth (Albanian “; mouth burning”), աղբյուր (Armenian “fountain, spring”), भुर्वन् (Sanskrit “runnel, spring”). More at brew (English).

From Northern Middle English burn, from Old English burne, burna (Old English “spring, fountain”), Proto-West Germanic *brunnō, from Proto-Germanic *brunnô, *brunō (Proto-Germanic).

Cognate with burn (Scots “stream”), - (Cimbric), prunn (mhn “well, spring”), bron (Dutch “well”), Bronnen (German), Brun (German), Brunnen (German “well”), Buer (lb), Bur (lb “well”), ברונעם (Yiddish “well”), brønd (Danish “well”), brunnur (Faroese), bruður (Faroese “well”), brunnur (Icelandic “well”), - (Norwegian Bokmål), brønn (gmq-scy “well”), brunn (Norwegian Nynorsk), brønn (Norwegian Nynorsk “well”), brunn (Swedish “well”), 𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌽𐌽𐌰 (Gothic “source, wellspring”), brunna (gme-cgo “spring, fountain, source”). Also burim (Albanian “spring, fountain”), φρέαρ (Ancient Greek “well, reservoir”), աղբիւր (Classical Armenian “fount”). . More at brew (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English bresten, bersten (Middle English), from Old English berstan, from Proto-West Germanic *brestan, from Proto-Germanic *brestaną, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰres- (“to burst, break, crack, split, separate”), enlargement of *bʰreHi- (Proto-Indo-European “to snip, split”).

See also boarste (Western Frisian), barsten (Dutch), briste (Danish), brista (Swedish); also bris (Irish “to break”)). More at brine (English). Also cognate to debris (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English birien, berien (Middle English), from Old English byrġan, from Proto-West Germanic *burgijan, from Proto-Germanic *burgijaną (“to keep safe”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰergʰ- (“to defend, protect”).

Cognate with byrgja (Icelandic “to cover, shut; to hold in”); bergje (Western Frisian “to keep”), bergen (German “to save/rescue something”), bjerge (Danish “to save/rescue something or somebody”); also Eastern bir̃ginti (Lithuanian “to save, spare”), бере́чь (Russian “to spare”), ӕмбӕрзын (Ossetic “to cover”).

The spelling with ⟨u⟩ represents the historical pronunciation of the West Midland and Southern dialects with (compare fury), while the Modern English pronunciation with is from the Kentish dialects.

Compare typologically хорони́ть (Russian) (akin to храни́ть (Russian)), chować (Polish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|right|A bush (woody plant)
From Middle English bush, from Old English *busċ, *bysċ (Old English “copse, grove, scrub”), from Proto-West Germanic *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, thicket”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to grow”). .

Cognate with Busk (Saterland Frisian “bush”), bosk (Western Frisian “forest”), bos (Dutch “forest, wood”), Busch (German “bush, shrub; small forest, grove”), Bësch (lb “forest, wood”), busk (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “bush, shrub”), buski (Icelandic “bush, shrub”), buske (Swedish “bush, shrub”), بیشه (Persian “woods”). Latin and Romance forms (boscus (Latin), bòsc (Occitan), bois (French), bûche (French) and buisson (French), bosco (Italian) and boscaglia (Italian), bosque (Spanish), bosque (Portuguese)) derive from the Germanic.

Compare typologically за́росли (Russian) (akin to расти́ (Russian)). Also compare быльё (Russian) (distantly cognate via *bʰuH- (Proto-Indo-European)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the sign of a bush usually employed to indicate such places.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: A semantic expansion of bush (English) (see Etymology 1, archaic and dialectal sense of “thicket” or “small wood”), which survived in English dialects and London‐area toponyms (such as Shepherd’s Bush).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5

Compare bin (English), about (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English buterflie, butturflye (Middle English), boterflye (Middle English), from Old English buterflēoge, equivalent to butter + fly (English). Cognate with botervlieg (Dutch), Butterfliege (German “butterfly”). The name may have originally been applied to butterflies of a yellowish color, or reflected a belief that butterflies ate milk and butter (compare Molkendieb (German “butterfly”) and Botterlicker (Low German “butterfly”)), or that they excreted a butter-like substance (compare boterschijte (Dutch “butterfly”)). Compare also Schmetterling (German) from Schmetten (German “cream”), Bottervögel (Low German (Germany) “butterfly”). More at butter (English), fly (English).

An alternate theory suggests that the first element may have originally been , a mutation of bēatan (Old English “to beat”), but this would not explain the cognates in other languages or the other names formed with milk products.

Superseded non-native papilion (Middle English “butterfly”) borrowed from papillon (Old French “butterfly”).

Contrary to popularised belief, the form "butterfly" was not derived from an earlier flutterby (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

From Middle English kampe (“battlefield, open space”), from Old English camp (“battle, contest, battlefield, open space”), from Proto-West Germanic *kamp (“open field where military exercises are held, level plain”), from Latin campus (“open field, level plain”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em- (“to bend; crooked”). Reinforced circa 1520 by Middle French can, camp (“place where an army lodges temporarily”), from Old Northern French camp, from the same Latin — (whence also champ (French) from Old French). Cognate with champf (Old High German “battle, struggle”) (Kampf (German)), kapp (Old Norse “battle”), hamf (Old High German “paralysed, maimed, mutilated”). .

The verb is from Middle English campen, from Old English campian, compian (“to fight, war against”), from Proto-West Germanic *kampōn (“to fight, do battle”), from *kamp (Proto-West Germanic “field, battlefield, battle”), see above. Cognate with kampen (Dutch), kämpfen (German “to struggle”), kæmpe (Danish), kämpa (Swedish).

Variant of earlier cass (English) under influence from cash above, from Tamil காசு, ultimately from Sanskrit — karsha ("weight of 1/400 tulā, तुला"). Extended to other similar forms of low-denomination coins in Southeast and East Asia following the example of cognate Portuguese cas, casse (Portuguese), caxa (Portuguese), caixa (Portuguese).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: A genericization of Cashpoint, originally a registered trademark of introduced in 1972, from cash + point (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English casten, from Old Norse kasta (“to throw, cast, overturn”), from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin.

Cognate with cast (Scots “to cast, throw”), kaste (Danish “to throw”), kasta (Swedish “to throw, cast, fling, toss, discard”), kasta (Icelandic “to pitch, toss”). In the sense of "flinging", displaced native warp (English).

The senses relating to broadcasting are based on that same term; compare -cast.
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English casten, from Old Norse kasta (“to throw, cast, overturn”), from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French casuel, from Late Latin cāsuālis (“happening by chance”), from cāsus (Latin “event”) (English case (English)), from cadere (Latin “to fall”) (whence English cadence (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English casually, casuelly (Middle English), casuali (Middle English), casuely (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English cathaloge, from Old French catalogue, from Late Latin catalogus, itself from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (“enrollment, register”), from καταλέγω (Ancient Greek “to recount, make a list”), from κατα- (Ancient Greek “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (Ancient Greek “to say, to speak, to tell”). Equivalent to cata- + -logue (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English cacchen, from Anglo-Norman cachier, variant of Old French chacier (Old French), from Late Latin captio (“captiāre”), from Latin captō (“captāre”), frequentative of capiō (Latin “capere”). Akin to Modern chasser (French) (from chacier (Old French)) and cazar (Spanish), and thus a . Compare . Via PIE cognate with have (English). Displaced fangen (Middle English) , from fōn (Old English “to seize, take”); lacchen (Middle English) , from læċċan (Old English).

The verb became irregular, possibly under the influence of the semantically similar latch (English) (from læċċan (Old English)), whose past tense was lahte (Middle English), lauhte (Middle English), laught (English) (læhte (Old English)), until becoming regularised in Modern English.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Middle English —, borrowed from French catégorie, from Middle French categorie, from Late Latin catēgoria (“class of predicables”), from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (“head of predicables”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English catel, from Anglo-Norman catel (“personal property”), from Old Northern French — (compare cheptel (French), chetel (Old French), chatel (Old French), also English ) from Medieval Latin capitāle, from Latin capitālis (“of the head”) (whence also , from caput (Latin “head”) + -alis (Latin “-al”)). For the sense evolution, compare pecuniary (English) and fee (English). Also compare поголо́вье (Russian “total number of livestock”) from голова́ (Russian “head”). .

Compare katēl (Old Dutch) , katêle (Middle Low German), katêl (Middle Low German), kachtele (Middle Low German “moveable property, cattle”), borrowed from the same Romance source.

etymologies.text:

* From Middle English causen, Old French causer and Medieval Latin causāre.

etymologies.text: From caution + ous (English). Compare cautus (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English cave, borrowed from Old French cave, from Latin cava (“cavity”), from cavus (Latin “hollow”). Cognate with kor (txb “throat”), cup (Albanian “odd, uneven”), κύαρ (Ancient Greek “eye of needle, earhole”), սոր (Classical Armenian “hole”), शून्य (Sanskrit “empty, barren, zero”). Displaced native sċræf (Old English). More at cavum (English), cavus (English) and cage (English).

From Middle English celle, selle (Middle English), from Old English cell (attested in inflected forms), from Latin cella (“chamber, small room, compartment”), later reinforced by Old French cel, sele (Old French), Old French cele. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *kelnā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelneh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”). . Displaced native cleofa (Old English) whence cleve (English). thumb|A jail cell

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English certeyn, certein (Middle English), certain (Middle English), borrowed from Old French certain, from a Vulgar Latin — unattested form *certānus (Latin), extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”), of the same origin as cretus (Latin), past participle of cernere (Latin “to separate, perceive, decide”). Displaced native - (Middle English) wis (Old English), iwis (Old English “certain, sure”) (from ġewiss (Old English “certain, sure”)) and alternative - (Middle English) spelling sertane (Middle English “some, certain”).

etymologies.label: Etymology

From Middle English chalenge, variant with palatalization (English) of Middle English kalange (“an accusation, claim”), from Old French chalenge, chalonge (Old French), palatalized Central French variants of Old Northern French calenge, calonge (Old French) (see Continental Norman calengier), from Latin calumnia (“a false accusation, calumny”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English champioun, from Old French champion, from Medieval Latin campio (“combatant in a duel, champion”), from Frankish *kampijō (“fighter”), from Proto-West Germanic *kampijō (“combat soldier”), a derivative of *kampijan (Proto-West Germanic “to battle, to campaign”), itself a derivative of *kamp (Proto-West Germanic “battlefield, battle”), ultimately a borrowing in West-Germanic from Latin campus (“a field, a plain, a place of action”).

Cognate with cempa (Old English “cæmpa”), cempa (Old English “soldier, warrior, champion”), kempfo (Old High German “kempfeo”), kempfo (Old High German “fighter, warrior, champion”), whence archaic Kempfe (German “fighter”).

chain.meaning: a field, a plain, a place of action

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English changen, chaungen (Middle English), from Old French changier, from Late Latin cambiāre, from Latin cambio (“cambīre”), derived from the noun cambium (Latin “change”) (whence was loaned the English ), from Gaulish cambion, earlier , related to Proto-Celtic *kambos (“twisted, crooked”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European —, . More at skimp (English), scam (English); see also *kh₂em- (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with cambiare (Italian), cambiar (Portuguese), schimba (Romanian), canciari (Sicilian), cambiar (Spanish). Used in English since the 13th century. , from wendan (Old English “to turn, change”) (whence wend (English)).

The noun is from Middle English change, chaunge (Middle English), from Old French change, from the verb changier (Old French). See also exchange (English). Possibly related from the same source is Old English gombe (Old English).

and related to capture (English). Displaced native ōht (Old English), ēhtnes (Old English), and wāþ (Old English). Broadly overtook huntaþ (Old English).

Noun from verb and/or Middle English chete, aphetic form of achete (Middle English), escheat (Middle English), eschete (Middle English “the reversion of property to the state”), from Anglo-Norman eschete and Old French eschet, escheit (Old French), escheoit (Old French “that which falls to one”), past participle of escheoir (Old French “to fall”) (modern échoir (French)), from Late Latin *excadēre (“fall away, fall out”), from ex- + cadō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English chek,chekke, borrowed from Old French eschec,eschek,eschac, from Medieval Latin scaccus, borrowed from Arabic شَاه (“king or check at chess, shah”), borrowed from Classical Persian شَاه (“king”), from Pahlavi 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠, from peo 𐏋 (“king”), from iir-pro *kšáyati (“he rules, he has power over”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to gain power over, gain control over”).

Compare Schak (Saterland Frisian), Schach (Saterland Frisian), schaak (Dutch), Schach (German), skak (Danish), schack (Swedish), skák (Icelandic), échec (French), scacco (Italian). , from the same source, as well as thig (English), which derives from the Germanic cognate.

All of the English senses developed from the chess sense.

Cognate with Sooke (Saterland Frisian “cheek”), tsjeak (Western Frisian “jaw”), kaak (Dutch “jaw; cheek”), käke (Swedish “jaw; jowl”), kjake (Norwegian “jaw”), kók (Old Norse “mouth; gullet”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested 1562, borrowed from French chimiste, from Medieval Latin chimista, from earlier alchimista (Latin), from Arabic كيمياء (“الْكِيمِيَاء”), with article اَلْ (Arabic) + Ancient Greek χυμεία (“art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (Ancient Greek “fluid”), from χυμός (Ancient Greek “juice”), from χέω (Ancient Greek “to pour”). The pronunciation with initial is based on the Graeco-Latin etymology rather than on the French word, where the pronunciation with is based on native French orthography.

As a synonym for pharmacy (English), a metonymous use of the proprietor to stand for their shop.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English chery, cherie (Middle English), chirie (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman cherise (mistaken as a plural) and Old English ċiris, ċirse (Old English “cherry”), from Proto-West Germanic *kirsijā, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, derived from Late Latin ceresium, cerasium (Latin), from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (“cherry fruit”), from κερασός (Ancient Greek “bird cherry”), and ultimately possibly of ine-ana — origin (the intervocalic suggests a pre-Greek origin for the word). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English chest, cheste (English), cheeste (Middle English), cheaste (Middle English), from Old English ċēast, ċēas (Old English “strife, quarrel, quarrelling, contention, murmuring, sedition, scandal; reproof”). Related to kāse (Old Frisian “strife, contention”), caest (Old Saxon “quarrel, dispute”), kōsa (Old High German “speech, story, account”).

Cognate with kôgje (Western Frisian), käwwen (Low German), kauwen (Dutch), kauen (German); also gingīva (Latin “gums”), śuwaṃ (txb “to eat”), żuć (Polish “to chew”), جویدن (Persian), ژُوَل (Pashto “to bite, gnaw”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

Cognate with obsolete kauw (Dutch “chewing”), gekauw (Dutch “chewing”), gekau (Western Frisian “chewing”).

Compare West Frisian/Dutch kin (Dutch), Low German/German Kinn (German), kind (Danish), kinn (Icelandic), gen (Welsh), gena (Latin), śanweṃ (xto), γένυς (Ancient Greek “jaw”), ծնոտ (Armenian), چانه (Persian), हनु (Sanskrit). .
