etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Noun from Middle English chip, chippe (Middle English), from Old English ċipp (“chip; small piece of wood, shaving”), from Old English *ċippian (“to cut; hew”) – attested in forċippian (Old English “to cut off”) –, from Proto-West Germanic *kippōn (“to cut; carve; hack; chop”), from Proto-Germanic *kippōną (“to chip, chop”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵeyb- (“to split; divide; germinate; sprout”). Related to kip (Dutch), keep (Dutch “notch; nick; score”), kippen (Dutch “to hatch”), kippen (Low German (Germany) “to cut; clip; trim; shorten”), kipfen (German “to chop off the tip; snip”), kippa (gmq-osw “to chop”). Compare also chop (English).

The formally similar ċipp (Old English), ċypp (Old English), ċyp (Old English “a beam; log; stock; post”), from *kippaz (Proto-Germanic “log; beam”) (whence kip (Old Saxon “post”), kipfa (Old High German), chipfa (Old High German “axle, stave”), keppr (Old Norse “cudgel, club”)) is a different, unrelated word either borrowed from cippus (Latin “stake; pale; post”) or borrowed from the same source language as the Latin.

Verb from Middle English chippen, from Old English *ċippian (“to cut; hew”) – attested in forċippian (Old English “to cut off”) – see above.

chain.meaning: chip; small piece of wood, shaving

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English chois, from Old French chois (“choice”), from choisir (Old French “to choose, perceive”), possibly via assumed Vulgar Latin *causīre (“to choose”), from Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (“to make a choice, taste, test, choose”), from Proto-Germanic *kauzijaną, from *keusaną (Proto-Germanic “to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose”). Akin to kiosan (Old High German “to choose”), ċēosan (Old English “to choose”), kjósa (Old Norse “to choose”). More at choose.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English choys, from a merger of the noun above and Middle English chyse, chuse (Middle English), chys (Middle English), chis (Middle English “choice, excellent”), from Old English ċīes (“choice; dainty; nice”), related to ċēosan (Old English “to choose”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English quer, quere (Middle English), from Old French quer, from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (“company of dancers or singers”). Modern spelling influenced by chorus (English) and chœur (French). . Displaced native hād (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English choppen, chappen (Middle English “to chop”), of origin, possibly (cf. tjoff (Swedish)), or a variant of chap (English “to become cracked”).

Cognate with chap (Scots “to chop”). Compare also kappe (Saterland Frisian), kapje (Saterland Frisian “to hack; chop; lop off”), kappen (Dutch “to chop, cut, hew”), kappen (Low German (Germany) “to cut off; clip”), kappen (German “to cut; clip”), German dialectal chapfen (German), kchapfen (German “to chop into small pieces”), copë (Albanian “piece, chunk”), *ċippian (Old English) (in forċippian (Old English “to cut off”)). Perhaps related to chip (English).

Compare couper (French “to chop”), κόπτω (Ancient Greek “to strike, cut”), kapa (Swedish / Norwegian), kappa (Swedish), kabba (Swedish “to chop/cut (off)”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: , perhaps a variant of chap (English “cheap”). Compare copen (Middle English “to buy”), kopen (Dutch “to buy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English choppe (“jaw, jawbone”), related to cheppe (Middle English “one side of the jaw, chap”). Perhaps ultimately related to Etymology 1 above.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Hindi छाप (“stamp”). Closely related to the similarly descended Malay word cap (Malay), which likely reinforced the English usage within the Malay world.

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Shortening.

etymologies.label: Etymology 6
etymologies.text: Shortening of chopper.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English circle, cercle (Middle English), from Old French cercle and Latin circulus, diminutive of Latin circus (“circle, circus”), from Ancient Greek κίρκος (“circle, ring”), related to hring (Old English “ring”). Compare also ċircul (Old English “circle, zodiac”), which came from the same Latin source. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English circuler, circuleer (Middle English), circulere (Middle English), from Old French circulier (circulaire (French)), from Late Latin circularis, from Latin circulus, diminutive of circus (Latin “ring”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English circumstaunce, from Old French circonstance, from Latin circumstantia.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English circus, circo (Middle English), from Latin circus (“ring, circle”), from Ancient Greek κρίκος, κίρκος (Ancient Greek “ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). . Cognate with hring (Old English) (whence ring (English)) and hringsetl (Old English “circus”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English citeseyn (“inhabitant of a city or town”), citezein (Middle English), citisein (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman citesain (“city-dweller, town-dweller”), citesein (Anglo-Norman), citezein (Anglo-Norman), alteration of citeien (Anglo-Norman) from (probable variant of cithein (Anglo-Norman) perhaps influenced by dainzain (Anglo-Norman “denizen”), deinzein (Anglo-Norman)), from Old French cite (“city”) + -ien (Old French) (whence citoyen (French)), from earlier citet (Old French), from Latin civitas, from civis (Latin). See also city (English). Displaced native burhsittend (Old English) and ceasterware (Old English).

chain.meaning: inhabitant of a city or town

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French civilisation, equivalent to civilize + -ation (English) or civil + -ization (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English claimen, borrowed from Old French clamer (“to call, name, send for”), from Latin clamo (“clāmō, clāmāre”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”), which is .

See also kalba (Lithuanian “language”), hlōwan (Old English “to low, make a noise like a cow”), halan (Old High German “to call”), καλέω (Ancient Greek “to call, convoke”), κλέδον (Ancient Greek “report, fame”), κέλαδος (Ancient Greek “noise”), cailech (mga “cock”), calō (Latin “to call out, announce solemnly”), उषःकल (Sanskrit “cock”). Cognate with llamar (Spanish) and clamar (Spanish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English clappen, from Old English clæppan, *clappian (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *klappijan, *klappōn (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *klappōną (“to clap”). Cognate with klappen (Dutch), klappa (Icelandic), klappa (Faroese) and klappe (Danish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
. Probably from Old French clapoir (“bubo, inflammation from infection”), from clapier (Old French “brothel”).
May also be from old, unsafe treatments for gonorrhea, such as clapping the penis between a book and a hard surface to break up obstructions in the urethra and permit urination. Attested from the 16th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle French classe, from Latin classis (“a class or division of the people, assembly of people, the whole body of citizens called to arms, the army, the fleet, later a class or division in general”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”). .

.

chain.meaning: a class or division of the people, assembly of people, the whole body of citizens called to arms, the army, the fleet, later a class or division in general

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French classique, from Latin classicus (“relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest”), from classis (Latin). . .

chain.meaning: relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English clause, claus (Middle English), borrowed from Old French clause, from Medieval Latin clausa (Latin diminutive clausula (Latin “close, end; a clause, close of a period”)), from Latin clausus, past participle of claudere (Latin “to shut, close”). See close (English), its doublet.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English clere, from Anglo-Norman cler, from Old French cler (Modern clair (French)), from Latin clarus. Displaced native Middle English schir (Middle English “clear, pure”) (from Old English scīr (Old English “clear, bright”)), Middle English skere (Middle English “clear, sheer”) (from Old English scǣre (Old English) and Old Norse skær (Old Norse “skǣr”)), Middle English smolt (Middle English “clear (of mind), serene”) (from Old English smolt (Old English “peaceful, serene”)). Cognate with klar (Danish / German / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), klaar (Dutch), clair (French), chiaro (Italian), claro (Portuguese), clar (Romanian), claro (Spanish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English clerli, clerely (Middle English), clerelych (Middle English), cleerliche (Middle English), clerliche (Middle English).
.

etymologies.label: Etymology
Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English client, from Anglo-Norman clyent, Old French client, from Latin cliēns, akin to clinare (Latin “to lean”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English clyf, from Old English clif, from Proto-West Germanic *klib, from Proto-Germanic *klibą.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English climat, from Old French climat, from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (“latitude”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English climben, clymben (Middle English), from Old English climban (“to climb”), from Proto-West Germanic *klimban, from Proto-Germanic *klimbaną (“to climb, go up by clinging”), believed to be a nasalised variant of Proto-Germanic *klibaną, *klibāną (Proto-Germanic “to stick, cleave”), from Proto-Indo-European *gley- (“to stick”). Cognate with klimme (Western Frisian “to climb”), klimmen (Dutch “to climb”), klimmen (German “to climb”), klembra (Old Norse “to squeeze”), klifra (Icelandic “to climb”). Related to clamber (English). See also clay (English), glue (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French clinique, from Late Latin clīnicus (“a bed-ridden person, one baptized on a sick-bed, a physician”), from Ancient Greek κλῑνικός (“pertaining to a bed”), from κλῑ́νη (Ancient Greek “bed”), from κλῑ́νω (Ancient Greek “to lean, incline”).

chain.meaning: a bed-ridden person, one baptized on a sick-bed, a physician

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English closen (“to close, enclose”), partly continuing (in altered form) earlier Middle English clusen (“to close”) from Old English clȳsan (“to close, shut”); compare beclose (English), foreclose (English), etc.), and partly derived from Middle English clos (“close, shut up, confined, secret”), from Old French clos (“close, confined”), from Latin clausus (“shut up”), from claudō (Latin “to bar, block, close, enclose, bring an end to, confine”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“key, hook, nail”), related to clāvis (Latin “key, deadbolt, bar”), clāvus (Latin “nail, peg”), claustrum (Latin “bar, bolt, barrier”), claustra (Latin “dam, wall, barricade, stronghold”). Cognate with κλείω (Ancient Greek), κλείς (Ancient Greek “bar, bolt, key”), заключи́ть (Russian) (via ключ (Russian)), schließen (German “to close, conclude, lock”), sluiten (Dutch “to close, conclude, lock”). Partially replaced lūcan (Old English “to close, lock, enclose”), (whence English lock). Doublet of clause (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: French clos, from Latin clausum, participle of claudō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From close + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English cloth, clath (Middle English), from Old English clāþ (“cloth, clothes, covering, sail”), from Proto-West Germanic *klaiþ, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“garment”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *gleyt- (“to cling to, cleave, stick”) (compare ngjit (Albanian “to stick, attach, glue”)), a form of *gleh₁y- (Proto-Indo-European “to smear; to stick”). Cognate with clath (Scots “cloth”), klaid (North Frisian “dress, garment”), Klood (Saterland Frisian “dress, apparel”), klaad (Western Frisian), kleed (Western Frisian “cloth, article of clothing”), kleed (Dutch “robe, dress”), kleed (Low German “dress, garment”), Kleid (German “gown, dress”), klæde (Danish “cloth, dress”), klede (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), kläde (Swedish “cloth”), klæði (Icelandic “cloth, dressing”), clīþan (Old English “to adhere, stick”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English clothing, clathing (Middle English), from Old English *clāþung, from Proto-West Germanic *klaiþungu (“clothing”), equivalent to . Cognate with clathing (Scots), claithing (Scots “clothing”), Klodenge (Saterland Frisian “clothing”), klaaiïng (Western Frisian “clothing”), kleding (Dutch “clothing”), Kleidung (German “clothing”), klædning (Danish “clothing, dress, attire”), kläding (Swedish), klädning (Swedish “clothing, dress”). Doublet of the dialectal English term , from clething (Middle English); compare also cladding (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English cloud, from Old English clūd (“mass of stone, rock, boulder, hill”), from Proto-West Germanic *klūt, from Proto-Germanic *klūtaz, *klutaz (Proto-Germanic “lump, mass, conglomeration”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to ball up, clench”).

Cognate with clood (Scots), clud (Scots “cloud”), kluit (Dutch “lump, mass, clod”), Kluute (Low German (Germany) “Kluut, Kluute”), Kloß (German “lump, ball, dumpling”), klode (Danish “sphere, orb, planet”), klot (Swedish “sphere, orb, ball, globe”), klót (Icelandic “knob on a sword's hilt”). Related to clod (English), clot (English), clump (English), club (English). Largely replaced welkne (Middle English), from wolcn (Old English) (whence welkin (English)), from *wulkną (Proto-Germanic), the original Germanic word for cloud (compare wolk (Dutch), Wolke (German), wolk (North Frisian / Western Frisian)).

chain.meaning: mass of stone, rock, boulder, hill

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English clubbe, from Old Norse klubba, klumba (Old Norse “cudgel”), from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“clip, clasp; clump, lump; log, block”). Doublets of clump (English), cloud (English), globus (Latin), glomus (Latin); and perhaps related to kolve (Middle Low German “bulb”), Kolben (German “butt, bulb, club”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Variant of clew (English “a ball of thread or yarn”), from Middle English clew, clewe (Middle English), clowe (Middle English), clue (Middle English), clwe (Middle English), clyw (Middle English), clywe (Middle English), from Old English clēowen, clīewen (Old English), clīowen (Old English), clīwen (Old English), clȳwe (Old English), clȳwen (Old English “ball, sphere; skein”), from Proto-West Germanic *kliuwīn (“ball, clump”), from Proto-Germanic *kliuwīną, *klewô (Proto-Germanic “bale, ball, clump, mass”), from Proto-Indo-European *glew- (“to ball up, clump together; lump, swelling”). Sense evolution with reference to the one which the mythical Theseus used to guide him out of the Minotaur's labyrinth. More at clew (English).

Cognate with khnaul (Cimbric “ball of yarn”), kluwe (Dutch), kluwen (Dutch “ball thread or yarn, clew”), Knäuel (German “ballyarn; tangle”), kljå (Norwegian Nynorsk “a loom weight”); also ग्लौ (Sanskrit “the moon; camphor; the earth”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly from an alteration of clumsed (English “benumbed”) or from . More at clumse (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Middle French coche, from German Kutsche, from Hungarian kocsi. According to historians, the coach was named after the small Hungarian town of Kocs (Hungarian), which made a livelihood from cart building and transport between Vienna and Budapest.

The meaning “instructor/trainer” is from Oxford University slang (c. 1830) for a “tutor” who “carries” one through an exam; the athletic sense is from 1861.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English coste (“rib; side of the body”), from Old French coste (“rib; side of an object; coast”) (modern côte (French “rib; coast; hill, slope”)), from Latin costa (“rib; side, wall”). .

Compare typologically cape (English) < caput (Latin), ness (English) (akin to nose (English)), нос (Bulgarian “nose; …; cape, promontory, foreland, gore”), ’рт (Macedonian), рт (Serbo-Croatian “cape, promontory, headland”) < *rъtъ (Proto-Slavic) (whence рот (Russian)).

chain.meaning: rib; side of an object; coast

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English costeien (“to travel along a border or coast; to go alongside (something), skirt; to accompany, follow; to travel across, traverse; to be adjacent to, to border;”), from Anglo-Norman —, Old French costoier (“to be at the side of”) (modern côtoyer (French “to pass alongside; (figuratively) to rub shoulders”)), from Latin costicāre, from Latin costa (“rib; side, wall”); see further at etymology 1.

chain.meaning: to travel along a border or coast; to go alongside (something), skirt; to accompany, follow; to travel across, traverse; to be adjacent to, to border;
to be at the side of

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From coast + -al (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From . In reference to assimilated Hispanic or black people, derived from the fruit's exotic origins. The slur originates from the idea that one is "brown on the outside, white on the inside". In reference to Polynesians, from the ubiquity of coconut palms in the area.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|a cod ()

From Middle English cod, codde (Middle English), of uncertain origin:
* Oldest English form cotfich (English) as a surname in the 13th century; for more see cot (Old English “chamber, cottage”).
* A bag or pouch, related to its bloated shape; see Etymology 2 below.
* From Latin gadus, from Ancient Greek γάδος (“cod”) with a possible pre-Greek or Semitic origin; for more see Atargatis, Cetus, and κῆτος (Ancient Greek). Cognate with the genus name, Gadus (Multiple languages).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English cod, codde (Middle English), from Old English cod, codd (Old English “bag, pouch”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuddō, from Proto-Germanic *kuddô, from Proto-Indo-European *gewt- (“pouch, sack”), from *gew- (Proto-Indo-European “to bend, bow, arch, vault, curve”). Cognate with cod (Scots), codd (Scots), coad (Scots), kod (Scots “pillow, cushion”), Koden (Low German (Germany)), Kon (Low German (Germany) “belly, paunch”), codde (Middle Dutch “scrotum”), kodde (Danish “testicle”), kudde (Swedish “cushion”), koddi (Faroese “pillow”), koddi (Icelandic “pillow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Origin . Attested in reference to a person (though not always a stupid or foolish person) from the end of the 17th century. The Oxford English Dictionary (1891) notes that a suggested link to codger (English) is unlikely, as cod appears much earlier.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English code (“system of law”), from Old French code (“system of law”), from Latin cōdex, later form of caudex (Latin “the stock or stem of a tree, a board or tablet of wood smeared over with wax, on which the ancients originally wrote; hence, a book, a writing.”). .

Verb is an .

From Middle English coyn, from Old French coigne (“wedge, cornerstone, die for stamping”), from Latin cuneus (“wedge”). . See also quoin (English “cornerstone”). Displaced mynt (Middle English), from mynet (Old English) (whence modern mint (English)), which was derived from monēta (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French coincidence (coïncidence (French)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English cold, from Anglian Old English cald. The West Saxon form, ċeald (Old English “cold”), survived as early Middle English cheald (Middle English), cheld (Middle English) or chald (Middle English). Both descended from Proto-West Germanic *kald, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz (“cold”), a participle form of *kalaną (Proto-Germanic “to be cold, to freeze”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to be cold, to freeze”).

Cognate with cauld (Scots “cold”), koold (Saterland Frisian “cold”), kâld (Western Frisian “cold”), chalt (Alemannic), choalt (Alemannic), cholt (Alemannic), chélte (Alemannic “cold”), ckolt (Bavarian), kholt (Bavarian), koid (Bavarian), kòlt (Bavarian “cold”), kalt (Central Franconian “cold”), kalt (Cimbric), khalt (Cimbric “cold”), koud (Dutch “cold”), kalt (German “cold”), kold (Low German), koolt (Low German “cold”), kal (lb “cold”), khòlt (mhn), kòlt (mhn “cold”), kāłt (Ripuarian “cold”), קאַלט (Yiddish “cold”), kold (Danish “cold”), kaldur (Faroese / Icelandic “cold”), kald (Norwegian Bokmål “cold”), kald (Norwegian Nynorsk), kald’u (Norwegian Nynorsk “cold”), kall (Swedish “cold”), 𐌺𐌰𐌻𐌳𐍃 (Gothic “cold”); also gelū (Latin), gelum (Latin), gelus (Latin “frost; chill, cold”), хо́лад (Belarusian “cold”), хлад (Bulgarian “chill, coolness”), chlad (Czech “cold”), лад (Macedonian “shade; coolness”), chłód (Polish “cold”), хо́лод (Russian / Ukrainian “cold”), хла̑д (Serbo-Croatian), hlȃd (Serbo-Croatian “shade”), जड (Sanskrit “cold; stiff”), जल (Sanskrit “water”). Related to cool (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Middle English cold, colde (Middle English), from Old English cald, ċeald (Old English “cold, coldness”), from Proto-West Germanic *kald, from Proto-Germanic *kaldą (“coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

Cognate with Keelde (Saterland Frisian “cold”), kjeld (Western Frisian “cold”), koude (Dutch “cold”), Kolle (Low German (Germany)), Koll (Low German (Germany) “cold”), Kälte (German “cold”), kulde (Danish “cold”), köld (Swedish “cold”), kulde (Norwegian “cold”), kuldi (Icelandic “cold”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Middle English colde, from Old English calde, ċealde (Old English “coldly”), from the adjective (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin collāpsus (past participle of collābor (Latin)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English coler, borrowed from Old French coler (Modern collier (French)), from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris, from collum (Latin “neck”). Cognate with 𐌷𐌰𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “neck”), heals (Old English “neck”). Compare cuello (Spanish “neck”). More at halse (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English collecten, a borrowing from Old French collecter, from Medieval Latin collectare (“to collect money”), from Latin collecta (“a collection of money, in Late Latin — a meeting, assemblage, in Medieval Latin a tax, also an assembly for prayer, a prayer”), feminine of collectus (Latin), past participle of colligo (Latin “colligere”), conligo (Latin “conligere”), from com- (Latin “together”) + lego (Latin “legere”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather, collect”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English collecte, from Ecclesiastical Latin collēcta (“assembly; collect”), originally designating the gathering at the beginning of a liturgical celebration.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English colleccioun, collection (Middle English), from Old French collection, from Latin collēctiō (“collēctiō, collēctiōnem”), from collēctus (Latin), from colligō (Latin “collect together”), composed of con + legō (Latin), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to gather, collect”). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English collectour, from Anglo-Norman collectour, from Late Latin collēctor, from Latin colligō (“to gather together”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English columne, columpne (Middle English), columpe (Middle English), borrowed from Old French columne, from Latin columna (“a column, pillar, post”), originally a collateral form of columen (Latin), contraction culmen (Latin “a pillar, top, crown, summit”). Akin to collis (Latin “a hill”), celsus (Latin “high”), probably to κολοφών (Ancient Greek “top, summit”). Displaced native sweor (Old English “pillar, column”) and stapol (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English comb, from Old English camb (“comb”), from Proto-West Germanic *kamb, from Proto-Germanic *kambaz (“comb”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth”), a . The verb is derived from the noun and displaced the older verb kemb (English).

Compare Koum (Saterland Frisian), Swedish/Dutch kam (Dutch), kam (Danish), kam (Norwegian), Kamm (German); also keme (txb), žam̃bas (Lithuanian “sharp edge”), зѫбъ (Church Slavonic), dhëmb (Albanian), γομφίος (Ancient Greek “backtooth, molar”), जम्भ (Sanskrit)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From combination (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English combinacioun, combynacyoun (Middle English), from Old French combination, from Late Latin combīnātiō. Morphologically combine + ation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English combynyn, from Middle French combiner, from Late Latin combīnō (“unite, yoke together”), from Latin con- (“together”) + [[binus (Latin “two by two”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English comen, cumen (Middle English), from Old English cuman, from Proto-West Germanic *kweman, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną (“to come”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémt (“to step; to arrive”), from *gʷem- (Proto-Indo-European “to come, step”).

Cognate from Proto-Germanic with cum (Scots “to come”), come (Yola), coome (Yola), cum (Yola “to come”), kaame (North Frisian), kame (North Frisian), keem (North Frisian), kem (North Frisian), kum (North Frisian), kååme (North Frisian), käme (North Frisian “to come”), kume (Saterland Frisian), kuume (Saterland Frisian “to come”), komme (Western Frisian “to come”), cha (Alemannic), cheemen (Alemannic), cheme (Alemannic), cho (Alemannic), chomu (Alemannic), chéeme (Alemannic “to come”), ckeman (Bavarian), kemma (Bavarian), kemman (Bavarian), khemen (Bavarian), kumma (Bavarian), kumman (Bavarian), kèmmin (Bavarian “to come”), komme (Central Franconian), kunn (Central Franconian), kumme (Central Franconian “to come”), ken (Cimbric), khemmen (Cimbric), khèmman (Cimbric “to come”), komen (Dutch), kommen (Dutch “to come”), kåmen (Low German (Netherlands) “to come”), kommen (de,lb “to come”), kamen (Low German), kuemen (Low German “to come”), kemmen (mhn “to come”), קימען (Yiddish), קומען (Yiddish “to come”), komme (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to come”), kumå (Elfdalian “to come”), koma (Faroese / Icelandic “to come; to arrive”), kuma (gmq-jmk “to come”), koma (Norwegian Nynorsk), komma (Norwegian Nynorsk), komme (Norwegian Nynorsk), kåmmå (Norwegian Nynorsk), kåmå (Norwegian Nynorsk “to come”), komma (Swedish “to come”), kommen (gme-cgo “to come”), 𐌵𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to come”).

Cognate from Proto-Indo-European with venio (Latin “to come; to approach”), βήμα (Greek (Modern) “pace, step”), ngah (Albanian), ngaj (Albanian “to hasten, run”), dzimt (Latvian “to be born”), gimti (Lithuanian “to be born”), եկ (Armenian “the act of coming, arrival; income”), 𐬔𐬀𐬨 (ae “to come, go”), gav (Kurmanji Kurdish “step”), گام (Persian “step”), kum- (xto “to come”), käm- (txb “to come”), गम् (Sanskrit “to come, go, move”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: See comma (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French comédien, from , from Old French comedie, from Latin cōmoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English comfort, from Old French cunfort, confort (Old French), from the stem of Late Latin confortō. It replaced frofor (Old English), frovre (Middle English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English comforten, from Old French conforter, from Late Latin confortō (“to strengthen greatly”), itself from Latin con- (“together”) + fortis (Latin “strong”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English comfortable, from Old French confortable, from conforter (Old French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: comfortable + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin comicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (“relating to comedy”), from κῶμος (Ancient Greek “carousal”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα, from κόπτω (Ancient Greek “to cut”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English commanden, commaunden (Middle English), comaunden (Middle English), comanden (Middle English), from Old French comander, from Late Latin commando (“commandāre”), from Latin commendo (“commendāre”). Ultimately from com- (Latin) + mandō (Latin) (whence ultimately also (a doublet), mandate (English), and recommend (English)), from manus (Latin) + -dō (Latin).

Compare typologically поручи́ть (Russian), поруче́ние (Russian), руководи́ть (Russian), руководи́тель (Russian) related to рука́ (Russian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English coment, comment (Middle English), from Old French coment (“commentary”), from Late Latin commentum (“comment, interpretation”), from Classical Latin commentum (“invention, fabrication”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English commenten, comenten (Middle English), from Latin commentor (“to consider thoroughly, think over, discuss, write upon”).

chain.meaning: to consider thoroughly, think over, discuss, write upon

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French commerce, from Latin commercium. . Displaced native mangung (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French commercial (“of, or pertaining to commerce”), from Late Latin commercialis, from Latin commercium. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English committen, itself borrowed from Latin committō (“to bring together, join, compare, commit (a wrong), incur, give in charge, etc.”), from com- (Latin “together”) + mittō (Latin “to send”). See mission (English).

chain.meaning: to bring together, join, compare, commit (a wrong), incur, give in charge, etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From commit + ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From commit + ee (English), or else revival of Anglo-Norman commite, past participle of commettre (Old French “to commit”), from Latin committere, from con- (Latin “with”) + mittere (Latin “to send”). The OED3 prefers the first etymology.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English comun, from Anglo-Norman comun, from Old French comun (rare in the , but reinforced as a Carolingian calque of *gamainī (Proto-West Germanic “common”) in Old French —), from Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to exchange, change”). Displaced native imene (Middle English), ȝemǣne (Middle English “common, general, universal”) (from ġemǣne (Old English “common, universal”)), mene (Middle English), mǣne (Middle English “mean, common”) (also from ġemǣne (Old English “common, universal”)), samen (Middle English), somen (Middle English “in common, together”) (from samen (Old English “together”)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: -ate, from commūnis + -icō (Latin). Compare communiquer (French) and its older (and now obsolete) cognate from , communique (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English communicate, an of Latin commūnicātus (see -ate), perfect passive participle of commūnicō (Latin “to make commune”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English comunicacioun, communicacion (Middle English “discussion, association”), from Old French communicacion, from Latin commūnicātiōnem, accusative singular of commūnicātiō (Latin “imparting, communicating”), from commūnicō (Latin “to share, to impart”). Morphologically .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English communite, borrowed from Old French communité, comunité (Old French), comunete (English) (modern communauté (French)), from Classical Latin commūnitās (“community; public spirit”), from commūnis (Latin “common, ordinary; of or for the community, public”) + -itās (Latin). . Displaced native ġemǣnsċipe (Old English). .

chain.meaning: common, ordinary; of or for the community, public

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English companion, from Old French compaignon (“companion”) (modern compagnon (French)), from Late Latin — (nominative singular compāniō (Latin), whence copain (French)), from com + pānis (Latin) (literally, with + bread), a word first attested in the Frankish Lex Salica as a calque of a gem — word, probably Frankish *galaibo, *gahlaibō (Proto-West Germanic “messmate”), from Proto-Germanic *gahlaibô. Compare also galeipo (Old High German “messmate”) and 𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌱𐌰 (Gothic “messmate”); and, for the semantics, compare ընկեր (Classical Armenian “friend”). More at co-, loaf. Displaced native ġefēra (Old English). Compare company (English) and mate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English companye (“a team; companionship”), from Old French compaignie (“companionship”) (Modern French: compagnie (French)), possibly from Late Latin —, but this word is not attested. compaignie (Old French) is equivalent to compaignon (Old French) (Modern French: compagnon (French)) + -ie (Old French). More at companion (English).

Displaced native werod (Old English), gefer (Old English), getæl (Old English), and hired (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English comparen, from Old French comparer, from Latin comparare (“to prepare, procure”), from compar (Latin “like or equal to another”), from com- (Latin) + par (Latin “equal”). Displaced native metan (Old English) (“to compare,” also “to measure”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English comparisoun

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French competer, from Latin competō (“to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of”), from com- (Latin “with”) + petō (Latin “to seek; to aim for, strive for”). Compare competītor (Latin “competitor”).

chain.meaning: to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French compétition, from Late Latin competitio (“competītiō, competītiōnem”), from Latin competō, from con- (Latin) + petō (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin competītus (past participle of competere (Latin))ive.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French compétiteur, from Latin competitor.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English complaynen, from Old French complaindre, from Medieval Latin complangere (“to bewail, complain”), from Latin com- (“together”) + plangere (Latin “to strike, beat, as the breast in extreme grief, bewail”); see plain, plaint.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English compleynte, from Anglo-Norman compleint, from Old French compleindre, eventually from Latin planctus (whence plaint (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English compleet (“full, complete”), borrowed from Old French complet or Latin completus, past participle of compleō (Latin “to fill up, to complete”) (whence also complement (English), compliment (English)), from com- (Latin) + pleō (Latin “to fill, to fulfill”) (whence also deplete (English), replete (English), plenty (English)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”) (full (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: complete + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French complexe, from Latin complexus, past participle of complector (Latin “to entwine, encircle, compass, infold”), from com- (Latin “together”) and plectō (Latin “to weave, braid”). May be analyzed as com- + -plex (English). See complect (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English composen, from Old French composer (“to compose, compound, adjust, settle”), from com- (Old French) + poser (Old French), as an adaptation of Latin componere (“to put together, compose”), from com- (Latin “together”) + ponere (Latin “to put, place”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: compose + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English composicioun, borrowed from Old French composicion, from Latin compositiō (“compositiō, compositiōnem”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French compromis, from Medieval Latin —, Late Latin compromissum (“a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration”), prop. neuter of , past participle of compromittere (Latin “to make a mutual promise to abide by the decision of an arbiter”), from com- (Latin “together”) + promittere (Latin “to promise”); see promise (English).

chain.meaning: a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Latin compulsorius, from Latin compulsus. Displaced native ġenīedelīċ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: (early 17th century) From a Romance language, see concentrer (French), concentrare (Italian “concentràre”), concentrar (Spanish); alternatively from Medieval Latin —/New Latin concentrō + -ate. Compare also earlier and konzentrieren (German). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Medieval Latin —/New Latin concentrātus, perfect passive participle of concentrō (New Latin “concentate”). See Etymology 1 and -ate for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From a substantivation of the above adjective. See also -ate. Compare concentré (French) and Konzentrat (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From New Latin concentrātiō (“(1550) action or an act of coming together at a single place; (1659) extraction or separation of one or more of the metals present in an alloy”). Compare concentration (French), concentración (Spanish), concentrazione (Italian) (last quarter of 16th century). Equivalent to . .

chain.meaning: (1550) action or an act of coming together at a single place; (1659) extraction or separation of one or more of the metals present in an alloy

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French concept, from Latin conceptus (“a thought, purpose, also a conceiving, etc.”), from concipiō (Latin “to take in, conceive”). . See conceive.

chain.meaning: a thought, purpose, also a conceiving, etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French concerner, from Medieval Latin concerno (“concernō, concernere”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- (Latin) + cernō (Latin “distinguish”).

chain.meaning: to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From concern + ing (English). The adjective and preposition follow from the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, borrowed from Old French conclusion, from Latin conclūsiō, from the past participle stem of conclūdō (Latin “conclūdere”), from con- + claudō (Latin), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kleh₂w- (“*kleh₂u-”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin concrētus, past participle of concrescō (Latin) (to curdle) from con- (Latin) (with, together) + crescō (Latin) (to grow, rise).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English condicioun, from Old French condicion (French condition (French)), from Latin condicio. An unetymological change in spelling due to a confusion with conditio (Latin). Displaced native hād (Old English “state, condition”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Latin conductus (“defense, escort”), from Latin conductus, perfect passive participle of condūcō (Latin “bring together”); see also conduce (English). Displaced native þēaw (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French conductour, from Old French conduitor, from Latin conductor.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle French conférence, from Medieval Latin cōnferentia, from Latin cōnferēns, omitting several steps, from con- (Latin) + ferō (Latin).

Compare parallel собра́ние (Russian), сбо́рище (Russian), akin to с- (Russian), со- (Russian) + брать (Russian), ultimately from the same Indo-European prefix and root. Also compare congress (English), convention (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English confessen, from Anglo-Norman confesser, from Old French confesser, from Latin confessus (confés (Old French)), past participle of cōnfiteor (Latin “to confess, admit”) from con- (Latin) + fateor (Latin “to admit”). Displaced andetten (Middle English “to confess, admit”) (from andettan (Old English)). .

.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English confessioun, from Old French confession, from Latin cōnfessiō (“confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith”). Displaced native andetnes (Old English). .

Morphologically confess + -ion (English).

Sense 6 is a calque of 告白 (kokuhaku).

chain.meaning: confession, acknowledgment, creed or avowal of one's faith

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English confidence, from Latin cōnfīdentia (possibly via Old French confidence), from cōnfīdō (Latin “believe, confide in”) from con- (Latin “with”) + fīdō (Latin “trust”).

.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French confident, from Latin confidens (“confident, i.e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent”), present participle of confidere (Latin “to trust fully, confide”). See confide (English).

chain.meaning: confident, i.e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: confident + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English confirmen, confermen (Middle English), from Old French confermer, from Latin confirmo (“cōnfirmāre”), from con- (Latin “together”) + firmo (Latin “firmāre”), from firmus (Latin “firm”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English confirmacioun, from Old French confirmacion, from Latin cōnfirmātiō, noun of process from cōnfirmātus (Latin “confirmed”), perfect passive participle of confirmo (Latin “cōnfirmāre”), from con- (Latin “with”) + firmo (Latin “firmāre”).

Morphologically confirm + ation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin cōnflīctus, from , past participle of conflīgō (Latin “to strike together”), from (whence con-).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: confused, from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English confus, from Old French confus, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally from Middle English confused (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman confus + Middle English -ed, from Latin cōnfūsus, past participle of cōnfundō (Latin); now equivalent to confuse (Middle English) (a ) ed.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English confusioun, from Old French confusion, from Latin confusio (“confusio, confusionem”).

Morphologically confuse + -ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: ; Latin congrātulātus, the perfect active participle of Latin congrātulor (“to wish joy, rejoice (with); to congratulate”) (see -ate), from con- + grātulor (Latin), from grātus (Latin “grateful, pleasing, agreeable, beloved”) + -ō (Latin “-or”). .

chain.meaning: to wish joy, rejoice (with); to congratulate

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French conjonction, from Latin coniūnctiō (“joining”), from coniungere (Latin “to join”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from con- + necto (Latin), which is cognate with knot (English) and knit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English conneccioun, connexioun (Middle English), conneccyon (Middle English), conneccion (Middle English), from Latin connexionem (nominative connexio (Latin “a conclusion, binding together”)), from connectō (Latin), an alternative spelling of cōnectō (Latin “to bind together”), from compound of co- (Latin “together”) and nectō (Latin “to bind”).

In American English mid-18c., spelling shifted from connexion (English) to connection (equivalent to connect + ion (English)), thus making connexion (English) British dated and connection in international use.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: conscious + -ness

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English consequence, from Old French consequence, from Latin consequentia. While analysable as , its adjective form has a different origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English consequentely, consequentliche (Middle English), consequently (Middle English); equivalent to consequent + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French —. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considero (“considerare”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: consider + -able

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: considerable + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English consideracioun, from Old French consideracion, from Latin cōnsīderātiō. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English consonant or consonaunt (Middle English), from Old French consonant, from Latin cōnsonāns (“sounding with”), from the prefix con- (Latin “with”) + the present participle sonāns (Latin “sounding”), from sonāre (Latin “to sound”). The Latin is a calque of Ancient Greek σύμφωνον.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English constant, from , from , accusative of constans (Latin), from consto (Latin “cōnstāre”). Displaced native singal (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From constant + -ly (English). Displaced native singallīċe (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctus, from cōnstruō (Latin “to heap together”), from com- (Latin “together”) + struō (Latin “to heap up, pile”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English construccioun, construction (Middle English), from Old French construction, from Latin cōnstructiō, from cōnstruō (Latin “cōnstruere”).

Morphologically construct + -ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French consultant, present participle of consulter (French), from Latin consulto (“to deliberate, consult”), frequentative of consulo (Latin “to consult, deliberate, consider, reflect upon, ask advice”), from com- (Latin “together”) + -sulere (Latin), of uncertain origin.
etymologies.uncertainNote: From French consultant, present participle of consulter (French), from Latin consulto (“to deliberate, consult”), frequentative of consulo (Latin “to consult, deliberate, consider, reflect upon, ask advice”), from com- (Latin “together”) + -sulere (Latin), of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English consumen, from Old French consumer, from Latin consumo (“cōnsūmere, cōnsūmō”), from con- + sūmō (Latin), from sub + emō (Latin), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁em- (“to take, distribute”), possibly related to the root *nem- (Proto-Indo-European “to take or give one's due”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: consume + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin contactus, from contingō (Latin “to touch on all sides”), from tangō (Latin “to touch”). Used in English since the 17th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English conteinen, borrowed from Old French contenir, from Latin continēre (“to hold or keep together, comprise, contain”), combined form of con- (Latin “together”) + teneō (Latin “to hold”).

chain.meaning: to hold or keep together, comprise, contain

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English conteiner, equivalent to contain + -er (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Medieval Latin contemporārius, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + temporārius (Latin), an adjective derived from tempus (Latin “time”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English contenten (“to satisfy”), from Latin contentus#Etymology_2 (“contained; satisfied”), past participle of continēre (Latin “to contain”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English content (plural contentes (Middle English), contence (Middle English)), from Latin contentus, past participle of continēre (Latin “to hold in, contain”), as Etymology 1, above. English apparently developed a substantive form of the adjective, which is not mirrored in Romance languages.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French contester, from Old French —, from Latin contestor (“to call to witness”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin contextus.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin continens, noun use of present participle of contineo (Latin “continēre”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English contynent, from Old French continent, from Latin continentem (“continuous; holding together”), present participle of continēre (Latin “to contain”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English continuen, from Old French continuer, from Latin continuō. Displaced native thurghwonen (Middle English), from þurhwunian (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin continuus, from contineō (Latin “hold together”). Displaced native singal (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: continuous + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from Old French contract, from Latin contractus, from contraho (Latin “contrahere”) [from con- (Latin “with, together”) + traho (Latin “trahere”)] .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from Middle French contracter, from Latin contractum, past participle of contraho (Latin “contrahere”), from con- (Latin “with, together”) + traho (Latin “trahere”). The verb developed after the noun, and originally meant only "draw together"; the sense "make a contract with" developed later.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French contraster, from Latin contrāstō (“contrāstāre”), from contrā (Latin “against”) + stō (Latin “stō, stāre”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin contribūtus, perfect passive participle of contribuō (Latin “to bring together; to unite”), from con + tribuō (Latin), from tribus (Latin “tribe”), derived from trēs (Latin “three”), from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English contribucioun, contribucion (Middle English), from Old French contribution, from Latin contribūtiōnem, contribūtiō (Latin), from Latin contribuēre. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English controllen, from Old French contrerole, from Medieval Latin contrārotulus (“a counter-roll or register used to verify accounts”), from Latin contrā (“against, opposite”) + Medieval Latin rotulus, Latin rotula (“roll, a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (Latin “a wheel”).

Partly displaced native wealdan (Old English) and wieldan (Old English), whence their merged reflex wield (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin contrōversiālis, from contrōversia (Latin) + -ālis (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin convenientia, from conveniens (Latin “suitable”), present participle of convenire (Latin “to come together, suit”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English convenient, from Latin conveniēns (“fit, suitable, convenient”), present participle of convenio (Latin “to come together, suit”); see convene (English) and compare covenant (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: convenient + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: convention + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English converten, from Old French convertir, from Latin converto (“turn around”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin convincō (“to refute, prove”), from con- (Latin) + vincō (Latin “to conquer, vanquish”). . Displaced native oferreċċan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English cool, from Old English cōl (“cool, cold, tranquil, calm”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōl(ī), from Proto-Germanic *kōluz (“cool”), from *kalaną (Proto-Germanic “to be cold, to freeze”), Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to be cold, to freeze”).

Cognate with kool (North Frisian), koul (North Frisian), kuul (North Frisian), kölj (North Frisian), kööl (North Frisian “cold”), köil (Saterland Frisian “cool”), koel (Western Frisian “cool”), khuul (Cimbric “chilly, cool”), koel (Dutch “cool”), kühl (German “cool”), köhl (Low German “cool”), kill (lb “cool”), kił (Ripuarian “cool”); also gelū (Latin), gelum (Latin), gelus (Latin “frost; chill, cold”), хо́лад (Belarusian “cold”), хлад (Bulgarian “chill, coolness”), chlad (Czech “cold”), лад (Macedonian “shade; coolness”), chłód (Polish “cold”), хо́лод (Russian / Ukrainian “cold”), хла̑д (Serbo-Croatian), hlȃd (Serbo-Croatian “shade”), जड (Sanskrit “cold; stiff”), जल (Sanskrit “water”). Related to cold (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English colen, from Old English cōlian (“to cool, grow cold, be cold”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlēn (“to become cold”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to freeze”).

Cognate with koelen (Dutch “to cool”), kühlen (German “to cool”), kyla (Swedish “to cool, refrigerate”). Also partially from Middle English kelen, from Old English cēlan (“to cool, be cold, become cold”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlijan, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną (“to cool”), altered to resemble the adjective cool (English). See keel (English).

chain.meaning: to cool, grow cold, be cold

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Alteration of cowl (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originated 1595–1605 from Late Latin cooperātus, perfect passive participle of cooperor (Late Latin “to work with”), see -ate for more. Equivalent to co- + operate (English). Displaced native efnwyrċan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The is Middle English coper, copper (Middle English “copper ore; copper metal; bronze”), from Old English coper, copor (Old English “copper”), from Proto-West Germanic *kopr, from Late Latin cuprum (“copper”), a of Latin aes Cyprium, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κῠ́προς (“Cyprus”) (a major source of copper during the Near East’s ), from the name of a sem-nwe — goddess from the root כ־ב־ר (Aramaic)/ (“related to being big, large; great; or old”). .

The is from an use of the noun. The is also derived from the noun.

* koper (Dutch “copper”)
* Kupfer (German “copper”)
* kopar (Icelandic “copper”)

Compare typologically Argentina (English) (< argentum (Latin), an opposite semantic shift); turquoise (English) (akin to Turk (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The is probably derived from cop + -er (English), although cop is attested slightly later.

The is derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English copy, copie (Middle English), from Old French copie (“abundance, plenty; transcript, copy”), from Medieval Latin copia (“reproduction, transcript”), from Latin cōpia (“plenty, abundance”), from *coopia (Latin), from co- (Latin “together”) + ops (Latin “wealth, riches”). More at opulent (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English copien, from Old French copier and Medieval Latin cōpiō.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English corn, from Old English corn, from Proto-West Germanic *korn, from Proto-Germanic *kurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵr̥h₂nóm (“grain; worn-down”), from *ǵerh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “grow old, mature”).

Cognate with koren (Dutch), Koorn (Low German (Germany)), Korn (German), korn (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish); see also grurë (Albanian), зерно́ (Russian), zrno (Czech), grānum (Latin) and žirnis (Lithuanian). .

The sense maize (English) () is an that developed in 18th century North America.

Middle English corne, from Old French corn (modern cor (French)), from Latin cornū. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English corporacion, corporation (Middle English), from Late Latin corporatio (“assumption of a body”), from Latin corporatus, past participle of corporō (Latin “corporare”); see corporate (English). .

Perhaps a play on the word corpulence (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French correct, from Latin correctus (“improved, amended, correct”), past participle of corrigere (Latin), conrigere (Latin “to make straight, make right, make better, improve, correct”), from con- (Latin “together”) + combining form of rego (Latin “regō, regere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English correcten, borrowed from Anglo-Norman correcter, from Latin correctus.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
From Middle English cost, from Old English cost (“option, choice, possibility, manner, way, condition”), from Old Norse kostr (“choice, opportunity, chance, condition, state, quality”), from Proto-Germanic *kustuz (“choice, trial”) (or Proto-Germanic *kustiz (“choice, trial”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus (“to enjoy, taste”).

Cognate with kostur (Icelandic), - (German) dialectal Kust (German “taste, flavour”), kust (Dutch “choice, choosing”), kest (North Frisian “choice, estimation, virtue”), kêst (Western Frisian “article of law, statute”), cyst (Old English “free-will, choice, election, the best of anything, the choicest, picked host, moral excellence, virtue, goodness, generosity, munificence”), gustus (Latin “taste”). , and related to choose (English).

chain.meaning: option, choice, possibility, manner, way, condition
choice, opportunity, chance, condition, state, quality

French costume, from Italian costume, from Latin consuetudo (“custom, habit”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Scots cosie, from Old colsie (Scots), but ultimate derivation is unknown. Possibly of gmq — origin, such as Norwegian kose seg (Norwegian “to have a cozy time”), from Old Norse kose sig (Old Norse), from koselig (Old Norse), koslig (Old Norse), perhaps ultimately from Old High German kōsa; see modern kosen (German “to cuddle”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Scots cosie, from Old colsie (Scots), but ultimate derivation is unknown.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Late Middle English —, from Anglo-Norman cotage and Medieval Latin cotagium, from Old Northern French cot, cote (Old French “cottage, hut”) + -age (Old French “surrounding property”), from Old Norse kot, from Proto-Germanic *kutą, *kuta- (Proto-Germanic “shed”), probably of non-Indo-European origin, possibly borrowed from fiu-pro —/Proto-Uralic *kota (“hut, tent”), probably akin to Proto-Iranian *kátah (“house; roof”). However, also compare hut (Dutch / English).

Cognate with Koate (Saterland Frisian “cottage, hut, small house”), kot (Dutch “ramshackle housing”), Kate (German), Kote (German “cot, cottage, hut”), kote (Norwegian Bokmål “cot, cottage, hut”), kot (Norwegian Nynorsk), kott (Norwegian Nynorsk “small house; small room”), kote (Norwegian Nynorsk), kotto (Norwegian Nynorsk), kåte (Norwegian Nynorsk “hut”), kåta (Swedish “cot, cottage, hut”), コタン (ain “village; town; island; land; country; place”), куэһть (sia “hut, tent”), کڈی (brh “hut, small house; wife”), кудо (Erzya “house”), koda (Estonian “building, house”), kota (Finnish “house, hut”), ház (Hungarian “house”), куэдтҍ (sjd “hut”), керку (koi “house, hut”) керка (kpv “house; family”), kuodā (liv “house”), കുടി (ml “dwelling, house; hut; clan”), куд (mdf “house”), хот (Mongolian), ᠬᠣᠲᠠ (Mongolian “city, town”), goahti (se “hut, tent; den, lair”), gåetie (sma “house; range; tent”), குடி (Tamil “ryot; tenants; citizens; family, household; descent, lineage; caste, race; house, mansion; village”), корка (udm “house, hut”), gåhtie (sju “tent”), kõta (vot “house”); also ақыҭа (ab “village; community”), քաղաք (Armenian “city, town”), ха́та (Belarusian / Russian / Ukrainian “house, hut”), chata (Czech / Polish “hut”), کەَ (hac “house”), کلی (Pashto “village”), کده (Persian “house; village”), kedî (Kurmanji Kurdish “domestic”), кат (yai “house”).

Old Northern French cote (Old French) is probably from kot (Old Norse “hut”), cognate of cot (Old English) of same Proto-Germanic — origin.

Slang sense “public toilet” from 19th century, due to resemblance.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English cotoun, from Anglo-Norman cotun, Old French coton, from (Genoese) Old Italian cotone, from Arabic قُطُن, from Hebrew כֻּתֹּנֶת (kuttónĕṯ).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: First use appears c. the 1560s, either from Welsh cydun, cytun (Welsh “agree, coincide”) (cyduno (Welsh), cytuno (Welsh)), from cyd (Welsh), cyt (Welsh) + un (Welsh “one”), literally “to be at one with”, or by metaphor with the textile, as cotton blended well with other textiles, notably wool in hat-making.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English coughen, coghen (Middle English “to cough; to vomit”), from Old English *cohhian (compare cohhetan (Old English “to bluster; to riot; to cough (?)”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kuh- (“to cough”), ultimately of onomatopoeic origin.

* cuchen (Middle Dutch “to cough”) (modern kuchen (Dutch “to cough”); kuchen (Low German (Germany) “to cough”))
* kûchen (Middle High German “to breathe (on); to exhale”), kîchen (Middle High German “to breathe with difficulty”) (modern keichen (German), keuchen (German “to breathe with difficulty; to gasp, pant”))
* cof (Spanish “coughing sound”)
* kiche (Western Frisian “to cough”), kochelje (Western Frisian “to cough persistently”)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English cough (“a cough; illness causing coughing”), from coughen (Middle English): see etymology 1.

The interjection is probably derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English coude, couthe (Middle English), cuthe (Middle English), from Old English cūþe, past indicative and past subjunctive form of cunnan (Old English “to be able”) (compare related cūþ (Old English), whence English couth (English)). Cognate with konnte (German), kunde (Swedish).

The -l- in the spelling was added in the early 16th century by analogy with should (English) and would (English); this analogy formerly affected the pronunciation as well and was probably assisted by the tendency for to be lost in those words (and so not written, leading to shudd, wode, etc).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English counseil (“meeting, conference, commune”), from Old French conseil (“advice, deliberation, thought”), from Latin cōnsilium (“plan, intention, design, purpose”), from cōnsulō (Latin “consult, seek counsel from, take counsel from, deliberate, reflect”), from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“take, grab”).

chain.meaning: consult, seek counsel from, take counsel from, deliberate, reflect

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English counten, borrowed from Anglo-Norman conter, from Old French conter (“add up; tell a story”), from Latin computō (“to compute”). In this sense, displaced native tellan (Old English), whence tell (English). .

Compare typologically reckon (English), счита́ть (Russian), счита́ться (Russian); the semantic evolution to санах (Mongolian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English counte, from Anglo-Norman conte and Old French comte (“count”), from Latin comes (“companion”) (more specifically derived from its accusative form comitem (Latin)) in the sense of "noble fighting alongside the king". .

etymologies.text: From Middle English countee, counte (Middle English), conte (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman counté, Old French conté (French comté (French)), from Latin comitātus (“jurisdiction of a count”), from comes (Latin “count, earl”). Cognate with condado (Spanish “county”) and contea (Italian “county”). , borrowed directly from Latin. Mostly displaced native sċīr (Old English), whence shire (English).

etymologies.text: From Middle English couple, from Old French couple, from Latin cōpula. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English corage, from Old French corage (courage (French)), from Vulgar Latin *corāticum, from Latin cor (“heart”). Distantly related to cardiac (English “of the heart”), which is from Greek, but from the same Proto-Indo-European root. Displaced Middle English elne, ellen (Middle English), from Old English ellen (“courage, valor”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: , diminutive of courge (French “vegetable marrow, marrow squash”). Ultimately related to zucchini (English) through Latin cucurbita.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (Latin “run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English court, from Old French cort (“cort, curt”), from Late Latin cōrs, contracted from Latin cohors. . Displaced native stapol (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English curteisie, curtesie (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman curtesie, from Old French curteisie, cortoisie (Old French). Equivalent to . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English coveren, borrowed from Old French covrir (“covrir, cueuvrir”) (modern couvrir (French)), from Late Latin coperire, from Latin cooperiō (“to cover completely”), from co- (Latin) + operiō (Latin “to close, cover”). Displaced native thecchen (Middle English) and bithecchen (Middle English “to cover”) (from þeccan (Old English), beþeccan (Old English “to cover”)), helen (Middle English “to cover, conceal”) (from helan (Old English “to conceal, cover, hide”)), wreon (Middle English “to cover”) (from wreon (Old English “to cover”)), hodren (Middle English “to cover up”) (from hudren (Low German “to cover up”)).

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the original sense of the verb and noun cover (English) was “hide from view” as in its cognate covert (English). Except in the limited sense of “cover again”, the word recover (English) is unrelated and is cognate with recuperate (English). Cognate with cubrir (Spanish) and cobrir (Portuguese).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English coward, from Old French coart, cuard (Old French) ( > couard (French)), from coue (Old French “tail”), coe + -ard (Old French); coue (Old French), coe is in turn from Latin cauda.

The reference seems to be to an animal "turning tail", or having its tail between its legs, especially a dog. Compare the expression tail between one's legs (English). Displaced native earg (Old English) (surviving in northern dialect argh (English)).

Unrelated to cower (English), which is of Germanic origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English *cowardly and cowardly (Middle English), equivalent to coward + ly (English). Displaced native earg (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English crabbe, from Old English crabba (“crab; crayfish; cancer”), from Proto-West Germanic *krabbō, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô, from *krabbōną (Proto-Germanic “to scratch”), from Proto-Indo-European —, a metathesised o-grade of *gerbʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to carve, scratch”). More at carve (English).

See also krab (Dutch), Low German Krabb (Low German (Germany)), Danish krabbe (Danish), Swedish krabba (Swedish).

Further cognates with frequentative-infix are krabbelje (Saterland Frisian “to creep, crawl”), krabbelen (Dutch “to scratch”) and krabbeln (German “to crawl”). Possibly related to creep (English) and krypa (Swedish “to creep, crawl”) etc.

Other origins have also been suggested, see κάραβος (Ancient Greek) (regarding the possibility of a substrate origin) and خرچنگ (Persian) (regarding possible ideophonic origin); compare also քարբ (Classical Armenian), Krebs (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English crabbe (“wild apple”), of gem — origin, plausibly from gmq —, cognate with Swedish dialect skrabba (Swedish “sour apple, apple cart”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Possibly a corruption of the genus name

etymologies.text: From carabiner (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English crakken, craken (Middle English), from Old English cracian (“to resound, crack”), from Proto-West Germanic *krakōn (“to crack, crackle, shriek”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to resound, cry hoarsely”).

Cognate with crak (Scots “to crack”), kreakje (Western Frisian “to crack”), kraken (Dutch “to crunch, creak, squeak”), kraken (Low German “to crack”), krachen (German “to crash, crack, creak”), gìrgžděti (Lithuanian “to creak, squeak”), կարկաչ (Classical Armenian), गर्जति (Sanskrit “to roar, hum”).

Compare typologically crevice (English) (<< crepō (Latin)), пукнатина (Bulgarian) (akin to пу́кам (Bulgarian)), тре́щина (Russian) (akin to треск (Russian)), щель (Russian) (akin to щёлкать (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Slang first attested 1793, perhaps from the verb in the sense of doing something quickly or with intelligence, or in the sense of "speaking boastingly" and having something to be proud of.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English craft (“strength, skill”), from Old English cræft (“strength, skill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (“strength, power”); further origin obscure.
Cognate with kracht (Dutch “strength, power, force”), Kraft (German “strength, power, force, energy, employee”), kraft (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “strength, power, force”), kraftur (Faroese / Icelandic “strength”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: Middle English craft (“strength, skill”), from Old English cræft (“strength, skill”), from Proto-West Germanic *kraftu, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz (“strength, power”); further origin obscure.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English crasshen, crasschen (Middle English), craschen (Middle English “to break into pieces”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a variant of earlier *crasken (Middle English), from crasen + k (Middle English); or from earlier *craskien (Middle English), *craksien (Middle English), a variant of craken (Middle English “to crack, break open”) (for form development compare break (English), brask (English), brash (English)).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English crasshen, crasschen (Middle English), craschen (Middle English “to break into pieces”), of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English crawlen, crewlen (Middle English), creulen (Middle English), crallen (Middle English), *cravelen (Middle English), from Old Norse krafla (compare kravle (Danish “to crawl, creep”), kravla (Swedish), kräla (Swedish “to creep, crawl”)), from Proto-Germanic *krabblōną (“*krablōną”) (compare krabbelje (Saterland Frisian), krabbelen (Dutch), krabbeln (Low German (Germany)), krabbeln (German)), frequentative of *krabbōną (Proto-Germanic “to scratch, scrape”). Compare also krauelje (Saterland Frisian “to crawl, scuttle”), kreauwelje (Western Frisian “to crawl”), krevelen (Dutch), krieuwelen (Dutch “to crawl”), kribbeln (Low German (Germany)), kribbeln (German “to creep, crawl, tingle”). , etymologically equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From craze + -y (English), akin to being "crazed up". Compare crack up (English “suffered a mental breakdown; be insane”), crackpot (English).

Compare typologically чо́кнутый (Russian).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English creime, creme, from Old French creme, cresme, blend of Late Latin chrisma (“ointment”) (from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (“unguent”)), and Late Latin crāmum (“cream”), from Gaulish *crama (compare cramen (Welsh “scab, skin”), crammen (Breton)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krama- (compare screm (mga “surface, skin”), schram (Dutch “abrasion”), kramas (Lithuanian “scurf”)). .

Displaced native rēam (Old English “cream”) (> modern ream (English)); and native flīete (Old English “cream”) related to flotian (Old English) (> modern float (English)) from *flutōną (Proto-Germanic “to float”).

Figurative sense of "most excellent element or part" appears from 1581. Verb meaning "to beat, thrash, wreck" is 1929, U.S. colloquial. The U.S. standard of identity is from [http://edocket.access.gpo.gov/cfr_2002/aprqtr/21cfr131.3.htm 21 CFR 131.3(a)].

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English createn, from Latin creātus, the perfect passive participle of creō (Latin), see -ate (English). In this sense, mostly displaced wyrċan (Old English) (whence work (English)) and ġesċieppan (Old English) (whence shape (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English creacion, from Old French creacion (modern création (French)), from Latin creātiō (“creātiō, creātiōnis”). . Displaced native ġesċeaft (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Latin creātīvus, from Latin creō. Equivalent to create + -ive (English). Displaced native orþanclīċ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English crue, from Old French creue (“an increase, recruit, military reinforcement”), the feminine past participle of creistre (Old French “grow”), from Latin cresco (“crescere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English cocodrill, cokadrill (Middle English), cokedril (Middle English), from Old French cocodril (modern crocodile (French)), from Medieval Latin cocodrillus, from Latin crocodilus, from Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος. The word was later refashioned after the Latin and Greek forms. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English crop, croppe (Middle English), from Old English cropp, croppa (Old English “the head or top of a plant, a sprout or herb, a bunch or cluster of flowers, an ear of corn, the craw of a bird, a kidney”), from Proto-West Germanic *kropp, from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz (“body, trunk, crop”), from Proto-Indo-European *grewb- (“to warp, bend, crawl”). .

Cognate with krop (Dutch “crop”), Kropp (Low German (Germany) “a swelling on the neck, the craw, maw”), Kropf (German “the craw, ear of grain, head of lettuce or cabbage”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian), and kropp (Swedish “body, trunk”), - (Faroese) and kroppur (Icelandic “body”). Related to crap (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English croppen (“to cut, pluck and eat”), from Old English *croppian. Cognate with crap (Scots “to crop”), kroppen (Dutch “to cram, digest”), kröppen (Low German “to cut, crop, stuff the craw”), kröpfen (German “to crop”), kroppa (Icelandic “to cut, crop, pick”). Literally, to take off the crop (top, head, ear) of a plant. See Etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English cross, cros (Middle English), from Old English cros (“rood, cross”), from Old Norse kross, from Old Irish cros, from Latin crux (crucī (Latin)). In this sense displaced native rode (Middle English), from rōd (Old English “cross”); see rood (English). . Compare croes (Welsh), crois (Irish).

The sense of "two intersecting lines drawn or cut on a surface; two lines intersecting at right angles" without regard to religious signification develops from the late 14th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
1706, from French crucial, a medical term for ligaments of the knee (which cross each other), from Latin crux (Latin “crux, crucis”) (English crux (English)), from the Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”).

The meaning “decisive, critical” is extended from a logical term, Instantias Crucis, adopted by in his influential ' (1620); the notion is of cross fingerboard signposts at forking roads, thus a requirement to choose.

etymologies.text: From Middle English cruel, borrowed from Old French cruel, from Latin crūdēlis (“hard, severe, cruel”), akin to crūdus (Latin “raw, crude”); see crude (English).
