etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is from Middle English crien (13th century), from Old French crier, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre, generally thought to derive from quirito (Classical Latin “quirītāre”) (*krītan (Proto-West Germanic) has also been suggested as a source). The noun corresponds to Middle English cry, crie (Middle English), from Old French cri, a deverbal of crier (Old French).

crien (Middle English) eventually displaced native galen (Middle English “to cry out”) (from galan (Old English)), greden (Middle English “to cry out”) (from grǣdan (Old English)), yermen (Middle English “to bellow, mourn, lament”) (from ġierman (Old English)), hoen (Middle English “hooen, hoen”) (from hóa (Old Norse)), remen (Middle English “to cry, shout”) (from hrīeman (Old English), compare hrēam (Old English “noise, outcry, lamentation, alarm”)), gretan (Middle English “greten, graten”) (from grǣtan (Old English) and gráta (Old Norse)). More at greet (English), regret (English).

Already in the 13th century, the meaning was extended to include the sense "to shed tears" (natively weep (English)); cry used in this sense had mostly replaced weep by the 16th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English cucumer, cucumber (Middle English), from Old French cocombre, ultimately from Latin cucumis (“cucumis, cucumerem”) (possibly through an pro — intermediate). Probably of Pre-Italic qfa-sub — origin. Displaced native earthapple (English) (see which for more), which has since acquired other senses.

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English cuppe, coppe (Middle English), from the merger of Old English cuppe (“cup”) and Old English copp (“cup, vessel”).

cuppe (Old English) is a borrowing from Late Latin cuppa, itself of origin, but probably from earlier Latin cūpa (“tub, cask”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“a hollow”). copp (Old English), however, is from Proto-West Germanic *kopp (“round object, bowl, vessel, knoll, summit, crown of the head”), from Proto-Germanic *kuppaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend, curve, arch”) (whence also obsolete cop (English “top, summit, crown of the head”), Kopf (German “top, head”)).

The Middle English word was further reinforced by cupe (Anglo-Norman) and cope (Old French), coupe (Old French), from cuppa (Latin). Compare also Kop (Saterland Frisian “cup”), kop (Western Frisian “cup”), kop (Dutch “cup”), Koppke (Low German (Germany)), Köppke (Low German (Germany) “cup”), kop (Danish “cup”), kopp (Swedish “cup”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English custume, borrowed from Anglo-Norman coustume (“custume”), inherited from Latin consuetudo (“consuētūdinem”), a noun derived from cōnsuēscō (Latin), from con- (Latin “with”) + suēscō (Latin “become used or accustomed to”). Displaced native ġewuna (Old English) and sidu (Old English). .

The adjectival form first appears c. 1830.

etymologies.text: Plural of custom (English). Perhaps influenced by or taken as a corruption of custom house (English “customhouse”), from Middle English custome hous.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English cutten, of gmq — origin, from Old Norse *kytja, *kutta (Old Norse), from Proto-Germanic *kutjaną, *kuttaną (Proto-Germanic “to cut”), of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *kwetwą (“meat, flesh”) (compare kvett (Old Norse “meat”)). Sometimes instead compared to couteau (French), itself from culter (Latin “knife”).

Copmare kut (Scots), kit (Scots “to cut”)); also akin to Middle kotta (Swedish “to cut or carve with a knife”) (compare dialectal kåta (Swedish), kuta (Swedish “to cut or chip with a knife”), kuta (Swedish), kytti (Swedish “a knife”)), kutte (Norwegian Bokmål “to cut”), kutte (Norwegian Nynorsk “to cut”), kuta (Icelandic “to cut with a knife”), kuti (Old Norse “small knife”), kyttel (Norwegian), kytel (Norwegian), kjutul (Norwegian “pointed slip of wood used to strip bark”). (from snīþan (Old English)), still attested in dialectal snithe (English) and snead (English). See snide (English).

The adjective sense of "drunk" (now rare and now usually used in the originally humorous derivative form of half-cut (English)) dates from the 17th century, from or , a for being very drunk.

Cognate with Deegeslucht (Saterland Frisian), Daisljoacht (Saterland Frisian “daylight”), deiljocht (Western Frisian “daylight”), daglicht (Dutch “daylight”), Tageslicht (German “daylight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ded, deed (Middle English), from Old English dēad, from Proto-West Germanic *daud, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz. Compare dead (Western Frisian), dea (Western Frisian), dood (Dutch), tot (German), død (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), daud (Norwegian Nynorsk), död (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: According to the Oxford English Dictionary, early usage refers to lines that do not move, such as one used in angling. Slightly later American usage refers to a boundary in a prison which prisoners must not cross. There is only indirect evidence that the sense of "due date" may be connected with this use of the term in prison camps during the American Civil War, when it referred to a physical line or boundary beyond which prisoners were shot. In 1904, in a report from the US Department of Commerce and Labor, the term is used for "minimum work goals" (and in contrast to bonus line): for example, as a typographer the line could be 18,000 ems per day; should one not cross this line, then that could have negative consequences. In 1917, the term is attested as a printing term for a guideline on the bed of a printing press beyond which text will not print. Three years later, the term is found in print in the sense of "time limit" in the closely connected publishing industry, indicating the time after which material would not make it into a newspaper or periodical.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dedly, dedlych (Middle English), dedlich (Middle English), from Old English dēadlīċ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþalīk, from Proto-Germanic *dauþalīkaz (“deadly”). . Cognate with dodelk (Saterland Frisian “deadly”), deadlik (Western Frisian “deadly”), dodelijk (Dutch “deadly”), tödlich (German “deadly”), dödlig (Swedish “deadly, fatal, mortal”), dauðlegur (Icelandic “mortal”).

The adverb is from Middle English dedliche, from Old English dēadlīċe, from the adjective.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English def, deef (Middle English), from Old English dēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *daub (“deaf”), from Proto-Germanic *daubaz (“deaf or stunned”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, smoke, darken, obscure”). Cognate with τυφλός (Ancient Greek “blind”). See also dumb (English). .

Cognate with doof (Dutch), taub (German), døv (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), dauv (Norwegian Nynorsk), döv (Swedish), deyvur (Faroese), daufur (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English del, dele (Middle English), from Old English dǣl (“part, share, portion”), from Proto-West Germanic *daili, from Proto-Germanic *dailiz (“part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European —. Cognate with dele (Scots “part, portion”), diel (Western Frisian “part, share”), deel (Dutch “part, share, portion”), Teil (German “part, portion, section”), del (Danish / Slovenian / Swedish “part”), deila (Icelandic “division, contention”), 𐌳𐌰𐌹𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “portion”). Related to dāl (Old English “portion”). More at dole.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English delen, from Old English dǣlan (“to divide, part”), from Proto-West Germanic *dailijan, from Proto-Germanic *dailijaną (“to divide, part, deal”), from Proto-Indo-European —.

Cognate with diele (Western Frisian “to divide, separate”), delen (Dutch), teilen (German), dela (Swedish); and with dalinti (Lithuanian “divide”), дели́ть (Russian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English dele (“plank”), from Middle Low German dele, from Old Saxon thili, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þiljǭ (“plank, board”); cognate with þille (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English delare, from Old English dǣlere, from Proto-West Germanic —. . Cognate with Deeler (Saterland Frisian), dieler (Western Frisian), deler (Dutch), Teiler (German), delare (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dere, from Old English dēore, dīere (Old English), dīore (Old English), dȳre (Old English “of great value or excellence, expensive, beloved”), from Proto-West Germanic *diurī, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz (“dear, precious; expensive”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn; hot, warm”).

Cognate with dear (Yola “dear”), djuur (Saterland Frisian “precious, dear, costly, expensive”), tüür (Alemannic “expensive”), dier (Dutch), duur (Dutch “expensive”), teuer (German “expensive”), taojer (Ripuarian), tojer (Ripuarian “dear”), diere (Flemish “expensive”), טײַער (Yiddish “expensive”), dyr (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “expensive”), dýrur (Faroese “expensive”), dýr (Icelandic “expensive”), tyyris (Finnish “expensive”), tõurõz (liv “dear”), divrras (se “expensive”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English dere (“fierce, severe, hard, deadly”), from Old English dēor, dȳr (Old English “brave, bold; severe, dire, vehement”), from Proto-Germanic *deuzaz. Cognate with the above.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English deth, deeth (Middle English), from Old English dēaþ, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰówtus. More at die (English).

Cognate with daeth (Scots), daith (Scots), death (Scots), deeth (Scots), deith (Scots “death”), Duar (North Frisian), duas (North Frisian), düüs (North Frisian “death”), Dood (Saterland Frisian “death”), dea (Western Frisian “death”), dood (Dutch “death”), Tod (German), Todt (German “death”), doead (Limburgish “death”), Doud (lb “death”), טויט (Yiddish “death”), død (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “death”), deyði (Faroese “death”), dauði (Icelandic “death”), daude (Norwegian Nynorsk), død (Norwegian Nynorsk “death”), död (Swedish “death”), 𐌳𐌰𐌿𐌸𐌿𐍃 (Gothic “death”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English debaten, from Old French debatre (“to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down”), from Romanic , from Latin dis- (“apart, in different directions”) + battuō (Latin “to beat, to fence”).

chain.meaning: to fight, contend, debate, also literally to beat down

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English debat, Old French debat, deverbal of debatre (Old French), see Etymology 1 for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French debet, from Latin debitum (“what is owed, a debt”), neuter of debitus (Latin), past participle of debere (Latin “to owe”); .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dette, dett (Middle English), borrowed from Old French dete (dette (French)), from Medieval Latin dēbita, from Latin dēbitum (“what is owed, a debt, a duty”), neuter of dēbitus (Latin), perfect passive participle of dēbeō (Latin “to owe”), contraction of *dehibeō (Latin “I have from”), from de (Latin “from”) + habeō (Latin “to have”). . Displaced native eofot (Old English).

The unpronounced "b" in the modern English spelling is a Latinisation from the Latin etymon dēbitum (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English decade, from Old French decade, from Late Latin decās (“(set of) ten”), from Ancient Greek δεκάς, from δέκα (Ancient Greek “ten”). In reference to a span of ten years, originally a clipping of the phrase decade of years (English). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English decaien (“to decrease, diminish”) and decai (Middle English “deterioration, decline in value”), from Anglo-Norman decheoir (“to fall away, decay, decline”), from Vulgar Latin —, etymologically restored form of Latin dēcidō (“to fall down, to fail, sink or perish”), from de- (Latin “of, from, away, down”) + cadō (Latin “to fall”). Compare decadent (English) and decadence (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English deceyven, from Anglo-Norman deceivre, from Latin dēcipiō (“to deceive; beguile; entrap”), from dē- (Latin “from”) + capiō (Latin “to seize”); see captive. Compare conceive, perceive, receive. Displaced native beswīcan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle French décent, or its source, Latin decēns, present participle of decet (Latin “it is fitting or suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to take, accept, to receive, greet, be suitable”) (compare δοκέω (Ancient Greek “to appear, seem, think”), δέχομαι (Ancient Greek “to accept”); दशस्यति (Sanskrit “shows honor, is gracious”), दाशति (Sanskrit “makes offerings, bestows”)). Meaning ‘kind, pleasant’ is from 1902.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French —, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis (Latin), from dēcīdō (Latin “to decide”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , equivalent to decide + ive (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English dekke, borrowed from Middle Dutch dec (“roof, covering”), from Middle Dutch decken, from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną. Formed the same: Decke (German “covering, blanket”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English dekken, from Middle Dutch dekken (“to cover”), from Old Dutch thecken, from Proto-West Germanic *þakkjan, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną (“to roof; cover”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English declaren, from Old French declarer, from Latin dēclārō (“to make clear”), from dē- (Latin) + clārus (Latin “clear”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English declinen, and ultimately Latin declīnō (“to bend, turn aside, deflect, inflect, decline”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean (English)). The senses arrived from two separate pathways in Middle English:
* The grammatical sense came from Old English declīnian, which was borrowed directly from the Latin etymon.
* All senses except the grammatical sense were derived from those of Old French decliner. Old French itself borrowed the verb from Latin.

chain.meaning: to bend, turn aside, deflect, inflect, decline

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English decorat (“adorned”), from Latin decorātus, perfect passive participle of decorō (Latin “to adorn, distinguish, honor”) (see -ate), from decus (Latin “ornament, grace, dignity, honor”), akin to decor (Latin “elegance, grace, beauty, ornament”), from decet (Latin “adorn, befit”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English decorat (“decorated, adorned”), see -ate and Etymology 1 for more. Originally also used as the past participle of decorate; compare generate (English) or communicate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin decoratio: compare . Morphologically decorate + ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin decorātus + -ive (English). Cognate with .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English decresen, alteration of discresen (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman —, Old French descreistre (French: décroître (French)), from Latin decrescere.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dep, deep (Middle English), depe (Middle English), from Old English dēop (“deep, profound; awful, mysterious; heinous; serious, solemn, earnest; extreme, great”), from Proto-West Germanic *deup, from Proto-Germanic *deupaz (“deep”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“deep”).

Cognate with depe (Scots “deep”), diip (North Frisian), jip (North Frisian “deep”), djoop (Saterland Frisian “deep”), djip (Western Frisian “deep”), diep (Dutch “deep”), deep (Low German “deep”), déif (lb “deep”), deep (Central Franconian), deef (Central Franconian “deep”), tief (German “deep”), tüüf (Alemannic “deep”), tiaf (mhn “deep”), tif (Ripuarian), tīf (Ripuarian), tiif (Ripuarian “deep”), טיף (Yiddish “deep”), dyb (Danish “deep”), djup (Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “deep”), djyber (gmq-scy “deep”), djup (Norwegian Bokmål), dyp (Norwegian Bokmål “deep”), djúpur (Faroese / Icelandic “deep”), 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐍃 (Gothic “deep”), dubùs (Lithuanian “deep, hollow”), det (Albanian “sea”), dwfn (Welsh “deep”).

chain.meaning: deep, profound; awful, mysterious; heinous; serious, solemn, earnest; extreme, great

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English deply, depely (Middle English), from Old English dēoplīċe (“deeply”), from dēoplīc (Old English “deep”), equivalent to deep + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English der, deer (Middle English “animal, deer”), from Old English dēor (“animal”), from Proto-West Germanic *deuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm (“living thing”), from *dʰéws (Proto-Indo-European “breath”), full-grade derivative of *dʰwes- (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with deer (Scots “deer”), dier (North Frisian “animal, beast”), dier (Western Frisian “animal, beast”), dier (Dutch “animal, beast”), Deer (Low German (Germany)), Deert (Low German (Germany) “animal”), Tier (German “animal, beast”), djur (Swedish “animal, beast”), dyr (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “animal, beast”), dýr (Icelandic “animal, beast”).

Related also to dash (Albanian “ram”) (possibly), daũsos (Lithuanian “upper air; heaven”), dùsti (Lithuanian “to sigh”), душа́ (Russian “breath, spirit”), dvė̃sti (Lithuanian “to breathe, exhale”), ध्वंसति (Sanskrit “he falls to dust”).

For the semantic development compare animālis (Latin “animal”), from anima (Latin “breath, spirit”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English defeten, from Middle English defet (“disfigured”) and defet (Middle English “defect”), see Etymology 2 below.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English defet, from French deffet, desfait (Old French), past participle of the verb desfaire (Old French) (compare modern French défaire (French)), from des- (Old French) + faire (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English defens, defense (Middle English), from Old French defens, defense (Old French), from Late Latin dēfēnsa (“protection”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English defencen, defensen (Middle English), from Old French defenser or its etymon, Latin dēfēnsō.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English defenden, from Old French defendre, deffendre (Old French) (Modern défendre (French)), from Latin dēfendō (“to ward off”), from Proto-Italic *fendō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰen-. Displaced native bewerian (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English defender, deffender (Middle English), defendere (Middle English), defendour (Middle English), defendoure (Middle English), partly from Anglo-Norman defendour, from Old French defendëor; partly from Middle English defenden + -ere (Middle English), equivalent to defend + -er (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English definen, from Old French definer, variant of definir (Old French), from Latin dēfīniō (“limit, settle, define”), from dē (Latin) + fīniō (Latin “set a limit, bound, end”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin dēfīnītus, past participle of dēfīniō (Latin), whence also English define (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: definite + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English diffinicioun, from Middle French definition, from Latin dēfīnītiō, from dēfīniō (Latin). Equivalent to define + -ition (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English degre, borrowed from Old French degré (French: degré (French)), itself from Latin gradus, with the prefix de- (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English delaien, borrowed from Anglo-Norman delaier, deslaier (Old French), from des- (Old French) + Old French laier (“to leave”), a conflation of Old Frankish *lattjan , and Old Frankish *laibijan . .

Akin to latian (Old English “to delay, hesitate”), latu (Old English “a delay, a hindrance”), lǣfan (Old English “to leave”). More at let (to hinder), late, leave.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English delaien, from Old French delaiier, a variant of delaissier (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Latin dēlētus, past participle of dēlēre (Latin “destroy, blot out, efface”), from dēlēvī (Latin), originally perf. tense of dēlinere (Latin “to daub, erase by smudging”), from dē- (Latin “from, away”) + linere (Latin “to smear, wipe”). Original sense first appears c. 1495. In common use for ordering the absence of features of products (such as automobiles) in the 1960s. The computing sense, including the noun form, first appears c. 1977 in Software: Practice & Experience. Not related to deleterious (English).
.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English deliberat, Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (Latin “to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate and -ate), from dē- + *līberō (Latin) / lībrō (Latin “to weigh”)), from *libera (Latin) / libra (Latin “a balance”); see librate (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: deliberate + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English delicat, from Latin dēlicātus (“giving pleasure, delightful, soft, luxurious, delicate, (in also) fine, slender”), from dēliciae + -ātus (Latin) (see -ate), usually in plural dēliciae (Latin “pleasure, delight, luxury”), from dēliciō (Latin “to allure, entice”), from dē- (Latin “away”) + laciō (Latin “to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. Compare delight (English), delicious (English) and delgado (Spanish “thin, skinny”). The noun is from a substantivization of the adjective (see -ate).

chain.meaning: giving pleasure, delightful, soft, luxurious, delicate, (in  also) fine, slender

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English delicious, from Anglo-Norman delicious, from Old French delicious (“delicious, delicieux”), from Late Latin deliciosus (“dēliciōsus”), from dēliciae (Latin “delights”), plural of dēlicia (Latin “pleasure”), from delicere (Latin “to allure, to entice”), from de- (Latin “away”) + laciō (Latin “to lure, deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. Displaced native ārlīċ (Old English “delicious”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested from the 13th century, from Middle English delite, from Old French deleiter, deliter (Old French), from Latin dēlectō (“dēlectāre”), frequentative of dēliciō (Latin “dēlicere”), from dē- (Latin “away”) + laciō (Latin “to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. . Related with delectation (English), delicate (English), delicious (English) and dilettante (English). The modern unetymological spelling (instead of expected ) is influenced by light (English) and other words ending in , such as might (English), bright (English), etc. The -gh- may also be an attempt to represent the Latin -c-; compare obsolete indight (English) for indict (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English deliteful, delitfull (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English deliveren, from Anglo-Norman — and Old French delivrer, from Latin dē + līberō (Latin “to set free”).

Compare typologically dispatch (English), analyzable as dis- (English) + impeach (English), from impedicō (Latin) (also akin to impede (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English deliveri et al., from Anglo-Norman —, from Old French delivrer.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From late Middle English demaunden, from Old French demander, from Latin demando (“dēmandō, dēmandāre”). Displaced native ġiwian (Old English “to demand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: demand + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle French democratie (French démocratie (French)), from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ.
.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French democratique (“pertaining to democracy, democratic”) (modern démocratique (French)), and its etymon Late Latin democraticus (“pertaining to democracy, democratic; democrat”), from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐκός (“of or for democracy; favouring or suited for democracy”), from δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (Ancient Greek “democracy”) + -ῐκός (Ancient Greek). is derived from δῆμος (Ancient Greek “the common people; free citizens, sovereign people; popular assembly; popular government, democracy”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- (“to divide; to share”)) + -κρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (Ancient Greek) (from κρᾰ́τος (Ancient Greek “might, strength; dominion, power”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kret- (“insight, intelligence; strength”)) + -ῐ́ᾱ (Ancient Greek)). or democrat + -ic (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested since the 16th century; from demoliss- , the stem of some conjugated forms of the verb demolir (Middle French “to destroy”, “to tear down”), from . Displaced native tōweorpan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin dēmonstrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēmonstrō (Latin “to show, point at”), see -ate. Cognate with démontrer (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English demonstracioun, from Old French demonstration, from Latin dēmōnstrātiō (“dēmōnstrātiōnem”), from dēmōnstrō (Latin “dēmōnstrāre”), from dē- (Latin “of or concerning”) + mōnstrō (Latin “mōnstrāre”).
Morphologically .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the phrase de Nîmes (French “from Nîmes”), after the French town of Nîmes, where denim fabric was originally produced.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also δασύς (Ancient Greek)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: dense + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French dental or Late Latin dentālis, from dēns + -ālis (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English denyen, from Old French denoier (“to deny, to repudiate”) (dénier (French)), from Latin denegare (“to deny, to refuse”), from de- (Latin “away”) and negare (Latin “to refuse”), the latter ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *né (“no, not”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French departir, from Late Latin departiō (“to divide”), from dē + partiō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent (Middle English), from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (Middle French “to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō (Latin “to depend”)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: , past participle of depono (Latin “put down”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English depression, depressioun (Middle English), from Old French depression, from Latin dēpressiō. Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English depryven, from Old French depriver, from Medieval Latin dēprīvō, from Latin dē- + prīvō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English depthe, from Old English *dīepþ (“depth”), from Proto-Germanic *diupiþō (“depth”), equivalent to .

Cognate with deepth (Scots), Djüpte (Saterland Frisian), djipte (Western Frisian “depth; abyss, chasm”), diepte (Dutch), Deepd (Low German (Germany)), Déift (lb), - (Danish), dybde (Norwegian Bokmål “depth”), dýpd (Faroese “depth”), dýpt (Icelandic), djupt (Norwegian Nynorsk), dypt (Norwegian Nynorsk), and 𐌳𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌹𐌸𐌰 (Gothic “depth”); further to diepe (Old English), Tiefe (German), dýpi (Icelandic), djup (Norwegian Nynorsk), djupn (Norwegian Nynorsk), djup (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Middle English descenden (“to move downwards, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to go from a better to a worse condition, decline, degenerate; to be a descendant, derive from (a source); etc.”), from Anglo-Norman descendere, descendre (Anglo-Norman), and Old French descendere, descendre (Old French “to move downwards, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to be a descendant, derive from (a source); etc.”) (modern descendre (French)), and from their etymon Latin dēscendere, the present active infinitive of dēscendō (Latin “to come or go down, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to be a descendant; etc.”), from de- (Latin) + scandō (Latin “to ascend, climb; to clamber”) (from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to climb, scale; to dart; to jump”)).

The noun is derived from the verb.

chain.meaning: to move downwards, fall, descend; to slope downwards; to go from a better to a worse condition, decline, degenerate; to be a descendant, derive from (a source); etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English descripcioun, from Old French description and its etymon, Latin dēscrīptiō, noun of action of dēscrībō (Latin “to describe”). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English deserven, from Old French deservir, from Latin dēserviō, from dē- (Latin) + serviō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English designen, from Old French designer, from Latin designō (“to mark out, point out, describe, design, contrive”), from de- (Latin) (or dis- (Latin)) + signō (Latin “to mark”), from signum (Latin “mark”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: design + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From .

Morphologically desire + able (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English desir, desire (Middle English) and desiren (Middle English), from Old French desirer, desirrer (Old French), from Latin dēsīderō (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”), apparently from de- (Latin) + sidus (Latin) (in the phrase de sidere, "from the stars") in connection with astrological hopes. Compare consider (English) and desiderate (English). The verb, along with Old Norse derived want (English), has mostly replaced native will (English) in modern English.

chain.meaning: to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: desk + top

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English dispeir, from Anglo-Norman despeir and Old French desperer (from Latin despero (“dēspērō, dēspērāre”)), or desesperer (Old French), from des- (Old French “dis-”) + esperer (Old French “hope”). See also desperate (English). Displaced native ormōdnes (Old English “despair”) and ortrīewan (Old English “to despair”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English desperat (“desperate”), borrowed from Latin dēspērātus, perfect passive participle of dēspērō (Latin “to be without hope”), see -ate. The noun is derived from the adjective or from the Latin source through substantivization, see -ate.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: desperate + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English despit, dispit (Middle English), from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from dēspiciō (Latin “to look down, despise”).

The preposition is derived from Middle English dispit, itself derived from the phrase in dispit of (Middle English) (in despite of (English)).

Compare typologically несмотря́ на (Russian) (< смотре́ть (Russian)); невзира́я на (Russian) (< взира́ть (Russian)), презре́в (Russian) (< презре́ть (Russian) <~ зреть (Russian)) (compare despite—despise (English) relation).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English despite, dispite (Middle English), dyspite (Middle English), dyspyte (Middle English), from Old French despitier.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin dēstinātiō, from dēstinō (Latin “to destine”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English destroyen, from Old French destruire, Vulgar Latin *destrugō, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (Latin “un-, de-”) + struō (Latin “to build”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English destruccioun, from Old French destrucion, from Latin destructio (“dēstructiō, dēstructiōnem”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle French détail, from Old French detail, from detaillier (Old French), from de- (Old French) + taillier (Old French “to cut”).

Compare typologically подробност (Bulgarian), podrobnost (Czech), подро́бность (Russian) (akin to дроби́ть (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The adjective is from Classical Latin —, past participial stem of dētegō (Latin “to detect”), ive. .

is an , or a similar construction. The later more general was derived by extension. The verb is also from the noun.

is a Dutch detective and Russian детекти́в, both from English.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English determinacion, determynacioun (Middle English), from Old French determinacion, from Latin dēterminātiō. Morphologically determine + ation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: determine + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from French développer, from Middle French desveloper, from Old French desveloper, from des- (Old French) + veloper (Old French “voloper, veloper, vloper”) (compare sviluppare (Italian “sviluppare”), - (Old Italian) alternative form goluppare (Italian “to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vloppō, *wloppō (“to wrap”) ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrappaną, *wlappaną (Proto-Germanic “to wrap, roll up, turn, wind”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (Proto-Indo-European “to turn, bend”) [http://www.wordnik.com/words/envelop].

Akin to wlappen (Middle English “to wrap, fold”) (Modern lap (English “to wrap, involve, fold”)), wrappen (Middle English “to wrap”), lappen (Middle Dutch “to wrap up, embrace”), dialectal vravle (Danish “to wind, twist”), wrempen (Middle Low German “to wrinkle, scrunch, distort”), wearp (Old English “warp”). The word acquired its modern meaning from the 17th-century belief that an egg contains the animal in miniature and matures by growing larger and shedding its envelopes.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English devil, devel (Middle English), deovel (Middle English), from Old English dēofol, from Proto-West Germanic *diubul, from Latin diabolus, ultimately from Ancient Greek διάβολος (“false accuser, slanderer”), also as "Satan" (in Jewish/Christian usage, translating שָׂטָן (hbo)), from διαβάλλω (Ancient Greek “to slander”), literally “to throw across”, from διά (Ancient Greek “through, across”) + βάλλω (Ancient Greek “throw”). The Old English word was probably adopted under influence of diabolus (Latin) (itself from the Greek). Other Germanic languages adopted the word independently: compare Düüwel (Saterland Frisian “devil”), duvel (Western Frisian “devil”), duivel (Dutch), duvel (Dutch “devil”), Düvel (Low German (Germany) “devil”), Teufel (German “devil”), Teifl (Bavarian “devil”), djævel (Danish “devil”), djävul (Swedish “devil”) (older: djefvul (Swedish), diævul (gmq-osw), djǫfull (Old Norse)). .

Also analyzable as di- + -alogue (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English difficult (ca. 1400), a from difficulte (Middle English) (whence modern difficulty (English)), from , from , from difficul (Latin), older form of difficilis (Latin “hard to do, difficult”), from dis- (Latin) + facilis (Latin “easy”); see difficile. Replaced native earveþ (Middle English “difficult, hard”), from earfoþe (Old English “difficult, laborious, full of hardship”), cognate to Arbeit (German “work”).

The verb is from the adjective, partly after Middle French difficulter and its etymon Latin difficultō. Compare difficilitate (English), difficultate (English), and difficoltare (Italian).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English difficulte, from Middle French — and Anglo-Norman difficulte and their etymon Latin difficultas, from difficul (Latin), older form of difficilis (Latin “hard to do, difficult”), from dis- (Latin) + facilis (Latin “easy”); see difficile and difficult. Equivalent to dis- + facile + -ty (English). Also analysable as difficult + -y (English), though the adjective is historically a backformation from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English diggen (“to dig”, 13th c.), an alteration of dīken (Middle English), from Old English dīcian (“to dig a ditch, mound up earth”), from Proto-West Germanic *dīkōn, which see for cognates. This verb is denominal from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (“pool, puddle; dyke, ditch”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stab, dig”).

The form with g may have been influenced by Old French —, a variant of dikier (Old French), itself from the West Germanic verb above. French forms with g are attested only in the 15th c., thus 200 years later than in English. On the other hand, French has according forms also for the underlying noun (cf. digue (French)) and the phonetic development is more plausible in French than in English.

chain.meaning: to dig a ditch, mound up earth

From Middle English drit (“excrement”), from Old Norse drit (“excrement”), from Proto-Germanic *dritą, *dritō (Proto-Germanic “excrement”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreyd-, *treydʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to have diarrhea”). Cognate with dialectal - (Danish) and drit (Norn “excrement”), dritt (Norwegian “excrement”), dialectal dret (Swedish “shit”), - (Faroese) and drit (Icelandic “bird excrement”), drijten (Dutch “to defecate”), drits (Dutch “dirt, mud, filth”), drijt (Dutch) and dreet (Dutch “excrement”), drieten (Low German “to defecate”), Driet (Low German “shit”), regional Driss (German “shit”), ġedrītan (Old English “to defecate”).

The word originally referred to excrement before shifting to the current sense of "soil". For a semantic parallel, see Norwegian skitt (Norwegian “dirt, filth, grime, mud”), from Old Norse skítr (Old Norse “shit”), which is cognate with English shit (English).

From Middle English distance, distaunce (Middle English), destance (Middle English “disagreement, dispute; discrimination; armed conflict; hostility; trouble; space between two points; time interval”), from Anglo-Norman distance, distaunce (Anglo-Norman), destance (Anglo-Norman), Middle French distance, and Old French destance, destaunce (Old French), distaunce (Old French “debate; difference, distinction; discord, quarrel; dispute; space between two points; time interval”) (modern distance (French)), and directly from their etymon Latin distantia (“difference, diversity; distance, remoteness; space between two points”) (whence also distantia (Late Latin “disagreement; discrepancy; gap, opening; time interval”)), from distāns (Latin “being distant; standing apart”) + -ia (Latin). is the present active participle of distō (Latin “to be distant; to stand apart; to differ”), from dis- (Latin) + stō (Latin “to stand”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”)).

The verb is derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The adjective is derived from Middle English divers, diverse (Middle English “different, divergent”), from Anglo-Norman divers, Anglo-Norman divers, and Old French divers (“different; of various kinds”) (modern divers (French)), and directly from their etymon Latin dīversus (“different, diverse”), an adjective use of the perfect passive participle of dīvertō (Latin “to divert, turn away”), from dī- (Latin) (variant of dis- (Latin)) + vertō (Latin “to turn”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to rotate; to turn”)). .

The adverb is derived from Middle English diverse (“differently; at various times”), from divers (Middle English), diverse (Middle English) (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English diversen (“to differ, diverge; to become different, change; to vary; to change or vary (something); to make a distinction, distinguish; to divert”), from Anglo-Norman diverser, Middle French diverser, and Old French diverser (“to alter, change; to differ, diverge; to disagree”), from Late Latin diversare (“to differ”), and then either:

* a frequentative form of Latin dīvertere, the present active infinitive of dīvertō (Latin) (see etymology 1); or
* from dī- (Latin) (variant of dis- (Latin)) + versāre (Latin) (the present active infinitive of versō (Latin “to alter, change; to keep turning, whirl”), a frequentative form of vertō (Latin): see etymology 1).

(“synonym of diversify”) became obsolete in the 16th century, and was probably coinage recoined in the 20th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English don, from Old English don (“dōn”), from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, do, make”).

For senses 4 and 5, compare duga (Old Norse), also Northern dow (English).

The past tense form is from Middle English didde, dude (Middle English), from Old English dyde, *diede (Old English), an unexpected development from Proto-Germanic *dedǭ/*dedē (Proto-Germanic) (the expected reflex would be *ded), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰédʰeh₁ti, an athematic e-reduplicated verb of the same root *dʰeh₁- (Proto-Indo-European).

The meaningless use of do in interrogative, negative, and affirmative sentences (e.g. "Do you like painting?" "Yes, I do"), existing in some form in most Germanic languages, is thought by some linguists to be one of the , calqued from Brythonic. It is first recorded in Middle English, where it may have marked the perfective aspect, though in some cases the meaning seems to be imperfective. In , any meaning in such contexts was lost, making it a dummy auxiliary, and soon thereafter its use became mandatory in most questions and negations.

Doublets include deed (English), deem (English), and -dom (English), but not deal (English).

Other cognates include, via Latin, feast (English), festival (English), fair (English “celebration”), via Greek, theo- (English), theme (English), thesis (English), and दधाति (Sanskrit “to put”), धातृ (Sanskrit “creator”) and धातु (Sanskrit “layer, element, root”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Circa 1845, back-formation from donation (English) on the basis of -ate (English), chiefly found in . Ultimately from Latin dono (“dōnāre”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English donacion, donation (Middle English), from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (Latin “to give”), from dōnum (Latin “a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: The origin is . Originally a slang term from the late eighteenth century. Perhaps from Middle English *donekie (“a miniature dun horse”), a double diminutive of Middle English don, dun (Middle English), dunne (Middle English), equivalent to modern dun (English “brownish grey colour”) + -ock + -ie, or similarly formed from the given name Duncan (English). Compare donning (Middle English “a dun horse”), dunnock (English). Became more common than the original term ass (English) due to the latter's homophony and partial merger with arse (English) (compare similar development between coney (English) and rabbit (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle French dose, from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (“a portion prescribed”), used by and other Greek physicians to mean an amount of medicine, from δίδωμι (Ancient Greek “to give”). Mostly displaced drench (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English *dot, dotte (Middle English), from Old English dott (“a dot, point”), from Proto-West Germanic *dott, from Proto-Germanic *duttaz (“wisp”). Cognate with Dot (Saterland Frisian), Dotte (Saterland Frisian “a clump”), dot (Dutch “lump, knot, clod”), Dutte (Low German “a plug”), dialectal dott (Swedish “a little heap, bunch, clump”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From French dot.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English double, from Old French doble, double (Old French), from Latin duplus (“twofold”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Middle English douten (“to doubt, fear, worry”), from Old French douter, doter (Old French), duter (Old French) (compare doubter (Middle French)), from Latin dubitō (“to be uncertain, doubt; to hesitate, waver in coming to an opinion; to consider, ponder”); the further etymology is uncertain, but one theory is that dubitō may be derived from dubius (Latin “fluctuating, wavering; doubtful, dubious, uncertain”), from duhibius (Latin “held as two”), from duo (Latin “two”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”)) + habeō (Latin “to have, hold”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab, take”)). Spelling reformers of the early modern period added the letter b (English) to reflect the Latin root dubitō, but it has never been pronounced in English.

The noun is derived from Middle English dout, doute (Middle English “uncertainty, hesitation; questionable point; anxiety, fear, reverence”),
from Old French doute, dote (Old French), dute (Old French “uncertain feeling, doubt”), from doter (Old French), douter (Old French), duter (Old French “to doubt, fear”) (compare doubter (Middle French); modern douter (French “to doubt, suspect”)); see further etymology above.

The "question" sense is a from Romance cognates: dúvida (Portuguese), duda (Spanish), dubte (Catalan), doute (French), dubbio (Italian) and others, which can all mean "question".

Displaced twēo (Old English “doubt”) and twēoġan (Old English “to doubt”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English doutfull, douteful (Middle English), equivalent to doubt + ful (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English doun, doune (Middle English “down”), from Old English dūne (“down”), aphetic form of adūne (Old English “down, downward”), from earlier ofdūne (Old English “down”), from of (Old English “of, off of”) + dūn (Old English “hill, mount, dune, down”). More at Etymology 2 below. For the development from directional phrases to prepositions, compare dene (Old Frisian “down”), dāle (Middle Low German “down, downwards”), whence dal (Low German (Germany) “down”). Compare also deel (Saterland Frisian “down”), del (Western Frisian “down”). Cognate with doon (Scots “down”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English doune, from Old English dūn, from Proto-West Germanic *dūnā (“sandhill, dune”), of . Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz, *dūnǭ (Proto-Germanic “pile, heap”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze, dust”).

Alternatively, perhaps borrowed from Proto-Celtic *dūnom (“hill; hillfort”) (compare din (Welsh “city, fort, stronghold”), dún (Irish “hill, fort”)), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to finish, come full circle”).

Cognate with dún (Western Frisian “dune, sandhill”), duin (Dutch “dune, sandhill”), Düne (German “dune”). More at town (English); akin to dune (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English doun, from Old Norse dúnn, from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz (“down”), which is related to *dauniz (Proto-Germanic “(pleasant) smell”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from the root *dʰewh₂- (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with Duune (Saterland Frisian “fluff, down”), Daune (German “down”) and dun (Danish “down”).

etymologies.text: Affix: down- + stair + -s

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English dozen, dozein (Middle English), doseyne (Middle English), from Old French dozaine (“a group of twelve”) (Modern French douzaine (French)), from doze (Old French “twelve”) + -aine (Old French “-ish”), from Latin duodecim (“twelve”) (from duo (Latin “two”) + decem (Latin “ten”)) + -ana (Latin “-ish”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From a deliberate misspelling of doesn't, originally referring to someone who "dozen sing, dozen rap, dozen do anything."

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: A phonetic spelling of draught (English) (compare laughter (English)), from Middle English draught, draght (Middle English “that which is pulled; that which is drawn up, a design”), from Old English *dreaht, *dræht (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *drahti, *drahtu (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz (“a pulling, drawing”). Cognate with dracht (Dutch), Tracht (German), dráttur (Icelandic). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English draggen (“to drag”), early Middle English dragen (“to draw, carry”), confluence of Old English dragan (“to drag, draw, draw oneself, go, protract”) and Old Norse draga (“to draw, attract”); both from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to draw, drag”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to draw, drag”).

Verb sense influenced due to association with the noun drag (English “that which is hauled or dragged”), related to dragge (Low German “a drag-anchor, grapnel”). Cognate with drægge (Danish “to dredge”), drage (Danish “to draw, attract”), dragga (Swedish “to drag, drag anchor, sweep”), draga (Swedish “to draw, go”), draga (Icelandic “to drag, pull”). .

chain.meaning: to drag, draw, draw oneself, go, protract

etymologies.text:
Possibly from drag (English “to pull along a surface”) because of the sensation of long skirts trailing on the floor, or from Yiddish טראָגן (“to wear”)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Middle English dragen, draghen (Middle English), draue (Middle English), drauen (Middle English), drauhen (Middle English), drawe (Middle English), drawen (Middle English), draȝe (Middle English), draȝen (Middle English), draȝhenn (Middle English “to drag, pull; to draw (out); to attract; to entice, lure; to lead; to make a drawing; to move, travel; etc.”), from Old English dragan (“to drag, draw”), from Proto-West Germanic *dragan (“to carry, haul”), from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to carry, draw, pull”); further etymology uncertain, often said to be from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to drag, pull, run”), but possibly from a non-Indo-European substrate root which is also the source of trahō (Latin “to pull, draw; etc.”). .

The noun is derived from Middle English drau, draue (Middle English “action of shooting with a bow”), from drauen (Middle English), drawen (Middle English).

Cognate with drai (North Frisian), dreeg (North Frisian), dreege (North Frisian “to carry; to wear”), drage (Western Frisian “to carry”), draan (Central Franconian), drage (Central Franconian), droon (Central Franconian “to bear, carry”), dragen (Dutch “to carry; to wear; to transfer”), tragen (German “to bear, carry; to wear; to support”), dregen (Low German “to carry, take”), droen (lb “to carry; to hold, support; to wear; to travel; to fruit”), טראָגן (Yiddish “to carry, to wear; to be pregnant”), draege (zea), draoge (zea “to carry”), drage (Danish “to draw”), drågå (Elfdalian “to drag, draw, pull”), draga (Faroese / Icelandic “to drag, draw, pull”), dräga (gmq-gut “to pull”), dra (Norwegian Bokmål), drage (Norwegian Bokmål “to drag, draw, pull”), dra (Norwegian Nynorsk), draga (Norwegian Nynorsk), drage (Norwegian Nynorsk), drågå (Norwegian Nynorsk), dråggå (Norwegian Nynorsk “to drag, pull; to leave”), dra (Swedish), draga (Swedish “to draw, pull; to consume; to leave; to run; to steep”), 𐌳𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to carry, draw, pull”); also droch (Old Irish “wheel; circlet”), tragō (Latin), trahō (Latin “to drag, pull; to trail; to extract; to plunder; to draw out; to protract; to consider, ponder, weigh”), τρέχω (Greek (Modern) “to run; to flee; to flow; to execute”), дро́га (Russian “rail or perch in a cart”), դուրգ (Armenian “to potter’s wheel”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English dredful, dredfull (Middle English), dredeful (Middle English) (also dreful (Middle English)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dream, dreem (Middle English), dreeme (Middle English), drem (Middle English), dreme (Middle English), dræm (Middle English), from Old English drēam, drēm (Old English), drīm (Old English “joy; melody, music; frenzy”), from Proto-West Germanic *draum, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz (“dream”), from earlier , from Proto-Indo-European —, from *dʰrewgʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to deceive”).

The sense of "dream", though not attested in Old English, may still have been present (compare drōm (Old Saxon “bustle, revelry, jubilation", also "dream”)), and was undoubtedly reinforced later in Middle English by draumr (Old Norse “dream”), from same Proto-Germanic root.

Cognate with dreme (Scots “dream”), Droom (Saterland Frisian “dream”), dream (Western Frisian “dream”), droom (Dutch “dream”), Traum (German “dream”), Droum (Limburgish “dream”), Dram (lb “dream”), טרוים (Yiddish “dream”), drøm (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “dream”), dreymur (Faroese “dream”), draumur (Icelandic “dream”), draum (Norwegian Nynorsk), drøm (Norwegian Nynorsk “dream”), dröm (Swedish “dream”); also drouk (Breton “bad; evil”), drog (Cornish “bad; evil; invalid; nasty; wicked; wrong”), droch- (Irish “bad; ill-”), drogh (Manx “bad; evil”), droch (Scottish Gaelic “bad”), drwg (Welsh “bad; naughty”), 𐬛𐬭𐬎𐬲𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (ae “to deceive, mislead”), λρωγο (xbc “lie; falsehood”), دروگ (bal “lie; falsehood”), درۆ (Central Kurdish “lie”), derew (Kurmanji Kurdish “lie”), دروغ (Pashto “lie; falsehood”), دُروغ (Persian “lie; falsehood”), द्रुह्यति (Sanskrit “to hurt; to bear malice or hatred; to be a foe or rival”).

The verb is from Middle English dreamen, dreme (Middle English), dremen (Middle English), dreomen (Middle English), possibly (see below) from Old English drēman, drīeman (Old English), drȳman (Old English “to rejoice; to play an instrument joyously; to sing a song joyfully”), from Proto-West Germanic *draumijan, from Proto-Germanic *draumijaną (“to be dream”), from the noun.

Cognate with drem (North Frisian), driime (North Frisian “to dream”), drööme (Saterland Frisian “to dream”), dreame (Western Frisian), dreamje (Western Frisian “to dream”), dramma (Bavarian), trama (Bavarian “to dream”), drööme (Central Franconian “to dream”), intruamen (Cimbric “to dream”), dromen (Dutch “to dream”), träumen (German “to dream”), draimen (Low German “to dream”), dreemen (lb “to dream”), טרוימען (Yiddish “to dream”), drømme (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to dream”), droyma (Faroese “to dream”), dreyma (Icelandic “to dream”), drømma (Norwegian Nynorsk), drømme (cog), drøyma (Norwegian Nynorsk), drøyme (Norwegian Nynorsk “to dream”), drömma (Swedish “to dream, muse”).

The derivation from Old English drēam is controversial, since the word itself is only attested in writing in its meaning of “joy, mirth, musical sound”. Possibly there was a separate word drēam meaning “images seen while sleeping”, which was avoided in literature due to potential confusion with the “joy” sense. Otherwise, the modern sense must have been borrowed from another Germanic language, most probably Old Norse. Since this is the common sense in all Germanic languages outside the British isles, a spontaneous development from “joy, mirth” to “dream” in Middle English is hardly conceivable. In - (Old Saxon), the cognate drōm (Old Saxon) did mean “dream”, but was a rare word.

Attested words for “sleeping vision” in Old English, both of which appeared in The Dream of the Rood, were mǣting (Old English) (Middle English mæte (Middle English), mete (Middle English)), from an unclear source, and swefn (Old English) (Modern sweven (English)), from *swefnaz (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *swepno- (Proto-Indo-European), *swep- (Proto-Indo-European); compare ὕπνος (Ancient Greek “sleep”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is from Middle English dressen, dresse (Middle English “to arrange, put in order”), from Anglo-Norman —, Old French dresser, drecier (Old French) (modern dresser (French)), from Late Latin *dīrēctiāre (“to guide, direct”), from Classical Latin dīrēctus, whence direct (English). Further akin to regō (Latin).

The noun is derived from the verb.

Compare typologically adorn (English) (<< ōrnō (Latin) < ōrdō (Latin), whence also ōrdinō (Latin), order (English), ornament (English)); наряжа́ть (Russian), наря́д (Russian) (akin to ряд (Russian), поря́док (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dryven, from Old English drīfan (“to drive, force, move”), from Proto-West Germanic *drīban, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”).

Cognate with drive (Scots “to drive”), dhreeve (Yola), dhrive (Yola), dreeve (Yola), drieve (Yola), drive (Yola “to drive”), driiv (North Frisian), driiw (North Frisian), driwe (North Frisian “to drive”), driuwe (Western Frisian “to drive; to float”), triibe (Alemannic “to drive”), drijven (Dutch “to drive, push”), treiben (German “to drive, push, propel”), drieven (Low German “to drive, drift, push”), dreiwen (lb “to drive, propel”), טרײַבן (Yiddish “to drive”), - (Danish), drive (Norwegian Bokmål “to drive, propel”), drífa (Icelandic “to drive”), driva (Norwegian Nynorsk), drive (Norwegian Nynorsk “to drive, move; to propel; to run”), driva (Swedish “to drive, compel; to drift; to run”), 𐌳𐍂𐌴𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to drive”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Late Middle English droppe, Middle English drope (“small quantity of liquid; small or least amount of something; pendant jewel; dripping of a liquid; a shower; nasal flow, catarrh; speck, spot; blemish; disease causing spots on the skin”), from Old English dropa (“a drop”), from Proto-West Germanic *dropō (“drop (of liquid)”), from Proto-Germanic *drupô (“drop (of liquid)”),, from *dreupaną (Proto-Germanic “to drip, droop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ- (“to drip, drop”).

Cognate with Droupe (Saterland Frisian), Druppe (Saterland Frisian “drop”), drop (Dutch), drup (Dutch “droplet”), Tropfen (German “drop”), Drüpp (Low German (Germany) “drop”), Drëps (lb “drop”), tropa (Ripuarian), troppa (Ripuarian “drop”), טראָפּן (Yiddish “drop”), dråbe (Danish “drop”), dropi (Faroese / Icelandic “drop”), dråpe (Norwegian Bokmål “drop”), drope (Norwegian Nynorsk “drop”), droppe (Swedish “drop”).

chain.meaning: small quantity of liquid; small or least amount of something; pendant jewel; dripping of a liquid; a shower; nasal flow, catarrh; speck, spot; blemish; disease causing spots on the skin

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English droppen, dropen (Middle English “to fall in drops, drip or trickle down; to scatter, sprinkle; to be covered with a liquid; to give off moisture; of an object: to drop, fall; of a living being: to fall to the ground”), from Old English droppian, dropian (Old English “to drop”), from Proto-West Germanic *dropōn, from Proto-Germanic *drupōną (“to fall in drops, drip”), ultimately from *dreupaną (Proto-Germanic “to hang, droop; drop, drip”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrebʰ- (“to drip, drop”).

Cognate with drippe (Western Frisian “to drip”), druipen (Dutch “to drip”), triefen (German “to drip”), טריפֿן (Yiddish “to drip”), drjúpa (Icelandic “to drip”), drjupa (Norwegian Nynorsk), drypa (Norwegian Nynorsk), drype (Norwegian Nynorsk “to drip”), drypa (Swedish “to drip”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English drownen, drounen (Middle English), drunen (Middle English “to drown”), of obscure and origin.

The OED suggests an unattested Old English form *drūnian (Old English). Harper 2001 points to Old English druncnian (Old English), ġedruncnian (Old English) (> drunknen (Middle English), dronknen (Middle English “to drown”)), "probably influenced" by drukkna (Old Norse) (cf. drukkna (Icelandic), drukne (Danish “to drown”)). Funk & Wagnall's has 'of uncertain origin'. It has been theorised (see e.g. ODS) that it may represent a direct loan of drukkna (Old Norse), but this is described by the OED as being "on phonetic and other grounds [...] highly improbable", unless one considers the possibility of an unattested variant in *drunkna (Old Norse).
etymologies.uncertainNote: Funk & Wagnall's has 'of uncertain origin'.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English drogge (“medicine”), from Middle French drogue, drocque (Middle French “tincture, pharmaceutical product”) (), from Middle Dutch — or Middle Low German droge, as in droge (Middle Dutch) vate (Middle Dutch “dry vats, dry barrels”), mistaking droge (Middle Dutch) for the contents, which were usually dried herbs, plants or wares. Droge comes from Middle Dutch droghe (“dry”), from Old Dutch drōgi (“dry”), from Proto-Germanic *draugiz (“dry, hard”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- (“to strengthen; become hard or solid”), from *dʰer- (Proto-Indo-European “to hold, hold fast, support”). Displaced native lybb (Old English “drug, medicine”). Cognate with dry (English), droog (Dutch “dry”), trocken (German “dry”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Germanic ablaut formation. If old, a doublet of drew (English), from Middle English drug, drog (Middle English), drugh (Middle English), drogh (Middle English), from Old English dragan (“drōg”), from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“*drōg”); compare droeg (Dutch), trug (German), drog (Swedish). If secondary, probably formed by analogy with dug (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English drunke, drunken (Middle English), ydrunke (Middle English), ydrunken (Middle English), from Old English druncen, ġedruncen (Old English “drunk”), from Proto-Germanic *drunkanaz, *gadrunkanaz (Proto-Germanic “drunk; drunken”), past participle of Proto-Germanic *drinkaną (“to drink”). Cognate with dronken (Saterland Frisian), dronken (Western Frisian), dronken (Dutch), gedronken (Dutch), drunken (Low German (Germany)), bedrunken (Low German (Germany)), trunken (German),
getrunken (German), betrunken (German), drucken (Swedish), drukkinn (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English dewe, dew (Middle English), due (Middle English), from Old French deu (“deü”), past participle of devoir (Old French “to owe”), from Latin dēbeō (“to owe”), from dē + habeō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dull, dul (Middle English) (also dyll (Middle English), dill (Middle English), dwal (Middle English)), from Old English dol (“dull, foolish, erring, heretical; foolish, silly; presumptuous”), from Proto-West Germanic *dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz, from earlier *dwulaz (Proto-Germanic), a variant of *dwalaz (Proto-Germanic “stunned, mad, foolish, misled”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwel-, *dʰewel- (Proto-Indo-European “to dim, dull, cloud, make obscure, swirl, whirl”).

Cognate with dull (Scots), doll (Scots “slow to understand or hear, deaf, dull”), dol (North Frisian “rash, unthinking, giddy, flippant”), dol (Dutch “crazy, mad, insane”), dul (Low German), dol (Low German “mad, silly, stupid, fatuous”), toll (German “crazy, mad, wild, fantastic”), dval (Danish “foolish, absurd”), dulur (Icelandic “secretive, silent”), West-Flemish dul (angry, furious).

chain.meaning: dull, foolish, erring, heretical; foolish, silly; presumptuous

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Probably from Irish dul, dol (Irish “loop, noose, snare”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English dust, doust (Middle English), from Old English dūst (“dust, dried earth reduced to powder; other dry material reduced to powder”), from the fusion of Proto-Germanic *dustą (“dust”) and *dunstą (Proto-Germanic “mist, dust, evaporation”), both from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust”).

Cognate with dust (Scots), dist (Scots “dust”), duist (Dutch “pollen, dust”) and dons (Dutch “down, fuzz”), Dust (German “dust”) and Dunst (German “haze”), dust (Swedish “dust”), dust (Icelandic “dust”), fūmus (Latin “smoke, steam”). Also related to dun (Swedish “down, fluff”), dúnn (Icelandic “down, fluff”). See down (English).

chain.meaning: dust, dried earth reduced to powder; other dry material reduced to powder

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From dust + bin (English), as used for disposing of dust (originally ash from domestic fires) and other rubbish.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English dusty, dusti (Middle English), from Old English dūstiġ, dystiġ (Old English), dȳstiġ (Old English “dusty”), equivalent to . Cognate with donzig (Dutch “cottony, downy, woolly”), dunstig (German “hazy, misty”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English duete, from Middle English dewe + Middle English -te. Equivalent to due (English) + -ty (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: duty + -free

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From French duvet, from Middle French duvet, from Old French duvet (“down, the feathers of young birds”), alteration of dumet (Old French), dumect (Old French), which in turn derives from dum (Old French), dun (Old French “down, feathers”), from Old Norse dúnn (“down, down feather”), from Proto-Germanic *dūnaz (“down”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, fume, raise dust”).

Cognate with dúnn (Icelandic “down”), dun (Danish “down”), Daune (German “down”), dons (Dutch “down”). More at down (English).

chain.meaning: down, the feathers of young birds

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French dynamique, from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (“powerful”), from δύναμις (Ancient Greek “power”), from δύναμαι (Ancient Greek “I am able”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English egre, eger (Middle English), from Old French aigre, egre (Old French) (modern aigre (French)), from Latin ācrus, variant of ācer (Latin “sharp, keen”); see acid (English), acerb (English), etc. Compare vinegar (English), alegar (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English erthe, from Old English eorþe, from Proto-West Germanic *erþu, from Proto-Germanic *erþō (“dirt, ground, earth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er- (“*h₁érteh₂”).

Cognate with erd (Scots), yerd (Scots), yird (Scots), yirth (Scots “earth, loam, mould, soil; ground”), eard (Yola), eart (Yola), eord (Yola), eorth (Yola), erth (Yola “earth”), eerd (North Frisian), eerde (North Frisian), iarde (North Frisian), Iart (North Frisian), iir (North Frisian), jard (North Frisian), örd (North Frisian), Öört (North Frisian “earth; world”), Idde (Saterland Frisian), Äid (Saterland Frisian), Äide (Saterland Frisian “earth; soil; ground”), ierde (Western Frisian “earth; soil; ground”), Ëërde (Alemannic “earth”), Erd (Bavarian), Erdn (Bavarian “world; soil; ground”), Ääd (Central Franconian “earth”), èerda (Cimbric “earth”), aard (Dutch), aarde (Dutch “earth”), Erde (German “earth; soil; ground; world”), Eer (Low German (Germany) “earth”), eerd (Limburgish “earth”), Äerd (lb “earth; soil”), Ād (Ripuarian “earth”), ערד (Yiddish “earth; soil”), jord (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “earth”), jørð (Faroese “earth”), jörð (Icelandic “earth”), yurn (Norn “the earth”), 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌸𐌰 (Gothic “earth”); also ōra (Latin “border, edge, rim”), erv (Breton “ridge between furrows”), erw (Welsh “acre”), ἔραζε (Ancient Greek “to the ground”), erdvė (Lithuanian “expanse, space”), varr (Albanian), vorr (Albanian “grave”), āre (txb “dust, loose earth”), उर्वरा (Sanskrit “fertile soil, field yielding crops”), 𒅕𒄩𒀸 (Hittite “border, boundary, line”).

Probably unrelated, but of unknown etymology, is երկիր (Classical Armenian “earth”). Likewise, the phonologically similar *ʔarṣ́- (sem-pro) – whence أَرْض (Arabic), אֶרֶץ (Hebrew) – is probably unrelated.

etymologies.text: From Middle English erthequake, corresponding to earth + quake (English). Displaced eorð byfung (Middle English “earthquake”) from eorþbeofung (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ese, eise (Middle English), aise (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (Old French “elbow room; opportunity”), of and obscure origin. Apparently related to Provençal ais (Occitan), agio (Italian) and asio (Italian), aciu (Sicilian) and azo (Portuguese). Sometimes ascribed to Vulgar Latin — or , possibly from Latin ānsa (“handle, haft”) or Frankish *ansiju (“handle, loophole, eyelet; cup-handle; arms akimbo, elbow room”), but more often derived from Vulgar Latin —, from Latin adiacēns (“adjacent, neighbouring”), present participle of adiaceō (Latin “lie next to, border on”), though the forms and senses are difficult to trace clearly.

Alternatively, possibly from a non-Latin source such as gem — or cel — on the basis of the conflicting forms which appear in various Romance languages. Compare īeþe (Old English “easy”), 𐌰𐌶𐌴𐍄𐌹 (Gothic “ease; pleasure”), *𐌰𐌶𐌴𐍄𐍃 (Gothic “easy”), eaz (Breton), ez (Breton “easy”), adhais (Irish “easy; leisure”). See also eath (English).

The verb is from Middle English esen, ultimately of the same origin.
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English ese, eise (Middle English), aise (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman ese (“ease”), from Old French eise, aise (Old French “elbow room; opportunity”), of and obscure origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The is derived from Middle English economike, iconomique (Middle English “household management”), and then:

* from Middle French iconomique, oeconomique (Middle French), and Old French iconomike (“(noun) household management; person in charge of household management; (adjective) relating to household management; relating to domestic or family matters; relating to management of a state; reducing costs or expenses, economical”) (modern économique (French)); and
* from their Latin oeconomicus (“(noun) household manager, housekeeper, steward; (adjective) relating to orderly arrangement of written material”) (whence economicus (Late Latin “relating to (management of) a household”)), and economica (Latin “household management”), both from Ancient Greek οἰκονομῐκός (“skilled in household management; frugal, thrifty, economical”) (whence οἰκονομῐκός (Koine Greek “relating to orderly arrangement of written material”));

from οἰκονόμος (Ancient Greek “master of a house; household manager, steward; administrator, manager”) + -ῐκός (Ancient Greek). is derived from οἶκος (Ancient Greek “dwelling place, house; estate”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyḱ- (“(verb) to enter in; to settle; (noun) settlement”)) + νόμος (Ancient Greek “law, ordinance”) (from νέμω (Ancient Greek “to distribute; to possess”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute; to give; to take”)) + -ος (Ancient Greek)).

(“one who manages the income of a vacant benefice”) is from Italian economo, from Late Latin oeconomus (“housekeeper, steward; administrator, especially of a religious foundation”), from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (“master of a house; household manager, steward; administrator, manager”): see above.

The is derived from the noun; compare the adjective senses in Middle and Old French, Latin, and Ancient Greek.

.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English yconomye, yconomy (Middle English), borrowed via Old French yconomie or Medieval Latin from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (“management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (Ancient Greek “house”) + νέμω (Ancient Greek “distribute, allocate”). . The first recorded sense of the word economy, found in a work possibly composed in 1440, is “the management of economic affairs”, in this case, of a monastery.

etymologies.label: Etymology

Displaced Old English fremming, fremednes (Old English) from fremman (Old English).

Of the verb: from Middle English effecten, partly from Medieval Latin effectuō, from Latin effectus, perfect passive participle of efficiō (Latin “accomplish, complete, do, effect”), from ex (Latin “out”) + faciō (Latin “do, make”) (see fact (English) and compare affect (English), infect (English)) and partly from the noun effect.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English eg, egg (Middle English), egge (Middle English “egg of a domestic or wild fowl; egg of a snake”) (originally Northern England and Northeast Midlands), from Old Norse egg (“egg”), from Proto-Germanic *ajją (“egg”) (by Holtzmann’s law), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (“egg”), probably from *h₂éwis (Proto-Indo-European “bird”), from *h₂ew- (Proto-Indo-European “to consume”). .

Cognate with ai (North Frisian “egg”), Oai (Saterland Frisian “egg”), aai (Western Frisian), aei (Western Frisian “egg”), Oa (Bavarian “egg”), ei (Dutch “egg”), Ei (German “egg”), Ai (Low German (Germany)), Ägg (Low German (Germany) “egg”), ei (Limburgish), Éï (Limburgish “egg”), Ee (lb “egg”), oi (mhn “egg”), e (Ripuarian “egg”), איי (Yiddish “egg”), æg (Danish “egg”), egg (Faroese / Icelandic / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “egg”), ägg (Swedish “egg”), ada (gme-cgo “egg”); also vi (Breton “egg”), oy (Cornish “egg”), wy (Welsh “egg”), ōvum (Latin “egg”), αβγό (Greek (Modern)), αυγό (Greek (Modern) “egg”), vo (Albanian “egg”), яйцо́ (Belarusian / Russian “egg”), яйце́ (Bulgarian “egg”), vejce (Czech “egg”), јајце (Macedonian “egg”), jajo (Polish “egg”), ја́јце (Serbo-Croatian), jájce (Serbo-Croatian “egg”), vajce (Slovak “egg”), jájce (Slovenian “egg”), яйце́ (Ukrainian “egg”), айк (Ossetic), айкӕ (Ossetic “egg”), ձու (Armenian “egg”), hêk (Kurmanji Kurdish “egg”), خا (sdh “egg”), hak (zza “egg”), هګۍ (Pashto), ويه (Pashto “egg”), خاگ (Persian), خایه (Persian “egg”).

The native ey (English) (plural eyren (English)) (obsolete), from ǣġ (Old English), is also derived from *ajją (Proto-Germanic). It survived into at least before being fully displaced by egg.

The verb is derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

From Middle English eggen (“to urge on; to entice, incite, lure, tempt; to encourage, exhort, stimulate; (reflexive) to bestir (oneself); to challenge, taunt; to enrage, irritate”), from Old English ġeeġġian (“to egg, excite”), from Old Norse eggja (“to incite, egg on”), from egg (Old Norse “an edge”), from Proto-Germanic *agjō (“a corner; an edge”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).

* ægge (Danish), egge (Danish “to incite, egg on; to excite, rouse”)
* egga (Swedish “to excite, egg on”)
* eggja (Faroese “to incite, egg on; to sharpen”)
* eggja (Icelandic “to incite, egg on”)
* eggia (Old Frisian “to fence”)
* eggen (Middle Low German “to sharpen”)
* ungiekkōt (Old High German “unworked, unformed”)
* ecken (Middle High German “to sharpen”), ecken (German)

Compare typologically another cognate: поощря́ть (Russian), akin to о́стрый (Russian), ultimately from the same PIE root.

Also compare typologically noncognate: потиквам (Bulgarian), nabádat (Czech “urge, exhort”), подстрека́ть (Russian).

Cognate to eclectic (English), which is via - (Ancient Greek) rather than - (Latin), hence prefix ἐκ (Ancient Greek), rather than e- (Latin) (from ex (Latin)).
