etymologies.text:
From Middle English ende, from Old English ende, from Proto-West Germanic *andī, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz (“end”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos (“forehead; front”), from *h₂ent- (Proto-Indo-European “face; forehead; front”), from *h₂en- (Proto-Indo-European “on, onto”).

Cognate with een (Yola), eene (Yola “end”), Eend (Saterland Frisian), Eende (Saterland Frisian “end”), ein (Western Frisian “end”), End (Alemannic), Endi (Alemannic “end”), Eng (Central Franconian), Enk (Central Franconian “end”), énte (Cimbric “end”), eind (Dutch), einde (Dutch), end (Dutch “end”), Ende (German “end”), Enn (lb “end”), end (Ripuarian), ent (Ripuarian “end”), ende (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “end”), endi (Faroese “end”), endi (Icelandic), endir (Icelandic “end”), ända (Swedish), ände (Swedish “end”), 𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌴𐌹𐍃 (Gothic “end”); also éadan (Irish “end; front”), eddin (Manx “face; front”), aodann (Scottish Gaelic “face; hillside”), antiae (Latin “forelock”), ἀντίος (Ancient Greek “opposite”), anë (Albanian “brink; edge; facet; side”), no (Latvian “for; from”), nuo (Lithuanian “for; from”), на (Belarusian / Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian / Ukrainian “on”), na (Czech / Kashubian / Lower Sorbian / Polish / Slovak / Slovenian “on”), на (Serbo-Croatian), na (Serbo-Croatian “on”), ընդ (Classical Armenian “in the place, instead of”), 𐎠𐎲𐎡𐎹 (peo “against; towards; upon”), ānt (xto “in front”), ānte (txb “in front of”), अन्त (Sanskrit “boundary; border, edge; end, termination”). More at and (English) and anti- (English).

The verb is from Middle English enden, endien (Middle English), from Old English endian (“to end, to make an end of, complete, finish, abolish, destroy, come to an end, die”), from Proto-Germanic *andijōną (“to finish, end”), denominative from *andijaz (Proto-Germanic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English endynge, endyng (Middle English), endinge (Middle English), from Old English endung, ġeendung (Old English “ending”), equivalent to end + -ing (English). Cognate with ending (Dutch “ending”), Endung (German “ending”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ending, endyng (Middle English), endende (Middle English), from Old English endiende, from Proto-Germanic *andijōndz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *andijōną (“to end”), equivalent to end + -ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English endeles, from Old English endelēas (“endless”), from Proto-Germanic *andijalausaz (“endless”), equivalent to end + less (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English enduren, from Old French endurer, from Latin indūrō (“to make hard”). Displaced Old English drēogan (Old English), which survives dialectally as dree (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English enemy, enemye (Middle English), enmy (Middle English), borrowed from Old French enemi, anemi (Old French) (Modern ennemi (French)), from Latin inimīcus, from in- (Latin “not”) + amīcus (Latin “friend”). Displaced fend (Middle English “enemy”), from fēond (Old English “enemy”), which survived into Modern - (English) as fiend (English), but with a different meaning. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From New Latin energeticus (16th c.), or its source, Ancient Greek ἐνεργητικός, from ἐνεργέω (Ancient Greek “to be active”), from ἐνεργός (Ancient Greek “active”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Possibly from a clipping of .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French énergie, from Late Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (“activity”), from ἐνεργός (Ancient Greek “active”), from ἐν (Ancient Greek “in”) + ἔργον (Ancient Greek “work”). The sense in physics was in his lectures on Natural Philosophy.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: engineer + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: enjoy + -able

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From enjoy + ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin ēnormis. An assimilated form of ex- + norma (Latin “rule, norm”) + -ous.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ynogh, from Old English ġenōg (“enough”), from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz (“enough”) (compare eneuch (Scots), genôch (Western Frisian), genoeg (Dutch), genug (German), (ge)noog (Low German), nok (Danish), nog (Swedish), nógur (Icelandic)), from *ganuganą (Proto-Germanic) 'to suffice' (compare ġeneah (Old English)), or from *ga- (Proto-Germanic) + an unattested *nōgaz, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂nó(n)ḱe (“he has reached, attained”), perfective of *h₂neḱ- (Proto-Indo-European “to reach”) (compare tánaic (Old Irish “he arrived”), nancisci (Latin “to get”), kënaq (Albanian “to please, satisfy”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French enquerre, from en- (Old French) + querre (Old French “to search, to look for”), from Latin quaero (“quaerere”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Old French enquerre, from en- (Old French) + querre (Old French “to search, to look for”), from Latin quaero (“quaerere”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English enquery, from the Old French — verb enquerre (Old French), from Latin inquīrō, composed of in- (Latin “in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (Latin “to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). The alternative form inquiry (English) was subsequently respelled to conform to the original Latin spelling, as opposed to the Old French spelling.
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English enquery, from the Old French — verb enquerre (Old French), from Latin inquīrō, composed of in- (Latin “in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (Latin “to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ensuren, from Anglo-Norman enseurer, from Old French seur (“sure”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English entren, from Old French entrer, from Latin intrō (“enter”), from intrā (Latin “inside”). Has been spelled as "enter" for several centuries even in the United Kingdom, although British English and the English of many Commonwealth Countries (e.g. Australia, Canada) retain the "re" ending for many words such as centre, fibre, spectre, theatre, calibre, sombre, lustre, and litre.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English entertenen, from Middle French entretenir, from Old French entretenir, from entre (Old French “among”) + tenir (Old French “to hold”), from Latin inter + teneō (Latin “hold, keep”). For the noun, compare entretien (French).

Sense of answering a phone call in is influenced by layan (Malay) “to serve, to attend to or engage with something”.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: entertain + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: entertain + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English entretenement (“support, maintenance”), from Old French entretenement; see entertain (English). Morphologically entertain + -ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested from , from Middle French enthousiasme, from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός, from ἐν (Ancient Greek “in”) + θεός (Ancient Greek “god”) + οὐσία (Ancient Greek “essence”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιαστικός, from either ἐνθουσιασμός (Ancient Greek) or ἐνθουσιάζω (Ancient Greek) + -τικός (Ancient Greek).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: enthusiastic + -ally

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English entere, enter (Middle English), borrowed from Anglo-Norman entier, from Latin integrum, accusative of integer (Latin “whole”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English entyerly, entierly (Middle English), enterely (Middle English), entyreliche (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Anglo-Norman entitler, from Old French entiteler, (intituler (French)), from Late Latin intitulāre.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From . Replaced native ingang (Middle English “entrance, admission”), from ingang (Old English “ingress, entry, entrance”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From en- (English) + trance (English “daze”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English entre, from Old French entree (feminine past participle of the verb entrer (Old French), Modern entrée (French)). From Latin intrō. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French environnement. Compare environnement (French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: environment + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: environmental + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English envie, from Old French envie, from Latin invidia (“envy”), from invidere (Latin “to look at with malice”), from in- (Latin “on, upon”) + videre (Latin “to look, see”). . Cognate to *zavistь (Proto-Slavic “envy”).

Displaced native æfest (Old English) and nīþ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French épisode, from New Latin *epīsodium, from Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (“a parenthetic addition, episode”), neuter of ἐπεισόδιος (Ancient Greek “following upon the entrance, coming in besides, adventitious”), from ἐπί (Ancient Greek “on”) + εἰς (Ancient Greek “into”) + ὁδός (Ancient Greek “way”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English equal, from Latin aequālis. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French equalité (modern French égalité (French)), from Latin aequalitas (“aequālitās, aequālitātem”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: equal + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From French équiper (“to supply, fit out”), originally said of a ship, Old French esquiper (“to embark”); of gem — origin, most probably from Old Norse skipa (“to man (a ship)”), from Proto-Germanic *skipōną (“to ship, sail, embark”).

Compare with schipfen (Middle High German), schiffern (German), skipa (Icelandic), scipian (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From equip + -ment (English), or from French équipement.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Late Latin aera

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English errour, from Anglo-Norman errour, borrowed from Old French error, from Latin error (“wandering about”), derived from the verb errō (Latin “to wander, to err”). Cognate with 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌶𐌴𐌹 (Gothic “error”), 𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌶𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to lead astray”). More at err (English). . Displaced native dwild (Old English “error”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: By genericization from the former trademark Escalator, created by American inventor in 1900, from Latin ex- (“from, out of”) + scala (Latin “ladder”) + -tor (Latin), which forms nouns of agency; see the appendix. Broader usage may be influenced by its derivative escalate (English), . For an alternative etymology, see the Online Etymology Dictionary.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English escapen, from Anglo-Norman — and Old Northern French escaper ( = Old French eschaper (Old French), modern French échapper (French)), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape a garment, get out of one's clothing”), from Latin ex- (“out”) + Late Latin cappa (“cape, cloak”). Cognate with escapade (English). Also .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: especial + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Since late 16th century, borrowed from Middle French essay, essai (Middle French “essay”), meaning coined by Montaigne at the same time, from the same words with the earlier meanings 'experiment; assay; attempt', from Old French essay, essai (Old French), assay (Old French), assai (Old French), from Latin exagium (“weight; weighing, testing on the balance”), from exigo (Latin “exigere”) + -ium (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle French essayer, essaier (Middle French), from Old French essaiier, essayer (Old French), essaier (Old French), assaiier (Old French), assayer (Old French), assaier (Old French), from essay (Old French), essai (Old French), assay (Old French), assai (Old French “attempt; assay; experiment”) as above.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Latin essentiālis, from Latin essentia (“being, essence”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: essential + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English establissen, from Old French —, stem of some of the conjugated forms of establir (Old French) (modern établir (French)), from Latin stabilio (“stabiliō, stabilīre”), from stabilis (Latin “firm, steady, stable”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English estat, from Anglo-Norman estat and Old French estat (French: état (French)), from Latin status. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English estimat, Latin aestimātus (“valuing, estimate”), from aestimō + -tus (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Latin aestimātus, perfect passive participle of aestimō (Latin “to estimate”) (see -ate), older form aestumō (Latin “to value, rate, esteem”); from itc-ola *ais-temos (“one who cuts copper”), meaning one in the Roman Republic who mints money. Compare estymatt (Middle English “reputed”) / estimat (Middle English). See also the doublet , as well as aim (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Latin aestimātus (“estimated”), see -ate and Etymology 2 for more. Originally used as the past participle of estimate; compare generate (English) or communicate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English even, from Old English efn (“flat; level, even, equal”), from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁émnos (“equal, straight; flat, level, even”).

Cognate with íeuwen (Saterland Frisian “even, flat”), even (Western Frisian “even”), ëben (Alemannic “even”), ébane (Cimbric “even”), even (Dutch “even, equal, same”), effen (Dutch “leveled”), eben (German “even, flat, level”), jævn (Danish “even, flat, smooth”), jafn (Icelandic “even”), jevn (Norwegian Bokmål “even, smooth”), jamn (Norwegian Nynorsk “even, smooth”), jämn (Swedish “even, level, smooth”), 𐌹𐌱𐌽𐍃 (Gothic “even”), eun (oco “equal, right”) (attested in Vocabularium Cornicum eun-hinsic (oco “iustus, i. e., just”)), eun (obt “equal, right”) (attested in Eutychius Glossary eunt (Latin “aequus, i. e., equal”)), effn (Middle Breton), eeun (Breton), अम्नस् (Sanskrit “(adverb) just, just now; at once”).

The traditional proposal connecting the Germanic adjective with the root *h₂eym- (Proto-Indo-European) (imāgō (Latin “picture, image, likeness, copy”), aemulus (Latin “competitor, rival”), यम (Sanskrit “pair, twin”)) is problematic from a phonological point of view.

For the meaning development compare with aequus (Latin “equal, level, even, flat, horizontal”), ро́вный (Russian “even, level, flat, smooth”), ра́вный (Russian “equal”), по́ровну (Russian “in equal parts”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English evene

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English evenen

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
From Middle English even, from Old English ǣfen, from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþ, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs (“evening”).

Cognate with Äivend (Saterland Frisian), Äiwend (Saterland Frisian), Eeuwend (Saterland Frisian “evening”), jûn (Western Frisian “evening”), avond (Dutch “evening”), Avend (Low German “evening”), Abend (German “evening”), aften (Danish “evening”). See also the related terms eve (English) and evening (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (Latin “to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (Latin “out of, from”), short form of ex (Latin) + veniō (Latin “come”); related to venture (English), advent (English), convent (English), invent (English), convene (English), evene (English), etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Derived from French éventer

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: The third sense is influenced by any of several European languages, including eventuálně (Czech), éventuellement (French), eventuellt (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English every,everich,everych, from Old English ǣfre ǣlċ,ǣfre ǣġhwelċ (“each and every”). or .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English evidence, from Old French —, from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (Latin “clear, evident”); see evident (English).

chain.meaning: clearness, in Late Latin a proof

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare ēvideor (Late Latin “to appear plainly”)), from ē (Latin “out”) + videō (Latin “see”), present participle vidēns (Latin), deponent videor (Latin “to appear, seem”). Displaced native .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English evidently, evydently (Middle English); equivalent to evident + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English yvel, evel (Middle English), ivel (Middle English), uvel (Middle English), from Old English yfel, from Proto-West Germanic *ubil, from Proto-Germanic *ubilaz, from Proto-Indo-European —, a deverbal derivative of *h₂wep- (Proto-Indo-European “*h₂wep(h₁)-, *h₂wop(h₁)-”). See -le (English) for the supposed suffix.

Alternatively from , from Proto-Indo-European *upo, *h₃ewp- (Proto-Indo-European “down, up, over”).

Cognate with euvel (Dutch “evil”), übel (German “bad, evil”), övel (Low German (Germany) “evil”), iwwel (lb “queasy, nauseous; bad”), 𐌿𐌱𐌹𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “bad, evil”). Compare fel (Old Irish “bad, evil”), from *uɸelos (Proto-Celtic), and 𒄷𒉿𒀊𒍣 (Hittite “to mistreat, harass”), 𒄷𒉿𒀊𒉺𒀸 (Hittite “evil, badness”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English yvele, yvel (Middle English), ivel (Middle English), from Old English yfele (“badly, evilly”), a derivative of the adjective yfel (Old English “bad, evil”). Often reinterpreted as the noun in the later language (as in "to speak evil").

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō (“ēvolūtiō, ēvolūtiōnis”), from ēvolūtus (Latin), perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (Latin “unroll, unfold”), from ex (Latin) + volvō (Latin “roll”).

Compare typologically vývoj (Czech), развој (Serbo-Croatian), разви́ть (Russian), развива́ть (Russian), разви́ться (Russian), развива́ться (Russian), разви́тие (Russian), related to *viti (Proto-Slavic) (whence vít (Czech), вить (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin exāctus (the verb via Middle English exact), perfect passive participle of exigō (Latin “demand, claim as due; measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (Latin “out”) + agō (Latin “drive”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From exact + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English examinacioun, from Old French examinacion, from Latin exāminātiō. Morphologically examine + -ation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English examinen, examenen (Middle English), from Old French examiner, from Latin examino (“exāmināre”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: examine + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English example, exaumple (Middle English), from Old French example, essaumple (Old French), from Latin exemplum (“sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.”); see exempt (English). . Displaced native forebisne (Middle English), from forebȳsn (Old English); and bisne (Middle English), from bȳsn (Old English) (modern bizen (English)).

chain.meaning: sample, pattern, specimen, copy for imitation, etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English exception, excepcioun (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman excepcioun, from Old French excepcion, from Latin exceptiō. Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: exception + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English eschaunge, borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschaunge, from Old French eschange (whence modern échange (French)), from the verb eschanger (Old French), from Vulgar Latin *excambiō (“*excambiāre”) (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō). Spelling later changed on the basis of ex- (English), with pronunciation following. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English eschaungen, from Anglo-Norman eschaungier, Old French eschanger, from the Old French — verb eschangier (Old French), eschanger (Old French) (whence modern échanger (French)), from Vulgar Latin *excambiō (“*excambiāre”) (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō). Gradually displaced native wrixlan (Old English), wixlan (Old English “to change, exchange, reciprocate”) and its descendants, wrixle (English) being one of them.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: excited + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English excitement, from Old French excitement, equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from excludere (Latin “to shut out, exclude”), from ex- (Latin “out”) + variant form of verb claudere (Latin “to close, shut”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English excusen and excuse (Middle English), borrowed from Old French escuser and excuse (Old French), from Latin excuso (“excūsō, excūsāre”), from ex (Latin “out”) + causa (Latin “a charge”); see cause, accuse and recuse. Displaced native lād (Old English “an excuse”) and lādian (Old English “to excuse”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English exercise, from Old French exercise, from Latin exercitium. Displaced native plega (Old English “an exercise”) whence Modern English play (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: exhaust + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: exhaust + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhaustiō, from exhauriō (Latin). Surface analysis: exhaust + -ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From . Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French exister, from Latin exsisto (“existō, exsistō”), from ex (Latin “out”) + sisto (Latin “sistere”) (related to stō (Latin “stare”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “stand”); see stand (English). Compare assist (English), consist (English), desist (English), insist (English), persist (English), resist (English). Cognate with existir (Spanish), exister (French), esistere (Italian), existieren (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English existence, from Old French existence, from Late Latin existentia (“existence”), from existēns (Latin), from exsisto (Latin “existō, exsistō”), from ex (Latin “out”) + sisto (Latin “sistere”) (related to stō (Latin “stare”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “stand”). Cognate with existencia (Spanish), existence (French), Existenz (German). Displaced native understandennes (Old English) (literally, "understanden-ness").

Morphologically exist + ence (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English exit, from Latin exitus (“departure, going out; way by which one may go out, egress; (figuratively) conclusion, termination; (figuratively) death; income, revenue”), from exeō (Latin “to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”) + -tus (Latin). Exeō is derived from ex- (Latin) + eō (Latin “to go”) (ultimately from ). The English word is cognate with esito (Italian), êxito (Portuguese), éxito (Spanish). .

The verb is derived from the noun.

chain.meaning: departure, going out; way by which one may go out, egress; (figuratively) conclusion, termination; (figuratively) death; income, revenue

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin exit, the third-person singular present active indicative of exeō (Latin “to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”); see further at etymology 1 above.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (“foreign”), from ἐξω- (Ancient Greek “outside”), from ἐξ (Ancient Greek “out of”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Recorded in Middle English — since 1422 (as expanden (Middle English), expaunden (Middle English)), from Anglo-Norman espaundre, from Latin expandō (“to spread out”), itself from ex- (Latin “out, outwards”) + pandō (Latin “to spread”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French expansion, from Latin expānsiō. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin expectāre, infinitive form of exspectō (Latin “look out for, await, expect”), from ex (Latin “out”) + spectō (Latin “look at”), frequentative of speciō (Latin “see”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French expectation, from Latin exspectātiō, from exspectō (Latin “expect”). . Displaced native wēn (Old English).

etymologies.text: From , and its source, .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English expense, from Anglo-Norman expense and Old French espense, from Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expendō. See expend. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English experience, from Old French —, from Latin experientia (“a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience”), from experiens (Latin), present participle of experiri (Latin “to try, put to the test, undertake, undergo”), from ex (Latin “out”) + peritus (Latin “experienced, expert”), past participle of ; see expert (English) and peril (English). Displaced native āfandung (Old English “experience”) and āfandian (Old English “to experience”).

chain.meaning: a trial, proof, experiment, experimental knowledge, experience

etymologies.text: Affix: experience + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English experiment, from Old French esperiment (expérience (French)), from Latin experimentum (“experience, attempt, experiment”), from experior (Latin “to experience, to attempt”), itself from ex (Latin) + *perior (Latin), in turn from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English expert, Old French expert (“experienced”), espert (Old French), from Latin expertus (contracted from *experitus (Latin)), of experior (Latin “to try”), from .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from explanare (Latin “explain”); see explain. Morphologically explain + ation (English). Displaced native racu (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First recorded around 1538, from the Latin — verb explodo (Latin “explōdere”). The meaning was originally theatrical, "to drive an actor off the stage by making noise," hence meaning to "to drive out" or "to reject". From ex- (Latin “out”) + plaudere (Latin “to clap; to applaud”). In English it used to mean to "drive out with violence and sudden noise" (from around 1660), and later meaning to "go off with a loud noise" (from around 1790). The sense of "bursting with destructive force" is first recorded around 1882.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French esploit, esploitier (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French explorer, from Latin explōrō (“explōrāre”), itself said to be originally a hunters' term meaning "to set up a loud cry", from ex- (Latin “out”) + plōrō (Latin “plōrāre”), but the second element is also explained as "to make to flow" (from pluō (Latin “pluere”)). Displaced native rāsian (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French explosion, from Latin explōsio, from explōdo (Latin “to drive out by clapping”), from ex- (Latin) and plōdo (Latin “to clap or strike”). For more information see explode (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin exportare.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (Old French “to lay, place”). (via Old French espondre (“to set forth, explain”)), from the same Latin term.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From French exprès, from Latin expressus, past participle of exprimere (Latin) (see Etymology 2, below).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

Middle French expression, from Late Latin expressiō (“expressiō, expressiōnem”).

Morphologically express + ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English extenden, from Anglo-Norman extendre, estendre (Old French), from Latin extendō (“to stretch out”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English extensioun, from Old French estension, from Latin extensiō (“extensiō, extensiōnem”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English —, from Medieval Latin externus (“outward, external”), from exter/exterus (Latin “on the outside, outward”).

etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin extractum, neuter perfect passive participle of extrahō (Latin), from ex- + trahō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed into late Middle English — from Old French extreme, from Latin extrēmus, the superlative of exter (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: extreme + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English eȝebreu, alteration of Old English ēaganbrū (“eyebrow”), equivalent to eye + brow (English). The corresponding Old English ēagbrǣw (Old English) meant "eyelid". Compare Dutch oogbrauw (Dutch “eyelid; eyelash; eyebrow”), German Augenbraue (German “eyebrow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From eye + lash (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English eyelidd, eye-led (Middle English), eiȝelid (Middle English), eghe-lydd (Middle English), yȝe-lydd (Middle English), ehlid (Middle English), yhelidd (Middle English), from an unrecorded Old English *ēaghlid (“eyelid”), from Proto-West Germanic *augahlid (“eyelid”), equivalent to . Cognate with Oogenlid (Saterland Frisian “eyelid”), eachlid (Western Frisian “eyelid”), ooglid (Dutch “eyelid”), Ooglidd (Low German (Germany) “eyelid”), Augenlid (German “eyelid”).

Generally superseded non-native palpebre (Middle English “eyelid”), borrowed from palpebra (Latin “eyelid”) (see Modern English palpebra (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English eiȝesiht, ieȝesihte (Middle English), ehsihthe (Middle English), eihsihthe (Middle English), eȝhesihthe (Middle English), equivalent to eye + sight (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English face, from Old French face, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“form, appearance”). . Displaced native onlete (Middle English “face, countenance, appearance”), anleth (Middle English “face”), from anwlite (Old English), andwlita (Old English), compare Antlitz (German); ansīen (Old English “face”), neb (Middle English “face, nose”) (from nebb (Old English)), leer (Middle English “ler, leor, leer”) (from hlēor (Old English)), and non-native vis (Middle English “face, appearance, look”) (from vis (Old French)) and chere (Middle English “face”) from chere (Old French).

In the sense of face as in reputation, influenced by Chinese 面子 or , both of which mean literally the front of the head and metaphorically one's public image. See lose face (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: face (English) + to (English) + face (English)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English facilite, from Middle French facilité, and its source, Latin facilitās. . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French fact, from Latin factum (“an act, deed, feat, etc.”); also Medieval Latin for “state, condition, circumstance”; neuter of factus (Latin “done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (Latin “do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). Old/Middle French later evolved it into faict and fait. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English factour, from Middle French facteur, Anglo-Norman factour, and their etymon Latin factor (“a doer, maker, performer”), from factus (Latin “done or made”), perfect passive participle of faciō (Latin “do, make”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English fade, vad (Middle English), vade (Middle English “faded, pale, withered, weak”), from Middle Dutch vade (“weak, faint, limp”), from Old French fade (“weak, witless”), of obscure origin. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fatidus, from Latin fatuus (“insipid”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English fade, vad (Middle English), vade (Middle English “faded, pale, withered, weak”), from Middle Dutch vade (“weak, faint, limp”), from Old French fade (“weak, witless”), of obscure origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fade, fede (Middle English), of uncertain origin. Compare gefæd (Old English “ġefæd”). See also fad (English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English fade, fede (Middle English), of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English failen, borrowed from Old French falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallire, alteration of Latin fallō (“to deceive, disappoint”), from Proto-Indo-European — or Proto-Indo-European *(s)gʷʰh₂el- (“to stumble”).

Compare fääle (Alemannic “to lack”), béelan (Cimbric), véelan (Cimbric “to fail”), veln (Cimbric “to be absent, missing”), falen (Dutch), feilen (Dutch “to fail, miss”), fallieren (German), fehlen (German “to fail, miss, lack”), fejle (Danish “to fail, err”), fallera (Swedish “to fail, break, malfunction”), fallar (Spanish “to fail, miss”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: . Compare fàl (Scottish Gaelic “hedge”), faill (Scots “turf”). Attested from the 16th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Anglo-Norman failer, from Old French faillir (“to fail”). Equivalent to fail + -ure (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English faynt, feynt (Middle English “weak; feeble”), from Old French faint, feint (Old French “feigned; negligent; sluggish”), past participle of feindre (Old French), faindre (Old French “to feign; sham; work negligently”), from Latin fingo (“fingere”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold”). Cognate with feign (English) and fiction (English) and more distantly dough (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English feynen, from the adjective (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fayr, from Old English fæġer (“beautiful”), from Proto-West Germanic *fagr, from Proto-Germanic *fagraz (“appropriate, fitting, nice, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ḱ- (“to attach, join; agreement, settlement”).

Cognate with fagar (Old High German / Old Saxon “beautiful, fair”), fager (Danish), favr (Danish “fair, pretty, wonderful”), fagur (Faroese / Icelandic “beautiful, fair”), fager (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “fair, pretty”), 𐍆𐌰𐌲𐍂𐍃 (Gothic “fair, proper”), vapper (Estonian “brave, courageous”), vauras (Finnish “substantial, wealthy”); also pāx (Latin “peace; ease, quiet, rest”), pase (xum “peace”), пе́кны (Belarusian “beautiful”), pěkný (Czech “nice; pretty”), piekny (Polish), piękny (Polish “beautiful; admirable, praiseworthy”), pekný (Slovak “nice; pretty”), पाश॑ (Sanskrit “bond, cord, noose; nature, outer world; border, edge, selvage”). See also peace (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English feyre, from Old French foire, from Latin fēriae.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fayrly, fayrely (Middle English), vayrliche (Middle English), equivalent to fair + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English feith (“faith”) (also fay (Middle English)), borrowed from Old French foi (“fei, feid”), from Latin fidēs (“fidem”). . Displaced native ġelēafa (Old English), which was also a word for belief (English).

* Old French had as a final devoiced allophone of from lenited Latin ; this eventually fell silent in the 12th century. The -th of the Middle English forms is most straightforwardly accounted for as a direct borrowing of a French . However, it has also been seen as arising from alteration of a French form with -d under influence of English abstract nouns in the suffix -th (English) (e.g., truth, ruth, health, etc.), or as a recharacterization of a French form like fay (Old French), fey (Old French), fei (Old French) with the same suffix. Compare fiate (roa-cha), fiaite (roa-cha), showing the same preservation of the final consonant.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English feithful, equivalent to faith + ful (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Verb from Middle English fallen, from Old English feallan (“to fall, fail, decay, die, attack”), from Proto-West Germanic *fallan (“to fall”), from Proto-Germanic *fallaną (“to fall”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃elh₁- (“to collapse, fall; to destroy”).

Cognate with faw (Scots “to fall”), vale (Yola), vall (Yola), vole (Yola “to fall”), faal (North Frisian), fåle (North Frisian “to fall”), faale (Saterland Frisian “to fall”), falle (Western Frisian “to fall”), foin (Bavarian “to fall”), ballan (Cimbric), vallan (Cimbric “to fall”), vallen (Dutch “to fall”), fallen (German / Low German “to fall”), falen (lb “to fall”), פֿאַלן (Yiddish “to fall”), falde (Danish “to fall”), falla (Faroese / Icelandic / Swedish “to fall”), falle (Norwegian Bokmål “to fall”), falla (Norwegian Nynorsk), falle (Norwegian Nynorsk “to fall”); also aboleō (Latin “to destroy; to die”), ὄλλῡμι (Ancient Greek “to destroy; to lose”), եղեռն (Armenian “crime; calamity, catastrophe; slaughter”), pùlti (Lithuanian “to fall; to attack, assault”).

Noun from Middle English fal, fall (Middle English), falle (Middle English), from Old English feall, ġefeall (Old English “a falling, fall”) and Old English fealle (“trap, snare”), from Proto-Germanic *fallą, *fallaz (Proto-Germanic “a fall, trap”). Cognate with vall (Yola “fall”), val (Dutch “fall”), Fall (German “fall”), fald (Danish “fall”), fall (Faroese / Icelandic / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “fall”).

Sense of "autumn" is attested by the 1660s in England as a shortening of fall of the leaf (1540s), from the falling of leaves during this season. Along with autumn, it mostly replaced the older name harvest as that name began to be associated strictly with the act of harvesting. Compare spring, which began as a shortening of “spring of the leaf”.

chain.meaning: to fall, fail, decay, die, attack

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Perhaps from the north-eastern Scottish pronunciation of whale (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English false, fals (Middle English), from Old English fals (“false; counterfeit; fraudulent; wrong; mistaken”), from Latin falsus (“counterfeit, false; falsehood”), perfect passive participle of fallō (Latin “deceive”). Reinforced in Middle English by - (Anglo-Norman) and fals (Old French), faus (Old French). Compare fals (Scots), false (Scots), falsk (Saterland Frisian), falsch (German), vals (Dutch), - (Swedish) and falsk (Danish); all from falsus (Latin). Displaced native les (Middle English), lese (Middle English), from lēas (Old English “false”); See lease (English), leasing (English). .

The verb is from Middle English falsen, falsien (Middle English), from Old French falser, from Latin falsō (“falsify”), itself also from falsus (Latin); compare fausser (French “to falsify, to distort”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fame, from Old French fame (“celebrity, renown”), itself borrowed from Latin fāma (“talk, rumor, report, reputation”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéh₂-meh₂, from *bʰeh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to speak, say, tell”). Cognate with φήμη (Ancient Greek “talk”). Related also to for (Latin “speak, say”), bōian (Old English “to boast”), bēn (Old English “prayer, request”), bannan (Old English “to summon, command, proclaim”). More at ban (English).

Displaced native hlīsa (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English familiar,familier, from Latin familiāris (“pertaining to servants; pertaining to the household”). . . Displaced native hīwcūþ (Old English).

From Late Middle English famylye, from Latin familia (“a household”). Displaced native hīred (Old English) and hād (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English fan, Old English fann (“a winnowing, fan”), Latin vannus (“fan for winnowing grain”), Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

* ventus (Latin “wind”)
* wan (Dutch “winnowing basket”)
* Wanne (German “winnowing basket”)
* vanna (Swedish “a fan for winnowing”)
* windwian (Old English “to fan, winnow”).

etymologies.text: fanatic, originally in US baseball slang. Possibly influenced by fancy (English “group of sport or hobby enthusiasts”), i.e. fancy boy (English “fan”).

etymologies.text: From Cantonese 分. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English fansy, fantsy (Middle English), a contraction of fantasy (Middle English), fantasye (Middle English), fantasie (Middle English), from Old French fantasie, from Medieval Latin fantasia, from Late Latin phantasia (“an idea, notion, fancy, phantasm”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία, from φαντάζω (Ancient Greek “to render visible”), from φαντός (Ancient Greek “visible”), from φαίνω (Ancient Greek “to make visible”); from the same root as φάος (Ancient Greek “light”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂nyéti, from the root *bʰeh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to shine”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fancien, fantasien (Middle English), fantesien (Middle English), from Old French fantasier, from the noun (see above)).

Noun Middle English fantasie, from Old French fantasie (“fantasy”), from Latin phantasia (“imagination”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (“apparition”), from φαντάζω (Ancient Greek “to render visible”), from φαντός (Ancient Greek “visible”), from φαίνω (Ancient Greek “to make visible”); from the same root as φάος (Ancient Greek “light”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂nyéti, from the root *bʰeh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to shine”). .

Verb from Middle English fantasien, from Old French fantasier. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English ferre, fer (Middle English), Old English feor, feorr (Old English), from Proto-Germanic *ferrai.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English fare, from a merger of Old English fær (“journey, road”) and faru (Old English “journey, companions, baggage”), from Proto-Germanic *farą and *farō (Proto-Germanic “journey, fare”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“a going, passage”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English faren, from Old English faran (“to travel, journey”), from Proto-West Germanic *faran, from Proto-Germanic *faraną, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“a going, passage”).

Cognate with farre (Western Frisian), varen (Dutch “to sail”), fahren (German “to travel”), - (Danish) and fare (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and fara (Icelandic “to go”) and fara (Swedish “to travel”).

etymologies.text: Affix: farm + -ing

etymologies.text: Middle English facioun, from Anglo-Norman fechoun (compare Jersey faichon (Norman)), variant of faceon (Old French), fazon (Old French), façon (Old French “fashion, form, make, outward appearance”), from Latin factiō (“a making”), from faciō (Latin “do, make”); see fact. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: fashion + -able

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fastenen, from Old English fæstnian, from Proto-West Germanic *fastinōn (“to secure, fasten”). Equivalent to fast + -en (English).

etymologies.text: From Middle English fat, fatt (Middle English), fatte (Middle English), from the adjective above, and possibly from Old English fǣt (“fat”), from Proto-West Germanic *fait, from Proto-Germanic *faitą, *faitaz (Proto-Germanic “fat”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English fat, from Old English fæt (“vat, vessel, jar, cup, casket, division”), from Proto-Germanic *fatą (“vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *pod- (“vessel”). etymologies.text: From Middle English fate, from Latin fāta (“prediction”), plural of fātum (Latin), from fātus (Latin “spoken”), from for (Latin “to speak”). In this sense, displaced native wyrd (Old English), whence weird (English).

etymologies.text: From Middle English fader in lawe, fadyr-in-lay (Middle English), fader yn lawe (Middle English), equivalent to father + in-law (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English faulte (“faute”), faulte (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman faute, Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita (“shortcoming”), feminine of , in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō (Latin “deceive”). Displaced native schuld (Middle English “schuld, schuild”) (from scyld (Old English “fault”)), lac (Middle English “fault, lack”) (from lak (Middle Dutch “lack, fault”)), last (Middle English “fault, vice”) (from lǫstr (Old Norse “fault, vice, crime”)). etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English feer, fere (Middle English), fer (Middle English “fear”), from Old English fǣr, ġefǣr (Old English “calamity, sudden danger, peril, sudden attack, terrible sight”), from Proto-Germanic *fērō, *fērą (Proto-Germanic “danger”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through, carry forth, try”). Cognate with gevaar (Dutch “danger, risk, peril”), Gefahr (German “danger, hazard, risk”), fare (Danish “danger, hazard, risk”), fár (Faroese / Icelandic “accident, anger, calamity”), fare (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “danger”), fara (Swedish “danger, risk, peril”), perīculum (Latin “danger, risk, trial”), πεῖρα (Ancient Greek “trial, experiment”), փորձ (Armenian “attempt”). .

The verb is from Middle English feren, from Old English fǣran (“to frighten, raven”), from the noun. Cognate with the archaic - (Dutch) verb varen (Dutch “to fear, to cause fear”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fere, feore (Middle English), from Old English fēre (“able to go, fit for service”), from Proto-Germanic *fēriz (“passable”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to put across, ferry”). Cognate with fere (Scots), feir (Scots “well, active, sound”), gevüere (Middle High German “able, capable, fit, serviceable”), för (Swedish “capable, able, stout”), fær (Icelandic “able”). Related to fare (English).

chain.meaning: able to go, fit for service

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fethere, from Old English feþer, from Proto-West Germanic *feþru, from Proto-Germanic *feþrō, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ (“feather, wing”), from *peth₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to fly”).

Cognate with fear (Western Frisian “feather”), bèdara (Cimbric), fòdara (Cimbric “pillowcase”), vèdara (Cimbric “feather”), veder (Dutch), veer (Dutch “feather”), Feder (German “feather”), Fedder (Low German (Germany) “feather”), Fieder (lb “feather”), faoder (Ripuarian “feather”), פֿעדער (Yiddish “feather”), fjeder (Danish), fjer (Danish “feather”), fjøður (Faroese “feather”), fjöður (Icelandic “feather”), fjær (Norwegian Bokmål), fjør (Norwegian Bokmål “feather”), fjøder (Norwegian Nynorsk), fjør (Norwegian Nynorsk “feather”), fjäder (Swedish “feather”). Also πέτομαι (Ancient Greek “to fly”), shpend (Albanian “bird”), penna (Latin “feather”), թիռ (Classical Armenian “flight”).

The sense correlated with splines and keys () probably reflects analogy with the fletching sense ().

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English feture, from Anglo-Norman feture, from Old French faiture, from Latin factūra, from Latin factus, from Latin faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place, set”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fee, fe (Middle English), feh (Middle English), feoh (Middle English), from Old English feoh (“cattle, property, wealth, money, payment, tribute, fee”) with contamination from Old French fieu, fief (Old French) (from Medieval Latin fevum, a variant of feudum (Latin) (see ), from Frankish *fehu (“cattle, livestock”); whence ), both from Proto-Germanic *fehu (“cattle, sheep, livestock, owndom”), from Proto-Indo-European *péḱu (“livestock”).

Cognate with Fäi (Saterland Frisian “cattle, livestock”), fee (Western Frisian “livestock”), biighe (Cimbric), viighe (Cimbric “animal, beast”), vee (Dutch “cattle, livestock”), Viech (German “animal, beast”), Vieh (German “livestock”), Veeh (Low German (Germany) “cattle, livestock, property”), Véi (lb “cattle”), fi (Ripuarian), fī (Ripuarian), fii (Ripuarian), fiih (Ripuarian “cattle, livestock”), פֿי (Yiddish), פֿיך (Yiddish “cattle, livestock”), fæ (Danish / Faroese “cattle, livestock”), fé (Icelandic “assets, livestock, money”), fe (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “cattle, livestock”), fä (Swedish “beast, cattle, dolt”), 𐍆𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍉 (Gothic), 𐍆𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌿 (Gothic “possessions, property; riches, wealth; money”); also pecū (Latin “cattle”), pecku (Old Prussian “cattle”), ասր (Armenian “fleece, wool”), 𐬞𐬀𐬯𐬎 (ae “livestock”), ποσο (xbc “sheep”), پەز (Central Kurdish “sheep”), pez (Kurmanji Kurdish “sheep”), фыс (Ossetic “sheep”), pəs (tly), пәс (tly “sheep”), पशु (Sanskrit “cattle”).

chain.meaning: cattle, property, wealth, money, payment, tribute, fee

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English feden, from Old English fēdan (“to feed”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōdijan, from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną (“to feed”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to guard, graze, feed”). Cognate with fiede (Western Frisian “to nourish, feed”), voeden (Dutch “to feed”), føde (Danish “to bring forth, feed”), föda (Swedish “to bring forth, feed”), fæða (Icelandic “to feed”), and more distantly with pāscō (Latin “feed, nourish”) through Indo-European. More at food (English), fodder (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fede, fed (Middle English), from the verb (see above). Alternatively, perhaps from Old Norse fǿða (“nourishment, food”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdijaną (“to feed”), whence also fēdan (Old English “to feed”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: feed + back

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English felen, from Old English fēlan, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan.

Cognate with voelen (Dutch) and fühlen (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: See fele (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English felynge, equivalent to feel + ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English felawe,felowe (“companion, good friend”) from Old English fēolaga, from Old Norse félagi, derived from félag (Old Norse “joint venture; partnership”), from fé (Old Norse “livestock, property; money”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“livestock; wealth”)) + lag (Old Norse “something laid down; right position; arrangement; companionship, fellowship; partnership”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie down”)).

* filaga (Old Norse), felaka (Old Norse “partner”), from which the other terms are derived:
* fælle (Danish “companion”)
* felagi (Faroese “member; partner”)
* félagi (Icelandic “companion, comrade, fellow; member; partner”)
* felle (Norwegian “companion”)
* fälaghi (gmq-osw) (modern felaga (Swedish), felaha (Swedish “partner”))
* falow (Scots), fallow (Scots), follow (Scots “associate, companion, comrade”)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English felauen, felow (Middle English “to join (someone) in companionship, friendship, partnership, etc.”), from felowe (Middle English), felau (Middle English), felawe (Middle English): see etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English female, an alteration of Middle English femele (Middle English), from Old French femele, femelle (Old French “female”), from Medieval Latin fēmella (“a female”), from Latin fēmella (“a girl, a young female, a young woman”), diminutive of fēmina (Latin “a woman”). The English spelling and pronunciation were remodelled under the influence of male (English), which is otherwise not etymologically related. Contrast woman (English), which is etymologically built on man (English) (as in, “person”).

chain.meaning: a girl, a young female, a young woman

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fence, fens (Middle English), short for defence (Middle English), defens (Middle English “the act of defending”), from Old French defens, defense (Old French) (see defence).

The sense "enclosure" arises in the mid 15th century.
Also from the 15th century is use as a verb in the sense "to enclose with a fence". The generalized sense "to defend, screen, protect" arises ca. 1500. The sense "to fight with swords (rapiers)" is from the 1590s (Shakespeare).

Displaced native heġe (Old English) (compare hedge (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is from Middle English ferien (“to carry, convey”), from Old English ferian, from Proto-West Germanic *farjan, from Proto-Germanic *farjaną, which see for cognates. This verb is the causative of *faraną (Proto-Germanic “to go, travel”), whence fare (English); ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European — root *per- (Proto-Indo-European).

The noun is from Middle English ferie (“place of crossing, ferry”), which was derived from the above verb under influence of Old Norse ferja, from *farjǭ (Proto-Germanic), itself also from the verb.

.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English festival, from Old French festival (“festive”), from Late Latin fēstīvālis, from Latin fēstīvus (“festive”). . Displaced native frēols (Old English). The noun is shortened from festival day (English), from festival dai (Middle English), festiuall day (Middle English “feast day, festival”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Middle English fecchen (“to get and bring back, fetch; to come for, get and take away; to steal; to carry away to kill; to search for; to obtain, procure”) , from Old English feċċan, fæċċan (Old English), feccean (Old English “to fetch, bring; to draw; to gain, take; to seek”), a variant of fetian (Old English), fatian (Old English “to bring near, fetch; to acquire, obtain; to bring on, induce; to fetch a wife, marry”) and possibly related to facian (Old English), fācian (Old English “to acquire, obtain; to try to obtain; to get; to get to, reach”), both from Proto-Germanic *fatōną, *fatjaną (Proto-Germanic “to hold, seize; to fetch”), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”).

The English word is cognate with vatten (Dutch “to apprehend, catch; to grasp; to understand”), fassen (German “to catch, grasp; to capture, seize”), fet (English “(obsolete) to fetch”), fata (Faroese “to grasp, understand”), fatte (Danish “to grasp, understand”), fatta (Swedish “to grasp, understand”), feta (Icelandic “to go, step”), fetsje (Western Frisian “to grasp”).

The noun is derived from the verb.

chain.meaning: to get and bring back, fetch; to come for, get and take away; to steal; to carry away to kill; to search for; to obtain, procure

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
; the following possibilities have been suggested:

* From fetch-life (English “(obsolete, rare) a deity, spirit, etc., who guides the soul of a dead person to the afterlife; a psychopomp”).
* From the supposed Old English *fæcce (“evil spirit formerly thought to sit on the chest of a sleeping person; a mare”).
* From Old Irish fáith (“seer, soothsayer”).

chain.meaning: (obsolete, rare) a deity, spirit, etc., who guides the soul of a dead person to the afterlife; a psychopomp

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fever, fevere (Middle English), from Old English fefer, fefor (Old English “fever”) and Old French fievre (“fever”), from Latin febris (“a fever”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”). Displaced native hriþ (Old English “fever”). Compare also Fiewer (Saterland Frisian), Fieber (German), feber (Danish), feber (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fewe, from Old English fēaw (“few”), from Proto-West Germanic *fau, from Proto-Germanic *fawaz (“few”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”).

Cognate with fā (Old Saxon “few”), fao (Old High German), fō (Old High German “few, little”), fár (Old Norse “few”), 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍃 (Gothic “few”). Also related with paucus (Latin “little, few”) and pauper (Latin “poor”), from which latter poor (English) and pauper (English); see these.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ficcioun, from Old French ficcion (“dissimulation, ruse, invention”), from Latin fictiō (“a making, fashioning, a feigning, a rhetorical or legal fiction”), from fingō (Latin “to form, mold, shape, devise, feign”). Displaced native lēasspell (Old English); see feign (English), feint (English), figment (English).

chain.meaning: to form, mold, shape, devise, feign

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English feld, feeld (Middle English “field”), from Old English feld (“field”), from Proto-West Germanic *felþu (“field”), from Proto-Germanic *felþuz (“field”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“field, plain”) or *pleth₂- (Proto-Indo-European “flat”) (with schwebeablaut).

Cognate with feld (Scots), feild (Scots “field”), fial (North Frisian), fälj (North Frisian “field”), Fäild (Saterland Frisian “field”), fjild (Western Frisian “field”), veld (Dutch “field”), Feld (de,lb “field”), fald (Ripuarian “field”), felt (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “field”), fält (Swedish “field”), pelto (Finnish “field”), - (Asturian) and platu (roa-leo “plate”), - (Aragonese) and plato (Spanish “plate”), plat (Catalan “plate”), plat (French “dish”), - (Galician), - (mwl), and prato (Portuguese “plate”), piatto (Italian “plate”), *plattus (Latin “flattened”), πλατύς (Greek (Modern) “wide, broad”). Doublet of plate (English). Related also to flat (Middle English “flat”), folde (Old English “earth, land, territory”), folm (Old English “palm of the hand”). More at flat, fold.

Not related to felt (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fers, fiers (Middle English), borrowed from Old French fers (“wild", "ferocious”), nominative of fer (Old French), from Latin ferus (“wild", "untamed”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fifthe, fifte (Middle English), fift (Middle English), from Old English fīfta (“fifth”), from Proto-Germanic *fimftô (“fifth”) or *femftô (Proto-Germanic), equivalent to five + -th (English). Cognate with fift (Scots), fyft (Scots “fifth”), fyfde (North Frisian “fifth”), fyfde (Western Frisian “fifth”), vijfde (Dutch “fifth”), fifte (Low German), föfte (Low German), füfte (Low German “fifth”), fünfte (German “fifth”), femte (Danish “fifth”), femte (Swedish “fifth”), fimmta (Icelandic “fifth”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fighten (“to fight”), from Old English feohtan (“to fight, combat, strive”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, tease, shear, struggle with”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“to comb, shear”).

Cognate with fecht (Scots “to fight”), fjochtsje (Western Frisian), fjuchte (Western Frisian “to fight”), vechten (Dutch “to fight”), fechten (Low German “to fight”), fechten (German “to fence”), fægte (Danish “to fence, to fight (using blade weapons)”), fekte (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “to fence”), fäkta (Swedish “to fence, to fight (using blade weapons), to wave vigorously (and carelessly) with one's arms”), pectō (Latin “comb, thrash”), pjek (Albanian “to hit, strive, fight”), πέκω (Ancient Greek “comb or card wool”). Related also to feht (Old English “wool, shaggy pelt, fleece”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fight, feyght (Middle English), fiȝt (Middle English), fecht (Middle English), from Old English feoht, ġefeoht (Old English “fight”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtą, *gafehtą (Proto-Germanic “fight, struggle”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to struggle with”). Cognate with gevecht (Dutch “fight”), Gefecht (German “fight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English feghtyng, fyȝtynge (Middle English), fightand (Middle English), feghtand (Middle English), feghtande (Middle English), feightand (Middle English), feȝtand (Middle English), viȝtinde (Middle English), feihtende (Middle English), from Old English feohtende, from Proto-Germanic *fehtandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, struggle, contend with”), equivalent to fight + -ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fightyng, fightynge (Middle English), fiȝtinge (Middle English), feȝtyng (Middle English), from Old English fihtung (“fighting”), equivalent to fight + -ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English figure, borrowed from Old French figure, from Latin figūra (“form, shape, form of a word, a figure of speech, - (Late Latin) a sketch, drawing”), from fingō (Latin “to form, shape, mold, fashion”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold, shape, form, knead”). Cognate with τεῖχος (Ancient Greek), देग्धि (Sanskrit), dāg (Old English “dough”). More at dough (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fillen, fullen (Middle English), from Old English fyllan (“to fill, fill up, replenish, satisfy; complete, fulfill”), from Proto-West Germanic *fullijan, from Proto-Germanic *fullijaną (“to make full, fill”), from *fullaz (Proto-Germanic “full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

Cognate with fill (Scots “to fill”), folje (Western Frisian “to fill”), füllen (Low German “to fill”), vullen (Dutch “to fill”), füllen (German “to fill”), fylde (Danish “to fill”), fylla (Swedish “to fill”), fylle (Norwegian “to fill”), fylla (Icelandic “to fill”) and plenus (Latin “full”)

chain.meaning: to fill, fill up, replenish, satisfy; complete, fulfill

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fille, vulle (Middle English “vülle”), fülle (Middle English), from Old English fyllu, from Proto-West Germanic *fullī, from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄ (“fullness”). Cognate with Fülle (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: See thill (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English filme, from Old English filmen (“film, membrane, thin skin, foreskin”), from Proto-West Germanic *filmīn-, from Proto-Germanic *filmīn- (“thin skin, membrane”) (compare *felma- (Proto-Germanic “skin, hide”)), from Proto-Indo-European —, from *pel- (Proto-Indo-European “to cover, skin”). Cognate with filmene (Old Frisian “thin skin, human skin”), velm (Middle Dutch), vilm (Middle Dutch “fleece, film, membrane”), felm (Old High German “peel, skin, wrap”), *felma (Old English) (in ǣġerfelma (Old English “egg membrane”)). Related also to vel (Dutch “sheet, skin”), Fell (German “skin, hide, fur”), fjäll (Swedish “fur blanket, cloth, scale”), fille (Norwegian “rag, cloth”), plėvē (Lithuanian “membrane, scab”), плева́ (Russian “membrane”), πέλμα (Ancient Greek “sole of the foot”). More at fell. Sense of a thin coat of something is 1577, extended by 1845 to the coating of chemical gel on photographic plates. By 1895 this also meant the coating plus the paper or celluloid.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English final, fynal (Middle English), fynall (Middle English), from Old French final, from Latin fīnālis (“of or relating to the end or to boundaries”), from fīnis (Latin “end”); see fine. Replaced native English endly (English “final”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English finally, fynaly (Middle English), fynally (Middle English), fynaliche (Middle English), fynalliche (Middle English), equivalent to final + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English finaunce, fynaunce (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman —, Middle French finance, from finer (Middle French “to pay ransom”) (whence also fine (English “to pay a penalty”)), from fin (Middle French “end”), from Latin fīnis.
Original English sense that appeared c. 1400 was “ending”. The sense of “ending or satisfying a debt” originated from French influence: in the sense of “ransom” appeared in the mid 15th century, in the sense of “taxation” appeared in the late 15th century. In the sense of “manage money” first recorded c. 1770.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: finance + -ial

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: financial + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English fynden, from Old English findan, from Proto-West Germanic *finþan, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, a secondary verb from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path bridge”).

See also fine (Western Frisian), finden (Low German), vinden (Dutch), finden (German), finde (Danish), finne (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and finna (Swedish); also path (English), étain (Old Irish “I find”), áitt (Old Irish “place”), pōns (Latin “bridge”), πόντος (Ancient Greek “sea”), հուն (Classical Armenian “ford”), 𐬞𐬀𐬧𐬙𐬃 (ae), पथ (Sanskrit “path”), *pǫtь (Proto-Slavic).

For the meaning development compare *najьti (Proto-Slavic) > найти́ (Russian), akin to *jьti (Proto-Slavic) > идти́ (Russian); находи́ть (Russian), нахо́дка (Russian), akin to ход (Russian), ходи́ть (Russian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English fin, fyn (Middle English), from Old French fin (“fine, minute, exact”), of obscure origin, but probably derived from Latin fīniō (“to finish”) or fīnis (Latin “boundary, limit, end”), with an abstract sense of fine or thin also arising in many Romance languages (compare fino (Italian / Portuguese / Spanish)). .
