etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fyn, fyne (Middle English), from Old French fin, from Medieval Latin fīnis (“a payment in settlement or tax”). .

chain.meaning: a payment in settlement or tax

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Italian fine (“end”). French fin (French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English finen, fynen (Middle English), from Old French finer, finir (Old French). See finish (English) (transitive verb).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English finely, fynely (Middle English), fynly (Middle English), fineliche (Middle English), finliche (Middle English), fynliche (Middle English), equivalent to fine + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English finger neiles (“finger neil(e)”); equivalent to . Compare nayl of fynger (Middle English “fingernail”) and handnæġl (Old English “fingernail”). Compare also Fingernail (Saterland Frisian “fingernail”), fingerneil (Western Frisian “fingernail”), vingernagel (Dutch “fingernail”), Fingernagel (German “fingernail”), fingernegl (Danish “fingernail”), fingernagel (Swedish “fingernail”), fingernegl (Norwegian “fingernail”), fingurnögl (Icelandic “fingernail”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English finishen, finisshen (Middle English), finischen (Middle English), from , stem of some of the conjugated forms of finir (Old French), from , from fīnis (Latin “end, limit, border, boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) or from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fyr, from Old English fȳr (“fire”), from Proto-West Germanic *fuir, from *fuïr (Proto-Germanic), a regularised form of Proto-Germanic *fōr (“fire”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥.

See also feier (Scots), fyre (Scots “fire”), vier (Yola), vire (Yola “fire”), Fjuur (Saterland Frisian), Fjúur (Saterland Frisian “fire”), fjoer (Western Frisian “fire”), Füür (Alemannic “fire”), Feia (Bavarian “fire”), Fauer (Central Franconian), Feier (Central Franconian), Füür (Central Franconian “fire”), bôar (Cimbric), vaür (Cimbric), vôar (Cimbric “fire”), vier (Dutch), vuur (Dutch “fire”), Feuer (German “fire”), Füer (Low German (Germany)), Füür (Low German (Germany) “fire”), Feier (lb “fire”), vaier (mhn “fire”), faojer (Ripuarian “fire”), vier (Flemish “fire”), פֿײַער (Yiddish “fire”), fyr (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “fire”), funi (Icelandic “fire”), 𐍆𐍉𐌽 (Gothic “fire”). Also, compare հուր (Armenian “fire”), πυρ (Greek (Modern) “fire”), pūrgō (Latin “to clean, cleanse, clear, purge, purify”), 𐌐𐌉𐌓 (xum “fire”), фир (Bulgarian “ooze, pickle, soak”), perz (Polish “smoke”), 𒉺𒄴𒄯 (Hittite “fire”), 𒉺𒀀𒄷𒌋𒌨 (Luwian “fire”), A/B por (xto)/puwar (txb “fire”). This was an inanimate noun whose animate counterpart was *h₁n̥gʷnis (Proto-Indo-European) (see ignite). Cognate to pyre (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English firen, fyren (Middle English), furen (Middle English), from Old English fȳrian (“to make a fire”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with fioria (Old Frisian “to light a fire”), fjuurje (Saterland Frisian “to fire”), vûren (Middle Dutch), vueren (Middle English), vieren (Middle English “to set fire”), vuren (Dutch “to fire, shoot”), fiuren (Old High German “to ignite, set on fire”), feuern (German “to fire”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From fire + fighter (English). Created as a gender-neutral term for fireman (English) and firewoman (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From . Compare Fjuurwierk (Saterland Frisian “firework”), fjoerwurk (Western Frisian “firework”), vuurwerk (Dutch “firework”), Füürwark (Low German), Füerwark (Low German “firework”), Feuerwerk (German “firework”), fyrværkeri (Danish “firework”), fyrverkeri (Swedish “firework”), fýrverk (Faroese “firework”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Italian firma (“signature”), from firmare (Italian “to sign”), from Latin firmāre (“to make firm, to confirm (by signature)”), from firmus (Latin “firm, stable”). The contemporary sense developed in the 18th century simultaneously with German Firma (“business, name of business”). There are conflicting statements in the literature as to which of the two languages influenced which. . Other cognates include держать (Russian “to hold”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ferme, from Old French ferme, from Latin firmus (“strong, steady”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English fermen (“to make firm”), partly from (either through Old French fermer or directly) Latin firmō, from firmus (Latin “firm”), and partly a new formation on the adjective.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fermely; equivalent to firm + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English first, furst (Middle English), ferst (Middle English), fyrst (Middle English), from Old English fyrest, from Proto-West Germanic *furist, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first, foremost”), superlative of Proto-Germanic *furai, *furi (Proto-Germanic “before”), from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”), from *per- (Proto-Indo-European “before; first”), equivalent to fore + est (English).

Cognate with first (Scots “first”), voorste (Dutch “foremost, first”), vorst (Dutch “prince”), Fürst (German “chief, prince”), Vürsch (Limburgish “prince”), viischt (lb “anterior; forward”), fiyśt (Ripuarian), fjəšt (Ripuarian), fjyśt (Ripuarian), fjyšt (Ripuarian “prince”), først (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “first”), fyrstur (Faroese / Icelandic “first”), fyrst (Norwegian Nynorsk), først (Norwegian Nynorsk “first”), först (Swedish “first”); also prīnceps (Latin “first, foremost; chief”), παρ' (Greek (Modern)), παρά (Greek (Modern) “despite; less”), 𐀞𐀫 (Mycenaean Greek “from”), parë (Albanian “first; chief, main”), pyrmais (ltg “first”), pirmais (Latvian “first; foremost”), pirmas (Lithuanian “first; primary”), пъ́рви (Bulgarian), пръ́в (Bulgarian “first”), prvý (Czech / Slovak “first”), прв (Macedonian), први (Macedonian “first”), piersy (Polish), pierwszy (Polish), pirszy (Polish “first”), пе́рвый (Russian “first”), пр̑вӣ (Serbo-Croatian), pȓvī (Serbo-Croatian “first”), prvi (Slovenian “first”), հարավ (Armenian “south”), 𐬞𐬀𐬎𐬭𐬎𐬎𐬀 (ae “before, first”), pärwat (xto “first”), parwe (txb “first”), पूर्व (Sanskrit “before”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English first, furst (Middle English), fyrst (Middle English), from Old English fyrst, fierst (Old English), first (Old English “period, space of time, time, respite, truce”), from Proto-Germanic *frestaz, *fristiz (Proto-Germanic), *frestą (Proto-Germanic “date, appointed time”), from Proto-Indo-European *pres-, *per- (Proto-Indo-European “forward, forth, over, beyond”). Cognate with ferst (North Frisian), frest (North Frisian “period, time”), Frist (German “period, deadline, term”), frist (Swedish “deadline, respite, reprieve, time-limit”), frestur (Icelandic “period”). See also frist (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined before 1475, from Middle English fyrst-lyk, equivalent to first + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fisch, from Old English fisċ (“fish”), from Proto-West Germanic *fisk, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz (“fish”), from Proto-Indo-European *péysks (“fish”).

Cognate with wish (Yola “fish”), fasch (North Frisian), fask (North Frisian), Fesk (North Frisian “fish”), Fisk (Saterland Frisian “fish”), fisk (Western Frisian “fish”), biss (Cimbric), visch (Cimbric), viss (Cimbric “fish”), vis (Dutch “fish”), visch (nds-nl,mhn “fish”), Fisch (German “fish”), Fösch (Low German (Germany) “fish”), Fësch (lb “fish”), פֿיש (Yiddish “fish”), fisk (Danish / Elfdalian / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “fish”), fiskur (Faroese / Icelandic “fish”), 𐍆𐌹𐍃𐌺𐍃 (Gothic “fish”), fisct (gme-cgo “fish”). Compare iasc (Irish “fish”), piscis (Latin “fish”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Deverbal from to fish (etymology 3).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Old English fiscian, from Proto-West Germanic *fiskōn, from Proto-Germanic *fiskōną.

Cognate with fiskje (Saterland Frisian “to fish”), vissen (Dutch “to fish”), fischen (German “to fish”), vésche (Limburgish), vèsse (Limburgish “to fish”), fëschen (lb “to fish”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian Bokmål) and fiske (Norwegian Nynorsk “to fish”), - (Faroese), - (Icelandic) and fiska (Swedish “to fish”), 𐍆𐌹𐍃𐌺𐍉𐌽 (Gothic “to fish”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French fiche (“peg, mark”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: fisher + -man

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Possibly from Middle English fit (“an adversary of equal power”), of further origin. The original sense appears to have been "to marshal or deploy troops", which shifted to "to suit (troops to a certain location" > "suitable", and may be further related to fitja (Icelandic “to web, knit, cast on”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: , possibly from Old English fitt (“song”), or from the sense of fitted to length. Compare *fittea (Old Saxon) (attested in the borrowed vittea (Latin)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: . From Middle English fit (“hardship, danger”), possibly from Old English fitt (“conflict”)—a word only attested once. Compare fit (Cornish “game match, bout”); or else, maybe cognate with fitta (Italian “sudden and stabbing pain”) (see further at Latin figo (“fīgere”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Formed from fight (English) on the model of bite (English):bit (English) and light (English):lit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Clipping: outfit

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From fit + -ness (English). , with the physical sense from 1935.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher (Old French), fichier (Old French); > English fitch (English)), from fix (Old French “fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (Latin “to drive in; stick; fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to jab; stick; set”). Related to dig (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English flag, flagge (Middle English “flag”), further etymology . Perhaps from or related to early Middle English flage and Old English flagg, flacg (Old English “cataplasm, poultice, plaster”). Or, perhaps ultimately , or otherwise drawn from Proto-Germanic *flaką (“something flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, broad, plain”), referring to the shape.

Germanic cognates include Saterland Frisian Flaage (Saterland Frisian “flag”), West Frisian flagge (Western Frisian “flag”), Dutch vlag (Dutch “flag”), Flagge (German “flag”), flagga (Swedish “flag”), flag (Danish “flag, ship's flag”). Compare also flacken (Middle English “to flutter, palpitate”), - (Swedish) dialectal flage (Swedish “to flutter in the wind”), flögra (Old Norse “to flap about”). Akin to flogarōn (Old High German “to flutter”), flogezen (Old High German “to flutter, flicker”), flakeren (Middle English “to move quickly to and fro”), flacor (Old English “fluttering, flying”). More at flack (English), flacker (English).

right|thumb|Several flagpoles with flags

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Perhaps from a variant of flack (English “to hang loose”), from Middle English flacken; or perhaps from Old Norse —. Compare flaggheren (Middle Dutch), vlaggheren (Middle Dutch “to droop, flag”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English flagge, of origin, perhaps from gmq —; compare flæg (Danish “yellow iris”). Or, possibly from flag#Etymology_1 (English “sense 1”), referring to its motion in the wind. Compare also vlag (Dutch).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English flag, flagge (Middle English), probably of Scandinavian/gmq — origin; compare flag (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English flawme, blend of Old French flame and flambe (Old French), flamble (Old French), the first from Latin flamma, the second from Latin flammula, diminutive of flamma (Latin), both from pre-Latin *fladma; Proto-Italic *flagmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shimmer, gleam, shine”). Displaced native līeġ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English flawmen, from Old French flamber, flammer (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: In some senses, from Middle English flasshen, a variant of flasken (Middle English), flaskien (Middle English “to sprinkle, [[splash#Verb”), which was likely of origin; in other senses probably of gmq — origin akin to Swedish dialectal flasa (Swedish “to [[burn#Verb”), related to flare (English). Compare also flasa (Icelandic “to rush, go hastily”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English flashe, flaske (Middle English), also found as flosche (Middle English) and flushe (Middle English) (whence modern English flosh (English) and flush (English)), used in Middle and modern English for bodies of water with varying emphasis on them being "pools" or "marshes". It is not entirely clear whether these constitute a single term with varied spellings, or have distinct etymologies. The form , flashe (Middle English) is often suggested to be from flache (Old French), flaque (French), which is of origin, akin to vlacke (Middle Dutch “an estuary, flats with stagnant pools”). See flush (English) for more on that form.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English flat, a borrowing from Old Norse flatr (compare Norwegian and flat (Swedish), flad (Danish)), from Proto-Germanic *flataz, from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“flat”); akin to flot (Saterland Frisian “smooth”), Flöz (German “a geological layer”), πλατύς (Ancient Greek), plats (Latvian), प्रथस् (Sanskrit “extension”). .

The noun is from Middle English flat (“level piece of ground, flat edge of a weapon”), from the adjective.

The algebraic sense was coined by in , originally as French plat.

chain.meaning: level piece of ground, flat edge of a weapon

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:

From an alteration (due to flatt (Scots “a level part of a structure”)) of Scots flet, flett (Scots “inner part of a house”), from Middle English flet (“dwelling”), from Old English flet, flett (Old English “ground floor, dwelling”), from Proto-West Germanic *flati, from Proto-Germanic *flatją (“floor”), from Proto-Germanic *flataz (“flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“flat”). Akin to flet (Old Frisian), flette (Old Frisian “dwelling, house”). More at flet (English), flat (English “flat 1 ”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English flatten, from Old French flatir (“to knock or strike down, dash”), from Frankish *flattjan (“to move the palm of the hand”), from Proto-Germanic *flatjaną (“to make flat, flatten”).

chain.meaning: to knock or strike down, dash

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French flexibilité, from Late Latin flexibilitās, from Latin flectō (“to bend, curve”). Equivalent to flexible + -ity (English) = flex + -ibility (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French flexible, from Latin flexibilis, from flectō (Latin “to bend, curve”). Morphologically flex + ible (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English floten, from Old English flotian (“to float”), from Proto-West Germanic *flotōn, from Proto-Germanic *flutōną (“to float”), from Proto-Indo-European *plewd-, *plew- (Proto-Indo-European “to float, swim, fly”). Compare flow (English), fleet (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English flote, from Old English flota (“sailor, boat”), from Proto-West Germanic *flotō, from Proto-Germanic *flutô, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd-.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with flude (Scots), fluid (Scots), Floud (Saterland Frisian), vloed (Dutch), Flut (German), flod (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), flóð (Icelandic), and 𐍆𐌻𐍉𐌳𐌿𐍃 (Gothic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English floor, floour (Middle English), flor (Middle English), flore (Middle English), flour (Middle English), flur (Middle English), vlor (Middle English), from Old English flōr (“floor, pavement; deck; gangplank”), from Proto-West Germanic *flōr, from Proto-Germanic *flōraz (“ground; floor”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂ros (“floor”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

Cognate with flair (Scots), fluir (Scots “floor”), Floor (Saterland Frisian “floor”), vloer (Dutch “floor”), Flur (German “corridor, hall, hallway, stairwell”), Vlǫǫr (Limburgish “floor”), Floor (Low German “hallway or entrance to a house”), Flouer (lb “countryside, farmland”); also leur (Breton / Cornish “floor, ground, surface”), lár (Irish “floor, ground”), làr (Scottish Gaelic “earth, floor, ground”), laare (Manx “bottom, deck, floor; level, storey”), llawr (Welsh “floor, ground”), plānus (Latin “even, flat, level”), απαλάμη (Greek (Modern)), παλάμη (Greek (Modern) “hand, palm”), pëllëmbë (Albanian “palm”), pluons (ltg “thin”), plāns (Latvian “thin”), plonas (Lithuanian “fine, slender, thin”), по́ле (Belarusian / Macedonian / Russian / Ukrainian “field”), поле́ (Bulgarian “field”), pole (Czech / Polish / Slovak “field”), по̏ље (Serbo-Croatian), pȍlje (Serbo-Croatian “field”), polje (Slovenian “field”), 𒁄𒄭𒅖 (Hittite “broad, wide”). Related to flat.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Spelled (until about 1830) and meaning flower (English) in the sense of flour being the "finest portion of ground grain" (compare fleur de farine (French), fine fleur (French)). . Partially displaced native meal (English).

The U.S. standard of identity comes from [https://web.archive.org/web/20100722051913/http://www.access.gpo.gov/nara/cfr/waisidx_02/21cfr137_02.html 21CFR137.105].

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English flowe, from the verb (see below). The psychology sense “state of focus” was .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English flowen, from Old English flōwan (“to flow”), from Proto-West Germanic *flōan, from Proto-Germanic *flōaną (“to flow”), from Proto-Indo-European *plōw-, lengthened o-grade form of *plew- (Proto-Indo-European “to fly, flow, run”).

Cognate with flouje (Saterland Frisian “to flow”), floeie (Western Frisian “to flow”), vloeien (Dutch “to flow”), flo (Norwegian “to flow”). Compare also float (English). Not cognate with fluō (Latin) despite similarity.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: . Perhaps from flói (Old Norse “a large bay, firth”), see floe (English). Compare flow (Scots “peat-bog, marsh”), flói (Icelandic “marshy ground”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fleute, floute (Middle English), flote (Middle English), from Old French flaute, fleüte (Old French), from oc-pro-old flaut (“flaüt”), of origin. Perhaps ultimately from three possibilities:
* Blend of Provencal flaujol (Occitan “flageolet”) + laüt (Occitan “lute”)
* From Latin flātus (Latin “blowing”), from flāre (Latin “to blow”)
* Imitative.
.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fflye, flehe (Middle English), flei (Middle English), fleie (Middle English), fley (Middle English), fleye (Middle English), fleȝe (Middle English), flie (Middle English), fliȝe (Middle English), flye (Middle English), vliȝe (Middle English), vlye (Middle English), from Old English flēge, flēoge (Old English), flīeġe (Old English “a fly”), from Proto-West Germanic *fleugā, from Proto-Germanic *fleugǭ (“a fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“to flow, fly, run; to splash”), enlargement of *plew- (Proto-Indo-European “to flow, fly, run”).

Cognate with flee (Scots), flei (Scots “fly”), fleeg (North Frisian “fly”), Fljooge (Saterland Frisian “fly”), Flüüge (Alemannic “fly”), blòiga (Cimbric), vlòiga (Cimbric “fly”), vlieg (Dutch “fly”), Fliege (German “fly”), Fleeg (Low German “fly”), fłig (Ripuarian), fłyjǵ (Ripuarian “fly”), פֿליג (Yiddish “fly”), flue (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “fly”), fluga (Faroese / Icelandic / Swedish “fly”), fluga (Norwegian Nynorsk), fluge (Norwegian Nynorsk), fluggu (Norwegian Nynorsk), flugu (Norwegian Nynorsk “fly”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English flei, fley (Middle English), fleye (Middle English), fleȝhenn (Middle English), flien (Middle English), fliȝe (Middle English), flyen (Middle English), flyyn (Middle English), from Old English flēgan, flēogan (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *fleugan, from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“to flow, fly, run; to splash”), enlargement of *plew- (Proto-Indo-European “to flow, fly, run”). Compare Etymology 1.

Cognate with flei (Scots “to fly”), vlee (Yola “to fly”), fli (North Frisian), fliin (North Frisian), fliine (North Frisian), fliinj (North Frisian), flä (North Frisian), fläie (North Frisian), flö (North Frisian “to fly”), fljoge (Saterland Frisian), fljooge (Saterland Frisian “to fly”), fleane (Western Frisian “to fly”), fleeje (Central Franconian “to fly”), vliegen (Dutch “to fly”), flegen (Low German “to fly”), fliegen (German “to fly”), fléien (lb “to fly”), fłig (Ripuarian “to fly”), פֿליִען (Yiddish “to fly”), flyve (Danish “to fly”), fljúgva (Faroese), flúgva (Faroese “to fly”), fljúga (Icelandic “to fly”), fly (Norwegian Bokmål), flyge (Norwegian Bokmål), flyve (Norwegian Nynorsk “to fly”), fljuga (Norwegian Nynorsk), fly (Norwegian Nynorsk), flyga (Norwegian Nynorsk), flyge (Norwegian Nynorsk “to fly”), flyğa (gmq-scy “to fly”), flyga (Swedish “to fly”); also lew (Cornish “rudder”), luí (Old Irish “rudder”), llyw (Welsh “rudder”), pluit (Latin), pluō (Latin “to rain”), πλέω (Ancient Greek “to sail; to float”), plaukti (Lithuanian “to swim; to float”), пля́скам (Bulgarian “to slap; to clap; to splash; to jabber; to blemish”), pleskat (Czech “to slap; to flap, lap”), плеска (Macedonian “to slap”), плеска́ть (Russian “to splash”), пље̏скати (Serbo-Croatian), pljȅskati (Serbo-Croatian “to applaud; to slap”), плеска́ти (Ukrainian “to splash”), լուանալ (Armenian), լվալ (Armenian), լվանալ (Armenian “to wash”), plu- (xto,txb “to fly”), प्लु (Sanskrit “to float; to sail”). etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The verb is from Middle English folden, from Old English fealdan, from Proto-West Germanic *falþan, from Proto-Germanic *falþaną (“to fold”), from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to fold”).

Cognate with vouwen (Dutch), falten (German).

The noun is from Middle English folde, falde (Middle English), itself derived from the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The noun is from Middle English fold, fald (Middle English), from Old English fald, falæd (Old English), falod (Old English “fold, stall, stable, cattle-pen”), from Proto-West Germanic *falud, from Proto-Germanic *faludaz (“enclosure”).

Akin to fald (Scots), fauld (Scots “an enclosure for livestock”), Dutch vaalt (Dutch “dung heap”), valt (Middle Low German “valt, vālt”), fold (Danish “pen for herbivorous livestock”), fålla (Swedish “corral, pen, pound”).

The verb is from Late Middle English fooldyn, itself derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English folde, from Old English folde (“earth, land, country, district, region, territory, ground, soil, clay”), from Proto-Germanic *fuldǭ, *fuldō (Proto-Germanic “earth, ground; field; the world”). Cognate with fold (Old Norse “earth, land, field”), - (Norwegian) and fold (Icelandic “land, earth, meadow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English fond, fonned (Middle English), past participle of fonnen (Middle English “to be foolish, be simple, dote”), equivalent to fon + -ed (English). More at fon (English).

etymologies.text: From French —, ultimately from Latin fundus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English force, fors (Middle English), forse (Middle English), from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”).

etymologies.label: Etymology

Equivalent to foreign + -er (English). Use of the -er suffix may be due to analogy with straunger (Middle English “stranger”). Displaced native elþēodiġ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology

From Middle English forme (“shape, figure, manner, bench, frame, seat, condition, agreement, etc.”), borrowed from Old French forme, from Latin fōrma (“shape, figure, image, outline, plan, mold, frame, case, etc., manner, sort, kind, etc.”).

In sense "division grouping school students" (now dated), derived from public school nomenclature later adopted by state schools. It is sometimes said to be from the sense of "bench", where students of certain ages would sit together, though this is disputed, or alternatively from the sense of "established method of expression or practice".

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

The adjective is derived from forth (English “forwards”) + coming (English “approaching (adjective)”); or from Middle English forth commyng, *forthcominge (Middle English), present participle of forth-comen (Middle English “to come forth; to appear, issue”), from Old English forþcuman (“to come forth, come forward”) (present participle *forþcumende (Old English)), from forþ- (Old English “forth; forward”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“before, in front; first”)) + cuman (Old English “to come”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (“to step”)). etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English fre, from Old English frēo, frēoh (Old English), frī (Old English), friġ (Old English), frīoh (Old English “free”), from Proto-West Germanic *frī, from Proto-Germanic *frijaz (“beloved, not in bondage”), from Proto-Indo-European *priHós (“pleased, loved”), from *preyH- (Proto-Indo-European “to please; to love”). Related to friend (English).

Germanic cognates include fre (Scots “free”), frai (North Frisian), frei (North Frisian), fri (North Frisian), Frii (North Frisian “free”), fräi (Saterland Frisian “free”), frij (Western Frisian “free”), vrij (Dutch “free”), frei (German “free”), free (Low German “free”), fräi (lb “free”), frȧj (Ripuarian “free”), פֿרײַ (Yiddish “free”), fri (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “free”), fríur (Faroese “free”), 𐍆𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃 (Gothic “free”).

Other cognates include rydh (Cornish “free”), rhydd (Welsh “free”), propriō (Latin “to appropriate”), přát (Czech “to wish; to favour”), sprzyjać (Polish “to favour, foster”), прѝјати (Serbo-Croatian), prìjati (Serbo-Croatian “to please, taste, suit; to be agreeable, relish”), priať (Slovak “to wish”), 𐬟𐬭𐬌𐬌𐬀 (ae “good, pleasant”), فری (Persian “beloved, dear; agreeable, pleasing”), प्रिय (Sanskrit “beloved”).

Germanic and Celtic are the only Indo-European language branches in which the PIE word with the meaning of "dear, beloved" acquired the additional meaning of "free" in the sense of "not in bondage". This was an extension of the idea of "characteristic of those who are dear and beloved", in other words friends and tribe members (in contrast to unfree inhabitants from other tribes and prisoners of war, many of which were among the slaves – compare the Latin use of liberi to mean both "free persons" and "children of a family").

etymologies.text: From Middle English frie (“spawn of fish, young or small fish, offspring, progeny, children”), probably from Old Norse frjó (“seed, semen”), from Proto-Germanic *fraiwą (“seed, semen, offspring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per-, *(s)prey- (Proto-Indo-European “to strew, sow”). Cognate with frjó (Icelandic “pollen, seed”), fræ (Icelandic “seed”), frö (Swedish “seed, embryo, grain, germ”), - (Danish) and frø (Norwegian “seed”), 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍅 (Gothic “seed”). Likely merging with Old French froiz, froie (Old French “spawn, spawning”), from froier (Old French), freier (Old French “to spawn”), from Latin fricō (“to rub”). Compare friable.

chain.meaning: spawn of fish, young or small fish, offspring, progeny, children

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Dialectal, of origin. Perhaps related to or a corruption of frith (English “a wood, forest", also "brushwood, wattle”), from Middle English fryth, frith (Middle English “forest, woodland, a fence of brush or wattle, hedge”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English fuayle, from Old French fouaille, feuaille (Old French “firewood, kindling”), from feu (Old French “fire”), from Late Latin focus (“fire”), from Latin focus (“hearth”), whence English focus (English). Cognate with fuego (Spanish “fire”), and fogo (Portuguese “fire”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ful, from Old English full (“full”), from Proto-West Germanic *full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

Germanic cognates include fol (Western Frisian), vull (Low German), vol (Dutch), voll (German), fuld (Danish), full (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish). Proto-Indo-European cognates include plenty (English) (via Latin, compare plēnus (Latin)), llawn (Welsh), по́лный (Russian), pilnas (Lithuanian), پر (Persian), पूर्ण (Sanskrit).

See also fele (English) and fou (Scots) (whence the English doublet ). For the "drunk, intoxicated" sense, compare also full (Swedish) and other Scandinavian languages.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English fulle, fylle (Middle English), fille (Middle English), from Old English fyllu, fyllo (Old English “fullness, fill, plenty”), from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄, *fulnō (Proto-Germanic “fullness, filling, overflow”), from Proto-Indo-European *plūno-, *plno- (Proto-Indo-European “full”), from *pelh₁- (Proto-Indo-European), *pleh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “to fill; full”). Cognate with Fülle (German “fullness, fill”), fylli (Icelandic “fulness, fill”). More at fill (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English fullen, fulwen (Middle English “to baptise”), from Old English fullian, fulwian (Old English “to baptise”), from full- (Old English) + (later ). Compare fulluht (Old English), fulwiht (Old English “baptism”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English fullen (“to full”), from Anglo-Norman fuller, fuler (Anglo-Norman), Middle French foller, fouler (Middle French), from Old French foler, fouler (Old French “to tread, stamp, full”), from Medieval Latin fullo (“fullāre”), from Latin fullō (“a fuller”). Compare fullian (Old English “to full”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From full + time (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English fully, fulliche (Middle English), volliche (Middle English), from Old English fullīċe (“fully”), equivalent to full + -ly (English). Compare völlig (German “fully”), fullt (Swedish “fully”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: A reference to the phrase "the prisoner was fully committed for trial".

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French function, from Old French fonction, from Latin functiō (“performance, execution”), from functus (Latin), perfect participle of fungor (Latin “to perform, execute, discharge”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to enjoy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: function + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Middle French funerailles (“funeral rites”), from Medieval Latin fūnerālia (“funeral rites”), originally neuter plural of Late Latin fūnerālis (“having to do with a funeral”), from Latin fūnus (“funeral, death, corpse”), origin unknown, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰew- (“to die”). Singular and plural used interchangeably in English until circa 1700. The adjective funereal (English) is first attested 1725, by influence of , from , from funus (Latin). .

Displaced native līcþeġnung (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Affix: fun + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English furre,forre, from Anglo-Norman forre,fuerre (“case; sheath”), from Frankish *fōdar, from Proto-West Germanic *fōdr, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“sheath”) (compare fōdor (Old English “sheaf”), voering (Dutch “lining”), Futter (German “lining”), 𐍆𐍉𐌳𐍂 (Gothic “sheath”)), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-, *poh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to protect”) (compare piemuō (Lithuanian “protection”), πῶῠ̈ (Ancient Greek “flock”), πῶμα (Ancient Greek “lid”), ποιμήν (Ancient Greek “shepherd”), հօրան (Classical Armenian “herd, flock”), pawan (Kurmanji Kurdish “to watch over”), पाति (Sanskrit “he watches, protects”).

The verb is from Middle English furren, from Anglo-Norman furrer, forrer (Old French), fourrer (Old French “to line, stuff, fill”), from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English furious, from Old French furieus, from Latin furiōsus. Displaced native hātheort (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English furiously; equivalent to furious + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English further, forther (Middle English), from Old English forþor, furþor (Old English “further”), from Proto-West Germanic *furþer, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (a common preposition), equivalent to fore (English) + ; or as sometimes stated, as . Cognate with forder (Scots), furder (Scots “further”), foarder (Saterland Frisian “further”), fierder (Western Frisian “further”), verder (Dutch “further”), fürder (German “further”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English furthermore, forthermore (Middle English), forthermar (Middle English) (also as forther mo (Middle English)), equivalent to further + -more (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English future, futur (Middle English), from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (Latin “to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”). Cognate with bēo (Old English “to become, will be; to be”). More at be (English). . Displaced native tōweard (Old English), which took on a different meaning as toward (English), and afterhede (Middle English “future”) in the given sense.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gayn, gain (Middle English), gein (Middle English “profit, advantage”), from Old Norse gagn (“benefit, advantage, use”), from Proto-Germanic *gagną, *gaganą (Proto-Germanic “gain, profit", literally "return”), from Proto-Germanic *gagana (“back, against, in return”), a reduplication of Proto-Germanic *ga- (“with, together”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”).

Cognate with gagn (Icelandic “gain, advantage, use”), gagn (Swedish “benefit, profit”), gavn (Danish “gain, profit, success”), 𐌲𐌰𐌲𐌴𐌹𐌲𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to gain, profit”), gegn (Old Norse “ready”), dialectal gen (Swedish “useful, noteful”), cum (Latin “with”); see gain- (English), again (English), against (English). Compare also gaynen (Middle English), geinen (Middle English “to be of use, profit, avail”), - (Icelandic) and gagna (Swedish “to avail, help”), gavne (Danish “to benefit”).

The Middle English word was reinforced by Middle French gain (“gain, profit, advancement, cultivation”), from Old French gaaing, gaaigne (Old French), gaigne (Old French), a noun derivative of gaaignier (Old French), gaigner (Old French “to till, earn, win”), from Frankish *waiþanōn (“to pasture, graze, hunt for food”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *waiþiz, *waiþō (Proto-Germanic), *waiþijō (Proto-Germanic “pasture, field, hunting ground”); compare weidōn (Old High German), weidanōn (Old High German “to hunt, forage for food”) (Modern Weide (German “pasture”)), veiða (Old Norse “to catch, hunt”), wǣþan (Old English “to hunt, chase, pursue”). Related to wide (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From dialectal English gen (English), gin (English), short for again (English), agen (English “against”); also Middle English gain, gayn (Middle English), gein (Middle English), ȝæn (Middle English “against”), from Old English gēan, geġn (Old English “against”). More at against (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English gayn, gein (Middle English), geyn (Middle English “straight, direct, short, fit, good”), from Old Norse gegn (“straight, direct, short, ready, serviceable, kindly”), from gegn (Old Norse “opposite, against”) (whence gagna (Old Norse “to go against, meet, suit, be meet”)); see above. Adverb from Middle English gayn, gayne (Middle English “fitly, quickly”), from the adjective.

chain.meaning: straight, direct, short, ready, serviceable, kindly

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compare gan (Welsh “a mortise”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English galery, gallerye (Middle English), from Middle French galerie, gallerie (Middle French), from Old French galerie, gallerie (Old French “a long portico, a gallery”), from Medieval Latin galeria (“gallery”), of . Perhaps an alteration of Latin galilea (“church porch”), probably from Latin Galilaea, Galilee, region of Israel. More at Galilee (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gangen, from Old English gangan (“to go, walk, turn out”), from Proto-West Germanic *gangan, from Proto-Germanic *ganganą (“to go, walk”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ- (“to step, walk”).

Cognate with gang (Scots “to go on foot, walk”), gånga (Swedish “to walk, go”), ganga (Faroese “to walk”), ganga (Icelandic “to walk, go”), ganga (Norwegian Nynorsk “to walk, go”), जंहस् (Vedic Sanskrit). Ultimately related to , which see below.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gang, from Old English gang (“a journey; way; passage”), from Proto-West Germanic *gang, from Proto-Germanic *gangaz, from Proto-Indo-European —, from *ǵʰengʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to step; stride”).

Cognate with Gong (Saterland Frisian), gang (Dutch), Gang (German), gang (Norwegian), gång (Swedish), gangur (Icelandic), जंहस् (Vedic Sanskrit).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: See gan (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Shortening of gangbang (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English gap//gappe, from Old Norse gap (“an empty space, gap, chasm”), from gapa (Old Norse “to gape, scream”), from Proto-Germanic *gapōną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂- (“to open wide, gape”). Related to gab (Danish “an expanse, space, gap”), ġeap (Old English “open space, expanse”). .

etymologies.text: From: gup

etymologies.text: French garage (“keeping under cover, protection, shelter”), derivative of French garer (“to keep under cover, dock, shunt, guard, keep”), from Middle French garer, garrer (Middle French), guerrer (Middle French); partly from Old French garir, warir (Old French) (from Old Frankish *warjan); and partly from Old French varer (“to fight, defend oneself, protect”), from Old Norse varask (“to defend oneself”), reflexive of vara (Old Norse “to ware, watch out, defend”); both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *warjaną (“to defend, ward off”), *warōną (Proto-Germanic “to watch, protect”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to close, cover, protect, save, defend”).

chain.meaning: to keep under cover, dock, shunt, guard, keep

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gardener, either calqued or loaned from Anglo-Norman — and Old Northern French gardinier.

See garden, and compare Gärtner (German “gardener”), which is equivalent to a derivative of the German cognate to garden (English), Garten (German “garden”), + -er (German).

Displaced native wyrtweard (Old English) (effectively "wortward").

etymologies.text: Affix: garden + -ing

etymologies.text: Dutch gas, in Ortus Medicinae. Derived from Ancient Greek χάος (“chasm, void, empty space”); perhaps also inspired by geest (Dutch “breath, vapour, spirit”). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gate (the forms ȝate (Middle English) and ȝeat (Middle English) yielded the dialectal doublet yate (English)), from the plural of Old English ġeat (specifically gatu (Old English)), from Proto-West Germanic *gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą (“hole, opening”).

See also gat (Old Norse), - (Swedish) and gat (Dutch), Gaat (Low German), Gööt (Low German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Old Norse gata, from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ. Cognate with gade (Danish), gata (Swedish), Gasse (German “lane”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English gaderen, from Old English gaderian (“to gather, assemble”), from Proto-West Germanic *gadurōn (“to bring together, unite, gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, assemble, keep”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
160px|thumb|Male gay couple
160px|thumb|Female gay couple

From Middle English gay, from Old French gai (“joyful, laughing, merry”), usually thought to be a borrowing of pro gai (“impetuous, lively”), from Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌴𐌹𐍃 (“impetuous”), merging with earlier Old French jai , from Frankish *gāhi; both from Proto-Germanic *ganhuz, *ganhwaz (Proto-Germanic “sudden”). This is possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ- (“to stride, step”), from *ǵʰeh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “to leave”), but Kroonen rejects this derivation and treats the Germanic word as having no known etymology.

Cognate with gauw (Dutch “fast, quickly”), Westphalian gau (Low German), gai (Low German “fast, quick”), jäh (German “abrupt, sudden”).

Anatoly Liberman, following Frank Chance and Harri Meier, believes Old French gai was instead a native development from Latin vagus (“wandering, inconstant, flighty”), with *[w] > [g] as in gaine (French).

The sense of homosexual (first recorded no later than 1937 by Cary Grant in the film Bringing Up Baby, and possibly earlier in 1922 in the poem "Miss Furr and Miss Skeene" by ) was shortened from earlier gay boy ("young male prostitute") and gay cat ("homosexual boy") in underworld and prison slang, itself first attested about 1935, but used earlier for a young tramp or hobo attached to an older one.

Pejorative usage is due to hostility towards homosexuality.

The sense of ‘upright’, used in reference to a dog’s tail, probably derives from the ‘happy’ sense of the word.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Pitman kay, which it is derived from graphically, and the sound it represents. The traditional name gee was considered inappropriate, as the Pitman letter never has the sound of that name.

etymologies.text: From Middle English general, in turn from Anglo-Norman general, generall (Old French), Middle French general, and their source, Latin generālis, from genus (Latin “class, kind”) + -ālis (Latin “-al”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English generally, generalliche (Middle English), equivalent to general + -ly (English).

etymologies.text: From generō + -ate (English), from genus + -ō (Latin); see genus. Compare generare (Italian), générer (French) (and its older (and now obsolete) cognate from , gender (English “engender, breed, copulate”)).

etymologies.text: From Middle French genereux, and its source, Latin generōsus (“of noble birth”), from genus (Latin “race, stock”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Ancient Greek γένεσις (“origin”). in a letter to zoologist Adam Sedgwick, and first used publicly by Bateson at a lecture to the International Conference on Plant Hybridization in 1906.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English gentil (“courteous, noble”), from Old French gentil (“high-born, noble”), from Latin gentilis (“of the same family or clan”), from gens (Latin “[Roman] clan”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English gentilman, morphologically gentle + man (English), .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English gentilly, gentlych (Middle English), gentilliche (Middle English), equivalent to gentle + -ly (English), with simplified to by haplology.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin genuīnus (“innate, native, natural”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: genuine + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English geten, from Old Norse geta, from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to find; to acquire, attain, get, hold, receive”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to find; to hold; to seize; to take”).

Cognate with get (Yola “to get”), gide (Danish “to care, like”), gita (Faroese “to be able”), geta (Icelandic “to be able; to beget, father; to achieve, obtain, to guess; to mention”), gjeta (Norwegian Nynorsk), gjete (Norwegian Nynorsk “to guess; to mention”), gida (gmq-scy “to have the energy to, to feel up for”), gæda (gmq-scy “to guess”), gita (Swedish), gitta (Swedish “to be able, to bring oneself to, to care”), 𐌱𐌹𐌲𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to discover, find”); also edera (Latin), hedera (Latin “ivy”), praeda (Latin “booty, pillage, plunder; prey; gain, profit”), prehendō (Latin), prēndō (Latin “to grab, grasp, seize; to attain, reach”), χανδάνω (Ancient Greek “to comprise, contain, hold”), gjej (Albanian “to find”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Variant of git (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Hebrew גֵּט.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The is derived from Middle English gost, from Old English gāst, gǣst (Old English “breath, spirit, soul, ghost”) (compare modern Holy Ghost (English)), from Proto-West Germanic *gaist, from Proto-Germanic *gaistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰéysdos, from *ǵʰéysd- (Proto-Indo-European “anger, agitation”).

The h in the spelling appears in the Prologue to ’s Royal Book, printed in 1484, in a reference to the “Holy Ghoost”. It was likely influenced by gheest (Middle Dutch), a common variant of geest (Middle Dutch). Both Caxton and his assistant had connections to the Low Countries. .

The and are derived from the noun. The verb gained prominence in the 2010s.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English geaunt, geant (Middle English), from Old French geant, gaiant (Old French) (Modern géant (French)) from Vulgar Latin *gagās, , from Latin gigās, gigant- (Latin), from Ancient Greek γίγας (“giant”). Cognate to giga- (English “1,000,000,000”). Largely Displaced native ent (Old English “giant”), eoten (Old English “giant or jötunn”), and þyrs (Old English “giant or ogre”). Compare ent (English “giant tree-man”), ettin (English “giant or troll”) and thurse (English “giant”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French giraffe, from Italian giraffa, from Arabic زُرَافَة, from Syriac ܙܪܝܦܐ, from Classical Persian زُرْنَاپَا. .

etymologies.text: Affix: girl + friend

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English given, yeven (Middle English), yiven (Middle English), ȝiven (Middle English), from merger of Old English ġefan, ġeofan (Old English), ġiefan (Old English), ġifan (Old English), ġiofan (Old English), ġyfan (Old English “to give”) and Old Norse gefa (“to give”), from Proto-Germanic *gebaną (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ- (“to give; to take”). , from yiven (Middle English), of the same origin, from influence of Old Norse gefa (Old Norse).

Cognate with gee (Yola), ye (Yola), yie (Yola), yive (Yola “to give”), gie (Scots “to give”), gjiuwe (North Frisian), iiv (North Frisian), jiiw (North Frisian), jiw (North Frisian), jeewe (North Frisian “to give”), jaan (Western Frisian “to give”), gë (Alemannic “to give”), gebn (Bavarian “to give”), jevve (Central Franconian “to give”), gem (Cimbric), ghèban (Cimbric “to give”), geven (Dutch “to give”), geben (German “to give”), ginn (lb “to give”), gaon (Ripuarian “to give”), געבן (Yiddish “to give”), give (Danish “to give”), djävå (Elfdalian “to give”), geva (Faroese “to give”), gefa (Icelandic “to give”), gi (Norwegian Bokmål “to give”), gi (Norwegian Nynorsk), giva (Norwegian Nynorsk), gje (Norwegian Nynorsk), gjeva (Norwegian Nynorsk), gjeve (Norwegian Nynorsk “to give”), ge (Swedish), gifva (Swedish), giva (Swedish “to give”), 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to give”); also κεφάλι (Greek (Modern)), κεφαλή (Greek (Modern) “head”), gobti (Lithuanian “cover up; to grab, snatch”), gabać (Polish “to touch; to tap; to accost”), ха̏бати (Serbo-Croatian), hȁbati (Serbo-Croatian “to abrade, wear out”), गभस्ति (Sanskrit “shining”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English glad, gled (Middle English), from Old English glæd (“shining; bright; cheerful; glad”), from Proto-Germanic *gladaz (“shiny; gleaming; radiant; happy; glossy; smooth; flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰladʰ-, from *ǵʰelh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to shine”).

Cognate with gled (Scots), glaid (Scots “shining; bright; glad”), glääd (Saterland Frisian “smooth; sleek”), glêd (Western Frisian “smooth”), glad (Dutch “smooth; sleek; slippery”), glatt (German “smooth; sleek; slippery”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian) and glad (Swedish “glad; happy; cheerful”), glaður (Icelandic “glad; joyful; cheery”), glaber (Latin “smooth; hairless; bald”), гла́дкий (Russian “smooth”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Late Middle English glenchen (“of a blow: to strike obliquely, glance; of a person: to turn quickly aside, dodge”), a blend of:

* Old French glacier, glachier (Old French), glaichier (Old French “to slide; to slip”) (whence also glacen (Middle English “of a blow: to strike obliquely, glance; to glide”)), from glace (Old French “frozen water, ice”) (from Vulgar Latin *glacia, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”), of uncertain origin, + -ier (Old French); and
* Old French guenchir, ganchir (Old French “to avoid; to change direction; to elude, evade”), from Proto-West Germanic *wankijan (“to move aside; to stagger, sway; to wave”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weng- (“to bend”).

The noun is derived from the verb.

The sense "to look briefly (at something)" is probably due to partial conflation with glenten (Middle English “to look askance”)—the ancestor of glint (English)—in the Middle English period. This conflation may also have reinforced the medial -n-. See glint (English)

chain.meaning: of a blow: to strike obliquely, glance; of a person: to turn quickly aside, dodge

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gon, goon (Middle English), from Old English gān (“to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave”).

The inherited past tense form yode (English) (compare ēode (Old English)) was replaced through suppletion in the 15th century by went (English), from wendan (Old English “to go, depart, wend”).

Cognate with gae (Scots), gan (Scots), gang (Scots), ging (Scots), gyang (Scots “to go”), go (Yola), goe (Yola), goeth (Yola), gow (Yola “to go”), gean (Western Frisian “to go”), gaa (Alemannic), go (Alemannic “to go, walk, step”), geh (Bavarian “to go”), ghéenan (Cimbric), gian (Cimbric “to go”), gaan (Dutch “to go”), gan (Low German (Netherlands)), gaon (Low German (Netherlands) “to go”), gehen (German “to go”), gahn (Low German (Germany) “to go”), gaon (Limburgish), goëne (Limburgish “to go”), goen (lb “to go”), gejn (Ripuarian), gyjn (Ripuarian “to go”), גיין (Yiddish “to go, walk”), gå (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “to go, walk”), geen (gme-cgo “to go”), 𐌲𐌰𐌲𐌲𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to go”). Compare also ngah (Albanian “to run, drive, go”), κιχάνω (Ancient Greek “to meet with, arrive at”), 𐬰𐬀𐬰𐬁𐬨𐬌 (ae), जहाति (Sanskrit “to shun, avoid, lay aside”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gol (“boundary, limit”), from Old English *gāl (“obstacle, barrier, marker”), from Proto-West Germanic *gailu, from Proto-Germanic *gailō (“crevice, gap”); compare the Old English's derivatives gǣlan (Old English “to hinder, delay”), and hyġegǣls (Old English “hesitating, slow, sluggish”), hyġegǣlsa (Old English “slow one, sluggish one”).

Possibly cognate with gãlas (Lithuanian “end”), gals (Latvian “end”), gallan (Old Prussian “death”), ngalem (Albanian “to be limping, lame, paralyzed”), ngel (Albanian “to remain, linger, hesitate, get stuck”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English god, from Old English god, originally neuter, then changed to masculine to reflect the change in religion to Christianity, from Proto-West Germanic *god, from Proto-Germanic *gudą; see there for further origin.

Cognate with God (Scots “God”), God (Yola), Gud (Yola “God”), gud (Yola “god”), God (Saterland Frisian “God”), God (Western Frisian “God”), god (Western Frisian “deity, god”), - (Alemannic), - (Cimbric), - (German), - (lb) and Gott (mhn “God”), Jott (Central Franconian “God”), god (Dutch “deity, god”), Gód (Limburgish “God”), gód (Limburgish “god”), Göt (Ripuarian “God”), גאָט (Yiddish “god; God”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian Bokmål) and gud (Swedish “god; God”), Gud (Faroese “God”), goð (Icelandic “idol, pagan god”), guð (Icelandic), Guð (Icelandic “God”), Gu (Norwegian Nynorsk), Gud (Norwegian Nynorsk “God”), gu (Norwegian Nynorsk), gud (Norwegian Nynorsk “god”), 𐌲𐌿𐌸 (Gothic “deity, god; God”).

Not related to the word good (English) or خدا (Persian “god”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English golden, a restored form (due to the noun gold (English)) of earlier Middle English gulden, gylden (Middle English), gilden (Middle English) , from Old English gylden (“golden”), from Proto-West Germanic *gulþīn, from Proto-Germanic *gulþīnaz (“golden, made of gold”), equivalent to gold + en (English).

Cognate with gouden (Dutch), gulden (Dutch “golden”), gülden (German), golden (German “golden”), gylden (Danish “golden”). . More at gold (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From gold + en (English), or perhaps a derivation from the adjective above.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English good, from Old English gōd, from Proto-West Germanic *gōd, from Proto-Germanic *gōdaz (“good”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, be associated, suit, fit”).

Related to gather (English) and together (English), but not to god (English)/God (English).

Eclipsed non-native bon (Middle English), bone (Middle English), boon (Middle English), boun (Middle English “good”) borrowed from bon (Old French “good”), from bonus (Latin “good”).

Cognate with gude (Scots), guid (Scots “good”), gayde (Yola), gooude (Yola), gude (Yola “good”), goud (North Frisian), gud (North Frisian), guid (North Frisian), gur (North Frisian), gödj (North Frisian), gööd (North Frisian “good”), goud (Saterland Frisian “good”), goed (Western Frisian “good”), guet (Alemannic “good”), guad (Bavarian “good”), gut (Central Franconian), jot (Central Franconian), jott (Central Franconian “good”), guat (Cimbric), guut (Cimbric “good”), goed (Dutch “good”), good (Low German (Netherlands) “good”), gut (German “good”), good (Limburgish), gott (Limburgish “good”), god (Low German), goot (Low German (Germany)), got (Low German (Germany)), gued (Low German (Germany) “good”), gutt (lb “good”), guat (mhn “good”), güt (Ripuarian “good”), גוט (Yiddish “good”), god (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “good”), guoð (Elfdalian “good”), góður (Faroese / Icelandic “good”), 𐌲𐍉𐌸𐍃 (Gothic “good”), *guths (xvn “good”); also nge (Albanian “chance, leisure, opportunity, time”), gods (Latvian “honor”), guõdas (Lithuanian “nobleness, virtue; glory, honour”), го́дны (Belarusian “worthy”), го́ден (Bulgarian “fit, suitable”), hodný (Czech “good, kind”), godny (Polish), godzien (Polish “dignified, worthy”), го́дный (Russian “fit, well-suited, good for; (coll.) good”), гі́дний (Ukrainian “deserving, worthy”), го́дний (Ukrainian “fit, well-suited, good for; (coll.) good”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English goode (“good, well”), from the adjective. Compare goed (Dutch “good, well”), gut (German “good, well”), godt (Danish “good, well”), gott (Swedish “good, well”), all from the adjective.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Middle English good, god (Middle English), from Old English gōd (“a good thing, advantage, benefit, gift; good, goodness, welfare; virtue, ability, doughtiness; goods, property, wealth”), from Proto-Germanic *gōdą (“goods, belongings”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ-, *gʰodʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to unite, be associated, suit”). Compare Gut (German “item of merchandise; estate; property”).

chain.meaning: a good thing, advantage, benefit, gift; good, goodness, welfare; virtue, ability, doughtiness; goods, property, wealth

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

From Middle Dutch grabben or Middle Low German grabben (“to grasp, grab, seize, snatch”), from Old Saxon gravan, from Proto-West Germanic *grabbōn, a secondary form of Proto-Germanic *grabōną (“to gather, rake”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrebʰ- (“to gather, rake, grab, seize”).

Related to archaic grappen (German “to grab”), grabbe (Danish “to grab”), grabba (Swedish “to grab”), grápa (Old Norse “to seize, appropriate”), grappen (Middle English “to feel, grope, grasp, clutch”), ġegræppian (Old English “to seize”).

Related also to गृह्णाति (Sanskrit), गृभ्णाति (Sanskrit “he seizes”), 𐬔𐬭𐬀𐬠 (ae “to seize”)), грабне (Macedonian “to snatch”), грабя (Bulgarian “to rob, to grab”).

Cognate with 𐌲𐍂𐌹𐌸𐍃 (Gothic “step, grade”), Gritt (Bavarian “step, stride”), grìdiju (Lithuanian “to go, wander”).

The noun is originally derived within Latin from the adjective via substantivization, see -ate. Sense 10 of the verb, relating to Japanese entertainment, is a .

Alternatively, a regular reflex of Medieval Latin *credentāre with regular voicing of /k/ before a liquid plus low vowel. More at guarantee (English), credit (English).

Cognate with graven (Dutch “to dig”), graben (German “to dig”), grave (Danish “to dig”), gräva (Swedish “to dig”), grafa (Icelandic “to dig”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English greet, grete (Middle English “great, large”), from Old English grēat (“big, massive; tall; thick; coarse”), from Proto-West Germanic *graut, from Proto-Germanic *grautaz (“coarse, crude; big, large”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd-, *gʰer- (Proto-Indo-European “to rub; to stroke; to grind; to remove”).

Cognate with graat (Scots), great (Scots), greet (Scots “great”), graat (Yola “great”), grat (North Frisian), groot (North Frisian), grot (North Frisian), grut (North Frisian), gråt (North Frisian), gurt (North Frisian “big, great, large”), groot (Saterland Frisian “big, large”), grut (Western Frisian “big, great, large”), groß (Alemannic), gruuss (Alemannic “very large”), jruß (Central Franconian “big, great, large”), gròas (Cimbric), groaz (Cimbric “big, great, large”), groot (Dutch / Low German (Germany) “big, great, large”), gross (German), groß (German “big, large”), grut (Limburgish), gruët (Limburgish “big, large; grand; tall; adult; pregnant”), grouss (lb “big, great, large”), groas (mhn “big, great, large”), grus (Ripuarian), grūs (Ripuarian “big, great, large”), גרויס (Yiddish “big, large”); also grandis (Latin “big, great, large”), χρίω (Greek (Modern) “to anoint”), grind (Albanian “to brawl, fight”), grauds (Latvian “grain”), grūdas (Lithuanian “grain”), hrouda (Czech), hruda (Czech “clod”), грутка (Macedonian “clod, clump, lump”), gruda (Polish “clod, lump; frozen ground; mud fever, scratches”), гру́да (Russian “clod, heap, mass, pile”), гру̏да (Serbo-Croatian), гру̏два (Serbo-Croatian), grȕda (Serbo-Croatian), grȕdva (Serbo-Croatian “clod, lump; snowball”), կորկոտ (Armenian “groats of wheat or barley”), घर्षति (Sanskrit “to brush, polish, rub”). Related to grit (English). .

The modern pronunciation shows an irregular change of Early Modern English to in the standard language; contrast this with the development of other words such as beat (English) and heat (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English gretnesse, gretnes (Middle English), greetnesse (Middle English), from Old English grēatnes. Equivalent to great + -ness (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gredy, from Anglian Old English grēdiġ (“greedy, hungry, eager”) (cognate West Saxon form grǣdiġ (Old English)), from Proto-Germanic *grēdagaz (“hungry”), from Proto-Germanic *grēdaz, *grēduz (Proto-Germanic), *grēdô (Proto-Germanic “hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer-. Equivalent to greed + -y (English).

Cognate with grādag (Old Saxon “greedy”), graag (Dutch “gladly, willingly”), grātag (Old High German “greedy”), grådig (Danish “greedy”), grådig (Norwegian Bokmål “greedy”) (from gráðigr (Old Norse “greedy”), gráði (Old Norse “greed, hunger”)), 𐌲𐍂𐌴𐌳𐌰𐌲𐍃 (Gothic “hungry”). गृद्धि (Sanskrit “greed”) is a false cognate.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English grene, from Old English grēne, from Proto-West Germanic *grōnī, from Proto-Germanic *grōniz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow”). More at grow. .

See also green (North Frisian), grien (Western Frisian), groen (Dutch), grön (Low German), green (Low German), greun (Low German (Germany)), grün (German), grøn (Danish / Norwegian Nynorsk), grön (Swedish), grønn (Norwegian Bokmål), grønur (Faroese), grænn (Icelandic).

The sense of obscene, pornographic, or sexual in the Philippines is a Spanish verde. In other varieties of English, blue is the color instead associated with obscenity or pornography.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English grenen, from Old English grēnian (“to become green, flourish”), from Proto-West Germanic *grōnijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōnijōną, *grōnijaną (Proto-Germanic “to become green”), from the adjective (see above).

Cognate with gräinje (Saterland Frisian), grönen (Low German (Germany)), grünen (German), gröna (Swedish), gróna (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From the colors used on traffic lights; green being the one that allows vehicles to move on.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English greten, from Old English grētan, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōtijaną.

Cognate with groeten (Dutch), grüßen (German), grüssen (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English greet, grete (Middle English “great”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From a blend of two Old English — verbs, grētan (Old English), grǣtan (Old English) (itself from Proto-West Germanic *grātan); and of grēotan (Old English) (itself from *greutan (Proto-West Germanic)), both meaning "to weep, lament".

Possibly reinforced in Northern England and Scotland by Old Norse gráta, whence also græde (Danish), gråte (Norwegian), gråta (Swedish), all meaning "to cry, to weep".

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English grey, from Old English grēġ (Anglian). The spelling grey (English) reflects the Anglian vowel development, whereas the variant gray (English) stems from the West Saxon form grǣġ (Old English) (through Middle English gray (Middle English)). Further derived from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz (compare grauw (Dutch), grau (German), grár (Old Norse)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁- (“to green, to grow”) (compare rāvus (Latin “grey”), зьрѭ (Church Slavonic “to see, to glance”), зреть (Russian “to watch, to look at”) (archaic), žeriù (Lithuanian “to shine”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English greef, gref (Middle English), from Old French grief (“grave, heavy, grievous, sad”), from Latin gravis (“heavy, grievous, sad”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: 1655, from French gril, from Middle French gril, from Old French greïl, graïl (Old French “gridiron”), from graïlle (Old French “grate, grating”), from Latin crātīcula (“gridiron”), diminutive of crātis (Latin “hurdle, wickerwork”), q.v. Related to griddle (English), hurdle (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English grillen (“to anger, provoke”), from Old English grillan, griellan (Old English “to annoy, vex, offend”), from Proto-West Germanic *gralljan (“to shout, make angry”). Cognate with grulje (Saterland Frisian “to make angry”), grillen (Dutch “to shudder, shiver”), vergrellen (Low German “to anger, provoke”), grollen (German “to rumble”) and perhaps also with grouiller (French “to swarm”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English gril, grille (Middle English “harsh, rough, severe”), from Old English *grielle, from Proto-West Germanic *grallī (“angry”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to rattle, make a noise, grumble”). Cognate with grell (German “harsh, angry”), grel (Danish “shrill, glaring, dazzling”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English grille, from Old English *grylla, *griella (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *gralljō.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Verb from Middle English grippen, from Old English grippan, from a Proto-Germanic *gripjaną (compare gripfen (Old High German)); compare the related grīpan (Old English), whence English gripe (English). See also grope (English), and the related *grīpaną (Proto-Germanic).

Noun from Middle English grippe, gripe (Middle English), an amalgam of Old English gripe (“grasp, hold”) (cognate with Griff (German)) and Old English gripa (“handful”) (cognate with grepp (Swedish)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English grip, grippe (Middle English), gryppe (Middle English “a ditch, drain”), from Old English grēp (“a furrow, burrow”) and grēpe (Old English “a furrow, ditch, drain”), from Proto-Germanic *grōpiz (“a furrow, groove”). Cognate with grippe (Middle Dutch), gruppe (Middle Dutch “ditch, drain”), greppe (Middle Dutch), Gruppe (Low German (Germany) “ditch, drain”). Related also to grōp (Old English “a ditch, drain”). More at groop (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: 1604, short for bridegroom (English “husband-to-be”), from Middle English brydgrome, alteration (with intrusive r) of earlier bridegome (Middle English “bridegroom”), from Old English brȳdguma (“bridegroom”), from brȳd (Old English “bride”) + guma (Old English “man, hero”). In Middle English, the second element was re-analyzed as or influenced by grom (Middle English), grome (Middle English “attendant”). guma (Old English “Guma”) derives from Proto-Germanic *gumô (“man, person”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰm̥mō; it is cognate to gumi (Icelandic) (cf. brúðgumi (Icelandic)) and gume (Norwegian) and, ultimately, human (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English grom, grome (Middle English “man-child, boy, youth”), of uncertain origin. Apparently related to grom (Middle Dutch “boy”), Old grómr (Icelandic), gromr (Icelandic “man, manservant, boy”), gromme (Old French “manservant”), and also to grom (Middle Dutch “fish guts”), grôm (Middle Low German “fish guts”), from the same Proto-Germanic — root. Possibly from Old English *grōm, from Proto-West Germanic *grōm (“swollen belly, stomach tumour, womb-child, fish roe, fish guts”), from Proto-Germanic *grōaną (“to grow”).

Alternative etymology describes Middle English grom, grome as an alteration of gome (Middle English “man”) with an intrusive r (also found in bridegroom (English), hoarse (English), cartridge (English), etc.), with the Middle Dutch and Old Icelandic cognates following similar variation of their respective forms.
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English grom, grome (Middle English “man-child, boy, youth”), of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ground, from Old English grund, from Proto-West Germanic *grundu, from Proto-Germanic *grunduz. Cognate with grûn (Western Frisian), grond (Dutch) and Grund (German).

Compare (bring (English “to bring”)) down to earth (English), come down to earth (English “to come down to earth”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Inflected form of grind (English). See also milled (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English growen, from Old English grōwan (“to grow, increase, flourish, germinate”), from Proto-West Germanic *grōan, from Proto-Germanic *grōaną (“to grow, grow green”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).

Cognate with groeien (Dutch “to grow”), grojen (Low German (Germany) “to green; thrive; take hold; flourish”), gro (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “to grow”), grógva (Faroese “to grow”), gróa (Icelandic “to grow”); also grāmen (Latin “grass, turf; herb, plant”), herba (Latin “grass, herbage; weeds; plant”), гря́ний (Ukrainian “green”). Related to growth, grass, green.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From grow + th (English). Compare grēd (Old Frisian) , gruote (Middle High German), gruot (Middle High German “greens, fresh growth, shoot”), gróðr (Old Norse) . More at grow (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French guarantie (perhaps via a later Spanish garante), from the verb guarantir (Old French “to protect, assure, vouch for”), ultimately from Old Frankish *warjand, *warand (Frankish “a warrant”), or from guaranty (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
right|thumb|A guard (person protecting or watching over something)

From Middle English garde, from early Middle French — or late Old French guarde (“a guardian, warden, keeper”) (whence modern garde (French)), from the verb guarder (Old French). , which is from - (Irish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From early Middle French garder or late Old French — (circa 14th cent) guarder (Old French “to keep, ward, guard, save, preserve, etc.”), from Early Medieval Latin wardo, from Frankish *wardēn, from Proto-Germanic *wardāną (“to guard, protect”). Cognate with garder (French), weardian (Old English) (whence also the English inherited doublet ). See also regard (English).

chain.meaning: to keep, ward, guard, save, preserve, etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gessen and Middle English gesse, probably of gmq — origin, from Old Danish getse, gitse (Old Danish), getsa (Old Danish “to guess”), from Old Norse *getsa, *gitsa (Old Norse), from Proto-Germanic *gitisōną (“to guess”), from Proto-Germanic *getaną (“to get”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to take, seize”).

Cognate with gisne (Danish “to guess”), gissa (Norwegian), gjette (Norwegian “to guess”), gissa (Swedish “to guess”), gisje (Saterland Frisian “to guess”), gissen (Dutch “to guess”), gissen (Low German “to guess”), gis (Dutch “a guess”). Related also to giska (Icelandic) . Compare also гада́ть (Russian “to conjecture, guess, divine”), gjëzë (Albanian “riddle”) from gjej (Albanian “find, recover, obtain”). More at get (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gest, from Old Norse gestr, which replaced or was merged with ġiest (Old English), both from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest, host, someone with whom one has reciprocal duties of hospitality”). , from Latin.
