etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: c. 1325–75. From Middle English guide, from the Old French guide, from pro guida, from guidar (pro), from Frankish *wītan (“to show the way, lead”), from Proto-Germanic *wītaną (“to see, know; go, depart”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, know”). Cognate with wītan (Old English “to see, take heed to, watch after, guard, keep”). Related also to wit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English guiden, from Old French guider, from pro guidar, from Frankish *wītan (“to show the way, lead”), from Proto-Germanic *wītaną (“to see, know; go, depart”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, know”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English gilt, gult (Middle English), from Old English gylt (“guilt, sin, offense, crime, fault”), of obscure origin. Possibly related with ġieldan (Old English “to pay, requite, punish”) (whence yield (English)), from Proto-West Germanic *guldijā (whence gülte (Middle High German “debt, fee, financial duty”), gülde (Middle Low German), Gülte (German)), from Proto-West Germanic *geldan (“to pay for”), from Proto-Germanic *geldaną (“to pay”). However, neither the Old English stem form nor its ending (instead of ) fit the continental form.
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English gilt, gult (Middle English), from Old English gylt (“guilt, sin, offense, crime, fault”), of obscure origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English gilten, gylten (Middle English), from Old English gyltan (“to commit sin, be guilty”), from gylt (Old English “guilt, sin, offense, crime, fault”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English gilty, gulty (Middle English), from Old English gyltiġ (“offending, guilty”); equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: guitar + -ist

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English gom, gome (Middle English), gomme (Middle English), goome (Middle English), gum (Middle English), gume (Middle English), gumme (Middle English), from Old English gōma (“palate”), from Proto-West Germanic *gōmō, from Proto-Germanic *gaumô, *gōmô (Proto-Germanic “palate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₂- (“to gape, yawn”).

Cognate with gaumo (Cimbric “palate”), Gaum (German), Gaumen (German “palate”), Gomm (lb), Gumm (lb “palate”), גומען (Yiddish “palate”), gumme (Danish “gums”), gómur (Icelandic “gum”), gom (Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “palate”); also hio (Latin “to gape, yawn”), χάσκω (Ancient Greek “to gape, yawn”), gomurỹs (Lithuanian “palate”), зе́я (Bulgarian “to gape”), zát (Czech), zet (Czech “to gape”), ziać (Polish “to pant”), зия́ть (Russian “to gape, yawn”), зи́јати (Serbo-Croatian), zíjati (Serbo-Croatian “to gape, yawn”), зя́яти (Ukrainian “to gape”), koy- (xto “mouth”), koyn (txb “mouth”). More at yawn.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English gomme, gumme (Middle English), borrowed from Anglo-Norman gome, from Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi (Latin), from Ancient Greek κόμμι, from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (Egyptian “acanthus resin, gum”). Cognate with goma (Spanish “rubber”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English gunne,gonne, possibly from Gunnhild, a female given name formerly used as a nickname for engines of war (compare Nordic Gunn, a female name meaning “battle”). The name is composed of the Norse elements gunnr (Old Norse) and hildr (Old Norse), both meaning "battle".

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Related to ganef (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From gunna (English), from gonna (English), from going to (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin gymnasticus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From gymnastic —: see -ics; from Latin gymnasticus, from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός, from γυμναστής (Ancient Greek “athlete, gymnast”), from γῠμνᾰ́ζω (Ancient Greek “to train, exercise”), from γυμνός (Ancient Greek “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English habit, from Latin habitus (“condition, bearing, state, appearance, dress, attire”), from habeō (Latin “to have, hold, keep”). Distantly related to gift. Replaced abit (Middle English), from abit (Old French), itself from the same Latin source. Displaced native þēaw (Old English), wuna (Old English), ġewuna (Old English), and sidu (Old English).

chain.meaning: condition, bearing, state, appearance, dress, attire

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English habiten, from Old French habiter, from Latin habitō (“to dwell, abide, keep”), frequentative of habeō (Latin “to have, hold, keep”); see have.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English her, heer (Middle English), hær (Middle English), from Old English hǣr, from Proto-West Germanic *hār, from Proto-Germanic *hērą (“hair”), from Proto-Indo-European *kes- (“to scrape, comb”).

Cognate with Hier (Saterland Frisian), Híer (Saterland Frisian “hair”), hier (Western Frisian “hair”), haar (Cimbric), har (Cimbric “hair”), haar (Dutch “hair”), - (German) and Haar (Low German “hair”), Hoer (lb “hair”), hor (mhn “hair”), האָר (Yiddish “hair”), hår (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “hair”), hár (Faroese / Icelandic “hair”). Eclipsed non-native cheveler (Middle English), chevelere (Middle English “hair”), borrowed from chevelëure (Old French “hair, head-hair, coiffure, wig”).

The modern spelling with ai is not a regular representation of the vowel developed from Middle English. Rather, it is from Middle English here (haircloth) influenced by haire (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From hair + cut (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: hair + dress + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From hair + dryer (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English half, halfe (Middle English) from Old English healf (“half”); as a noun, 'half', 'side', 'part', from Proto-West Germanic *halb, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz.

Cognate with - (Old Saxon), - (Old Frisian), and half (Old Dutch), heal (Western Frisian), half (Dutch), halb (German), halv (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), hálfur (Icelandic) and 𐌷𐌰𐌻𐌱𐍃 (Gothic). Compare halve (English), behalf (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hamer, from Old English hamor, from Proto-West Germanic *hamar, from Proto-Germanic *hamaraz (“tool with a stone head”) (compare hammer (Western Frisian), Hamer (Low German), hamer (Dutch), Hammer (German), hammer (Danish), hammare (Swedish)). This is traditionally ascribed to Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱmoros, from *h₂éḱmō (Proto-Indo-European “stone”), but see *hamaraz (Proto-Germanic) for further discussion.

Originally signalled by knocking with a wooden mallet.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hond, hand (Middle English), from Old English hand, from Proto-West Germanic *handu, from Proto-Germanic *handuz.

See also - (Dutch) and hand (Swedish “hand”), hånd (Danish), Hand (German), hân (Western Frisian). Perhaps compare Old Swedish hinna (Swedish “to gain”), 𐍆𐍂𐌰𐌷𐌹𐌽𐌸𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “𐍆𐍂𐌰-𐌷𐌹𐌽𐌸𐌰𐌽”); and sīts (Latvian “hunting spear”), κεντέω (Ancient Greek “prick”), çandër (Albanian “pitchfork, prop”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English handen, honden (Middle English), from the noun (see above); and also from henden (Middle English) (> hend (English)), from Old English *hendan, ġehendan (Old English “to seize by hand, grasp, hold”), from Proto-West Germanic *handijan, from Proto-Germanic *handijaną (“to take by hand, grasp”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with handa (Old Frisian), henda (Old Frisian “to grasp, seize”), handen (Middle Low German), henden (Middle Low German) (in derivatives), handen (Dutch), henden (Dutch “to arrange, dispose, be handy”), overhandigen (Dutch “to hand, hand over”), handen (Middle High German “to cut, hew”), henden (Middle High German “to give hands to; take hold of, seize”), henda (Old Norse “to grasp, seize, take by hand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From hand + held (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From hand + ball (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
thumb|A linen handkerchief.

From hand + kerchief (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English handel, handle (Middle English), from Old English handle (“handle”), from Proto-West Germanic *handulā (“handle”). See verb below. Cognate with Hantel (German “dumbbell, barbell”), handel (Danish “handle”). Related to hand (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English handlen, from Old English handlian (“to handle, feel, deal with, discuss”), from Proto-West Germanic *handulōn, from Proto-Germanic *handulōną (“to take, grip, feel”), equivalent to . Cognate with handelje (Western Frisian), hanneljen (Western Frisian), hanljen (Western Frisian “to handle, treat”), handelen (Dutch “to handle, deal, act, negotiate”), handeln (German “to act, trade, negotiate, behave”), handla (Swedish “to buy, trade, deal”), höndla (Icelandic “to handle”).

chain.meaning: to handle, feel, deal with, discuss

etymologies.text:

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English handsum, hondsom (Middle English), equivalent to hand + some (English). Compare handzaam (Dutch), handsaam (Low German (Germany)). The original sense was “easy to handle or use”, hence “suitable” and “apt, clever” (mid-16th century), giving rise to the current appreciatory senses (late 16th century).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , equal to .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hangen, hongen (Middle English), from a fusion of Old English hōn (“to hang, be hanging”) and hangian (Old English “to hang, cause to hang”), respectively from the transitive verb Proto-West Germanic *hą̄han and the intransitive verb *hangēn (Proto-West Germanic); also probably influenced by hengja (Old Norse “to suspend”) and hanga (Old Norse “to be suspended”); all from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną and *hangāną (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱenk- (“to waver, be in suspense”).

See also hangen (Dutch), hangen (Low German) and hängen (Low German), hängen (German), henge (Norwegian Bokmål), henga (Norwegian Nynorsk); also 𐌷𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (Gothic), 𒂵𒀀𒀭𒂵 (Hittite “to hang”), शङ्कते (Sanskrit “is in doubt, hesitates”), cunctor (Latin “cūnctārī”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From hang sangwich (English), Irish colloquial pronunciation of sandwich.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Alteration of dang (English), itself a minced oath of damn (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English happily, happyly (Middle English), happyliche (Middle English), happylyche (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: happy + -ness

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hard, from Old English heard, from Proto-West Germanic *hard(ī), from Proto-Germanic *harduz, from Proto-Indo-European —, from *kret- (Proto-Indo-European “strong, powerful”).

Cognate with hard (Yola “hard”), hurd (Western Frisian “hard”), hert (Alemannic “hard”), hoat (Bavarian “hard”), haat (Central Franconian “hard”), hard (Dutch “hard”), hart (German “hard”), haart (lb “hard”), hård (Danish / Swedish “hard”), harður (Faroese / Icelandic “hard”), hard (Norwegian Bokmål “hard”), hard (Norwegian Nynorsk), hard’u (Norwegian Nynorsk “hard”), 𐌷𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (Gothic “hard”), κρατύς (Ancient Greek “strong, mighty”), क्रतु (Sanskrit “power, might, ability”), 𐬑𐬭𐬀𐬙𐬎 (ae).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English harden, herden (Middle English), from Old English heardian (“to become hard”) and hierdan (Old English “to make hard”), from Proto-West Germanic *hardēn and *hardijan (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną.

Cognate with harden (Dutch “to harden”), härten (German “to harden”), hærde (Danish “to harden; to temper”), herða (Icelandic “to harden”), herde (Norwegian Bokmål “to harden; to toughen”), herda (Norwegian Nynorsk “to make hard, temper; harden”), härda (Swedish “harden, temper”), 𐌲𐌰𐌷𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic), *𐌷𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to harden”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hardely, hardliche (Middle English), from Old English heardlīċe (“boldly; hardily; without ease; in a way that causes pain; not easily; only by degrees”), equivalent to hard + -ly (English). Compare hardelijk (Dutch), härtlich (German).

chain.meaning: boldly; hardily; without ease; in a way that causes pain; not easily; only by degrees

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hardware; equivalent to hard + -ware (English); attested since the mid-15th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English harm, herm (Middle English), from Old English hearm, from Proto-West Germanic *harm, from Proto-Germanic *harmaz (“harm; shame; pain”). Cognate with harm (Dutch “harm”), Harm (German “harm”), harme (Danish “indignation, resentment”), harmur (Icelandic “sorrow, grief”), harm (Swedish “anger, indignation, harm”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English harmful, from Old English *hearmful (suggested by hearmfullīċ (Old English “harmful; hurtful”)), equivalent to harm + ful (English).

Cognate with harmvoll (German), harmfuld (Danish), harmfull (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English harmles, from Old English *hearmlēas, from Proto-Germanic *harmalausaz (“without harm; harmless”), equivalent to harm + less (English).

Cognate with harmlos (German “harmless”), harmløs (Danish “harlmess”), harmlös (Swedish “harmless”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English armonye, from Old French harmonie,armonie, from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (“joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”), either from or cognate with ἁρμόζω (Ancient Greek “to fit together”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to join, fit, fix together”). . .

chain.meaning: joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English harvest, hervest (Middle English), from Old English hærfest (“autumn, harvest-time; August”), from Proto-West Germanic *harbist, from Proto-Germanic *harbistaz (“harvest-time, autumn, fall”), from *harbaz (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *kerp-.

Cognate with Sylt Hārefst (North Frisian), hjerst (Western Frisian), herfst (Dutch), Herbst (German), dated Harvst (Low German (Germany)), - (Danish) and høst (Norwegian Bokmål), haust (Norwegian Nynorsk); further with carpere (Latin “to seize”), καρπός (Ancient Greek “fruit”), κείρω (Ancient Greek “to cut off”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English haunten (“to reside, inhabit, use, employ”), from Old French hanter (“to inhabit, frequent, resort to”), from Old Northern French hanter (“to go back home, frequent”), from Old Norse heimta (“to bring home, fetch”) or/and from Old English hāmettan (“to bring home; house; cohabit with”); both from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną (“to house, bring home”), from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“village, home”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village”).

Cognate with hǣman (Old English “to cohabit, lie with, marry”); related to hām (Old English “home, village”), hantin (Old French “a stay, a place frequented by”) from the same Germanic source. Another descendant from the French is hanteren (Dutch), whence hantieren (German), hantera (Swedish), håndtere (Danish). More at home.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English haven, from Old English habban (“to have”), from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną (“to have”), durative of *habjaną (Proto-Germanic “to lift, take up”), from Proto-Indo-European *kapyéti, an imperfective formation to the root *kap- (Proto-Indo-European “to take, seize, catch”). Related to heave (English).

Since there is no common Indo-European root for a transitive possessive verb have (notice that habeō (Latin) is not etymologically related to English have), Proto-Indo-European probably lacked the have structure. Instead, the third person forms of be were used, with the possessor in dative case, compare Latin mihi est / sunt, literally to me is / are.

The nonstandard is a semantic loan from other languages’ term for , such as French avoir, Polish mieć, and Spanish tener.

Cognate with hae (Scots “to have”), haa (North Frisian), heewe (North Frisian “to have”), häbe (Saterland Frisian), hääbe (Saterland Frisian “to have”), hawwe (Western Frisian “to have”), hê (Afrikaans “to have”), haa (Alemannic), heen (Alemannic), hoh (Alemannic), hä (Alemannic), häbä (Alemannic), hè (Alemannic “to have”), hobm (Bavarian), hobn (Bavarian), hoom (Bavarian), håbn (Bavarian “to have”), haban (Cimbric), hen (Cimbric), håm (Cimbric “to have”), hebben (Dutch / Low German “to have”), haben (German “to have”), haane (Limburgish), höbbe (Limburgish “to have”), hunn (lb “to have”), hom (mhn “to have”), hon (Ripuarian “to have”), האָבן (Yiddish “to have”), have (Danish “to have”), åvå (Elfdalian “to have”), hava (Faroese “to have”), hafa (Icelandic “to have”), ha (Norwegian Bokmål “to have”), ha (Norwegian Nynorsk), hava (Norwegian Nynorsk), have (Norwegian Nynorsk), hå (Norwegian Nynorsk “to have”), ha (Swedish), hafva (Swedish), hava (Swedish “to have”), 𐌷𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to have”), kap (Albanian “to grab, catch, grip”), capiō (Latin “take”), хапать (Russian “to seize”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English efd, had (Middle English), hafd (Middle English), heafd (Middle English), hed (Middle English), heed (Middle English), hefet (Middle English), heid (Middle English), het (Middle English), hevd (Middle English), heved (Middle English), hevid (Middle English), hiede (Middle English), hæfd (Middle English), hæfedd (Middle English), from Old English hēafod (“head; top; leader; origin”), from Proto-West Germanic *haubud, from Proto-Germanic *haubudą (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”), from *kap- (Proto-Indo-European “head; bowl, cup”).

Cognate with heid (Scots “head”), haade (Yola), hade (Yola), heade (Yola “head”), Haur (North Frisian), hood (North Frisian “head”), Haud (Saterland Frisian), Hööft (Saterland Frisian “head”), haad (Western Frisian “head”), Haupt (Alemannic “head”), hoofd (Dutch “head”), Haupt (German), Häupt (German “head”), hiöet (Ripuarian), hiöt (Ripuarian), huöt (Ripuarian), huø̄t (Ripuarian “head”), הויפּט (Yiddish “head”), hode (Danish), hoved (Danish “head”), ovuð (Elfdalian “head”), høvd (Faroese), høvur (Faroese “head”), höfuð (Icelandic “head”), huvu (gmq-jmk “head”), hode (Norwegian Bokmål), hue (Norwegian Bokmål “head”), haud (Norwegian Nynorsk), hauv (Norwegian Nynorsk), hove (Norwegian Nynorsk), hovu (Norwegian Nynorsk), hovud (Norwegian Nynorsk), hue (Norwegian Nynorsk), huggu (Norwegian Nynorsk), hugu (Norwegian Nynorsk), hugud (Norwegian Nynorsk), huvu (Norwegian Nynorsk), huvud (Norwegian Nynorsk “head”), huweð (gmq-scy “head”), hufvud (Swedish), hufwud (Swedish), huve (Swedish), huvud (Swedish), hövve (Swedish “head”), hoef (gme-cgo “head”), 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌱𐌹𐌳 (Gothic), 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌱𐌹𐌸 (Gothic “head”); also cuach (Irish / Scottish Gaelic “bowl; dome (of head)”), cawg (Welsh “basin, bowl, vessel”), capud (Latin), capus (Latin), caput (Latin “head”), κεφάλι (Greek (Modern)), κεφαλή (Greek (Modern) “head”), کاپۆڵ (Central Kurdish “skull”), कपाल (Sanskrit “skull; bowl”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English heed, from Old English hēafod- (“main”), from Proto-West Germanic *haubida-, derived from the noun *haubid (Proto-West Germanic “head”).

Cognate with hööft- (Saterland Frisian), haad- (Western Frisian), hoofd- (Dutch), höövd- (Low German (Germany)), haupt- (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From head + line (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: head + quarter

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English helen, from Old English hǣlan (“to heal, cure, save, greet, salute”), from Proto-West Germanic *hailijan, from Proto-Germanic *hailijaną (“to heal, make whole, save”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos (“healthy, whole”). Derived from the adjective at hand in whole (English).

Cognate with hale (Scots), hail (Scots “to heal”), heila (Saterland Frisian), heilen (Saterland Frisian “to heal”), hielje (Western Frisian), helen (Dutch “to heal”), heilen (German “to heal”), hele (Danish), hela (Swedish “to heal”), and further цели́ть (Russian “to heal”), ocalić (Polish “calić”), celit (Czech “to heal”), céliti (Serbo-Croatian “to heal”).

chain.meaning: to heal, cure, save, greet, salute

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English har, heoren (Middle English), her (Middle English), here (Middle English), heren (Middle English), from Old English hēran, hīeran (Old English), hīran (Old English), hȳran (Old English “to hear”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti (“to be sharp-eared”), from *h₂eḱ- (Proto-Indo-European “sharp”) + *h₂ows- (Proto-Indo-European “ear”) + *-yéti (Proto-Indo-European) (denominative suffix).

Cognate with hear (North Frisian), hiar (North Frisian), hiir (North Frisian), hiire (North Frisian “to hear”), heere (Saterland Frisian), here (Saterland Frisian “to hear”), hearre (Western Frisian “to hear”), hearn (Bavarian “to hear”), hüre (Central Franconian “to hear”), hòrran (Cimbric), höarn (Cimbric “to hear”), horen (Dutch “to hear”), hören (German / Low German “to hear”), héieren (lb “to hear”), הערן (Yiddish “to hear”), høre (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to hear”), ära (Elfdalian “to hear”), hoyra (Faroese “to hear”), heyra (Icelandic “to hear”), haur (Norwegian Nynorsk), høra (Norwegian Nynorsk), høre (Norwegian Nynorsk), høyra (Norwegian Nynorsk), høyre (Norwegian Nynorsk “to hear”), höra (Swedish “to hear”), 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to hear”); also ακούγω (Greek (Modern)), ακούω (Greek (Modern) “to hear”), κούω (grk-ita “to hear”), āks- (txb “to awaken”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English harte, heorrte (Middle English), hert (Middle English), herte (Middle English), hierte (Middle English), hirte (Middle English), horte (Middle English), huerte (Middle English), hurte (Middle English), from Old English heorte (“heart”), from Proto-West Germanic *hertā, from Proto-Germanic *hertô (“heart”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”), from *ḱerd- (Proto-Indo-European “heart”). ; see also core (English).

Cognate with hert (Scots “heart”), hart (Yola), hearth (Yola “heart”), hart (North Frisian), härt (North Frisian “heart”), Haat (Saterland Frisian “heart”), hert (Western Frisian “heart”), hart (Dutch “heart”), erte (Flemish “heart”), Hart (Low German), Hiärt (Low German “heart”), Häerz (lb “heart”), Hertz (German), Herz (German), Herze (German “heart”), Härz (Alemannic “heart”), Hatz (Central Franconian), Hätz (Central Franconian “heart”), hèertze (Cimbric), hèrtz (Cimbric “heart”), hèrz (mhn “heart”), haoc (Ripuarian “heart”), האַרץ (Yiddish), הערץ (Yiddish “heart”), hierte (Danish), hjerte (Danish), hjærte (Danish “heart”), järta (Elfdalian “heart”), hjarta (Faroese / Icelandic “heart”), jaart (jut “heart”), hjerte (Norwegian Bokmål “heart”), hjarta (Norwegian Nynorsk), hjarte (Norwegian Nynorsk), hjerta (Norwegian Nynorsk), hjerte (Norwegian Nynorsk “heart”), hjärta (Swedish “heart”), 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍄𐍉 (Gothic “heart”); also kres (Cornish “centre, middle; waist”), croí (Irish), croidhe (Irish “heart; core; hub; sweetheart”), cree (Manx “heart”), cridhe (Scottish Gaelic “heart; courage; core; nucleus; sweetheart”), craidd (Welsh “centre, core, middle”), cor (Latin “heart”), καρδιά (Greek (Modern) “heart”), kërth (Albanian “askew”), sirds (ltg “heart”), sirde (Latvian), sirds (Latvian “heart”), širdis (Lithuanian “heart”), seyr (Old Prussian “heart”), сэ́рца (Belarusian “heart”), сърце́ (Bulgarian “heart; centre”), srdce (Czech / Slovak “heart”), срце (Macedonian “heart”), serce (Polish “heart”), се́рдце (Russian “heart”), ср̏це (Serbo-Croatian), sȑce (Serbo-Croatian “heart”), srce (Slovenian “heart”), се́рце (Ukrainian “heart”), սիրտ (Armenian “heart”), 𐬰𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬛 (ae “heart”), زرد (bal “heart; conscience”), زر (Central Kurdish “heart”), دل (Persian “heart; stomach; mind; courage”), زێڵ (hac “heart”), dil (Kurmanji Kurdish “heart”), зӕрдӕ (Ossetic “heart; soul”), زړه (Pashto “heart”), dıl (tly “heart”), zerri (zza “heart”), 𒆠𒅕 (Hittite), 𒊮𒅕 (Hittite “heart”), 𒍝𒀀𒅈𒍝 (Luwian), 𔖪𔖱𔖪 (Luwian “heart”), židi (ask “heart”), j̈arë (bsh), zërë (bsh “heart”), zër (Prakrit “heart”), kri (xto “will”), *käryā- (txb “heart”), हृद् (Sanskrit “heart; soul; breast, chest”).

Most of the modern figurative senses (such as passion or compassion, spirit, inmost feelings, especially love, affection, and courage) were present in Old English. However, the meaning “center” dates from the early 14th century. The verb sense “to love” is from the 1977 advertising campaign.

The spelling ⟨ear⟩ for is paralleled by hearken (English) and hearth (English), but is problematic since an Early Modern variant with can be posited for those words, but not heart. Perhaps it represents hart (Middle Scots) (reflecting the Scots lengthening of before then a consonant, then the early actuation of the in Scots) or a parallel development in Northern England. Alternatively, a back-spelling by speakers of dialects where preconsonantal was shortened early, allowing it to undergo the late Middle English lowering to (reflected in forms such as larn (English) "learn") is possible.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English hete, from Old English hǣtu, from Proto-West Germanic *haitī, from Proto-Germanic *haitį̄ (“heat”), from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (“heat; hot”). Cognate with hete (Scots “heat”), Hatte (Saterland Frisian “heat”), heizī (Old High German “heat”). Related also to hitte (Dutch “heat”), Hitze (German “heat”), hetta (Swedish “heat”), hiti (Faroese / Icelandic “heat”). Related to hot.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English heten, from Old English hǣtan (“to heat; become hot”), from Proto-Germanic *haitijaną (“to heat, make hot”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Either an alternative spelling of het (English “heated”), a continuation of late Middle English heet, het (English) (an analogical simple past of heten (Middle English “to heat”) created on the basis of bet (English), the past tense of beten (Middle English “to beat”)), or a later analogical formation from the past forms of beten (Middle English)'s modern reflex beat (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: heat + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From a wide variety of Middle English — forms including hevene (Middle English), heven (Middle English), hevin (Middle English) and hewin (Middle English “heaven, sky”), from Old English heofon, heofone (Old English “heaven, sky”), from Proto-West Germanic *hebun (“heaven, sky”), of uncertain origin.

Cognate with heiven (Scots), hewin (Scots “heaven, sky”), heven (Middle Dutch “sky, heaven”), Heven (Low German “heaven, sky”), and possibly the rare - (Icelandic) and hifinn (Old Norse “heaven, sky”), which are all probably dissimilated forms of the Germanic root which appears in himinn (Old Norse “heaven, sky”), 𐌷𐌹𐌼𐌹𐌽𐍃 (Gothic “heaven, sky”), himin (gmq-osw), himæn (Old Danish) and probably also (in another variant form) himil (Old Saxon), himil (Old Dutch) (modern hemel (Dutch)) and himil (Old High German) (Himmel (German)).

Accepting these as cognates, some scholars propose a further derivation from Proto-Germanic *himinaz (“cover, cloud cover, firmament, sky, heaven”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hevely, hevyliche (Middle English), from Old English hefiġlīċe (“heavily; grievously”), equivalent to heavy + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hevy, heviȝ (Middle English), from Old English hefiġ, hefeġ (Old English), hæfiġ (Old English “heavy; important, grave, severe, serious; oppressive, grievous; slow, dull”), from Proto-West Germanic *habīg (“heavy, hefty, weighty”), from Proto-Germanic *habīgaz (“heavy, hefty, weighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to take, grasp, hold”). Equivalent to . Related to have (English).

Cognate with hevy (Scots), havy (Scots), heavy (Scots “heavy”), heeuwich (Saterland Frisian), häwich (Saterland Frisian “violent, angry”), hevich (Western Frisian “violent”), hevig (Dutch “violent, severe, intense, acute”), hevig (Low German (Germany) “violent, fierce, intense, angry”), hebig (German) (compare heftig (German “fierce, severe, intense, violent, heavy”)), höfugur (Icelandic “heavy, weighty, important”).

Compare typologically взять,объёмный,ёмкий (Russian), and capāx (Latin “large, wide, roomy, spacious, capacious, capable, apt”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: heave + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English hegge, from Old English heċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *haggju, from Proto-Germanic *hagjō, from Proto-Indo-European *kagʰyóm (“enclosure”). Cognate with heg (Dutch), Hecke (German). . More at haw (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English heggen, from the noun (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hele, from Old English hēla, from Proto-West Germanic *hą̄hilō, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *hanhaz (“heel, hock”), equivalent to . More at hock (English).

Compare haiel (North Frisian), hyl (Western Frisian), hiel (Dutch), Hiel (Low German (Germany)), - (Danish) and hæl (Norwegian), häl (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Probably inferred from hielded (English), the past tense of hield (English), from Middle English helden, heelden (Middle English), from Old English hyldan, hieldan (Old English “to incline”), cognate with hella (Old Norse “to pour out”) (whence Danish hælde (Danish “lean, pour”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: See hele (English “conceal, keep secret, cover”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English heighte, heiȝþe (Middle English), from Old English hēahþu, hēhþo (Old English), hīehþu (Old English “height”), Proto-West Germanic *hauhiþu, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō (compare *hauhaz (Proto-Germanic)). Equivalent to high + -t (English). The regular pronunciation is now obsolete (as with other words in ); the modern form developed early on, at first as a variant, by analogy with the underlying adjective.

See also Höchte (Saterland Frisian), Hööchte (Saterland Frisian “height”), hichte (Western Frisian “height”), hoogte (Dutch “height”), hœhede (Middle High German), hœhte (Middle High German “height”), hæð (Old Norse “height”) (compare höjd (Swedish), høyde (Norwegian)), 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌹𐌸𐌰 (Gothic “height”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hel, hell (Middle English), helle (Middle English), hælle (Middle English), from Old English hel, hell (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *hallju, from Proto-Germanic *haljō (“hell, netherworld”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover”). .

Cognate with helle (Yola “hell”), Hälle (Saterland Frisian “hell”), hel (Western Frisian “hell”), Hell (Alemannic “hell”), hélla (Cimbric “hell”), hel (Dutch “hell”), Hölle (German “hell”), hel (Limburgish), Héll (Limburgish), Höll (Limburgish “hell”), Häll (lb “hell”), heł (Ripuarian), hełł (Ripuarian “hell”), helvede (Danish “hell”), ihjel (Danish “to death”), helviti (Faroese “hell”), hel (Icelandic “death, hell”), helvíti (Icelandic “hell”), hel (Norwegian Nynorsk “death, underworld”), helvete (Norwegian Nynorsk “hell”), helvete (Swedish “hell”), ihjäl (Swedish “to death”), 𐌷𐌰𐌻𐌾𐌰 (Gothic “hell”), koll (Estonian “bugbear”), koljo (Finnish “giant; evil spirit; devil”); also keles (Cornish “to conceal, hide”), ceil (Irish “to conceal, hide; to cover up”), celu (Welsh “to conceal, hide”), 𐌂𐌄𐌋𐌀 (xfa “tomb”), cella (Latin “hut, storeroom; barn, granary”), κολεός (Greek (Modern) “vagina; sheath; scabbard; coleus”), šalmas (Lithuanian “helmet”), шало́м (Belarusian “helmet”), шлем (Bulgarian / Macedonian “helmet”), szłom (zlw-opl “helmet”), шело́м (Russian), шлем (Russian “helmet”), шле̏м (Serbo-Croatian), шље̏м (Serbo-Croatian), šlȅm (Serbo-Croatian), šljȅm (Serbo-Croatian “helmet”), шолом (Ukrainian “helmet”), शर्मन् (Sanskrit “safety, shelter; house; bliss, happiness, joy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From German hellen (“to brighten, burnish”). Related to hel (Dutch “clear, bright”) and hell (German “clear, bright”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English hellen, from Old Norse hella (“to pour”), from Proto-Germanic *halþijaną (“to incline, tip; to pour out, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to lean, incline”). Cognate with hella (Icelandic “to pour”), helle (Norwegian “to pour”), hälla (Swedish “to pour”). See also hield (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English helmet, helmett (Middle English), a borrowing from Old French helmet, heaumet (Old French), a diminutive of helme (Old French) (Modern French heaume (French)), equivalent to helm + et (English). The Old French is itself of gem — origin (whence helm (Old English)). Used in English since the 15th century, it has largely displaced helm (English) as the general word.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English help, from Old English help (“help, aid, assistance, relief”), from Proto-Germanic *helpō (“help”), *hilpiz (Proto-Germanic), *hulpiz (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (Proto-Indo-European “to help”).

Cognate with Hälpe (Saterland Frisian “help”), help (Western Frisian “help”), hölfe (Cimbric “help”), hulp (Dutch “help”), Hilfe (German “help, aid, assistance”), Hëllef (lb “help”), hilf (mhn “help”), hyłf (Ripuarian “help”), הילף (Yiddish “help”), hjælp (Danish “help”), hjálp (Faroese / Icelandic “help”), hjelp (Norwegian Bokmål “help”), hjelp (Norwegian Nynorsk), hjølp (Norwegian Nynorsk “help”), hjälp (Swedish “help”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English helpen, from Old English helpan (“to help, aid, assist, benefit, relieve, cure”), from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, Proto-Germanic *helpaną (“to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (Proto-Indo-European “to help”).

chain.meaning: to help, aid, assist, benefit, relieve, cure

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English helpere, from Old English *helpere, from Proto-West Germanic *helpārī (“helper”), equivalent to help + -er (English). Cognate with Hälper (Saterland Frisian “helper”), helper (Western Frisian “helper”), helper (Dutch “helper”), Helper (Low German (Germany) “helper”), Helfer (German “helper”), hjælper (Danish “helper”), hjälpare (Swedish “helper”), hjálpar (Icelandic “helper”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English helpful; equivalent to help + ful (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English herbe, erbe (Middle English), from Old French erbe (French herbe (French)), from Latin herba. Initial h was restored to the spelling in the 15th century on the basis of Latin, but it remained mute until the 19th century and still is for many speakers. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English her, from Old English hēr (“at this place”), from Proto-West Germanic *hēr, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r, from *hiz + *r (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European —, from *ḱe (Proto-Indo-European) + *ís (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with hier (Saterland Frisian), hjir (Western Frisian), hier (Dutch), hier (Low German (Germany)), hier (German), her (Danish), här (Swedish), her (Norwegian), her (Faroese), hér (Icelandic). Also related to the English pronoun he (English “this/that person”), and the words hither (English “to this place”) and hence (English “from this place”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English heroes, from Old French heroes, from Latin hērōs (“hero”), from Ancient Greek ἥρως (“demi-god, hero”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to watch over, protect”); if so, related to servo (Latin “protect”). Displaced heleð (Middle English), haleð (Middle English), from hæle (Old English “hæleþ”), hæle (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —. Equivalent to her#Pronoun + -self (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin haesitātus, perfect passive participle of haesitō (Latin) (see -ate), intensive of haereō (Latin “to hesitate, stick fast; to hang or hold fast”). Displaced native wandian (Old English). Compare hésiter (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: hi + tech

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Morphologically hid + en (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hiden, huden (Middle English), from Old English hȳdan (“to hide, conceal, preserve”), from Proto-West Germanic *huʀdijan (“to conceal”), from Proto-Germanic *huzdijaną (“to hoard”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, wrap, encase”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover”).

The verb was originally weak. In the of the Bible (1611), both hid and hidden are used for the past participle.

Cognate with huiden (Dutch), (ver)hüden (Low German), (ver)hüen (Low German “to hide, cover, conceal”), cuddio (Welsh “to hide”), custōs (Latin), κεύθω (Ancient Greek “to conceal”), कुहरम् (Sanskrit “cave”). Related to hut (English) and sky (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hyde, from Old English hȳd, from Proto-West Germanic *hūdi, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European — (compare cutis (Latin “skin, rind, hide”)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover”), ultimately the same root as the above etymology. More at sky (English).

See also hûd (Western Frisian), huid (Dutch), Haut (German), hud (Danish), cwd (Welsh “scrotum”), cutis (Latin “skin”), kutys (Lithuanian “purse, money-belt”), κύτος (Ancient Greek “hollow vessel”), σκῦτος (Ancient Greek “cover, hide”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English hide, from Old English hīd, hȳd (Old English), hīġed (Old English), hīġid (Old English “a measure of land”), for earlier *hīwid (Old English “the amount of land needed to support one family”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *hīwaz, *hīwō (Proto-Germanic “relative, fellow-lodger, family”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“to lie with, store, be familiar”). Related to hīwisc (Old English “hide of land, household”), hīwan (Old English “members of a family, household”). More at hewe (English), hind (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English high, heigh (Middle English), heih (Middle English), from Old English hēah (“high, tall, lofty, high-class, exalted, sublime, illustrious, important, proud, haughty, deep, right”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauh (“high”), from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz (“high”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewk- (“to bend; crooked”).

Cognate with heich (Scots “high”), heegh (Yola), heigh (Yola), heighe (Yola), hia (Yola), hie (Yola “high”), hoog (North Frisian), huuch (North Frisian “high”), hooch (Saterland Frisian), hoog (Saterland Frisian “high”), heech (Western Frisian “high”), hooch (Alemannic “high”), huh (Central Franconian “high”), hoach (Cimbric), hòach (Cimbric “high”), hoog (Dutch “high”), hoch (German “high”), hooch (Low German (Germany) “high”), hoeg (Limburgish “high”), héich (lb “high”), heach (mhn “high”), huch (Ripuarian “high”), הויך (Yiddish “high”), høj (Danish “high”), háur (Faroese), høgur (Faroese “high”), haugar (gmq-gut “high”), hár (Icelandic “high”), høg (Norwegian Bokmål), høy (Norwegian Bokmål “high”), høg (Norwegian Nynorsk), håg (Norwegian Nynorsk), hå (Norwegian Nynorsk “high”), hög (Swedish “high”), 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐌷𐍃 (Gothic “high”), *oas (xvn “high”), haut (Old French “high”) (from hoh (Old High German “high”)); also with Καύκᾰσος (Ancient Greek “Caucasus”), koks (Latvian “tree”), kúoka (Lithuanian “stick with thick end, pounder, pestle”), ку́ка (Bulgarian “hook”), çukë (Albanian “peak, summit, top”).

chain.meaning: high, tall, lofty, high-class, exalted, sublime, illustrious, important, proud, haughty, deep, right

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English hegen,heghen,heien, a conflation of Old English ġehēgan (“to perform, conduct”) (from Proto-West Germanic *hauwjan) and hēan (Old English “to raise up, exalt”) (from *hauhijan (Proto-West Germanic)), also influenced by heigh (Middle English “high”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: See hie (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: high + light

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hiȝly, heȝly (Middle English), heyȝliche (Middle English), from Old English hēalīce (“highly”), equivalent to high + -ly (English). Cognate with hoogelijk (Dutch “highly”), höchlich (German “highly”), højlig (Danish “highly”), högligen (Swedish “highly”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hymself, from Old English him selfum. Equivalent to him + -self (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hinten, hynten (Middle English), variant of henten (Middle English “to lay hold of, catch”), from Old English hentan (“to seize, grasp”), from Proto-West Germanic *hantijan, from Proto-Germanic *hantijaną. . Related also to hunt (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English hipe, hupe (Middle English), from Old English hype, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz (compare heup (Dutch), Huop (Low German), Hüfte (German)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb- (compare cysgu (Welsh “to sleep”), cubāre (Latin “to lie”), κύβος (Ancient Greek “hollow in the hips”), sup (Albanian “shoulder”), शुप्ति (Sanskrit “shoulder”)), from *ḱew- (Proto-Indo-European “to bend”). More at high (English). The sense "drug addict" derives from addicts lying on their hips while using certain drugs such as opium.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hepe, heppe (Middle English), hipe (Middle English), from Old English hēope, from Proto-Germanic *heupǭ (compare joop (Dutch), Hiefe (German), hjúpa (Faroese)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb- (“briar, thorn”) (compare kaāubri (Old Prussian “thorn”), kaubre (Lithuanian “kaubrė̃”)).
right|thumb|Rose hips.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: or disputed. Probably a variant of hep#Adjective (English “hep”); both forms are attested from the first decade of the 20th century. Some sources suggest derivation from Wolof hepi (“to see”) or hipi (Wolof “to open one’s eyes”). Others suggest connection to the noun, as opium smokers were said to lie on a hip#Etymology 1 (English). Neither of these suggestions is widely accepted, however.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hire, hyre (Middle English), here (Middle English), hure (Middle English), from Old English hȳr (“employment for wages; pay for service; interest on money lent”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀiju (“payment”), from the verb *hūʀijan (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *hūzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kewHs- or . Compare 𒆪𒊭𒀭 (Hittite “fee, pay, wages, price”).

Cognate with hier (Western Frisian “hire”), huur (Dutch “lease, rental”), Hüür (Low German (Germany) “lease, rental”).

chain.meaning: employment for wages; pay for service; interest on money lent

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hiren , hyren (Middle English), from Old English hȳrian (“to hire”), from the noun (see above). Compare hiere (Western Frisian “to rent, lease”), huren (Dutch “to rent, lease”), hüren (Low German “to rent”), hyre (Danish “to hire”), hyra (Swedish “to hire”).

Eclipsed souden (Middle English “to hire, employ, enlist”), borrowed from souder (Old French), soudre (Old French), souldre (Old French “to take into employ, pay”); see obsolete sold (English “salary, military pay”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin historicus (“historical”), from Ancient Greek ἱστορικός (“exact; historical”). Cognate with French historique (French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English hitten (“to hit, strike, make contact with”), from Old English hittan (“to meet with, come upon, fall in with”), from Old Norse hitta (“to strike, meet”), from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną (“to come upon, find”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- (“to fall; fall upon; hit; cut; hew”).

Cognate with hitte (Western Frisian “to meet”), hitten (Dutch “to hit, encounter”), hitte (Danish “to find”), - (Faroese), - (Icelandic), hitta (Swedish “to meet”), hitta (Norwegian Nynorsk), hitte (Norwegian Nynorsk “to meet; to find”), caedō (Latin “to kill”), qit (Albanian “to hit, throw, pull out, release”). Probably also related to hei (Dutch “mallet”), Heie (German “wooden hammer, mallet”).

Compare typologically striking (English), порази́тельный (Russian) (<~ порази́ть (Russian) <~ рази́ть (Russian)).

chain.meaning: to hit, strike, make contact with
to meet with, come upon, fall in with

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English hit (“it”), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (Proto-Indo-European “this, here”). Cognate with het (Dutch “it”). More at it (English); also note 'it (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From hitch + hike (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English holden, Old English healdan, Proto-West Germanic *haldan, Proto-Germanic *haldaną (“to tend, herd”), maybe Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to drive”). .

*hâlde (Western Frisian)
*holden (Low German), holen (Low German)
*houden (Dutch)
*halten (German)
*holde (Danish)
*holde (Norwegian Bokmål)
*halda (Norwegian Nynorsk).

Compare celer (Latin “quick”), käl- (txb “to goad, drive”), κέλλω (Ancient Greek “to drive”), कलयति (Sanskrit “to impel”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Alteration (due to hold) of hole (English). Cognate with hol (Dutch “hole, cave, den, cavity, cargo hold”), holte (Dutch “cavity, hollow, den”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hold, holde (Middle English), from Old English hold (“gracious, friendly, kind”), from Proto-West Germanic *holþ, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz (“favourable, gracious, loyal”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to tend, incline, bend, tip”).

Cognate with hold (German “gracious, friendly, sympathetic, grateful”), - (Danish) and huld (Swedish “fair, kindly, gracious”), hollur (Icelandic “faithful, dedicated, loyal”), Huld (German “grace, favour”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English hole, hol (Middle English), from Old English hol (“orifice, hollow place, cavity”), from Proto-West Germanic *hol (“hole”), from Proto-Germanic *hulą (“hollow space, cavity”), noun derivative of Proto-Germanic *hulaz (“hollow”), which is of uncertain ultimate origin. Related to hollow (English).

Cognate with hol (Dutch / Faroese / Icelandic “hole”), hul (Danish “hole”), hola (Faroese / Icelandic / Norn “hole”), hol (Norwegian Bokmål “depression, hole, cavern”), hål (Swedish “hole”), houle (French “swell of water”). Compare unrelated Finnish kolo (Finnish “hole”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hom, from Old English hām, from Proto-West Germanic *haim, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, village”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village, home”), from the root *tḱey- (Proto-Indo-European). .

Cognate with hame (Scots “home”), haime (Yola), hime (Yola), hyme (Yola “home”), Heem (Saterland Frisian “home”), haim (Alemannic), hei (Alemannic), heim (Alemannic), hemmu (Alemannic “home”), hama (Bavarian), hame (Bavarian “home”), hòam (Cimbric), huam (Cimbric “home”), heem (Dutch), heim (Dutch “home”), Heim (German “home”), heim (Limburgish), Héïm (Limburgish “home”), Heem (lb “home”), hoa'm (mhn “home”), ham (Ripuarian), hām (Ripuarian), haom (Ripuarian “home”), היים (Yiddish “home”), hjem (Danish “home”), - (Faroese), heim (Icelandic “home”), heimur (Icelandic “world”), heim (Norwegian Bokmål), hjem (Norwegian Bokmål “home”), heim (Norwegian Nynorsk “home”), hem (Swedish “home”), 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐌼𐍃 (Gothic “village”), caoimh (Irish “dear”), kaimas (Lithuanian “village”), šeima (Lithuanian “family”), komb (Albanian “nation, people”), κώμη (Ancient Greek “village”), from *ḱey- (Proto-Indo-European “to lie”) (compare , κεῖμαι (Ancient Greek “to lie down”), civis (Latin “citizen”), 𐬯𐬀𐬉𐬙𐬈 (ae “he lies, rests”), शये (Sanskrit “he lies”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English honest, honeste (Middle English “honourable, appropriate, excellent”), from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus, from honor (Latin). For the verb, see honestāre (Latin “to clothe or adorn with honour”), and compare honester (French). Displaced native Old English sōþfæst.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English honestly, honestlyche (Middle English), honestliche (Middle English), equivalent to honest + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English honeste (“honour, integrity”), from Old French honesté (compare modern French honnêteté (French)). . Displaced native sōþfæstnes (Old English) and non-native prodonomee (Middle English), from prodomie (Old French). The plant is named so after the visibility of the seeds through the translucent pods.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From earlier hony moone (English), originally denoting the period of time following a wedding, equivalent to . The original reference was to affection waning like the moon, but later the sense became "the first month, or moon after marriage", which tends to be the sweetest.

Compare suckermânt (Middle Low German “honeymoon”), Hönnigweken (Low German (Germany) “honeymoon”). The Honigmond (German) is a calque of lune de miel (French), itself a calque of the English term.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hood, hod (Middle English), from Old English hōd, from Proto-West Germanic *hōd, from Proto-Germanic *hōdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kadʰ- (“to cover”).

See also Houd (Saterland Frisian “hat; hood”), hoed (Western Frisian / Dutch “hat”), huat (Cimbric), huut (Cimbric “hat”), Hut (German “hat”), Hood (Low German (Germany) “hat; hood”), Hutt (lb “hat”); also *xawdaH (Proto-Iranian “hat”) (𐬑𐬂𐬛𐬀 (ae), 𐎧𐎢𐎭 (peo)). More at hat.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: hoodlum.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: neighborhood; compare nabe (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: hoodie, influenced by existing sense “hoodlum”.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hoke, from Old English hōc (“angle, point, hook”), from Proto-West Germanic *hōk, from Proto-Germanic *hōkaz, variant of *hakô (Proto-Germanic “hook”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kog-, *keg- (Proto-Indo-European), *keng- (Proto-Indo-European “peg, hook, claw”).

Cognate with huke (Scots), huik (Scots “hook”), - (Western Frisian) and hoek (Dutch “hook, angle, corner”), Hook (Low German), Huuk (Low German), Hook (German “small cluster of farms”), høkja (Faroese “crutch”), hækja (Icelandic “crutch”), hek (Norn “crutch”), kuokka (Finnish “hoe, mattock”). Related to hake (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hopen, from Old English hopian (“hope”), from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn; further etymology unclear.

Cognate with - (Saterland Frisian), hoopje (Western Frisian “to hope”), hòffan (Cimbric “to hope”), hopen (Dutch “to hope”), - (German), hoffen (lb “to hope”), höfnan (Ripuarian “hope”), האָפֿן (Yiddish “to hope”), håbe (Danish “to hope”), håpe (Norwegian Bokmål “to hope”), håpa (Norwegian Nynorsk), håpe (Norwegian Nynorsk “to hope”), hoppas (Swedish “to hope”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English hopen, from Old English hopian (“hope”), from Proto-West Germanic *hopōn; further etymology unclear.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hope, from Old English hopa (“hope, expectation”), from the same source as the verb hope (English).

Eclipsed non-native early modern esperance (English), borrowed from Middle French esperance.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English hope (“a valley”), from Old English hōp (found only in placenames). More at hoop (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Icelandic hóp (“a small bay or inlet”). Cognate with hoop (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From hope + -ful (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: The use as a sentence adverb first gained currency in the United States and has been explained as a possible .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compare hopplös (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English horn, horne, from Old English horn, from Proto-West Germanic *horn, from Proto-Germanic *hurną. Compare hoarn (Western Frisian), hoorn (Dutch), Hoorn (Low German), horn (Low German), Horn (German), - (Danish) and horn (Swedish), 𐌷𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌽 (Gothic).

Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European —, from *ḱerh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “head, horn”). Compare kern (Breton “horn”), cornū (Latin), κέρας (Ancient Greek), *sьrna (Proto-Slavic), сьрна (Church Slavonic “roedeer”), , سر (Persian), शृङ्ग (Sanskrit “horn”). .

From the horn-shaped earpieces of old communication systems that used air tubes.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English horer, horrour (Middle English), from Old French horror, from Latin horror (“a bristling, a shaking, trembling as with cold or fear, terror”), from horrere (Latin “to bristle, shake, be terrified”). Displaced native ōga (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English hoste, from Old French oste (French: hôte (French)), from Latin hospitem, accusative of hospes (Latin “a host, also a sojourner, visitor, guest; hence, a foreigner, a stranger”), from *hostipotis (Proto-Italic), an old compound of hostis (Latin) and the root of potis (Latin), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstipotis (“master of guests”), from *gʰóstis (Proto-Indo-European “stranger, guest, enemy”) and *pótis (Proto-Indo-European “owner, master, host, husband”). Used in English since 13th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English oost, borrowed from Old French ost, hoste (Old French “oste, hoste”), from Latin hostis (“foreign enemy”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (as opposed to inimicus (Latin “personal enemy”)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English host, oist (Middle English), ost (Middle English), from Old French hoiste, from Latin hostia (“sacrificial victim”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English hostel, from Old French hostel, ostel (Old French), from Late Latin hospitale (“hospice”), from Classical Latin hospitalis (“hospitable”) itself from hospes (Latin “host”) + -alis (Latin “-al”). . Not in use from late 17th c. (in the usual sense from mid 16th c.) to 1808, when it was revived by in his poem Marmion (see the quotation).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hot, hoot (Middle English), from Old English hāt (“hot”), from Proto-West Germanic *hait, from Proto-Germanic *haitaz (“hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (“to heat; to become hot”).

Cognate with hoat (Yola), hoate (Yola), hote (Yola “hot”), hjit (Western Frisian), hyt (Western Frisian “hot”), hoaß (Bavarian “hot”), heeß (Central Franconian “hot”), heet (Dutch “hot”), heiss (German), heiß (German), heyß (German “hot”), haas (Ripuarian), haes (Ripuarian), hȧś (Ripuarian), hǡs (Ripuarian “hot”), הייס (Yiddish “hot”), hed (Danish “hot”), heitur (Faroese / Icelandic “hot”), het (Norwegian Bokmål / Swedish “hot”); also kaitra (Lithuanian “heat”). Related to heat.

Superseded non-native chaud (Middle English), from chaut (Old French “hot”); and early Modern calent (English), from calēns (Latin “hot”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: hour + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English houshold. .

Cognate with houshald (Scots), housald (Scots), housell (Scots), howsell (Scots “household”), huishouden (Dutch “household”) (earlier huishoud (Dutch)), Huushollen (Low German (Germany) “household”) (hūsholt (Middle Low German)), Haushalt (German “household”), hushåll (Swedish “household, family”), husholdning (Norwegian “household”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From house + work (English). Cognate with huiswerk (Dutch “homework”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English how, hou (Middle English), hu (Middle English), hwu (Middle English), from Old English hū, from Proto-West Germanic *hwō, from Proto-Germanic *hwō (“through what, how”), from the same root as hwæt (Old English “who, what”). /hw/ > /h/ due to wh-cluster reduction in Old English; compare who (English), which underwent this change later, and thus is spelt wh (Middle English spelling of /hw/) but pronounced /h/ (it previously had a different vowel, hence avoided the spelling and sound change in Old English). Vowel change per Great Vowel Shift.

Akin to hoo (Scots), foo (Scots “how”), ho (North Frisian), hü (North Frisian), hur (North Frisian “how”), wo (Saterland Frisian “how”), hoe (Western Frisian “how”), hoe (Dutch “how”), ho (Low German), wo (Low German), wu (Low German “how”), wie (German “how”), hur (Swedish “how”). See who (English) and compare why (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English howe, hough (Middle English), hogh (Middle English), partly from Old English hōh (“promontory”), and partly from Old Norse haugr (“a how, mound”). Compare höe (Old French “hillock, hill”), from the same source.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From a sio — language; compare háu (lkt). Alternatively from Wyandot haau.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From earlier hugge (English “to embrace, clasp with the arms”) (1560), probably representing a conflation of huck (English “to crouch, huddle down”) and Old Norse hugga (“to comfort, console”), from hugr (Old Norse “mind, heart, thought”), from Proto-Germanic *hugiz (“mind, thought, sense”), cognate with hugga (Icelandic “to comfort”), hyġe (Old English “thought”) (whence high (English) (Etymology 2)).

chain.meaning: to embrace, clasp with the arms

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English huge, from Old French ahuge (“high, lofty, great, large, huge”), of origin.

One theory derives it from an underlying , from a (Old French “at, to”) + hoge (Old French “a hill, height”), the latter from Frankish *haug or cognate Old Norse haugr (“hill”); both from Proto-Germanic *haugaz (“hill, mound”), from Proto-Indo-European *kowkós (“hill, mound”), from the root Proto-Indo-European *kewk-, whence also high (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English humaigne, humayne (Middle English), humain (Middle English), from Middle French humain, from Old French humain, umain (Old French “of or belonging to man”), from Latin hūmānus (“of man, human”); see there for further details. Spelling has been predominant since the early 18th century. Compare man (English), to which it is possibly related.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Old French humide, from Latin humidus (“moist”). Via Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ- (“wet”) related to weaky (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English humour, from Old French humor, humour (Old French), from Latin hūmor, correctly ūmor (Latin “liquid”), from hūmeō (Latin), correctly ūmeō (Latin “to be moist”). The h in these words, which was silent in late Classical Latin, is folk etymological, due to the erroneous association with the word humus (Latin “soil”).

The shift in meaning "liquid" > "mood" is attributed to the classical system of physiology, where human behaviour is regulated by four bodily humours (fluids). The sense "mood" gave rise to the verb sense "to give in to someone's mood or whim" and, by narrowing of meaning, the sense "wit".

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hunger, from Old English hungor (“hunger, desire; famine”), from Proto-West Germanic *hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hungruz, *hunhruz (Proto-Germanic “hunger”), from Proto-Indo-European *kenk- (“to burn, smart, desire, hunger, thirst”).

Cognate with honger (Western Frisian), hûnger (Western Frisian “hunger”), honger (Dutch “hunger”), Hunger (Low German (Germany) “hunger”), Hunger (German “hunger”), hunger (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “hunger”), hungur (Faroese / Icelandic “hunger”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English hungren, from Old English hyngran, hyngrian (Old English), ġehyngrian (Old English “to be hungry”), from Proto-West Germanic *hungrijan, from Proto-Germanic *hungrijaną.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hunten, from Old English huntian (“to hunt”), from Proto-West Germanic *huntōn (“to hunt, capture”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱent- (“to catch, seize”). Related to hunda (Old High German “booty”), 𐌷𐌿𐌽𐌸𐍃 (Gothic “body of captives”), hūþ (Old English “plunder, booty, prey”), hentan (Old English “to catch, seize”). More at hent (English), hint (English).
In some areas read as a collective form of hound (English) by folk etymology (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English hunting, from Old English huntung, equivalent to hunt + ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English horien (“to rush, impel”), probably a variation of hurren (Middle English “to vibrate rapidly, buzz”), from Proto-Germanic *hurzaną (“to rush”) (compare hurren (Middle High German “to hasten”), hurre (Norwegian “to whirl around”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”) (compare currō (Latin “to run”), kursär (xto)/kwarsär (txb “league; course”)). Related to hurr (English), horse (English), rush (English).

Alternative etymology derives hurry as a variant of harry (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English hurten, hirten (Middle English), hertan (Middle English “to injure, scathe, knock together”), from Old Northern French hurter , perhaps from Frankish *hūrt (“a battering ram”), cognate with hwrdd (Welsh “ram”) and hordh (Cornish “ram”). Compare *hrūtaną (Proto-Germanic), *hreutaną (Proto-Germanic “to fall, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *krew- (“to fall, beat, smash, strike, break”); however, the earliest instances of the verb in Middle English are as old as those found in Old French, which leads to the possibility that the Middle English word may instead be a reflex of an unrecorded Old English *hyrtan, which later merged with the Old French verb. Germanic cognates include horten (Dutch “to push against, strike”), hurten (Middle Low German “to run at, collide with”), hurten (Middle High German “to push, bump, attack, storm, invade”), hrútr (Old Norse “battering ram”).

Alternate etymology traces hurter (Old Northern French) rather to Old Norse hrútr (“ram (male sheep)”), lengthened-grade variant of hjǫrtr (Old Norse “stag”), from Proto-Germanic *herutuz, *herutaz (Proto-Germanic “hart, male deer”), which would relate it to English hart (English “male deer”). See hart (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Unclear. Suggestions include: from its resemblance to a blue hurtleberry, or from French heurt (French) (a blow, leaving a blue bruise), the latter of which would make it a doublet of hurt (English) Etymology 1; compare the theories about golpe (English “purple roundel”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:

Cognate with Hütte (German “hut”), hut (Dutch “hut”), hutte (Western Frisian “hut”), Hutte (Saterland Frisian “hut”), hytte (Danish “hut”), hytte (Norwegian Bokmål “hut”), hydda (Swedish “hut”). Related to hide (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English intenden, entenden (Middle English “direct (one’s) attention towards”), borrowed from Old French entendre, from Latin intendo (“intendō, intendere”). See also intensive. .

Largely displaced native myntan (Old English “to mean, intend; to think, suppose”), whence dialectal mint (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The adjective is derived from Late Middle English intensive (“fervent, great, intense”), borrowed from Old French intensif, intensive (Old French) (modern intensif (French)) + -ive (Middle English), equivalent to intense + -ive (English). is from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus (“attentive; eager, intent; intensive”) + -īvus (Latin); and is the perfect passive participle of intendō (Latin “to stretch out, strain”), from in- (Latin) + tendō (Latin “to extend, stretch, stretch out”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tend- (“to extend, stretch”)). .

The noun is derived from the adjective.

Cognate with airn (Scots), ern (Scots “iron”), eeren (Yola “iron”), Iersen (Saterland Frisian “iron”), izer (Western Frisian “iron”), Eisn (Bavarian “iron”), aizarn (Cimbric “iron”), ijzer (Dutch “iron”), - (German), Eisen (lb “iron”), Isen (Low German (Germany) “iron”), Ise (Alemannic “iron”), iezer (Limburgish “iron”), aisn (mhn “iron”), ȧjza (Ripuarian “iron”), yzer (Flemish “iron”), אײַזן (Yiddish “iron”), jern (Danish), jærn (Danish “iron”), jarn (Faroese “iron”), járn (Icelandic “iron”), járn (gmq-jmk), jáðn (gmq-jmk “iron”), jern (Norwegian Bokmål “iron”), jarn (Norwegian Nynorsk), jern (Norwegian Nynorsk), jønn (Norwegian Nynorsk “iron”), jern (Swedish), jaͤrn (Swedish), järn (Swedish “iron”), 𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐍂𐌽 (Gothic “iron”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English issue, from Old French issue (“an exit, a way out”), feminine past participle of issir (Old French “to exit”), from Latin exeō (“go out, exit”), from prefix ex- (Latin “out”) + eō (Latin “go”).

The legal meaning originated from the concept of "the end or result of pleadings in a suit (by presenting the point to be determined by trial)," leading to the sense of "the controversy over facts in a trial" (early 14th century, Anglo-French). This later extended to mean "a point of contention between two parties" (early 15th century) and more generally, "an important point to be decided" (1836). Consequently, the verbal phrase take issue with emerged in 1797 (preceded by join issue in the 1690s), meaning "to adopt an affirmative or negative stance in a dispute with another." The expression to have issues, meaning "to have unresolved conflicts," dates to 1990.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English it, hit (Middle English) ( > dialectal hit (English “it”)), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-West Germanic *hit, from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe (“here; here”).

Cognate with it (Yola), t' (Yola), yt (Yola “it”), at (North Frisian), et (North Frisian), 't (North Frisian “it”), et (Saterland Frisian “it”), it (Western Frisian “it”), het (Dutch “it”), hatt (lb “her, it, she”), eð (Elfdalian “it”); also ᚕᚑᚔ (pgl “here”), cis (Latin “short of; before”), hic (Latin “this”), εκείνος (Greek (Modern) “that; those”). Compare es (Cimbric), is (Cimbric), 's (Cimbric), 'z (Cimbric “it”), es (German), 's (German “it, there”), s (mhn,wym “it”), עס (Yiddish “it”), ið (Faroese “that, which, who”), 𐌹𐍄𐌰 (Gothic “it”), which instead descends from *it (Proto-Germanic “it”). More at he (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English item, from Latin item (“also; in the same manner”). The present English meaning derives from a usage in lists, where the first entry would begin in (Latin) primis (Latin) (“firstly”) or imprimis, and the other entries with . Later, the members of lists were referred to as "items".

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
First attested in the early 18th c. as a verb meaning “to press, be pressed, be wedged in”. Compare dialectal jammock (English “to press, squeeze, crush into a soft mass, chew food"; also "a soft, pulpy substance”). Perhaps from Middle English chammen, champen (Middle English) , of origin; probably originally .

The "performance" sense is first attested with regards to jazz in 1929, and its origin, though , is likely metaphorical, "something sweet made by the combination of many things", with influence from jamboree (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English jarre (“jar”), from Medieval Latin jarra, or from Middle French jarre (“liquid measure”) (from Old French jare; modern jarre (French “earthenware jar”)), or from Spanish jarra, jarro (Spanish “jug, pitcher; mug, stein”), all from Arabic جَرَّة (“earthen receptacle”).

The word is cognate with giara (Italian “jar; crock”), jarro (Occitan), jarra (Portuguese), jarro (Portuguese “jug; ewer, pitcher”).

The verb is derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From earlier , jur (English), jarre (English), jurre (English), of origin. Possibly from earlier *char (English), *chur (English), *charre (English), *churre (English) (now spelt chirr (English), churr (English “to make a sound”); compare also nightjar (English) and its variant nightchurr (English)), from Middle English *chirren, *cherren (Middle English), *churren (Middle English “to sound, cry, murmur, complain”), from Old English ċeorian (“to murmur, gripe, complain with just cause”), from Proto-West Germanic *karēn (“to complain”). For the change of ch to j, compare also charm (English), jarm (English “chirping”); achar (English), ajar (English “slightly turned or open”), chaw (English), jaw (English), etc. The noun is derived from the verb.

chain.meaning: to murmur, gripe, complain with just cause

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English jowe (“jaw; sides of the lower face”), the further origin of which is . Either:
* From Anglo-Norman jowe, from Old French joe (“cheek; jaw”), from Vulgar Latin *ga(v)ota (“cheek”), of uncertain further origin.
** It has been objected that the rhyming of with in Middle English demonstrates that it did not have the vowel /uː/. This would be a concern if /uː/ were the vowel to expect from a borrowing of the Old French word, which it is not. Compare paw (English) < pawe (Middle English “pawe/powe”) < powe (Anglo-Norman) < poe (Old French).

* From , from *ċēowe (Old English). The main difficulties with this theory are the notable lack of evidence and the late attestation of (early 16th century). If it is correct, then the further origin would be *keuwā (Proto-West Germanic “jaw”), whence Kiuwe (Saterland Frisian), kieuw (Dutch), Keu (German), Käu (German). For the initial consonant, compare jowl (English) as a variant of chavel (English)/chawl (English).

It is also conceivable that the word is a merger of two coincidentally similar sources. Gradually (from ċeafl (Old English)).

chain.meaning: jaw; sides of the lower face

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Of origin. Originally with the meaning of "to shake up and down." Possibly from Middle English joggen, a variant of jaggen (Middle English “to pierce, prod, stir up, arouse”); see jag (English “sharp projection”).

Or, perhaps an early alteration of shog (English “to jolt, shake; depart, go”), from Middle English shoggen, schoggen (Middle English “to shake up and down, jog”), from Middle Dutch schocken (“to jolt, bounce”) or Middle Low German schoggen, schocken (Middle Low German “to shog”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skukkōn (“to move, shake, tremble”), possibly related to *skakan (Proto-West Germanic “to shake, stir”). More at shock (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is from Middle English joynt (attested since the late 13th century), from Old French joint (“joint of the body”) (attested since the 12th century). The adjective (attested since the 15th century) is from jointiz (Old French). Both Old French words are from Latin iūnctus, the past participle of iungō (Latin). See also join (English), jugular (English), junction (English). Displaced fōg (Old English) and partially displaced lith (English).

The meaning of "building, establishment", especially in connection with shady activities, appeared in Anglo-Irish by 1821 and entered general American English slang by 1877, especially in the sense of "opium den". The sense "marijuana cigarette" is attested since 1935. The development to meaning "any thing" also happened to the Scots and Memphian form junt (English) and the Mid-Atlantic/Philadelphian form jawn (English).
