etymologies.text:
thumb|125px|A tap dancer jumping.
From Middle English jumpen (“to walk quickly, run, jump”), probably of Middle Low German — or gmq — origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *gumbōną (“to hop, skip, bounce”), an iterative verb. The OED suggests an origin. Related to jumble (English). In the sense “to propel oneself” it displaced leap (English) partially and spring (English) largely.

Cognate with jumpen (Low German (Germany) “to jump”), archaic gumpen (German “to jump, hop, bounce”), dialectal gampen (German “to hop”), gumpe (Alemannic “to leap, jump”), Walser dialect kumpu (German), gopta (Old Norse “to jump; make jump”) gumpe (Danish “to jolt”), gumpa (Swedish “to jump”), gimpe (Danish “to move up and down”), jumpren (Middle English), jumbren (Middle English “to mix, jumble”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compare jupe (French “a long petticoat, a skirt”) and jupon (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: inc-hnd — (Hindi जंगल / Urdu جَن٘گَل), from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀚𑀁𑀕𑀮, from Sanskrit जङ्गल (“arid or sterile region, desert”), from a qfa-sub — language. First appears c. 1776 in a translation by .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin junior, a contraction of iuvenior (Latin “younger”) which is the comparative of iuvenis (Latin “young#Adjective”); see [[juvenile.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English jure, from Anglo-Norman juree, from Medieval Latin iūrāta, from Latin iūrō (“to swear or take an oath”).

thumb|right|The Jury, painting of a jury in Aylesbury assizes dated 1861

chain.meaning: to swear or take an oath

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Early 1600s, of origin. Perhaps ultimately from Old French ajurie, from Latin adiūtō.

Alternatively, perhaps ultimately from Frankish *garu (“ready, prepared”), related to yore (Middle English), ȝare (Middle English), from ġeoro (Old English), ġearu (Old English “ready, prompt, prepared, quick”), related to gear (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English juste, from Old French juste, from Latin iūstus (“just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate”), from Proto-Italic *jowestos, related to Latin iūs (Latin “law, right”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-. Compare juist (Scots “just”), juust (Saterland Frisian “just”), just (Western Frisian “just”), juist (Dutch “just”), jüst (Low German (Germany) “jüst”), just (German “just”), just (Danish “just”), just (Swedish “just”). .

chain.meaning: just, lawful, rightful, true, due, proper, moderate

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Variation of joust, presumably ultimately from Latin iuxta (“near, besides”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English justice, from Old French justise, justice (Old French) (Modern justice (French)), from Latin iūstitia (“righteousness, equity”), from iūstus (Latin “just”), from iūs (Latin “right”), from Proto-Italic *jowos, perhaps literally "sacred formula", a word peculiar to Latin (not general Italic) that originated in the religious cults, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-. .

Partly displaced native rihtwīsnes (Old English) ( righteousness (English) < rightwiseness (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English justifien, from Old French justifier, from Late Latin justificare (“make just”), from Latin justus, iustus (Latin “just”) + ficare (Latin “make”), from facere (Latin), equivalent to just + ify (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru (“eastern grey kangaroo”). Despite a popular misconception, the Guugu Yimidhirr term does not mean "I don't know".

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English kene (“[[bold#Adjective”), from Old English cēne (“keen, fierce, bold, brave, warlike, powerful; [[learned#Adjective”), from Proto-Germanic *kōniz (“knowledgeable, skilful, experienced, clever, capable”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).

Cognate with køn (Danish “handsome, pretty”), kien (Dutch “[[smart#Adjective”), koen (Dutch “[[daring#Adjective”), kühn (German “bold, daring, audacious, hardy, valiant, venturesome”), kænn (Icelandic “wise, crafty, clever, able”), kønur (Faroese “expert (in, on), experienced, skilful, able, capable”), keen (Scots “lively, brisk; avaricious”). Related to cunnan (Old English “to know how to, be able to”). More at cunning (English), can (English).

chain.meaning: keen, fierce, bold, brave, warlike, powerful; [[learned#Adjective

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Irish caoin (“to lament, keen”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English kepen (“to keep, guard, look after, watch”), from Old English cēpan (“to seize, hold, observe”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōpijan, from Proto-Germanic *kōpijaną (“to look, heed, watch, observe”) (compare kypje (Western Frisian “to look”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵab-, *ǵāb- (Proto-Indo-European “to look after”) (compare žẽbti (Lithuanian “to eat reluctantly”), забо́та (Russian “care, worry”)).

The dialectal keep (English “sense of the verb meaning “to put back” or “put away””) may be analyzed as a semantic loan from a local language—compare cadw (Welsh) and - (Mandarin Chinese) .

chain.meaning: to keep, guard, look after, watch

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English kepe, kep (Middle English), from the verb (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English kepere. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ketel, also chetel (Middle English), from Old English ċietel (“kettle, cauldron”) and in Middle English possibly influenced by Old Norse ketill and both from Proto-Germanic *katilaz (“kettle, bucket, vessel”), of uncertain origin and formation. Usually regarded as a borrowing of Late Latin catīllus (“small bowl”), diminutive of Latin catinus (“deep bowl, vessel for cooking up or serving food”), however, the word may be Germanic confused with the Latin: compare cete (Old English “cooking pot”), chezzi (Old High German “a kettle, dish, bowl”), kati (Icelandic), ketla (Icelandic “a small boat”). Cognate with tsjettel (Western Frisian “kettle”), ketel (Dutch “kettle”), Kessel (German “kettle”), kittel (Swedish “cauldron, kettle”), 𐌺𐌰𐍄𐌹𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “kettle”), kattila (Finnish), kocioł (Polish “cauldron”), kotel (Czech “boiler”), котёл (Russian “boiler, cauldron”).

Cockney rhyming slang from 'kettle and hob' to 'fob' (fob watch).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English ketel, also chetel (Middle English), from Old English ċietel (“kettle, cauldron”) and in Middle English possibly influenced by Old Norse ketill and both from Proto-Germanic *katilaz (“kettle, bucket, vessel”), of uncertain origin and formation.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English keye, kaye (Middle English), keiȝe (Middle English), from Old English cǣġ (“key, solution, experiment”) (whence also key (Scots) and kay (Scots “key”)), from Anglo-Frisian Proto-West Germanic *kaiju, of uncertain origin. The only sure cognates are Koai (Saterland Frisian “key”), kaai (Western Frisian “key”), and kai (North Frisian), koie (North Frisian “key”). Possibly from Proto-Germanic *kēgaz, *kēguz (Proto-Germanic “stake, post, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵogʰ-, *ǵegʰ- (Proto-Indo-European), *ǵegʰn- (Proto-Indo-European “branch, stake, bush”), which would make it cognate with kāk (Middle Low German “whipping post, pillory”), and perhaps to keige (Middle Dutch “javelin, spear”) and keie (Middle Low German), keige (Middle Low German “spear”).

For the semantic development, note that medieval keys were simply long poles (ending in a hook) with which a crossbar obstructing a door from the inside could be removed from the outside, by lifting it through a hole in the door. Liberman has noted, however, "The original meaning of *kaig-jo- was presumably '*pin with a twisted end.' Words with the root *kai- followed by a consonant meaning 'crooked, bent; twisted' are common only in the North Germanic languages."
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English keye, kaye (Middle English), keiȝe (Middle English), from Old English cǣġ (“key, solution, experiment”) (whence also key (Scots) and kay (Scots “key”)), from Anglo-Frisian Proto-West Germanic *kaiju, of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Variant of cay (English), from Spanish cayo, from Taíno cayo (“small island”)

etymologies.text: kilogram,kilo.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English kyllyng; equivalent to kill + -ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English kyndely, kyndeliche (Middle English), from Old English cyndelīċ (“natural, kindly”); equivalent to kind + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English kyndely, kyndly (Middle English), kyndeliche (Middle English), from Old English ġecyndelīċe, equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English kyndenesse, equivalent to kind + -ness (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English kingdom, kyngdom (Middle English), from Old English cyningdōm from Proto-Germanic *kuningadōmaz, equivalent to king + -dom (English). Cognate with kingdom (Scots), keuningdom (Western Frisian), koningdom (Dutch), Königtum (German), kongedømme (Danish), kungadöme (Swedish), and konungdómur (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English kyt,kytt,kytte, from Middle Dutch kitte (“a wooden vessel made of hooped staves”). Related to kit (Dutch “tankard”) (see below). The further etymology is unknown. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *kitjō-,*kut-, which would be related to the root of kot (Dutch “ramshackle house”), itself of non-Indo-European origin.

The transfer of meaning to the contents of a soldier's knapsack dates to the late 18th century, extended use of any collection of necessaries used for travelling dates to the first half of the 19th century.
The further widening of the sense to a collection of parts sold for the buyer to assemble emerges in American English in the mid 20th century.

chain.meaning: a wooden vessel made of hooped staves

etymologies.uncertainNote: The further etymology is unknown.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|alt=A young red fox emerging from a burrow, looking at the camera|A red fox kit ()

A short form of kitten (English) or kitling (English). From the 16th century, spelled kytte (English), kitt (English). From the 19th century also extended to other young animals (beaver, fox, mink, muskrat, etc.), and to a species of small fox (kit fox). Later usage (for other animals) perhaps influenced by chit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: 16th century, perhaps from cithara.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Borrowed from German kitte, Kütte (German “flock of doves”) (circa 1880).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English kitoun, kytton (Middle English), kyton (Middle English), keton (Middle English “kitten”), of origin. Seemingly from, and usually explained as being from, unattested Anglo-Norman *kitoun, *ketun (Old French) (compare chitoun (Old French), cheton (Old French), chaton (Old French “kitten”), diminutive of cat (Old French), chat (Old French “cat”)); whence Modern chaton (French “kitten”). Similar words of Germanic origin may have reinforced this word; compare kitling (English “kit, kitten”), Kitten (Low German “kitten”), kettlingur (Icelandic “kitten”), chitte (Middle English) . The idea that kitoun (Middle English), rather than being of Anglo-Norman origin, was in fact a purely Germanic derivation from one of these words is etymologically problematic, but cannot be definitively ruled out.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English kne, from Old English cnēow, from Proto-West Germanic *kneu, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European —, a derivative of *ǵónu (Proto-Indo-European).

See also knibbel (Western Frisian), Knee (Low German), Knie (Low German), knie (Dutch), Knie (German), knæ (Danish), kne (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), knä (Swedish); also 𒄀𒉡 (Hittite), genū (Latin), kanweṃ (xto), keni (txb “kenī”), γόνυ (Ancient Greek “knee”), γωνία (Ancient Greek “corner, angle”), glin (Welsh “knee”), ծունր (Classical Armenian), 𐬲𐬥𐬎𐬨 (ae), जानु (Sanskrit).

The obsolete plural kneen is from Middle English kneen, knen (Middle English), kneon (Middle English), kneuwene (Middle English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English knelen, from Old English cnēowlian (“to kneel”), equivalent to knee + le (English). Cognate with knielen (Dutch), knelen (Low German), dialectal knielen (German), chnüle (Alemannic), knæle (Danish), all meaning “to kneel”.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: knickerbockers.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with knütten (Low German) and knýta (Old Norse) (whence knytte (Danish), knyta (Norwegian Nynorsk)). More at knot (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English knokken, from Old English cnocian, ġecnocian (Old English), ġecnucian (Old English), cnucian (Old English “to knock, pound on, beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *knokōn, from Proto-Germanic *knukōną (“to knock”), a suffixed form of *knu- (Proto-Germanic), *knew- (Proto-Germanic “to pound on, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gnew-, *gen- (Proto-Indo-European “to squeeze, pinch, kink, ball up, concentrate”). The English word is cognate with knochen (Middle High German “to hit”), cnuian (Old English), cnuwian (Old English “to pound, knock”), knoka (Old Norse) (compare knuge (Danish “to squeeze”), knocka (Swedish “to hug”)). More at knuckle.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English knowen, from Old English cnāwan (“to know, perceive, recognise”), from Proto-West Germanic *knāan, from Proto-Germanic *knēaną (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- (“to know”).

* from Proto-Germanic: knaw (Scots “to know, recognise”), knega (Icelandic “to know, know how to, be able”), knājan (Old High German “to know, recognise”), kná (Old Norse “to know how”). Remotely related also - (Dutch) and kennen (German), kenne (Western Frisian) (see English ken (English)).
* from Indo-European: gnoscō (Latin), cognoscō (Latin) (conocer (Spanish), connaître (French), cunoaște (Romanian), conoscere (Italian), conhecer (Portuguese)), γνωρίζω (Ancient Greek “to know”) and γνῶσις (Ancient Greek “knowledge”), njoh (Albanian “to know, recognise”), знать (Russian “to know”), žinoti (Lithuanian “to know”), شناختن (Persian “to know”) and जानना (Hindi “to know, understand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Shortening of you know (English)—Singapore English favours pro-drop constructions (Wee, 2003).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English knowleche, knaweleche (Middle English), cnawlece (Middle English “knowledge”), from knowen (Middle English “to know, recognise”) + -leche (Middle English). Related to knowlechen (Middle English “to find out, acknowledge”). For more on the Middle English suffix -leche, compare freelage (English). Compare also cnāwelǣċ (Old English), cnāwelǣċing (Old English “acknowledging, acknowledgement”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English knowen, from Old English cnāwen.

Morphologically know + n (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English label (“narrow band, strip of cloth”), from Old French label, lambel (Old French) (Modern lambeau (French)), from Frankish *lappā (“torn piece of cloth”), from Proto-Germanic *lappǭ, *lappô (Proto-Germanic “cloth stuff, rag, scraps, flap, dewlap, lobe, rabbit ear”), from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“blade”). Cognate with lappa (Old High German “rag, piece of cloth”), læppa (Old English “skirt, flap of a garment”). More at lap (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Medieval Latin labōrātōrium

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lack, lakke (Middle English), lak (Middle English), from Old English *læc (“deficiency, lack, want”), from Proto-West Germanic *lak, from Proto-Germanic *laką, *lakaz (Proto-Germanic “slackness”), from Proto-Germanic *lakaz (“limp, slack, loose, low”), related to *lak(k)ōną (Proto-Germanic “to blame, reproach”), from Proto-Indo-European *lok-néh₂-. Cognate with Lak (Saterland Frisian “lack”), lack (Middle Low German), lak (Middle Low German “lack”), lak (Dutch “lack, deficiency, calumny”), lakur (Icelandic “lacking”). Related also to laken (Middle Dutch “to blame, lack”).

Eclipsed non-native carence (Middle English “absence, lack”), from carence (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English lacken, lakken (Middle English), laken (Middle English), from Old English læccian, *lacian (Old English “to blame, criticise, lack”), from Proto-West Germanic *lak(k)ōn (“to blame, be lacking”), from Proto-Germanic *lak(k)ōną (“to reproach, blame, be lacking”), from Proto-Indo-European *lok-néh₂-. Cognate with lakia (Old Frisian), lekia (Old Frisian “to contest, blame”), lacken (Middle Low German), laken (Middle Low German “to reproach, blame, criticise”), laken (Middle Dutch “to disapprove, blame, lack”), laken (Dutch “to blame, reproach”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English ladder, laddre (Middle English); from Old English hlǣder, from Proto-West Germanic *hlaidriju, from Proto-Germanic *hlaidrijō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlóydʰrom, from *ḱley- (Proto-Indo-European “to lean”).

Compare ledder (Scots), ladder (North Frisian), Laadere (Saterland Frisian), ljedder (Western Frisian), ladder (Dutch), Leiter (German); also clithar (Old Irish “hedge”), and 𐌊𐌋𐌄𐌈𐌓𐌀𐌌 (xum “stretcher”). See lean (English), which is related to lid (English).

Further include istrī (ask), c̣ik (bsh), čik (Prakrit), čix (Prakrit); c̣iř (wbk), श्रिति (Sanskrit).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lady, laddy (Middle English), lafdi (Middle English), lavedi (Middle English), from Old English hlǣfdīġe (“mistress of a household, wife of a lord, lady”), from hlāf (Old English “bread, loaf”) + dǣġe (Old English “kneader”), related to dǣġe (Old English “maker of dough”) (whence dey (English “dairymaid”)). Compare also lord (English). More at loaf (English), dairy (English), dough (English). Unrelated to lad (English).

chain.meaning: mistress of a household, wife of a lord, lady

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lamb, from Old English lamb, from Proto-West Germanic *lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁onbʰos, enlargement of *h₁elh₁én (Proto-Indo-European), ultimately from *h₁el- (Proto-Indo-European).

See also lam (Dutch), Lamm (German), Lamperl (Bavarian), lam (Danish), lamm (Swedish), lammas (Finnish), lon (Scottish Gaelic “elk”), ἔλαφος (Ancient Greek “red deer”). More at elk.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lond, land (Middle English), from Old English land, from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).

Cognate with laund (Scots “land”), lhoan (Yola), lloan (Yola), loan (Yola), londe (Yola), lone (Yola “land”), loun (North Frisian), luin (North Frisian), lun (North Frisian), Lön (North Frisian), lönj (cog), löön (North Frisian “land”), Lound (Saterland Frisian “land”), lân (Western Frisian “land”), Land (Limburgish), landj (Limburgish), Laïnt (Limburgish “land”), land (Dutch “land, country”), - (lb) and Land (German “land, country, state”), łaond (Ripuarian “land”), - (Danish), - (Elfdalian), - (Faroese), - (Icelandic), - (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and land (Swedish “land, country, shore, territory”). Non-Germanic cognates include lann (Old Irish “heath”), llan (Welsh “enclosure”), lann (Breton “heath”), лѧдо (Church Slavonic), from *lędo (Proto-Slavic “heath, wasteland”), lande (French “heath”) and lëndinë (Albanian “heath, grassland”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English *land, from Old English hland. More at lant (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From land + lady (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English londlord, landlorde (Middle English), from Old English landhlāford, equivalent to land + lord (English). Cognate with landlaird (Scots), lantlord (Middle Low German “homeowner, landlord”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From an alteration (due to Dutch landschap (Dutch)) of earlier landskip (English), lantschip (English), from Middle English *landschippe, *landschapp (Middle English), from Old English landsċipe, landsċeap (Old English “region, district, tract of land”); in some senses from Dutch landschap (“region, district, province, landscape”), from landscap (Middle Dutch), lantscap (Middle Dutch “region”), from *landskepi (Old Dutch), *landskapi (Old Dutch “region”). Cognate with landskape (Scots), landskep (Scots), landskip (Scots “landscape”), lânskip (Western Frisian “landscape”), landschop (Low German “landscape, district”), Landschaft (German “landscape, countryside, scenery”), landskab (Danish “landscape, countryside”), landskap (Swedish “landscape, scenery, province”), landskapur (Icelandic “countryside”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lane, lone (Middle English), from Old English lanu (“a lane, alley, avenue”), from Proto-West Germanic *lanu, from Proto-Germanic *lanō (“lane, passageway”).

Cognate with lone (Scots “cattle-track, by-road”), leane (Western Frisian), loane (Western Frisian “a walkway, avenue”), laan (Dutch “alley, avenue”), Lane (Low German (Germany)), Laan (Low German (Germany) “lane”), lån (Swedish “covered walkway encircling a house”), lön (Icelandic “a row of houses”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English langage, language (Middle English), from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”), from itc-ola dingua (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue, speech, language”). . . Mostly, but not fully, displaced native tongue (English), in this specific sense, in common as well as academic usage.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Alteration of languet (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English lappe, from Old English læppa (“skirt or flap of a garment”), from Proto-West Germanic *lappō, from Proto-Germanic *lappô (“cloth; rag”), of origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Cognate with lap (Dutch “cloth; rag”), Lappen (German “cloth; lobe; flap”), leppur (Icelandic “rag; patch”).

chain.meaning: skirt or flap of a garment

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lappen (“to fold, wrap”) from earlier wlappen (Middle English “to fold, wrap”), from Old English *wlappan, *wlæppan (Old English), *wlappian (Old English “to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wlapp-, *wrapp- (Proto-Germanic “to wrap, fold, roll up, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to bend, turn”).

Cognate with lappen (Middle Dutch “to wrap up, embrace”), dialectal vravle (Danish “to wind”), goluppare (Old Italian “to wrap, fold up”) (from ). . Also related to envelop (English), develop (English).

The sense of "to get a lap ahead (of someone) on a track" is from 1847, on notion of "overlapping." The noun meaning "a turn around a track" (1861) is from this sense.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English lappen, from Old English lapian, from Proto-West Germanic *lapōn, from Proto-Germanic *lapōną, *lapjaną (Proto-Germanic “to lick; lap”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂b- (“to lap, lick”); akin to laffen (Old High German “to lick”), lepja (Old Norse), labe (Danish), lepil (Old Saxon), Löffel (German “spoon”). Cognate with lambo (Latin “lick”). lamper (French) is a loanword from German. Compare leffe (Danish), dialect läffeln (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: large + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From LASER, w:light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. . Originally called an optical maser.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin laser

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English laste, latst (Middle English), syncopated variant of latest (Middle English), both ultimately from Old English latost. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English lasten, from Old English lǣstan, from Proto-West Germanic *laistijan, from Proto-Germanic *laistijaną. Cognate with leisten (German “yield”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
thumb|A pair#Noun|pair of [[wooden lasts.]]

The is derived from Middle English lest, leste (Middle English “shoemaker’s model shaped like a foot, last”), from Old English lǣste (“shoemaker‘s last”), from Proto-Germanic *laistiz, from *laisǭ (Proto-Germanic “track, trail”), from Proto-Indo-European *leys-eh₂-, from *leys- (Proto-Indo-European “to trace; to track”). .

The is derived from the noun.

* leest (Dutch)
* Leisten (German)
* *laistaz (Proto-Germanic “footprint”)
* läst (Swedish)

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English last, from Old English hlæst (“burden, load, freight”), from Proto-Germanic *hlastuz (“burden, load, freight”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂- (“to put, lay out”). Cognate with lêst (Western Frisian), last (Dutch), Last (German), last (Swedish), lest (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: last + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English late, lat (Middle English), from Old English læt (“slow; slack, lax, negligent; late”), from Proto-West Germanic *lat, from Proto-Germanic *lataz (“slow, lazy”). .

Cognate with laate (Yola “late”), leed (North Frisian), leet (North Frisian), lääs (North Frisian “late”), leet (Saterland Frisian “late”), - (Dutch), laat (Low German (Germany) “late, tardy”), lass (German “lazy, sluggish”), lad (Danish “languid, lazy, indolent”), - (Faroese), latur (Icelandic “lazy”), - (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and lat (Swedish “lazy”), 𐌻𐌰𐍄𐍃 (Gothic “lazy, slothful”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lately, latly (Middle English), equivalent to . Compare lætlīċe (Old English “slowly, tardily”), lātlîk (Middle Low German “careless, slack, sloppy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
* Adverb: From Middle English later, latere (Middle English), from Old English lator, equivalent to late + er (English).
* Adjective: From Middle English later, latere (Middle English), from Old English lætra, equivalent to late + er (English).

Cognate with leeter (Saterland Frisian “later”), letter (Western Frisian “later”), later (Dutch “later”), later (Low German (Germany) “later”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English latter, lattere (Middle English), lattre (Middle English), from Old English lætra, comparative form of læt (Old English “late”). Equivalent to , thus a ; also, related to last (English), whose doublet is latest (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English laughen, laghen (Middle English), from (Anglian) Old English hlæhhan, hlehhan (Old English), (West Saxon) hliehhan (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *hlahhjan, from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.

Germanic: lauch (Scots “to laugh”), leeigh (Yola), leigh (Yola “to laugh”), laache (North Frisian), lachi (North Frisian), laake (North Frisian), loache (North Frisian), lååke (North Frisian “to laugh”), laachje (Saterland Frisian “to laugh”), laitsje (Western Frisian “to laugh”), lache (Alemannic “to laugh”), lachan (Cimbric “to laugh”), lachen (Dutch / German / Low German “to laugh”), laachen (lb “to laugh”), לאַכן (Yiddish “to laugh”), le (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “to laugh”), läa (Elfdalian “to laugh”), læa (Faroese “to laugh”), hlæja (Icelandic “to laugh”), le (Norwegian Nynorsk), læ (Norwegian Nynorsk), læja (Norwegian Nynorsk “to laugh”), lachen (gme-cgo “to laugh”), 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌷𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to laugh”).

Indo-European: kloc'h (Breton “bell”), clog (Irish “bell; clock”), clag (Manx / Scottish Gaelic “bell”), cloch (Welsh “bell”), клекота́ть (Russian), клокота́ть (Russian), клохта́ть (Russian “to cluck, cackle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English laughter, laghter (Middle English), laȝter (Middle English), from Old English hleahtor (“laughter, jubilation, derision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (Proto-Indo-European “to shout”). Cognate with Gelächter (German “laughter, hilarity, merriment”), Danish and Norwegian latter (Danish “laughter”), Icelandic hlátur (Icelandic “laughter”). More at laugh (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English launchen (“to throw as a lance”), Old French lanchier, another form (Old Northern French —/Norman variant, compare Jèrriais lanchi (Norman)) of lancier (Old French), French lancer (French), from lance (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Portuguese lancha (“barge, launch”), apparently from Malay lancar (“quick, agile”). Spelling influenced by the verb above.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lavendrie, from Old French lavanderie, from Latin lavandaria. See launder (English).
thumb|upright=1.1|A laundry (sense 2, room where laundering is done).
thumb|upright=1.1|Laundry (sense 3, clothes in the process of being laundered) hanging on a clothesline to dry.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lawe, laȝe (Middle English), from Old English lagu (“law”), borrowed from Old Norse lǫg (“law”), originally the plural of lag (Old Norse “layer, stratum, a laying in order, measure, stroke”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą (“that which is laid down”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”). Cognate with law (Scots “law”), lög (Icelandic “things laid down, law”), lóg (Faroese “law”), lov (Norwegian “law”), lag (Swedish “law”), lov (Danish “law”), laki (Finnish “law”). Compare typologically distant cognate уложе́ние (Russian). Displaced native ǣ (Old English) and ġesetnes (Old English). More at lay (English).

Not related to legal (English), nor to loi (French), ley (Spanish), all of which ultimately derive from lēx (Latin), from *leǵ- (Proto-Indo-European “to gather”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Northern Middle English lawe, from Old English hlāw (“burial mound”). Also spelled low. See also law (Scots).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English lagh, from Old Norse lag (“that which is lying or laid, position, price, way, sting, blow”), from Proto-Germanic *lagą (“that which is laid”). Cognate with lauch (Scots “one's tavern-reckoning or one's share of the cost, a score; a payment for drink or entertainment”), lai (Middle English “one's share of expenses, one's bill or account”).

chain.meaning: that which is lying or laid, position, price, way, sting, blow

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compare la (English) and Lawd (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lawiere, lawier (Middle English), lawer (Middle English), equivalent to law + yer (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Appears at first glance to be from Middle English leyer, leyare (Middle English “a layer of stones or bricks”), equivalent to lay + er (English). In which case, ultimately identical to etymology 2 below. For the pronunciation compare prayer (English).

However, this word layer (referring to a thickness of a material covering a surface) has also been argued to be from a respelling of an obsolete sense of the word lair (English) that was once used by farmers, which had to do with soil. The connecting sense between the usual meaning of lair (English) and the specialised farming meaning was: an area where cows typically rest, the ground being fertilised by their waste. Related to lie#Etymology_1 (English “lie”), ledger (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: lay + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: lazy + -ness

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Attested since 1540, origin uncertain. Probably from Low German — and Middle Low German lasich (“slack, feeble, lazy”), from las (Middle Low German), from Old Saxon lask, from Proto-Germanic *lasiwaz, *laskaz (Proto-Germanic “feeble, weak”), from Proto-Indo-European *las- (“weak”).

Akin to leuzig (Dutch “lazy”), lässig (German “casual, nonchalant, laid-back, easy-going”), lasinn (Old Norse “limpy, tired, weak”), lesu (Old English), lysu (Old English “false, evil, base”). More at lush (English).

An alternative etymology traces lazy to Early Modern English laysy (English), a derivative of lay (English) (plural lays + -y (English)) in the same way that tipsy (English) is derived from tip (English). See lay (English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: Attested since 1540, origin uncertain.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English led, leed (Middle English), from Old English lēad (“lead”), from Proto-West Germanic *laud (“lead”), possibly borrowed from Proto-Celtic *ɸloudom, from Proto-Indo-European *plewd- (“to flow”).

Cognate with leid (Scots), lede (Scots “lead”), lud (North Frisian), luad (North Frisian “lead”), lead (Western Frisian “lead”), lood (Dutch “lead”), Lod (Low German “solder, plummet”), Lot (German “solder, plummet, sounding line”), lod (Swedish “solder, plummet”), lóð (Icelandic “a plumb, weight”), luaidhe (Irish “lead”) plumbum (Latin “lead”), luoti (Finnish “bullet”). . More at flow (English).
* Graphite was once believed to be a form of lead; see black lead (English) and plumbago (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English leden, from Old English lǣdan (“to lead”), from Proto-West Germanic *laidijan, from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną (“to cause one to go, lead”), causative of Proto-Germanic *līþaną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“to leave, die”).

Cognate with liede (Western Frisian “to lead”), leiden (Dutch “to lead”), leiten (German “to lead”), lede (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to lead”), leia (Norwegian Nynorsk “to lead”), leda (Swedish “to lead”), leiða (Faroese / Icelandic “to lead”). Related to līþan (Old English “to go, travel”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
Perhaps from a confusion or conflation with read, which has a single spelling for both past and present tenses, but has differing pronunciations in the same way as lead, i.e. the present's vowel is , and the past's is .
See also red#Verb_2 (English) and redd#Verb_3 (English), the obsolete spellings of read.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: . Cognate with leader (Scots “leader”), lieder (Western Frisian “leader”), leider (Dutch “leader”), Leiter (German “leader, conductor, manager”), leder (Danish “leader, manager”), ledare (Swedish “leader, conductor, director”), leiðari (Icelandic “leader, conductor”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English ledinge, ledynge (Middle English), ledand (Middle English), ledande (Middle English), ledende (Middle English), from Old English lǣdende, from Proto-West Germanic *laidijandī, from Proto-Germanic *laidijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *laidijaną (“to lead”), equivalent to . Compare liedend (Western Frisian), leidend (Dutch), leitend (German), ledande (Swedish), leiðandi (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English leding, ledyng (Middle English), ledinge (Middle English), ledunge (Middle English), equivalent to . Cognate with leiding (Dutch “conduit, leading, guidance, leadership”), Leitung (German “line, conduit, cable”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English leedynge, equivalent to lead + ing (English); so named because in metal typesetting (letterpress and hot metal typesetting), pieces of lead (slugs, strips, blocks, etc) were often the mechanical means of producing the gap.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lef, leef (Middle English), from Old English lēaf, from Proto-West Germanic *laub, from Proto-Germanic *laubą (“leaf”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from *lewbʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to cut off”).

Cognate with leaf (Scots “leaf”), laafe (Yola “leaf”), luuf (North Frisian “leaf”), Loof (Saterland Frisian “leaf”), leaf (Western Frisian “leaf”), loap (Cimbric “leaf”), loof (Dutch “foliage”), Laub (German “leaves”), Loov (Low German (Germany) “leaf”), Laf (lb “foliage, leaves”), lap (mhn “leaf”), łaub (Ripuarian), łaup (Ripuarian), łojp (Ripuarian “leaf”), løv (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “leaf”), leyv (Faroese “leaf”), lauf (Icelandic “leaf”), lauv (Norwegian Nynorsk “leaf”), löv (Swedish “leaf”), 𐌻𐌰𐌿𐍆𐍃 (Gothic “leaf”); also luibh (Irish “herb, plant”), liber (Latin “bast; book”), labë (Albanian “rind”), lúobas (Lithuanian “bark; bast”), łub (Polish “bark”), луб (Russian “bast”).

In reference to the maple leaf as national symbol.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: leaf + -let

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English liege, ligg (Middle English), lige (Middle English “a pact between governments, an agreement, alliance”), from Middle French ligue, from Italian lega, from the verb legare (Italian), from Latin ligō (“to tie”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English lege (“league”), from Late Latin leuca, leuga (Latin “the Gaulish mile”), from Gaulish —, from Proto-Celtic *lougā (compare leau (Middle Breton), lew (Middle Breton), lev (Breton) / leo (Breton “league”)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English leken (“to let water in or out”), from Old English *lecan (“to leak”), Middle Dutch leken (“to leak, drip”) or Old Norse leka (“to leak, drip”); all from Proto-Germanic *lekaną (“to leak, drain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leg- (“to leak”).

Cognate with lekken (Dutch “to leak”), lechen (German), lecken (German “to leak”), lække (Danish “to leak”), läcka (Swedish “to leak”), lekke (Norwegian Bokmål “to leak”), leka (Faroese / Icelandic / Norwegian Nynorsk “to leak”). Related also to leċċan (Old English “to water, wet”), lag (Albanian), lak (Albanian “to damp, make wet”). See also leach (English), lake (English).

Compare typologically изтичане (Bulgarian), przeciek (Polish), уте́чка (Russian) (akin to течь (Russian)).

chain.meaning: to let water in or out

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lernen (“to learn", also, "to teach"”), from Old English leornian (“to learn", rarely also, "to teach”), from Proto-West Germanic *liʀnōn, from Proto-Germanic *lizaną, from Proto-Indo-European —, stative from the root *leys- (Proto-Indo-European “track, furrow, trace, trail”).

The spelling with ⟨ea⟩ is of origin and reflects a lengthening of to before in Late Old English or Early Middle English, then later lowering to ; the modern pronunciation reflects still later reshortening. The dialect form with reflects the Middle English pronunciation which either retained the short or reshortened it earlier, enabling the a development to before which yielded modern .

Cognate with lernia (Old Frisian), lerna (Old Frisian “to learn”), lernen (Middle Low German “to learn", also, "to teach”), leernen (Middle Dutch “to learn", also, "to teach”) (whence lernen (Dutch “to study scripture”)), lernen (German “to learn”). See also lore (English) and lear#Verb (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: learn + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lernyng, lernynge (Middle English), from Old English leornung (“learning, study”), from Proto-West Germanic *liʀnungu (“learning”), equivalent to . Cognate with lernunga (Old Saxon), Lernung (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The , , and are derived from Middle English leste, lest (Middle English), last (Middle English “(adjective) smallest, least; (noun) smallest thing, etc.; person or thing least in importance; etc.”), from Old English lǣst, a contraction of læsast (Old English), læsest (Old English “least”) (also lærest (Old English) in only one source), from Proto-Germanic *laisistaz (“smallest, least”), from *laisiz (Proto-Germanic “less”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂is- or *leh₃is- (Proto-Indo-European); whence modern less (English)) + *-istaz (Proto-Germanic “forming forms of some adjectives”).

The and are derived from the adjective or determiner.

* leist (Old Frisian)
* lēs (Old Saxon)

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English leven, from Old English lǣfan (“to leave”), from Proto-West Germanic *laibijan, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną (“to let stay, leave”), causative of *lībaną (Proto-Germanic “to stay, remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick; fat”).

Cognate with lēva (Old Frisian “to leave”), dialectal loven (Dutch “to have left over, save, keep”), lēvian (Old Saxon), leiban (Old High German “to leave”), leifa (Old Norse “to leave over”) (whence leifa (Icelandic “to leave food uneaten”), leva (Swedish “to leave”)), lifna (Icelandic “to be left”) (whence levne (Danish)). More at lave, belive.

The noun is attested since the 19th century, with earliest references to billiards.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English leve, from Old English lēaf (“permission, privilege”), from Proto-Germanic *laubō, *laubą (Proto-Germanic “permission, privilege, favour, worth”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to love, hold dear”). Cognate with obsolete Laube (German “permission”), lov (Swedish “permission”), leyfi (Icelandic “permission”). Related to verlof (Dutch), Urlaub,Erlaubnis,Verlaub (German). See also love (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English leven, from Old English līefan (“to allow, grant, concede; believe, trust, confide in”), from Proto-West Germanic *laubijan, from Proto-Germanic *laubijaną (“to allow, praise”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“to love, hold dear”). Cognate with erlauben (German “to allow”), glauben (German “to believe”), leyfa (Icelandic “to allow”).

chain.meaning: to allow, grant, concede; believe, trust, confide in

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English leven, from lef (Middle English “leaf”). More at leaf (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From French lever. Compare levy (English). Compare also leve (Middle English), a variant of levy that may have been monosyllabic.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lecture, lectour (Middle English), letture (Middle English), letteur (Middle English), lettur (Middle English), lectury (Middle English), from Medieval Latin — or Late Latin lectura (“reading”), from Latin lectus, past participle of legō (Latin “to read, recite”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: lecture + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English leek, leeke (Middle English), lek (Middle English), leke (Middle English), leyke (Middle English), from Old English lēac, lēc (Old English “allium; garlic or leek”), from Proto-West Germanic *lauk, from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“leek”), from *leukaną (Proto-Germanic), *lūkaną (Proto-Germanic “to close, shut”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewg- (“to bend”).

Cognate with Làuich (Alemannic “leek”), look (Dutch “leek”), Luak (pdt “leek”), Lauch (German “leek”), løg (Danish “onion”), leykur (Faroese “onion”), laukur (Icelandic “garlic, leek, onion”), løk (Norwegian Bokmål “onion”), lauk (Norwegian Nynorsk), løk (Norwegian Nynorsk “onion”), lök (Swedish “onion”), лук (Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian “onion”), lauk (pox “garlic”), лу̏к (Serbo-Croatian), lȕk (Serbo-Croatian “onion; garlic”), lauk (Estonian “allium”), laukka (fi,izh “onion”), lōka (liv “onion”), laukku (olo “onion”), lauk (lud “leek; onion”); also lunget (Gaulish “to load”), fulaing (Irish “to bear; to support; to sustain; to mountain”), fuiling (Scottish Gaelic), fulaing (Scottish Gaelic “to suffer; to stand; to allow; to bear”), gollwng (Welsh “to drop, release; to leak; to dissolve”), luxus (Latin “dislocated”), λύγος (Ancient Greek “chaste tree; flexible twig, withe”), vlug (Albanian “peak”), रुग्ण (Sanskrit “bent, broken, checked; diseased, infirm, sick”). See garlic (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: , from lēx (Latin “law”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From legal + -ly (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English legende, from Old French legende, from Medieval Latin legenda (“a legend, story, especially the lives of the saints”), from Latin legendus (“legenda”), from lego (Latin “to read”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English leyser, from Anglo-Norman leisir, variant of Old French loisir (“to enjoy oneself”) (Modern loisir (French) survives as a noun), substantive use of a verb, from Latin licēre (“be permitted”). Displaced native ǣmetta (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From earlier len (English) (with excrescent -d, as in sound (English “sound”)), from Middle English lenen, lænen (Middle English), from Old English lǣnan (“to lend; give, grant, lease”), from Proto-West Germanic *laihnijan, from Proto-Germanic *laihnijaną (“to loan”), from Proto-Germanic *laihną (“loan”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave, leave over”).

Cognate with len (Scots), lend (Scots “to lend”), liene (Western Frisian “to lend, borrow, loan”), lenen (Dutch “to lend, borrow, loan”), låne (Danish “to lend, loan”), låna (Swedish “to lend, loan”), lána (Icelandic “to lend, loan”), léna (Icelandic “to grant”), linquō (Latin “quit, leave, forlet”), λείπω (Ancient Greek “leave, release”). See also loan (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lende (usually in plural as lendes (Middle English), leendes (Middle English), lyndes (Middle English)), from Old English lendenu, lendino (Old English “loins”), plural of Old English lenden (“loin”), from Proto-West Germanic *landī, from Proto-Germanic *landį̄ (“loin”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“loin, kidney”). Cognate with lend (Scots), leynd (Scots “the loins, flank, buttocks”), lendenen (Dutch “loins, reins”), Lenden (German “loins”), länder (Swedish “loins”), lænd (Danish “loin”), lendar (Icelandic “loins”), lumbus (Latin “loin”) (whence loin (English)),
lędźwie (Polish “loins”),
ля́двея (Russian “thigh, haunch”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lengthe, from Old English lengþ, lengþu (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *langiþu, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō, equivalent to long + th (English). Cognate with lenth (Scots), lainth (Scots “length”), Loangte (Saterland Frisian “length”), lingte (Western Frisian), langte (Western Frisian “length”), lengte (Dutch “length”), Längde (Low German (Germany)), Längd (Low German (Germany)), Längte (Low German (Germany)), Längt (Low German (Germany) “length”), længde (Danish “length”), längd (Swedish “length”), lengd (Icelandic “length”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English leopard, leopart (Middle English), lepard (Middle English), leperd (Middle English), from Old French leopard (“leopard”), from Late Latin leopardus (“leopon, lipard”) from late Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (“leopon, lipard”), from λέων (Ancient Greek “lion”) + πάρδος (Ancient Greek “pard, male leopard”), from earlier πάρδαλις (Ancient Greek “leopard”), probably from an unattested peo — term ancestral to , , , پړانګ (Pashto “پړانګ”) (pṛāng). Compare پلنگ (Persian) and पृदाकु (Sanskrit “panther”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lessoun, from Old French leçon, from Latin lēctiō (“lēctiō, lēctiōnem”), from legō (Latin “to read; to gather”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English leten, læten (Middle English), from Old English lǣtan (“to allow, let go, bequeath, leave, rent”), from Proto-West Germanic *lātan, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną (“to leave behind, allow”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to be tired, leave”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

Akin to latian (Old English “to delay”), letten (Dutch), læt (Old English “late”). More at late, delay.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English letuse, of uncertain precise origin, probably from the plural form Old French laitue (“laitues”), derived from Latin lactūca (“lettuce”), from lac (Latin “milk”), because of the milky fluid in its stalks. Replaced Old English lēactric (“lēahtric”).

Likely from the green color of US banknotes.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English level, from Old French livel, liveau (Old French), later nivel (Old French), niveau (Old French), from Latin libella (“a balance, a level”), diminutive of libra (Latin “a balance, a level”); see libra, librate. .

The verb is from Middle English levelen, from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English lier, liere (Middle English), lyere (Middle English), liȝer (Middle English), lieȝer (Middle English), legher (Middle English), from Old English lēgere, lēogere (Old English “liar, false witness, hypocrite”), from Proto-West Germanic *leugārī, from Proto-Germanic *leugārijaz (“liar”), from *leuganą + *-ārijaz (Proto-Germanic), equivalent to . More at lie (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English liberte, from Old French liberté, from Latin libertas (“freedom”), from liber (Latin “free”); see liberal (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English likken, from Old English liccian, from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn, from Proto-Germanic *likkōną (“to lick”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”). Sense evolution towards violence unclear; not paralleled in any other Germanic language.

etymologies.text:
From Middle English lie, from Old English lyġe (“lie”), from Proto-Germanic *lugiz (“lie”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to announce, tell publicly”).

Cognate with Löägene (Saterland Frisian “a lie”), leugen (Dutch), logen (Dutch), loogen (Dutch “a lie”), Lug (German), Lüge (German), Lügen (German “a lie”), Lögen (Low German (Germany) “a lie”), Ligen (lb “a lie”), ליגן (Yiddish “a lie”), løgn (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “a lie”), lygi (Icelandic), lygn (Icelandic “a lie”), lygn (Norwegian Nynorsk), løgn (Norwegian Nynorsk “a lie”), lögn (Swedish “a lie”); also лъжа́ (Bulgarian “а lie”), lež (Czech “a lie”), ложь (Russian “а lie”), łeż (Polish “a lie”), ла̑ж (Serbo-Croatian), laž (Serbo-Croatian “a lie”), lož (Slovak “a lie”), lȃž (Slovenian “a lie”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lyf, from Old English līf, from Proto-West Germanic *līb, from Proto-Germanic *lībą (“life, body”), from *lībaną (Proto-Germanic “to remain, stay, be left”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”).

Cognate with life (Scots), leif (Scots “life”), Lieuw (Saterland Frisian “body”), liif (Western Frisian “body”), laip (Cimbric “body”), lijf (Dutch “body”) and leven (Dutch “life”), Leib (German “body; womb”) and Leben (German “life”), Lief (Low German “body; life”), Leif (lb), Läif (lb “body”), łaowa (Ripuarian “life”), לײַב (Yiddish “body”), liv (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “life; waist”), lív (Faroese “life”), líf (Icelandic “life”). etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lyftyme, equivalent to life + time (English). Cognate with líftími (Icelandic “lifetime”). Compare also Lieuwendstied (Saterland Frisian), leeftijd (Dutch) and levenstijd (Dutch), Levenstied (Low German (Germany)), Lebenszeit (German), livstid (Danish), livstid (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English liften, lyften (Middle English), from Old Norse lypta (“to lift, air”), from Proto-Germanic *luftijaną (“to raise in the air”), related to *luftuz (Proto-Germanic “roof, air”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“to peel, break off, damage”) or from a root meaning roof (see *luftuz (Proto-Germanic)). Cognate with - (Danish) and løfte (Norwegian Bokmål “to lift”), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and lyfta (Swedish “to lift”), lüften (German “to air, lift”), lyft (Old English “air”). See above. 1851 for the noun sense "a mechanical device for vertical transport".

For this sense Cleasby suggests perhaps a relation to the root of Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌹𐍆𐍄𐌿𐍃 (Gothic) "thief", cognate with cleptus (Latin) and Greek κλέπτω (Ancient Greek)). But perhaps simply from the idea of removing an item from a surface.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lifte, luft (Middle English), lefte (Middle English “air, sky, heaven”), from Old English lyft (“atmosphere, air”), from Proto-West Germanic *luftu, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz (“roof, sky, air”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“to peel, break off, damage”).

Cognate with luft (Old High German “air”) (Luft (German)), lucht (Dutch “air”), lopt (Old Norse “lopt, loft”). .

* leuchten (German “to shine”)

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English light, liht (Middle English), leoht (Middle English), from Old English lēoht (“luminous, bright, light, clear, resplendent, renowned, beautiful”), from Proto-Germanic *leuhtaz (“light”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light”). Cognate with ljoacht (Saterland Frisian “light”), licht (Dutch), licht (German).

chain.meaning: luminous, bright, light, clear, resplendent, renowned, beautiful

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
From Middle English light, liȝt (Middle English), lyghte (Middle English), from Old English lēht, lēoht (Old English), līht (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz or *līhtaz (Proto-Germanic “light (in weight)”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“lightweight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The is derived from Late Middle English lighter, lightere (Middle English), lyghtere (Middle English “type of barge or tender for transporting cargo”), from lighten (Middle English “to reduce the weight of, lighten; to alight, dismount; to descend; etc.”) + -er (Middle English), -ere (Middle English). is from Old English līehtan (West Saxon), līhtan (Old English “to reduce the weight of, lighten; to alight, dismount; to descend”) (Anglian; Late West Saxon), from Proto-West Germanic *lį̄htijan (“to reduce the weight of, lighten”), from Proto-Germanic *linhtijaną (“to reduce the weight of”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“lightweight; to move lightly or effortlessly”). .

The is derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Verb from Middle English liken, from Old English līcian (“to like, to please”), from Proto-West Germanic *līkēn, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg- (“image; likeness; similarity”).

Cognate with liekje (Saterland Frisian “to be similar, resemble”), lykje (Western Frisian “to seem, appear, look”), lijken (Dutch “to seem”), lieken (Low German “to be like; resemble”), gleichen (German “to resemble”), lika (Swedish “to like; put up with; align with”), like (Norwegian “to like”), - (Icelandic) and líka (Faroese “to like”).

Noun from Middle English like (“pleasure, will, like”), from the verb Middle English liken (“to like”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Adjective from Middle English lik, lyk (Middle English), lich (Middle English), like (Middle English), from Old English ġelīċ by shortening, influenced by Old Norse líkr, glíkr (Old Norse); both from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz (“like, similar, same”). Related to alike (English); more distantly, with lich (English) and -ly (English). Cognate with like (Western Frisian “like; as”), gliek (Saterland Frisian “like”), lig (Danish “alike”), gelijk (Dutch “like, alike”), gleich (German “equal, like”), líkur (Icelandic “alike, like, similar”), lik (Norwegian “like, alike”) lik (Swedish “like, similar”)

Adverb from Middle English like, lyke (Middle English), liche (Middle English), lyche (Middle English), from Old English ġelīċe (“likewise, also, as, in like manner, similarly”) and Old Norse líka (“also, likewise”); both from Proto-Germanic *galīkê, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz (“same, like, similar”).

Conjunction from Middle English like, lyke (Middle English), lik (Middle English), lyk (Middle English), from the adverb Middle English like.

Preposition from Middle English like, lyke (Middle English), liche (Middle English), lyche (Middle English), lijc (Middle English), liih (Middle English “similar to, like, equal to, comparable with”), from Middle English like and like (Middle English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From like (English) and like (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English likely, likly (Middle English), lykly (Middle English), likliche (Middle English), from Old English ġelīclīċ (“suitable”) and Old Norse líkligr (“likely”) (probably independent formations), equivalent to like + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

chain.meaning: a cross-path or balk between fields, hence a boundary, boundary line or wall, any path or road, border, limit

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English limiten, from Old French limiter, from Latin līmitō (“to bound, limit, fix, determine”), from līmes (Latin); see noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English line, lyne (Middle English), from Old English līne (“line, cable, rope, hawser, series, row, rule, direction”), from Proto-West Germanic *līnā, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“line, rope, flaxen cord, thread”), from Proto-Germanic *līną (“flax, linen”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”).
Influenced in Middle English — by Middle French ligne (“line”), from Latin linea. More at linen (English).

The oldest sense of the word is “rope, cord, thread”; from this the senses “path”, “continuous mark” were derived.

chain.meaning: line, cable, rope, hawser, series, row, rule, direction

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Old English līn (“flax, linen, cloth”). For more information, see the entry linen (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French ligner

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English linke, lenke (Middle English), from a merger of Old English hlenċe, hlenċa (Old English “ring; chainlink”) and Old Norse *hlenkr, hlekkr (Old Norse “ring; chain”); both from Proto-Germanic *hlankiz (“ring; bond; fettle; fetter”), from Proto-Germanic *hlankaz (“bendsome, flexible”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng-, *klenk- (Proto-Indo-European “to bend; twist; wind”). Used in English since the 14th century. Related to lank (English).

Cognate with Lenk (Low German “link”), lænke (Danish “chain; link”), lekk (Elfdalian “link”), hlekkur (Icelandic “link”), lenke (Norwegian Bokmål “chain; link”), lenke (Norwegian Nynorsk), lenkje (Norwegian Nynorsk “chain; link”), länk (Swedish “chain; link”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Plausibly a modification of Medieval Latin — linchinus (Latin “candle”), an alteration of Latin lynchinus, itself from Ancient Greek λύχνος (“lamp”).

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The sense of “burden” first arose in the 13th century as a secondary meaning of Middle English lode, loade (Middle English), which had the main significance of “way, course, journey”, from Old English lād (“course, journey; way, street, waterway; leading, carrying; maintenance, support”) (ultimately from Proto-Germanic *laidō (“leading, way”), Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“to go, go forth, die”).

Cognate with leide (Middle Low German “entourage, escort”), Leite (German “line, course, load”), led (Swedish “way, trail, line”), leið (Icelandic “way, course, route”). As such, is a , which has preserved the older meaning.

Most likely, the semantic extension of the Middle English substantive arose by conflation with the (etymologically unrelated) verb lade (English); however, Middle English occurs only as a substantive; the transitive verb is recorded only in the 16th century (frequently in Shakespeare),
and (except for the participle laden (English)) has largely supplanted lade (English) in modern English.

For the meaning development from PIE, compare carrus (Latin) (whence carry (English)) akin to currō (Latin).

chain.meaning: course, journey; way, street, waterway; leading, carrying; maintenance, support

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English local, from Late Latin locālis (“belonging to a place”), possibly also via Old French local; ultimately from Latin locus (“a place”).

The local (English “ring-theoretic senses”) derive from , who first referred to Noetherian commutative rings with a unique maximal ideal as "Stellenring" (Stellen + ring (German)) in 1938. The term was inspired by algebraic geometry, where local rings encode information about the behavior of curves (surfaces, etc.) at points; hence, describe "local" behavior.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
Now widely believed (due to historical written record) to be from the idea that when one does a thing “for love” it is for no monetary gain, the word “love” thus implying “nothing”. Use of “love” for having no score extends to the 18th century in tennis as well as certain card games.

The former assumption that it had originated from French œuf (French “l’œuf”), due to its shape, has largely been discredited and is no longer widely accepted. However, the apparent similarity of the shape of an egg to a zero has inspired similar analogies, such as the use of duck (English) (reputed to be short for duck's egg) for a zero score at cricket, and goose egg (English) for "zero".

etymologies.text:
From Middle English lah, loue (Middle English), from Old Norse lágr (“low”), from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz (“low; flat”), from *ligjaną (Proto-Germanic “to lie; to lead”), from Proto-Indo-European *légʰyeti (“to be lying down”), from *legʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to lie”).

Cognate with laich (Scots “low”), läich (Saterland Frisian “low”), leech (Western Frisian “low”), laag (Dutch “low”), leeg (Low German (Germany)), leeg' (Low German “low; inferior”), leeg (Flemish “lazy”), lav (Danish “low”), lágur (Faroese / Icelandic “low”), låg (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “low”), laaka (Finnish “flat”), laaku (izh “gentle”); also laigh (Irish), luigh (Irish “to lie”), lhie (Manx “lie; lay”), laigh (Scottish Gaelic “lie; lay”), 𐌋𐌄𐌂𐌄𐌕 (xfa “he lies down”), lectus (Latin “bed”), 𐌅𐌄𐌉𐌀𐌕 (spx “to lie”), λέχομαι (Ancient Greek “to lie down”), lag (Albanian “band, encampment, troop”), ляжа́ць (Belarusian “to lie”), лежа́ (Bulgarian “to lie”), ležet (Czech “to lie”), лежи (Macedonian “to lie”), leżeć (Polish “to lie”), лежа́ть (Russian “to lie”), лѐжати (Serbo-Croatian), lèžati (Serbo-Croatian “to lie”), ležáti (Slovenian “to lie”), лежа́ти (Ukrainian “to lie”), lyäk- (txb “to lie”). More at lie (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English lough, from Old English hlōh, first and third person singular preterite of hliehhan (Old English “to laugh”). More at laugh (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lowen (“to low”), from Old English hlōwan (“to low; to bellow; to roar”), from Proto-Germanic *hlōaną (“to call; shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call”).

Cognate with loeien (Dutch “to low”), lüejen (Middle High German “to roar”), dialectal lumma (Swedish “to roar”), calō (Latin “to call”), καλέω (Ancient Greek), clāmō (Latin “to shout, claim”). More at claim (English).

chain.meaning: to low; to bellow; to roar

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
From Middle English lowe, loghe (Middle English), from Old Norse logi (“fire, flame, sword”), from Proto-Germanic *lugô (“flame, blaze”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“light”).

Cognate with logi (Icelandic “flame”), låga (Swedish “flame”), lue (Danish “flame”), Lohe (German “blaze, flames”), leag (North Frisian “fire, flame”), līeġ (Old English “fire, flame, lightning”). More at More at leye (English) and More at light (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From Middle English lowe, from Old English hlāw, hlǣw (Old English “burial mound”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlaiw. Obsolete by the 19th century, survives in toponymy as -low (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From low + er (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French loyal, from Old French loial, leial, leal, from Latin lēgālis. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English loialte, borrowed from Old French loialte, loiauté (Old French) (Modern loyauté (French)) from loial (Old French) + -té (Old French), equivalent to loyal + -ty (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English luk, lukke (Middle English), from Middle Dutch luc, geluc (Middle Dutch), gelucke (Middle Dutch “good luck, fortune”) or Middle Low German lücke, gelücke (Middle Low German “lot, fortune, fate, luck”), of origin; perhaps ultimately related to Lücke (German “gap, opening”) in the sense of "space or opportunity", hence "chance". Cognate with gelok (Western Frisian “luck”), Gluk (Saterland Frisian “luck”), luk (Dutch), geluk (Dutch “luck, happiness”), luk (Low German (Netherlands) “luck”), - (Low German (Germany)) and Glück (German “luck, good fortune, happiness”), lykke (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “luck, happiness”), lukke (Norwegian Nynorsk “luck, happiness”), lycka (Swedish “luck, happiness”), lukka (Icelandic “happiness”). According to the OED, it may be related to lock (English).

A loanword into English in the 15th century (probably as a gambling term), luc (Middle Dutch), geluc (Middle Dutch “gelucke”) has parallels with lücke (Middle High German), gelücke (Middle High German) . The word occurs only from the 12th century, apparently first in Rhine Frankish. Perhaps from a Frankish *galukki, derived from Proto-Germanic *lukjǭ (“opening”). The word enters standard Middle High German during the 13th century, and spreads to English and Scandinavian in the Late Middle Ages. Its origin seems to have been regional or dialectal, and there were competing German words such as gevelle (Middle High German) or schick (Middle High German), or the Latinate fortūne (Middle High German) from Latin fortūna (Latin). Its etymology is unknown, although there are numerous proposals as to its derivations from a number of roots.

Use as a verb in American English is late (1940s), but there was a Middle English verb lukken (Middle English “to chance, to happen by good fortune”) in the 15th century.
etymologies.uncertainNote: Its etymology is unknown, although there are numerous proposals as to its derivations from a number of roots.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: lucky + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lukky, equivalent to luck + -y (English). Cognate with lucky (Scots “lucky”), lokkich (Western Frisian “lucky, fortunate”), gelukkig (Dutch “lucky, fortunate, happy”). Compare also lykkelig (Danish “happy”), lycklig (Swedish “happy, lucky”), glücklich (German “happy”), glukkelk (Saterland Frisian “happy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English lunge, longe (Middle English), from Old English lungen, from Proto-Germanic *lunganjō, an enlargement of *lungô (Proto-Germanic “the light organ, lung”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-, whence ultimately also light (English). Cognate with long (Western Frisian), long (Dutch), Lunge (German), lunge (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), lunga (Swedish), lunga (Icelandic), and also лёгкое (Russian) (lung), Ancient Greek ἐλαφρός (Ancient Greek “light in weight”) and perhaps Albanian lungë (Albanian “blister, bulge”). Compare levis (Latin) and lēoht (Old English) (Modern English light (English)). See also lights (English “lungs”). Superseded non-native pomoun (Middle English “lung”), borrowed from poumon (Old French), pomon (Old French “lung”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English luxurie, from Old French luxurie, from Latin luxuria (“rankness, luxury”), from luxus (Latin “extravagance, luxury”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English mad, madde (Middle English), madd (Middle English), medd (Middle English), from Old English ġemǣd, ġemǣded (Old English “enraged”), past participle of ġemǣdan (Old English), *mǣdan (Old English “to make insane or foolish”), from Proto-Germanic *maidijaną (“to change; damage; cripple; injure; make mad”), from Proto-Germanic *maidaz , from Proto-Indo-European *mey- .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compare ġemǣdan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English madame, from Old French madame, from ma (Old French “my”) + dame (Old French “lady”), from post-classical Latin mea domina. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English magik,magyk, from Old French magique, from Latin magicus, magica (Latin), from Ancient Greek μαγικός (“magical”), from μάγος (Ancient Greek “magician, magus”). Ultimately from , probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“*meh₂gʰ-”). . . (whence galder (Middle English)) and dwimmer (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: magic + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English magnificent, from Middle French magnificent, from Latin magnificentior, comparative of magnificus (Latin “great in deeds or sentiment, noble, splendid, etc.”), from magnus (Latin “great”) + -ficēns (Latin), a form of -ficiēns (Latin), the regular form, in compounds, of faciēns (Latin), a participle of faciō (Latin “facere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mayn, main (Middle English), maine (Middle English), mæin (Middle English), meyn (Middle English), from main (Middle English) (see further at etymology 2); compare Old English mæġen (“strong, main, principal”) (used in combination) and Old Norse megn, megenn (Old Norse “strong, main”).

The word is cognate with megīn (Old High German “strong, mighty”) (modern Möge (German), Vermögen (German “power, wealth”)), and also akin to magan (Old English “to be able to”). See also may (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mayn, main (Middle English), maine (Middle English), mæine (Middle English), mæȝen (Middle English), from Old English mæġen (“strength”), from Proto-Germanic *maginą (“strength, power, might”), *maginaz (Proto-Germanic “strong”), from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“be able”).

The word is cognate with magen (Old High German), megin (Old High German), magn (Old Norse), megn (Old Norse), megin (Old Norse), megin (Old Saxon). More recent senses are derived from the adjective.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: ; probably from the adjective main. Evidence is lacking for a derivation from main (French “hand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: , possibly from French main (“hand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English maynly; equivalent to main + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mayntenen, from Old French maintenir, from Late Latin manuteneo (“manūteneō, manūtenēre”), from Latin manū (“with/in/by the hand”) + teneo (Latin “tenēre”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mayntenaunce, from Old French maintenance, from maintenir (Old French), from Latin —. .

Note that maintain (English) has undergone a sound and spelling change, hence is spelt with , rather than the still found in .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English major, from Latin maior, comparative of magnus (Latin “great, large; noble, important”), from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂yōs (“greater”), comparative of *meǵh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “great”). Compare majoar (Western Frisian “major”), majoor (Dutch “major”), majeur (French). .

is a shortening of sergeant major (English), perhaps after Spanish mayor in the same sense.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French maiorité (“maiorité”), from Medieval Latin maiōritātem, accusative of Latin maiōritās, from Latin maior (“greater”). Morphologically major + ity (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English maken, make (Middle English), from Old English macian (“to build, make, work”), from Proto-West Germanic *makōn (“to build, make, work”), from *mak (Proto-West Germanic “agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ-, *meh₂ḱ- (Proto-Indo-European “to knead”) or *meg- (Proto-Indo-European “to be comfortable, pleasant”). Related to match (English).

Cognate with mak (Scots “to make”), maak (Yola), maake (Yola “to make”), maage (North Frisian), maaki (North Frisian), mååge (North Frisian “to make”), moakje (Saterland Frisian “to make; to repair; to prepare; to preach; to earn”), meitsje (Western Frisian “to make”), mache (Alemannic “to make; to do”), måcha (Bavarian), måchn (Bavarian “to make; to do; to go; to cause; to play; to matter; to look”), machan (Cimbric “to make”), maken (Dutch / Low German “to make”), machen (German “to make; to do; to go; to cause; to play; to fare; to look”), maachen (lb), man (lb “to make; to do; to take; to equal; to put”), mòchen (mhn “to make”), mahha (Ripuarian “to make; to do”), מאַכן (Yiddish “to create, make; to do; to say”); also probably mám (Irish “yoke; duty, obligation; function, service”), mācerō (Latin “to soften; to weaken; to mortify; to torture”), μάσσω (Ancient Greek “to handle, knead; to wipe”), ма́жа (Bulgarian “to smear; to oil”), mazat (Czech “to lubricate; to spread; to smear; to scribble; to erase”), mazać (Polish “to smear; to scribble; to pule, whimper”), ма́зать (Russian “to oil; to paint; to smear; to soil; to miss”), ма̏зати (Serbo-Croatian), mȁzati (Serbo-Croatian “to smear; to dirty”), ма́зати (Ukrainian “to smear”), մած (Classical Armenian “glued together, joined; coagulated, curdled; adhesive, sticking; compact; dense”), मचाना (Hindi “to cause, raise, wreak”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English make, imake (Middle English), ȝemace (Middle English), from Old English ġemaca (“a mate, an equal, companion, peer”), from Proto-West Germanic *gamakō, from Proto-Germanic *gamakô (“companion, comrade”), from Proto-Indo-European *maǵ- (“to knead, oil”). Reinforced by maki (Old Norse “an equal”).

Cognate with maki (Icelandic “spouse”), make (Swedish “spouse, husband”), mage (Danish “companion, fellow, mate”). .

chain.meaning: a mate, an equal, companion, peer

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English maker, makere (Middle English), equivalent to make + -er (English). Compare makar (Scots), Moaker (Saterland Frisian), makker (Western Frisian), maker (Dutch), Macher (German), -mager (Danish “mager”), -makare (Swedish “makare”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English male, borrowed from Old French malle, masle (Old French) (Modern French mâle (French)), from Latin masculus (“masculine, a male”), diminutive of mās (Latin “male, masculine”). . Displaced native wǣpned (Old English “male”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably from The Mall, a major street in London, England, which was originally a pall mall (English) alley.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English man, from Old English mann (“human being, person, man”), from Proto-West Germanic *mann, from Proto-Germanic *mann- (“man”), from Proto-Indo-European *mon- (“human being, man”). .

This word has many s, in every Germanic language (whether extant or extinct), with similarities in form and meaning.
Virtually all the words below mean “man” and “husband”, with some specific cases noted.

In (the languages closest to English):
:* Mann (Low German)
:* maan,man,moon,muon (North Frisian)
:* Mon (Saterland Frisian)
:* man (Scots)
:* man (Western Frisian)
:* man (Yola)

In the remainder of West Germanic:
:* ma,Maa,Mann,mo,mà,Mànn (Alemannic)
:* Mo,mon,moon,Må,mònn (Bavarian)
:* man,mann,månn (Cimbric)
:* man (nl,li,zea)
:* Mann (de,lb)
:* mònn (mhn)
:* maon,mon,mōn (Ripuarian)
:* מאַן (Yiddish)

In East Germanic:
:* 𐌼𐌰𐌽𐌽𐌰 (Gothic), which meant “man”, “human“ and “person”, but likely also “husband”

In North Germanic:
:* mand (Danish)
:* maður (Faroese / Icelandic), both additionally meaning “human” and “person”, as in Old Norse
:* man (gmq-gut,sv)
:* mann (Norn / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk)
:* mainnj (Norwegian Nynorsk)
:* maðr (Old Norse)

Outside Germanic:
: Indo-Iranian:
::* 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬎𐬱 (ae “human”)
::* मनुस् ,मनु (Sanskrit)
::* Also म॒नु॒ष्य॑ (Sanskrit “human; man; huband”)
: Slavic (all of these mean “man” and “husband”, though in some cases the former is no longer part of the modern standard):
::* муж (Belarusian / Russian / Ukrainian)
::* мъж (Bulgarian)
::* muž (Czech / Slovak)
::* маж (Macedonian)
::* mąż (Polish)
::* му̑ж,mȗž (Serbo-Croatian)
::* mož (Slovenian)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mannen, from Old English mannian, ġemannian (Old English “to man, supply with men, populate, garrison”), from mann (Old English “human being, man”).

* bemannen (Dutch “to man”)
* bemannen (German “to man”)
* bemande (Danish “to man”)
* bemanna (Swedish “to man”)
* manna (Icelandic “to supply with men, to man”)
