etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Modern English manage, menage (English), from Middle English *manage, *menage (Middle English), from Old French manege (“the handling or training of a horse, horsemanship, riding, maneuvers, proceedings”), probably from Old Italian maneggiare (“to handle, manage, touch, treat”), from Vulgar Latin *manizāre (“handle”), from Latin manus (“hand”) + -izō (Latin “-izāre”). .

Compare typologically handle (English); руководи́ть (Russian) (< рука́ (Russian)).

chain.meaning: the handling or training of a horse, horsemanship, riding, maneuvers, proceedings

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: manage + -ment

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mankynde, alteration (due to kynde (Middle English) = “kind, nature, sort”) of earlier mankyn (Middle English), from Old English mancynn. Equivalent to man + kin (English), and/or man + kind (English). Cognate with mankind (Scots), mankünne (Middle High German), mandkøn (Danish), mannkyn (Icelandic “mankind”). See also mankin (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English manere, maner (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman manere, from Old French maniere, from Vulgar Latin *manāria, from feminine of Latin manuarius (“belonging to the hand”), from manus (Latin “hand”). Compare manière (French), mannaia (Italian “ax, axe”), maneira (Portuguese) and maneiro (Portuguese “handy, portable”), mâner (Romanian “handle”), and manera (Spanish). Displaced native hād (Old English “nature, manner”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: man + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English manuel, from Old French manuel, from Late Latin manuāle (“handbook, manual”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English manuel, from Anglo-Norman manuel, Old French manual, from Latin manuālis, from manus (Latin “hand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle French manufacture, from Old French —, from Medieval Latin manūfactūra (“a making by hand”), from manūfactus (Latin), a compound of , manū (Latin) being ablative of manus (Latin “hand”), and factus (Latin) past participle of faciō (Latin “to do, make”).

Compare manual (English), facture (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: manufacture + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French marathon, coined in 1894 by linguist for the first modern time Olympic Games after Ancient Greek Μαραθών, a town northeast of Athens. Phidippides the Greek ran the distance from Marathon to Athens to deliver a message regarding the . The modern sport of marathon running is based on a run approximately the same distance. The toponym itself comes from μάραθον (Ancient Greek “fennel”) and refers to the prevalence of the plant in the area.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mark, merk (Middle English), merke (Middle English), from Old English mearc (“mark, sign, line of division; standard; boundary, limit, term, border; defined area, district, province”), from Proto-West Germanic *marku, from Proto-Germanic *markō (“boundary; boundary marker”), from Proto-Indo-European *mórǵs (“edge, boundary, border”).

Compare march (English).

* mark (Dutch), merk (Dutch “mark, brand”)
* Mark (German “mark; borderland”), Marke (German “mark, brand”)
* mark (Swedish “mark, land, territory”)
* mark (Icelandic “mark, sign”)
* margō (Latin “edge, margin”)
* مرز (Persian “limit, boundary”)
* मर्या (Sanskrit “limit, mark, boundary”), मार्ग (Sanskrit “mark, section”).

chain.meaning: mark, sign, line of division; standard; boundary, limit, term, border; defined area, district, province

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English mark, from Old English marc (“a denomination of weight (usu. half a pound), mark (money of account)”), from Proto-West Germanic *mark, from Proto-Germanic *marką (“mark, sign”). Cognate with mark (Dutch “mark”), mark (Swedish “a stamped coin”), mörk (Icelandic “a weight, usu. a pound, of silver or gold”). .

chain.meaning: a denomination of weight (usu. half a pound), mark (money of account)

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From German Mark, from Middle High German marc, marche (Middle High German), marke (Middle High German), from Old High German marc, from Proto-West Germanic *mark (whence etymology 2 via marc (Old English)). The identical plural is also from German.

etymologies.text: An alternative form supposedly easier to pronounce while giving commands.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mariage, from Old French mariage, from marier (Old French “to marry”), from Latin marītō (“marry”), from maritus (Latin “marītus”), from mas (Latin “male, masculine, of the male sex”). Equivalent to marry + age (English). . Displaced native sinsċipe (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English marien, from Anglo-Norman marïer, from Latin marito (“to wed”), from marītus (Latin “husband, suitor”), from mās (Latin “man, male”), of origin. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *méryos (“young man”), same source as मर्य (Sanskrit “suitor, young man”). Compare its feminine derivatives: morwyn (Welsh “girl”), merch (Welsh “daughter”), marzus (gme-cgo “wedding”), μεῖραξ (Ancient Greek “boy; girl”), martì (Lithuanian “bride”), 𐬨𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌𐬌𐬀 (ae “yeoman”).) Displaced native hīwian (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English Marie, referring to Mary, the Virgin Mary. Mid-14th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested from 1300 as Middle English merveilous, from Old French merveillus, from merveille (Old French “a wonder”) + -us (Old French). . See also marvel (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Middle French masque (“a covering to hide or protect the face”), from Italian maschera (“mask, disguise”), from (a byform of, see it for more) Medieval Latin masca, mascha (English), a borrowing of Proto-West Germanic *maskā, from which English and are inherited. .

Replaced grīma (Old English “mask”), whence grime (English), and displaced non-native viser (Middle English “visor, mask”) borrowed from viser (Old French), visier (Old French).

chain.meaning: a covering to hide or protect the face

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English *mask, masch (Middle English), from Old English māx, māsc (Old English “mash”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English masken, short for *maskeren (Middle English), malskren (Middle English “to bewilder; be confused, wander”). More at masker (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English massif, from Middle French massif, equivalent to . The Irish sense is possibly derived from .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English maister, mayster (Middle English), meister (Middle English) and maistren (Middle English), from Old English mǣster, mæġster (Old English), mæġester (Old English), mæġister (Old English), magister (Old English “master”), from Latin magister (“chief, teacher, leader”), from itc-ola magester, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (as in magnus (Latin “great”), also cognate of much (English) and mickle (English)) + -ester (Latin)/-ister (Latin) (compare minister (Latin “servant”)). Reinforced by Old French maistre, mestre (Old French) and maistriier (Old French), maister (Old French) from the same Latin source. Compare also Mäster (Saterland Frisian “master”), master (Western Frisian “master”), meester (Dutch “master”), Meister (German “master”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: mast + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English macche, mecche (Middle English), from Old English mæċċa, ġemæċċa (Old English “companion, mate, wife, one suited to another”), from Proto-West Germanic *makkjō, *gamakkjō (Proto-West Germanic “partner, equal”), from Proto-Germanic *makô, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, work”). Compare mage (Danish “mate”), maki (Icelandic “spouse”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English macchen (“to marry; be paired with”), from the noun (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mate, a borrowing from Middle Low German mate (“messmate”) (replacing mett (Middle English), mette (Middle English “table companion, mate, partner”), from ġemetta (Old English “sharer of food, table-guest”)), from Old Saxon gimato, derived from Proto-Germanic *gamatjô, itself from *ga- (Proto-Germanic “together”) (related to - (German) and ge- (Dutch)) + *matjô (Proto-Germanic) (from *matiz (Proto-Germanic “food”)), related to mete (Old English “food”)). From the same Middle Low German source stems Maat (Low German (Germany) “journeyman, companion”), Maat (German “naval non-commissioned officer”). Cognates include Moat (Saterland Frisian “friend, buddy, comrade, mate”), maat (Dutch “mate, partner, colleague, friend”). More at ġe- (Old English), co- (English), meat (English). .

Compare typologically compāniō (Latin) (whence companion (English)) (< con- (Latin) + panis (Latin) + -ō (Latin)), однока́шник (Russian) (< одно- (Russian) + ка́ша (Russian) + -ник (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English magen, mauen (Middle English), mawe (Middle English), mawen (Middle English), mayen (Middle English), maȝen (Middle English), mouin (Middle English), mow (Middle English), mowen (Middle English), moȝen (Middle English), mugen (Middle English), from Old English magan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able”), from *megʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to be able”).

Cognate with mey (Scots “may”), ma (Yola), maa (Yola), mai (Yola), mey (Yola), mye (Yola “may”), mai (North Frisian), mei (North Frisian), mooge (North Frisian “like to, would”), meie (Western Frisian “may; to like”), möge (Alemannic “may; can”), megn (Bavarian “to like; to want to”), mugge (Central Franconian “to like; may”), mögan (Cimbric), möng (Cimbric “may”), mogen (Dutch “to be allowed; may; to like”), mögen (German / Low German “to like; would like; may”), מעגן (Yiddish “may”), måtte (Danish “have to; may”), mega (Faroese / Icelandic “may; must”), måtta (Norwegian Bokmål “may; must”), måtta (Norwegian Nynorsk), måtte (Norwegian Nynorsk “may; must”), må (Swedish “may; must”), 𐌼𐌰𐌲𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to be able, can, may”); also smacht (Irish “ordinance, regulation, rule; dominion, sway; control, discipline, restraint; fine, penalty”), mėgti (Lithuanian “to like”), магчы́ (Belarusian “to be able”), мо́га (Bulgarian “to be able”), moci (Czech “to be able”), mòc (Kashubian “to be able”), moc (Lower Sorbian), móc (Lower Sorbian), moz (Lower Sorbian “to be able”), може (Macedonian “to be able”), мочи (rsk “to be able”), móc (Polish “to be able”), мочь (Russian “to be able”), мо̏ћи (Serbo-Croatian), mȍći (Serbo-Croatian “to be able”), môcť (Slovak “to be able; be allowed to”), moči (Slovenian “to be able”), môc (zlw-slv “to be able”), могти́ (Ukrainian “to be able”), مغ (Persian “magus”), मघ (Sanskrit “power, wealth; bounty, gift, reward”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3

etymologies.label: Etymology

Cognate with meior (Old High German “estate manager, steward, bailiff”) (modern Meier (German)), meier (Middle Dutch “administrator, steward, bailiff”) (modern meier (Dutch)). , burhġerēfa (Old English “boroughreeve”), and portġerēfa (Old English “portreeve”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English menen (“to intend; remember; lament; comfort”), from Old English mǣnan (“to mean, complain”), Proto-West Germanic *mainijan, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną (“to mean, think; complain”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyn- (“to think”), or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *meyno-, extended form of Proto-Indo-European *mey-.

Germanic cognates include miene (Western Frisian “to deem, think”) (mēna (Old Frisian “to signify”)), menen (Dutch “to believe, think, mean”) (menen (Middle Dutch “to think, intend”)), meinen (German “to think, mean, believe”), mēnian (Old Saxon). Indo-European cognates include mían (Old Irish “wish, desire”) and mienić (Polish “to signify, believe”). Non-Indo-European cognates include mainita (Finnish “to mention”), meinata (Finnish “to mean, to plan, to intend”) mainima (Estonian “to mention”), máinnastit (se “to tell”). Related to moan (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mene, imene (Middle English), from Old English mǣne, ġemǣne (Old English “common, public, general, universal”), from Proto-West Germanic *gamainī, from Proto-Germanic *gamainiz (“common”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to change, exchange, share”). .

Cognate with mien (Western Frisian “general, universal”), gemeen (Dutch “common, mean”), gemein (German “common, mean, nasty”), gemen (Danish), 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (Gothic “common, unclean”), commūnis (Latin “shared, common, general”) (comoinem (itc-ola)). For a similar change in definition, see vulgar (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English meene, borrowed from Old French meien (moyen (French)), mediānus (Late Latin “that is in the middle, middle”), from Latin medius (“middle”). Cognate with mid (English). For the musical sense, compare the cognate mezzano (Italian). .

Cognate with mening (Scots “intent, purpose, sense, meaning”), miening (Western Frisian “opinion, mind”), mening (Dutch “view, opinion, judgement”), Meinung (German “opinion, view, mind, idea”), - (Danish) and mening (Swedish “meaning, sense, sentence, opinion”), meining (Icelandic “meaning”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mesure, from Old French mesure, from Latin mēnsūra (“a measure”), mētior (Latin “to measure”) + -tūra (Latin). Largely displaced native metan (Old English) ("to measure" whence modern mete (English)) and ġemet (Old English “a measure”). See also -ure.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from Middle French medaille, medale (Middle French), from Italian medaglia (originally "half a denarius"), from Early Medieval Latin medālia, feminine derived via dissimilation (/dj–lj/ > /d–lj/) from mediālia (Latin), neuter plural of Late Latin mediālis (“middle”), from Classical Latin medius.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French médical, from Medieval Latin medicālis, from Latin medicus. Replaced lǣċe (Old English “doctor (physician)”), which is cognate with læknir (Icelandic “doctor”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English medicin, from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicīnus (Latin “of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (Latin “a physician, surgeon”). The extended sense of "Indigenous magic" is a oj mashkiki (“medicine”) or mide (oj) (or cognates in ) when used in compounds such as Grand Medicine Society, medicine lodge, medicine dance, medicine bag, medicine wheel, medicine man, Medicine Line, and bad medicine or place names such as Medicine Hat, Medicine Creek, etc. Displaced native lybb (Old English “drug, medicine”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French médiéval (“medieval”), from Latin — medium + aevum (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin medium, neuter of medius (Latin “middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare middle (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English meten, from Old English mētan (“to meet, find, encounter”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōtijan (“to meet”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to come, meet”).

Cognate with met (Scots), mete (Scots), meit (Scots “to meet”), meet (North Frisian), mätje (North Frisian), möt (North Frisian “to meet”), mette (Western Frisian), moetsje (Western Frisian “to meet”), ontmoeten (Dutch “to meet”), möten (Low German “to meet”), møde (Danish “to meet”), my̨öt (Elfdalian “to meet”), møta (Faroese “to meet”), mæta (Icelandic “to meet”), møte (Norwegian Bokmål “to meet”), møta (Norwegian Nynorsk), møte (Norwegian Nynorsk “to meet”), möta (Swedish “to meet”). Related to moot (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English mete, imete (Middle English), from Old English ġemǣte (“suitable, having the same measurements”), from the Proto-Germanic *gamētijaz, *mētiz (Proto-Germanic “reasonable; estimable”) (cognate with meten (Dutch “measure”), gemäß (German “suitable”) etc.), itself from collective prefix *ga- (Proto-Germanic) + Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English melten, from a merger of Old English meltan (intransitive) and mieltan (Old English) (transitive), both meaning “to melt, digest,” from Proto-West Germanic *meltan and *maltijan (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *meltaną and *maltijaną (Proto-Germanic), both from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“melt”). Cognate with melta (Icelandic “to digest”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Anglo-Norman memorie, Old French memoire etc., from Latin memoria (“the faculty of remembering, remembrance, memory, a historical account”), from memor (Latin “mindful, remembering”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (to remember), related to μνήμη (Ancient Greek “memory”) μέρμερος (Ancient Greek “anxious”), μέριμνα (Ancient Greek “care, thought”), ġemimor (Old English “mindful, remembering”). More at mimmer (English). . Displaced native myne (Old English) (whence min (English)) and ġemynd (Old English), which took on a different meaning as modern mind (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mere, mer (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman meer, from Old French mier, from Latin merus (“pure, unmixed, undiluted”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to sparkle, gleam”).

Cognate with āmerian (Old English), āmyrian (Old English “to purify, examine, revise”). The Middle English word was perhaps influenced by or conflated with sound-alike Middle English mere (“glorious, noble, splendid, fine, pure”), from Old English mǣre (“famous, great, excellent, sublime, splendid, pure, sterling”), from Proto-West Germanic *mārī, from Proto-Germanic *mērijaz.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English mere, from Old English mǣre, ġemǣre (Old English “boundary; limit”), from Proto-Germanic *mairiją (“boundary”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to fence”). Cognate with meer (Dutch “a limit, boundary”), mærr (Icelandic “borderland”), landamäre (Swedish “border, borderline, boundary”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English mere, from Old English mere (“lake, pool,” in compounds and poetry “sea”), from Proto-West Germanic *mari (“sea”), from Proto-Germanic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Cognate with mar (Western Frisian “lake”), meer (Dutch “lake”), Meer (Low German), and Meer (German “sea”). Non-Germanic cognates include mare (Latin), mor (Breton), and мо́ре (Russian). .

See mission (English), and compare Mass (English “religious service”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English myddel, middel (Middle English), from Old English middel (“middle, centre, waist”), from Proto-Germanic *midlą, *midilą (Proto-Germanic), *medalą (Proto-Germanic “middle”), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *midjō (“middle, midst”) (compare *midjaz (Proto-Germanic “mid, middle”)), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between, in the middle, middle”).

Cognate with Middel (Saterland Frisian “middle”), mul (Western Frisian “middle”), middel (Dutch “means; medicine, cure”), mittel (German “middle”), Mittel (German “means; medicament, remedy”), Mëttel (lb “means, method; medicament”), mytuł (Ripuarian “middle”), מיטל (Yiddish “middle”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian Bokmål) and middel (Norwegian Nynorsk “means”), meðal (Icelandic “average; means, medicine”), medel (Swedish “average, mean, middle”). See also mid (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English maught, might (Middle English), miȝt (Middle English), myght (Middle English), from Old English maht, meaht (Old English), meht (Old English), mieht (Old English), miht (Old English), mæht (Old English “ability, power; strength; virtue”), from Proto-West Germanic *mahti, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz (“ability, power; force, strength”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able to, to have power”), from *megʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to be able”), corresponding to Germanic *maganą (Proto-Germanic “to be able, may”) + *-þiz (Proto-Germanic). Equivalent to may (English) .

Cognate with micht (Scots “might”), mought (Yola “might”), macht (Dutch “might, power”), Macht (German “might, power”), Muecht (lb “authority, might, power”), מאַכט (Yiddish “might, power”), máttur (Faroese / Icelandic “might, strength”), magt (Danish “power; force”), makt (Norwegian Bokmål “power”), makt (Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “power; force”), mått (Swedish “might, power”), 𐌼𐌰𐌷𐍄𐍃 (Gothic “ability, might, power”), and further to smacht (Irish “ordinance, regulation, rule; dominion, sway; control, discipline, restraint; fine, penalty”), μάγος (Greek (Modern) “magician; sorcerer, wizard”), mėgti (Lithuanian “to like”), моц (Belarusian “might, power”), мощ (Bulgarian “might, power”), moc (Czech / Polish “might, power”), моќ (Macedonian “might, power”), мочь (Russian “power, might”) and мощь (Russian “force, strength”), мо̑ћ (Serbo-Croatian), mȏć (Serbo-Croatian “power; strength; potency; authority”), moč (Slovenian “power; strength”), міч (Ukrainian) and міць (Ukrainian “might, power”), մոգ (Armenian “magus; fire-worshiper, Zoroastrian; astrologer; diviner, enchanter, sorcerer, wizard”), مغ (Persian “magus”), मघ (Sanskrit “power, wealth; bounty, gift, reward”). See more at may (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Old English meahte and mihte (Old English), inflections of magan (Old English), whence English may (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English milde, from Old English milde (“mild”), from Proto-Germanic *mildijaz (“mild”), from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to beat, pound, grind”).

Cognate with mild (Scots), myld (Scots “mild”), milde (Saterland Frisian “mild”), myld (Western Frisian “mild”), mild (Dutch “mild”), milde (Low German “mild”), mild (German “mild”), - (Danish), - (Swedish) and mild (Norwegian Bokmål “mild”), mildur (Icelandic “mild”), mollis (Latin “soft, gentle”), malonus (Lithuanian “pleasing, pleasant, kind”), mildr (Old Norse).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English myle, mile (Middle English), from Old English mīl, from Proto-West Germanic *mīliju, a borrowing of Latin mīlia, mīllia (Latin), plural of mīle (Latin), mīlle (Latin “mile”) (literally ‘thousand’ but used as a short form of mīlle passūs (Latin “a thousand paces”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English militari, from Old French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris, from mīles (Latin “soldier”) + -āris (Latin) (whence ). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English minde, munde (Middle English), imynde (Middle English), imunde (Middle English), ȝemynde (Middle English), ȝemunde (Middle English), from Old English mynd, ġemynd (Old English “mind, memory”), from Proto-West Germanic *mundi, *gamundi (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *mundiz, *gamundiz (Proto-Germanic “memory, remembrance”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”) (compare also mantis (English), via Greek), from the root *men- (Proto-Indo-European “to think”).

Cognate with gimunt (Old High German) , mynd (Old Norse “image, model”), 𐌲𐌰𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (Gothic “remembrance, memory, mind”). Related also to minde (Danish “memory”), minne (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “memory”), minni (Faroese / Icelandic “memory, recall, recollection”), mēns (Latin “mind, reason”), मनस् (Sanskrit), μένος (Ancient Greek), mënd (Albanian “mind, reason”). Related to mantra (English). Compare also myntan (Old English “to mean, intend, purpose, determine, resolve”). More at mint#Etymology 3 (English).

From Middle English min, myn (Middle English), from Old English mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.

Cognate with mien (Saterland Frisian), myn (Western Frisian), mijn (Dutch), mien (Low German), mein (German), min (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), mín (Faroese / Icelandic).
