etymologies.text: , neuter form of minimus (Latin “least, smallest”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English ministre, from Old French ministre, from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other under official”), from minor (Latin “less”) + -ter (Latin); see minor. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English mynystren, from Middle French ministrer, from Old French menistrer, ministrer (Old French) and Latin ministrō, from minister (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English minor, menor (Middle English), menour (English), etc., from Latin minor (“lesser; young; young person”) both directly and via Norman — and Middle French menor, menour (Middle French), etc. but not mini- (English). Cognate with minister (English), minify (English), Minorca (English), Menshevik (English) and possibly minnow (English). Compare minimum (Latin) and minuō (Latin), minniro (Old High German), minow (Cornish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English minoritie, from Middle French minorité, and its source Late Latin minōritās, from Latin minor. Morphologically minor + ity (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English mynt, munet (Middle English “münet”), from Old English mynet (“coin”), from late Proto-West Germanic *munit, from Latin monēta (“place for making coins, coined money”), from the temple of (named for Monēta (Latin) mother of the Muses), where coins were made. . The verb is from the noun; mynetian (Old English “to mint”) is a parallel formation.

chain.meaning: place for making coins, coined money

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|right|A mint plant.

From Middle English mynte, from Old English minte (“mint plant”), from Proto-West Germanic *mintā (“mint”), from Latin menta, probably from a lost Mediterranean language either through Ancient Greek μίνθη, μίνθα (Ancient Greek) or directly. Akin to minta (Old Norse “mint”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English minten, from Old English myntan (“to mean, intend, purpose, determine, resolve”), from Proto-West Germanic *muntijan (“to think, consider”), from Proto-Indo-European *men-, *mnā- (Proto-Indo-European “to think”). Cognate with mintsje (Saterland Frisian), muntsje (Saterland Frisian “to aim, target”), munten (Dutch “to aim at, target”), münten (Low German (Germany) “to aim at”), münzen (German “to aim at”), monter (Dutch “cheerful, gladsome, spry”), 𐌼𐌿𐌽𐍃 (Gothic “thought, opinion”), munan (Old English “to be mindful of, consider, intend”). More at mind (English).

chain.meaning: to mean, intend, purpose, determine, resolve

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (Latin “to wonder at”), from mīrus (Latin “wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). . Partially displaced native wonder (English), from wundor (Old English “miracle, wonder”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French miserable, from Old French —, from Latin miserabilis, equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English miserie, from Old French miserie (modern: misère (French)), from Latin miseria, from miser (Latin), equivalent to . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: mislead + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Verb from Middle English missen, from Old English missan (“to miss, escape the notice of a person”), from Proto-West Germanic *missijan, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną (“to miss, go wrong, fail”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to change, exchange, trade”). Cognate with misse (Western Frisian “to miss”), missen (Dutch “to miss”), missen (German “to miss”), - (Norwegian Bokmål) and miste (Danish “to lose”), missa (Swedish “to miss”), - (Norwegian Nynorsk), missa (Icelandic “to lose”) and mittere (Latin “to send, let go”).

Noun from Middle English misse, mis (Middle English), from Old English miss (“loss, absence”), from Proto-West Germanic *miss, from Proto-Germanic *miss- (“loss”). Cognate with miss (Scots “a loss, want, cause of grief or mourning”), misse (Middle High German), mis (Middle High German “lack, missing, absence”), missir (Icelandic “loss”). Related also to mis (Scots “wrongdoing, sin, guilt”), mis (Dutch “misdeed, wrongdoing, mistake”), misse (Middle Low German “sin, wrong”).

chain.meaning: to miss, escape the notice of a person

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From mistress (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is from Middle English mist, from Old English mist (“mist; darkness; dimness (of eyesight)”), from Proto-Germanic *mihstaz (“mist, fog”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from the root *h₃meygʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “cloud, fog, drizzle”). Cognate with mist (Scots “mist, fog”), mist (Western Frisian “mist”), mist (Dutch “mist”), mist (Swedish “mist, fog”), mistur (Icelandic “mist”), miegelje (Western Frisian “to drizzle”), - (Dutch) dialectal miggelen (Dutch), miegelen (Dutch “to drizzle”), miglà (Lithuanian “fog”), मेघ (Sanskrit “cloud”), мгла (Russian “fog, haze”).

The verb is from Middle English misten, from Old English mistian.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English misty, mysty (Middle English), misti (Middle English), from Old English mistiġ (“misty, dark”), from Proto-West Germanic *mistig (“misty”), equivalent to mist + -y (English). Cognate with misty (Scots), mistie (Scots “misty”), mistich (Western Frisian “misty, foggy”), mistig (Dutch “misty, foggy”), mistig (Low German (Germany) “foggy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mys-understanden, equivalent to mis + understand (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mys undirstonding, equivalent to misunderstand + ing (English). Compare misverstand (Dutch “misunderstanding”), Missverständnis (German “misunderstanding”), missförstånd (Swedish “misunderstanding”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mixen (attested in past tense as mixed (Middle English), myxyd (Middle English)), from Old English *mixian, miscian (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan, from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from *meyǵ- (Proto-Indo-European), *meyḱ- (Proto-Indo-European “to mix”).

Cognate with miskje (Saterland Frisian “to mix, blend”), mischen (Middle Dutch “to mix”), Low German misken (Low German (Germany)), mischen (Low German (Germany) “to mix”), miskian (Old High German), miskēn (Old High German “to mix”) (mischen (German)), mysgu (Welsh “to mix”), misceō (Latin “mix”), μῑ́γνῡμῐ (Ancient Greek “to mix”), мѣсити (Church Slavonic “to mix”), mišti (Lithuanian) and maišyti (Lithuanian “to mix”), मिश्र (Sanskrit “mixed”), آمیختن (Persian “to mix”), māsc (Old English “mixture, mash”). More at mash.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: A merger of a nominal use of the verb and a borrowing from Anglo-Norman mixte, from Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (Latin “mix”). Nowadays regarded automatically as the nominal form of the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus (Latin), perfect passive participle of misceō (Latin “mix”); compare mix.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (Latin “measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (Latin “measure”); see mode, and compare module, modulus, mould, mold.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French moderne, from Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (Latin “measure”); hence, by measure, "just now". See also mode (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English moment, from Old French moment, from Latin mōmentum. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from perfect passive participle monitus (Latin “warning”), from verb monere (Latin “to warn, admonish, remind”). Warship sense is from , the first ship of this type.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English monstre, from Old French monstre, mostre (Old French), moustre (Old French), from Latin mōnstrum. Displaced native fīfel (Old English) and þyrs (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From month + -ly (English), perhaps via Middle English *monethly (attested only adverbially), from Old English mōnaþlīċ (“monthly”), from Proto-West Germanic *mānōþlīk, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþlīkaz (“monthly”). Cognate with moundelk (Saterland Frisian “monthly”), monatlich (German “monthly”), månedlig (Danish “monthly”), månatlig (Swedish “monthly”), månedlig (Norwegian Bokmål “monthly”), mánaðarlegur (Icelandic “monthly”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English monethly, equivalent to month + -ly (English). Cognate with moundelk (Saterland Frisian “monthly”), maandelijks (Dutch “monthly”), monatlich (German “monthly”), månatligen (Swedish “monthly”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English monument, from Old French monument, from Latin monumentum (“memorial, monument, tomb”), from monēre (Latin “to remind”).

Partially displaced bēacn (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mood, mode (Middle English), mod (Middle English), from Old English mōd (“mind,” in poetry also “heart, spirit, courage”), from Proto-West Germanic *mōd, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz (“sense, courage, zeal, anger”), from Proto-Indo-European *moh₁-, *meh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “endeavour, will, temper”).

Cognate with Moud (Saterland Frisian “courage”), moed (Western Frisian “courage; mind; spirit; will; intention”), moed (Dutch “bravery, courage; mood”), Mut (German “bravery, courage; mood”), Mood (Low German (Germany) “boldness, bravery, courage”), Mutt (lb “courage”), מוט (Yiddish “bravery, courage”), mod (Danish / Swedish “courage”), móður (Faroese / Icelandic “anger, wrath; fierce mood”), mot (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “courage”), 𐌼𐍉𐌸𐍃 (Gothic “mood; anger”), *muths (xvn “mind”); also mōs (Latin “behavior, conduct, manner; inclination, temperament; humour, will”), сме́я (Bulgarian “to dare”), smět (Czech “to be allowed; may”), сме́е (Macedonian “to be allowed”), śmieć (Polish “dare”), сметь (Russian “to dare”), сме̏ти (Serbo-Croatian), смје̏ти (Serbo-Croatian), smȅti (Serbo-Croatian), smjȅti (Serbo-Croatian “to dare, venture”), smieť (Slovak “to be allowed; may”), smeti (Slovenian “to be allowed; may”) смі́ти (Ukrainian “to dare”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Alteration of mode (English), from Latin modus, with specialized uses in grammar, music and logic.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The is derived from Middle English moonelight,monelight,mone lyght (“light of the moon; (heraldry) pattern of moons on the field of a heraldic banner”), from mon (Middle English), mone (Middle English “moon”) (from Old English mōna (“moon”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon; month”)) + light (Middle English “light”) (from Old English lēoht (“light”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”)). .

The is derived from the noun. (“to secretly leave premises without paying the rent”) is a moonlight flit, while (“to make a night-time attack on a tenant farmer”) is probably a .

* maanlicht (Dutch)
* Mondlicht (German)
* muinlicht (Scots), munelicht (Scots)
* moanneljocht (Western Frisian)

chain.meaning: light of the moon; (heraldry) pattern of moons on the field of a heraldic banner

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English moral, from Old French moral, from Latin mōrālis (“relating to manners or morals”)
(first used by Cicero, to translate ἠθικός (Ancient Greek “moral”)), from mos (Latin “manner, custom”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English morali,moralli,morally, equivalent to moral + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English more, from Old English māra (“more”), from Proto-West Germanic *maiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *maizô (“more”), from Proto-Indo-European *mē- (“many”).

Cognate with mair (Scots “more”), moor (Saterland Frisian “more”), mear (Western Frisian “more”), meer (Dutch “more”), mehr (Low German “more”), mehr (German “more”), mere (Danish “more”), mera (Swedish “more”), mer (Norwegian Bokmål “more”), meir (Norwegian Nynorsk “more”), meira (Faroese / Icelandic “more”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English more, moore (Middle English “root”), from Old English more, moru (Old English “carrot, parsnip”) from Proto-West Germanic *morhā, from Proto-Germanic *murhǭ (“carrot”), from Proto-Indo-European *merk- (“edible herb, tuber”).

Akin to moraha (Old Saxon “carrot”), morha (Old High German), moraha (Old High German “root of a plant or tree”) (Möhre (German “carrot”), Morchel (German “mushroom, morel”)). More at morel (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English moren, from the noun. See above.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: mores.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English moreover, moreovere (Middle English), morover (Middle English), mooreover (Middle English), more-overe (Middle English), mare over (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Spanish mosquito (“gnat”), diminutive of mosca (Spanish “fly”), from Latin musca (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”). Cognate with meuzie (Flemish “mosquito”), dialectal mausa (Swedish “fly”), musė (Lithuanian “a fly”) and muschitta (Sicilian “midge”). See also midge (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English most, moste (Middle English), from Old English mǣst, māst (Old English), from Proto-Germanic *maistaz, *maist (Proto-Germanic). Cognate with mast (Scots), maist (Scots “most”), maast (Saterland Frisian “most”), meast (Western Frisian “most”), meest (Dutch “most”), meist (German “most”), - (Danish) and mest (Swedish “most”), mestur (Icelandic “most”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Clipping: almost

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: The sense “probably” is a calque from Indian languages such as அனேகமாக (Tamil).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English moder in lawe; equivalent to mother + -in-law (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From motive#Verb + ation (English), probably after French motivation and German Motivation.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English motif, from Anglo-Norman motif, Middle French motif, and their source, Late Latin motivum (“motive, moving cause”), neuter of motivus (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English motour (“controller, prime mover; God”), from Latin mōtor (“mover; that which moves something”), from mōtō (Latin “to set in motion”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: motor + -ist

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Used in English since the 16th century. From Middle French moustache from Italian mostaccio, from Early Medieval Latin mustācium, from Medieval Greek μουστάκιον, diminutive of (Doric) Ancient Greek μύσταξ (“upper lip”), of unknown origin (probably a qsb-grc — substrate). Replaced native kemp (English “moustache”), from cenep (Old English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle French moustache from Italian mostaccio, from Early Medieval Latin mustācium, from Medieval Greek μουστάκιον, diminutive of (Doric) Ancient Greek μύσταξ (“upper lip”), of unknown origin (probably a qsb-grc — substrate).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English moven, moeven (Middle English), meven (Middle English), borrowed from Old Northern French mover, moveir (Old French) and Old French mouver, moveir (Old French “to move”) (compare modern French mouvoir (French) from Old French movoir (Old French)), from Latin moveō (“move; change, exchange, go in or out, quit”), from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move, drive”). Cognate with mauti (Lithuanian “to push on, rush”), मीवति (Sanskrit “pushes, presses, moves”), mouwe (Middle Dutch “sleeve”). Largely displaced native stir (English), from stiren (Middle English), sturien (Middle English), from styrian (Old English). See also hrēran (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English mevement, from Old French movement (modern mouvement (French)), from movoir (Old French) + -ment (Old French); cf. also Medieval Latin movimentum, from Latin movere (“move”). . In this sense, displaced native styring (Old English), which led to stirring (English).

Morphologically move + ment (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English muche (“much, great”), apocopated variant of muchel (Middle English “much, great”), from Old English myċel, miċel (Old English “big, much”), from Proto-West Germanic *mikil, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“great, many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“big, stour, great”). See also mickle (English), muckle (English).

Cognate with mickle (Scots), mukill (Scots), mekil (Scots), mikil (Scots “big, large, great, much”), mekel (Middle Dutch “mēkel”), michel (Middle High German) , mye (Norwegian Bokmål “much”), mykje (Norwegian Nynorsk “much”), mycket (Swedish “much”), meget (Danish “much”), 𐌼𐌹𐌺𐌹𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “great, many”), μέγας (Ancient Greek “large, great”), Modern μεγάλος (Greek (Modern) “large, great”).

Note that much (English) is not related to mucho (Spanish), and their resemblance in both form and meaning is purely coincidental, as mucho (Spanish) derives from multus (Latin) and is not related to the forms. Instead, related to maño (Spanish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English mud, mudde (Middle English), mode (Middle English), probably a borrowing from Middle Dutch mod, modde (Middle Dutch) or Middle Low German mudde, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mud-, *mudra- (Proto-Germanic “mud”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *mū-, *mew- (Proto-Indo-European “moist”). Cognate with Mudde (Saterland Frisian “mud”), mot (Middle High German “mud”), modd (Swedish “slush”). Compare also suffixed variants mother#Etymology 3 (English “mother”), modder (Western Frisian “mud”), modder (Dutch “mud”), Mudder (Low German (Germany) “mud”), Moder (German “moldiness, mildew, decay”), mudder (Danish “mud”). Alternative etymology suggests the Proto-Germanic word is possibly borrowed from a urj — language (compare e.g. muta (Finnish “mud”), mođđi (se “mud”), мода (Erzya “earth, ground”) from *muďa (Proto-Uralic “earth”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Dutch mud, from gmw —, from Latin modius. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From MUD (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The adjective is derived from Late Middle English muddi, moddy (Middle English), muddy (Middle English “covered with or full of mud, muddy”), from mud (Middle English), mudde (Middle English “mud; turbid water”) + -i (Middle English). , is possibly borrowed from Middle Dutch modde, and/or Middle Low German modde, mudde (Middle Low German), from Proto-Germanic *mud-, *mudra- (Proto-Germanic “mud”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mū-, *mew- (Proto-Indo-European “moist”). The English word is analysable as mud + y (English). .

The verb is derived from the adjective.

* moddich (Middle Low German), muddich (Middle Low German) (muddig (Low German (Germany) “muddy; mouldy”))

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|mud crab or mangrove crab () is [[informally called a muddy in Australia, especially in Queensland.]]

From mud crab + y (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English momelen, a frequentative of mum#Etymology 3 (English “silent”). Compare mümmeln (German), mommelen (Middle Dutch) and mompelen (Dutch). Perhaps related to mumpa (Norwegian Nynorsk “to gum, to chew without teeth”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English murder, murdre (Middle English), mourdre (Middle English), alteration of earlier murthre (Middle English “murder”) (see murther (English)), from Old English morþor (“secret slaying, unlawful killing”) and myrþra (Old English “murder, homicide”), both from Proto-West Germanic *morþr, from Proto-Germanic *murþrą (“death, killing, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥tro- (“killing”), from Proto-Indo-European *mer-, *mor- (Proto-Indo-European), *mr̥- (Proto-Indo-European “to die”). Akin to 𐌼𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌸𐍂 (Gothic “murder”), mord (Old High German “murder”), morð (Old Norse “murder”), myrþrian (Old English “to murder”) and morþ (Old English).

The -d- in the - (Middle English) form may have been influenced in part by murdre (Anglo-Norman), from murdre (Old French), from murdrum (Medieval Latin) (whence the English ), from *morþr (Frankish), *murþr (Frankish “murder”), from the same gem — root, though this may also have been wholly the result of internal development (compare burden (English), from burthen (English) and spider (English), from spiþra (Old English)).

Attested at least since 1475.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English murderere; equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English muscle, muscule (Middle English), muskylle (Middle English), and in part from Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from mūs (Latin “mouse”). . More at mouse (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English musical, from Old French —, from Medieval Latin mūsicālis, from Latin mūsica (“music”) ālis; equivalent to music + al (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English musician, musicien (Middle English), from Old French musicien (“musician”), equivalent to musike +‎ -ien. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English moste , from Old English mōste (“had to”), 1st & 3rd person singular past tense of mōtan (Old English “to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be compelled to, must, may”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną. Cognate with moest (Dutch “had to”), musste (German “had to”), måste (Swedish “must, have to, be obliged to”). More at mote.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English must, from Old English must and Old French must, most (Old French), both from Latin mustum.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: See musth (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English muteren, moteren (Middle English), of origin.

Compare mustern (Low German), musseln (Low German “to whisper”), muttern (German “to mutter; whisper”), muðla (Old Norse “to murmur”). Compare also muttīre (Latin), mutīre (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Hindi मटर

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English myself, meself (Middle English), from Old English mē selfum (Old English) and similar phrases, equivalent to me + self (English), later partly reinterpreted as my + self (English) / -self. Cognate with mysel (Scots), mysell (Scots “myself”), mysels (Western Frisian “myself”), mijzelf (Dutch “myself”), mich selbst (German), mir selbst (German “myself”), meg selv (Norwegian Bokmål “myself”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English *misterius (implied in misteriusly (Middle English)), probably partly from Middle French mystérieux and partly from la:mystērium + ous (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English mysterie, from Anglo-Norman misterie (mistere (Old French)), from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (“a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (Ancient Greek “initiated one”), from μυέω (Ancient Greek “to initiate”), from μύω (Ancient Greek “to shut”). Displaced native ġerȳne (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Ancient Greek μῦθος (“word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable”). Attested in English since 1830. .

chain.meaning: word, humour, companion, speech, account, rumour, fable

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nail, nayl (Middle English), Old English næġl, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl, from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ- (“nail”).

Compare Nail (North Frisian “nail”), Nail (Saterland Frisian “nail”), neil (Western Frisian), Nagel (German / Low German), nagel (Dutch / Swedish), negl (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), nagl (Norwegian Nynorsk), naula (Finnish “nail”), nael (Estonian “nail”), (compare ionga (Irish), unguis (Latin), nyell (Albanian “ankle, hard part of a limb”), nagas (Lithuanian), нога́ (Russian “foot, leg”), но́готь (Russian “nail”), ὄνυξ (Ancient Greek), ناخن (Persian), नख (Sanskrit).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English naylen, from Old English næġlan.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English naked, from Old English nacod, from Proto-West Germanic *nak(k)wad, from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷ- (“naked”). (remotely).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English name, nome (Middle English), from Old English nama, noma (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *namō, from Proto-Germanic *namô (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”).

Germanic Cognates: naame (Yola), name (Yola), naume (Yola “name”), Naam (North Frisian), neem (North Frisian), noome (North Frisian), nööm (North Frisian “name”), Nome (Saterland Frisian), Noome (Saterland Frisian “name”), namme (Western Frisian “name”), Naame (Alemannic), namä (Alemannic), noame (Alemannic), nomu (Alemannic), nàmund (Alemannic “name”), naamo (Cimbric), name (Cimbric), nåm (Cimbric “name”), naam (Dutch), name (Dutch “name”), Nahme (German), Name (German “name”), Naam (Low German (Germany) “name”), Numm (lb “name”), nu'm (mhn “name”), noma (Ripuarian “name”), נאָמען (Yiddish “name”), - (Danish), - (Faroese) and navn (Norwegian Bokmål “name”), nafn (Icelandic “name”), nabn (Norwegian Nynorsk), namn (Norwegian Nynorsk “name”), namn (Swedish “name”), 𐌽𐌰𐌼𐍉 (Gothic “name”).

Indo-European Cognates: nōmen (Latin “name”) (whence nombre (Spanish “name”)), имя (Russian “name”), nām (ask “name”), nom (bsh), num (bsh “name”), nom (Prakrit), nëmë (Prakrit “name”), nām (wbk “name”), नामन् (Sanskrit “name”).

Possible cognates outside of Indo-European include nimi (Finnish “name”) and név (Hungarian “name”). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English namen, from Old English namian (“to name, mention”) and ġenamian (Old English “to name, call, appoint”), from Proto-West Germanic *namōn (“to name”). Cognate with neame (Western Frisian “to name; to mention”). Compare also nemnan (Old English), nemnian (Old English “to name, give a name to a person or thing”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Spanish ñame, substituting n for the unfamiliar Spanish letter ñ. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English narow, narowe (Middle English), narewe (Middle English), narwe (Middle English), naru (Middle English), from Old English nearu (“narrow, strait, confined, constricted, not spacious, limited, petty; limited, poor, restricted; oppressive, causing anxiety (of that which restricts free action of body or mind), causing or accompanied by difficulty, hardship, oppressive; oppressed, not having free action; strict, severe”), from Proto-West Germanic *naru, from Proto-Germanic *narwaz (“constricted, narrow”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ner- (“to turn, bend, twist, constrict”).

Cognate with naar (North Frisian), noar (North Frisian), noor (North Frisian), nåår (North Frisian “narrow”), noar (Saterland Frisian “narrow”), naar (Dutch “nasty, scary; sickening, unpleasant”), nor (Danish / Swedish “narrow strait”); also नृत् (Sanskrit “to dance; act on stage, represent”).

chain.meaning: narrow, strait, confined, constricted, not spacious, limited, petty; limited, poor, restricted; oppressive, causing anxiety (of that which restricts free action of body or mind), causing or accompanied by difficulty, hardship, oppressive; oppressed, not having free action; strict, severe

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English narwen (“to narrow”); see there for more details, but ultimately derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English narowly, equivalent to narrow + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nasty, nasti (Middle English), naxty (Middle English), naxte (Middle English “unclean, filthy”), whence also Early Modern nasky (English “nasty”), of origin. Probably from earlier Middle English *naskty, *naskedy (Middle English), from Middle English *nasked (“dirty, messy”) + -y (Middle English), ultimately of gmq — origin (comparable to nasket (Danish “dirty, foul, unpleasant”), naskot (Swedish “dirty, filthy”), naskig (Swedish), naskug (Swedish “nasty, dirty, messy”)), themselves all probably related to Proto-Germanic *hnaskuz (“tender, soft”). Likely . Cognate with nastie (Scots), nestie (Scots “dirty, filthy”).

Alternative theories have also been proposed, which include:
* From Low German nask (“nasty”) .
* Middle Dutch nestich, nistich (Middle Dutch) , perhaps ultimately connected to the Scandinavian word above, or related to *nest (Proto-West Germanic “nest”).
* From Old French nastre (“lowly, strange”), shortened form of villenastre (Old French “infamous, bad”), from vilein (Old French “villain”) + -astre (Old French), from Latin -aster.
* Other suggestions include Old High German naz (“wet”), hardening of nesh (English “soft”), or alteration of naughty (English).
* Modern use of the word is sometimes attributed to the popular and often derogatory 19th century American political cartoons of , but the word predates him.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English nacioun,nacion, from Old French nacion, from Latin nātiōnem, accusative of nātiō (Latin “nation”). and cynewīse (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Short for damnation (English) or tarnation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: nation + -wide

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English natif, from Old French natif, from Latin nātīvus, from nātus (Latin “birth”). . Displaced native Middle English thedisch (Middle English), equivalent to (puristic) theed (English) + -ish (English). .

Compare also inborn (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English natural, borrowed from Old French natural, naturel (Old French), from Latin nātūrālis, from nātus (Latin), the perfect participle of nāscor (Latin “be born”). Displaced native ġecynde (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English naturally, naturaly (Middle English), naturely (Middle English), naturaliche (Middle English), natureliche (Middle English), equivalent to natural + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nature, natur (Middle English), from Old French nature, from Latin nātūra (“birth, origin, natural constitution or quality”), future participle from perfect passive participle natus (Latin “(g)natus”), from deponent verb nasci (Latin “(g)nasci”) + future participle suffix -urus (English).

Displaced native erd (Middle English “character, nature, disposition”) from eard (Old English) (compare Art (German “nature, character, kind, type”)); and kynde (Middle English “character, disposition, nature”) from ġecynd (Old English). More at kind (English). Also displaced native hād (Old English “nature, manner”).

chain.meaning: birth, origin, natural constitution or quality

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From late Middle English noughti, naughty (Middle English “evil, immoral, wicked”), from nought (Middle English “evil, immoral”) + -ī̆ (Middle English). Analysable as naught + y (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nave, navye (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman —, Old French navie, from Latin nāvigia < nāvigium (Latin), from Latin nāvigō, nāvis (Latin “boat”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare ναῦς (Ancient Greek “ship”), ناو (Persian “boat, warship”), नाव (Sanskrit “ship”), nōwend (Old English “mariner, sailor”). .

Displaced native sċiphere (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nere, ner (Middle English), from Old English nēar (“nearer”), influenced by Old Norse nær (“near”), both originating from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz (“nearer”), comparative of the adverb *nēhw (Proto-Germanic “near”), from the adjective *nēhwaz (Proto-Germanic), ultimately from Pre-Proto-Germanic , a lengthened-grade adjective derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

Cognate with nai (North Frisian), noi (North Frisian), näi (North Frisian “close, near”), nai (Saterland Frisian “close, near”), na (Dutch “close”), naar (Dutch “to, towards”), nao (Low German (Netherlands) “after”), nach (German “after”), nahe (German “near”), näher (German “nearer”), nao (Low German (Germany)), nå (Low German (Germany) “towards”), no (lb “after”), nær (Danish / Faroese / Icelandic / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “close, near”), när (Swedish), nära (Swedish “close, near”), 𐌽𐌴𐍈 (Gothic “close, near”). See also nigh (English).

Near appears to be derived from (or at the very least influenced by) the North Germanic languages; as opposed to nigh (English), which continues the inherited West Germanic adjective. Both, however, are ultimately derived from the same Proto-Germanic root: *nēhw (Proto-Germanic “near, close”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nēre, neere (Middle English “kidney, abdomen; (pl.) seat of emotions”), probably from unattested Old English *nēora, *nīora (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *neurō, from Proto-Germanic *neurô; but alternatively borrowed from Middle Low German nêre. Cognate with nere (Scots), neir (Scots), Niere (German), nier (Dutch), nyre (Norwegian), nýra (Icelandic), and more distantly nefronēs (Latin), νεφρός (Ancient Greek), all meaning both and .

In most English dialects, this word survived only as a fossilized fossil in the second syllable of kidney (English) (earlier kidenēre (English “kide-nēre”)), wherein the original r was apparently replaced with y.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ner-bi, neer by (Middle English), equivalent to near + by (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English nete, net (Middle English), nette (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman neit (“good, desirable, clean”), a variant of Old French net, nette (Old French “clean, clear, pure”), from Latin nitidus (“gleaming”), derived from niteo (Latin “to shine”). . Cognate with nett (German “nice, kind”). Compare also nait (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English net, neet (Middle English), from Old English nēat (“animal, beast, ox, cow, cattle”), from Proto-West Germanic *naut, from Proto-Germanic *nautą (“foredeal, profit, property, livestock”), from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to acquire, make use of”). Cognate with noot (Dutch “cow, cattle”), dialectal German Noß (Bavarian “livestock”), Alemannic German Nooss (Alemannic “young sheep or goat”), Swedish nöt (Swedish “cattle”), naut (Icelandic “cattle, bull”) and neyt (Faroese “cattle”). More at note (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: necessary + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English necessarye, from Old French necessaire, from Latin necessārius (“unavoidable, inevitable, required”), variant of necesse (Latin “unavoidable, inevitable”), probably from ne (Latin) or non (Latin) cessus (Latin “cessum”), from the perfect passive participle of cēdō (Latin “yield; avoid, withdraw”); see cede.

Older use as a noun in reference to an outhouse or lavatory under the influence of English and necessārium (Latin), a medieval term for the place for monks’ “unavoidable” business, usually located behind or attached to monastic dormitories.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nede, a merger of two terms:
* Old English nīed (West Saxon), nēd (Old English) (Mercian), nēad (Old English “necessity, compulsion, want”), from Proto-West Germanic *naudi, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, from Proto-Indo-European *neh₂w- (“death”).
* Old English nēod (“desire, longing”), from Proto-West Germanic *niudi (“desire, eagerness”), from Proto-Indo-European *new- (“to incline, tend, move, push, nod, wave”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English neden, from Old English nēodian.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nedle, from Old English nǣdl, from Proto-West Germanic *nāþlu, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō, from pre-Germanic *neh₁-tleh₂ (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₁- (“to spin, twist”).

Cognate with Näddele (Saterland Frisian “sewing needle”), naald (Dutch “needle”), Nadel (German “needle, pin, crochet hook”), nähen (German “sew”), Nol (lb “needle”), nöłd (Ripuarian “needle”), נאָדל (Yiddish “needle, pin”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk), nål (Swedish “needle”), ną̊l (Elfdalian “needle”), - (Faroese), nál (Icelandic “needle”), 𐌽𐌴𐌸𐌻𐌰 (Gothic “sewing needle”), neula (Finnish “needle”). Further related with nyddu (Welsh), nēre (Latin), स्नायति (Sanskrit “wraps up, winds”). Related to snood (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nedes (“of necessity, necessarily; inevitably, unavoidably”), from Old English nēdes, nīedes (Old English “of necessity; not willingly”), from nīed (Old English) + -es (Old English).

The English word is equivalent to need + -'s (English) and hence to need + s (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English negative, negatif (Middle English), from Old French negatif, from Latin negātīvus (“that denies, negative”), from negāre (Latin “to deny”); see negate (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: negative + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English neighebour, neighbour (Middle English), neyghebour (Middle English), from Old English nēahġebūr (“neighbour”), from Proto-West Germanic *nāhwagabūrō, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwagabūrô (“neighbour”), from *nēhwaz (Proto-Germanic “close, near”) + *gabūrô (Proto-Germanic “dweller”). Equivalent to .

Cognate with nebour (Scots), neebour (Scots), neibour (Scots “neighbour”), nipore (Yola), nypore (Yola “neighbour”), Naiber (North Frisian), naibüür (North Frisian), näiber (North Frisian “neighbour”), Noaber (Saterland Frisian “neighbour”), Naachpuur (Alemannic), Nochbär (Alemannic “neighbour”), Nohber (Central Franconian “neighbour”), nabuur (Dutch “neighbour”), Naber (Low German), Nahwer (Low German “neighbour”), Nachbar (German “neighbour”), Noper (lb “neighbour”), nokwer (Ripuarian), nökver (Ripuarian), nökwer (Ripuarian “neighbour”), nabo (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “neighbour”), nábúgvi (Faroese “neighbour”), nábúi (Icelandic “neighbour”), naboo (Manx “neighbour”), nàbaidh (Scottish Gaelic “neighbour”), naaber (Estonian “neighbour”), naapuri (Finnish “neighbour”).

Eclipsed non-native prome (Middle English “neighbour”), borrowed from proeme (Old French), proime (Old French), proisme (Old French “neighbour”) (<< proximus (Latin “nearest, next”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: neighbour + -hood

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration (after either (English)) of nauther (English), from Middle English neiþer, from Old English nāwþer, contraction of nāhwæþer (Old English), corresponding to no (English) + whether (English). Compare neuter (Latin “neither”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nevew, neveu (Middle English “nephew, grandson”), from Old French neveu, from Latin nepos (“nepos, nepōtem”), from Proto-Italic *nepōts (“nephew, grandson”), whence also neveu (French), nipote (Italian). Displaced or absorbed the inherited neve (English “nephew, grandson, male cousin”), from neve (Middle English), from nefa (Old English), from *nefō (Proto-West Germanic), from *nefô (Proto-Germanic “nephew, grandson”), whence neef (Dutch), Neffe (German). All ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts (“grandchild, sister's son”). Cognate with nećak (Serbo-Croatian), nia (Irish), نوه (Persian). .

Spelt with -ph- by readaptation to since the 15th century, which later triggered the with .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nervous (“composed of or incorporating nerves”), from Latin nervōsus (“nervous; sinewy; energetic, vigorous”), from nervus (Latin “nerve; muscle; sinew, tendon; (figuratively) energy, power; nerve; force, strength, vigour”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥ (“sinew, tendon”)) + -ōsus (Latin). The English word is analysable as nerve + ous (English).

chain.meaning: nerve; muscle; sinew, tendon; (figuratively) energy, power; nerve; force, strength, vigour

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: nervous + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English net, from Old English net, nett (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *nati, from Proto-Germanic *natją (“net”), from Proto-Indo-European *neHd- (“to knot, turn, twist”).

Cognate with näät (North Frisian “net”), Nät (Saterland Frisian “net”), net (Western Frisian / Dutch “net”), Netz (de,lb “net”), נעץ (Yiddish “net”), net (Danish / Elfdalian / Faroese / Icelandic “net”), nett (Norwegian Bokmål “net”), net (Norwegian Nynorsk), nett (Norwegian Nynorsk “net”), nät (Swedish “net”), 𐌽𐌰𐍄𐌹 (Gothic “net”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English net, nette (Middle English), from Old French net, from Latin nitidus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Middle French nettoyer (“to cleanse”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From ; the nonliteral sense and its subsenses are extended from the literal sense; they are now the dominant senses. Cognate with Netzwerk (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nevere, navere (Middle English), nævere (Middle English), from Old English nǣfre (“never”), equivalent to ne + ever (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nevertheles, never-þe-les (Middle English), nevere-þe-lesse (Middle English). ; compare never the wiser (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English neowe, neue (Middle English), new (Middle English), newe (Middle English), nywe (Middle English), from Old English nēowe, nīewe (Old English), nīowe (Old English), nīwe (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *niwi, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz (“new”), from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, *néwyos (Proto-Indo-European “new”). Compare also nū (Old English “now”). More at now (English). .

Cognate with new (Scots “new”), nai (North Frisian), nei (North Frisian), nii (North Frisian “new”), näi (Saterland Frisian “new”), nij (Western Frisian “new”), nöi (Alemannic), nüüw (Alemannic “new”), neich (Bavarian “new”), naüge (Cimbric “new”), nieuw (Dutch), nij (Dutch “new”), nij (Low German (Netherlands) “new”), neu (German), new (German), neuw (German “new”), nee (Low German), neei (Low German (Germany) “new”), nei (lb “new”), noj (Ripuarian), noü (Ripuarian “new”), נײַ (Yiddish “new”), ny (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “new”), nýggjur (Faroese “new”), nýr (Icelandic “new”), 𐌽𐌹𐌿𐌾𐌹𐍃 (Gothic “new”); also nevez (Breton “new”), nowydh (Cornish), nowyth (Cornish “fresh, new”), nua (Irish), nuadh (Irish “new”), noa (Manx “fresh, new”), nuadh (Scottish Gaelic “fresh, new”), newydd (Welsh “new”), novus (Latin “new”), νέος (Greek (Modern) “young, youthful; modern, new”), naũjas (Lithuanian “new”), но́вы (Belarusian “new”), нов (Bulgarian / Macedonian “new”), nový (Czech / Slovak “new”), nowy (Polish “new”), но́вый (Russian “new”), но̏в (Serbo-Croatian), nȍv (Serbo-Croatian “new”), nov (Slovenian “new”), нови́й (Ukrainian “new”), նոր (Armenian “new”), نوک (bal “new”), نوێ (Central Kurdish “new”), нӕуӕг (Ossetic), ног (Ossetic “fresh, new; young”), نو (Persian “new”), نو (mzn “new”), nû (Kurmanji Kurdish “new”), نوی (Pashto “new”), newe (zza “new”), nuy (bsh), nuyĩ (bsh “new”), unü (Prakrit “new”), 𒉋𒀸 (Hittite “fresh, new”), 𒈾𒀀𒌑𒉿𒋾 (Luwian “new”), ñu (xto “new”), ñuwe (txb “new”), नव (Sanskrit “fresh, modern, new”), नव्य (Sanskrit “new”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English newly, newely (Middle English), neweliche (Middle English), from Old English nīewlīċe (“newly”), equivalent to new + -ly (English). Compare nieuwelijks (Dutch), neulich (German), nylig (Danish), nýlega (Icelandic). More at new (English), -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nexte, nexste (Middle English), nixte (Middle English), from Old English nīehsta, nīehste (Old English), etc., inflected forms of nīehst (Old English “nearest, next”), superlative form of nēah (Old English “nigh”) (the comparative would become near (English)), corresponding to Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”); equivalent to nigh + est (English).

Cognate with naist (Saterland Frisian “next”), naast (Dutch “next to”), nächster (German “next”), נעקסט (Yiddish “next”), næste (Danish “next”), nest (Elfdalian “by, near”), næst (Icelandic “next”), neste (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “next”), näst (Swedish), nästa (Swedish “next”), نزد (Persian “near, with”).

Compare typologically proximus (Latin “nearest, next”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nycely; equivalent to nice + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nece (“niece, granddaughter”), from Old French nece (“niece, granddaughter”) (Modern nièce (French “niece”)) from Late Latin neptia, representing Latin neptis (“granddaughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *néptih₂ (“granddaughter, niece”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: night + club

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From night + life (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with nichtmare (Scots) and nichtmeer (Scots), nachtmerrie (Dutch), nachtmār (Middle Low German), Nachtmahr (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nodden, probably from an unrecorded Old English *hnodian (“to nod, shake the head”), from Proto-West Germanic *hnodōn, from Proto-Germanic *hnudōną (“to beat, rivet, pound, push”), from Proto-Indo-European *kendʰ-, from *ken- (Proto-Indo-European “to scratch, scrape, rub”). Compare hnotōn (Old High German “to shake”), hnutten (Old High German “to shake, rattle, vibrate”) (> modern dialectal notteln (German), nütteln (German “to rock, move back and forth”)), njóða (Faroese “to clench a nail”), hnjóða (Icelandic “to rivet, clinch”), noða (Faroese “to double by bending”), hnoða (Icelandic “to clinch, rivet”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From non- + smoking (English). The noun is back-formed from the adjective.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English none, noon (Middle English), non (Middle English “not one”), from Old English nān (“not one, not any, none”), from Proto-West Germanic *nain, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz (“none, nought, nothing”), equivalent to ne + one (English). (Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one (English).)

Cognate with nane (Scots “none”), naan (Saterland Frisian), neen (Saterland Frisian “no, not any, none”), neen (Western Frisian) & gjin (Western Frisian “no, none”), neen (Dutch) & geen (Dutch “no, none”), nen (Low German “nēn”), neen (Low German), keen (Low German “no, none, no one”), nein (German) & kein (German “no, none”), nōn (Latin “not”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the first sense, since they respond “none” when asked about their religion; also a play on words on nun (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From French none, from Latin nōna (“ninth; ninth hour”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From non- + sense (English), from c. 1610. Compare the semantically similar ûnsin (Western Frisian “nonsense”), onzin (Dutch “nonsense”), Unsinn (German “nonsense”), unsense (English “nonsense”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Contraction of Middle English nauther, from nother (Middle English). Cognate with neither (Middle English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Etymology 1 (sense 2 above), reinterpreted as not (English) + or (English) or negation (English) + or (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: normal + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English northest, from Old English norþēast, equivalent to north + east (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English northerne, from Old English norþerne, from Proto-West Germanic *norþrōnī, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz. Cognate with nordrōni (Old High German) and norrœnn (Old Norse).

Morphologically north + -ern (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English northwest, from Old English norþwest, equivalent to north + west (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English not,nat, a variant of noght (Middle English), naht (Middle English “not, nothing”), from Old English *nōht,nāht (“nought, nothing”), shortening of nōwiht (Old English), nāwiht (Old English “nothing”), from Proto-West Germanic *naiwwiht, corresponding to ne (Old English “not”) + ōwiht (Old English), āwiht (Old English “anything”), corresponding to ā (Old English “ever, always”) + wiht (Old English “thing, creature”).

Cognate with nat (Scots), naucht (Scots “not”), nit (Saterland Frisian “not”), net (Western Frisian “not”), niet (Dutch “not”), nicht (German “not”). Compare nought (English), naught (English) and aught (English). More at no (English), wight (English), whit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English note , from Old English not, nōt (Old English “note, mark, sign”) and Old French note (“letter, note”), both from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English note (“use, usefulness, profit”), from Old English notu (“use, enjoyment, advantage, profit, utility”), from Proto-West Germanic *notu, from Proto-Germanic *nutō (“enjoyment, utilisation”), from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to acquire, make use of”). Cognate with not (Western Frisian “yield, produce, crop”), genot (Dutch “enjoyment, pleasure”), nut (Dutch “usefulness, utility, behoof”), Nutzen (German “benefit, usefulness, utility”), not (Icelandic “use”). Related also to notian (Old English “to enjoy, make use of, employ”), nēotan (Old English “to use, enjoy”), niozan (Old High German “to use, enjoy”) (Modern genießen (German “to enjoy”)), Modern benutzen (German “to use”). Related to nait (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English nothyng, noon thing (Middle English), non thing (Middle English), na þing (Middle English), nan thing (Middle English), nan þing (Middle English), from Old English nāþing, nān þing (Old English “nothing”), equivalent to no + thing (English). Compare nāwiht (Old English “nothing”), ingenting (Swedish “nothing”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French notice, from the Latin nōtitia. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English novel, from Old French novel (“new, fresh, recent, recently made or done, strange, rare”) (modern nouvel (French), nouveau (French)), from Latin novellus (“new, fresh, young, modern”), diminutive of novus (Latin “new”). .

chain.meaning: new, fresh, recent, recently made or done, strange, rare

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|200px|Front page of ', by , a notable example of a novel

Borrowed from Italian novella, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English novel, from Old French novelle, from Latin novella, feminine of novellus (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Latin novella, feminine of novellus (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: novel + -ist

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nou, nu (Middle English), from Old English nū, from Proto-West Germanic *nū, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”). ("well?").

Cognate with noo (Scots), nou (Scots), now (Scots “now”), neow (Yola), now (Yola), nowe (Yola “now”), nü (North Frisian “now”), no (Western Frisian “now”), nu (Dutch), nou (Dutch “now”), nu (German), nun (German “now”), noe (Limburgish), Nuu (Limburgish “now”), nu (Danish / Swedish “now”), nų (Elfdalian “now”), nú (Faroese), núgv (Faroese “now”), nú (Icelandic), núna (Icelandic “now”), no (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), nu (Norwegian Nynorsk), nå (Norwegian Nynorsk “now”), 𐌽𐌿 (Gothic “now”); also nu (Gaulish “now”), num (Latin “now”), νυν (Greek (Modern) “currently, now”), ni (Albanian), tani (Albanian “now”), ни́не (Bulgarian “currently, now”), nyní (Czech “now”), ninie (zlw-opl “now”), но́не (Russian), ны́не (Russian “now, today”), ни́ні (Ukrainian “nowadays; today”), 𐬥𐬏 (ae “currently, now”), نون (bal “now”), اکنون (Persian), کنون (Persian), نون (Persian “now”), ana (Kurmanji Kurdish), anaka (Kurmanji Kurdish), anêka (Kurmanji Kurdish), aniha (Kurmanji Kurdish), anika (Kurmanji Kurdish), naga (Kurmanji Kurdish), naha (Kurmanji Kurdish), naka (Kurmanji Kurdish), niha (Kurmanji Kurdish), niho (Kurmanji Kurdish), nika (Kurmanji Kurdish), noke (Kurmanji Kurdish), ئانا (Kurmanji Kurdish), نکا (Kurmanji Kurdish “now”), ныр (Ossetic “now”), 𒆠𒉡𒌦 (Hittite “now”), 𒈾𒀀𒉡𒌦 (Luwian “now”), nuṃ (xto “again, once more”), nano (txb “again, once more”), नु (Sanskrit “now”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: See know (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From now + adays (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English nowher, from Old English nōhwēr, nāhwǣr (Old English), from nā- (Old English) + hwǣr (Old English). .

Adjective usage is taken from phrases like nowhere on the map (signifying the location was too small or too insignificant to be listed), nowhere you want to be, etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin nū̆cleus, a contraction of the adjective nuculeus (Latin), masculine of feminine nuculea (Latin “pertaining to a small nut”) from nucula (Latin) + adjectival suffix -eus, -ea, -eum (Latin). The nucula (Latin) + -āris (Latin) adds up to nuculāris (Latin), a term that in English becomes nucular (English); the nuculea (Latin) + -āris (Latin), becomes nuculeāris (Latin “relative to what pertains to small nut”), later contracted into nuclear. . Compare muscle (English) and mūsculus (Latin); muscular (English) and mūsculāris (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English noysaunce, from Anglo-Norman nusaunce, nussance (Old French) and Old French nuisance, from nuisir (Old French “to harm”), from Latin noceō (“nocēre”). and nocency (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English number, nombre (Middle English), numbre (Middle English), noumbre (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman noumbre, Old French nombre, from Latin numerus (“number”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nem- (“to distribute, to give, to take”). Compare Nummer (Saterland Frisian), Nuumer (Saterland Frisian), nûmer (Western Frisian), nummer (Dutch “number”), Nummer (German “number”), nummer (Danish “number”), nummer (Swedish “number”), númer (Icelandic “number”). and rime (Middle English); more at tell (English), tale (English) and rhyme (English). Distantly related (via ) to nim (English “to take, seize”) and its Germanic cognates (e.g. nehmen (German)), hence also to numb (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From numb (English) + -er (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Equivalent to numb + -er (English)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English noricerie, norserye (Middle English “children's nursery; state of being fostered or nursed; education, upbringing”), from Old French norricerie, nourricerie (Old French), from norrice (Old French), nourrice (Old French) (modern nourrice (French “childminder, nanny; wet nurse”)) + -erie (Old French). Norrice and nourrice are derived from Late Latin nūtrīcia (“wet nurse”), from Latin nūtrīcius (“that nurses or suckles; nourishing”), from nūtriō (Latin “to breastfeed, nurse, suckle”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂- (“to flow”). The English word may be analysed as nourice (English), nurse (English) ery.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English note, nute (Middle English), from Old English hnutu, from Proto-West Germanic *hnut, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts (“nut”), from a root *knu- possibly shared with *knūs (Proto-Celtic) and nux (Latin “nut”). Based on the form of the nouns and the restriction of the root to Germanic, Celtic and Italic, it has been argued to be of non-Indo-European (qfa-sub —) origin.

See also nút (Western Frisian), noot (Dutch), Nuss (German), nød (Danish), nöt (Swedish), nøtt (Norwegian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Variant of not (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English ake, hok (Middle English), oek (Middle English), ok (Middle English), oke (Middle English), from Old English aac, āc (Old English), ǣċ (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *aik, from Proto-Germanic *aiks (“oak”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“oak”).

From Proto-Germanic: aik (Scots), ake (Scots), yik (Scots “oak”), iake (North Frisian), iik (North Frisian “oak”), Eeke (Saterland Frisian “oak”), iik (Western Frisian “oak”), aicha (Cimbric), oach (Cimbric “oak”), eik (Dutch “oak”), Eiche (German “oak”), Eech (lb “oak”), aach (Ripuarian), aeh́ (Ripuarian), ǡh́ (Ripuarian “oak”), eg (Danish “oak”), eik (Faroese / Icelandic / Norwegian Nynorsk “oak”), eik (Norwegian Bokmål), ek (Norwegian Bokmål “oak”), ek (Swedish “oak”).

From Proto-Indo-European: aesculus (Latin “Italian oak”), αἰγίλωψ (Ancient Greek “Turkey oak”), enjë (Albanian “English yew; stinking juniper”), ozols (Latvian “oak”), ąžuolas (Lithuanian “oak”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English obeyen, from Anglo-Norman obeir, obeier (Old French) et al., Old French obeir, from Latin oboediō (also obēdiō (Latin “to listen to, harken, usually in extended sense, obey, be subject to, serve”)), from ob- (Latin “before, near”) + audiō (Latin “to hear”). Compare audient (English). In Latin, ob + audire would have been expected to become Classical Latin *obūdiō (compare in + claudō becoming inclūdō), but it has been theorized that the usual law court associations of the word for obeying encouraged a false archaism from ū to oe, to oboediō (compare Old Latin oinos → Classical Latin ūnus).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French object, from Medieval Latin obiectum (“object”), from obiectus (Latin), perfect passive participle of obiciō (Latin “to throw against”), from ob iaciō (Latin “to throw”), as a calque of Ancient Greek ἀντικείμενον. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from , from . Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English obgectyf, from Middle French objectif and its etymon Medieval Latin obiectīvus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English obligacioun, from Old French obligacion, from Latin obligatio (“obligatio, obligationem”), from obligatum (Latin) (past participle of obligare (Latin)), from ob- (Latin “to”) + ligare (Latin “to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Also a borrowing from French observation and a Latin observatio (“observātiō(n-)”).
Morphologically observe + ation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (Latin “before”) + servō (Latin “to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (Gothic “weapons, armour”), searu (Old English “device”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from obsidere (Latin “to besiege”); see obsess (English). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner (Old French) et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- (Latin) + tenere (Latin “tenēre”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: 16th century, from la:obvius + -ous (English), from ob- (Latin “before”) + via (Latin “way”).

parts: la:obvius<t:being in the way so as to meet, meeting, easy to access, at hand, ready, obvious>

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: obvious + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English occasioun, from Middle French occasion, from Old French occasiun, from Latin occāsiō (“occāsiōnem”), noun of action from perfect passive participle occāsus (Latin), from verb occidō (Latin), from prefix ob- (Latin “down", "away”) + verb cadō (Latin “fall”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English occasionally, occasionaly (Middle English), occasyoneely (Middle English), occasyonly (Middle English), equivalent to occasional + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English occupien, occupyen (Middle English), borrowed from Old French occuper, from Latin occupō (“to take possession of, seize, occupy, take up, employ”), from ob (Latin “to, on”) + capiō (Latin “to take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). , now obsolete.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally "meet (in argument)", borrowed from Middle French occurrer, from Latin occurrō (“run to meet, run against, befall, present itself”) from prefix ob- (Latin “against”) + verb currō (Latin “run, hurry, move”).

chain.meaning: run to meet, run against, befall, present itself

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English *ocean, occean (Middle English), occian (Middle English), occyan (Middle English), from Old French occean (later reborrowed or reinforced by Middle French ocean), from Latin Ōceanus, originally from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (“Oceanus”). Displaced native gārseċġ (Old English). Also commonly referred to as the ocean sea, the sea of ocean (compare Latin mare ōceanum; Old French mer oceane, occeanne mer). Compare Oceoan (Saterland Frisian “ocean”), oseaan (Western Frisian “ocean”), oceaan (Dutch “ocean”), Ozeaan (Low German (Germany) “ocean”), Ozean (German “ocean”), ocean (Danish “ocean”), ocean (Swedish “ocean”), océan (French “ocean”), oceano (Italian “ocean”). /Okeanos (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English odde, od (Middle English “odd (not even); leftover after division into pairs”), from Old Norse oddi (“odd, third or additional number; triangle”), from oddr (Old Norse “point of a weapon”), from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz (“point”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to stick, prick, pierce, sting”) + *dʰeh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “to set, place”).

Cognate to oddi (Icelandic “triangle, point of land, odd number”), udda (Swedish “odd”), udd (Swedish “a point”), od (Danish “point of weapon”) and odde (Danish “a headland, point”), odde (Norwegian Bokmål “a point”, “odd”, “peculiar”); related to ord (Old English “a point”). .

chain.meaning: odd, third or additional number; triangle

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English of, from Old English of (“from, out of, off”), an unstressed form of æf (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab (“away; away from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“away”). , which is the stressed descendant of the same Old English word. More at off (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: A spelling of influenced by Etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English of, from Old English of, af (Old English), æf (Old English “from, off, away”), from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab (“from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“from, off, back”). .

Cognate with aff (Scots “away, off”), oawe (Saterland Frisian), ou (Saterland Frisian “from”), ôf (Western Frisian “away, off”), af (Dutch “from, off”), ab (German “from, off”), - (Low German (Germany)), of (lb “off”), אָפּ (Yiddish “off”), - (Danish), af (Icelandic “from, off”), - (Faroese), - (Norwegian Bokmål) and av (Norwegian Nynorsk “off”), af (Swedish), av (Swedish “off”), 𐌰𐍆 (Gothic “of, from”); and with ab (Latin “of, from, by”), ἀπό (Ancient Greek “from”), and others.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from , from ob- (Latin “against”) + *fendō (Latin “strike”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English offendour, offender (Middle English), offendir (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French offensif, from offendre (Middle French) + -if (Middle French) by analogy with défensif (French). Offendre is from Latin offendo (“to offend”); see offend.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English offer, from Old English offrian (“offer or make a sacrifice”) rather than from Old French offre (“offer”), from offrir (Old French “to offer”), from Latin offerō (“to present, bring before”). Compare offer (North Frisian “sacrifice, donation, fee”), offer (Dutch “offering, sacrifice”), Opfer (German “victim, sacrifice”), offer (Danish “victim, sacrifice”), offr (Icelandic “offering”). See verb below.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English offren, offrien (Middle English). In the religious senses inherited from Old English offrian (“to offer, sacrifice, bring an oblation”); otherwise from Old French ofrir. Both ultimately from Latin offerō (“to present, bestow, bring before”), from Latin ob + ferō (Latin “bring, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carry, bear”), later reinforced by offrir (Old French “to offer”). Cognate with offria (Old Frisian “to offer”), offrōn (Old Dutch “to offer”), opfern (German “to offer”), offra (Old Norse “to offer”). More at ob- (English), bear (English).

chain.meaning: to offer, sacrifice, bring an oblation

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Affix: off + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English officer, from Anglo-Norman officer, officier (Old French), from Old French officer, Late Latin officiarius (“official”), from Latin officium (“office”) + -ārius (Latin “-er”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English official, from Old French official, from Latin officiālis, from Latin officium (“duty, service”), .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English often, alteration (with final -n added due to analogy with selden (Middle English “seldom”)) of Middle English ofte, oft (Middle English), from Old English oft (“often”), from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (Proto-Germanic “often”).

Cognate with affen (Scots), aften (Scots), af'en (Scots), oaffen (Scots), oaften (Scots), oftin (Scots “often”), aaft (North Frisian), oftem (North Frisian), oofting (North Frisian “often”), oafte (Saterland Frisian “often”), - (German), - (lb) and oft (Pennsylvania German “often”), אָפֿט (Yiddish “often”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian Bokmål) and ofte (Norwegian Nynorsk “often”), - (Faroese), ofta (Swedish “often”), oft (Icelandic “often”), 𐌿𐍆𐍄𐌰 (Gothic “often”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English oyle, oile (Middle English “olive oil”), borrowed from Old French oile, from Latin oleum (“oil, olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (“olive oil”), from ἐλαία (Ancient Greek “olive”). Compare *lojь (Proto-Slavic). More at olive (English). . Supplanted ele (Middle English “oil”), from ele (Old English “oil”), also from Latin. Displaced native smireness (Old English “ointment, oil”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English oylen, from the noun (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From old + fashioned (English). The cocktail (which goes back to at least the early 1800s) got its name in the late 1800s as more complicated cocktails became common and those who preferred simpler drinks began asking for old-fashioned cocktails.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English olyve, from Old French olive (“olive, olive tree”), from Latin olīva (“olive”), itself from either ett *𐌄𐌋𐌄𐌉𐌅𐌀, Proto-Greek *elaíwā (compare 𐀁𐀨𐀷 (Mycenaean Greek), ἐλαίᾱ (Ancient Greek)), or the same source as those two. In any case, ultimately from a Mediterranean qsb-grc — source, possibly ber-pro *wlw (“wild olive”). More questionably, maybe from Proto-Indo-European *loiwom (compare лои (Church Slavonic “tallow”), եւղ (Classical Armenian “oil”)). . Displaced native eleberġe (Old English), literally "oil berry."

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English on, from Old English on, an (Old English “on, upon, onto, in, into”), from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana (“on, at”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“on, onto”).

Cognate with a (Yola), an (Yola), ana (Yola), on (Yola “on”), an (Saterland Frisian “on; at”), oan (Western Frisian “on; to, towards”), aan (Cimbric), å (Cimbric “on, onto”), aan (Dutch “on; at”), an (Low German “on; at, to”), an (German “at, in; on”), un (lb “on; at, to”), אָן (Yiddish “on, onward”), å (Danish / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “on”), ą̊ (Elfdalian “on”), á (Faroese / Icelandic “in; on”), 𐌰𐌽𐌰 (Gothic “at, on”); also 𐌀𐌌- (xum), 𐌀𐌍- (xum “up, upon”), ἀνά (Ancient Greek “on, upon”) (whence ανά (Greek (Modern) “by, through, per”)), në (Albanian “in; on”), no (Latvian “from; out of; for; of; with”), nuo (Lithuanian “from, off; for, of”), на (Belarusian / Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian / Ukrainian “on”), na (Czech / Polish / Slovak / Slovenian “on”), на (Serbo-Croatian), na (Serbo-Croatian “on”), ան- (Classical Armenian “at, on, unto”); and from Old Norse upp á (Old Norse): på (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Swedish “on”), paa (Norwegian Nynorsk), på (Norwegian Nynorsk “on”), see upon (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Norse ón, án (Old Norse “without”), from Proto-Germanic *ēnu, *ēno (Proto-Germanic), *ino (Proto-Germanic “without”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḗnu (“without”). Cognate with on (North Frisian “without”), an (Middle Dutch), on (Middle Dutch “without”), āne (Middle Low German “without”), ohne (German “without”), 𐌹𐌽𐌿 (Gothic “without, except”).

Unlikely to be related to ἄνευ (Ancient Greek “without”), which is likely akin to *sundraz (Proto-Germanic) instead (whence sunder (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Japanese 音読み.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English ones, from Old English ānes, a remodelling (after ān (Old English “one”)) of ǣnes (Old English), itself an extension of ǣne (Middle English “once”) with the genitive suffix -es (Old English). Equivalent to . Cognate with enst (Saterland Frisian), insen (Saterland Frisian “once”), iens (Western Frisian “once”), eens (Dutch “once”), eens (Low German (Germany)), ins (Low German (Germany) “once”), einst (German “once”). More at one (English) (including regarding the development of the pronunciation) and -s.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English oon, on (Middle English), oan (Middle English), an (Middle English), from Old English ān (“one”), from Proto-West Germanic *ain, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“single, one”). .

Cognate with ae (Scots), ane (Scots), wan (Scots), yin (Scots “one”); ån (North Frisian “one”); aan (Saterland Frisian “one”); ien (Western Frisian “one”); een (Dutch), één (Dutch “one”); een (Low German (Germany)); ein (German), eins (German “one”); en (Danish “one”); en (Swedish “one”); ein (Norwegian Nynorsk “one”), einn (Icelandic “one”); ūnus (Latin “one”) (oinos (itc-ola)); оди́н (Russian), uno (Spanish). , ஒன்னு (Tamil), ஒண்ணு (Tamil), ஒன்று (Tamil).

The use as an indefinite personal pronoun may have been influenced by unrelated on (French), although the Germanic languages widely use cognates for the same sense (usually in non-subject function, but also in subject function, e.g. een (lb)).

Verb form from Middle English onen.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Analogous to several senses of and . This semantic loan might have stemmed from the apparent similarity between one as a prop-word and 的 (Mandarin Chinese) or 個 (Hokkien) as a nominalizer (e.g. 青色的 (Hokkien “the green one”)). Compare 嘅 (Cantonese).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English oonly, only (Middle English), from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (Old English “only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz. Cognate with obsolete eenlijk (Dutch), ähnlich (German “similar”), álíkr (Old Norse), enlig (Swedish “unified”). .
* Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one (English).

* eepen (Saterland Frisian “open”)
* iepen (Western Frisian “open”)

* open (Dutch “open”)

Verb from Middle English openen, from Old English openian (“to open”), from Proto-West Germanic *opanōn, from Proto-Germanic *upanōną (“to raise; lift; open”), from Proto-Germanic *upanaz (“open”). Related to up (English).

Noun from Middle English open (“an aperture or opening”), from the verb. In the sports sense, however, a shortening of “open competition”.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English panne, from Old English panne, from Proto-West Germanic *pannā, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ. Further origin uncertain.

Alois Walde firstly suggests that it might be from Late Latin panna, from Latin patina (“broad, shallow dish, pan, stewpan”), from Ancient Greek πατάνη (“kind of flat dish”), which is probably from qsb-grc —. But the sound shifting from /patina/ → /patna/ → /panna/ raises questions as -tn- to -nn- is rarely seen in Latin.

The mainstream theory as of now (Friedrich Kluge, Julius Pokorny, Guus Kroonen) suggests that it is from Late Latin panna. But its sparse attestation only in the frontier inscriptions and not widespread in most Romance languages raises doubts among a few scholars (notably Michiel de Vaan), being skeptical about its origin, and open for any interpretations (Oxford English Dictionary).

Vladmir Orel, in his work Albanian Etymological Dictionary, suggests that both Proto-Germanic *pannǭ and Late Latin panna could be from a non-IE Mediterranean qfa-sub — word, considering that classical Latin attestations are scarce and distributed in a specific region, and Proto-Germanic loanwords from non-IE substrates often include agricultural terms, seafaring vocabulary, or animal names. Although, this substrate hypothesis is controversial and most scholars remain skeptical about it.

In either case of relationship to the Latin, the English word is a ; see there for more doublets and further detail.

Cognate with panne (Western Frisian), Ponne (Saterland Frisian), pan (Dutch), Panne (Low German (Germany)), Pann (Low German (Germany)), Pfanne (German), pande (Danish), panna (Swedish), panna (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English pancake, panne cake (Middle English), pankake (Middle English), ponkake (Middle English). .

Perhaps adapted from Middle Low German pankôke, pannekôke (Middle Low German), from Old Saxon *pannakōko (suggested by derivatives pannakōkilo (Old Saxon) and pannakōkilīn (Old Saxon)), where the compound is much older; compare phankuohho (Old High German) (8th century), whence phankuoche (Middle High German), Pfannkuchen (German “pancake”); further
Ponkouke (Saterland Frisian), Ponkuuke (Saterland Frisian “pancake”), pankoek (Western Frisian “pancake”), pannenkoek (Dutch “pancake”), Pannkook (Low German (Germany) “pancake”).
The juggling sense is by analogy with a pancake being tossed in a pan.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The adjective is borrowed from Middle French panique, a word itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πανικός (“pertaining to Pan”); Pan, the Greek god of fields and woods, was believed to be the source of mysterious sounds that caused contagious, groundless fear in herds and crowds, or in people in lonely spots.

Adjective sense 3 (“pertaining to or resulting from overpowering fear or fright”) is partly an attributive use of the noun.

The noun is derived from the adjective, while the verb is derived from the noun. Verb sense 1.3 (“to highly amuse, entertain, or impress (an audience watching a performance or show”) is derived from noun sense 4 (“a highly amusing or entertaining performer, performance, or show”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested in 1525. From , either a diminutive of Pierre (Middle French) or a shortened form of perroquet (Middle French) (whence also parakeet (English)). Compare pierrot (French) and parrat (Occitan). A number of origins have been suggested for perroquet (French), such as Spanish periquito (Spanish) and Italian parrocchetto (Italian). The relationship between these various words is disputed. Replaced earlier popinjay (English).

Akin to portiō (Latin “a portion, part”), parō (Latin “parāre”). , dele (Middle English “part”) (from dǣl (Old English “part, distribution”) > Modern English deal (English “portion; amount”)), dale (Middle English), dole (Middle English “part, portion”) (from dāl (Old English “portion”) > Modern English dole (English)), sliver (Middle English “part, portion”) (from sliven (Middle English “to cut, cleave”), from tōslifan (Old English “(tō)slifan”)).
