From Middle English path, peth (Middle English), from Old English pæþ (“path, track”), from Proto-West Germanic *paþ, from Proto-Germanic *paþaz (“path”). The Proto-Germanic term is possibly borrowed from ira —, from Proto-Iranian *pántaHs, from iir-pro *pántaHs, from Proto-Indo-European *póntoh₁s, from the root *pent- (Proto-Indo-European “to pass”), but this is disputed.

Cognate with Paad (Saterland Frisian), Pad (Saterland Frisian “path”), paad (Western Frisian “path”), pad (Dutch “path”), Pfad (German “path”), Padd (Low German (Germany) “path”), Pad (lb “path”). Indo-Iranian cognates could be 𐬞𐬀𐬧‎𐬙𐬃 (ae “way”), 𐎱𐎰 (peo), पथ (Hindi), पन्था (Sanskrit “path”). See also find (English). .

etymologies.text: From . Cognate to for, sweet.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: pessimist + -ic

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: pharmacy + -ist

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pharmacy, borrowed from Middle French pharmacie (“the art of creating drugs; a drug, especially a laxative”), from Old French farmacie, from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (“the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (Ancient Greek “a drug, charm, enchantment”), of uncertain but likely qsb-grc — origin. Attested since late 14th century.

chain.meaning: the art of creating drugs; a drug, especially a laxative

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compare phantasm (English) and see face (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Latin phase (“passover”), Phasa (Latin), from Hebrew פָּסַח.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English philosophre, from Anglo-Norman — or Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος + -er (English).

Credited as having been coined by to describe himself.

Displaced native ūþwita (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English philosophie, from Old French philosophie, from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία, from φίλος (Ancient Greek “loving”) + σοφία (Ancient Greek “wisdom”). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: photo- + copy

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From photo + graph (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (“manner of expression”), from φράζω (Ancient Greek “to tell, express”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Latin physicālis, from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική, feminine singular of φυσικός (Ancient Greek “natural; physical”), from φύσις (Ancient Greek “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (Ancient Greek “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From physic + -ally (English) or physical + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English piken, picken (Middle English), pikken (Middle English), from Old English *piccian, *pīcian (Old English) (attested in pīcung (Old English “a pricking”)), and pīcan (Old English), pȳcan (Old English “to pick, prick, pluck”), both from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick, knock”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (Proto-Indo-European “to make a dull, hollow sound”). .

Cognate with pikken (Dutch “to pick”), picken (German “to pick, peck”), pikka (Old Norse), pjakka (Old Norse) (whence pikka (Icelandic “to pick, prick”), picka (Swedish “to pick, peck”)). Compare also puken (Low German (Germany) “to pick out, rip out, pull away, extract”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English picture, from Latin pictūra (“the art of painting, a painting”), from pingō (Latin “to paint”). .

chain.meaning: the art of painting, a painting

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , a French pittoresque, from picture (French “a picture, painting”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pye, pie (Middle English), pey (Middle English “baked dish, filled pastry”), possibly attested earlier () in the surname Piehus (Middle English “pie-house?”). Further origin .

Relation to pie (Middle English), pye (Middle English “magpie”) has been suggested due to correspondences between other similar foods and the names of birds (compare haggis (English “Scottish dish”) and haggess (English “magpie”); and chewet (English “meat pie”) and chewet (English “chough, jackdaw”); however, the baked dish may instead be named after a creator with the surname Pie, a common name at the time.

The surname is ultimately derived from the bird above, and thus from Old French pie, from Latin pīca (“magpie”). If true, then .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English pye, from Old French pie, from Latin pīca, feminine of pīcus (Latin “woodpecker”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Hindi पाई (“low-denomination coin”), from Sanskrit पादिका (“foot, shoe”), from पाद (Sanskrit “foot, base, quarter”) + -इक (Sanskrit “-ic: forming adjectives”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Hindi पाहि (“migrant farmer, passer-through”), from Sanskrit पार्श्व (“side, vicinity”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From Spanish pie (“foot, Spanish foot”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pece, peece (Middle English), peice (Middle English), from Old French piece, from Late Latin pettia (“pecia”), pettia (Latin “broken piece, fragment; parcel of land”), of origin. Possibly ultimately from Gaulish *pettyā, from Proto-Celtic *kʷezdis (“piece, portion, quota”). Compare peth (Welsh “thing, stuff, junk”), pez (Breton “thing”), cuid (Irish “part, portion”). Compare pièce (French), peça (Portuguese), pieza (Spanish), pezza (Italian), pezzo (Italian). Displaced native sticche (Middle English), stucche (Middle English “piece, fragment”) from styċċe (Old English “piece, portion”), whence also styca (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English pyle, from Old French pile, from Latin pīla#pillar-pier-Latin (“pillar, pier”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English pile, from Old English pīl, from Proto-West Germanic *pīl, from Latin pīlum (“heavy javelin”). Cognate with pijl (Dutch), Pfeil (German). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Apparently from Late Latin pilus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English pile, partly from Anglo-Norman pil (a variant of peil (Old French), poil (Old French “hair”)) and partly from its source, Latin pilus (“hair”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From French pile (“battery”), with the pronunciation adapted to the existing English word . , which may have influenced the sense development by emphasizing the stack (“pile”) out of which early batteries were made.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pille (also pillem (Middle English)), a borrowing from Middle Low German pille or Middle Dutch pille (whence pil (Dutch)), probably from Latin pila, pilula (Latin).
* Generalized from red pill (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English pillen, pilen (Middle English), from Old English pilian (“to peel”), from Latin pilō (“depilate”), from pilus (Latin “hair”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English *pill, *pyll (Middle English), from Old English pyll (“a pool, pill”), from Proto-Germanic *pullijaz (“small pool, ditch, creek”), diminutive of Proto-Germanic *pullaz (“pool, stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *bl̥nos (“bog, marsh”). Cognate with pull (Old English “pool, creek”), poll (Scots “slow moving stream, creek, inlet”), pollur (Icelandic “pond, pool, puddle”). More at pool (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pinne, from Old English pinn (“pin, peg, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *pinnaz, *pinnō (Proto-Germanic), *pint- (Proto-Germanic “protruding point, peak, peg, pin, nail”), from Proto-Indo-European *bend- (“protruding object, pointed peg, nail, edge”). Related to pen (English “enclosure”).

Cognate with pin (Dutch “peg, pin”), pin (Low German), pinne (Low German “pin, point, nail, peg”), Pinn (German), Pinne (German “pin, tack, peg”), Pfonzer (Bavarian), Pfunzer (Bavarian “sharpened point”), pind (Danish “pin, pointed stick”), pinn (Norwegian “stick”), pinne (Swedish “peg, rod, stick”), pinni (Icelandic “pin”). More at pintle.

No relation to classical pinna (Latin “fin, flipper, wing-like appendage, wing, feather”), which was extended to mean "ridge, peak, point" (compare pinnacle), and often confused with penna (Latin “wing, feather”). More at feather and pen (Etymology 3).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|a Turkish pine Turkish pine () (1)
From Middle English pyne, from Old English *pīne, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā, from Latin pīnus, see there for more. . Possibly related to fat (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pyne, pine (Middle English), probably from Old English *pīne (“pain”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā (“pain, torment, torture”), possibly from Latin poena (“punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (“penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate to pain (English).

Entered Germanic with Christianity; cognate to pinen (Middle Dutch), pīnōn (Old High German), pína (Old Norse).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English pynen, from Old English pīnian (“to torment”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā (“pain, torment, torture”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with peinigen (German “to torment, torture”), pine (Danish “to torment, torture”), pína (Icelandic “to torment”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
thumb|A pineapple with a slice
thumb|100px|A pineapple-style hand grenade
From Middle English pinappel (“pinecone”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīnapplu. Later applied to the fruit of the pineapple plant due to its resemblance to a pinecone. Compare the - (Middle Dutch) and pijnappel (Dutch “pinecone", formerly also "pineapple”), pynappel (Afrikaans “pineapple”), pinappel (Middle Low German), pīnapful (Old High German), pīnaphel (Middle High German), and early Modern pinapfel (German) — all in the sense of “pine cone”. Compare also the post-Classical pomum pini (Latin), the pume de pin (Old French), the - (Middle French) and pomme de pin (French) and piña (Spanish). .

Sense "An Australian fifty dollar note": From the yellow colour of a $50 banknote in the first, second, and third series of rice Australian dollar notes. Compare with lobster for a $20 Australian banknote, and watermelon for a $100 Australian banknote.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pinte, from Old French pinte, assumed from Vulgar Latin *pincta (“a mark used to indicate a level of quantity against a larger measure”), from Latin picta (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pipe (“pīpe”), pype (Middle English “hollow cylinder or tube used as a conduit or container; duct or vessel of the body; musical instrument; financial records maintained by the English Exchequer, pipe roll”), from Old English pīpe (“pipe (musical instrument); the channel of a small stream”), from Proto-West Germanic *pīpā. Reinforced by Vulgar Latin *pīpa, from Latin pipire, pipiare (Latin), pipare (Latin), from pīpiō (Latin “to chirp, peep”), of origin. Displaced native fealh (Old English) and þrūh (Old English). .

Cognate with pijp (Dutch), Pfeife (German), pibe (Danish), pipe (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), pipa (Swedish), pípa (Faroese / Icelandic).

The “storage container” and “liquid measure” senses are derived from Middle English pipe (“pīpe”), from pīpe (above) and Old French pipe (“liquid measure”). In specific contexts, calques similar units of measure such as Portuguese pipa.

The verb is from Middle English pipen (“pīpen”), pypyn (Middle English “to play a pipe; to make a shrill sound; to speak with a high-pitched tone”), from Old English pīpian (“to pipe”).

chain.meaning: pipe (musical instrument); the channel of a small stream

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pirate, pirat (Middle English), pyrat (Middle English), from Old French pirate, from Latin pīrāta (“pirate”), from Ancient Greek πειρατής, from πεῖρα (Ancient Greek “trial, attempt, plot”). Displaced native wīċing (Old English), which was the word for both "pirate" and "viking".

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English picche, piche (Middle English), pich (Middle English), from Old English piċ, from Proto-West Germanic *pik, from Latin pix. Cognate with πίσσα (Ancient Greek “pitch, tar”), pīnus (Latin “pine”). More at pine (English). Cognate with Pik (Saterland Frisian “pitch, tar”), pek (Dutch “pitch, tar”), Pick (Low German (Germany) “pitch, tar”), Pech (German “pitch, tar”), pega (Catalan “pitch”), pegar (Spanish “to stick, glue”), pouatche (frp “sap from a pine”) and poix (French “sap”). The adjective is probably back-formed from pitch-black (English), reinterpreting "pitch" as meaning "intense(ly)".

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English picchen, pycchen (Middle English “to thrust in, fasten, settle”), from Old English *piċċan, from Proto-West Germanic *pikkijan, a variant of *pikkōn (Proto-West Germanic “to pick, peck”), whence pikken (Middle English), picken (Middle English “to pick, pierce”), modern pick (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: . Perhaps from the above sense of "inclination", "level", or "degree", or influenced by it.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pitye, pitie (Middle English), pittye (Middle English), pitee (Middle English), pite (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman pité, pittee (Old French) etc., from Old French pitet, pitié (Old French), from Latin pietās. See also the doublets .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English place, conflation of Old English plæċe (“place, an open space, street”) and Old French place (“place, an open space”), both from Latin platēa (“plaza, wide street”), from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα, shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (Ancient Greek “broad way”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“to spread”), extended form of *pleh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “flat”). Displaced native stōw (Old English), stede (Old English) (partially), and -ern (Old English). Compare also pleck (English “plot of ground”), plak (Western Frisian “place, spot, location”), plek (Dutch “place, spot, patch”). .

In the etymological chain from platēa (Latin), note place (Old French), which has multiple descendants — including Platz (German), itself with many descendants (e.g., плац (Russian)). Also note a more distant chain node πλατύς (Ancient Greek), whence Plato (English) and plate (English) (via Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English placen, from the noun (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman pleyn, playn (Old French), Middle French plain, plein (Middle French), and Old French plain, from Latin plānus (“flat, even, level, plain”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Old French plain, from Latin plānum (“level ground, a plain”), neuter substantive from plānus (Latin “level, even, flat”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Anglo-Norman plainer, pleiner (Old French), variant of - (Anglo-Norman) and Old French pleindre, plaindre (Old French), from Latin plangō (“plangere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Old French plein, from Latin plēnus (“full, filled, complete”). Ultimately from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: French plan (“flat surface, ground plot, map”), from Latin plānus. Some sources also argue for influence or alteration of French plant, from plantar (French), from Latin plantāre (“set, fix in place”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English planete, from Old French planete, from Latin planeta, planetes (Latin), from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (“wanderer”) (itself an ), from Ancient Greek πλανάω (“wander about, stray”), of unknown origin. Cognate with pālor (Latin “wander about, stray”), flana (Old Norse “to rush about”), and flanta (Norwegian “to wander about”). More at flaunt (English). So called because they have apparent motion, unlike the "fixed" stars. Originally including also the moon and sun but not the Earth; modern scientific sense of "world that orbits a star" is from 1630s in English. The Greek word is an enlarged form of πλάνης (Ancient Greek “who wanders around, wanderer”), also "wandering star, planet", in medicine "unstable temperature." Displaced native tungol (Old English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English planete, from Old French planete, from Latin planeta, planetes (Latin), from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (“wanderer”) (itself an ), from Ancient Greek πλανάω (“wander about, stray”), of unknown origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English plante, from Old English plante (“young tree or shrub, herb newly planted”), from Proto-West Germanic *plantu, from Latin planta (“sprout, shoot, cutting”). Broader sense of "any vegetable life, vegetation generally" is from plante (Old French). (borrowed through Celtic languages) and (directly from Latin).

The verb is from Middle English planten, from Old English plantian (“to plant”), from Latin plantō (“plantāre”), later influenced by planter (Old French). Compare also planten (Dutch “to plant”), pflanzen (German “to plant”), plantera (Swedish “to plant”), planta (Icelandic “to plant”).

The factory and machinery senses comes from the Latin sense of "any vegetable production that serves to propagate the species," which refers to something that produces.

chain.meaning: young tree or shrub, herb newly planted

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French plateforme (“a flat form”), from plate (Middle French “flat”) (from Old French plat, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (“flat”)) + forme (Middle French “form”) (from Latin forma (“fōrma”)); compare flatscape (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pleyen and Middle English pleye, from Old English plegian and plegan (Old English), plagian (Old English “to play, exercise, etc.”), from Proto-West Germanic *plehan (“to care about, be concerned with”) and Proto-West Germanic *plegōn (“to engage, move”), of uncertain origin.

Cognate with play (Scots “to act or move briskly, cause to move, stir”), pleegje (Saterland Frisian “to look after, care for, maintain”), pleegje (Western Frisian), pliigje (Western Frisian “to commit, perform, bedrive”), pleyen (Middle Dutch) , plegen (Dutch “to commit, bedrive, practice”), pflegen (German “to care for, be concerned with, attend to, tend”). Related also to plēon (Old English “to risk, endanger”). More at plight (English), pledge (English).

The noun is from Middle English pleye, from Old English plæġ, plega (Old English), plæġa (Old English “play, quick motion, movement, exercise; (athletic) sport, game; festivity, drama; battle; gear for games, an implement for a game; clapping with the hands, applause”), deverbative of plegian (Old English “to play”); see above.
etymologies.uncertainNote: ”), from Proto-West Germanic *plehan (“to care about, be concerned with”) and Proto-West Germanic *plegōn (“to engage, move”), of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pleasauntly; equivalent to pleasant + ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English plesen, plaisen (Middle English), borrowed from Old French plaise, conjugated form of plaisir (Old French) or plaire (Old French), from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleHk- (“pleasingness, permission”). In this sense, displaced native līcian (Old English), whence like (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Short for if you please (English), an intransitive, ergative form taken from which is a French s'il vous plaît, which replaced pray. If it please you is a present subjunctive form, but most current uses of please are not parsed that way.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: German bitte (“please; excuse me”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Early Modern English pleasur (English), plesur (English), alteration (with ending accommodated to -ure) of Middle English plaisir (“pleasure”), from Old French plesir, plaisir (Old French “to please”), infinitive used as a noun, conjugated form of plaisir (Old French) or plaire (Old French), from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-k- (“wide and flat”). Related to plezier (Dutch “pleasure, fun”). More at please (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from Middle English plentie, plentee (Middle English), plente (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman plenté, from Old French plenté, from Latin plēnitātem, accusative of plēnitās (Latin “fullness”), from plenus (Latin “complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”), from which English full (English) also comes, via Proto-Germanic. Related to the Latin derivatives replenish (English), plenary (English), complete (English), deplete (English), replete (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English plot, plotte (Middle English), from late Old English plot (“a plot of ground”), of origin. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *plataz, *platjaz (Proto-Germanic “a patch”); or alternatively, perhaps from a rebracketing of landsplott (Old English “small portion, or plot, of ground”) taken as . Compare plet (Middle Low German “patch, strip of cloth, rags”), Bletz (German “rags, bits, strip of land”), and possibly 𐍀𐌻𐌰𐍄 (Gothic “a patch, rags”). See also plat (English). See also complot (English) for an influence and reinforcement of .

is a .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Dutch plug, from Middle Dutch plugge (“peg, plug”), from Old Dutch *pluggi, from Proto-West Germanic *plugi. Further origin . Possibly from Proto-Germanic *plugjaz, but the word seems originally restricted to northern continental West Germanic. Perhaps ultimately from the same source as plag (Dutch “cut-out sod”), itself considered to be from a substrate.

Compare Plüg (Low German (Germany)), plug (Norwegian “peg, wedge”), Pflock (German “peg”). Possibly akin to plúkti (Lithuanian “to strike, hew”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English plumber, from Old French plummier (French plombier (French)); from Latin plumbārius, from plumbum (Latin “lead or lead shot”).

The verb sense “to botch” is perhaps from the negative stereotype of the occupation.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin plūs (“more”)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pocket (“bag, sack”), from Anglo-Norman fro (“poket”), Old Northern French poquet, poquete (Old French), diminutive of poque (Old French), poke (Old French “bag, sack”) (compare modern Norman pouquette (Norwegian) and modern French pochette (French) from Old French pochete (Old French), from puche (Old French)), from Frankish *pokō (“pouch”), from Proto-Germanic *puhô (“bag; pouch”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). Equivalent to . . Cognate with poke (Middle Dutch), Pfoch (Alemannic “purse, bag”), pocca (Old English), pohha (Old English “poke, pouch, pocket, bag”), poki (Old Norse “bag, pocket”). Compare the related poke (English “sack or bag”). See also Modern pochette (French) and bucca (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French poème, from Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα, from ποιέω (Ancient Greek “to make”). Widely .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English poete, from Old French poete, from Latin poēta (“poet, author”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (“creator, maker, author, poet”), from ποιέω (Ancient Greek “to make, compose”). Displaced native sċop (Old English) and lēoþwyrhta (Old English) (literally, "leedwright" or "poem-writer"). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English poetrye, poetrie (Middle English), a borrowing from Old French pöeterie, pöetrie (Old French), from Medieval Latin poētria, from poēta (Latin “poet”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (“poet; author; maker”). Displaced native lēoþcræft (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English poynt, from Old French point (“dot; minute amount”), from Latin pūnctum (“a hole punched in; a point, puncture”), substantive use of pūnctus (Latin), perfect passive participle of pungō (Latin “to prick, punch”); alternatively, from Old French pointe (“sharp tip”), from Latin pūnctus (“pūncta”), all from Proto-Italic *pungō (“to sting, prick”).

Mostly displaced native ord (Middle English “point”), from ord (Old English “point”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English pointen, poynten (Middle English), from Old French pointier, pointer (Old French), poynter (Old French), from point (Old French) from Latin pūnctum.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English pointen, poynten (Middle English), by apheresis of apointen (Middle English), appointen (Middle English), appoynten (Middle English). See appoint (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English poysoun, poyson (Middle English), pusoun (Middle English), from Old French poison, poisun (Old French), from Latin pōtio (“drink, a draught, a poisonous draught, a potion”), from pōtō (Latin “to drink”). See also potion (English) and potable (English) (from the same root). Mostly displaced native ātor (Old English) and lybb (Old English). See more at atter (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English poisounous, poysonouse (Middle English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English policie, from Old French policie, pollicie (Old French) and police (Old French), from Late Latin — politia (Latin “citizenship; government”), classical Latin polītīa (in Cicero), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (“citizenship; polis, (city) state; government”), from πολίτης (Ancient Greek “citizen”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle French police, from Italian polizza, from Medieval Latin — apodissa (Latin “receipt for money”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (“proof, declaration”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: polite + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: polite + -ness

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: politic + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: politic + -ian

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: By analogy with Aristotle’s τά πολῑτῐκᾱ́ (Ancient Greek “affairs of state”), a plural noun phrase.

etymologies.label: Etymology

1. From French poule (“collective stakes in a game”). The French word "poule" in this context is an abbreviation of "poulain, pouliche" (foal, filly), and referred to races with female horses under 3 years old. It then became used by punters to designate bets on that race, and started to be used from the racetrack to the stadiums.

2. The OED suggests that this may be a transferred use of poule (French “hen”), which has been explained anecdotally as deriving from an old informal betting game in France - 'jeu de poule' - Game of Chicken (or Hen, literally) in which poule became synonymous with the combined money pot claimed by the winner.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
.

Most likely derived from Romani posh (“half”), either because (originally a substantial sum of money) was used metaphorically for anything pricey or upper-class, or because came to refer to money generally.

A period slang dictionary defines "posh" as a term used by thieves for "money : generic, but specifically, a halfpenny or other small coin". An example is given from James Payn's The Eavesdropper (1888): "They used such funny terms: 'brads,' and 'dibbs,' and 'mopusses,' and 'posh' ... at last it was borne in upon me that they were talking about money."

Evidence exists for a slang sense from the 1890s meaning dandy#Noun (English “dandy”), which is quite possibly related.

A popular folk etymology holds that the term is an acronym for "port out, starboard home", describing the cooler, north-facing cabins taken by the most aristocratic or rich passengers travelling from Britain to India and back. However, there is no evidence for this claim.

It could also possibly be a polished.

See also the articles mentioned in the References section below for additional discussion.

etymologies.text:
From Middle English pot, potte (Middle English), from Old English pott (“pot”) and Old French pot (“pot”) (probably from Frankish *pott); both Old English and Frankish from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar; tub”), of unknown origin.

Cognate with Pot (Saterland Frisian “pot”), pot (Dutch “pot”), Pott (Low German (Germany) “pot”), Pott (German “pot”), potta (Swedish “chamber pot”), pottur (Icelandic “tub, pot”) (from pottr (Old Norse “pot, tub, basin”)), and perhaps պույտ (Armenian “pot”) (from պոյտն (Classical Armenian “pot, earthen pot”)) and bocë (Albanian “bottle, decanter”), related either via late Proto-Indo-European — or as a '. pot (Middle English) gave rise to pota (Irish), poit (Scottish Gaelic) and pot (Welsh) through . Further cognates in languages are via pottus//pōtus (Late Latin), pottum (Latin), which either was borrowed from the Germanic word or, less likely, is its source; see more on the Proto-Germanic entry.

The sense of or was originally a general allusion to “being chopped up and tossed in a (normally fiery) pot, like a piece of meat” (i.e. “to get wasted or done with (by someone)”). The slang term which was used in reference to toilet rooms and lavatories apparently derives from English chamberpots, although now usually encountered as potty (English) in the context of children's toilet training.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
First attested early 1400s as various Middle English — forms prayne (Middle English), prane (Middle English), praune (Middle English), and prawne (Middle English), which present no clear cognates in languages other than English. The forms suggest a hypothetical Old English — form *prægn, where *æg would have evolved into Middle English *ay, but it is unclear if the word is of Germanic origin, from another European language, or loaned from a qfa-sub —. In the Isle of Wight, a word prankle ("prawn") is recorded and thought to be related. Century, following Skeat, suggested transposition of an unrecorded Old French *parne, *perne related to perna (Spanish “a flat shellfish”), Old Italian perna and diminutive pernochie, parnocchie, glossed as "shrimps or prawne, fishes" by John Florio, but the OED considers Florio's entry incorrect and the suggested connection semantically and phonologically implausible.

("woman with attractive body and unattractive face") is from the idea of discarding the head of a prawn before eating it.

etymologies.text: From Old French president, from Latin praesidēns (“presiding over; president, leader”) (accusative: praesidentem (Latin)). The Latin word is the substantivized present active participle of the verb praesideō (Latin “preside over”). The verb is composed from prae (Latin “before”) and sedeō (Latin “sit”). The original meaning of the verb is 'to sit before' in the sense of presiding at a meeting. A secondary meaning of the verb is 'to command, to govern'. etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English pryde, pride (Middle English), from Old English prȳde, prȳte (Old English “pride”) (compare prýði (Old Norse “bravery, pomp”)), derivative of Old English prūd (Old English “proud”). More at proud (English). The verb derives from the noun, at least since the 12th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English pryde, from Middle Low German lampride, from Medieval Latin lampreda.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English prest, preest (Middle English), from Old English preost (“prēost”), from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος, from πρέσβυς (Ancient Greek “elder, older”). Reinforced in Middle English by Old French prestre, also from Latin presbyter (Latin). .

* The uses native elder (English) instead.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: primary + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin prīmārius (“of the first (rank); chief, principal; excellent”), from prīmus (Latin) (first; whence the - (English) adjective prime (English)) + -ārius (Latin) (whence the - (English) suffix -ary (English)); compare the primaire (French), primer (French), and premier (French). .

chain.meaning: of the first (rank); chief, principal; excellent

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English prince, from Anglo-Norman prince, from Latin prī̆nceps (“first, foremost (person)”), from prīmus + capiō (Latin). Cognate with fruma (Old English “prince, ruler”). .

, from atheling (Middle English “Middle English”), from æþeling (Old English “prince”). Displaced also kinebarn (Middle English) (from cynebearn (Old English), , i.e. “royal child”), alder (Middle English) < ealdor (Old English “elder, leader, chief, prince, king”), and drighten (Middle English) < dryhten (Old English “lord”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English princesse, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman princesse, Old French princesse. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English principal, from Old French principal, from Latin prīncipālis.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English *printen, prenten (Middle English), preenten (Middle English), an apheretic form of emprinten (Middle English), enprinten (Middle English “to impress; imprint”) (see imprint (English)). Compare prenten (Dutch “to imprint”), prenten (Middle Low German “to print; write”), prente (Danish “to print”), prenta (Swedish “to write German letters”). Compare also Late printer (Old French), preindre (Old French “to press”), from premere (Latin “to press”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old French priorite, from Latin priōritās.

Surface analysis: prior + ity (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English prisoun, prison (Middle English), from Old English prisūn, a borrowing from Old French prison, from Latin prehensiōnem, accusative singular of prehensiō (Latin), from the verb prehendō (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English prisoner, from Old French prisonier (compare prisōnārius (Medieval Latin)), equivalent to prison + -er (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: private + -acy

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English privat (“individual, exclusive, private”), from Latin prīvātus (“bereaved, deprived, set apart from, release”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (Latin “to bereave, deprive, release”) (see -ate for more), from prīvus (Latin “private, one's own, proper”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per; compare prime (English), prior (English), pristine (English). .

chain.meaning: bereaved, deprived, set apart from, release

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: private + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English probable, from Old French probable, from Latin probābilis (“that may be proved, credible”), from probāre (Latin “to test, examine”); see probe (English), probity (English), prove (English). Compare recent doublet provable (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French procédure, from Old French —, from Latin procedo (“procedere”); see proceed.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English proces, from Old French procés (“journey”), from Latin prōcessus (“course, progression”), nominalization of prōcēdō (Latin “proceed, advance”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English produce, from Latin prōdūcō (“to lead forth”), from prō- (Latin “forth, forward”) + dūcō (Latin “to lead, bring”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: produce + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English product, from Latin prōductus, perfect participle of prōdūcō (Latin), first attested in English in the mathematics sense.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English produccioun, from Old French production, from Latin productio (“prōductiō, prōductiōnem”). Equivalent to . See produce (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Latin productivus, equivalent to product + -ive (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English professioun, from Anglo-Norman professioun, Old French profession (“declaration of faith, religious vows, occupation”), from Latin professiō (“avowal, public declaration”), from the participle stem of profitērī (Latin “to profess”). .

chain.meaning: declaration of faith, religious vows, occupation

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English professhennalle, professhynalle (Middle English); equivalent to profession + al (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English professor,professour, from Anglo-Norman proffessur and its etymon Latin professor (“declarer, person who claims knowledge”), from the past participle stem of profiteor (Latin “profess”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French profil, from Italian profilo (“a border”), later also proffilo (Italian “a side-face, profile”), from Latin pro (“before”) + filo (Italian “a line, stroke, thread”), from filum (Latin “a thread”); see file (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English profit, from Old French profit (Modern profit (French)), from Latin prōfectus (“advance, progress, growth, increase, profit”), from proficiō (Latin “to go forward, advance, make progress, be profitable or useful”). .

chain.meaning: to go forward, advance, make progress, be profitable or useful

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French profitable, equivalent to profit + -able (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From program//programme + ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English progresse, from Old French progres (“a going forward”), from Latin prōgressus (“an advance”), from the participle stem of prōgredī (Latin “to go forward, advance, develop”), from pro- + gradior (Latin). Displaced native forþgang (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the noun. Lapsed into disuse in the 17th century, except in the US. Considered an Americanism on reintroduction to use in the UK.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the , from the , from prōgredior + -īvus (Latin). Displaced native forþgenġe (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English prohibiten, from Latin prohibeō (“to fend off, prevent, prohibit”) (through past participle prohibitus (Latin)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (Latin “throw forth, extend; expel”).

Compare typologically прики́дывать (Russian), прики́дка (Russian) (akin to кида́ть (Russian)); набро́сок (Russian) (akin to броса́ть (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English promis (“promis, promisse”), borrowed from Old French promesse, from Medieval Latin prōmissa, Latin prōmissum (“a promise”), feminine and neuter past participles of prōmittō (Latin “to send forth, to say beforehand, to promise”), from pro (Latin “forth”) + mittere (Latin “to send”); see mission (English). Compare admit (English), commit (English), permit (English), etc. Displaced native ġehātan (Old English “to promise”) and ġehāt (Old English “a promise”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin prōmōtus, perfect passive participle of prōmoveō (Latin “move forward, advance”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Late Middle English —, from Old French promocion, from Late Latin prōmotiō, from Latin prōmoveō (“to move forward”). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The adjective is from Middle English prompte, from Middle French prompt and its etymon Latin prōmptus (“visible, apparent, evident”), past participle of prōmō (Latin “to take or bring out or forth, produce, bring to light”), from prō (Latin “forth, forward”) + emō (Latin “to take, acquire, buy”). .

The verb is from Middle English prompen, apparently from the adjective. The noun is from the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: prompt + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From pro- + noun (English), modeled on Middle French pronom, from Latin pronomen, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ντωνῠμῐ́ᾱ.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Recorded since c.1330 as Middle English pronouncen (“to utter, declare officially”), from Old French prononcier, from Latin prōnūntiō, itself from pro (Latin “prō-”) + nūntiō (Latin “to announce”) from nūntius (Latin “messenger”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English pronunciacioun, from Middle French prononciation, pronunciation (Middle French), from Latin prōnūntiātiō, noun of action from perfect passive participle prōnūntiātus (Latin), from verb prōnūntiāre (Latin “proclaim”), from prō- (Latin “for”) + nūntiāre (Latin “announce”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English proof, from Old French prove, from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from Latin probō (“to prove”); see prove (English); compare also the doublet .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English propre, from Anglo-Norman proper, propre (Old French), Old French propre (French: propre (French)), from Latin proprius.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: proper + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English propertee, properte (Middle English), propirte (Middle English), proprete (Middle English), borrowed from Anglo-Norman — and Old French propreté, proprieté (Old French “propriety, fitness, property”), from Latin proprietās (“a peculiarity, one's peculiar nature or quality, right or fact of possession, property”), from proprius (Latin “special, particular, one's own”). Equivalent to proper + ty (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: propose + -al

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English proposen, from Anglo-Norman proposer, propos (Old French), Middle French proposer, propos (Middle French), from Latin propono (“prōpōnō, prōpōnere”), with conjugation altered based on poser (Old French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English prospecte, from Latin prōspectus (“view, sight, prospect; panorama”), from prōspiciō (Latin “to look forward”) + -tus (Latin), from pro (Latin “before, forward”) + speciō (Latin), spiciō (Latin “to look, to see”). . . is a Russian проспе́кт. The verb is from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested in English since 1530, from Latin prōtēctus (“covered, protected”), past participle of prōtegō (Latin “prōtegō, prōtegere”) from prō (Latin), prō- + tegō (Latin), see tegument (English). Largely displaced native Middle English shelden (Middle English), from Old English sċildan (Old English) (“to protect,” literally “to shield”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from Old French —, from stem of Late Latin prōtectiō (“a covering over”), from Latin prōtēctus, perfect passive participle of protego (Latin “prōtegere”). Displaced native ġesċildnes (Old English). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōtēctīvus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the Middle English — verb protesten (Middle English), from Old French protester, from Latin prōtestor (“prōtestārī”), from prō (Latin) + testor (Latin), from testis (Latin “witness”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English proud, prout (Middle English), prut (Middle English), from Old English prūd, prūt (Old English “proud, arrogant, haughty”) (compare prȳtung (Old English “pride”); prȳde (Old English), prȳte (Old English “pride”), see also deal (Old English)), probably from Old French prod, prut (Old French “brave, gallant”) (modern preux (French)), from Late Latin prode (“prōde”), derived from prosum (Latin “to be of value”); however, the Old English umlaut derivatives prȳte (and), prȳtian (Old English), etc. suggest the word may be older and possibly native. Compare prýði (Old Norse “ornament; gallantry, bravery”). See also pride (English).

Cognate with praud (Low German (Germany)), prúðr (Old Norse “gallant, brave, magnificent, stately, handsome, fine”) (prúður (Icelandic), Middle prudh (Swedish), prud (Danish)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English proutly, proudliche (Middle English), prudeliche (Middle English), prudliche (Middle English), prouteliche (Middle English), from Old English prūtlīċe, equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English proven, from Old English prōfian (“to esteem, regard as, evince, try, prove”) and Old French prover (“to prove”), both from Latin probō (“test, try, examine, approve, show to be good or fit, prove”), from probus (Latin “good, worthy, excellent”), from Proto-Indo-European *pro-bʰuH-s (“being in front, prominent”), from *pro- (Proto-Indo-European), *per- (Proto-Indo-European “toward”) + *bʰuH- (Proto-Indo-European “to be”). Displaced native sothen (Middle English “to prove”), from sōþian (Old English “to prove”). . More at for (English), be (English), soothe (English).

chain.meaning: to esteem, regard as, evince, try, prove

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Simple past form of proove (English), conjugated as a Germanic strong verb, on the pattern of choose (English) → chose (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English providen, from Latin prōvideō (“to foresee, act with foresight”). .

etymologies.text: Affix: psychology + -ical

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French psychologie, from Renaissance Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (“soul”) + -λογία (Ancient Greek “study of”), equivalent to psycho- + -logy (English). The Latin term is believed by some to have been coined in a lost treatise by Croatian humanist (1450–1524), but this is disputed by other scholars. It is , at which time it was apparently already current, and may be a Hellenization of the established expression dē animā (Latin “on the soul”) in titles.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The adjective and noun are derived from Late Middle English publik, publike (Middle English “(adjective) generally observable, public; relating to the general public or public affairs; (noun) a generally observable place or situation”), from Anglo-Norman public, publik (Anglo-Norman), publique (Anglo-Norman), Middle French public, publique (Middle French), and Old French public (“(adjective) generally observable, public; relating to the general public; official; (noun) community or its members collectively; nation, state; audience, spectators collectively”) (modern public (French), publique (French) (obsolete)); and from their etymon Latin pūblicus (“of or belonging to the community, people, or state; general, public”), an alteration of poplicus (Latin) (influenced by pūbēs (Latin “adult men; male population”)), from poplus (Latin “community; the people, public; nation, state”) (later populus (Latin); from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”); further origin uncertain, possibly from ett — or from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”)) + -icus (Latin). Related to people (English), populus (English) etc.

The Middle English word displaced native ceorlfolc (Old English) and folclic (Old English).

The verb is derived from the adjective.

etymologies.text: Russian па́блик and Ukrainian па́блік (“public webpage on a blog or on social media”), both borrowed from English public: see etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English publicacioun, from Old French publicacion, from Latin pūblicātiō. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French publicité, From Medieval Latin pūblicitātem, accusative singular of pūblicitās (Latin), from Latin pūblicus (“public, general”). Morphologically public + ity (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English publicen (by analogy with banish (English), finish (English)), from Old French publier, from Latin publicare (“to make public, show or tell to the people, make known, declare, also (and earlier) confiscate for public use”), from publicus (Latin “pertaining to the people, public”); see public (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: publish + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From circa 1305, Middle English podynge (“kind of sausage; meat-filled animal stomach”), puddynge (Middle English), from Old French boudin (“blood sausage, black pudding”), from Latin botellus (“sausage, small intestine”). .
* An alternative etymology assumes origin from Proto-Germanic *put-, *pud- (Proto-Germanic “to swell”) (compare dialectal pod (English “belly”), puduc (Old English “wen, sore”), puddig (Low German “swollen”), Westphalian Puddek (German “lump, pudding”), Puddewurst (German “black pudding”). More at pout (English).

chain.meaning: kind of sausage; meat-filled animal stomach

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Deverbal: pull over

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English pumpe, possibly from Middle Dutch pompe (“pipe, water conduit”) or Middle Low German pumpe (“pump”), probably ultimately .

Compare pompen (Dutch), pumpen (German), and pompe (Danish); also bomba (Spanish “pump”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: The etymology of the term is unclear and disputed. One possibility is that it comes from pomp (English “ornamentation”). Another is that it refers to the sound made by the foot moving inside the shoe when dancing. The Oxford English Dictionary claims that it appeared in the 16th century, and lists its origin as "". It has also been linked to the Dutch pampoesje, possibly borrowed from Javanese pampus, ultimately from Persian پاپوش, borrowed from Arabic بَابُوش.
etymologies.uncertainNote: The etymology of the term is unclear and disputed.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English punchen, partially from Old French ponchonner (“to punch”), from ponchon (Old French “pointed tool”), from Latin punctio, from punctus (Latin), perfect passive participle of pungo (Latin “pungō”); and partially from Middle English punchen (Middle English), a syncopated variant of punischen (Middle English) . Also influenced by Middle English punchon (Middle English) . Compare also bunchen (Middle English), bonchen (Middle English “to punch, deliver a blow, pound, beat”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shortened form of puncheon (English), from Middle English punchoun, from Old French ponchon (“pointed tool”), from Latin punctio, from punctus (Latin), perfect passive participle of pungō (Latin “to prick”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Hindi पाँच (“five”)/Urdu پانچ, because of the drink's original five ingredients (spirits, water, lemon juice, sugar, and spice), from Sanskrit पञ्च. ; related to Punjab (English) and Pompeii (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Punch (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: . Perhaps shortened from puncheon (English) (compare Punze,Punzen (German “cask; short fat person or thing”)) or Punchinello (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Medieval Latin punctuātiō (“a marking with points, a writing, agreement”), from punctuō (Latin “to mark with points, settle”). Morphologically, punctuate + ion (English). Coined in the French dialogue book Orthoepia Gallica, translated by John Eliot in 1593.

chain.meaning: a marking with points, a writing, agreement

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English punischen, from Anglo-Norman —, Old French — puniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of punir (Old French), from Latin puniō (“to inflict punishment upon”), from poena (Latin “punishment, penalty”); see pain (English). Displaced wītnian (Old English) and (mostly, in this sense) wrecan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English punishement, from Old French punissement, from punir (Old French “to punish”). Equivalent to punish + -ment (English). Displaced native wīte (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From earlier puppie (English “a woman's pet dog”), of origin, but probably from Middle English *puppee, *poupee (Middle English), from , popée (Old French “a doll; puppet”). More at puppet (English).

Mostly displaced native whelp (Middle English “puppy”), from hwelp (Old English), whence Modern whelp (English) and whelpie (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (Old French) (from Latin pro-) + chacier (Old French “chac(i)er”). Compare porchacier (Old French “to follow, to chase”), which has given pourchasser (French “to chase without relent”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English pure, pur (Middle English), from Old French pur, from Latin pūrus (“clean, free from dirt or filth, unmixed, plain”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“to cleanse, purify”). Displaced native lutter (Middle English “pure, clear, sincere”) (from hlūtor (Old English), hluttor (Old English)), skere (Middle English “pure, sheer, clear”) (from scǣre (Old English) and skǣr (Old Norse)), schir (Middle English “clear, pure”) (from scīr (Old English)), smete (Middle English “smete, smeate”) (from smǣte (Old English); compare mǣre (Old English “pure”)).

chain.meaning: clean, free from dirt or filth, unmixed, plain

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English purpos, from Old French purposer (“to propose”) (with conjugation altered based on poser (Old French)), from Latin prō- (“forth”) + pono (Latin “pōnere”), hence Latin propono (“prōpōnō, prōpōnere”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English purposen, from Old French purposer (“to propose”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English pushen, poshen (Middle English), posson (Middle English), borrowed from Middle French pousser (Modern French pousser (French)) from , from Latin pulsare (“to beat, strike”), frequentative of pellere (Latin) (past participle pulsus (Latin)). . Partly displaced native sċūfan (Old English), whence shove (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Probably . See pouch (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English putten, pitten (Middle English), pytten (Middle English), puten (Middle English), poten (Middle English), from Old English putian, *pūtian (Old English) and potian (Old English “to push, thrust, strike, butt, goad”), both from Proto-West Germanic *putōn, from Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to stick, stab”), which is of origin. Possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bud- (“to shoot, sprout”), which would make it cognate with बुन्द (Sanskrit “arrow”), budė (Lithuanian), and budis (Lithuanian “mushroom, fungus”). Compare also related pȳtan (Old English “to push, poke, thrust, put out (the eyes)”). Cognate with poten (Dutch “to set, plant”), paten (Low German “to set, plant”), putte (Danish “to put”), putta (Swedish), pötta (Swedish), potta (Swedish “to strike, knock, push gently, shove, put away”), putte (Norwegian “to set, put”), pota (Norwegian “to poke”), pota (Icelandic “to poke”), peuteren (Dutch “to pick, poke around, dig, fiddle with”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: . Perhaps related to pwt (Welsh), itself possibly borrowed from butt (English “stub, thicker end”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Old French pute.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: inc-hnd — (Hindi पैजामा / Urdu پائِجامَہ), from Classical Persian پایجامه, archaic form of پاجامه (Classical Persian).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French qualification in the 1540s, which in turn derives from Medieval Latin quālificātiō. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French qualifier (“to qualify”). Equivalent to quality + -fy (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English qualite, from Old French qualité, from Latin quālitās (“quālitās, quālitātem”), from quālis (Latin “of what kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷo- (“who, how”). Cicero coined qualitas (Latin) as a calque to translate the - (Ancient Greek) word ποιότης (Ancient Greek “quality”), coined by Plato from ποῖος (Ancient Greek “of what nature, of what kind”).

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
1560s, via Middle French race from Italian razza (early 14th century), of origin. Partially displaced native kinde (Middle English “kind, type, sort, race, nature”), whence kind (English). Fully displaced native cnōsl (Old English) and hād (Old English).

* Diez and some other scholars suggest derivation from Proto-Germanic *raitō (whence reiza (Old High German “line”) and ríta (Old Norse “to score, log, outline”)), perhaps via Lombardic *raiza (“line”), which Körting notes is a literal rendering of Latin linea sanguinis (“bloodline of descent”). Anatoly Liberman says "the semantic fit is good" but the chronology falters; he says the Germanic word went out of use before the Italian word arose, and he says the intermediary is not attested.
* Some scholars suggest derivation from raza (osp), rasa (osp), from earlier ras (osp), res (osp “head of cattle”), from Arabic رَأْس (“head”), but razza (Italian) predates the Spanish word according to Diez and Meyer-Lübke.
* Meyer-Lübke suggested generatio (Latin) as the root; Körting says "the disappearance of two initial syllables hardly seems credible", but Meyer-Lübke notes the Venetian form narazza and the Old Bellunesian form naraccia, positing that after the first syllable ge- was lost, the remaining (una) narazza came to be reanalysed as una razza.
* Gianfranco Contini suggests the Italian word comes from Old French haraz (“troop of horses”), whence Modern haras (French “breeding farm for horses; stud farm”), from Old Norse hárr (“grey-haired; hoary”). Liberman considers this derivation the most likely.
* Other suggested Latin etyma:
** radius (Latin) (perhaps via *radia (Vulgar Latin)) (per Baist).
** radix (Latin “root”) (per Ulrich); Liberman says "the semantic match is excellent", and race (English “rhizome of ginger”) (which definitely derives from radix) shows that the phonology is plausible.
** *raptiare (Latin “breed falcons”) (per Körting).
** The nominative of ratio (Latin) (perhaps via an unattested intermediate form *razzo), as opposed to ragione (Italian) which derives from the accusative rationem.
* Other implausible suggestions include Slavic raz and Basque arraca, supposedly meaning "stud animal" (Basque arrazza, "race", derives from Spanish).

* from Anglo-Norman racer, an aphetic form of aracer (Anglo-Norman) (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English rapen, rappen (Middle English “to abduct; ravish; seduce; rape; seize; snatch; carry off; transport”), probably from Latin rapiō (verb), possibly through or influenced by Anglo-Norman — rap (Old French), rape (Old French) (noun) (compare also ravish (English)). But compare rappa (Swedish “to snatch, seize, carry off”), rapen (Low German “to snatch, seize”), rapen (Dutch “to pick up, gather, collect”); the relationship with Germanic forms is not clear. Compare also rap (English “seize, snatch”). Further, some senses may be from rape (English “3=Etymology 3”), an Old Norse word. Displaced native seorþan (Old English) whence sard (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Generally considered to derive from Old English rāp (“rope”), in reference to the ropes used to delineate the courts that ruled each rape. Compare reep (Dutch) and the parish of .

In the 18th century, proposed derivation from Old Norse hreppr (“tract of land”), but this was rejected by the New English Dictionary and is considered "phonologically impossible" by the . Others, considering it improbable that the Normans would have adopted a local word, suggest derivation from Old French raper (“take by force”).

Related to rise and raise, which is used for several of its now archaic or obsolete senses and for some of its senses that are currently more common in other dialects of English.

etymologies.text: From Middle English resoun, reson (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman raisun (Old French raison), from Latin ratiō, from ratus (Latin), past participle of reor (Latin “reckon”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂reh₁- (“to think”), reanalysed root of *h₂er- (Proto-Indo-European “to put together”). Displaced racu (Old English “logic, reason”) and native -rede (Middle English “reden”), from rǣden (Old English “condition, stipulation, calculation, direction”), from the same Proto-Indo-European source (compare reden (Western Frisian “reason”), reden (Dutch “reason”)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English reason, reson (Middle English), resen (Middle English), rasen (Middle English), from Old English ræsn (“beam, rafter, ceiling, wall panel”), probably from Proto-West Germanic *raʀn (“house”), from Proto-Germanic *razną (“house, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erh₁- (“to rest”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English resonable, from Old French resnable, from Classical Latin ratiōnābilis, from ratiō (Latin). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English resonably, equivalent to reasonable + -ly (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English rebel, rebell (Middle English), from Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis (“waging war again; insurgent”), from rebellō (Latin “to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (Latin “again, back”) + bellō (Latin “to wage war”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English rebellen, from Old French rebeller, from Latin rebellō (“to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (Latin “again, back”) + bellō (Latin “to wage war”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: re- + build

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From re- + call (English), probably modelled on revocāre (Latin), rappeler (French), withcall (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English receyt, recorded since c. 1386 as "statement of ingredients in a potion or medicine," from Anglo-Norman — or Old Northern French receite (“receipt, recipe”) (1304), altered (by influence of receit (Old French “he receives”), from recipit (Latin)) from Old French recete, from Latin receptus, perfect passive participle of recipiō (Latin), itself from re- (Latin “back”) + capiō (Latin “to take”). The unpronounced p was later inserted to make the word appear closer to its Latin root. . (whence رسید (Urdu)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin recēns (genitive recentis (Latin)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: recent + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English recepcion,reception, from Middle French reception, from Latin receptiō (“the act of receiving; reception”), from recipiō (Latin “receive”), from re- (Latin “back”) + capiō (Latin “to hold”). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin recessiō, from recēdō (Latin “recede, retreat”), from re- (Latin “back”) + cēdō (Latin “to go”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French récipé, from Latin recipe, second person singular imperative of Latin recipiō (“receive”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rekenen, from Old English recenian (“to pay; arrange, dispose, reckon”) and ġerecenian (Old English “to explain, recount, relate”); both from Proto-West Germanic *rekanōn (“to count, explain”), from Proto-West Germanic *rekan (“swift, ready, prompt”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to make straight or right”).

Cognate with rekkin (Scots “to enumerate, mention, narrate, rehearse, count, calculate, compute”), reekenje (Saterland Frisian “to calculate, figure, reckon”), rekkenje (Western Frisian “to account, tally, calculate, figure”), rekenen (Dutch “to count, calculate, reckon, charge”), reken (Low German (Germany) “to reckon”), rechnen (German “to count, reckon, calculate”), regne (Danish “to calculate”), räkna (Swedish “to count, calculate, reckon”), rekna (Norwegian Nynorsk “to calculate”), reikna (Icelandic “to calculate”), rectus (Latin “straight, right”). See also reck (English), reach (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French reconoistre, from Old French reconoistre, from Latin recognosco (“recognoscere”), first attested in the 16th century. Displaced native acknow (English “to recognize, perceive as”), compare erkennen (German) and erkänna (Swedish). Latin had rare recognizare (Latin “to try by jury”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: re- + cognize

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English recommenden, from Old French recommender (compare recommander (French)), from Latin re- + commendo (Latin “commendāre”), from con- + mando + mandāre (Latin), from .

Compare typologically препоръчам (Bulgarian), препоручити (Serbo-Croatian), priporočiti (Slovenian), doporučit (Czech), odporučiť (Slovak) (the same meaning); поручи́ться (Russian), пору́ка (Russian), поручи́тельство (Russian) (close meaning), all related to *rǫka (Proto-Slavic) (ръка (Bulgarian), рука́ (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English recommendacioun, from Anglo-Norman recomendacion, from Medieval Latin recommendatio. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English recorde (“recorde”), borrowed from Old French record, from recorder (Old French). See record (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English recorden (“to repeat, to report”), borrowed from Old French recorder (“to get by heart”), from Latin recordor (“remember, call to mind”), from re- (Latin “back, again”) + cor (Latin “heart; mind”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English recoveren, rekeveren (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman recoverer and Old French recovrer, from Latin recupero (“recuperāre”), alternative form of recipero (Latin “reciperāre”). .

The noun is from Middle English recover, from the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: re- + cover

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from Middle English recoveree, from Old French recovree, from recovrer (Old French “recover”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English recreacion; equivalent to re- + creation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (Latin “back”) + dūcō (Latin “lead”). See duke (English), and compare with redoubt (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English reduccion, a borrowing from Old French reducion, from Latin reductio (“reductiō, reductiōnem”). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin redundāns, present participle of redundō (Latin “to overflow, redound”), from red- (Latin “again, back”) + undō (Latin “to surge, flood”), from unda (Latin “a wave”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English —, from past participle of Old French referer (“to relate, to refer”), from Latin refero (“referre”); as if refer + ee (English), that is, the person to whom something is referred for consideration.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French référence, from Medieval Latin referentia, nominative neuter plural of referēns (Latin), present participle of referō (Latin “return, reply”). Morphologically refer + ence (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , from , from re- (Latin “again”) + flectō (Latin “to bend, to curve”). Compare reflex (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English refleccion,refleccioun,refleccioune,reflection, from Middle French reflection,reflexion, and its source Late Latin reflexiō, from the participle stem of reflectō (Latin). The current spelling is influenced by reflect (English). Equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French réfugié, past participle of réfugier (French “to take refuge, to seek refuge”), from Old French refuge (“hiding place”) from Latin refugium (“a place of refuge, place to flee back to”), originally describing French Huguenots fleeing religious persecution after the in 1685. was "one seeking asylum" until 1914, when it evolved to mean more generally "one fleeing home" (first applied in this sense to civilians in Flanders heading west to escape fighting in World War I). . Displaced native flīema (Old English).

chain.meaning: a place of refuge, place to flee back to

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English refunden, refounden (Middle English), from , refonder (Old French), refunder (Old French “to restore; pay back”), from ; prefix re- (Latin “re-”) + fundere (Latin “to pour”): compare refondre (French), refonder (French). Not related to fund (English). See fuse (English “to melt”), and compare refound (English “to cast again”), and refuse (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed into late Middle English — from Middle French refusé, past participle of refuser (Middle French “to refuse”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (Middle English “to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding warnen (Middle English)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English refusen, from Old French refuser, from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, either from a blend of Classical Latin refutō (“refūtāre”) (whence also refute (English)) and recūsō (Latin “recūsāre”) (whence also recuse (English)) or from Latin refūsus, the perfect passive participle of refundo (Latin “refundere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Affix: re- + fuse

etymologies.text: From (French regagner (French)). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English regard, regarde (Middle English), reguard (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman reguard, from regarder (Old French), reguarder (Old French). Attested in Middle English starting around the mid 14th century. ; compare also guard (English), ward (English), guardian (English), and so on.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English regarden, from Old French regarder, reguarder (Old French). First attested in late Middle English, circa the early 15th century.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Popularized about 2022 along with regarded (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English regioun, from Anglo-Norman regiun, from Latin regiō, from regō (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French régional, from Latin regiōnālis, equivalent to region + -al (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regero (“regerō”), from re- (Latin) + gero (Latin “to carry, bear”). Compare registoria (Latin “a treasurer”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated rego (Latin “regō”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: register + -ation

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English regretten, regreten (Middle English), from Old French regreter, regrater (Old French “to lament”), from re- (Old French) + *greter (Old French), *grater (Old French “to weep”), from Frankish *grātan (“to weep, mourn, lament”), from Proto-Germanic *grētaną (“to weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁d- (“to sound”); and Frankish *greutan (“to cry, weep”), from Proto-Germanic *greutaną (“to weep, cry”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd- (“to weep, be sad”), equivalent to re- + greet (English). Cognate with grāzan (Old High German “to cry”), grǣtan (Old English “to weep, greet”), grēotan (Old English “to weep, lament”), gráta (Old Norse “to weep, groan”), 𐌲𐍂𐌴𐍄𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to weep”). More at greet (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English reguler, from Anglo-Norman reguler, Middle French reguler, regulier (Middle French), and their source, Latin rēgulāris (“continuing rules for guidance”), from rēgula (Latin “rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“move in a straight line”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: regular + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From regulate + ion (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English rehercel, rehersail (Middle English), rehersall (Middle English), from rehersen (Middle English) and apparently partly Middle French rehercel. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin reiectus, past participle of reicio (Latin “reicere”), from re- (Latin “back”) + iacio (Latin “iacere”). Displaced native āweorpan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English relacion, relacioun (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman relacioun and Old French relacion (whence relation (French)), from Latin relātiō, noun of process form from perfect passive participle relātus (Latin “related”), from verb referō (Latin “to refer, to relate”), from prefix re- (Latin “again”) + ferō (Latin “to bear, to carry”). . .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Displaced native sibb (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French relatif, from Late Latin relātīvus, from Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (Latin “to carry back, to ascribe”), from re- (Latin “again”) + ferō (Latin “to bear or carry”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English relaxen, from Old French relaxer, from Latin relaxāre (“relax, loosen, open”), from re- (Latin “back”) + laxāre (Latin “loosen”), from laxus (Latin “loose, free”). .

thumb|A man relaxing and reading a book.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin relaxatio (“relaxatio, relaxationis”); equivalent to relax + ation (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From relax + ed (English), originally after Latin relaxātus.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English relesen, relessen (Middle English), from Old French relaisser (variant of relascher (Old French)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: re- + lease

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Scots relevant meaning "legally pertinent," used in Scottish legal circles starting in the early 1500s, and first used in English in the 1700s. Borrowed from Latin relevāns (“relevāns, relevāntem”), present active participle of relevō (Latin “lift up again, lighten, relieve”), from re- (Latin “again”) + levō (Latin “lift”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: rely + -able

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old French relief (“assistance”), from Old French relever (“to relieve”), from Latin relevo (“relevare”). See also relieve (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Italian rilievo, from rilevare (Italian “to raise”), from Latin relevō (“to raise”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English religioun, from Old French religion, from Latin religiō (“scrupulousness, pious misgivings, superstition, conscientiousness, sanctity, an object of veneration, cult-observance, reverence”). Most likely from the Proto-Indo-European *h₂leg- with the meanings preserved in Latin dīligere (Latin) and legere (Latin) (“to read repeatedly”, “to have something solely in mind”). .

chain.meaning: scrupulousness, pious misgivings, superstition, conscientiousness, sanctity, an object of veneration, cult-observance, reverence

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English religiouse, religious (Middle English), religius (Middle English), religeous (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman religieus, religius (Old French), from Old French religious, religieux (Old French), and their source, Latin religiōsus (“religious, superstitious, conscientious”), from religiō (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English remainen, from Old French —, stressed stem of remanoir (Old French), from Latin remaneō, maneō (Latin), from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay”).

Displaced native beliven (Middle English), bliven (Middle English “to remain”) (from belīfan (Old English “to remain, stay”)) due to confluence with related beleven (Middle English “to leave behind”), with which it merged. More at beleave and belive.

etymologies.text: From Middle French remarquer, from Old French remarquer, from re- (Old French “again”) + marquer (Old French “to mark”), equivalent to re- + mark (English).
