etymologies.text: From Middle English remedie, from Old French *remedie, remede (Old French), from Latin remedium (“a remedy, cure”), from re- (Latin “again”) + mederi (Latin “to heal”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From mid 17th century, equivalent to re- + mind (English). Probably suggested by obsolete rememorate (English) with the same sense. Displaced myndgian (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English remote, from Old French remot, masculine, remote (Old French), feminine, from Latin remotus, past participle of removere (Latin “to remove”), from re- (Latin) + movere (Latin “to move”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English removen, from Anglo-Norman remover, removeir (Old French), from Old French remouvoir, from Latin removeo (“removēre”), from re- (Latin) + moveo (Latin “movēre”), equivalent to re- + move (English). Displaced native āfierran (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English renewen, an alteration (possibly on analogy with renovāre (Latin)) of earlier anewen (Middle English “to renew”), from Old English nīewian (“to restore; renovate; renew”), equivalent to re + new (English). Cognate with giniuwōn (Old High German “to renew”), geniuwen (Middle High German “to renew”), nýja (Old Norse “to renew”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English rent, rente (Middle English), from Old French rente, from Early Medieval Latin rendita, from Late Latin rendo (“rendere”), from Latin reddo (“reddere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: See rend (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Coined between 1300 and 1350 from Middle English repairen, from Middle French reparer, from Latin reparō (“renew, repair”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English repairen (“to return”), from Old French repairier, from Late Latin repatriare (“to return to one's country”), from re- (Latin) + patria (Latin “homeland”). Cognate to repatriate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English repeten, from Old French repeter, from Latin repetō, from the prefix re- (Latin “again”) + petō (Latin “to attack, beseech”).

Doublet of replicate (English) and replica (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reporto (“reportāre”), from re- + porto (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English reportour, from Old French reporteur; equivalent to report + -er (English).

etymologies.text: From Middle English representative, from Middle French representatif and its etymon Medieval Latin repraesentātīvus. ; See representation. Displaced native spala (Old English “a representative”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: 14c. "credit, good reputation", from Middle English reputacion,reputacioun,reputation,reputatioun, from Anglo-Norman reputacion,reputacioun, Middle French reputation (réputation (French)), and their etymon Latin reputātiō (“reputātiōnem”), noun of action from past participle stem of reputō (Latin “reflect upon, reckon, count over”), from the prefix re- (Latin “again”) + putō (Latin “reckon, consider”). . Displaced native hlīsa (Old English “reputation, fame”)

Compare to requérir (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English rescouen, from Old French rescoure, rescurre (Old French), rescorre (Old French); from Latin — prefix re- (Latin “re-”) + excutiō (Latin “to shake or drive out”), from ex (Latin “out”) + quatiō (Latin “to shake”). Displaced native nerian (Old English).

etymologies.text: Early Modern , from , .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English resident, from Anglo-Norman resident, from Latin residēns, present participle of resideō (Latin “to remain behind, reside, dwell”), equivalent to , from re- (Latin “back”) + sedeō (Latin “to sit”). . The espionage sense is a Russian резиде́нт.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French ressource, from Old French resourse, resource (Old French “a source, spring”), from resourdre (Old French), from Latin resurgō (“to rise again, spring up anew”). Equivalent to re- + source (English). See resourd, resurgent, source.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English respect, from Old French respect, also respit (Old French “respect, regard, consideration”), from Latin respectus (“a looking at, regard, respect”), perfect passive participle of respiciō (Latin “look at, look back upon, respect”), from re- (Latin “back”) + speciō (Latin “to see”), equivalent to re + spect (English). .

The verb is derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English respounden, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondō, from Latin respondeō. Cf. Modern répondre (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English respounse, respons (Middle English), from Old French respons, respuns (Old French), responce (Old French), ultimately from the Latin respōnsum, a nominal use of the neuter form of respōnsus (Latin), the perfect passive participle of respondeō (Latin), from re (Latin “again”) + spondeō (Latin “promise”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From responsible + ity (English). Although the components are of French origin, the compound appears to have been formed in English. Later-attested responsabilité (French) is modeled on the English word, and responsabilità (Italian) is in turn modeled on the French.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French responsable, from Old French responsable, responsible (Old French), formed from the root of Latin responsus, from respondeō (Latin “respondeō, respondēre”). The spelling of the English word is taken from the Old French variant responsible. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English rest, reste (Middle English), from Old English ræst, from Proto-West Germanic *rastu, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, of uncertain origin; possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to rest”) or *Hre(h₁)s- (Proto-Indo-European “to flow, rush”). Cognate with rêst (Western Frisian “rest”), rust (Dutch “rest”), Rast (German “rest”), rast (Swedish “rest”), rest (Norwegian “rest”), röst (Icelandic “rest”), árus (Old Irish “dwelling”), Ruhe (German “calm”), resht (Albanian “to stop, pause”), araf (Welsh “quiet, calm, gentle”), rovà (Lithuanian “calm”), ἐρωή (Ancient Greek “rest, respite”), 𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌𐬨𐬈 (ae “calm, peaceful”), रमते (Sanskrit “he stays still, calms down”), 𐍂𐌹𐌼𐌹𐍃 (Gothic “tranquility”). Related to roo (English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English rest, reste (Middle English), from Old English ræst, from Proto-West Germanic *rastu, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, of uncertain origin; possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to rest”) or *Hre(h₁)s- (Proto-Indo-European “to flow, rush”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English resten, from Old English restan, from Proto-West Germanic *rastijan (“to rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ros-, *res- (Proto-Indo-European), *erH- (Proto-Indo-European “rest”). Cognate with rusten (Dutch “to rest”), resten (Middle Low German “to rest”), rasten (German “to rest”), raste (Danish “to rest”), rasta (Swedish “to rest”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English reste, from Old French reste, from Old French rester (“to remain”), from Latin restō (“to stay back, stay behind”), from re- (Latin) + stō (Latin “to stand”). Replaced native lave (Middle English “rest, remainder”) (from lāf (Old English “remnant, remainder”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English resten, from Old French rester, from Latin restō.

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Aphetic form of arrest (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English restoren, from Old French restorer, from Latin restauro (“rēstaurāre”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Recorded since 1432 as Middle English resulten, from Medieval Latin resulto (“resultare”), in Classical Latin — "to spring forward, rebound", the frequentative of the past participle of resilio (Latin “to rebound”), from re- (Latin “back”) + salio (Latin “to jump, leap”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle French retirer (“draw back”), from Old French retirer, built from re- (Middle French “back”) + tirer (Middle French “draw, pull”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre, of highly uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English returnen, retornen (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman returner, from Old French retourner, retorner (Old French), from Medieval Latin retornare (“to turn back”), from re- (Latin) + tornare (Latin “to turn”). . Compare beturn (English). Displaced native eftċierran (Old English), literally "eft-char".

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English revelen (“revēlen”), from Old French reveler, from Latin revēlāre (“to reveal, uncover”), from re- (Latin “back, again”) + vēlāre (Latin “to cover”), from vēlum (Latin “a cloth, covering, curtain, veil, awning, sail”) (whence also veil (English), unveil (English), voile (English), вуаль (Russian), завуали́ровать (Russian “to veil”) (compare typologically)).

Also compare typologically uncloak (English), dismantle (English), divest (English), invest (English), unmask (English), разобла́чать (Russian) (akin to облаче́ние (Russian), срыва́ть покро́вы (Russian) (покро́в (Russian “cover, covering”)).

chain.meaning: a cloth, covering, curtain, veil, awning, sail

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle French revenge, a derivation from revenger (Middle French), from Old French revengier (possibly influenced by pro revènge (“revenge, comeback”), from revenir (pro “to come back”)), a variant of revancher (Middle French) (whence deverbal revanche (French)), from revenchier (Old French). The variants vengier (Old French) (whence venger (French)) and venchier (Old French) are both descended from Latin vindicō, with stress-conditioned different parallel development in the inflectional forms. . Compare avenge (English) and vengeance (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English revengen, from Old French revengier, revenger (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English revers, from Anglo-Norman revers, Middle French revers, and their source, Latin reversus, perfect passive participle of reversō (Latin), from re- (Latin) + versō (Latin). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English reversen, from Anglo-Norman reverser, Middle French reverser, and their source, Latin reversō, from re- (Latin) + versō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English revewe, reveue (Middle English), from Old French reveue (“reveüe”), revue (Old French) (Modern French: revue (French)), feminine form of reveu (Old French “reveü”), past participle of reveoir (Old French) (French: revoir (French)), from Latin revideō, from re- (Latin) +videō (Latin “see, observe”) (English: video (English)). Equivalent to re + view (English). Compare retrospect (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French réviser, from Latin revīsō, from re- (Latin) + vīsō (Latin “examine”), frequentative of videō (Latin “see”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French révision, from Latin revīsiō.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English revolucion, borrowed from Old French revolucion, from Late Latin revolūtiō (“the act of revolving; revolution”), from Latin revolvō (“roll back, revolve”).

etymologies.text: Compare ; equivalent to revolution + -ary (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English reward, rewarde (Middle English), from Old French reward (“reward”) (compare regard (Old French), whence modern French regard (French), and also English regard (English) through Middle French), from rewarder (Old French “to reward”) (compare reguarder (Old French)), from re- (Old French) + warder (Old French “to guard, keep”) (compare guarder (Old French)); the Anglo-Norman forms are derived from Old Northern French — variants of Old French, ultimately of gem — (Frankish —) origin. Compare regard (English), warden (English), guard (English). See more below.

Mostly displaced mēd (Old English), whence meed (English). Displaced lēan (Old English) and edlēan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rewarden, from Anglo-Norman rewarder (“to reward”), from re- (Old French) + warder (Old French “to guard, keep”), from Old Northern French —, from Frankish *wardēn (“to guard, keep”), from Proto-Germanic *wardōną (“to guard, defend”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, shelter, defend, guard, shut”). Cognate with wardōn (Old Saxon “to guard, provide for, protect”), weardian (Old English “to guard”), wartēn (Old High German “to watch, keep, look after”). More at ward (English). .

Displaced lēanian (Old English). In this sense, displaced ġieldan (Old English), whence yield (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: re- + write

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First coined in 1557, from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (“any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm”), from ῥέω (Ancient Greek “to flow, run, stream, gush”).

chain.meaning: any measured flow or movement, symmetry, rhythm

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rib, ribbe (Middle English), from Old English ribb (“rib”), from Proto-West Germanic *ribi, from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib, reef”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ- (“arch, ceiling, cover”).

Cognate with rib (Dutch “rib”), ribbe (Norwegian “sparerib”), ribben (Norwegian “rib”), ribbe (Low German “rib”), Rippe (German “rib”), rif (Old Norse “rib, reef”), rèbro (Serbo-Croatian “rib”).

In reference to the creation of Eve from Adam's rib in the Bible.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ribbe, from Old English ribbe (“hound's-tongue”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English riche (“strong, powerful, rich”), from Old English rīċe (“powerful, mighty, great, high-ranking, rich, wealthy, strong, potent”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīkī (“powerful, rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz (“kingly, powerful, rich”), from Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king, ruler”), an early borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs. Reinforced by riche (Old French), from the same gmw — source.

Cognate with rijk (Dutch), reich (German), rig (Danish), rik (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), ríkur (Faroese / Icelandic), rico (Portuguese / Spanish), riche (French), ricco (Italian).

chain.meaning: powerful, mighty, great, high-ranking, rich, wealthy, strong, potent

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English riden, from Old English rīdan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīdan, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną (“to ride”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreydʰ- (“to ride”), from *h₃reyH- (Proto-Indo-European “to move”), from *h₃er- (Proto-Indo-European “to move, stir”).

From Proto-Germanic: ride (North Frisian), ridj (North Frisian), rir (North Frisian “to ride”), ride (Western Frisian “to ride”), rijden (Dutch), ryden (Dutch “to ride; to drive”), reiten (German), reuten (German “to ride”), rieden (Low German (Germany) “to ride; to drive”), rieje (Limburgish “to ride; to drive”), reiden (lb “to ride”), raeita (Ripuarian), rajta (Ripuarian “to ride”), ride (Danish “to ride”), ríða (Faroese / Icelandic “to ride”), ri (Norwegian Bokmål), ride (Norwegian Bokmål “to ride”), ri (Norwegian Nynorsk), rida (Norwegian Nynorsk), ride (Norwegian Nynorsk “to ride”), rida (Swedish “to ride”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ryder, ridere (Middle English), from Late Old English rīdere (“rider, knight”). Compare rijder (Dutch), Reiter (German). .

etymologies.text: Latin rīdiculus (“laughable, ridiculous”); Equivalent to ridicule + -ous (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English reȝt, right (Middle English), righte (Middle English), riht (Middle English), riȝt (Middle English), riȝte (Middle English), ryght (Middle English), ryȝt (Middle English), from Old English reht, reoht (Old English), rieht (Old English), riht (Old English), ryht (Old English “right,” also the word for “straight” and “direct”), from Proto-West Germanic *reht, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz (“right, straight; just, morally upright”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós (“right, straightened”), from *h₃reǵ- (Proto-Indo-European “to straighten; to righten”).

The Germanic adjective which has been used also as a noun since the common Germanic period.

Cognate with richt (Scots “right”), reights (Yola), rights (Yola “rights”), recht (North Frisian), rocht (North Frisian), rucht (North Frisian “right”), gjucht (Saterland Frisian “right”), rjocht (Western Frisian “straight”), rääch (Central Franconian “right”), recht (Dutch “straight”), recht (German), Recht (German “right”), réët (Limburgish “right”), Recht (lb), riets (lb “right”), riicht (lb “straight”), רעכט (Yiddish “right”), ret (Danish “right”), rættur (Faroese “right”), réttur (Icelandic “right”), rett (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “right”), rät (Swedish “straight”), rätt (Swedish “right”), 𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌷𐍄𐍃 (Gothic “straight; correct”). The Indo-European root is also the source of reiñ (Breton “to give”), ri (Cornish “to give; to grant; to present”), reachd (Irish), reacht (Irish “law, statute; authority; dispensation”), reachd (Scottish Gaelic “law, right; command, power”), rhoddi (Welsh), rhoi (Welsh “to give; to put”), rēctus (Latin “led straight along; correct, right; just, lawful”), ὀρεκτός (Ancient Greek “stretched out; longed for”), redzēt (Latvian “to see”), regėti (Lithuanian “to see, view”), 𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬰𐬎 (ae “straight”), راست (bal “right”), ڕاست (Central Kurdish “right; straight”), rast (Kurmanji Kurdish “straight; right; true; erect; direct”), раст (Ossetic “honest, true; correct; exact; straight; fair; direct”), راس (Persian), راست (Persian “straight; direct; true; erect”), raşt (zza “right; straight”), ऋजु (Sanskrit “straight; honest, sincere”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English right, righte (Middle English), from Old English rihte, rehte (Old English “right; rightly; due; directly; straight”), from Proto-Germanic *rehta, from *rehtaz (Proto-Germanic “right; straight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English right, from Old English riht, reht (Old English), ġeriht (Old English “that which is right, just, or proper”), from Proto-West Germanic *reht, from Proto-Germanic *rehtą (“a right”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵt- (“to straighten; direct”).

Cognate with recht (Dutch “a right; privilege”), Recht (German “a right”), ret (Danish “a right”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English righten, reghten (Middle English), riȝten (Middle English), from Old English rihtan, ġerihtan (Old English “to straighten, judge, set upright, set right”), from Proto-West Germanic *rihtijan, from Proto-Germanic *rihtijaną (“to straighten; rectify; judge”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ryȝtly, rihtliche (Middle English), from Old English rihtlīċe, from Proto-West Germanic *rehtalīkā, *rehtalīkō (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *rehtalīkê, *rehtalīkô (Proto-Germanic “rightly”), equivalent to right + -ly (English). Cognate with rjochtlik (Western Frisian), rechtelijk (Dutch), rechtlich (German), rätteligen (Swedish), réttilega (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ryng, from Old English hring (“ring, circle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krengʰ-, extended nasalized form of *(s)ker- (Proto-Indo-European “to turn, bend”). , as well as indirectly .

* Ring (Low German)

More distantly cognate with *krǫgъ (Proto-Slavic) (whence кръг (Bulgarian), krąg (Polish), круг (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ryngen, from Old English hrinġan (“to ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *hringijan, from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną (“to ring”), of imitative origin. Cognate with ringen (Dutch “to ring”), ringe (Danish “to ring”), ringa (Swedish “to ring”), ringja (Faroese “to ring up, telephone”), hringja (Icelandic “to ring”), ringelje (Western Frisian “to ring”), rinkelen (Dutch “to ring, jingle”), ringla (Faroese “to tinkle, jingle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rippen, from earlier ryppen (Middle English “to pluck”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rupjaną and/or *ruppōną (Proto-Germanic), intensive of *raupijaną (Proto-Germanic), causative of Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to break”). Possible .

Cognate with rippe (Western Frisian), ripje (Western Frisian), roppe (Western Frisian), ropje (Western Frisian “to rip”), - (Dutch) dialectal rippen (Dutch), ruppen (Low German), röpen (Low German (Germany)), rupfen (German), also rīpan (Old English), rīepan (Old English “to plunder”) (whence reap (English)), rippe (Western Frisian “to rip, tear”), raufen (German “to rip”); perhaps also, less likely, rrabe (Albanian “maquis”) and rubus (Latin “bramble”). More at reave, rob and rub.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English ripe, rype (Middle English), from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīpī, from Proto-Germanic *rīpijaz, *rīpiz (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyb- (“to snatch”). Cognate with ryp (Western Frisian “ripe”), rijp (Dutch “ripe”), reif (German “ripe”). Related to reap (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ripe, from Latin ripa.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: An alteration of rife (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English risen, from Old English rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to arise, rise”). According to Kroonen (2013), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to rise, spring”). See also raise (English).

Cognate with rijzen (Dutch “to rise”), reisen (German “to fall”), rieze (Limburgish “to rise”), rísa (Faroese / Icelandic “to rise”), risa (Norwegian Nynorsk), rise (Norwegian Nynorsk “to rise”), *𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to rise”) (whence 𐌿𐍂𐍂𐌴𐌹𐍃𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to arise”)). Non-Germanic cognates include ardh (Cornish “height”), arad (Irish), ard (Irish), árd (Irish “high, tall”), ard (Manx “high, tall”), àrd (Scottish Gaelic “high”), ardd (Welsh “hill, upland”), orior (Latin “to rise”), ἔρις (Ancient Greek “quarell, strife; contention, rivalry”) (whence έριδα (Greek (Modern) “feud”)), rashë (Albanian “to have fallen; to have flopped”), ръст (Bulgarian “size; stature; growth”), růst (Czech “growth”), раст (Macedonian “growth, height”), rost (Polish), wzrost (Polish “growth”), рост (Russian “growth”), ра̑ст (Serbo-Croatian), rȃst (Serbo-Croatian “growth”), rȃst (Slovenian “growth”), յառնեմ (Classical Armenian “to arise, rise”) (whence հառնել (Armenian “to rise up”)), رمبیدن (Persian “to collapse”), ar- (xto “to evoke”), er- (txb “to evoke”), 𒀀𒊏𒀀𒄑𒍣 (Hittite “to rise”), ऋ (Sanskrit “to rise”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ris, rys (Middle English), from Old English hrīs, from Proto-Germanic *hrīsą (“twig; shoot”). More at rice (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From earlier risque (English), from Middle French risque, from Old Italian risco (“risk”) (modern rischio (Italian)) and rischiare (Italian “to run into danger”). Displaced native pleoh (Old English “risk”) and plēon (Old English “to risk”).

Most dictionaries consider the etymology of these Italian terms , but some suggest they perhaps come from Vulgar Latin *resecum (“that which cuts, rock, crag”) (> resicu (Medieval Latin)), from Latin resecō (“cut off, loose, curtail”), in the sense of that which is a danger to boating or shipping; or from Ancient Greek ῥιζικόν (“root, radical, hazard”).

A few dictionaries express more certainty. Collins says the Italian risco comes from Ancient Greek ῥίζα (“cliff”) due to the hazards of sailing along rocky coasts. The American Heritage says it probably comes from Medieval Greek ῥιζικό (“sustenance obtained by a soldier through his own initiative, fortune”), from Arabic رِزْق (“sustenance, that which God allots”), from Syriac ܪܙܩܐ (“daily ration”), from Pahlavi — (whence روزِی (Classical Persian)), from Pahlavi — (whence روز (Classical Persian)), from peo 𐎼𐎢𐎨𐏃 (cognate with रोचस् (Sanskrit “light, lustre”)), from Proto-Iranian *ráwčah, from iir-pro *ráwčas, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *léwkos (“*léwk-os”), from . Karla Mallette derives the word from Arabic رِزْق (“sustenance, that which God allots”) via pml —.

Cognate with riesgo (Spanish), risco (Portuguese)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: risk + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English robben, from Anglo-Norman rober (“robber”), from Late Latin raubō (“raubāre”), from Frankish *raubōn (compare roven (Dutch)) and Old High German roubōn, raubōn (Old High German “to rob, steal, plunder”), from Proto-Germanic *raubōną. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Medieval Latin rob, from Arabic ربّ (“thickened fruit juice”). Compare rob (French), rob (Spanish), rob (Italian), robbo (Italian), robe (Portuguese), arrobe (Portuguese), ربودن (Persian).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English robberie, robry (Middle English), roberie (Middle English), from Old French roberie, from the verb rober (Old French “to steal; to pillage”) + -ie (Old French). Ultimately from unattested Frankish *raubōn. . Compare roverij (Dutch “robbery”), røveri (Norwegian Bokmål “robbery”), Räuberei (German “robbery, banditry”).

Displaced native rēaflāc (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From German Robot, from a zlw — language, ultimately related to Etymology 2, below.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|An industrial robot () engraving on a metal plate

Czech robot, from robota (Czech “drudgery, servitude”). in the play ' after having been suggested to him by his brother . Largely displaced automaton (English).

Ultimately a cognate with from , and ; see dialectal erf (English). . Related to orphan (English), but with a -t- suffix from Proto-Slavic — instead of the -an- from - (Ancient Greek).

Compare robotnik (Polish) and работник (Russian “worker”), sometimes mistakenly cited as the direct source of the English word.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
Referencing the origin of the name of the imageboard (created in 2008), so-called because it implements the algorithm by to prevent the reposting of content.

Possibly overlapping with the sense of robot (English “a person who does not seem to have any emotions”), alluding to , due to the prevalence of personal stories describing awkward or embarrassing situations on the board.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English rocke, rokke (Middle English “rock formation”), from Old English *rocc (“rock”), as in stānrocc (Old English “high stone rock, peak, obelisk”), and also later from Anglo-Norman roche (“roque”), (compare Modern roc (French), roche (French), rocher (French)), from Medieval Latin rocca (attested 767), of origin, sometimes said to be of cel — (in particular, perhaps Gaulish —) origin (compare roc'h (Breton)). Related also to rocke (Middle Low German “rock ledge”). One suggestion is that it derives from Vulgar Latin *rupica, from rupes (Latin) (compare rupico (Latin)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Middle English rokken, from Old English roccian, from Proto-West Germanic *rokkōn, from Proto-Germanic *rukkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ruknéh₂ti, from *h₃rewk- (Proto-Indo-European), *h₃runk- (Proto-Indo-European).

See also obsolete rokken (Dutch), rocken (Middle High German “to drag, jerk”), Modern rücken (German “to move, shift”), rukka (Icelandic “to yank”); also runcāre (Latin “to weed”), rũķēt (Latvian “to toss, dig”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Shortened from rock and roll (English). Since the meaning of has adapted to mean a simpler, more modern, metal-like genre, has generally been left referring to earlier forms such as that originating in the 1950s, notably more swing-oriented style.

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English rok, rocke (Middle English), rokke (Middle English), perhaps from Middle Dutch rocke (whence rokken (Dutch)), Middle Low German rocken, or Old Norse rokkr (whence - (Icelandic) / rokkur (Faroese), rok (Danish), spinnrock (Swedish “spinning wheel”)). Cognate with rocko (Old High German “distaff”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Compound: roc

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Italian rocchetta, from Old Italian rocchetto (Italian “rocket”), diminutive of rocca (Italian “a distaff”), from Lombardic rocko (“spinning wheel”), from Proto-West Germanic *rokkō, from Proto-Germanic *rukkô (“a distaff, a staff with flax fibres tied loosely to it, used in spinning thread”). Cognate with rocco (Old High German), rocko (Old High German), roccho (Old High German), rocho (Old High German) , rock (Swedish “a distaff”), rokkur (Icelandic “a distaff”), rocke (Middle English “a distaff”). More at rock⁴.

For the meaning development, compare fuselage (English), ultimately from fūsus (Latin “spindle, spinning wheel”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from French roquette, from Italian ruchetta, diminutive of ruca (Italian), from Latin eruca. Cognate to arugula (English), rucola (English), eruca (English), roquette (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From French rôle, from Middle French rolle, from Old French role, from Medieval Latin rotulus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rollen, partly from Old French roller, roler (Old French), röeler (Old French), röoler (Old French), from Medieval Latin rotulāre (“to roll; to revolve”), from Latin rotula (“a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (Latin “a wheel”); partly from Anglo-Latin rollāre, from the same ultimate source.

Displaced native welt (English) and partially displaced wallow (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English rolle, from Old French rolle, role (Old French), roule (Old French), from Medieval Latin rotulus (“a roll, list, catalogue, schedule, record, a paper or parchment rolled up”); as such, it is a .

chain.meaning: a roll, list, catalogue, schedule, record, a paper or parchment rolled up

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English romauns, roumance (Middle English), borrowed from Anglo-Norman — and Old French romanz, romans (Old French) (the vernacular language of France, as opposed to Latin), from Medieval Latin rōmānicē, Vulgar Latin rōmānicē (“in the Roman language”), from Latin rōmānicus (“roman”) from rōmānus (Latin “a Roman”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From romant + -ic (English), or borrowed from . Compare romantique (French), which is borrowed from English. Also compare romántico (Spanish), romântico (Portuguese), romantico (Italian), romantisch (Dutch), and romantisch (German) and Romantiker (German “a composer of Romantic music”), all of which are borrowed from English or French.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English roum (“room, space”), from Old English rūm (“room, space”), from Proto-West Germanic *rūm (“room”), from Proto-Germanic *rūmą (“room”), from Proto-Indo-European *(H)rewH- (“to root; to rip, tear”), from *Hrew- (Proto-Indo-European “to tear out, open”).

Cognate with rüm (North Frisian “room, space”), Ruum (Saterland Frisian / Low German “room, space”), ruim (Dutch “open space; cargo hold”), Raum (de,lb “room, space”), raojm (Ripuarian “room”), rum (Danish / Swedish “room, space”), rúm (Faroese / Icelandic “space, room”), rom (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “room, space”), 𐍂𐌿𐌼 (Gothic “room, space”); also rúsc (Irish “bark”), roost (Manx “bark; peel, rind”), rùsg (Scottish Gaelic “rind; bark; fleece; shell”), rhisgl (Welsh “bark”), rūs (Latin “country, fields, lands; estate, farm; village”), ὀρύσσω (Ancient Greek), ὀρύττω (Ancient Greek “to dig”), raut (Latvian “to pull with force”), rauti (Lithuanian “to grub, pull”), рыць (Belarusian “to dig”), ри́я (Bulgarian “to excavate”), rýt (Czech “to dig; to engrave”), ryć (Polish “to dig”), рыть (Russian “to dig; to burrow, mine”), ryť (Slovak “to dig; to engrave”), riti (Slovenian “to dig”), ри́ти (Ukrainian “to dig, excavate”), ڕێو (Central Kurdish “public hair”), kärpi (xto “raw, rough; common”), kärpiye (txb “raw, rough; common”), लोमन् (Sanskrit), रोमन् (Sanskrit “body hair; down, wool”). More at rural (English). , a surname from German.

The word superficially appears to be an exception to the , which might have produced the pronunciation , but the retention of Middle English before is regular. In fact, does not occur before non-coronal consonants in Standard Modern English native vocabulary. Some dialects did undergo diphthongization in such a position and the pronunciation occurs, for example, in Lancashire.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English roum, rom (Middle English), rum (Middle English), from Old English rūm (“roomy, spacious, ample, extensive, large, open, unencumbered, unoccupied, temporal, long, extended, great, liberal, unrestricted, unfettered, clear, loose, free from conditions, free from occupation, not restrained within due limits, lax, far-reaching, abundant, noble, august”), from Proto-Germanic *rūmaz (“roomy, spacious”), from Proto-Indo-European *rewh₁- (“free space”). Cognate with roum (Scots “spacious, roomy”), ruim (Dutch “roomy, spacious, wide”), rum (Danish “wide, spacious”), raum (German “wide”), rúmur (Icelandic “spacious”).

chain.meaning: roomy, spacious, ample, extensive, large, open, unencumbered, unoccupied, temporal, long, extended, great, liberal, unrestricted, unfettered, clear, loose, free from conditions, free from occupation, not restrained within due limits, lax, far-reaching, abundant, noble, august

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English rome, from Old English rūme (“widely, spaciously, roomily, far and wide, so as to extend over a wide space, liberally, extensively, amply, abundantly, in a high degree, without restriction or encumbrance, without the pressure of care, light-heartedly, without obstruction, plainly, clearly, in detail”). Cognate with ruim (Dutch “amply”).

chain.meaning: widely, spaciously, roomily, far and wide, so as to extend over a wide space, liberally, extensively, amply, abundantly, in a high degree, without restriction or encumbrance, without the pressure of care, light-heartedly, without obstruction, plainly, clearly, in detail

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: room + -mate

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rote, root (Middle English), roote (Middle English “the underground part of a plant”), from late Old English rōt, from Old Norse rót (“root”), from Proto-Germanic *wrōts (“root”), from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”); .

Cognate with ruit (Scots), rute (Scots “root”), rod (Danish “root”), rót (Faroese / Icelandic “root”), rot (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “root”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wroten (“wrōten”), from Old English wrōtan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrōtan, from Proto-Germanic *wrōtaną (“to dig out, to root”). Related to wrōt (Old English “snout; trunk”). Loss of initial w- probably due to influence from the related noun (Etymology 1).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Possibly an alteration of rout (English “to make a loud noise”), influenced by hoot (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rop, rope (Middle English), from Old English rāp (“rope, cord, cable”), from Proto-West Germanic *raip, from Proto-Germanic *raipaz, *raipą (Proto-Germanic “rope, cord, band, ringlet”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁roypnós (“strap, band, rope”), from *h₁reyp- (Proto-Indo-European “to peel off, tear; border, edge, strip”).

Cognate with rape (Scots), raip (Scots “rope”), Roop (Saterland Frisian “rope”), reap (Western Frisian “rope, cord”), roop (Dutch), reep (Dutch “rope, cord, ring, strip, bar”), Reep (Low German (Germany) “rope”), Reif (German “ring, hoop”), rep (Norwegian Bokmål / Swedish “rope”), reip (Faroese / Norwegian Nynorsk “rope”), reb (Danish “rope”), reipi (Icelandic “rope”), rrip (Albanian “belt, rope”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English ropen, rope (Middle English “to form ropes”), from rop (Middle English “rope”); see above.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rop (“gut, intestine”), from Old English rop, ropp (Old English); compare rop (Middle Dutch), roppe (Middle Dutch “fish guts”).

The modern pronunciation results from phonological assimilation to Etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rose, roose (Middle English), from Old English rōse, but with its vowel influenced by Old French rose, both from Latin rosa.

The Latin is of origin, but likely via Oscan — from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (“rose”) (Aeolic ϝρόδον (Ancient Greek)), from peo *vr̥dah (“flower”) (compare 𐬬𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬜𐬀 (ae “𐬬𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬜𐬀-”), , wâr (xpr), late , گل (Persian “rose, flower”), and Middle Iranian borrowings including վարդ (Classical Armenian “rose”), וַרְדָּא (Aramaic) / ܘܪܕܐ (Syriac), وَرْدَة (Arabic), וֶרֶד (Hebrew)), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥dʰos (“sweetbriar”) (compare word (Old English “thornbush”), rubus (Latin “bramble”), hurdhe (Albanian “ivy”)). Possibly ultimately a derivation from a verb for "to grow" only attested in Indo-Iranian (*Hwardʰ- (iir-pro), compare वर्धति (Sanskrit), with relatives in Avestan).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From French rosé (“pinkish”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English roten, from Old Norse rotinn (“decayed, rotten”), past participle of an unrecorded verb related to rotna (Old Norse “to rot”) and rotian (Old English “to rot”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rutāną (“to rot”). See rot (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rough, roughe (Middle English), roȝe (Middle English), row (Middle English), rou (Middle English), ru (Middle English), ruȝ (Middle English), ruh (Middle English), from Old English rūg, rūh (Old English), from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz.

Cognate with ruch (Scots), rouch (Scots “rough”), ruuch (Saterland Frisian), rouch (Saterland Frisian “rough”), rûch (Western Frisian “rough”), ruuch (Low German “rough”), ruig (Dutch “rough”), rau (German “rough”), ru (Danish “uneven on the surface, "rough", "rugged"”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: rough + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English round, rounde (Middle English), from Old Northern French rount (“roünt”), rund (Old French), Old French ront, runt (Old French), reont (Old French) ( > rond (French)), from both Late Latin retundus and the original Latin rotundus. The noun developed partly from the adjective and partly from the corresponding French noun rond (French). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English rounen, from Old English rūnian (“to whisper, talk low, talk secrets, consipre, talk secretly”), from Proto-Germanic *rūnōną (“to talk secrets, whisper, decide”), *raunijaną (Proto-Germanic “to investigate, examine, prove”), from Proto-Indo-European *(e)rewə-, *(e)rwō- (Proto-Indo-European “to trace, find out, look out”). Cognate with roun (Scots “to converse with in whispers, speak privately”), rūnen (Middle Low German “to whisper”), ruinen (Middle Dutch “to whisper”), raunen (German “to whisper, murmur”), rūn (Old English “whisper, secret, mystery”), röna (Swedish “to meet with, experience”). More at rune (English).

chain.meaning: to whisper, talk low, talk secrets, consipre, talk secretly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English route, from Old French rote (“route”), from Latin rupta via (“rupta [via]”). Compare Modern route (French). See routine (English). Further via ruptus (Latin) related with bankrupt (English). Unrelated to road (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
. Further from Latin rupta via.

Compare typologically travel (English) << tripālium (Latin), whence also travail (English), note the inverse semantic vector from a subjective state (toil) to an objective action (journey). Also compare běžný (Czech) (< běžet (Czech)), обихо́д (Russian), обихо́дный (Russian) (akin to ходи́ть (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English rewe, rowe (Middle English), rawe (Middle English), from Old English rǣw, rāw (Old English), probably from Proto-Germanic *raiwō, *raigwō (Proto-Germanic), *rīgǭ (Proto-Germanic “row, streak, line”), from Proto-Indo-European *Hreyk- (“to carve, scratch, etch”).

Cognate with raw (Scots “row”), dialectal rå (Norwegian “boundary line”), Riege (Saterland Frisian “row”), rige (Western Frisian “row”), rij (Dutch “row, line”), Reeg (Low German (Germany)), Riege (Low German (Germany)), Rieg (Low German (Germany) “row”), Reihe (German “row”), Riege (German “sports team”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English rowen (“to row”), from Old English rōwan (“to row”), from Proto-Germanic *rōaną (“to row”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to row”). Compare roeie (Western Frisian), roeien (Dutch), ro (Danish). More at rudder. Related to Russia (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Unclear; some suggest it is a , verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English royal, from Old French roial (Modern French royal (French)), from Latin rēgālis, from rēx (Latin “king”). . Cognate with real (Spanish), reale (Italian), reial (Catalan). Displaced native cynelīċ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English rubben, of origin; possibly ultimately from Proto-Germanic —, a hypothetical variant of *ruppōną (Proto-Germanic “to tear (off), rip; to wear away, rub”), related to *reufaną (Proto-Germanic “to tear”) (> reave (English)). If so, a .

Cognate with rubje (Saterland Frisian “to rub, scrape”), rubben (Low German (Germany) “to rub”), rubblig (Low German “rough, uneven”), robben (Dutch), rubben (Dutch “to rub smooth; scrape; scrub”), rubbe (Danish “to rub, scrub”), - (Icelandic) and - (Norwegian) rubba (Icelandic “to scrape”).
More at reave (English).

Compare typologically fricō (Latin) < friō (Latin) < *bʰreyH- (Proto-Indo-European) (whence also брить (Russian “to shave”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From .

The sense of the substance comes from its ability to function as an eraser, displacing earlier caoutchouc (English). The senses not pertaining to rubbing or erasing are secondarily derived from the name of the substance.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
thumb|A pile#Noun|pile of rubbish in [[India]]

Middle English robous (“rubbish, building rubble”), further origin ; possibly from Anglo-Norman rubous, rubouse (Old French), rubbouse (Old French “refuse, waste material; building rubble”), and compare Anglo-rebbussa (Latin), robousa (Latin), robusium (Latin), robusum (Latin), rubisum (Latin), rubusa (Latin), rubusium (Latin) (although the Anglo-Norman and Anglo-Latin words may be derived from the English word instead of the other way around, as there are no known Old French cognates of the word). The English word may be related to rubble (English), though the connection is unclear. Possibly derived ultimately from Old Norse rubba (“to huddle, crowd together, heap up", also possibly "to rub, scrape”), from Proto-Germanic *rubbōną (“to rub, scrape”). Compare rubba (Swedish “to move, displace, dislodge, upset”).

The verb is derived from the noun.

chain.meaning: to huddle, crowd together, heap up", also possibly "to rub, scrape

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English rude, from Old French rude, ruide (Old French), from Latin rudis (“rough, raw, rude, wild, untilled”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
; probably of gmq — origin; perhaps inherited via Middle English *rugge (suggested by ruggy (Middle English “hairy, shaggy, bristly”) and rugged (Middle English “hairy, shaggy, rugged”)), from Old Norse rǫgg (“shagginess, tuft”), from Proto-Germanic *rawwō (“long wool”), probably related to *rūhaz (Proto-Germanic “rough”), related to English rag (English) and rough (English).

Cognate with dialectal rugga (Norwegian “coarse coverlet”), rugg (Swedish “rough entangled hair”), related to rag (English) and rough (English). Compare also rȳhe (Old English “rug, rough covering, blanket”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English ruyne, ruine (Middle English), from Old French ruine, from Latin ruīna (“overthrow, ruin”), from ruō (Latin “to fall down, tumble, sink in ruin, rush”).

chain.meaning: to fall down, tumble, sink in ruin, rush

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English reule, rewle (Middle English), rule (Middle English), borrowed from Old French riule, reule (Old French), from Latin regula (“straight stick, bar, ruler, pattern”), from regō (Latin “to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃réǵeti (“to straighten; right”), from the root *h₃reǵ- (Proto-Indo-European); see regent (English). .

chain.meaning: to keep straight, direct, govern, rule

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English reulen, rulen (Middle English), borrowed from Old French riuler, from Latin regulāre (“to regulate, rule”), from regula (Latin “a rule”); see regular (English) and regulate (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Related to revel (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English rumour, from Old French rumour, rumor (Old French), from Latin rūmor (“common talk”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *rewH- (“to shout, roar”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English runnen, rennen (Middle English “to run”), alteration (due to the past participle runne (Middle English), runnen (Middle English),
yronne (Middle English)) of rinnen (Middle English “to run”), from Old English rinnan, iernan (Old English “to run”) and Old Norse rinna (“to run”), both from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to boil, churn”).

Cognate with rin (Scots “to run”), rinne (Western Frisian “to walk, march”), archaic rinnen (Dutch) (“to flow”, still in geronnen (Dutch)), rinnen (German “to flow”), rinna (Swedish “to flow”), and renna (Icelandic “to flow”). From the causative *rannijaną (Proto-Germanic “to make run”) are rennen (Dutch), rennen (German), rende (Danish), ränna (Swedish) (all “to run”). Non-Germanic cognates include rend (Albanian “to run, run after”), راندن (Persian “to move, set in motion”). See also random (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French rural, from Latin rūrālis (“rural”), from rūs (Latin “countryside”) + -ālis (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Perhaps from Middle English ruschen, russchen (Middle English “to rush, startle, make a loud rushing noise”), from Old English hrysċan (“to jolt, startle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hurskijan, from Proto-Germanic *hurskijaną (“to startle, drive”), from *hurskaz (Proto-Germanic “fast, rapid, quick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run, hurry”).

Cognate with hursken (Old High German “to hurry, speed, incite, accelerate”), horsċ (Old English “quick, quick-witted, clever”), rosk (Old Frisian), rosch (Old Frisian “quick, rapid, sudden”).

An alternative etymology traces rush via Middle English ruschen (“to rush”) from *rūscian (Old English “to rush”) from Proto-Germanic *rūskōną (“to rush, storm, be fierce, be cruel”), a variant (with formative k) of Proto-Germanic *rūsōną (“to be cruel, storm, rush”) from Proto-Indo-European *(o)rewə- (“to drive, move, agitate”), making it akin to rosci (Old High German “rosc, rosci”), rûschen (Middle Low German “to rush”), ruschen (Middle High German “to rush”) (rauschen (German “to rush”)), ruse (North Frisian “to rush”), ruuscen (Middle Dutch “to make haste”), rusen (Middle Dutch “to rush”) (ruisen (Dutch “to rush”)), ruse (Danish “to rush”), rusa (Swedish “to rush”). Compare rūsch (Middle High German “a charge, rush”). Influenced by Middle English russhen (“to force back”) from russer (Anglo-Norman “russher, russer”) from ruser (Old French “ruser, rëuser”).

Alternatively, according to the OED, perhaps an adaptation of Anglo-Norman — russher (Old French), russer (Old French “to force back, down, out of place, by violent impact", "to pull out or drag off violently or hastily”), from Old French rehusser (“re(h)usser”), ruser (Old French) (although the connection of the forms with single -s- and double -ss- is dubious; also adopted in English ruse (English); French ruser (French “to retreat, drive back”)), from an assumed *refūsāre (Vulgar Latin) and Latin refundō (Old French “I cause to flow back”), although connection to the same gem — root is also possible. More at rouse (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English risshe, rusch (Middle English), risch (Middle English), from Old English rysċ, rysċe (Old English), risċ (Old English), risċe (Old English), from a merger of Proto-West Germanic *riskijā, from Proto-Indo-European *(H)resg- (“to weave”) and Proto-West Germanic *ruskijā, possibly borrowed from Latin rūscum (“butcher's broom”), of unknown origin + *-jā (Proto-West Germanic).

Cognates include risk (Western Frisian), rus (Dutch “bulrush”), rusk (Norwegian Bokmål), dialectal ryskje (Norwegian “hair-grass”). Further cognates include ро́зга (Russian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English rusty, from Old English rūstiġ (“rusty”), from Proto-Germanic *rustagaz (“rusty”), equivalent to rust + -y (English). Cognate with rusterch (Saterland Frisian “rusty”), rustich (Western Frisian), roastich (Western Frisian “rusty”), roestig (Dutch “rusty”), rusterig (Low German (Germany)), rüsterig (Low German (Germany) “rusty”), rostig (German “rusty”), rostig (Swedish “rusty”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: more often used for this, or from the general epithet rusty given to various particular firearm names—earlier both were applied in Cockney rhyming slang for other machines, including swords in their day, but the present coinage has not more than a loose connection to this and is from the preference for used or antique firearms due to their being easier or cheaper to obtain.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Variant form of resty (English); compare also reasty (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sak, sek (Middle English), sach (Middle English), zech (Middle English “bag, sackcloth”), from Old English sacc (“sack, bag”) and sæċċ (Old English “sackcloth, sacking”); both from Proto-West Germanic *sakku, from late Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), borrowed from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (“bag of coarse cloth”), from sem —, possibly Phoenician — or Hebrew.

Cognate with zak (Dutch), Sack (German), säck (Swedish), sæk (Danish), sekk (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), sekkur (Faroese / Icelandic), שַׂק (Hebrew “sack, sackcloth”), סַקָּא (Aramaic), ܣܩܐ (Syriac), ሠቅ (gez), 𒆭𒊓 (Akkadian), sꜣgꜣ (Egyptian). .

Černý and Forbes suggest the word was originally Egyptian, a nominal derivative of sꜣq (Egyptian “to gather or put together”) that also yielded ⲥⲟⲕ (Coptic “sackcloth”) and was borrowed into Greek perhaps by way of a Semitic intermediary. However, Vycichl and Hoch reject this idea, noting that such an originally Egyptian word would be expected to yield Hebrew rather than שַׂק (Hebrew). Instead, they posit that the Coptic and Greek words are both borrowed from Semitic, with the Coptic word perhaps developing via sꜣgꜣ (Egyptian).

* “Pillage” senses from the use of sacks in carrying off plunder. From Middle French sac, shortened from the phrase mettre à sac (“put it in a bag”), a military command to pillage; also parallel meaning with Italian sacco (“plunder”), from Medieval Latin — saccō (Latin “pillage”). From Vulgar Latin — saccare (Latin “to plunder”), from saccus (Latin “sack”). See also ransack (English). American football “tackle” sense from this “plunder, conquer” root.
* “Removal from employment” senses attested since 1825; the original formula was “to give (someone) the sack”, likely from the notion of a worker going off with his tools in a sack, or being given such a sack for his personal belongings as part of an expedient severance. Idiom exists earlier in French — (on luy a donné son sac, 17c.) and Middle Dutch — (iemand den zak geven). English verb in this sense recorded from 1841. Current verb, to sack (“to fire”) carries influence from the forceful nature of “plunder, tackle” verb senses.
* Slang meaning “bunk, bed” is attested since 1825, originally nautical, likely in reference to sleeping bags. The verb meaning “go to bed” is recorded from 1946.
* Slang meaning "scrotum" is an ellipsis of ballsack (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English salarie, from Anglo-Norman salarie, from Old French salaire, from Latin salārium (“wages”), the neuter form of the adjective salārius (Latin “related to salt”), from sal (Latin “salt”). There have been various attempts to explain how the Latin term for “wages” came from the adjective “related to salt”. It is generally assumed that salārium (Latin) was an abbreviation of salārium argentum (Latin “salt money”), though that phrase is not attested. A commonly cited theory states that the phrase meant “money consisting of salt”, because, supposedly, Roman soldiers were sometimes paid in salt, but there is no evidence for either of these claims from ancient sources. Another is that the phrase meant “money used to buy salt [and other miscellaneous items]”.

From Middle English sexe (“sex [distinction between male and female] and gender”), from Old French sexe (“genitals; gender”), from Latin sexus (“gender; gender traits; males or females; genitals”), from Proto-Italic *seksus, from Proto-Indo-European *séksus, from *sek- (Proto-Indo-European “to cut, cut off, sever”), thus meaning "section, division" (into male and female). etymologies.text:
From Middle English schare, schere (Middle English), from Old English sċearu (“a cutting, shaving, a shearing, tonsure, part, division, share”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaru, from Proto-Germanic *skarō (“a division, detachment”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut, divide”).

Cognate with skar (Saterland Frisian), sker (Saterland Frisian “a share in a communal pasture”), schare (Dutch “share in property”), Schar (German “band, troop, party, company”), skor (Icelandic “department”). Compare shard (English), shear (English). .

chain.meaning: a cutting, shaving, a shearing, tonsure, part, division, share

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English schar, schare (Middle English), from Old English sċear, sċær (Old English “ploughshare”), from Proto-Germanic *skaraz (“ploughshare”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut”). Cognate with schaar (Dutch “ploughshare”), dialectal Schar (German “ploughshare”), plovskær (Danish “(plov)skær”). More at shear (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English shark (used by in 1442 to refer to a kind of fish), of origin. Most likely from a semantic extension of the German —-derived , see below. The fish was originally called a dogfish (English) or haye (English) in English and Middle English. Its name in Old English is unknown, although some uses of the word hranfisċ (Old English) that do not appear to carry the sense of "whale (English)" may have been referencing it.

Some older dictionaries derived the word from carcharias (Latin “c(h)archarias”), carcharus (Latin “c(h)acharus”) (from - (Ancient Greek)), but admit that "the requisite [Old French] forms intermediate between E. shark and L. carcharus are not found, and it is not certain that the name [shark] was orig. applied to the fish; it may have been first used of a greedy man".

Other older authorities speculated that the word might derive from xok (yua “fish”) (), as John Hawkins brought a specimen from the area where Mayan was spoken to England in the 1560s. However, the 1442 use rules out a New World origin for the word.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From German Schurke (“scoundrel”); compare schurk (Dutch).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Probably from the "steal" senses above, but perhaps related to shear (English). Compare shirk (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English scharp, from Old English sċearp, from Proto-West Germanic *skarp, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (Proto-Indo-European “to cut”).

Cognate with skerp (Western Frisian), scherp (Low German), scharp (Low German), schaarp (Low German), scherp (Dutch), scharf (German), skarp (Danish). Compare cearb (Irish “keen; cutting”), acerbus (Latin “tart, bitter”), Tocharian B kärpye (xtb “rough”), Latvian skârbs (Lithuanian “sharp, rough”), Russian щерба (Russian “notch”), Polish szczerba (Polish “gap, dent, jag, chip, nick, notch”), Albanian harb (Albanian “rudeness”). More at shear (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English sharply, scharply (Middle English), from Old English sċearplīċe (“sharply, smartly”), equivalent to sharp + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English shaven, schaven (Middle English), from Old English sċafan (“to shave, scrape, shred, polish”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaban, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną (“to scrape”), from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to cut, split, form, carve”).

Cognate with skave (Western Frisian), schaven (Dutch), schaven (Low German), schaben (German), skave (Danish), skava (Norwegian Nynorsk), skava (Swedish), skafa (Icelandic), 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌽 (Gothic), all roughly “to scrape, chafe, shave, plane, remove the outer lay of”.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English shave, from Old English sceafa, from Proto-Germanic *skabô.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English scheden, schede (Middle English), from Old English scēadan, scādan (Old English “to separate, divide, part, make a line of separation between; remove from association or companionship; distinguish, discriminate, decide, determine, appoint; shatter, shed; expound; decree; write down; differ”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþan, from Proto-Germanic *skaiþaną (compare skiede (Western Frisian), - (Dutch) and scheiden (German)), from Proto-Indo-European *skeyt- (“to cut, part, divide, separate”), from *skey- (Proto-Indo-European).

See also scian (Irish “knife”), skėsti (Lithuanian “to spread”), skíesti (Lithuanian “to separate”), цѣдити (Church Slavonic “to filter, strain”), σχίζω (Ancient Greek “to split”), ցտեմ (Classical Armenian “to scratch”), च्यति (Sanskrit “he cuts off”)). Related to shoad (English), shit (English), sheath (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English sched, schede (Middle English), schad (Middle English), from a combination of Old English scēada (“a parting of the hair, top of the head”) and Old English ġesċēad (“distinction, reason”).

chain.meaning: a parting of the hair, top of the head

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Dialectal variant of a specialized use of shade (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schete; partly from Old English sċīete (“a sheet, a piece of linen cloth”); partly from Old English sċēata (“a corner, angle; the lower corner of a sail, sheet”); and Old English sċēat (“a corner, angle”); all from Proto-Germanic *skautijǭ, *skautaz (Proto-Germanic “corner, wedge, lap”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to throw, shoot, pursue, rush”).

Cognate with skut (North Frisian “the fold of a garment, lap, coattail”), skoat (Western Frisian “sheet; sail; lap”), schoot (Dutch “the fold of a garment, lap, sheet”), Schote (Low German (Germany) “a line from the foot of a sail”), Schoß (German “the fold of a garment, lap”), skød (Danish “lap, skirt”), skaut (Icelandic “the corner of a cloth, a line from the foot of a sail, the skirt or sleeve of a garment, a hood”), skaut (Norwegian “headdress”), sköt (Swedish “sheet”).

chain.meaning: a sheet, a piece of linen cloth
a corner, angle; the lower corner of a sail, sheet

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: A minced oath of shit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schelle, from Old English sċel, sċell (Old English), sċiell (Old English), sċil (Old English), sċill (Old English), sċyl (Old English), sċyll (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *skallju, from Proto-Germanic *skaljō (“shell; husk; rind; peel”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to cut; to separate, split”).

Cognate with schil (Dutch “bark, rind, skin; crust; shell; slice”), skæl (Danish “scale; dandruff”), skel (Faroese / Icelandic “shell”), skjell (Norwegian Bokmål “shell; scale”), skjel (Norwegian Nynorsk “shell; bivalve; scale; carapace”), 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌻𐌾𐌰 (Gothic “brick, tile”), écaille (French “scale; shell”), scae (Friulian “scale”), scaglia (Italian “scale; flake, sliver; splinter”); also killi (Breton “grove”), kelli (Cornish “grove”), coill (Irish “forest, wood”), keyll (Manx “forest, wood; grove, plantation”), coille (Scottish Gaelic “forest”), celli (Welsh “grove”), scalpō (Latin “to scratch; to carve”), σκᾰ́λλω (Ancient Greek “to hoe, stir up”), çel (Albanian “to open up; to sprout; to hatch up; to rise”), skelti (Lithuanian “to crack, split”), скала́ (Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian “cliff, rock”), skála (Czech “rock”), skała (Polish), skáła (Polish), szkała (Polish “rock”), skala (Slovak / Slovenian “rock”), скала́ (Ukrainian), ска́ля (Ukrainian “cliff, rock”), քաղել (Armenian “to pick; to gather; to mow”), कॢप् (Sanskrit “to order; to manage; to perform; to create; to cut”). More at shale (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sheltron, sheldtrume (Middle English “roof or wall formed by locked shields”), from Old English sċildtruma, sċyldtruma (Old English “a phalanx, company (of troops), a tortoise, a covering, shed, shelter”), from sċyld (Old English), sċield (Old English “shield”) + truma (Old English “a troop of soldiers”). Cognate with schilthrum (Scots), schiltrum (Scots). More at shield (English), and trymman (Old English “to strengthen”), from trum (Old English “strong, firm”) at trim (English).

Doublet of sheltron (a kind of military formation), which is the more conservative of the two.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The verb is from Middle English schiften, from Old English sċiftan (“to divide, separate into shares; appoint, ordain; arrange, organise”), from Proto-West Germanic *skiftijan, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną, *skiptijaną (Proto-Germanic), from earlier *skipatjaną (Proto-Germanic “to organise, put in order”), from Proto-Indo-European *skeyb- (“to separate, divide, part”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, divide, separate, part”). Cognate with schift (Scots), skift (Scots “to shift”), skifte (Western Frisian), skiftsje (Western Frisian “to sort”), schiften (Dutch “to sort, screen, winnow, part”), schichten (Low German “to stack, layer”), schichten (German “to stack, layer”), skifta (Swedish “to shift, change, exchange, vary”), skifte (Norwegian “to shift”), skipta (Icelandic “to switch”). See ship (English).

The noun is from Middle English schyft, shyffte (Middle English). Cognate with schift (Dutch “split, fissure”), Schicht (German “layer, shift”).

chain.meaning: to divide, separate into shares; appoint, ordain; arrange, organise

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English shinen, schinen (Middle English) (preterite schon (Middle English), past participle schinen (Middle English)), from Old English sċīnan , from Proto-West Germanic *skīnan (“to shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skīnaną (“to shine”).

Cognate with schijnen (Dutch), scheinen (German), skinne (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), skina (Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish), skína (Faroese / Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the noun shine (English), or perhaps continuing Middle English schinen in its causative uses, from Old English scīn (“brightness, shine”), and also Middle English schenen, from Old English scǣnan (“to render brilliant, make shine”), from Proto-Germanic *skainijaną, causative of *skīnaną (Proto-Germanic “to shine”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle Dutch schokken (“to push, jolt, shake, jerk”) or Middle French choquer (“to collide with, clash”), from Old Dutch *skokkan (“to shake up and down, shog”), from Proto-Germanic *skukkaną (“to move, shake, tremble”). Of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *skakaną (“to shake, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kek-, *(s)keg- (Proto-Indo-European “to shake, stir”); see shake (English).

Cognate with schocken (Middle Low German “collide with, deliver a blow to, move back and forth”), scoc (Old High German “a jolt, swing”), schocken (Middle High German “to swing”) (schaukeln (German)), skykkr (Old Norse “vibration, surging motion”), skykkjun (Icelandic “tremulously”), schiggen (Middle English “to shake”). .
etymologies.uncertainNote: Of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English schok, from Old English *sċoc or Middle Low German schok; in any case, from Proto-West Germanic *skok and possibly related to kàudze (Latvian) and kiūgis (Lithuanian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English scheten,schoten, from Old English scēotan, from Proto-West Germanic *skeutan, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European —, thematic present of *(s)kewd- (Proto-Indo-European “to shoot, throw”).

Cognate with sjitte (Western Frisian), scheten (Low German), schieten (Dutch), schießen (German), skyde (Danish), skyte (Norwegian Bokmål), skyta (Norwegian Nynorsk), skjuta (Swedish); and also, through Indo-European, with кида́ть (Russian), hedh (Albanian “to throw, toss”), چست (Persian “quick, active”), skudrùs (Lithuanian).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English shoting, schoting (Middle English), from Old English scotung (“shooting”), from Proto-Germanic *skutungō, equivalent to shoot + ing (English). Cognate with schieting (Dutch), Erschießung (German “shooting”), skjutning (Swedish “shooting”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English shoppe, schoppe (Middle English), from Old English sċoppa (“shed; booth; stall; shop”), from Proto-Germanic *skupp-, *skup- (Proto-Germanic “barn, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *skub-, *skup- (Proto-Indo-European “to bend, bow, curve, vault”). Cognate with schop (Dutch “shed”), Schuppen (German “shed”), Schober (German “barn”), échoppe (French “booth, shop”) (< Germanic). The verb is denominal. The noun senses “act of shopping”, “purchased items” are backformed from the verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From shop + keeper (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schore, from Old English *sċora (attested as sċor- in placenames), from Proto-Germanic *skurô (“rugged rock, cliff, high rocky shore”). Possibly related to sċieran (Old English “to cut”), which survives today as shear (English).

Cognate with scorre (Middle Dutch “land washed by the sea”), schor (Middle Low German “shore, coast, headland”), schorre (Middle High German) , and sjaor (Limburgish “riverbank”). Maybe connected with skjær (Norwegian Bokmål).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English shore (“a prop, a support”), from Middle Dutch schore, schare (Middle Dutch “a prop, a stay”) (modern schoor (Dutch)), and Middle Low German schōre, schāre (Middle Low German “a prop, a stay; barrier; stockade”) (compare skorða (Old Norse “a prop, a stay”) (skor (Norwegian), skorda (Norwegian))); further etymology unknown.

From Late Middle English shoren (“to prop, to support”), from Middle English shore (“a prop, a support”) (see etymology 2) + -en (Middle English); compare schooren (Middle Dutch “to prop up, support”) and schore (Middle Low German “to shovel; to sweep”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 6
etymologies.text: Uncertain. The word is attested in Northern English and Scots; the DSL states that schore "to threaten" is attested before 1400 (a corresponding noun schoyr is attested since 1375: "vith gret schoyr and mannasyng" in Barbour's Bruce), and suggests it might ultimately be related to Old Scots schoir "steep (of a crag)", related to shear. Alternatively, it has been suggested that it might be a variant of score (English) or sure (English) and related to assure (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schort, short (Middle English), from Old English sċeort, sċort (Old English “short”), from Proto-West Germanic *skurt, from Proto-Germanic *skurtaz (“short”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. .

Cognate with short (Scots), schort (Scots “short”), court (French), kort (Dutch), kurz (German), scurz (Old High German “short”) (whence schurz (Middle High German)), skorta (Old Norse “to lack”) (whence skorte (Danish)), shkurt (Albanian “short, brief”), curtus (Latin “shortened, incomplete”) and *kortъkъ (Proto-Slavic). See more at shirt (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English scholde, from Old English sċolde, first and third person preterite form of sċulan (Old English “should,” “have to,” “to owe”), the ancestor of shall (English). . Cognate with sollen (German “sollte”), 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐌻𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “𐍃𐌺𐌿𐌻𐌳𐌰”), skulle (Swedish). Related to shild (Middle English) and shildy (Middle English).

The loss of in this word is probably due to weak stress, as in would (English) and could (English) (though in the latter, the was due to the analogy of the former two).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English schuldre, sholder (Middle English), shulder (Middle English), schulder (Middle English), from Old English sċuldra, sċuldor (Old English “shoulder”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuldru (“shoulder”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to Proto-Germanic *skelduz (“shield”), see shield (English). Cognate with skuldere (Old Frisian “shoulder”) (skouder (Western Frisian “shoulder”)), scholder (Middle Low German “shoulder”), Schuller (Low German), Schulder (Low German “shoulder”), schouder (Dutch “shoulder”), Schulter (German “shoulder”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English shouten. Further origin . Possibly related to shooten (Middle English “to shoot (out)”) or from or akin to , skúti (Old Norse), skúta (Old Norse “a taunt”). See also the second, rare sense of the verb scout (English “to reject with contempt”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English shout (“shout(e)”), from Middle Dutch schûte (“boat or light ship”). , see there for more. Compare scout (English “swift sailing boat”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schewen, from Old English scēawian (“to look, look at, exhibit, display”), from Proto-West Germanic *skauwōn, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, see”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to heed, look, feel, take note of”); see haw (English), gaum (English), caveat (English), caution (English).

Cognate with shaw (Scots “to show”), schouwen (Dutch “to inspect, view”), schauen (German “to see, behold”), skue (Danish “to behold”). Related to sheen (English).

Wider cognates include κῦδος (Ancient Greek), caveō (Latin) whence caution (English) and caveat (English), कवि (Sanskrit “seer, prophet, bard”), *čuti (Proto-Slavic) (whence чу́ять (Russian) and many more).

chain.meaning: to look, look at, exhibit, display
