etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schour (“shower”), from Old English sċūr (“shower”), from Proto-West Germanic *skūru (“shower”), from Proto-Germanic *skūrō (“storm, short shower”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱēwer- (“north, north wind, cold wind, rain shower”).

Cognate with schoer (Dutch “downpour, heavy rainshower”), Schauer (German “shower”), - (Danish), - (Norwegian), and skur (Swedish “shower”), skúrur (Faroese “shower”), skúr (Icelandic “shower”), skur (Norn “squall”), 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐍂𐌰 (Gothic “storm”), coro (Italian “northwestern wind”), cauro (Spanish “northwestern wind”), се́вер (Belarusian), сі́вер (Belarusian), - (Bulgarian) and се́вер (Russian “north”), - (Czech) and sever (Slovak “north”), север (Macedonian “north”), sȅvēr (Serbo-Croatian), sjȅvēr (Serbo-Croatian “north”), sẹ́ver (Slovenian “north”), сі́вер (Ukrainian “cold, cold, bitter wind”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English schewere, schewer (Middle English), shewere (Middle English “one who exhibits something, actor; watchman; sign; mirror; index finger”), from Old English sċēawere (“an observer, one who examines into a matter; a spy; mirror; actor, buffoon”), equivalent to . Cognate with schouwer (Dutch “observer, visionary, clairvoyant”), Schauer (German “an inspector”).

chain.meaning: an observer, one who examines into a matter; a spy; mirror; actor, buffoon

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schrynken, from Old English sċrincan, from Proto-Germanic *skrinkwaną. Cognate with schrinken (Dutch “to shrink”).

The sense is a head-shrinker.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English schitten, schetten (Middle English), from Old English sċyttan (“to cause rapid movement, shoot a bolt, shut, bolt”), from Proto-West Germanic *skuttjan, from Proto-Germanic *skutjaną, *skuttijaną (Proto-Germanic “to bar, bolt”), from Proto-Germanic *skuttą, *skuttjō (Proto-Germanic “bar, bolt, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd- (“to drive, fall upon, rush”). The Modern English word was originally a dialect form; the Old English word would have normally merged with shit (English).

Cognate with schutten (Dutch “to shut in, lock up”), schütten (Low German “to shut, lock in”), schützen (German “to shut out, dam, protect, guard”).

chain.meaning: to cause rapid movement, shoot a bolt, shut, bolt

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Variation of chute (English) or shute (English) (archaic, related to shoot (English)) from Old English scēotan.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English shy (“shy”), from Old English sċēoh (“shy”), from Proto-West Germanic *skeuh (“shy, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, fearful”). Cognate with skjou (Saterland Frisian “shy”), schuw (Dutch “shy”), scheu (German “shy”), sky (Danish “shy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English sikness, from Old English sēocnes, sēocness (Old English), sēocnys (Old English), sēocnyss (Old English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English side, from Old English sīde (“side, flank”), from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ (“side, flank, edge, shore”), derived from *sīdaz (Proto-Germanic), probably from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). Cognate with Siede (Saterland Frisian “side”), side (Western Frisian “side”), zijde (Dutch), zij (Dutch “side”), Sied (Low German (Germany) “side”), Seite (German “side”), side (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “side”), sida (Swedish “side”).

The LGBTQ slang sense was and popularized in 2013. The sense was coined by analogy with top (English) and bottom (English) and based on the metaphor of a box which has a top, bottom, and sides.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English side, syde (Middle English), syd (Middle English), from Old English sīd (“wide, broad, spacious, ample, extensive, vast, far-reaching”), from Proto-West Germanic *sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīdaz (“drooping, hanging, low, excessive, extra”), from Proto-Indo-European *sēy- (“to send, throw, drop, sow, deposit”). Cognate with obsolete zijd (Dutch “wide, vast”), sied (Low German “low”), sid (Swedish “long, hanging down”), síður (Icelandic “low hanging, long”).

chain.meaning: wide, broad, spacious, ample, extensive, vast, far-reaching

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English sighen (“to sigh”), from sighte (Middle English), past tense form of siken (Middle English), from Old English sīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *sīkan, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“to pour out”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English sighe (“sigh”), from sighen (Middle English “to sigh”) (see #Etymology 1).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sighte, from Old English sihþ (“something seen; vision”), from Proto-West Germanic *sihti (“seeing, sight”), equivalent to see + t (English).

Cognate with gazicht (Cimbric “sight, vision; pupil”), gezicht (Dutch “face; sight, vision”), zicht (Dutch “sight, vision”), Gesicht (German “face; sight, vision”), Sicht (German “view; sight; visibility”), Gesiicht (lb “face”), Siicht (lb “view; sight”), געזיכט (Yiddish “face”), sigt (Danish “sight; visibility”), sikt (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “visibility”), sikt (Swedish “visibility”), sikte (Swedish “sight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English signe, sygne (Middle English), syng (Middle English), seine (Middle English), sine (Middle English), syne (Middle English), from Old English seġn (“sign; mark; token”) and Old French signe, seing (Old French “sign; mark; signature”); both from Latin signum (“a mark; sign; token”); root uncertain. . Partially displaced native token (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English signen, seinen (Middle English), seinien (Middle English), partly from Old English seġnian (“to mark; sign”) and partly from Anglo-Norman en (“seigner”), seiner (English) et al., et al., and their source Latin signare (“signāre”); all from Latin signum (“a mark, sign”); see Etymology 1, above. Compare sain (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French segnal, seignal (Old French) or Medieval Latin signāle; noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum; verb use from 1805, as a shortened from signalize (1650s). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French signature, or from Medieval Latin signātūra, future active periphrastic of verb signo (Latin “signāre”) from signum (Latin “sign”), + -tūra (Latin), feminine of -tūrus (Latin), future active periphrastic suffix. Displaced native handseten (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin significans, present participle of significare (Latin), from signum (Latin “sign”) + ficare (Latin “do, make”), variant of facere (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: significant + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From sign + post (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English silence, from Old French silence, from Latin silentium (“silence”), from silēns + -ium (Latin). Displaced native swīġe (Old English) and sālnes (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin silēns (“silent”), present participle of sileō (Latin “be silent”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyl- (“still, windless, quiet, slow”). Related to Gothic 𐌰𐌽𐌰𐍃𐌹𐌻𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to cease, grow still, be silent”), Old English sālnes (Old English “silence”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: silent + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English silk, sylk (Middle English), selk (Middle English), selc (Middle English), from Old English sioloc, seoloc (Old English), seolc (Old English “silk”). The immediate source is uncertain; it probably reached English via the Baltic trade routes (cognates in silki (Old Norse) (> silke (Danish), silke (Swedish “silk”)), шёлк (Russian), obsolete zilkaĩ (Lithuanian)), all ultimately from Late Latin sēricus, from Ancient Greek σηρικός, ultimately from an Oriental language (represented now by e.g. 絲 (Chinese “silk”)). Displaced sīde (Old English “silk”). Compare Seres (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English seely, seli (Middle English “sēlī”), from Old English sǣliġ, ġesǣliġ (Old English “lucky, fortunate”), from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg, from *sāli (Proto-West Germanic); equivalent to seel + -y (English). .

The semantic evolution is “lucky” to “innocent” to “naive” to “foolish”. Compare the similar evolution of daft (English) (originally meaning “accommodating”), and almost the reverse with nice (English) (originally meaning “ignorant”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From French similaire, from Medieval Latin similaris, extended from Latin similis (“like”); akin to simul (Latin “together”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From . Morphologically similar + ity (English)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English symple, from Old French simple, from Latin simplex (“simple”) (as opposed to duplex (Latin “double”)), from semel (Latin “the same”) + plicō (Latin “to fold”). See same and fold. Compare single, singular, simultaneous, etc. Partially displaced native English onefold (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English symply, symplely (Middle English); equivalent to simple + -ly (English), with simplified to by haplology.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: simultaneous + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English syns, synnes (Middle English), contraction of earlier sithens (Middle English), sithence (Middle English), from sithen (Middle English “after, since”) ( + -s (Middle English), adverbial genitive suffix), from Old English sīþþan, from the phrase , from sīþ (Old English “since, after”) + þǣm (Old English) dative singular of þæt (Old English). Cognate with sinds (Dutch “since”), seit (German “since”), siden (Danish “since”), síðan (Icelandic “since”) syne (Scots “since”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English single, sengle (Middle English), from Old French sengle, saingle (Old French), sangle (Old French), from Latin singulus, a diminutive derived from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one”). Akin to simplex (Latin “simple”). See simple (English), and compare singular (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English synken, from Old English sincan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷ- (“to fall, sink”).

Compare sinke (Western Frisian), sinken (Low German), zinken (Dutch), sinken (German), synke (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), sjunka (Swedish). In the causative sense, it replaced senċan (Old English “make sink”) from *sankwijaną (Proto-Germanic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire (Middle English), borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (Latin “old”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English suster-in-lawe; equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sitten, from Old English sittan, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”).

Cognate with sitte (Western Frisian), sitten (Low German), zitten (Dutch), sitzen (German), sitta (Swedish), sitte (Norwegian Bokmål), sitja (Norwegian Nynorsk), sidde (Danish), sita (Faroese), sitja (Icelandic); and with suigh (Irish), sedeo (Latin), сиде́ть (Russian).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English site, from Anglo-Norman site, from Latin situs (“position, place, site”), from sino (Latin “sinere”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English situacioun, situacion (Middle English), from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio (“position, situation”), from situare (Latin “to locate, place”), from . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: from Dutch schaats, from Middle Dutch schāetse, from Old Northern French — escache (Old French “a stilt, trestle”) (compare échasse (French) and scatch (English)), from a gem — language, perhaps Frankish *skakkjā (“stilt”), related to *skakan (Frankish “to shake, swing”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|A drawing of a cuckoo skate (w:Leucoraja|Leucoraja naevus)

From Middle English skat, scate (Middle English) (also schat (Middle English)), from Old Norse skata (“skate”). Cognate with skata (Icelandic “skate, ray”), skate (Norwegian “skate”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Origin , but probably related to skite (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From New Latin sceleton, from Ancient Greek σκελετός (“σκελετόν”), the neuter of σκελετός (Ancient Greek “dried up, withered, dried body, parched, mummy”), from σκέλλω (Ancient Greek “dry, dry up, make dry, parch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”); compare σκληρός (Ancient Greek “hard”).

chain.meaning: dry, dry up, make dry, parch

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The etymology of the term is disputed between two versions.
* From the sled used, which originally was a bare frame, like a skeleton.
* From Norwegian kjaelke through a bad anglicization as "skele".
etymologies.uncertainNote: The etymology of the term is disputed between two versions.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Norwegian — ski (Norwegian Bokmål), from Old Norse skíð (“stick of wood, snowshoe”), from Proto-Germanic *skīdą (“stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to cut, split”) (see also shed (English)). Cognate with sċīd (Old English “stick of wood”) (modern ), skit (Old High German) (Modern Scheit (German “log”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English skill, skille (Middle English) (also schil (Middle English), schile (Middle English)), from Old Norse skil (“a distinction, discernment, knowledge”), from Proto-Germanic *skilją (“separation, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cut”). Cognate with skel (Danish “a separation, boundary, divide”), skäl (Swedish “reason”), verschil (Dutch “difference”) and schillen (Dutch “to separate the outer layer () from the product”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English skilen (also schillen (Middle English)), partly from Old English scilian (“to separate, part, divide off”); and partly from Old Norse skilja (“to divide, separate”); both from Proto-Germanic *skilōną, *skiljaną (Proto-Germanic “to divide, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cut”). Cognate with skille (Danish “to separate, discard”), skilja (Swedish “to distinguish, differentiate, part”), skilja (Icelandic “to understand”), schelen (Low German “to make a difference; to be squint-eyed”), schelen (Dutch “to make a difference”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Affix: skill + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English skyn, skinn (Middle English), from Old English scinn, from Old Norse skinn (“animal hide”), from Proto-Germanic *skinþą, from Proto-Indo-European *sken- (“to split off”), nasal variant of *skeh₁i-d- (Proto-Indo-European “to cut”). Partially displaced native Old English hȳd (Old English “skin, hide”), from which derives hide (English).

Cognate with schinde (Dutch “bark”), dialectal German Schinde (German “fruit peel”); also skant (Breton “scales”), cenn (Old Irish “covering, shell”), scáin (Irish “to tear, burst”), scindō (Latin “to split, divide”), छिनत्ति (Sanskrit “to split”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English skippen, skyppen (Middle English), of gmq — origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skupjaną, perhaps related to *skeubaną (Proto-Germanic “to drive, push”), iterative *skuppōną (Proto-Germanic “to push/move repeatedly, skip”), from Proto-Indo-European *ksewbʰ- (“*skewbʰ-”).

Related to skopa (Icelandic “to take a run”), skuppa (gmq-osw “to skip”), modern dialectal skopa (Swedish), skimpa (Swedish “to skip, leap”), and shove (English). See also dialectal skimp (English “to mock”) (Etymology 1), considered by some to be related.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English skep, skeppe (Middle English), from Old English sceppe, from Old Norse skeppa, skjappa (Old Norse “basket, bushel, measure”), perhaps from Middle Low German scheppe (“a unit of weight”), perhaps related to schēpel (Middle Low German “buschel, measurement for grain”), Scheffel (German “bushel”). These could all ultimately be related to *skap (Proto-West Germanic “shape”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Late Middle English skipper, borrowed from Middle Dutch — and Middle Low German schipper (“captain”), earlier "seaman", from schip (Dutch “ship”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: A reference to the television series Skippy the Bush Kangaroo; coined and used by Australians (particularly children) of non-British descent to counter derogatory terms aimed at them. Ultimately from etymology 1 (above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: 17th-century Ireland. Possibly a skip-kennel + young lackey or assistant (English). Used at .

etymologies.label: Etymology 6
etymologies.text: skip-level manager.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English *slammen (not recorded), apparently from a Scandinavian source ultimately from Old Norse slæma, slœma (Old Norse “to slam, swing a weapon, strike an object out of reach”), related to slamra (Old Norse), slambra (Old Norse “to slam”). Cognate with slamre (Norwegian Bokmål “to slam”), slamra (Swedish “to pound, beat, make a clatter, rattle”), slamra (Norwegian Nynorsk “to sway, dangle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: and long-speculated, though perhaps at least reinforced by Etymology 1. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compare slomp (Dutch), Schlampe (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English slappen, of origin, possibly . Compare Slappe (Low German “slap”), whence also Schlappe (German “defeat”). Compare also sleppa (Italian “slap”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Late Middle English —, originally a verb of uncertain etymology. Perhaps of origin, or possibly from Old French esclachier (“to break in pieces”), a variant of esclater (Old French), which is likely a gem — borrowing, from Frankish *slītan (“to slit, tear”).

Used in the as slascht (see 1 Kings 5:18) but otherwise unattested until 16th century. Conjunctive use from various applications of the punctuation mark ⟨/⟩. See also slash fiction (English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: Late Middle English —, originally a verb of uncertain etymology.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: . Compare slash (Scots “large splash”), possibly from esclache (Old French). Slang use for urination attested from the 1950s.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
. Compare British dialectal slashy (English “wet and dirty, miry”) and slash (Scots “act of walking forcefully through water or mud”) and slatch (Scots “wet and muddy place, mire”). Perhaps related to slask (Swedish “slush”).

Compare also slash (English “clearing in a forest”): in many cases it is difficult to tell whether that sense or this one is meant. (Also compare flash (English “a marsh; a pool of water”).)

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: See slatch (English)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English sclave, from Old French esclave, from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“Slav”), traditionally assumed to be because Slavs were often forced into slavery in the Middle Ages. The Latin word is from Medieval Greek Σκλάβος; see that entry and Slav (English) for more. Displaced native þēow (Old English). thrall (English “Thrall”) and bondsman (English)/bondswoman (English), however, remain common synonyms. .

An alternative hypothesis derives sclavus (Latin) from Ancient Greek σκῡλεύω, σκῡλάω (Ancient Greek “to strip or despoil a slain enemy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English slepen, from Anglian Old English slēpan (slǣpan (ang-wsx)), from Proto-West Germanic *slāpan, from Proto-Germanic *slēpaną (“to sleep”).

Cognate with sleepe (North Frisian), sliap (North Frisian), sliip (North Frisian), släipe (North Frisian “to sleep”), släipe (Saterland Frisian “to sleep”), sliepe (Western Frisian “to sleep”), schlaaffe (Alemannic), schlaafä (Alemannic), schlafe (Alemannic), schloafe (Alemannic), schloafen (Alemannic), schlofe (Alemannic), schlàfu (Alemannic “to sleep”), schlofn (Bavarian), schlåfn (Bavarian), sghlofn (Bavarian “to sleep”), schlofe (Central Franconian “to sleep”), slaafan (Cimbric), slafan (Cimbric), slavan (Cimbric “to sleep”), slapen (Dutch / Low German “to sleep”), schlafen (German “to sleep”), schloëpe (Limburgish), slaope (Limburgish “to sleep”), schlofen (lb “to sleep”), schloven (mhn “to sleep”), šłȫfa (Ripuarian), śłöfa (Ripuarian “to sleep”), שלאָפֿן (Yiddish “to sleep”), schlipen (gme-cgo “to sleep”), 𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to sleep”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English slepe, sleep (Middle English), sleepe (Middle English), from Old English slǣp (“sleep”), from Proto-West Germanic *slāp, from Proto-Germanic *slēpaz (“sleep”).

Cognate with slepe (Yola “sleep”), Släip (Saterland Frisian “sleep”), sliep (Western Frisian “sleep”), slaap (Dutch “sleep”), Schlaf (German “sleep”), Schlof (lb “sleep”), šłȫf (Ripuarian), śłöf (Ripuarian “sleep”), שלאָף (Yiddish “sleep”), 𐍃𐌻𐌴𐍀𐍃 (Gothic “sleep”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English slepy, from Old English *slǣpiġ (attested in unslǣpiġ (Old English “sleepless”)), from Proto-West Germanic *slāpag (“sleepy”), equivalent to sleep + -y (English). Cognate with släipich (Saterland Frisian “sleepy”), sliepich (Western Frisian “sleepy”), dialectal slapig (Dutch), slepig (Dutch “sleepy”), slapig (Low German (Germany)), släpig (Low German (Germany)), slöpig (Low German (Germany) “sleepy”), archaic schlafig (German “sleepy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sleve, slefe (Middle English), from Old English slīef and slīefe (Old English “sleeve”). Cognate with Sleeuwe (Saterland Frisian “sleeve”), slúf (Western Frisian), sloof (Dutch “apron”), sluve (Low German), dialectal Schlaube (German).

The Canadian sense of “measure smaller than a pint” is due to a former conflict between federal law and provincial law in British Columbia. According to federal law, a pint must be 20 imperial ounces (~568 ml), but according to provincial law at the time, the maximum individual serving size was 500 ml, so an individual portion could not be called a “pint” in British Columbia, and required a different term. The provincial law has been changed, allowing servings of up to 24 oz (~682 ml), but the term remains in use. The term sleeve itself for a cylindrical glass of beer is also found in the UK and Australia (as sleever (English)), and may be due to stacked glasses resembling a sleeve.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English sclise, sklise (Middle English), from Old French esclice, esclis (Old French “a piece split off”), deverbal of esclicer (Old French), esclicier (Old French “to splinter, split up”), from Frankish *slitjan (“to split up”), from Proto-Germanic *slitjaną, from Proto-Germanic *slītaną (“to split, tear apart”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyd- (“to rend, injure, crumble”). Akin to sliz (Old High German), gisliz (Old High German “a tear, rip”), slīȥan (Old High German “to tear”), slītan (Old English “to split up”), modern éclisse (French). More at slite, slit.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English slight (“bad, of poor quality, unimportant, trivial, slender, slim, smooth, level”), from Old English sliht (“smooth, level”), from Proto-Germanic *slihtaz (“slippery, flat, level, plain”), related to slick (English). Cognate with slicht (Scots “bad, of poor quality”), sljocht (Western Frisian “smooth, level, plain, simple”), slecht (Dutch “bad”), slecht (Low German “bad”), schlecht (German “bad”) and schlicht (German “plain, artless, natural”), slet (Danish “bad, evil, poor, nasty, wrong”), slät (Swedish “smooth”), slett (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “even”), sléttur (Icelandic “even, smooth, level”).

chain.meaning: bad, of poor quality, unimportant, trivial, slender, slim, smooth, level

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: slight + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English slippen, probably from Middle Low German slippen, from Old Saxon *slippian, from Proto-West Germanic *slippjan, from Proto-Germanic *slipjaną (“to glide”), an iterative form of *slīpaną (Proto-Germanic “to slip, slide”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyb- (“slimy; to slide”). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *slewbʰ- (“slip, slide”), or related to Proto-Germanic *slībaną (“to split”); related to slipor (Old English “slippery”).

Cognate with slipje (Saterland Frisian “to slip”), slippen (Dutch “to slip”), slippen (Low German (Germany)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Probably from Middle Dutch slippe or Middle Low German slippe, probably ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *slīban (“to split”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English slyp, slep (Middle English), slyppe (Middle English), from Old English slyp, slyppe (Old English), slipa (Old English “a viscous, slimy substance”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-West Germanic *sleupan, from Proto-Germanic *sleupaną (“to slip, sneak”), possibly connected with Proto-Indo-European *slewb-, *slewbʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “slip, slide”), from Proto-Indo-European *sel- (“to sneak, crawl”); or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *slippijaną (“to glide”), from Proto-Indo-European *sleyb- (“slimy; to glide”).

Compare slūpan (Old English “to slip, glide”), cūslyppe (Old English), cūsloppe (Old English “cowslip”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English slyp, slep (Middle English), slyppe (Middle English), from Old English slyp, slyppe (Old English), slipa (Old English “a viscous, slimy substance”), of uncertain origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From aslope (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English slaw, slow (Middle English), from Old English slāw (“lazy; inert, slow”), from Proto-West Germanic *slaiw, from Proto-Germanic *slaiwaz (“blunt; dull; exhausted, faint, sluggish, weak, weary; listless, torpid; dim-witted, slow; lazy, slack”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leyH- (“*sleyH-u-”).

Cognate with slee (Dutch), sleeuw (Dutch “cramped, stiff; blunt; sour”), sløv (Danish “blunt; dull; apathetic, lethargic, listless, sluggish, torpid; drowsy”), sljór (Icelandic “dim-witted; blunt; jaded”), sljo (Norwegian Nynorsk), slø (Norwegian Nynorsk), sløv (Norwegian Nynorsk “blunt; weak; lazy”), slö (Swedish “dull; lazy, lethargic, slow, sluggish”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English smerten, from Old English *smeortan (“to smart”), from Proto-West Germanic *smertan, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną (“to hurt, ache”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with smert (Scots), smarten (Dutch), schmerzen (German), smerte (Danish), smärta (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English smert, smart (Middle English), from Old English smeart (“smarting, smart, painful”), from Proto-West Germanic *smart, from Proto-Germanic *smartaz (“hurting, aching”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with smert (Scots “painful, smart”), smert (Old Frisian “sharp, painful”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English smerte, from smerten (Middle English “to smart”); see above. Cognate with smert (Scots), smart (Dutch), smart (Low German), Schmerz (German), smerte (Danish), smärta (Swedish). More above.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: , probably of onomatopoeia onomatopoeic origin. Compare smask (Swedish “to smack with the lips”), dialectal smaska (Swedish “to smack, kiss”), smaske (Danish “to smack with the lips”), smaksen (Low German “to smack with the lips, kiss”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English smellen, smillen (Middle English), smyllen (Middle English), smullen (Middle English), from Old English *smyllan, *smiellan (Old English “to smell, emit fumes”), from Proto-West Germanic *smallijan (“to glow, burn, smoulder”), from Proto-Indo-European *smel- (“to burn, smoke, smoulder; tar, pitch”). The noun is from Middle English smel, smil (Middle English), smul (Middle English “smell, odour”). Related to smeele (Saterland Frisian “to smoulder”), smolen (Middle Dutch “smōlen”) (whence smeulen (Dutch “to smoulder”)), smölen (Middle Low German “to be hazy, be dusty”) (whence smölen (Low German “smoulder”)), smullen (Low German “emit smoke”), smoel (Flemish “stuffy, muggy, hazy”), smul (Danish “dust, powder”), smilkyti (Lithuanian “to incense, fumigate”), smilkti (Lithuanian “to smudge, smolder, fume, reek”), smalkinti (Lithuanian “to fume”), smál (mga), smól (mga), smúal (mga “fire, gleed, embers, ashes”), смола́ (Russian “resin, tar”). Compare smoulder (English), smother (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English snesen (“to sneeze”), alteration of earlier fnesen (Middle English “to sneeze”), from Old English fnēosan (“to sneeze, snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *fneusan, from Proto-Germanic *fneusaną, from Proto-Indo-European *pnew- (“to breathe, pant, snort, sneeze”). Cognate with dialectal fniezen (Dutch “to sneeze”), fnýsa (Old Norse “to snort”).

Compare neeze (English), from nesen (Middle English), from *hnēosan (Old English “to sneeze”), cognate with niosan (Old High German “to sneeze”), hnjósa (Old Norse “to sneeze”). See neeze (English).

It has been suggested that the change could be due to a misinterpretation of the uncommon initial sequence fn- as ſn- (sn- written with a long s), although the change is regular, seen also in snore (English) and snort (English) from fnoren (Middle English) and fnorten (Middle English), and in late snatted (Middle English) from earlier fnatted (Middle English “snub-nosed”). The fn- forms of all these words fell out of use in the 1400s. Due to this rather universal adoption of the fn- > sn- shift within English by such a time frame, the idea of it being a simple sound shift has been suggested as well, with it specifically being a type of assimilation as the labial f- becomes alveolar s- to match the place of articulation of the following n-.

etymologies.label: Etymology

Compare also *snarkōn (Proto-West Germanic), snorren (Middle Low German “to drone”), snorren (Dutch “to hum, purr”).

The change fn → sn in this word is regular, seen also in sneeze (English), from fnesen (Middle English) (see sneeze (English) for more).

etymologies.label: Etymology

From Middle English speke, speken (Middle English “to speak”), from Old English specan (“to speak”). This is usually taken to be an irregular alteration of earlier sprecan (Old English), spreocan (Old English “to speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *sprekan, from Proto-Germanic *sprekaną (“to speak, make a sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *spreg- (“to make a sound, utter, speak”). Finding this proposed loss of r from the stable cluster spr unparalleled, Hill instead sets up a different root, Proto-West Germanic *spekan (“to negotiate”) from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂g- (“to distribute”) with *s-mobile, which collapsed in meaning with *sprekan ("to speak" < "to crackle, prattle") and so came to be seen as a free variant thereof.

Cognate with speak (Scots), speik (Scots “to speak”), spreke (Saterland Frisian “to speak”), sprekke (Western Frisian “to speak”), sjprèche (Central Franconian “to speak”), spreken (Dutch / Low German “to speak”), sprechen (German “to speak”), spriechen (lb “to speak”), and also with shpreh (Albanian “to express, manifest, show”) through Indo-European.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English speden, from Old English spēdan (“to speed, prosper, succeed, have success”), from Proto-West Germanic *spōdijan (“to succeed”).

Cognate with spede (Scots), speid (Scots “to meet with success, assist, promote, accomplish, speed”), spoeden (Dutch “to hurry, rush”), spoden (Low German), spöden (Low German “to hasten, speed”), sputen (German), spuden (German “to speed”).

chain.meaning: to speed, prosper, succeed, have success

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English spice, from Old French espice (modern épice (French)), from Late Latin speciēs (“spice, good, ware”), from Latin speciēs (“kind, sort”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Formed by analogy with lice (English) and mice (English) as the plurals of louse (English) and mouse (English).
First attested use Christopher Morley in “Morley's Magnum” (1935).
Made popular by in ' (1973).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: spice + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English spithre, spider (Middle English), from Old English spīþra (“spider”), from Proto-West Germanic *spinþrijō, from Proto-Germanic *spinnaną (“to spin”). Mostly displaced attercop (English “spider, unpleasant person”), now a dialectal term.

Compare typologically *mězgyrь (Proto-Slavic) (whence мизги́рь (Russian)) (akin to mežģīt (Latvian)), örümcek (Turkish) (akin to örmek (Turkish)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English spillen, from Old English spillan, spildan (Old English “to kill, destroy, waste”), from Proto-West Germanic *spilþijan, from Proto-Germanic *spilþijaną (“to spoil, kill, murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to sunder, split, rend, tear”).

Cognate with spillen (Dutch “to use needlessly, waste”), gaspiller (French) , spillen (Bavarian “to split, cleave, splinter”), spilde (Danish “to spill, waste”), spilla (Swedish “to spill, waste”), spilla (Icelandic “to contaminate, spoil”). See also spool (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English spinach, from Anglo-Norman spinache, from Old French espinoche, from pro espinarc, from Arabic إِسْفَانَاخ, from Classical Persian اسپناخ.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English spirit, from Old French espirit (“spirit”), from Latin spīritus (“breath; spirit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”). Compare inspire (English), respire (Latin), transpire (Latin), all ultimately from Latin spīrō (Latin “to breathe, blow, respire”). In this sense, displaced native gast (Middle English) (from gāst (Old English)), whence modern ghost (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English spiritual, spirituel (Middle English), from Old French spirituel, from Late Latin spīrituālis, from Latin spīritus. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Probably an alteration of plash (English) (compare spatter (English), spill (English) for the initial s-).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Attested since about 1567, from Middle Dutch splitten (“to split”) and/or Middle Low German splitten (“to split”), both ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *splittjan, an intensive form of Proto-West Germanic *splītan (“to split”), from Proto-Germanic *splītaną (whence splitte (Danish), splieten (Low German), spleißen (German)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pley- (“to split, splice”).

Compare ysplett (Middle English “split”), speld (Old English “splinter”), spaltan (Old High German “to split”), slis (mga “splinter”), spaliai (Lithuanian “flax sheaves”), půl (Czech “half”), расплитати (Church Slavonic “рас-плитати”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English spoilen, spuylen (Middle English), borrowed from Old French espoillier, espollier (Old French), espuler (Old French), from Latin spoliō (“pillage, ruin, spoil”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Affix: sport + -s

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: sport + -s

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English spot, spotte (Middle English), partially from Middle Dutch spotte (“spot, speck”), and partially merging with Middle English splot, from Old English splott (“spot, plot of land”), from Proto-West Germanic *splott, from Proto-Germanic *spluttaz (“segment”), from Proto-Indo-European *splt-no- (“an off-split, segment”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to split”).

Cognate with spot (North Frisian “speck, piece of ground”), spot (Low German “speck”), spotti (Old Norse “small piece”). See also splot (English), splotch (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle Dutch spraien (“sprāien”), sprayen (Middle Dutch), spraeyen (Middle Dutch “to spray, sprinkle, spread”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sprēwijaną (“to spray, sprinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per- (“to sow, scatter”).

Cognate with spræjen (Middle High German), spræwen (Middle High German “to squirt, spray, dust, splash, straw”), Danish dialectal språe (Danish “to open up, burst forth”), Swedish dialectal språ (Swedish “to sprout, shoot forth, burst”), Norwegian dialectal spra (Norwegian), spræ (Norwegian “to splash, splatter, spout, burst forth”), sproeien (Dutch “to spray, sprinkle”), sprühen (German “to spray, sparkle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English spray, from Old English *spræġ, sprei (Old English) (found in place names such as that of , England), of unknown origin. Compare sprig (English “shoot, twig”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English spray, from Old English *spræġ, sprei (Old English) (found in place names such as that of , England), of unknown origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English spreden, from Old English sprǣdan (“to spread, expand”), from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną (“to spread”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per- (“to strew, sow, sprinkle”).

Cognate with spreede (Saterland Frisian “to spread”), spriede (Western Frisian “to spread”), spriedjen (North Frisian “to spread”), spreiden (Dutch “to spread”), spreden (Low German “to spread”), spreiten (German “to spread, spread out”), sprede (Danish “to spread”), spre (Norwegian), spreie (Norwegian “to spread, disseminate”), sprida (Swedish “to spread”), spernō (Latin), spargō (Latin), σπείρω (Ancient Greek), سپردن (Persian “to deposit”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: speed + read (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From spread + sheet (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English spien, aphetic variant of earlier espien (Middle English “to espy”), from Old French espier (“to spy”), from Frankish *spehōn (“to spy”), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”). Akin to spähen (German “to spy”), spieden (Dutch “to spy”).

The noun displaced native sċēawere (Old English), which was also the word for "mirror." In this sense, the verb displaced sċēawian (Old English), which was also the word for "to watch" and became the Modern English word show (English).

Distant cognate vie PIE with speculātor (Latin), κατάσκοπος (Ancient Greek).

Compare typologically согляда́тай (Russian) (akin to гляде́ть (Russian)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English squachen, squatchen (Middle English), from Old French esquacher, escachier (Old French), from Vulgar Latin *excoāctiāre, from Latin ex + coāctāre (Latin). Probably influenced by quashen (Middle English), quassen (Middle English), from esquasser (Old French), escasser (Old French “to crush, shatter, destroy, break”), from *exquassare (Vulgar Latin), from ex- (Latin) + quassare (Latin “to shatter”) (see quash (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shortening of Narragansett askutasquash (“[a vegetable] eaten green (or raw)”), from askut + asquash (Narragansett).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: musquash.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From earlier squize (English), squise (English) (whence also dialectal English squizzen (English) and squeege (English)), first attested around 1600, further origin ; probably an alteration of quease (English) (which is attested since 1550), from Middle English queisen (“to squeeze”), from Old English cwȳsan (“to crush, squeeze”), itself also of unknown origin, perhaps imitative (compare qväsa (Swedish), kväsa (Swedish “to squeeze, bruise, crush; quell”), kwetsen (Dutch “to injure, hurt”), quetschen (German “to squeeze”)). Or, a blend of obsolete squiss (English “to squeeze”) (whence also squash (English) and squish (English)) with quease. Compare also esquicher (French) from esquichar (pro “to press, squeeze”).

The slang expression "to put the squeeze on (someone or something)", meaning "to exert influence", is from 1711. The baseball term "squeeze play" is first recorded 1905. "Main squeeze" ("most important person") is attested from 1896, the specific meaning "one's sweetheart, lover" is attested in 1970s.

The nonstandard strong forms squoze (English) and squozen (English), attested dialectally since at least the mid-19th century, are by analogy with freeze (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
First attested in Scottish English (compare stob (Scots), stobbe (Scots), stabb (Scots “a pointed stick or stake; a thrust with a pointed weapon”)), from Middle English stabbe (“a stab”), probably a variant of Middle English stob, stub (Middle English), stubbe (Middle English “pointed stick, stake, thorn, stub, stump”), from Old Norse stobbi, stubbi (Old Norse), cognate with stybb (Old English). Cognate with stobbe (Middle Dutch).

Supposed by some to derive from Scottish Gaelic stob (“to prick, to prod, to push, to thrust”); supposed by others to be from a Scots — word.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: stabilizer,stabiliser.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English stage, from Old French estage (“dwelling, residence; position, situation, condition”), from Old French ester (“to be standing, be located”). Cognate with stæþþan (Old English “to make staid, stay”), steðja (Old Norse “to place, provide, confirm, allow”), stede (Old English “state, status, standing, place, station, site”). More at stead (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: French stage (“internship”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English steinen, steynen (Middle English “to stain, colour, paint”), of gmq — origin, from Old Norse steina (“to stain, colour, paint”), from steinn (Old Norse “stone, mineral blue, colour, stain”), from gmq-pro ᛊᛏᚨᛁᚾᚨᛉ, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”), from Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- (“to stiffen”). Cognate with stān (Old English “stone”). More at stone (English).

Replaced native wem (Middle English “spot, blemish, stain”), from wamm (Old English “spot, stain”).

In some senses, influenced by unrelated disteynen (Middle English “to discolor, remove the colour from"; literally, "de-colour”), from desteindre (Anglo-Norman “to remove the colour from, bleach”), from destaindre (Old French “to remove the color from, bleach”), from des- (Old French “dis-, de-, un-”) + teindre (Old French “to dye”), from tingo (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English stall, stalle (Middle English), from Old English steall (“standing place, position”), from Proto-Germanic *stallaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to place, put, post, stand”). Cognate with étal (French), stallo (Italian), Stall (German), stall (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English stallen (“to abide, dwell, place in a location, stop, come to a standstill”), partly from Old French estaler, ultimately from the same origin as Etymology 1 (see above); and partly from Middle English stalle (“fixed position, stall”).

chain.meaning: to abide, dwell, place in a location, stop, come to a standstill

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stampen (“to pound, crush”), from assumed Old English *stampian, variant of stempan (Old English “to crush, pound, pound in mortar, stamp”), from Proto-West Germanic *stampōn, *stampijan (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *stampōną, *stampijaną (Proto-Germanic “to trample, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *stemb- (“to trample down”).

Cognate with stampen (Dutch “to stamp, pitch”), stampfen (German “to stamp”), stampe (Danish “to stamp”), stampa (Swedish “to stomp”), estampar (Occitan), stąpać (Polish “to step, treat”). See also stomp (English), step (English). Marks indicating that postage had been paid were originally made by stamping the item to be mailed; when affixed pieces of paper were introduced for this purpose, the term “stamp” was transferred to cover this new form.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English standard, from Old French estandart (“gathering place, battle flag”), from Frankish *standahard, equivalent to . An alternative etymology derives the second element from Frankish *oʀd (“point, spot, place”) (compare ordé (Old French “pointed”), ord (Old English “point, source, vanguard”), Standort (German “location, place, site, position, base”)). Merged with Middle English standar, stander (Middle English), standere (Middle English “flag, banner”), equivalent to stand + -er (English). More at stand (English), hard (English), ord (English).

As a hill-naming term possibly a ; equivalent to lluman (Welsh “standard”), arising with confusion with the hill-naming element llumon (Welsh “chimney”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sterre, from Old English steorra (“star”), from Proto-West Germanic *sterrō, variant of *sternō (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *sternô, *sternǭ (Proto-Germanic “star”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr (“star”). ; related to estoile (English), étoile (English), stella (English), and stelo (English).

Cognate with starn (Scots), ster (Scots “star”), starr (Yola), steor (Yola “star”), Stiern (Saterland Frisian “star”), stjer (Western Frisian “star”), stèrn (Cimbric “star”), ster (Dutch “star”), Stern (German “star”), Stär (lb “star”), stern (mhn “star”), śtaom (Ripuarian “star”), שטערן (Yiddish “star”), stjerne (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “star”), stjørna (Faroese “star”), stjännå (gmq-gut “star”), stjarna (Icelandic “star”), skjødna (Norwegian Nynorsk), stjerne (Norwegian Nynorsk “star”), stjärna (Swedish “star”), stein (gme-cgo “star”), 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌽𐍉 (Gothic “star”), étoile (French “star”), stila (ist “star”), ste (ruo “star”), stella (Italian “star”), steau̯ă (ruq “star”), streilha (mwl “star”), estela (Occitan “star”), estrela (Portuguese “star”), staila (Romansh “star”), stea (Romanian “star”), isteddu (Sardinian “star”), stidda (Sicilian “star”), estrella (Spanish “star”), stéła (Venetian “star”), sitoele (wa “star”), stēlla (Latin “star”), ἀστήρ (Ancient Greek “star”), αστέρι (Greek (Modern) “star”), աստղ (Classical Armenian “star”), ستاره (Persian “star”), ситора (Tajik “star”), ستوری (Pashto “star”), اساره (mzn “star”), stêr (Kurmanji Kurdish “star”), ئەستێرە (Central Kurdish “star”), astare (zza “star”), стъалы (Ossetic “star”), तारा (Hindi “star”), تارا (Urdu “star”), ਤਾਰਾ (Punjabi “star”), તારો (Gujarati “star”), तारा (Sanskrit “star”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English staren, from Old English starian (“to stare”), from Proto-West Germanic *starēn, from Proto-Germanic *starjaną, *starāną (Proto-Germanic “to be fixed, be rigid”), from Proto-Indo-European *ster-.

Cognate with staren (Dutch “to stare”), starren (German “to stare”), starr (German “stiff”). More at start (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English star, ster (Middle English), from Old English stær (“starling”), from Proto-Germanic *starô (“starling”), from Proto-Indo-European *stor- (“starling”).

Cognate with Star (German “starling”), stær (Danish “starling”), stare (Swedish “starling”), stare (Norwegian Nynorsk “starling”), stari (Icelandic “starling”). Compare also stearn (Old English “a type of bird, starling”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English stert, from the verb sterten (Middle English “to start, startle”). See below.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English sterten (“to leap up suddenly, rush out”), from Old English styrtan (“to leap up, start”), from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan (“to startle, move, set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter- (“to be stiff”). Cognate with stirta (Old Frisian “to fall down, tumble”), sterten (Middle Dutch “to rush, fall, collapse”) (storten (Dutch)), sturzen (Old High German “to hurl, plunge, turn upside down”) (stürzen (German)), sterzan (Old High German “to be stiff, protrude”). More at stare (English).

chain.meaning: to leap up suddenly, rush out

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English stert, start (Middle English “tail, handle, projection”), from Old English steort (“tail”), from Proto-West Germanic *stert, from Proto-Germanic *stertaz (“tail”). Cognate with start (Scots), stairt (Scots “side post, shaft, upright post”), staart (Dutch “tail”), Sterz (German “tail, handle”), stjert (Danish “tail of a bird”), stertur (Faroese “tail”), stertur (Icelandic “short horse tail”), skjårt (Norn “tail”), sterti (Norn “tail of a large fish”), stjårt (Norn “tail of a large fish”), stjert (Norwegian “tail of a bird”), stjärt (Swedish “tail, arse”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Variant of stark (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English stat (as a noun); adopted c. 1200 from both Old French estat and Latin stātus (“manner of standing, attitude, position, carriage, manner, dress, apparel; and other senses”), from stō (Latin “stāre”). . The sense of "polity" develops in the 14th century. Compare être (French), στέω (Greek (Modern)), stare (Italian), estar (Portuguese), sta (Romanian), and estar (Spanish). The verb is first attested around the beginning of the 16th century. Related to stand (English). Displaced native hād (Old English “state, condition”) and cynewīse (Old English “state, nation”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Affix: state + -ment

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: or .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English stacioun, borrowed from Anglo-Norman estation, from Latin statiōnem, accusative of statiō (Latin “standing, post, job, position”), whence also Italian stazione (Italian). . Cognate with ἵστημι (Ancient Greek), στάσις (Ancient Greek), standan (Old English) (whence stand (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From German Statistik, from New Latin statisticum (“of the state”) and Italian statista (“statesman, politician”), compare statist (English). Statistik introduced by (1749), originally designated the analysis of data about the state.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French statue, from Latin statua, derived from statuō (Latin “set up or erect”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English steyen, staien (Middle English), from Old French estayer, estaier (Old French “to fix, prop up, support, stay”), from estaye (Old French), estaie (Old French “a prop, stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede (Middle Dutch), stade (Middle Dutch “a prop, stay, help, aid”) (compare staeyen (Middle Dutch), staeden (Middle Dutch “to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)), from Proto-West Germanic *stadi (“a site, place, location, standing”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“a standing, place”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing”). Influenced by stæġ (Old English) . Cognate with stede (Old English “a place, spot, locality, fixed position, station, site, standing, status, position of a moving body, stopping, standing still, stability, fixity, firmness, steadfastness”), stödja (Swedish “to prop, support, brace, hold up, bolster”), stöðug (Icelandic “continuous, stable”). More at stead (English), steady (English).

Sense of "remain, continue" may be due to later influence from ester (Old French), esteir (Old French “to stand, be, continue, remain”), from stāre (Latin “stand”), from the same Proto-Indo-European root above; however, derivation from this root is untenable based on linguistic and historical grounds.

An alternative etymology derives Old French estaye, estaie (Old French), from Frankish *stakā, *stakō (Frankish “stake, post”), from Proto-Germanic *stakô (“stake, bar, stick, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg- (“rod, pole, stick”), making it cognate with staca (Old English “pin, stake”), stician (Old English “to stick, be placed, lie, remain fixed”). Cognate with Albanian shtagë (Albanian “a long stick, a pole”). More at stake (English), stick (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English stay, from Old French estaye, estaie (Old French “a prop, a stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede (Middle Dutch), stade (Middle Dutch) , from Old Dutch *stad (“a site, place, location, standing”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“a standing, place”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). See above.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English stay, from Old English stæġ (“stay, a rope supporting a mast”), from Proto-West Germanic *stag, from Proto-Germanic *stagą (“stay, rope”), from Proto-Indo-European *stek-, *stāk- (Proto-Indo-European “stand, pole”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). Cognate with stag (Dutch “stay”), Stag (German “stay”), stag (Swedish “stay”), stag (Icelandic “stay”).

chain.meaning: stay, a rope supporting a mast

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English *steȝe, from Old English *stǣġe, an apocopated variant of stǣġel (Old English “steep, abrupt”), from Proto-West Germanic *staigil (“steep”), see sty (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: steady + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stedy, studi (Middle English), stidiȝ (Middle English), perhaps continuing Old English stæþþiġ, ġestæþþiġ (Old English “steadfast, stable, firm, staid”), equivalent to ; or calque calquing Middle Low German — or Middle Dutch stēdig. Cognate with stoadig (Saterland Frisian “steady”), stadich (Western Frisian “slow”), stedig (Danish), stadig (Danish), steeg (Danish), stadig (Swedish), stöðugur (Icelandic), stätig (German), stetig (German).

Compare also ġestedegian (Old English “to bring to a standstill”) and steeds (Dutch “more and more”).

Adjective sense 8 is a 在 (Chinese “confident, skilled”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English steem, stem (Middle English), from Old English stēam (“steam, hot exhalation, hot breath; that which emits vapour; blood”), from Proto-Germanic *staumaz (“steam, vapour, breath”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to whirl, waft, stink, shake; steam, haze, smoke”). Cognate with stem (Scots), steam (Scots “steam”), steam (Western Frisian “steam, vapour”), stoom (Dutch “steam, vapour”), stom (Low German “steam”), - (Swedish) dialectal stimma (Swedish “steam, fog”), fūmus (Latin “smoke, steam”).

chain.meaning: steam, hot exhalation, hot breath; that which emits vapour; blood

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English stele, stel (Middle English), from Old English stīele, from Proto-West Germanic *stahlī (“something made of steel”), enlargement of *stahl (Proto-West Germanic “steel”), from Proto-Germanic *stahlą, from *stah- (Proto-Germanic) or *stag- (Proto-Germanic “to be firm, rigid”), from Proto-Indo-European *stak- (“to stay, to be firm”). Compare stele (Scots), stehli (Yola), Stahl (German), staal (Dutch), stål (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From French Bastille (a French prison).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English steep, from Old English stēap (“high”), from Proto-Germanic *staupaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp- (“to push, stick”).

Compare stāp (Old Frisian) , stoop (Dutch “grand; proud”), stouf (Middle High German “towering cliff, precipice”), stief (Middle High German “steep”)). The Proto-Indo-European root (and related) has many and varied descendants, including English stub (English); compare also stap (Scots “to strike, to forcibly insert”).

The sense of “sharp slope” is attested circa 1200; the sense “expensive” is attested US 1856.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English stepen, from Old Norse steypa (“to make stoop, cast down, pour out, cast (metal)”), from Proto-Germanic *staupijaną (“to tumble, make tumble, plunge”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewb- (“to push, hit”). Cognate with støbe (Danish “cast (metal)”), støpe (Norwegian), støype (Norwegian), stöpa (Swedish “to found, cast (metal)”), stūpian (Old English “to stoop, bend the back, slope”). Related to stoop (English).

chain.meaning: to make stoop, cast down, pour out, cast (metal)

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English steeren, steren (Middle English), stiren (Middle English), sturen (Middle English), steoren (Middle English), from Old English stēoran, stīeran (Old English), stȳran (Old English “to steer; guide a vessel”), from Proto-West Germanic *stiurijan (“to steer”), from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną (“to steer”).

The noun is from Middle English steere, stere (Middle English “rudder”), steor (Middle English), from Old English stēor, stȳr (Old English “steering; guidance; direction”). Compare stuur (Dutch), Steuer (German), stýri (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English steer, ster (Middle English), from Old English stēor (“a young bull or cow; steer”), from Proto-Germanic *steuraz (“bull; steer”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros (“wild bull; aurochs”). Cognate with stier (Dutch), Stier (German), stjór (Icelandic), taurus (Latin “bull”), ταύρος (Greek (Modern)). .

chain.meaning: a young bull or cow; steer

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English steppen, from Old English steppan (“to step, go, proceed, advance”), stepe (Old English “step”), from Proto-West Germanic *stappjan, from Proto-Germanic *stapjaną (“to step”), *stapiz (Proto-Germanic “step”), from Proto-Indo-European *stebʰ- (“to support, stomp, curse, be amazed”).

Cognate with stappe (Western Frisian “to step”), stape (North Frisian “to walk, trudge”), stappen (Dutch “to step, walk”), steper (wa “to walk away, leave”), stapfen (German “to trudge, stomp, plod”) and further to Slavic stąpać (Polish “to stomp, stamp, step, tread”), ступать (Russian) and stopień (Polish “step, stair, rung, degree”), степень (Russian). Related to stamp (English), stomp (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Clipping: stepchild + stepsibling

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stepfader, from Old English stēopfæder, from Proto-Germanic *steupafadēr (“stepfather”), equivalent to step + father (English).

Cognate with Stäiffoar (Saterland Frisian “stepfather”), stiefvader (Dutch “stepfather”), Steevvader (Low German (Germany) “stepfather”), Stiefvater (German “stepfather”), styvfar (Swedish “stepfather”), stjúpfaðir (Icelandic “stepfather”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English stepmoder, from Old English stēopmōdor, from Proto-Germanic *steupamōdēr (“stepmother”), corresponding to step + mother (English). Cognate with Stäifmuur (Saterland Frisian “stepmother”), stiefmoeder (Dutch “stepmother”), Steevmoder (Low German (Germany) “stepmother”), Stiefmutter (German “stepmother”), stedmor (Danish “stepmother”), styvmor (Swedish “stepmother”), stjúpmóðir (Icelandic “stepmother”). Compare also styfmem (Western Frisian “stepmother”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sticke, stik (Middle English), stikke (Middle English “branch, twig; kindling; mast; pale; stick, stylus”), from Old English sticca (“stick; peg; beam, rod”), from Proto-West Germanic *stikkō, from Proto-Germanic *stikkô (“pole, stick”), from *stikkōną (Proto-Germanic “to fix, stick”), from *stikaną (Proto-Germanic “to stick; to stab”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp; to sting”).

Cognate with stek (Dutch “home, spot; cutting, a leaf, stem, branch, or root removed from a plant and cultivated to grow a new plant”), Stecken (German “stick”), śtakia (Ripuarian “stick”); also wosa (Cornish “after”), wedi (Welsh “past (time); after”), instigo (Latin “to stimulate”), στῐ́ζω (Ancient Greek “to tattoo; to mark; to punctuate”), تێژ (Central Kurdish), تیژ (Central Kurdish “sharp; hot, spicy”), tîj (Kurmanji Kurdish), tûj (Kurmanji Kurdish “sharp; hot, spicy; severe”), цыхт (Ossetic “cheese”), تیز (Persian “sharp; pungent; shrill; piercing; penetrating; nimble, swift; smart”), तेज॑ते (Sanskrit “to be or become sharp; to activate, energize”). Related to stigma (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stiken (“to stick, pierce, stab, remain embedded, be fastened”), from Old English stician (“to pierce, stab, remain embedded, be fastened”), from Proto-West Germanic *stikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *stikkōną (“to pierce, prick, be sharp”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tig-, *(s)teyg- (Proto-Indo-European “to pierce, prick, be sharp”).

See also the related *stikaną (Proto-Germanic), whence stekke (Western Frisian), steken (Low German), steken (Dutch), stechen (German); compare also stikke (Danish), sticka (Swedish).

Cognate with the first etymology (same PIE root, different paths through Germanic and Old English), to stitch (English), and to etiquette (English), via French étiquette (French) – see there for further discussion.

chain.meaning: to stick, pierce, stab, remain embedded, be fastened
to pierce, stab, remain embedded, be fastened

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English stick, stik (Middle English), steik (Middle English), from Middle Dutch stic, stec (Middle Dutch), stuc (Middle Dutch “piece”), from Old Dutch *stukki, from Proto-West Germanic *stukkī, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją (“piece”). Cognate with Stück (German “piece”), stucche (Middle English), sticche (Middle English “piece”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: stick + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stiff, stiffe (Middle English), stif (Middle English), from Old English stīf, from Proto-West Germanic *stīf, from Proto-Germanic *stīfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *steypós.

See also stiif (Western Frisian), stijf (Dutch), stiv (Norwegian Bokmål), steif (German); also stīpes (Latin), stīpō (Latin), from which English stevedore (English).

The expected Modern English form would be ; is probably originally from compounds such as stiffly (English), where the vowel was shortened before a consonant cluster.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stille (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English stille (“still, quiet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stillī, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)telH- (“to be silent; to be still”). Cognate with stil (Scots “still”), stil (Saterland Frisian “motionless, calm, quiet”), stil (Western Frisian “quiet, still”), stil (Dutch “quiet, silent, still”), still (Low German “quiet, silent, still”), still (German “still, quiet, tranquil, silent”), stilla (Swedish “quiet, silent, peaceful”), stilltur (Icelandic “set, quiet, calm, still”). Related to stall (English).

Military slang, short for still a Benny, since the military had been instructed not to refer to the islanders by the derogatory term Benny (English) (which see).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Via Middle English stillen, clip of distillen; Old French distiller; Latin distillare, from dis- + stillare, from Latin stilla.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Inherited from Old English stillan

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Aphetic form of distil (English), or from Latin stillare.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin stimulātus, perfect passive participle of stimulō (Latin “to urge, goad on”) (see -ate), from .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English stiren, sturien (Middle English), steren (Middle English), from Old English styrian (“to be in motion, move, agitate, stir, disturb, trouble”), from Proto-Germanic *sturiz (“turmoil, noise, confusion”), related to *staurijan (Proto-West Germanic “to destroy, disturb”). Cognate with styrr (Old Norse “turmoil, noise, confusion”), stören (German “to disturb”), storen (Dutch “to disturb”).

chain.meaning: to be in motion, move, agitate, stir, disturb, trouble

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Romani stariben (“prison”), nominalisation of astar (Romani “seize”), causative of ast (Romani “remain”), probably from Sanskrit आतिष्ठति (“stand or remain by”), from तिष्ठति (Sanskrit “stand”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stok, from Old English stocc, from Proto-West Germanic *stokk, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“tree-trunk”).

Modern senses are mostly referring either to the trunk from which the tree grows (figuratively, its origin and/or support/foundation), or to a piece of wood, stick, or rod. The senses of "supply" and "raw material" arose from a probable conflation with steck (English “an item of goods, merchandise”) or the use of split tally sticks consisting of foil or counterfoil and stock to capture paid taxes, debts or exchanges. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Italian stoccata.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ston, stone (Middle English), stan (Middle English), from Old English stān, from Proto-West Germanic *stain, from Proto-Germanic *stainaz (“stone”), from Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- (“to stiffen”).

Cognate with stane (Scots “stone”), sthoan (Yola “stone”), stean (North Frisian), stian (North Frisian), stiin (North Frisian), stiinj (North Frisian “stone”), Steen (Saterland Frisian “stone”), stien (Western Frisian “stone”), Steei (Alemannic “rock, stone”), Staa (Bavarian “rock, stone”), Steen (Central Franconian), Stään (Central Franconian “stone”), steen (Dutch “stone”), Stein (German “rock, stone”), Steen (Low German (Germany)), Stein (Low German (Germany) “stone”), Steen (lb “stone”), śtan (Ripuarian “stone”), שטיין (Yiddish “stone”), sten (Danish / Swedish “stone”), stien (Elfdalian “stone”), steinur (Faroese “stone”), stain (gmq-gut “rock, stone”), steinn (Icelandic “rock, stone”), stein (Norwegian Bokmål), sten (Norwegian Bokmål “stone”), steidn (Norwegian Nynorsk), stein (Norwegian Nynorsk “stone”), 𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌽𐍃 (Gothic “stone”). Compare also στία (Ancient Greek “pebble”), στέαρ (Ancient Greek “tallow”), sténgti (Lithuanian “to be able, make an effort; to oppose”), стена́ (Russian “wall”), shtëng (Albanian “hardened or pressed matter”), स्तिया (Sanskrit “still or stagnant water”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stonen, stanen (Middle English), from Old English *stānian (“to stone”), from Proto-West Germanic *stainōn, from Proto-Germanic *stainōną (“to stone”).

Cognate with stane (Scots “to stone”), stenen (Low German (Germany) “to stone”), stene (Danish “to stone”), stena (Swedish “to stone”), steina (Faroese “to stone”). Compare also stenigje (Saterland Frisian “to stone”), stiennigje (Western Frisian “to stone”), stenigen (Dutch “to stone”), steinigen (German “to stone”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stool, from Old English stōl (“chair, seat”), from Proto-West Germanic *stōl, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz (“chair”), from Proto-Indo-European —, from *steh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to stand”).

Cognate with stuul (North Frisian), stölj (North Frisian), Stööl (North Frisian “chear”), Stoul (Saterland Frisian “chear”), stoel (Western Frisian “chair, seat”), stoel (Dutch “chair”), Stuhl (German “chair”), Stohl (Low German “chair”), Stull (lb “chair”), śtül (Ripuarian “chair”), שתוהל (Yiddish), שטול (Yiddish “chair”), stol (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “chair”), stólur (Faroese “chair”), stóll (Icelandic “chair”), stul (gme-cgo “seat”), 𐍃𐍄𐍉𐌻𐍃 (Gothic “chair; throne”), стул (Russian “chair”), tool (Estonian “chair”), tuoli (Finnish “chair”); also sevel (Breton / Cornish “to erect, rise; to build; to lift; to compose; to earn”), sáil (Irish), sál (Irish “heel”), sàil (Scottish Gaelic “heel”), sefyll (Welsh “to stand; to stop; to sit”), sistō (Latin “to set; to stop; to stand; to stabilise”), 𐌔𐌄𐌔𐌕𐌖 (xum “to place”), στέκω (Greek (Modern)), στέκομαι (Greek (Modern) “to stand up”), shtoj (Albanian “to add; to augment; to accumulate”), stálas (Lithuanian “table”), stallan (Old Prussian “table”), стол (Belarusian / Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian “table”), stůl (Czech “table”), stół (Polish “table”), сто̑ (Serbo-Croatian), сто̑л (Serbo-Croatian), stȏ (Serbo-Croatian), stȏl (Serbo-Croatian “table”), stôl (Slovak “table”), stol (Slovenian “chair”), երթալ (Armenian), էթալ (Armenian “to go”), ستوون (Central Kurdish “column”), ستن (Pashto “needle; awl; pin; syringe; post; hand; dragonfly”), ایستادن (Persian), وایسادن (Persian), وایستادن (Persian “to stand up; to step; to stay”), ستون (Persian “column”), rawestîn (Kurmanji Kurdish “to stand up”), stûn (Kurmanji Kurdish “column”), стын (Ossetic “to stand up”), 𒋾𒄑𒍣 (Hittite “to step; to place oneself”), ṣtäm- (xto “to stand”), stäm- (txb “to stand”), तिष्ठति (Sanskrit “to stand; to stay”). More at stand (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Latin stolo. See stolon (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stoppen, stoppien (Middle English), from Old English stoppian (“to stop, close”), from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn, from Proto-Germanic *stuppōną (“to stop, close”), *stuppijaną (Proto-Germanic “to push, pierce, prick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-, *(s)tewb- (Proto-Indo-European “to push; stick”), from *(s)tew- (Proto-Indo-European “to bump; impact; butt; push; beat; strike; hit”).

Cognate with stopje (Saterland Frisian “to stop, block”), stopje (Western Frisian “to stop”), stoppen (Dutch “to stop”), stoppen (Low German “to stop”), stopfen (German “to be filling, stuff”), stoppen (German “to stop”), stoppe (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to stop”), stoppa (Icelandic / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “to stop”), stupfen (Middle High German), stüpfen (Middle High German “to pierce”). More at stuff, stump.

Alternative etymology derives Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn from an assumed *stūpāre (Vulgar Latin), *stuppāre (Latin “to stop up with tow”), from stūpa (Latin), stīpa (Latin), stuppa (Latin “tow, flax, oakum”), from στύπη (Ancient Greek), στύππη (Ancient Greek “tow, flax, oakum”). This derivation, however, is doubtful, as the earliest instances of the Germanic verb do not carry the meaning of "stuff, stop with tow". Rather, these senses developed later in response to influence from similar sounding words in Latin and Romance.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stoppe, from Old English stoppa (“bucket, pail, a stop”), from Proto-Germanic *stuppô (“vat, vessel”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teub- (“to push, hit; stick, stump”). See stoup.

Cognate with stopp (Norwegian), stoppa (Norwegian “deep well, recess”), stubech (Middle High German), stübich (Middle High German “barrel, vat, unit of measure”) (German Stübchen (German)). Related also to stōp (Middle Low German “beaker, flask”), stouf (Middle High German “beaker, flask”), staupa (Norwegian “goblet”), staupa (Icelandic “shot-glass”), stēap (Old English “a stoup, beaker, drinking vessel, cup, flagon”). Cognate to shtambë (Albanian “amphora, bucket”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Affix: s- + top

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Deverbal: stop over
