etymologies.text: Affix: store + -age

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English store

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English story, via Medieval Latin historia (“narrative, illustraton, frieze”) from Ancient Greek ἱστορίᾱ (“learning through research”). The current sense arose from narrative friezes on upper levels of medieval buildings, esp. churches. .

An alternative etymology derives story (Middle English) from Old French *estoree (“a thing built, building”), from estoree (Old French “built”), feminine past participle of estorer (Old French “to build”), from Latin instaurare (“to construct, build, erect”), but this seems unlikely since historia already had the meaning "storey of a building" in Anglo-Latin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English stormy, stormi (Middle English), from Old English *stormiġ (“stormy”), equivalent to . Cognate with stormig (Dutch “stormy”), stürmisch (German “stormy”), stormig (Swedish “stormy”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English storie, storye (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman estorie by aphesis, from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ῐ̔στορῐ́ᾱ (“learning through research”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Alternative form of what's the story (English “how are you?”)

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From: storey

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English streight, streght (Middle English), streiȝt (Middle English), the past participle of strecchen (Middle English “to stretch”), from Old English streċċan (past participle ġestreaht (Old English), ġestreht (Old English)), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch”). Cognate with straicht (Scots “straight”), gestrekt (Dutch “stretched”), gestreckt (German “stretched”), strakt (Danish “stretched”), - (Faroese) and strekti (Norn “stretched”), strekkti (Icelandic “stretched”), strekte (Norwegian “stretched”), sträckte (Swedish “stretched”). Doublet of straught (English). Equivalent to stretch + ed (English).

In some senses, conflated with strait (English “narrow, constricted”), which is from strictus (Latin) via estreit (Old French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From straight + forward (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English streen, strene (Middle English), streon (Middle English), istreon (Middle English “race, stock, generation”), from Old English strēon, ġestrēon (Old English “gain, wealth”), from Proto-West Germanic *streun, from Proto-Germanic *streuną (“heap, treasure, profit, gain”), from Proto-Indo-European *strew- (“to spread, strew”) (cognate with gistriuni (Old Saxon), gistriuni (Old High German “gain, property, wealth, business”), strues (Latin “heap”)). Confused in Middle English with the related noun strend (Middle English), strynd (Middle English), strund (Middle English), from Old English strȳnd (“race; stock”), from strēonan (Old English), strȳnan (Old English “to beget; acquire”). Related also to struinen (Dutch “to prowl, root about, rout”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English straynen, streinen (Middle English), streynen (Middle English), from Old French estreindre (whence étreindre (French “to grip”)), from Latin stringō (“to draw tight together, to tie”).

chain.meaning: to draw tight together, to tie

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English strenen (“to beget, father, procreate”), from Old English strēonan, strīenan (Old English), strȳnan (Old English “to beget, generate, gain, acquire”), from Proto-West Germanic *striunijan, from Proto-Germanic *striunijaną (“to furnish, decorate, acquire”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English straunge, strange (Middle English), stronge (Middle English), from Old French estrange, from Latin extrāneus (“that which is on the outside”). . Cognate with étrange (French “strange, foreign”) and extraño (Spanish “strange, foreign”). Largely displaced native fremd (English), selcouth (English), and uncouth (English), from fremede (Old English), seldcūþ (Old English), and uncūþ (Old English).

chain.meaning: that which is on the outside

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English straungely (“strangely, aloofly, intricately”); equivalent to strange + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English straunger, from , from estrange (Old French), from (whence also English estrange (English)), from extra (Latin “outside of”). Cognate with étranger (French “foreigner, stranger”) and extranjero (Spanish “foreigner”). Displaced native fremde (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Latin stratēgia, from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (“office of general, command, generalship”), from στρατηγός (Ancient Greek “the leader or commander of an army, a general”), from στρατός (Ancient Greek “army”) + ἄγω (Ancient Greek “to lead, conduct”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English strawberie, strawbery (Middle English), from Old English strēawberġe, corresponding to straw + berry (English).

Of various theories advanced to explain the name, the two most plausible are:
1. the fact that wild strawberries grow on straw-like runners (or stolons) (compare stråbær (Norwegian Nynorsk), denoting , which grow in a similar way);
2. the practice, still common in parts of Europe, of gathering strawberries by stringing them on a straw or stalk.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English streem, strem (Middle English), from Old English strēam, from Proto-West Germanic *straum, from Proto-Germanic *straumaz (“stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *srowmos (“river”), from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”). .

Cognate with strem (Scots), streme (Scots), streym (Scots “stream, river”), Stroom (North Frisian), struum (North Frisian “stream”), stream (Western Frisian “stream”), Stroom (Low German “stream”), stroom (Dutch “current, flow, stream”), Strom (German “current, stream”), strøm (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “current, stream, flow”), straum (Norwegian Nynorsk “current, stream, flow”), ström (Swedish “current, stream, flow”), streymur (Faroese “stream”), straumur (Icelandic “current, stream, torrent, flood”), ῥεῦμα (Ancient Greek “stream, flow”), srovė (Lithuanian “current, stream”) strumień (Polish “stream”), ffrwd (Welsh “stream, current”), sruth (Scottish Gaelic “stream”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English strengthe, from Old English strengþu (“strength”), from Proto-West Germanic *strangiþu (“strongness; strength”), equivalent to strong + -th (English). Cognate with strengte (Dutch “strength”), Strengde (Low German (Germany)), Strengte (Low German (Germany) “harshness; rigidity; strictness; severity”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From rare Middle English strengthenen (14th c.), from earlier strengthen (Middle English) (12th c.), where -en is the infinitive ending. Probably the original form was reinterpreted as strength + -en (English) around the time when the infinitive ending was being apocopated in late Middle English.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From a shortening of Middle English destresse, borrowed from Old French destrecier, from Latin distringō (“to stretch out”). This form probably coalesced with Middle English stresse, from Old French estrece (“narrowness”), from Vulgar Latin *strictia, from Latin strictus (“narrow”). Displaced native swēġ (Old English “accent, stress”), though strictly in the grammatical sense.

In the sense of "mental strain" or “disruption”, used occasionally in the 1920s and 1930s by psychologists, including (1934); in “biological threat”, used by endocrinologist , by metaphor with stress in physics (force on an object) in the 1930s, and popularized by same in the 1950s.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From stress + -ful (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English strecchen, from Old English streċċan (“to stretch, hold out, extend, spread out, prostrate”), from Proto-West Germanic *strakkjan (“to stretch, make taut or tight”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)treg-, *streg- (Proto-Indo-European), *treg- (Proto-Indo-European “stiff, rigid”). Cognate with strekke (Western Frisian), strekken (Dutch “to stretch, straighten”), strecken (German “to stretch, straighten, elongate”), strække (Danish “to stretch”), sträcka (Swedish “to stretch”), strak (Dutch “taut, tight”), shtriqem (Albanian “to stretch”). More at stark (English).

chain.meaning: to stretch, hold out, extend, spread out, prostrate

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Latin strictus, past participle of stringere (Latin “to draw tight, bind, contract”). . See stringent (English), strain (English). Related to strong (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: strict + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English stryken, from Old English strīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *strīkan, from Proto-Germanic *strīkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to stroke, rub, press”).

Cognate with strijken (Dutch), streichen (German), stryge (Danish), strýkja (Icelandic), strýkva (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English string, streng (Middle English), strynge (Middle English), from Old English strenġ, from Proto-West Germanic *strangi, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz (“string”), from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“rope, cord, strand; to tighten”).

Cognate with string (Scots “string”), streng (Dutch “cord, strand”), strenge (Low German “strand, cord, rope”), Strang (German “strand, cord, rope”), streng (Danish “string”), sträng (Swedish “string, cord, wire”), strengur (Icelandic “string”), stringt (Latvian “to be tight, wither”), stringō (Latin “to tighten”), στραγγαλόομαι (Ancient Greek “to strangle”), from στραγγάλη (Ancient Greek “halter”), στραγγός (Ancient Greek “tied together, entangled, twisted”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English stryngen, strengen (Middle English), from the noun (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English stripe, strype (Middle English), from Middle Dutch — or Middle Low German strîpe, from Proto-West Germanic *strīpā, *strīpō (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *strīpô. Cognate with Striepe (Saterland Frisian “stripe, strip”), stripe (Western Frisian “stripe”), streep (Dutch “stripe”), Striepe (Low German (Germany)), Striep (Low German (Germany)), Streep (Low German (Germany) “stripe”), Streifen (German “stripe, strip, band”), stribe (Danish “stripe”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English strok, stroke (Middle English “blow from a weapon, cut”), from Old English strāc, from Proto-West Germanic *straik, from Proto-Germanic *straikaz (“stroke”), from Proto-Indo-European *streyg- (“to rub, stroke; to shear; to strike”).

Sense 3.5.2.2 (“the oblique, slash, or virgule (‘/’)”) is a contraction of oblique stroke (English), a variant of oblique (English) which was originally used in telegraphy.

The verb is derived from the noun.

* Streich (German “stroke”)
* strēk (Middle Low German “stroke, trick, prank”)
* strak (Scots), strake (Scots), straik (Scots “blow, stroke”)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Middle English stroken, straken (Middle English “to caress, fondle, pat, rub, smooth, stroke; to pass something over (someone or something); to brush or rub against;”), from Old English strācian (“to stroke”), from Proto-West Germanic *straikōn (“to caress, stroke”), from *straik (Proto-West Germanic “a line, stroke; a dash”) (see further at etymology 1) + *-ōn (Proto-West Germanic).

The noun is derived from the verb.

* streicheln (German “to stroke, fondle”)
* straken (Low German (Germany)), strieken (Low German (Germany)), strakeln (Low German (Germany)), striekeln (Low German (Germany) “to stroke; caress; fondle”)
* strēken (Middle Low German), strēken (Middle Dutch) (modern streeken (Dutch))
* strīhhan (Old High German), streihhōn (Old High German), strīchen (Middle High German) (modern streichen (German “to stroke; to rub; to spread; to apply; to paint; to cancel; to cross out, strike out; to delete; to discard”))
* strookje (Saterland Frisian “to stroke; caress”)
* streakje (Western Frisian “to stroke; caress”)

Cognate with strang (Scots “strong”), strang (Western Frisian), string (Western Frisian “strict, harsh, severe, stern, stark, tough, strong, intense”), streng (Dutch “strict, severe, tight”), dialectal strang (Dutch “tight, strict, powerful, intense, mighty, strong”), streng (German “strict, severe, austere”), - (Danish) and streng (Norwegian “strong, hard”), strang (Norwegian “strong, harsh, bitter”), sträng (Swedish), strang (Swedish “severe, strict, harsh”), - (Faroese) and strangur (Icelandic “strict”), stringō (Latin “tighten”). Related to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English struglen, stroglen (Middle English), strogelen (Middle English), of obscure origin; perhaps from a variant of *strokelen (Middle English), *stroukelen (Middle English) , from Middle Dutch struyckelen , the frequentative form of Old Dutch *strūkon (“to stumble”), from Proto-Germanic *strūkōną, *strūkēną (Proto-Germanic “to be stiff”), from Proto-Indo-European *strug-, *ster- (Proto-Indo-European “to be stiff; to bristle, strut, stumble, fall”),

Cognate with strugil (Scots “to struggle, grapple, contend”). Also related to strûkelen (Middle Low German) , strūhhēn (Old High German), strūhhōn (Old High German) .

Alternative etymology derives the base of struggle from Old Norse strúgr (“arrogance, pride, spitefulness, ill-will”) + -le, from Proto-Germanic *strūkaz (“stiff, rigid”), ultimately from the same Proto-Indo-European root above, which would make it cognate with dialectal strug (Swedish “contention, strife, discord”), stru (Norwegian “obstinate, unruly”), struende (Danish “reluctantly”), strug (Scots “difficulty, perplexity, a laborious task”).

See also swill (English).

The noun is from Middle English swolow, swolwe (Middle English), from Old English swelh, swelg (Old English “gulf, chasm”) and ġeswelge (Old English “gulf, chasm, abyss, whirlpool”), both from Proto-West Germanic *swelg, *swalgi (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *swelgaz, *swalgiz (Proto-Germanic). Cognate with swiliġe (Old English “pit”), swelch (Scots), swellie (Scots), swallie (Scots “an abyss in the sea, whirlpool”), swelch (Middle Low German “whirlpool, eddy”), zwelg (Dutch “gorge, chasm, gullet, throat”), svelgr (Old Norse “whirlpool, current, stream”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English sweren, swerien (Middle English), from Old English swerian (“to swear, take an oath of office”), from Proto-West Germanic *swarjan, from Proto-Germanic *swarjaną (“to speak, swear”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“to swear”).

Cognate with swarre (Western Frisian “to swear”), swera (Saterland Frisian “to swear”), zweren (Dutch “to swear, vow”), swören (Low German “to swear”), sweren (Low German), schwören (German “to swear”), sværge (Danish), svära (Swedish “to swear”), sverja (Icelandic “to swear”), свара (Russian “quarrel”). Also cognate to var (Albanian “to hang, consider, to depend from”) through Proto-Indo-European.

The original sense in all Germanic languages is “to take an oath”. The sense “to use bad language” developed in Middle English and is based on the Christian prohibition against swearing in general (cf. 5:33-37) and invoking God’s name in particular (i.e. frequent swearing was considered similar to the use of obscene words).

chain.meaning: to swear, take an oath of office

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the above verb, or from Middle English sware, from Old English swaru, from Proto-Germanic *swarō.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English swere, swer (Middle English), swar (Middle English), from Old English swǣr, swār (Old English “heavy, heavy as a burden, of great weight, oppressive, grievous, painful, unpleasant, sad, feeling or expressing grief, grave, slow, dull, sluggish, slothful, indolent, inactive from weakness, enfeebled, weak”), from Proto-West Germanic *swār, from Proto-Germanic *swēraz (“heavy”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).

Cognate with swier (Western Frisian “heavy”), zwaar (Dutch “heavy, hard, difficult”), schwer (German “heavy, hard, difficult”), svær (Danish “heavy, hard, severe”), svår (Swedish “heavy, hard, severe”), sērius (Latin “earnest, grave, solemn, serious”) and varrë (Albanian “wound, plague”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English swete, swet (Middle English), swate (Middle English), swote (Middle English), from Old English swāt, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, , from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), o-grade of *sweyd- (Proto-Indo-European “to sweat”). Cognate with swit (Western Frisian), zweet (Dutch), Schweiß (German), sved (Danish), svette (Norwegian Bokmål), sveitte (Norwegian Nynorsk), svett (Swedish), שוויצן (Yiddish) (shvitz (English)), sudor (Latin), sueur (French), sudore (Italian), sudor (Spanish), suor (Portuguese), خوی (Persian “sweat”), स्वेद (Sanskrit), sviedri (Lithuanian), syā- (txb), djersë (Albanian), and chwys (Welsh).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English sweten, from Old English swǣtan, from Proto-Germanic *swaitijaną (“to sweat”). Compare zweten (Dutch), schwitzen (German), svede (Danish). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From sweat + shirt (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English swepen, from Proto-West Germanic *swaipijan (unattested in Old English), from Proto-Germanic *swaipijaną. Cognate with Early Modern swiepe (Western Frisian “whip, cleanse, sweep”), from swēpa (Old Frisian), suepa (Old Frisian “sweep”). More distantly related to sveipa (Old Norse) (whence svepa (Swedish)). See also swoop (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English soot, sweete (Middle English), swete (Middle English), swoote (Middle English), from Old English swēte, swoete (Old English), swōt (Old English), swœ̄te (Old English “sweet”), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtī, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz (“sweet”), from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus (“sweet”), from *sweh₂d- (Proto-Indo-European “sweet”) + *-us (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with sweet (Yola “sweet”), swäit (Saterland Frisian “sweet”), swiet (Western Frisian “sweet”), süeß (Alemannic “sweet”), siaß (Bavarian “sweet; cute”), söß (Central Franconian “sweet”), zoet (Dutch “sweet”), süss (German), süß (German “sweet; cute”), söüt (Limburgish “sweet; cute”), seut (Low German), sööt (Low German “sweet”), séiss (lb “sweet”), ziss (Ripuarian “sweet”), זיס (Yiddish “sweet; cute”), sød (Danish “sweet; cute, pretty”), søtur (Faroese “sweet”), sætur (Icelandic “sweet; cute, pretty”), søt (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “sweet; cute”), söt (Swedish “sweet; cute”); also suāvis (Latin “delicious, pleasant, sweet”), ἡδύς (Ancient Greek “sweet; pleasant; glad, pleased”), shije (Albanian “flavour, taste”), sūdyti (Lithuanian “to add salt; to brine, souse”), քաղցր (Armenian “sweet”), swār (xto “sweet”), swāre (txb “sweet, tender”), स्वादु (Sanskrit “delicious, palatable, savoury, sweet, tasty; dainty, delicate”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English swimmere, equivalent to swim + -er (English). The dumplings are so called because they are often served in stew.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English swyngen, from Old English swingan, from Proto-West Germanic *swingan, from Proto-Germanic *swinganą (compare swingen (Low German), schwingen (German), zwingen (Dutch), svinga (Swedish)), from Proto-Indo-European *swenk-, *sweng- (Proto-Indo-European) (compare seang (Scottish Gaelic “thin”)). Related to swink (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Perhaps from Middle Dutch swijch (“twig”), . The mechanical device for altering the direction of something sense is , pertaining to pivoted rails on minecart railways, which were once wooden.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English swollen, i-swolle (Middle English), y-swolle (Middle English), yswolle (Middle English), ȝeswollen (Middle English), from Old English swollen, ġeswollen (Old English), from Proto-Germanic *swullanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *swellaną (“to swell”). Cognate with swollen (Western Frisian “swollen”), gezwollen (Dutch “swollen”), geschwollen (German “swollen”), svullen (Swedish “swollen”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
West Midland Middle English sword (swerd (Middle English) in most dialects), from Old English sweord (“sword”), from Proto-West Germanic *swerd (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *swerdą (“sword”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂w- (“sharp”).

Cognate with Swērt (North Frisian), Swiirt (North Frisian), swörd (North Frisian “sword”), Swid (Saterland Frisian), Swäid (Saterland Frisian “sword”), swurd (Western Frisian “sword”), zwaard (Dutch “sword”), Schwert (German “sword”), Schwäert (lb “sword”), świert (Ripuarian “sword”), שווערד (Yiddish “sword”), sværd (Danish “sword”), svørð (Faroese “sword”), sverð (Icelandic “sword”), svird (Norn “small longish object”), sverd (Norwegian Bokmål “sword”), sverd (Norwegian Nynorsk), svørd (Norwegian Nynorsk “sword”), svärd (Swedish “sword”); also све́рдзел (Belarusian “drill, drill bit”), свре́дел (Bulgarian “drill, drill bit”), svider (Czech “drill bit”), świder (Polish “drill”), сверло́ (Russian “auger, bore, drill, drill bit”), свр̏дло (Serbo-Croatian), svȑdlo (Serbo-Croatian “auger”), sveder (Slovenian “drill”), све́рдел (Ukrainian), све́рдло (Ukrainian “drill bit”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English syllable, sillable (Middle English), syllabylle (Middle English), sylabul (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman sillable, from Old French sillebe, from Latin syllaba, from Ancient Greek συλλαβή, from συλλαμβάνω (Ancient Greek “to gather together”), from συν- (Ancient Greek “together”) + λαμβάνω (Ancient Greek “to take”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
thumb|upright|Symbols of various religions.
From French symbole, from Latin symbolus, symbolum (Latin “a sign, mark, token, symbol, in Late Latin also a creed”), from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (“a sign by which one infers something; a mark, token, badge, ticket, tally, check, a signal, watchword, outward sign”), from συμβάλλω (Ancient Greek “to throw together, dash together, compare, correspond, tally, come to a conclusion”), from σύν (Ancient Greek “with, together”) + βάλλω (Ancient Greek “to throw, put”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Mid 17th century in the sense , from Latin sympathēticus. ; compare pathetic (English). Displaced native efnþrōwiende (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (“fellow feeling”), from σῠμπᾰθής + -ῐᾰ (Ancient Greek). Equivalent to sym- + -pathy (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English sinthoma, from Medieval Latin sinthoma, altered by Late Latin symptoma, from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (“a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), from stem of συμπίπτω (Ancient Greek “Ι befall”), from συν- (Ancient Greek “together”) + πίπτω (Ancient Greek “to fall”). See also syn- (English), -oma (English), -ome (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Partly Middle French sisteme, systeme (Middle French), partly directly from its etymon Late Latin systēma (“harmony; musical scale; set of celestial objects; set of troops; system”), from Ancient Greek σύστημα (“musical scale; organized body; whole made of several parts or members”), from σῠνίστημῐ (Ancient Greek “to combine, organize”) + -μᾰ (Ancient Greek). is from σῠν- (Ancient Greek “with, together”) + ἵστημι (Ancient Greek “to stand”), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand (up)”).

Cognate with systeem (Dutch), modern système (French), System (German), sistema (Italian), sistema (Portuguese), sistema (Spanish). .

chain.meaning: harmony; musical scale; set of celestial objects; set of troops; system

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English table, tabel (Middle English), tabil (Middle English), tabul (Middle English), from Old English tabele, tabul (Old English), tablu (Old English), tabule (Old English), tabula (Old English “board”); also as tæfl (Old English), tæfel (Old English), an early borrowing of Latin tabula (“tablet, board, plank, chart”). The sense of “piece of furniture” is from Old French table, of same Latin origin; Old English used bēod (Old English) or bord (Old English) instead for this meaning: see board (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English tablet, from Old French tablete (Modern tablette (French)), diminutive of table (Old French “table”). Compare table (English), -et.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
thumb|Tabloids () on sale#Noun|sale at a [[newsstand in the United Kingdom.]]

The noun is derived from tablet + -oid (English), originally as a brand name for their medicines and other products such as tea in tablet form and registered as a trademark on 14 March 1884.

is influenced by .

The adjective and verb are derived from the noun.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English takel (“gear, apparatus”), from Middle Dutch — or Middle Low German takel (“ship's rigging”), perhaps related to taken (Middle Dutch “to grasp, seize”). Akin to takkel (Danish “tackle”), tackel (Swedish “tackle”). More at take (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English tail, taile (Middle English), taille (Middle English), tayil (Middle English), tayl (Middle English), tayle (Middle English), tayll (Middle English), teil (Middle English), tæȝel (Middle English), from Old English tæġel, tæġl (Old English “tail”), from Proto-West Germanic *tagl, from Proto-Germanic *taglą (“hair, fiber; hair of a tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ- (“hair of the tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to tear, fray, shred”).

Cognate with Zagel (German “tail”), tagl (Danish / Faroese / Icelandic “tail”), tagel (Swedish “horsehair”), 𐍄𐌰𐌲𐌻 (Gothic “hair”); also дла̏ка (Serbo-Croatian), dlȁka (Serbo-Croatian “single hair”), dlaka (Slovenian “single hair”), dezî (Kurmanji Kurdish “cotton, thread”), दशा (Sanskrit “border, fringe, hem”).

In some senses, apparently by a generalization of the usual opposition between head and tail.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Anglo-Norman —, probably from a shortened form of entail.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English taken (“to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike”), from Old English tacan (“to grasp, touch”), probably of gmq — origin, from Old Norse taka (“to touch, take”). Alternatively, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *takan (“to take; grasp, touch”). Both from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to touch”), from pre-Germanic , possibly a phonetically altered form of Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g- (“to touch, take”) (see there for details).

Gradually displaced native nim (English), from nimen (Middle English), from niman (Old English “to take”).

Cognate with tak (Scots “to take”), - (Icelandic) and taka (Norwegian Nynorsk “to take”), ta (Norwegian Bokmål “to take”), ta (Swedish “to take”), tage (Danish “to take, seize”), take (Western Frisian), taakje (Western Frisian “to grab, steal”), taken (Dutch “to take; grasp”), tacken (Middle Low German “to grasp”). thack (English) may be from the same root. Compare tackle (English). Despite superficial similarity, unrelated to *tek- (Proto-Indo-European “to take by hand, obtain”), which is instead cognate with thig (English “to beg”).

chain.meaning: to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Deverbal: take away

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English tale, from Old English talu (“tale, series, calculation”), from Proto-West Germanic *talu, from Proto-Germanic *talō (“calculation, number”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to reckon, count”).

Cognate with taal (Western Frisian “speech, language”), taal (Dutch “language, speech”), Zahl (German “number, figure”), tale (Danish “speech”), tala (Icelandic “speech, talk, discourse, number, figure”), dolus (Latin “guile, deceit, fraud”), δόλος (Ancient Greek “wile, bait”), ndjell (Albanian “to lure”), til (Kurmanji Kurdish “finger”), տող (Classical Armenian “row”). Related to tell (English), talk (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English talen, from Old English talian (“to count, calculate, reckon”), from Proto-West Germanic *talōn, from Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to count”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to count, reckon, aim, calculate, adjust”).

Cognate with talen (Dutch “to long, care”), zahlen (German “to pay”), tala (Swedish “to speak, talk”), tala (Icelandic “to talk”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English talent, from Old English talente, borrowed from the plural of Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (“balance, a particular weight, especially of gold, sum of money, a talent”). Compare talenta (Old High German “talent”). Later figurative senses are from Old French talent (“talent, will, inclination, desire”), derived from the biblical .

chain.meaning: balance, a particular weight, especially of gold, sum of money, a talent

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: talent + -ed

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English talken, talkien (Middle English), from Old English *tealcian (“to talk, chat”), from Proto-West Germanic *talkōn, from Proto-Germanic *talkōną (“to talk, chatter”), frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to count, recount, tell”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol-, *del- (Proto-Indo-European “to aim, calculate, adjust, count”), equivalent to tell (English) + -k (English).

Cognate with taalken (Low German “to chatter, gossip, talk”). Related also to zoin (Bavarian “to pay”), zaln (Cimbric “to pay”), talen (Dutch “to care, long; to speak; to say”), zahlen (German “to pay”), zoln (mhn “to pay”), tale (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to talk, speak”), tala (Faroese / Icelandic / Swedish “to speak, talk”), tala (Norwegian Nynorsk “to speak, talk”); also dolus (Latin “deceit, deception, fraud, guile, treachery, trickery; malice; artifice, device, stratagem”), δόλος (Ancient Greek “deceit, trick; wiles; bait”), տող (Armenian “line (in a text)”). More at tale (English). Despite the surface similarity, unrelated to *telkʷ- (Proto-Indo-European “to talk”) (due to Grimm's law), which is the source of loquacious (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English talk, talke (Middle English “conversation; discourse”), from the verb (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English tan, from Old French tan (“tanbark”), from Gaulish *tannos (“green oak”) – compare tann (Breton “red oak”), tannen (oco) –, from Proto-Celtic *tannos (“green oak”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dʰonu (“*(s)dʰonu”). Per this hypothesis, related to , femur (Latin), genitive feminis (Latin “thigh”), Tann (German “woods”), Tanne (German “fir”), thanë (Albanian “cranberry bush”), θάμνος (Ancient Greek “thicket”), 𐬚𐬀𐬥𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬭𐬆 (ae), धनु (Sanskrit).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English tan, from Old French tan (“tanbark”), from Gaulish *tannos (“green oak”) – compare tann (Breton “red oak”), tannen (oco) –, from Proto-Celtic *tannos (“green oak”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *dʰonu (“*(s)dʰonu”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: As a verb, from Middle English tannen, from late Old English tannian (“to tan a hide”), from Latin tannare.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3

etymologies.text: Cantonese — .

etymologies.label: Etymology 6
etymologies.text: From Middle English *tan, from Old English tān (“twig, shoot, switch”), from Proto-West Germanic *tain, from Proto-Germanic *tainaz (“rod, twig, straw, lot”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 7
etymologies.text: It may either be a figurative use of the usual verb or a jam — pronunciation of turn (English), compare bun (English “to kill particularly by gunshot”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English tappe (“hollow device for controlling the flow of liquid from a hole, cock, faucet, spigot; hole through which the liquid flows; the liquid which thus flows”), from Old English tæppa, from Proto-West Germanic *tappō, from Proto-Germanic *tappô (“a plug, tap; peg; tapering stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂p- (“to lose; to sacrifice”). .

The verb is derived from Middle English tappen (“to obtain (liquid, chiefly liquor) from a tap; to obtain and sell (liquor)”), from Old English tæppian (“to provide (a container) with a stopper; to obtain (liquid) from a tap”), and then either:

* from Old English tæppa (see above) + -ian (Old English); or
* from Proto-Germanic *tappōną, from *tappô (Proto-Germanic) (see above).

Verb (“to turn over (a playing card or playing piece) to remind players that it has already been used in that round”) alludes to the abilities or resources of the card or piece having been drawn on to the point of temporary exhaustion: see verb .

chain.meaning: hollow device for controlling the flow of liquid from a hole, cock, faucet, spigot; hole through which the liquid flows; the liquid which thus flows
to obtain (liquid, chiefly liquor) from a tap; to obtain and sell (liquor)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
The verb is derived from Middle English tappen, teppen (Middle English “to give (something) a knock or tap; to hit (something) lightly, pat, tap”), either:

* imitative of the making of a tapping sound; or
* from Old French tapper, taper (Old French “to tap”) (modern taper (French)), from Frankish *tappōn, *dabbōn (Proto-West Germanic “to strike”), or from Middle Low German tappen, tapen (Middle Low German “to rap, strike, tap”), or from Proto-Germanic *tabōną (“to grope, to grapple, to claw”), maybe via a *tapa (Old Norse “to strike”), as seen in the derivative tapsa (Old Norse “to tap”) .

Verb (“to arrest (someone)”) and (“to choose or designate (someone) for a duty, etc.”) allude to a police officer or other person tapping someone on their shoulder to catch their attention or to select them.

The noun is derived from Middle English tap, tappe (Middle English “light blow or hit”), and then either:

* from Middle English tappen (see above); or
* from Old French tape (“light slap or touch, pat”) (modern tape (French)), from tapper (Old French), taper (Old French) (see above).

* tappen (German “to fumble; to grope”)
* tappa (Icelandic), tapsa (Icelandic), tæpta (Icelandic “to tap”)

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From - (Persian) or تب (Urdu “malarial fever”), ultimately from Sanskrit ताप (“fever; heat; pain, torment”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French targette, targuete (Middle French), diminutive of targe (Middle French “light shield”), from Old French —, from Frankish *targa (“buckler”), akin to targa (Old Norse “small round shield”) (whence also targe (Old English), targa (Old English “shield”)) from Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge”), from Proto-Indo-European *derǵʰ- (“fenced lot”). Akin to zarga (Old High German “side wall, rim”) (German Zarge (German “frame”)), tarjeta (Spanish “card”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English taske (“task, tax”), from Old Northern French tasque, (compare Old French variant tasche (Old French)), from Medieval Latin tasca, alteration of taxa (Latin), from Latin taxō (“to censure; to charge”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The verb is from Middle English tasten, borrowed from Old French taster (“to taste, touch or hit”), from unattested Vulgar Latin *tastāre (“to touch or feel”), from , an innovated form of Classical Latin taxo (“taxāre”), from tango (Latin “tangere”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-, which is assumed to have had the same meaning as .
The noun came from the verb, and the two conflated after English lost its infinitive suffix -en (English), though tasten (Middle English) was most likely already used nominatively (as a ), similar to tasting (English).

Almost fully , from smac,smak,smacke (Middle English), from smæc,smæċċ (Old English “taste, smatch”).
, from smacchen,smecchen (Middle English), from smæċċan (Old English “to taste; to smack”); displaced also buriȝen (Middle English), from bierġan (Old English “to taste”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From taste + -y (English). The Philippine sense is due to a genericized trademark from Taystee Bread Company, a defunct American company.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English taxe, from Middle French taxe, from Medieval Latin taxa, from taxō (Latin “to appraise, value, estimate; (medieval) to tax”). . Displaced native gafol (Old English), which was also the word for “tribute” and “rent”.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English taxen, from Anglo-Norman taxer (“to impose a tax”), from Latin taxō (“to handle, to censure, to appraise, to compute”).

chain.meaning: to handle, to censure, to appraise, to compute

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
First appears c. 1655, in the English translation ’s writings. From Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (), from och —, ultimately from sit-pro *s-la (“leaf, tea”). Introduced to English and other Western European languages by the , who sourced their tea in ; compare teh (Malay) along the same trade route. (and, distantly, the first element of lahpet (English)), from same Proto-Sino-Tibetan root; see discussion of cognates.

The word for “tea” in many languages is of Sinitic origin (due to China being the origin of the plant), and thus there are many cognates; see translations. These are from one of two proximate sources, reflected in the phonological shape: forms with a stop (e.g. ) are derived from Min Nan tê, while forms with an affricate (e.g. ) are derived from other Sinitic languages, like Mandarin chá or Cantonese caa4 (all written as ). Different languages borrowed one or the other form (specific language and point in time varied), reflecting trade ties, generally Min Nan tê if by ocean trade from Fujian, Cantonese caa4 if by ocean trade from Guangdong, or northern Chinese chá if by overland trade or by ocean trade from India.

Thus Western and Northern European languages borrowed tê (with the exception of Portuguese, which uses chá (Portuguese); despite being by ocean trade, their source was in , not Amoy), while chá borrowings are used over a very large geographical area of Eurasia and Africa: Southern and Eastern Europe, and on through Turkish, Arabic, North and East Africa, Persian, Central Asian, and Indic languages. In Europe the tê/chá line is Italian/Slovene, Hungarian/Romanian, German/Czech, Polish/Ukrainian, Baltics/Russian, Finnish/Karelian, Northern Sami/Inari Sami. tê was also borrowed in European trade stops in Southern India and coastal Africa, though chá borrowings are otherwise more prevalent in these regions, via Arabic or Indic, due to earlier trade. The situation in Southeast Asia is complex due to multiple influences, and some languages borrowed both forms, such as Malay teh (Malay) and ca (Malay).

(“information, especially gossip”) may be originally from T standing for truth (English), which evolved into tea. An alternative explanation dates back to gay African-American culture in the 1970s and alludes to women gossiping over afternoon tea.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English techen, from Old English tǣċan (“to show, declare, demonstrate; teach, instruct, train; assign, prescribe, direct; warn; persuade”), from Proto-West Germanic *taikijan, from Proto-Germanic *taikijaną (“to show”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”).

Cognate with tech (Scots), teich (Scots “to teach”), zeigen (German “to show, point out”), zeihen (German “accuse, blame”), 𐌲𐌰𐍄𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to announce, declare, tell, show, display”), dīcō (Latin “speak, say, tell”), δείκνυμι (Ancient Greek “show, point out, explain, teach”), दिशति (Sanskrit “to point out, show, tell, teach”). More at token (English).

chain.meaning: to show, declare, demonstrate; teach, instruct, train; assign, prescribe, direct; warn; persuade

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Clipping: teacher

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English teching, techinge (Middle English), from Old English tǣċing, tǣċung (Old English “instruction, direction, teaching”), equivalent to teach + -ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2

etymologies.label: Etymology 1

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English þe, from Old English þē (“the, that”), a late variant of sē (Old English), the s- (which occurred in the masculine and feminine nominative singular only) having been replaced by the þ- from the oblique stem.

Originally neutral nominative, in Middle English it superseded all previous Old English nominative forms (sē (Old English), sēo (Old English), þæt (Old English), þā (Old English)); sē (Old English) is from Proto-West Germanic *siz, from Proto-Germanic *sa, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *só.

Cognate with die (Saterland Frisian “the”), de (Western Frisian “the”), de (Dutch “the”), de (Low German (Germany) “the”), der (German “the”), de (Danish “the”), de (Swedish “the”), sá (Icelandic “that”) within Germanic and with स (Sanskrit “the, that”), ὁ (Ancient Greek “the”), se (txb “this”) among other Indo-European languages.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English the, thy (Middle English), thi (Middle English), from Old English þe (“þē̆”), probably a neuter instrumental form ("by that, thereby")—alongside the more common þȳ (Old English) and þon (Old English)—of the demonstrative pronoun sē (Old English) ("that"). Compare des te (Dutch “des te”) ("the, the more"), desto (German “desto”) ("the, all the more"), fordi (Norwegian “fordi”) and av di (Norwegian “av di”) ("because"), því (Icelandic “the; because”), tí (Faroese), ty (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Late Middle English thesis (“lowering of the voice”) and also borrowed directly from its etymon Latin thesis (“proposition, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from Ancient Greek θέσῐς (“arrangement, placement, setting; conclusion, position, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from τῐ́θημῐ (Ancient Greek “to place, put, set; to put down in writing; to consider as, regard”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to place, put”)) + -σῐς (Ancient Greek). The English word is a .

Sense 1.1 (“proposition or statement supported by arguments”) is adopted from antithesis (English). Sense 1.4 (“initial stage of reasoning”) was first used by the German philosopher (1762–1814), and later applied to the dialectical method of his countryman, the philosopher (1770–1831).

The plural form theses (English) is borrowed from Latin thesēs, from Ancient Greek θέσεις.

chain.meaning: proposition, thesis; lowering of the voice

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English þei, borrowed in the 1200s from Old Norse þeir, plural of the demonstrative sá (Old Norse) which acted as a plural pronoun. Displaced native he (Middle English) from hīe (Old English) — which vowel changes had left indistinct from he (Middle English “he”) — by the 1400s, being readily incorporated alongside native words beginning with the same sound (the (English), that (English), this (English)). Used as a singular pronoun since 1300, e.g. in the 1325 Cursor Mundi.

The Norse term (whence also þeir (Icelandic “they”), teir (Faroese “they”), de (Danish “they”), de (Swedish “they”), dei (Norwegian Nynorsk “they”)) is from Proto-Germanic *þai (“those”) (from Proto-Indo-European *só (“*to-”)), whence also þā (Old English “those”) (whence obsolete English ), thae (Scots), thai (Scots), thay (Scots “they; those”), dia (swg “they”).

The origin of the determiner they (English “the, those”) is unclear. The OED, English Dialect Dictionary and Middle English Dictionary define it and its Middle English predecessor thei (Middle English) as a demonstrative determiner or adjective meaning “those” or “the”. This could be a continuation of the use of the English pronoun they (English)'s Old Norse etymon þeir (Old Norse) as a demonstrative meaning “those”, but the OED and EDD say it is limited to southern, especially southwestern, England, specifically outside the region of Norse contact.

etymologies.text: From Middle English thef, theef (Middle English), þef (Middle English), from Old English þēof, from Proto-West Germanic *þeub, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz. etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English thing, from Old English þing, from Proto-West Germanic *þing, from Proto-Germanic *þingą.

Cognate with Ding (Saterland Frisian “thing”), ting (Western Frisian), ding (Western Frisian “thing”), ding (Dutch “thing”), Ding (Low German (Germany) “thing”), Ding (German “thing”), ting (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “thing”), ting (Faroese “parliament, assembly”), þing (Icelandic “congress, assembly”), hing (Scots “thing”).

The word originally meant "assembly", then came to mean a specific issue discussed at such an assembly, and ultimately came to mean most broadly "an object". Compare rēs (Latin), also meaning "legal matter", and same transition from causa (Latin “legal matter”) to "thing" in Romance languages. Modern use to refer to a Germanic assembly is likely influenced by cognates (from the same Proto-Germanic root) like þing (Old Norse “thing”), ting (Danish), ting (Swedish), and ding (Old High German) with this meaning.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English thirst,thurst, from Old English þurst, from Proto-West Germanic *þurstu, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters- (“dry”).

Germanic cognates include thurst (Old High German), durst (Middle High German), Durst (German), thurst (Old Saxon), thursti (Old Dutch), dorst (Middle Dutch), dorste (Middle Dutch), dorst (Dutch), þorsti (Old Norse) (törst (Swedish), þorsti (Icelandic), tosti (Faroese), tørst (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), tørste (Norwegian Nynorsk)). Indo-European cognates include τέρσομαι (Ancient Greek), djersë (Albanian “sweat”), तृष्णा (Sanskrit “desire; thirst”), तृष्यति (Sanskrit), terra (Latin), torridus (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English thoruȝ, þoruȝ (Middle English), from Old English þuruh, a byform of Old English þurh, whence comes through (English). The adjective derives from the preposition and adverb. The word developed a syllabic form in cases where the word was fully stressed: when it was used as an adverb, adjective, or noun, and less commonly when used as a preposition.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From thorough + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From though (Middle English), thogh (Middle English), from Old Norse *þóh (later þó (Old Norse)). Superseded (in most dialects) Middle English thegh, from Old English þēah (“though, although, even if, that, however, nevertheless, yet, still; whether”). Both the Old Norse and Old English are from Proto-Germanic *þauh (“though”), from Proto-Indo-European *to-, suffixed with Proto-Germanic *-hw < Proto-Indo-European *-kʷe (“and”).

Akin to tho (Scots “though”), dach (Saterland Frisian “though”), dôch (Western Frisian), dochs (Western Frisian “though”), doch (Dutch “though”), doch (German “though”), dog (Danish “though, however”), dock (Swedish “however, still”), þó (Icelandic “though”). More at that.

chain.meaning: though, although, even if, that, however, nevertheless, yet, still; whether

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English thought, ithoȝt (Middle English), from Old English þōht, ġeþōht (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *þą̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtaz, *gaþanhtą (Proto-Germanic “thought”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think”). Cognate with thocht (Scots “thought”), Toacht (Saterland Frisian “thought”), oandacht (Western Frisian “dacht”), gedachte (Dutch “thought”), Andacht (German “Andacht”), þóttur (Icelandic “thought”). Related to thank, think.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English thoȝtful, thohtful (Middle English), equivalent to thought + ful (English). Compare gedachtenvol (Dutch), tankfull (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English threte, thret (Middle English), thrat (Middle English), thræt (Middle English), threat (Middle English), from Old English þrēat (“crowd, swarm, troop, army, press; pressure, trouble, calamity, oppression, force, violence, threat”), from Proto-Germanic *þrautaz, closely tied to *þrautą (Proto-Germanic “displeasure, complaint, grievance, labour, toil”), from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, push, press”). Cognate with thret, threte, threit (Scots “threat”), drōz (Middle High German “annoyance, disgust, horror, terror, fright”), drōt (Middle Low German “threat, menace, danger”), treyt (Faroese “struggle, labour, distress”), þraut (Icelandic “struggle, labour, distress”), - (Belarusian), - (Bulgarian), - (Macedonian), - (Russian), and труд (Ukrainian “work, labour”), trud (Czech “effot, hard work”), trud (Polish “hard work”), trȗd (Serbo-Croatian “effort, hard work”).

chain.meaning: crowd, swarm, troop, army, press; pressure, trouble, calamity, oppression, force, violence, threat

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English threten, from Old English þrēatian (“to press, oppress, repress, correct, threaten”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, push, press”). Cognate with threit (Scots “to threaten”), verdrieten (Dutch “to sadden, displease”), drēten (Middle Low German “to threaten”), verdrießen (German “to bother, vex”), tróta (Faroese “to run out”), þrjóta (Icelandic “to run out, end”), tryte (Norwegian “to run out, end”), tryda (Swedish “to run out”), 𐌿𐍃𐌸𐍂𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to harass, torment”), trūdō (Latin “to push”), ndrydh (Albanian “to sprain, supress, withdraw”), трудзіць (Belarusian “to burden, tire”), тру̀дя (Bulgarian “to work”), trudit (Czech “to toil, worry”), trudzić (Polish “to toil, worry”), труди́ть (Russian “to burden, tire”), trúditi (Serbo-Croatian “to try, make and effot”), труди́ти (Ukrainian “to toil, tire”).

chain.meaning: to press, oppress, repress, correct, threaten

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English thretenen, from Old English þrēatnian (“to urge, force, compel”), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: thrill + -er

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English throte, from Old English þrote, þrota (Old English), þrotu (Old English “throat”), from Proto-West Germanic *þrotu, from Proto-Germanic *þrutō (“throat”), from Proto-Indo-European *trud- (“to swell, become stiff”). Cognate with strot (Dutch “throat”), Drossel (German “throttle, gorge of game (wild animals)”), troti (Faroese “swelling”), þroti (Icelandic “swelling”), trut (Norwegian “mouth”), trut (Swedish).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English thurgh, thrugh (Middle English), thruch (Middle English), thruh (Middle English), metathetic variants of thurgh (Middle English), thurh (Middle English), from Old English þurh, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw (“through”), from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥h₂kʷe, suffixed zero-grade from *terh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to pass through”) + *-kʷe (Proto-Indo-European “and”).

Cognate with döör (North Frisian “through”), truch (Saterland Frisian “through”), troch (Western Frisian “through”), door (Dutch “through”), durch (German “through”), duerch (lb “through”), deur (Flemish “through”), דורך (Yiddish “through”), 𐌸𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌷 (Gothic “through”), trans (Latin “across, over, through”), tërthor (Albanian “through, around”), tra (Welsh “through”). See also thorough.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English thrugh, þrouȝ (Middle English), throgh (Middle English), from Old English þrūh (“trough, conduit, pipe; box, chest; coffin, tomb”), from Proto-Germanic *þrūhs (“hollowed-out wood”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₃u- (“to rub, turn, drill, bore”). Not directly related with Truhe (German “chest”), which belongs to the root of trough (English). However, these two Germanic roots seem to have influenced each other early on.

chain.meaning: trough, conduit, pipe; box, chest; coffin, tomb

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old English þurh ūt (Old English), equivalent to . Compare durchaus (German “all the way, fully, absolutely”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived from Middle English thombe, thoume (Middle English), thoumbe (Middle English “thumb”), from Old English þūma (“thumb”), from Proto-West Germanic *þūmō (“thumb”), from Proto-Germanic *þūmô (“thumb”), from Proto-Indo-European *tūm- (“to grow”).

Cognate with tomme (Western Frisian “thumb”), duim (Dutch “thumb”), Duum (Low German “thumb”), Daumen (German “thumb”), tomme (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “inch”), tum (Norn “thumb”), tumme (Swedish “thumb”), tum (Swedish “inch”), дюйм (Russian “inch”), τύμβος (Ancient Greek “burial mound”). Also compare tyfu (Welsh “to grow”), tumēre (Latin “to swell”), tumėti (Lithuanian “to thicken, clot”), 𐬀𐬨𐬏𐬙 (ae “strong”), तुम्र (Sanskrit “strong, thick”). The parasitic ‐b has existed since the late 13th century. Doublet of tomb (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English thunder, thonder (Middle English), thundre (Middle English), thonre (Middle English), thunnere (Middle English), þunre (Middle English), from Old English þunor (“thunder”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunr, from Proto-Germanic *þunraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ten-, *(s)tenh₂- (Proto-Indo-European “to thunder”).

Compare astound (English), astonish (English), stun (English). Germanic cognates include tonger (Western Frisian), donder (Dutch), Donner (German), Þórr (Old Norse) (Thor (English)), torden (Danish), tore (Norwegian Nynorsk). Other cognates include تندر (Persian), tonō (Latin), detonō (Latin), στένω (Ancient Greek), στενάζω (Ancient Greek), στόνος (Ancient Greek), Στέντωρ (Ancient Greek), torann (Irish), taran (Welsh), Taranis (Gaulish). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English thundren, from Old English þunrian (“to thunder”), from Proto-West Germanic *þunrōn, from Proto-Germanic *þunrōną (“to thunder”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English thus, þus (Middle English), from Old English þus (“thus, in this way, as follows, in this manner, to this extent”), from Proto-West Germanic *þus (“so, thus”), perhaps originally from a variant of the instrumental form of this (English), related to þȳs (Old English “by this, with this”), thius (Old Saxon “by this, with this”). Cognate with thus (Scots “thus”), aldoz (North Frisian “thus”), dus (Saterland Frisian), düs (Saterland Frisian “thus”), dus (Western Frisian “thus”), dus (Dutch “thus, so”), dus (Middle High German “thus, as follows”).

Compare also zus (Dutch “thus, hence”), sus (Low German “thus, hence”), sus (Middle High German “thus, hence”), a similar formation from the stem of *swā (Proto-West Germanic “so”).

chain.meaning: thus, in this way, as follows, in this manner, to this extent

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|A tick ()
From Middle English tyke, teke (Middle English), from Old English ticia (“parasitic animal, tick”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīkō, compare teek (Dutch), Zecke (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English *tik, tek (Middle English), tyche (Middle English “light touch, tap”), from the verb (see Etymology 3 below). Compare tik (Dutch “a pat, tap”), zic (Middle High German “a slight touch”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English ticken, tiken (Middle English), probably from Old English *ticcian (“to touch, tap”), from Proto-West Germanic *tikkōn (“to touch, tap”), cognate with zecken (German “to nudge, poke, jab”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle English tike, probably from Middle Dutch tike and Middle Low German teke, both ultimately from Latin theca (“cover”). Compare also Zieche (German “duvet, pillowcase”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: ticket.

etymologies.label: Etymology 6
etymologies.text: From Middle English tik-, tic- (Middle English), tike- (Middle English), tiken- (Middle English), an unassibilated form of Middle English tiche, tichen (Middle English “young goat”), from Old English tiċċen (“young goat; kid”), from Proto-West Germanic *tikkīn (“goatling”), diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *tigā (“goat”). Cognate with regional Zicke (German “nanny goat”), from Ziege (German “goat; nanny goat”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Related to time (English).

Cognate with tijd (Dutch “time”), Zeit (German “time”), tid (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “time”), tíð (Faroese / Icelandic “time”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English tiden, tide, from Old English tīdan (“to happen”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English teye (“cord, chain”), from Old English tēag, tēah (Old English “cord, chain”), from Proto-West Germanic *taugu, from Proto-Germanic *taugō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-. Compare tov (Danish), taug (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English teien, teiȝen (Middle English), from Old English tīġan, tīeġan (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *taugijan, from Proto-Germanic *taugijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to tug, draw”). Cognate with teygja (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English tygre, in part from Old English tigras (pl.), in part from Anglo-Norman tigre, both from Latin tigris, from Ancient Greek τίγρις, from ira — (compare 𐬙𐬌𐬔𐬭𐬌 (ae “arrow”), 𐬙𐬌𐬖𐬭𐬀 (ae “pointed”)). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to pierce, prick, be sharp”). Compare English stick (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From the mascot of Princeton (a tiger), which led to early cheerleaders calling out "Tiger" at the end of a cheer for the Princeton team.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English tight, tyght (Middle English), tyȝt (Middle English), tiht (Middle English), variants of thight (Middle English), thiht (Middle English), from Old English *þiht, *þīht (Old English) (attested in meteþiht (Old English)), from Proto-West Germanic *þį̄ht(ī), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *tenkt- (“dense, thick, tight”), from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, pull”).

Cognate with ticht (Scots), ticht (Western Frisian), tæt (Danish), þéttur (Icelandic “dense”), tett (Norwegian), tät (Swedish), dicht (Dutch “dense”), dicht (German “dense”).

The current form with t- /t/ rather than etymologically-expected th- /θ/ arose in Middle English under the influence of the etymologically-unrelated verbs tighten (English) and tight, which come from a different Proto-Indo-European root (starting with *d- and thus regularly having t-).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English tighten, thyhten (Middle English “to make tight”); see tighten (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Synchronically equivalent to tight + en (English), but actually derived from Middle English tighten, from Old English tyhtan, thus originally unrelated to tight (English) (Old English *þiht (Old English)).

etymologies.text: Affix: tight + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English til, from Northern Old English til, from or akin to Old Norse til (“to, till”); both from Proto-Germanic *til (“to, toward”), from Proto-Germanic *tilą (“planned point in time”). Not a contraction of until (English); rather, until comes from till with the prefix un- (English “against; toward; up to”) also found in unto (English). Cognate with til (Old Frisian “to, till”), til (Danish “to”), till (Swedish “to, till”), til (Icelandic “to, till”). Also related to til (Old English “good”), Ziel (German “goal”), 𐍄𐌹𐌻 (Gothic “something fitting or suitable”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English tylle (“till”), possibly from Middle English tillen (“to draw”) from Old English *tyllan (“to draw, attract”) (as in betyllan (Old English “to lure, decoy”) and fortyllan (Old English “to draw away”); related to *tollian (Old English) > tollen (Middle English)). Cognate with ndjell (Albanian “to lure, attract”).

Alternatively, tylle (Middle English) is from Anglo-Norman tylle (“compartment”), from Old French tille (“compartment, shelter on a ship”), from Old Norse þilja (“plank”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English tilyen, from Old English tilian.

etymologies.text:
From Middle English tyme, time (Middle English), from Old English tīma (“time, period, space of time, season, lifetime, fixed time, favorable time, opportunity”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīmō, from Proto-Germanic *tīmô (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂imō, from *deh₂y- (Proto-Indo-European “*deh₂-i-”), from the root *deh₂- (Proto-Indo-European). Related to tide (English). Not related to tempus (Latin). Distant (or , if the Greek and Germanic words were suffixed independently).

* tym (Scots), tyme (Scots “time”)
* Zimen (Alemannic), Zimmän (Alemannic “Zīmmän”)
* time (Danish “hour, lesson”)

* tími (Faroese “hour, lesson, time”)
* tími (Icelandic “time, season”)

* timma (Swedish), timme (Swedish “hour”).

etymologies.text: From Middle English tin, from Old English tin, from Proto-West Germanic *tin, from Proto-Germanic *tiną.

etymologies.text: From Late Middle English tippen, possibly from gmq —/Scandinavian (compare tippa (Swedish “to topple over”)), or a special use of Etymology 1.

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: , perhaps related to tip#Etymology 1 (English “Etymology 1”) and cognate with tippen (Dutch), tippen (German), tippa (Swedish).

etymologies.text: From Middle English tiredness, terednesse (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English tissu, from Old French tissu (“woven”), past participle of tistre (Old French “to weave”), from Latin texō (“to weave”).

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English to, from Old English tō, from Proto-Germanic *tō ~ *ta (Proto-Germanic), from Proto-Indo-European *de ~ *do (Proto-Indo-European “to”). Cognate with tae (Scots), to (Scots “to”), to (North Frisian), tö (North Frisian), tu (North Frisian “to”), tou (Saterland Frisian “to”), to (Low German “to”), toe (Dutch), te (Dutch “to”), zu (German “to”), ta (Western Frisian “to”). Non-Germanic cognates include ndaj (Albanian “towards”), Irish do (Irish “to, for”), Breton da (Breton “to, for”), Welsh i (Welsh “to, for”), до (Russian “to”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English today, to-daie (Middle English), todæig (Middle English), from Old English tōdæġ, tō dæġe (Old English “today”), equivalent to to + day (English). Compare däälich (Saterland Frisian “today”), vandaag (Dutch “today”), hindag (Old Saxon “today”), vandage (Low German (Germany)), vandaag (Low German (Germany) “today”), i dag (Swedish), idag (Swedish “today”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Late Middle English together, from earlier togedere (Middle English), togadere (Middle English), from Old English tōgædere (“together”), from Proto-West Germanic *tōgadura, *tegadura (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *tō (“to”) + *gadar (Proto-Germanic “together”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- (“to unite, keep”), equivalent to to-#Etymology_2 + gather (English). Cognate with thegither (Scots “together”), togadera (Old Frisian) (whence togearre (Western Frisian “together”)), tegader (Dutch “together”), tōgāder (Middle Low German “together”), zegater (Middle High German “together”). Compare also ætgædere (Old English “together”), ġeador (Old English “together”). More at gather (English).

From Middle English tombe, toumbe (Middle English), borrowed from Old French tombe, from Latin tumba from Ancient Greek τύμβος (“a sepulchral mound, tomb, grave”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂- (“to swell”). Displaced native þrūh (Old English).

The verb is from Middle English tomben.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English tongue, a late spelling of tonge (Middle English “tong(e)”), tunge (Middle English “tung(e)”), from Old English tunge, from Proto-West Germanic *tungā (“tongue”), from Proto-Germanic *tungǭ (“tongue”), from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue”). .

* Germanic: tonge (Western Frisian), tong (Dutch), Zong (lb), Zunge (German), tunge (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), tunga (Faroese / Icelandic / Swedish), 𐍄𐌿𐌲𐌲𐍉 (Gothic).
* Italic: llengua (Asturian / Catalan), luenga (Aragonese), langue (French), lingua (Galician / Italian / Latin), llingua (roa-leo), lhéngua (mwl), língua (Portuguese), lengua (Spanish).
* Celtic: teanga (Irish).
* Slavic: язык (Belarusian / Russian), ези́к (Bulgarian), jazyk (Czech / Slovak), јазик (Macedonian), język (Polish), jèzik (Serbo-Croatian “tongue”), jézik (Slovenian), язи́к (Ukrainian).
* Indo-Iranic: زبان (Persian), जि॒ह्वा (Sanskrit).

* The expected modern spelling, both phonetically and etymologically, would be tung (English). Using ⟨on⟩ for ⟨un⟩ was fairly common in - (Middle English); compare e.g. yong (Middle English “young”). The final ⟨gue⟩ arose to prevent being misread with a soft . However, this spelling only became common at a time when the final ⟨e⟩ was already largely silent, so it is not clear why it was not simply dropped instead. Perhaps the spelling was influenced directly by langue (Middle French “tongue”).
* (“a language”) is an ancient metonym, already in use more than one thousand years ago in Old English, going back all the way to Proto-Germanic (the oldest-possible form of English and other tongues), and common across Indo-European languages (cf. լեզու (Armenian), teanga (Irish), lingua (Latin), زبان (Persian) and язык (Russian)). Its persistent modern usage, which prevented it from becoming fully or in favor of the Gallicism language (English), is likely due to its natural metonymicity and to steady historical reinforcement by langue (Anglo-Norman) (which had both meanings too) and by, to a lesser extent, native poetic imitation of lingua (Latin) during the Renaissance.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English tool, tol (Middle English), from Old English tōl (“tool, implement, instrument”), perhaps borrowed from Old Norse tól, but at any rate ultimately from Proto-Germanic *tōlą (“that which is used in preparation, tool”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂- (“to tie to, secure”), equivalent to taw + le (English) . Cognate with tuil (Scots “tool, implement, instrument, device”), tól (Icelandic “tool”), tól (Faroese “tool, instrument”). Related to tāwian (Old English “to make, prepare, or cultivate”); see taw (English), and tow (English) ("fibres used for spinning").

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From tooth + paste (English). Compare Tuskepasta (Saterland Frisian “toothpaste”), toskpoetserguod (Western Frisian “toothpaste”), tandpasta (Dutch “toothpaste”), Zahnpasta (German), Zahnpaste (German “toothpaste”), tandpasta (Danish “toothpaste”), tandpasta (Swedish “toothpaste”), tannkrem (Icelandic “toothpaste”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English top, toppe (Middle English), from Old English topp (“top, highest part; summit; crest; tassel, tuft; (spinning) top, ball; a tuft or ball at the highest point of anything”), from Proto-West Germanic *topp, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz (“braid, pigtail, end”), of unknown ultimate origin. Compare typologically apex (Latin) (<< *h₂ep- (Proto-Indo-European “to join, attach, fasten, fit”)).

Cognate with Top (Saterland Frisian “top”), sòpf (Cimbric “braid”), top (Dutch “top, summit, peak”), Topp (German “top of a mast”), Zopf (German “braid, pigtail, plait, top”), Zapp (lb “plait, tress”), cöp (Ripuarian “braid, plait”), צאָפּ (Yiddish “braid”), top (Danish “top”), toppur (Icelandic “top”), - (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and topp (Swedish “top, peak, summit, tip”), zuffa (Italian “brawl”).

The sense of a spinning toy is separated from this, obscurely related to top (Dutch) and dop (Dutch) in this sense, against Standard tol (Dutch), and toupie (French) having this sense.

chain.meaning: top, highest part; summit; crest; tassel, tuft; (spinning) top, ball; a tuft or ball at the highest point of anything

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin topica, from Ancient Greek τοπικός (“pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical”), from τόπος (Ancient Greek “a place”).

chain.meaning: pertaining to a place, local, pertaining to a common place, or topic, topical

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English torch, torche (Middle English “large candle; lighted stick; (figurative) sunbeam”), from Old French torche, torque (Old French “torch; bundle of (twisted) straw”) (modern torche (French)); further etymology uncertain, probably from Vulgar Latin *torca (“coiled object”) (referring to a torch made from twisted plant fibres dipped in a flammable substance such as pitch), from Latin torqua, a variant of torquis (Latin “collar of twisted metal, torque; wreath”), from torqueō (Latin “to twist, wind”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- (“to spin; to turn”).

() is either due to the plant’s spike of yellow flowers, or because its leaves and stalks were used to make torches (noun ). (“precious cause, etc., which needs to be protected and transmitted to others”) is derived from lampada trādere (Latin), from [[λᾰμπᾰ́ς (Ancient Greek “to hand over the torch”), a reference to the torch race held at various festivals such as the in Ancient Greece, which involved a relay where a torch was passed from one runner to another.

The verb is derived from the noun.

etymologies.text: Borrowed from French torcher (“to daub; to wipe; to build or plaster with clay mixed with chopped straw”), from torche (French “bundle of (twisted) straw; torch”) (see further at etymology 1) + -er (French).

chain.meaning: to daub; to wipe; to build or plaster with clay mixed with chopped straw

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From earlier English ternado (English), attested since the 1550s as a nautical term for a windy thunderstorm. From Spanish tronada (“thunderstorm”), from tronar (Spanish “to thunder”), from Latin tonō (“to thunder”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). The o and r were reversed in English () under influence of tornar (Spanish “to twist, to turn”), from tornō (Latin “to turn”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English total, from Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from tōtus + -ālis (Latin), the former element of unknown origin. Perhaps related to touto (Oscan “community, city-state”), 𐌕𐌏𐌕𐌀𐌌 (xum “tribe”), þēod (Old English “a nation, people, tribe”), from *tewtéh₂ (Proto-Indo-European “people”). More at Dutch (English), thede (English).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English total, from Old French total, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, from tōtus + -ālis (Latin), the former element of unknown origin.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English touchen, tochen (Middle English), from Old French tochier (“to touch”) (whence Modern toucher (French); compare French doublet toquer (French “to offend, bother, harass”)), from Vulgar Latin *tuccō (“to knock, strike, offend”), from Frankish *tukkōn (“to knock, strike, touch”), from Proto-Germanic *tukkōną (“to tug, grab, grasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to draw, pull, lead”). Largely displaced native rinen (Middle English), from hrīnan (Old English) (whence rine (English)). Doublet of tuck (English).

Cognate with zochhōn (Old High German), zuhhōn (Old High German “to grasp, take, seize, snatch”) (whence zucken (German “to jerk, flinch”)), tucken (Low German (Germany)), tocken (Low German (Germany) “to fidget, twitch, pull up, entice, throb, knock, repeatedly tap”), tocken (Middle Dutch), tucken (Old Dutch “to touch, entice”) (whence tokkelen (Dutch “to strum, pluck”)), tucian (Old English), tūcian (Old English “to disturb, mistreat”) (whence Modern tuck (English)). Compare also tokkōn (Old High German), tockōn (Old High German “to abut, collide”). More at tuck.

Via *dewk- (Proto-Indo-European) cognate with tie (English), tow (English), tug (English), team (English), dūcō (Latin), dux (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English tough, towgh (Middle English), tou (Middle English), toȝ (Middle English), from Old English tōh (“tough, tenacious, holding fast together; pliant; sticky, glutinous, clammy”), from Proto-West Germanic *tą̄h(ī), from Proto-Germanic *tanhuz (“fitting; clinging; tenacious; tough”), from *tinganą (Proto-Germanic “to press upon, throng”), from Proto-Indo-European *denḱ- (“to bite”).

Cognate with toai (Saterland Frisian “tough”), zaach (Bavarian), zach (Bavarian “tough”), taai (Dutch “tough”), zäh (German), zähe (German “tough”), tiee (Limburgish “tough”), zéi (lb “tough”); also δάκνω (Ancient Greek “to bite”), danë (Albanian), darë (Albanian “tongs; pincers; pliers”), दशति (Sanskrit “to bite”).

chain.meaning: tough, tenacious, holding fast together; pliant; sticky, glutinous, clammy

Compare tour (Scots), towr (Scots), towre (Scots “tower”), toer (Western Frisian “tower”), toren (Dutch “tower”), Turm (German “tower”), tårn (Danish “tower”), torn (Swedish “tower”), turn (Icelandic “tower”), tŵr (Welsh).

Cognate with trade (Dutch), tra (Dutch “path, trail, course, trade”), Traad (Low German (Germany) “track, wagon trail”), Tratt (lb “step, pace”), tröð (Icelandic “a lane between fences, enclosure, pen”).

Cognate with trap (Dutch “step, stair”), Trapp (Low German (Germany) “step, stair”). Akin also to traap (Western Frisian “stepping, treading, stairway”), Treppe (German “step, stair”), træppan (Old English “to step, tread”). etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English travelen (“to make a laborious journey, travel”) from Middle Scots travailen (“to toil, work, travel”), alteration of travaillen (Middle English “to toil, work”), from Old French travailler (“to trouble, suffer, be worn out”). See the doublets .

Compare typologically routine (English) << rupta via (Latin). Note the inverse semantic vectors: travel moves from a subjective state (toil) to an objective action (journey), while routine moves from an objective object (beaten path) to a subjective pattern (habit).

Largely displaced native fare (English), from faran (Old English “to go [a long distance], to travel”). More at fare (English).

Cognate with tregi (Icelandic “sorrow, grief”), 𐍄𐍂𐌹𐌲𐍉 (Gothic “grief”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English trikke, from Old Northern French trique (related to trichier (Old French “to defraud, act dishonestly, conceal, deceive, cheat”); > modern tricher (French)), itself possibly from Middle High German trechen (“to launch a shot at, play a trick on”), or one of its derivatives (e.g. ūftrechen (Middle High German “to do something to someone, hurt someone”), vertrechen (Middle High German “to conceal, get over on someone”), zuotrechen (Middle High German “to obtain falsely or deceitfully, wangle, finagle”), etc.); yet the Old French verb is equally likely to be derived from Vulgar Latin *triccāre, from Late Latin tricāre, from Latin tricor (“trīcor, trīcārī”).

The term has been connected to Middle Dutch treck, trec (Middle Dutch “draw, line, desire, game move, cord, stratagem, ruse, trick”), from Middle Dutch trekken, treken (Middle Dutch “trēken”), from *trekken (Old Dutch), *trekan (Old Dutch “to move, drag”), from Proto-Germanic *trakjaną, *trekaną (Proto-Germanic “to drag, scrape, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dreg- (“to drag, scrape”). If they are related, trick would be cognate with trekken (Low German), trecken (Middle High German), trechen (Middle High German), trække (Danish), and trekka (Old Frisian), truc (Romanian) and other Romance languages.

Compare track (English), treachery (English), trig (English), and trigger (English).

Cognate with trjou (Saterland Frisian “honest”), trüüw (Alemannic “loyal”), trouw (Dutch “loyal, true”), treu (German “loyal, true”), trei (lb “loyal”), tryg (Danish “safe, secure”), tryggur (Faroese / Icelandic “faithful, loyal; safe”), trygg (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “safe, secure”), 𐍄𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌲𐍅𐍃 (Gothic “true; faithful, loyal”); also dearbh (Irish “sure”), druwis (Old Prussian “faith”), δροόν (Ancient Greek “firm”)), extension of *dóru (Proto-Indo-European “tree”) (possibly also *sъdorvъ (Proto-Slavic “healthy”) from the same root). etymologies.text:
From Middle English trust (“trust, protection”). Long considered a borrowing from traust (Old Norse “confidence, help, protection”), from *traustą (Proto-Germanic), but the root vocalism is incompatible, so trust has come to be considered a reflex of an unattested Old English *trust, from a rare zero-grade Proto-Germanic variant of the same root also attested in getrüste (Middle High German “host”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deru- (“be firm, hard, solid”).

Cognate with Traast (Saterland Frisian “comfort, solace”), treast (Western Frisian “comfort, consolation, solace”), troost (Dutch “comfort, consolation”), Trost (German “comfort, consolation”), Troost (Low German “comfort, consolation”), Trouscht (lb “consolation”), trøst (Danish “comfort, solace”), traust (Icelandic “faith, trust; confidence”), trøst (Norwegian Nynorsk), trøyst (Norwegian Nynorsk “consolation”), tröst (Swedish “comfort, consolation”), 𐍄𐍂𐌰𐌿𐍃𐍄𐌹 (Gothic “covenant, pact”). . More at true, tree.
