etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English trien (“to separate out, sift, choose, select, evaluate, try a legal case”), from Anglo-Norman trier, triher (Anglo-Norman), triere (Anglo-Norman “to divide, separate, choose, select, prove, determine, try a case”), Old French trier (“to choose, pick out or separate from others, sift, cull”), of origin. Cognate with triar (Occitan “to choose, sort, scrutinise, peel”), triar (Catalan “to pick, choose, decide”). Suggested to be derived from Late Latin *trītō (“to crush, grind, trample, wear out”), itself derived from trītus (Classical Latin “rubbed, worn down, pulverised”), the past participle of tero (Latin “to rub, wear down, trample”), though this derivation is incompatible with the Occitan form. Additionally, the shift in meaning from "rub, crush, trample" to "pick out, choose, cull" is difficult to explain. One suggestion is that the semantic shift might have originated from a Latin phrase , which has a parallel in the modern trier le grain (French “to sort the grain”). Alternatively, perhaps derived from Vulgar Latin *trīāre, a metathetic alteration of *tīrāre (Vulgar Latin “to tear off, pull, draw”), whence also Old French tirer (“to draw, pull, pluck, tug, peck at, extract”), tirar (Occitan “to take, draw, retrieve, remove, extract”).

Replaced native cunnen (Middle English “to try”) (from cunnian (Old English)), fandien (Middle English “to try, prove”) (from fandian (Old English)), and costnien (Middle English “to try, tempt, test”) (from costnian (Old English)).

etymologies.text: From Middle English upon, uppon (Middle English), uppen (Middle English), from Old English upon, uppon (Old English), uppan (Old English “on, upon, up to, against, after, in addition to”), equivalent to . Cognate with uppan (Old Saxon “upon”), ūfan (Old High German), ūffan (Old High German “upon”), upp (Icelandic) á (Icelandic), upp á (Icelandic “up on, upon”), uppå (Swedish “up on, upon”) (thence på (Swedish)), på (Danish “up on, upon”), på (Norwegian “up on, upon”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from Middle English upper. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English upright, uppryght (Middle English), upriht (Middle English), from Old English upriht (“upright; erect”), from Proto-Germanic *upprehtaz, equivalent to up + right (English). Cognate with apgjucht (Saterland Frisian “upright”), oprjocht (Western Frisian “upright”), oprecht (Dutch “upright”), uprecht (Low German (Germany) “upright”), aufrecht (German “upright”), upprätt (Swedish “upright”), uppréttur (Icelandic “upright”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English upset (“the act of setting up; establishment”), from Middle English upsetten, corresponding to up- + set (English). Cognate with upset (Middle Low German “setup; arrangement”).

chain.meaning: the act of setting up; establishment

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle French urbain (“belonging to a city, urban; courteous, refined, urbane”) (modern urbain (French)), or from its etymon Latin urbānus (“of or belonging to a city, urban; of manners or style: like those of city dwellers: cultivated, polished, refined, sophisticated”) + -an (English). is derived from urbs (Latin “city; walled town; Rome”) (further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- (“to encircle, enclose; a belt; an enclosure, fence”) or *werbʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to enclose”)) + -ānus (Latin).

For the euphemistic or proscribed term, it was coined by New York radio DJ Frankie Crocker in the early to mid-1970s as a synonym for Black music.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French urgent (“pressing, impelling”), from Latin urgēns, from urgeo (Latin “to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”). Equivalent to urge + ent (English). Related to würgen (German “to strangle”), verzti (Lithuanian “ver̃žti”), - (Russian) (poetic) отверза́ть (Russian “to open”), otwierać (Polish “to open”)) and worry (English), wring (English), wreak (English), wreck (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: urgent + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English use, from Old French us, from Latin ūsus (“use, custom, skill, habit”), from past participle stem of ūtor (Latin “use”). Displaced native note (Middle English “use”) (see note) from notu (Old English); nutte (Middle English “use”) from nytt (Old English); as well as fricu (Old English) and sidu (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English usen, from Old French user (“use, employ, practice”), from Medieval Latin uso (“use”), frequentative form of past participle stem of Latin uti (“to use”). Displaced native noten (Middle English), nutten (Middle English “to use”) (from notian (Old English), nēotan (Old English), nyttian (Old English)) and brouken (Middle English), bruken (Middle English “to use, enjoy”) (from brūcan (Old English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: use + -less

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English usere, equivalent to use + -er (English). Cognate with usar (Scots), uiser (Scots “user”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English usual, from Old French usuel, from Latin ūsuālis (“for use, fit for use, also of common use, customary, common, ordinary, usual”), from ūsus (Latin “use, habit, custom”), from the past participle stem of utor (Latin “to use”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃eyt- (“to take along, fetch”). Displaced native ġewunelīċ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old French vacant, from Latin vacāns.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle French valide (“healthy, sound, in good order”), from Latin validus, from valeō + -idus (Latin), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“be strong”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English valeye, valey (Middle English), from Anglo-Norman valey, Old French valee (compare vallée (French)), from Latin vallēs/vallis (Latin). . Displaced native dene (English), from dene (Old English) and partially displaced native dale (English), from dæl (Old English).

Aphetic for obsolete evanish (English), from Middle English evanisshen, esvanisshen (Middle English), from Old French esvanir, esvaniss- (modern French évanouir (French)), from Vulgar Latin *exvanire (“to vanish, disappear, to fade out”), from Latin ēvānēscō (“ēvānēscō, ēvānēscere”), from vānus (Latin “empty”). . .

Displaced native cwincan (Old English), whose causative persists as quench (English “put out (fire)”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle French varieté (“variety”) (modern variété (French “variety; genre, type”)) or directly from its etymon Latin varietās (“difference; diversity, variety”) + -ty (English); . is derived from varius (Latin “different, diverse, various; variegated”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to abandon; to give out; to leave”)) + -tās (Latin). The English word displaced the native mislīcnes (Old English).

Sense 1.3.2 (“total number of distinct states of a system; logarithm to the base 2 of the total number of distinct states of a system”) was coined by the English psychiatrist William Ross Ashby (1903–1972) in his work ' (1956).

* variedade (Galician “variety”)

etymologies.text: From Middle English varien, from Old French varier, from Latin variō (“to change, alter, make different”), from varius (Latin “different, various”); see various (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle French victime, from Latin victima (“sacrificial animal”). Although this root and victor (English) drive from homophonous PIE roots, they are traditionally reconstructed as separate words and thus not cognates.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English victory, victori (Middle English), victorie (Middle English “supremacy, victory; a defeat or vanquishing, conquest; superior military force; might, power, strength; triumphal celebration or procession; monument commemorating a defeat; superior position, dominance; mastery; moral victory, vindication; success, triumph; redemption, salvation; resurrection of Jesus; means of achieving spiritual victory; reward for or token of perseverance in a spiritual struggle”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman victorie and Old French victorie, a variant of victoire (Old French “victory, win”) (modern victoire (French)), from Latin victōria (“victory”), from victor (Latin “champion, winner, victor; conqueror, vanquisher”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to contain, envelop; to overcome”)) + -ia (Latin). The English word is analysable as victor + y (English), and , sye (Middle English).

The interjection is derived from the noun.

Cognate with victoire (French), vittoria (Italian), vitoria (Portuguese), victoria (Spanish), victorie (Romanian).

வெற்றி (Tamil) (pronounced roughly like "vetri") is a false cognate.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English victorien (“to overcome, vanquish”), from Old French victorier, or from Medieval Latin victōriāre, from Latin victōria; see further at etymology 1.

* vittoriare (Italian)

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.text: From Middle English violent, from Old French violent, from Latin violentus, from vīs (Latin “strength”). Displaced native stræc (Old English). For the verb, compare violenter (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English violently; equivalent to violent + -ly (English).

etymologies.text:
The adjective is derived from Middle English vertual, virtual (Middle English), from Old French vertüal, vertüelle (Old French) (modern virtuel (French)), or from their etymon Medieval Latin virtuālis (“of or pertaining to potency or power; having power to produce an effect, potent; morally virtuous”), from Latin virtūs (“goodness, virtue; manliness, virility”) (from vir (Latin “adult male, man”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wiHrós (“man”), possibly from *weyh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “to chase, hunt, pursue”)) + -tūs (Latin)) + -ālis (Latin), modelled after virtuōsus (Latin “good, virtuous”).

is borrowed from French virtuel, from Middle French virtuel, from Old French vertüal, vertüelle (Old French): see above.

The noun is derived from the adjective.

* virtuel (French)
* virtuale (Italian)
* virtual (Spanish)

etymologies.text: From Middle English vertually; equivalent to virtual + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English virus, from Latin vīrus (“poison, slime, venom”), via rhotacism from Proto-Italic *weizos, from Proto-Indo-European *wisós (“fluidity, slime, poison”). First use in the computer context by David Gerrold in his 1972 book When HARLIE Was One.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 1831, "official signature or endorsement on a passport," from French visa, from Latin charta vīsa (“paper that has been seen”) from feminine perfect passive of Latin video (“vidēre”). Compare vision (English), video (English), vista (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English visible, from Old French visible, from Late Latin visibilis (“that may be seen”), from Latin videre (“to see”), past participle visus (Latin); see vision. Displaced native ġesewenlīċ (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English visioun, from Anglo-Norman visioun, from Old French vision, from Latin vīsiō (“vision, seeing”), noun of action from the perfect passive participle visus (Latin “that which is seen”), from the verb videō (Latin “to see”) + action noun suffix -iō (Latin).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English visiten, from Old French visiter, from Latin vīsitō, frequentative of vīsō (Latin “behold, survey”), from videō (Latin “see”). Cognate with wīsōn (Old Saxon “to visit, afflict”), archaic weisen (German “to visit, afflict”). Displaced native sēċan (Old English “to visit”) and sōcn (Old English “a visit”).

The noun is from French visite or the verb. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English visual, from French visuel, visual (French) and directly from Late Latin vīsuālis (“of sight”), from , from vidēre (Latin “to see, perceive; look (at)”); see visage (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English vital, from Old French vital, from Latin vītālis (“of life, life-giving”), from vīta (Latin “life”), from vīvō (Latin “to live”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: First use appears c. 1920, originally vitamine (1912), from (see vital (English)) + amine (English) (see amino acid (English “amino acids”)). Vitamine coined by Polish biochemist after the initial discovery of aberic acid (thiamine), when it was thought that all such nutrients would be amines. The term had become ubiquitous by the time it was discovered that vitamin C, among others, had no amine component. In 1920, British biochemist proposed that the final -e be dropped to deemphasize the amine reference. The ending -in was acceptable because it was used for natural substances of undefined composition. Drummond also introduced the lettering system of nomenclature (Vitamin A, B, C, etc.) at this same time.

etymologies.label: Etymology

, from vivo (Latin “to live”), akin to vita (Latin “life”), βίος (Ancient Greek “life”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English voice, voys (Middle English), vois (Middle English), borrowed from Anglo-Norman voiz, voys, voice, Old French vois, voiz (Modern voix (French)), from Latin vōcem, accusative form of vōx (Latin “voice”).

Cognate with वाच् (Sanskrit), ὄψ (Ancient Greek), آواز (Persian). Displaced native steven (Middle English “voice”) (from stefn (Old English) (see steven (English))), hlēoþor#Noun (Old English), woþ#Noun_2 (Old English), and reord#Noun (Old English). Compare advocate (English), advowson (English), avouch (English), convoke (English), vocal (English), vouch (English), vowel (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English voysen, voicen (Middle English), from the noun (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English volume, from Old French volume, from Latin volūmen (“book, roll”), from volvō (Latin “roll, turn about”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle French voluntaire, from Latin voluntārius (“willing, voluntary”); or from voluntary + -eer (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin vōtum, a form of voveō (Latin “to vow”) (cognate with εὔχομαι (Ancient Greek “to vow”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wegʷʰ- (“to promise, to vow”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English vowel, from Old French vouel, a variant of voyeul (Old French) (whence voyelle (French)), from Latin vōcālis (“voiced”), itself a semantic loan of φωνῆεν (Koine Greek). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English viage, borrowed from Anglo-Norman viage and Old French voiage, from Latin viaticum. The modern spelling is under the influence of Modern French voyage. .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English wage, from Anglo-Norman wage, from Old Northern French wage, a northern variant of Old French gauge, guage (Old French) (whence modern French gage (French)), Medieval Latin wadium, from Frankish *wadi (“*waddī”) (cognate with wedd (Old English)), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge”). Akin to veðja (Old Norse “to pledge”), 𐍅𐌰𐌳𐌹 (Gothic), wedde (Dutch). Compare also the doublet gage (English). More at wed (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wagen (“to pledge”), from Anglo-Norman —, Old Northern French wagier, a northern variant of Old French guagier (whence modern gager (French)), itself either from guage (Old French) or from a derivative of Frankish *wadi (“*waddī”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin — intermediate *wadiō (Latin) from *wadium (Latin) (see the noun above). See wadiō (Medieval Latin) and wadium (Medieval Latin) for more.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English wast (“waist”), probably from Old English *wæst, *wǣst (Old English), *weaxt (Old English), *wæhst (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *wahstu, from Proto-Germanic *wahstuz (“growth, development, stature, build”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weks- (“to multiply, increase”). Cognate with wacste (Middle English “growth, increase, might, power”), wahst (Middle High German “growth”), vækst (Danish “growth”), växt (Swedish “growth, development, size”), vöxtur (Icelandic “growth”), 𐍅𐌰𐌷𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (Gothic “growth”). Related to weaxan (Old English “to grow, increase”). More at wax (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English waiten, from Anglo-Norman waiter, waitier (Old French) (compare guetter (French) from gaitier (Old French), guaitier (Old French)), from Frankish *wahtwēn (“to watch, guard”), derivative of Frankish *wahtu (“guard, watch”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō (“guard, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be fresh, cheerful, awake”).

Cognate with wahtēn (Old High German “to watch, guard”), wachten (Low German (Germany) “to wait”), wachten (Dutch “to wait, expect”), guetter (French “to watch out for”), wachtje (Saterland Frisian “to wait”), wachtsje (Western Frisian “to wait”), wachtjen (North Frisian “to stand, stay put”). More at watch (English).

In some senses, merged or influenced by Middle English waiten, weiten (Middle English “to do good to, lie in wait for, to contrive good or harm on, catch, snare”), from Old Norse veita (“to give help to, assist, grant, cause to happen”), from Proto-Germanic *waitijaną (“to show, guide, advise, direct”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to see, know”).

Largely overtook native biden (Middle English), from bīdan (Old English), source of bide (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Japanese 待ち.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
A merger of two verbs of related/similar form and meaning:
* Middle English waken, Old English wacan, from Proto-West Germanic *wakan, from Proto-Germanic *wakaną.
* Middle English wakien, Old English wacian, from Proto-West Germanic *wakēn, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wake, from Old English wacu, from Proto-Germanic *wakō, related to the verb *wakjaną (Proto-Germanic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Probably from Middle Low German — or Middle Dutch wake, from or akin to Old Norse vǫk (“a hole in the ice”) ( > våge (Danish), vök (Icelandic)), from Proto-Germanic *wakwō (“wetness”), from Proto-Indo-European *wegʷ- (“moist, wet”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wandren, from Old English wandrian (“to wander, roam, fly around, hover; change; stray, err”), from Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn (“to wander”), from *wandōn + *-rōn (Proto-West Germanic). Cognate with wander (Scots “to wander”), wandern (German “to wander, roam, hike, migrate”), wandelen (Dutch “to wander, roam, hike, migrate”), vandre (Danish “to wander, roam, hike, migrate”), vandra (Swedish “to wander, hike”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English warde, from Old English weard (“keeper, watchman, guard, guardian, protector; lord, king; possessor”), from Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard, keeper”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, defend”). Cognate with waard (Dutch), Wart (German).

chain.meaning: keeper, watchman, guard, guardian, protector; lord, king; possessor

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English ward, warde (Middle English), from Old English weard (“watching, ward, protection, guardianship; advance post; waiting for, lurking, ambuscade”), from Proto-West Germanic *wardu, from Proto-Germanic *wardō (“protection, attention, keeping”), an extension of the stem (wary (English), beware (English)), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover”).

Cognate with Warte (German “watchtower”), warten (German “wait for”); guard (English) is a parallel form which came via Old French.

chain.meaning: watching, ward, protection, guardianship; advance post; waiting for, lurking, ambuscade

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English warden, from Old English weardian (“to watch, guard, keep, protect, preserve; hold, possess, occupy, inhabit; rule, govern”), from Proto-West Germanic *wardēn, from Proto-Germanic *wardōną, *wardāną (Proto-Germanic “to guard”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, defend”). .

chain.meaning: to watch, guard, keep, protect, preserve; hold, possess, occupy, inhabit; rule, govern

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English warderobe, from Old Northern French warderoube, wardereube (Old French), northern variants of Old French garderobe, from garder (Old French “to keep safe”) + robe (Old French). Subsequently influenced by various senses of garderobe (French) as they developed in French. . .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English warm, werm (Middle English), from Old English wearm, from Proto-West Germanic *warm, from Proto-Germanic *warmaz, from one of:
* Proto-Indo-European —, from , which is related to 𒉿𒊏𒀀𒉌 (Hittite “to burn”), վառել (Armenian “to burn, heat, warm”), варити (Church Slavonic “to cook, boil”).
* Proto-Indo-European —, from the root *gʷʰer- (Proto-Indo-European “warm, hot”), in which case cognate with θερμός (Ancient Greek) (making perhaps a distant ), formus (Latin), घर्म (Sanskrit).
In any case cognate within Germanic to waarm (Western Frisian), woorm (Saterland Frisian), warm (Dutch), warm (German), varm (Swedish), varmur (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English warmen, wermen (Middle English), wyrmen (Middle English), from Old English wierman (“to make warm”) and wearmian (Old English “to become warm”), from Proto-West Germanic *warmijan and *warmōn (Proto-West Germanic). Cognate with warmen (Dutch), wärmen (German), värma (Swedish).

etymologies.text: Affix: warm + -ly

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English warmth, warmeth (Middle English), wermþe (Middle English), from Old English *wiermþu (“warmth”), from Proto-West Germanic *warmiþu (“warmness; warmth”), corresponding to warm + th (English). Cognate with Waarmte (Saterland Frisian “warmth”), waarmte (Western Frisian “warmth”), warmte (Dutch “warmth”), Warmte (Low German (Germany)), Warmt (Low German (Germany) “warmth”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English warnen, warnien (Middle English “to warn; admonish”), from Old English warnian (“to take heed; warn”), from Proto-Germanic *warnōną (“to warn; take heed”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to be aware; give heed”). Cognate with waarnen (Dutch) (obsolete), warnen (Low German (Germany)), warnen (German), varna (Swedish), varna (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
thumb|A wasp ()

Middle English wappes, waps (Middle English), wasp (Middle English), waspe (Middle English), from Old English wæfs, wæps (Old English), wæsp (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *wapsu, from Proto-Germanic *wapsō (“wasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *wóbʰseh₂ (“wasp”), from *webʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to braid, weave”), referring to the insect's woven nests.

Cognate with wesp (North Frisian “wasp”), Häspe (Saterland Frisian “wasp”), waps (Western Frisian “wasp”), Wespi (Alemannic “wasp”), Weps (Bavarian), Wepsn (Bavarian “wasp”), bèspa (Cimbric “wasp”), wesp (Dutch / Ripuarian “wasp”), Wespe (German “wasp”), Weps (Low German), Wepse (Low German “wasp”), וועספּ (Yiddish), וועספּע (Yiddish “wasp”), hveps (Danish “wasp”), veps (Norwegian Bokmål “wasp”), kvefs (Norwegian Nynorsk “wasp”); also goghi (Cornish “wasp”), foich (Irish), foiche (Irish), puch (Irish “wasp”), gwchi (Welsh “drone”), vespa (Latin “wasp”), ανυφαίνω (Greek (Modern)), υφαίνω (Greek (Modern) “to weave”), vej (Albanian “to weave”), lapsene (Latvian “wasp”), vapsvà (Lithuanian “wasp”), wobse (Old Prussian “wasp”), аса́ (Belarusian “wasp”), оса́ (Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian / Ukrainian “wasp”), vosa (Czech “wasp”), osa (Polish / Slovenian / Slovak “wasp”), о̀са (Serbo-Croatian), òsa (Serbo-Croatian “wasp”), մոզ (Armenian “a kind of fly that bites horses and cattle”), 𐬬𐬀𐬡𐬲𐬀𐬐𐬀 (ae “scorpion”), مۆز (Central Kurdish “gadfly, horsefly”), ماز (mzn “fly”), moz (Kurmanji Kurdish “wasp; gadfly, horsefly; bee; bumblebee”), بوز (Persian “wasp”), wäp- (xto “to weave”), wāp- (txb “to weave”), उभ्नाति (Sanskrit “to hurt, kill; to cover”).

of and was both a process of some generality within English (compare grasp (English) from grapsen (Middle English), and—affecting other plosives—ascian (Old English) ~ acsian (Old English “to ask”)) and common in the reflexes of *wóps (Proto-Indo-European “wasp”) in particular, as the aforementioned Germanic cognates (and non-Germanic cognates like vespa (Latin)) evince.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English wast, waste (Middle English “a waste”), from Anglo-Norman —, Old Northern French wast, waste (Old French “a waste”), from Frankish *wōstī (“a waste”), from Proto-Germanic —, , from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty, wasted”). Displaced native Middle English wernen (Middle English “to refuse”) likely due to the similar sounding warnen (Middle English)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wast, waste (Middle English “waste”), from Anglo-Norman —, Old Northern French wast (“waste”), from Frankish *wōstī (“waste, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty, wasted”). Cognate with wuosti (Old High German), wuasti (Old High German “waste, empty”), wüst (German), wōsti (Old Saxon “desolate”), wēste (Old English “waste, barren, desolate, empty”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wasten (“to waste, lay waste”), from Anglo-Norman —, Old Northern French waster (“to waste, devastate”) (compare also the variant gaster (Old French) and gâter (French) from a related Old French word); the Anglo-Norman form waster was either from Frankish *wōstijan (“to waste”), from Proto-Indo-European *wāsto- (“empty, wasted”), or alternatively from Latin vastō (“vastāre”) and influenced by the Frankish; the English word was assisted by similarity to native westen (Middle English) . Cognate with wuostan (Old High German), wuastan (Old High German), wuostjan (Old High German “to waste”) (Modern wüsten (German)), wēstan (Old English “to lay waste, ravage”).

Displaced native essian (Old English) and strȳndan (Old English). Largely overtook forspillan (Old English) and wēstan (Old English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: As a noun, from Middle English wacche, from Old English wæċċe. See below for verb form.

etymologies.text:

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English waterfal, waterfalle (Middle English), from Old English wæterġefeall (“waterfall”), equivalent to water + fall (English). etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English waven, from Old English wafian (“to wave, fluctuate, waver in mind, wonder”), from Proto-West Germanic *wabōn, from Proto-Germanic *wabōną, *wabjaną (Proto-Germanic “to wander, sway”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to move to and from, wander”).

Cognate with waben (Middle High German “to wave”), wabern (German “to waft”), váfa (Icelandic “to fluctuate, waver, doubt”). See also waver (English).

chain.meaning: to wave, fluctuate, waver in mind, wonder

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|The wave after a ferry (1)
From Middle English *wave, partially from waven (Middle English “to fluctuate, wave”) (see above) and partially from Middle English wawe, waghe (Middle English “wave”), from Old English wǣg (“a wave, billow, motion, water, flood, sea”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (“motion, storm, wave”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to drag, carry”).

Cognate with waag (North Frisian “wave”), weach (Western Frisian “wave”), waag (Dutch “wave”), Woge (German), Wooge (German “wave”), vove (Danish), våg (Danish “wave”), vágur (Faroese “bay”), vogur (Icelandic “bay”), - (Norwegian Bokmål), - (Norwegian Nynorsk) and våg (Swedish “wave”), 𐍅𐌴𐌲𐍃 (Gothic “wave”), vague (French “wave”) (from vágr (Old Norse “ocean, sea; wave”)). See also waw (English).

chain.meaning: a wave, billow, motion, water, flood, sea

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: See waive (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English way, wey (Middle English), from Old English weġ, from Proto-West Germanic *weg, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. and possibly .

Cognate with wai (North Frisian), wäi (North Frisian “way”), Wai (Saterland Frisian “way”), wei (Western Frisian “road; way”), Wääch (Central Franconian “way”), bege (Cimbric), bèg (Cimbric “way”), weg (Dutch “way”), - (German), Weg (Low German “way”), waeg (Limburgish “way”), Wee (lb “way”), be (mhn “way”), וועג (Yiddish “way”), vej (Danish “way”), vegur (Faroese / Icelandic “way”), veg (Norwegian Bokmål), vei (Norwegian Bokmål “way”), veg (Norwegian Nynorsk “way”), väg (Swedish “way”), 𐍅𐌹𐌲𐍃 (Gothic “path; road”).

etymologies.text: From the sound it represents, by analogy with other (velar) letters such as kay (English) and gay#Etymology_2 (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English we, from Old English wē (“we”), from Proto-West Germanic *wiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *wīz, *wiz (Proto-Indo-European “we”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéy (“we (plural)”). Cognate with wee (Scots), we (Scots “we”), we (North Frisian “we”), wy (Western Frisian “we”), wi (Low German “we”), we (Dutch), wij (Dutch “we”), wir (German “we”), - (Danish), - (Swedish) and vi (Norwegian “we”), vér (Icelandic), við (Icelandic “we”), 𐬬𐬀𐬉𐬨 (ae), वयम् (Sanskrit).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Case extension of nominative we (English), used in the objective case in Tyneside English.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English waik, wayk (Middle English), wayke (Middle English), weik (Middle English), weyk (Middle English), borrowed from Old Norse veikr (“weak”), from Proto-Germanic *waikwaz (“weak, yielded, pliant, bendsome”), from *wīkwaną (Proto-Germanic “to cease, fold, yield; to retreat”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, turn, wind”), from *weh₁y- (Proto-Indo-European “to plait, twist, weave, wind; to cover, enclose, wrap”).

Cognate with wāc (Old English “bendsome, weak”), wook (Saterland Frisian “soft, gentle, tender”), weak (Western Frisian “soft”), week (Dutch “soft, weak”), weich (German “soft, weak”), weech (lb “weak”), ווייך (Yiddish “soft”), veg (Danish “weak”), veikur (Faroese / Icelandic “weak”), veik (Norwegian Bokmål), vek (Norwegian Bokmål “weak; pliant”), veik (Norwegian Nynorsk “weak”), vek (Swedish “weak, pliant”), vaik (Estonian), vaikne (Estonian “quiet”), vaieta (Finnish “to fall silent; to be silent; to keep silent; to suppress by not discussing”), vaiketa (izh “quiet down”); also gwigh (Cornish “winkles”), faocha (Irish), faochóg (Irish “periwinkle”), vicis (Latin “change; time; season; succession; lot; place, room, stead”), vieo (Latin “to bend”), οἴγω (Ancient Greek “to open”), vig (Albanian “bier, litter, stretcher”), vyti (Lithuanian “to twist, wind”), віць (Belarusian “to twist, weave”), ви́я (Bulgarian “to bend, twist; to roam; to swirl”), vít (Czech “to weave, wind; to wrap”), wić (Polish / Upper Sorbian “to plait, weave; to wriggle, writhe”), вить (Russian “to wind; to twist, weave”), ви̏ти (Serbo-Croatian), vȉti (Serbo-Croatian “to twist”), viti (Slovenian “to twist”), ви́ти (Ukrainian “to twist, wind; to plait; to build a nest; to curl”), avêtin (Kurmanji Kurdish), avitin (Kurmanji Kurdish), avîtin (Kurmanji Kurdish), havêtin (Kurmanji Kurdish), havîtin (Kurmanji Kurdish “to cast, throw”), آویختن (Persian “to hang, suspend”), بیختن (Persian “to sift”), वेग (Sanskrit “speed, impetus; stream; agitation; impetuosity; strength; haste; the flight of an arrow; love; delight; expulsion; semen; attack; constipation”).
