etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English weyknesse, replacing earlier wocnesse (Middle English), wakenes (Middle English), wacnesse (Middle English “weakness”), from wācnes (Old English “weakness”). Equivalent to weak + -ness (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Middle English welth, welthe (Middle English “happiness, prosperity”), from Old English *welþ, *welþu (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *waliþu (“wealth”). Alternatively, possibly an alteration (due to similar words in -th (Middle English): compare helth (Middle English “health”), derth (Middle English “dearth”)) of wele (Middle English “wealth, well-being, weal”), from Old English wela (“wealth, prosperity”), from Proto-Germanic *walô (“well-being, prosperity”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“good, best”); equivalent to weal + th (English). Cognate with wielde (Western Frisian “wealth”), weelde (Dutch “wealth”), Weelde (Low German “wealth”), welida (Old High German), welitha (Old High German “wealth”). Related also to Wohl (German “welfare, well-being, weal”), vel (Danish “weal, welfare”), väl (Swedish “well-being, weal”). More at weal (English), well (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English welthy, welþi (Middle English), equivalent to wealth + -y (English). Cognate with weldech (Middle Dutch), weeldech (Middle Dutch “magnificent, luscious, lavish”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wepen, from Old English wǣpn, from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną (“weapon”), of unknown origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wēbnom.

Cognate with weepon (Scots “weapon”), woopen (North Frisian “weapon”), Woapen (Saterland Frisian “weapon”), wapen (Western Frisian “weapon; coat of arms”), Waaffe (Alemannic “tool”), wapen (Dutch “weapon”), Waffe (German “weapon”) and Wappen (German “coat of arms”), Waff (lb “weapon”), וואָפֿן (Yiddish “weapon”), våben (Danish “weapon; coat of arms”), vákn (Faroese), vápn (Faroese “weapon; whaling lance”), vopn (Icelandic “weapon”), våpen (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “weapon”), vapen (Swedish “weapon; coat of arms”), 𐍅𐌴𐍀𐌽 (Gothic “weapon”).
etymologies.uncertainNote: From Middle English wepen, from Old English wǣpn, from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną (“weapon”), of unknown origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *wēbnom.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Middle English weren , from Old English werian (“to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *waʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *wazjaną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to dress, put on (clothes)”). Compare weary (English).

Cognate to वस्ते (Sanskrit), ἕννυμι (Ancient Greek “put on”), vestis (Latin “garment”) (vest (English)), vesh (Albanian “dress up, wear”), wäs- (txb), զգենում (Classical Armenian), gwisgo (Welsh), 𒉿𒀸- (Hittite).

Originally a weak verb (i.e. with a past tense in -ed), it became irregular during the Middle English period by analogy with verbs like beren (Middle English) (whence bear) and teren (Middle English) (whence tear).

chain.meaning: to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock (land)

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English weren, werien (Middle English), from Old English werian (“to guard, keep, defend; ward off, hinder, prevent, forbid; restrain; occupy, inhabit; dam up; discharge obligations on (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną (“to defend, protect, ward off”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to close, cover, protect, save, defend”).

Cognate with wer (Scots), weir (Scots “to defend, protect”), weren (Dutch “to aver, ward off”), wehren (German “to fight”), värja (Swedish “to defend, ward off”), verja (Icelandic “to defend”).

chain.meaning: to guard, keep, defend; ward off, hinder, prevent, forbid; restrain; occupy, inhabit; dam up; discharge obligations on (land)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English web, webbe (Middle English), from Old English webb, from Proto-West Germanic *wabi, from Proto-Germanic *wabją (“web”), from Proto-Germanic *webaną (“to weave”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to braid, weave”).

Cognate with wab (Scots “web”), wääb (North Frisian “web”), Wäb (Saterland Frisian “web”), web (Western Frisian / Dutch “web”), væv (Danish “web”), vevur (Faroese “web”), vefur (Icelandic “web”), vev (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “web”), väv (Swedish “web”); also goghi (Cornish “wasps”), foich (Irish), foiche (Irish), puch (Irish “wasp”), gwchi (Welsh “drone”), vespa (Latin “wasp”), ὑφή (Ancient Greek “web”), ὑφαίνω (Ancient Greek “to weave”) (whence ανυφαίνω (Greek (Modern)), υφαίνω (Greek (Modern) “to weave”)), vej (Albanian “to weave”), lapsene (Latvian “wasp”), vapsvà (Lithuanian “wasp”), wobse (Old Prussian “wasp”), аса́ (Belarusian “wasp”), оса́ (Bulgarian / Macedonian / Russian / Ukrainian “wasp”), vosa (Czech “wasp”), osa (Polish / Slovak / Slovenian “wasp”), о̀са (Serbo-Croatian), òsa (Serbo-Croatian “wasp”), մոզ (Armenian “a kind of fly that bites horses and cattle”), moz (Kurmanji Kurdish “hornet; wasp”), بافتن (Persian “to weave”), wäp- (xto “to weave”), wāp- (txb “to weave”), उभ्नाति (Sanskrit “to hurt, kill; to cover; fill”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Web + cam (English), shortened from camera (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English wedding, weddynge (Middle English), from Old English weddung (“betrothal, espousal”), equivalent to . Cognate with weddinghe (Middle Dutch).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: A conversion of wedding (English) to a verb.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English weyen, from Old English wegan, from Proto-West Germanic *wegan, from Proto-Germanic *weganą (“to move, carry, weigh”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéǵʰeti, from *weǵʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to bring, transport”).

Cognate with wey (Scots), wee (Scots), wegen (Dutch), wiegen (German), wägen (German), veje (Danish), veie (Norwegian Bokmål), vega (Norwegian Nynorsk). .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English weight, weiȝte (Middle English), weght (Middle English), wight (Middle English), from Old English wiht, ġewiht (Old English “weight”), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz , from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to move; pull; draw; drive”). Equivalent to weigh + t (English).

Cognate with wecht (Scots), weicht (Scots “weight”), Wächte (Saterland Frisian “scale”), Gewicht (Saterland Frisian “weight”), gewicht (Western Frisian “weight”), gewicht (Dutch “weight”), Wicht (Low German (Germany)), Gewicht (Low German (Germany) “weight”), Wucht (German “massiveness, force”), Gewicht (German “weight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English werde, wierde (Middle English), wirde (Middle English), wyrede (Middle English), wurde (Middle English), from Old English wyrd (“fate”), from Proto-West Germanic *wurdi, from Proto-Germanic *wurdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, wind”). Cognate with urður (Icelandic “fate”). Related to weorþan (Old English “to become”); more at worth#Etymology_2 (English).

, a reborrowing of the original sense and spelling.

Obsolete by the 16th century in standard English. Its reintroduction is due to Shakespeare, who borrowed weird sister (Middle Scots “3=weird sisters”), denoting the Fates of classical mythology, for the witches in his play Macbeth. Though originally a noun in this context, it was subsequently reinterpreted as an adjective meaning “supernatural” or “uncanny”. The sense “strange” is a development of this.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English welcome, wolcume (Middle English), wulcume (Middle English), wilcume (Middle English), from Old English wilcuma , from Proto-West Germanic *willjakwemō, from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a wished-for arrival or guest”), possibly from *wiljakwemaną (Proto-Germanic “to be welcome”), equivalent to . The component wil- was replaced by wel- when the sense “guest” of the second component was no longer understood, likely under influence from the adverb well (English).

Cognate with walcome (Scots), welcome (Yola), welkome (Yola), welkimen (North Frisian), wilkemen (Saterland Frisian), wäilkeemen (Saterland Frisian), wülkemen (Saterland Frisian), wolkom (Western Frisian), wol chomne (Alemannic), wolgcheemen (Alemannic), woul chemne (Alemannic), wéllkòmm (Alemannic), bóolkhèmm (Cimbric), welkom (Dutch) (earlier willecome), willkommen (German), willkamen (Low German (Germany)), welkom (Limburgish), wéllekemm (Limburgish), wëllkomm (lb), velkommen (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), welkumin (Elfdalian), vælkomin (Faroese), velkominn (Icelandic), velkomen (Norwegian Nynorsk), välkommen (Swedish), and wilecome (Old French) (whence willecomme (Middle French “welcome”)), from Germanic.

The verb is from Middle English welcomen, wolcumen (Middle English), wilcumen (Middle English), from Old English wellcumian, wylcumian (Old English), wilcumian (Old English “to welcome, receive gladly”).

Similar constructions are found in Modern καλώς ορίσατε (Greek (Modern)), South Slavic languages, such as добре́ дошъ́л (Bulgarian), dobrodošao (Serbo-Croatian),
and also in Romance languages, such as benvenuto (Italian), bienvenido (Spanish), bienvenu (French), benvingut (Catalan), bem-vindo (Portuguese) and bun venit (Romanian), meaning “[may you have fared] well [in] coming [here]”. These Romance terms do not derive from a Classical Latin root, as no similar construction in Latin is found to exist, but are instead presumed (considering the ruling elite of the Germanic kingdoms which succeeded the ) to be the result of a calque from a Germanic language into Proto-Romance (Vulgar Latin; see *bene venūtus (Latin), and compare perdōnō (Latin) and compāniō (Latin) for similar historical calques).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English welefare, probably from the Old English — phrase wel faran (Old English “to fare well, get along successfully, prosper”) (cognate with welvare (Middle Dutch “welfare”), wolvare (Middle Low German “welfare”), wolvar (Middle High German), wolfar (Middle High German “welfare”)). Equivalent to well + fare (English). Compare also wolfeart (Western Frisian), welvaart (Dutch), Wohlfahrt (German), velferð (Old Norse) (whence välfärd (Swedish “welfare”)). The first recorded use in the sense of "social concern for the well-being of children, the unemployed, etc." is from 1904 and in the sense of "organized effort to provide for maintenance of members of a group" from 1918.

chain.meaning: to fare well, get along successfully, prosper

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wel, wal (Middle English), wol (Middle English), wele (Middle English), from Old English wel (“well, abundantly, very, very easily, very much, fully, quite, nearly”), from Proto-Germanic *wela, *wala (Proto-Germanic “well”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“wish, desire”).

Cognate with vella (Yola), waal (Yola), wel (Yola), well (Yola), wull (Yola “well”), boll (Cimbric), bóol (Cimbric “well”), wel (Dutch “well”), wohl (German), wol (German), woll (German “well”), vel (Danish / Icelandic / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “well”), væl (Faroese “well”), väl (Swedish), waͤl (Swedish “well”), 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐌻𐌰 (Gothic “well”). Related to will (English).

chain.meaning: well, abundantly, very, very easily, very much, fully, quite, nearly

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle English welle, from Old English wielle (“well”), from Proto-West Germanic *wallijā, from Proto-Germanic *wallijǭ (“well, swirl, wave”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn; wind; roll”).

Cognate with wel (Western Frisian “well”), wel (Dutch “well”), Welle (Low German (Germany) “well”), Welle (German “wave”), væld (Danish “well; spring”), väl (Swedish “well”), vella (Icelandic “boiling; bubbling; eruption”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wellen, from a merger of Old English weallan (intransitive) and wiellan (Old English) (transitive), both meaning “to boil.” Further from Proto-Germanic *wallaną and *wallijaną (Proto-Germanic). Doublet of wall (English).

Cognate with wallen (German “boil, seethe”), vælde (Danish “gush”), vella (Norwegian Nynorsk) and outside Germanic, with valë (Albanian “hot, boiling”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From well + built (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wel-paied, equivalent to well + paid (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English westerne, from Old English westerne, from Proto-Germanic *westrōnijaz.

.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wet (“wet, moistened”), wett (Middle English), wette (Middle English), past participle of Middle English weten (“to wet”), from Old English wǣtan (“to wet, moisten, water”), from Proto-West Germanic *wātijan, from Proto-Germanic *wētijaną (“to wet, make wet”), from Proto-Indo-European *wed- (“water, wet”) (also the source of water (English)).

Cognate with weit (Scots), wete (Scots “to wet”), wäitje (Saterland Frisian “to wet; drench”), væta (Icelandic “to wet”). Compare also weet (Middle English “wet”), from wǣt (Old English “wet, moist, rainy”), from *wāt (Proto-West Germanic), from *wētaz (Proto-Germanic “wet, moist”), related to weit (Scots), weet (Scots), wat (Scots “wet”), wiat (North Frisian), weet (North Frisian), wäit (North Frisian “wet”), wäit (Saterland Frisian “wet”), wiet (Western Frisian “wet”), wet (Middle Dutch “wet, damp, watery”), - (Swedish) and våt (Norwegian “wet”), våd (Danish “wet”), vátur (Faroese “wet”), votur (Icelandic “wet”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English whal, whale (Middle English), from Old English hwæl (“whale”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwal, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz (“whale”) (compare Wal (German), val (Swedish), hval (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål), kval (Norwegian Nynorsk); compare also walvis (Dutch), walfisk (Western Frisian), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”) (compare Wels (German), squalus (Latin “big sea fish”), kalis (Old Prussian), ἄσπαλος (Ancient Greek), 𐬐𐬀𐬭𐬀 (ae “kind of fish”)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: . Perhaps a variant of wale (English) influenced by whack (English), whap (English), etc.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English what, from Old English hwæt (“what”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat (“what”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód (“what”), neuter form of *kʷós (Proto-Indo-European “who”).

Cognate with what (Scots), whit (Scots “what”), wat (North Frisian “what”), wat (Saterland Frisian “what”), wat (Western Frisian “what”), wat (Dutch “what”), wat (Low German “what”), was (German “what”), hvad (Danish “what”), hva (Norwegian Bokmål “what”), vad (Swedish “what”), kva (Norwegian Nynorsk “what”), hvað (Icelandic “what”), quod (Latin “what, which”).

Its use as a particle of contradiction or objection in colloquial Malaysian and Singaporean Englishes is semantic loan analogous to and . It is possible that this was historically reinforced by the dated use of what (English “what as a sentence-final question tag”) in British English.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whatever. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whete, from Old English hwǣte, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaitī, from Proto-Germanic *hwaitijaz (compare weet (Western Frisian), weit (Dutch), Weten (Low German), Weizen (German), hvede (Danish), vete (Swedish), hvete (Norwegian Bokmål), kveite (Norwegian Nynorsk), hveiti (Faroese / Icelandic)), from *hwītaz (Proto-Germanic “white”). More at white (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: wheel + chair

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English when (“when(ne)”), whan (Middle English “whan(ne)”), from Old English hwonne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannē, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan (“at what time, when”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís.

Cognate with whan (Scots “when”), wanneer (Dutch “when”), wan (Dutch “when”) and wen (Dutch “when, if”), wannehr (Low German “when”), wann (Low German “when”) and wenn (Low German “if, when”), wann (German “when”) and wenn (German “when, if”), 𐍈𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “when, how”), quandō (Latin “when”). More at who (English).

Interjection sense: a playful misunderstanding of "say when" (i.e. say something / speak up when you want me to stop) as "say [the word] when".

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whan evere, whanne ever (Middle English), whanne evere (Middle English), whener (Middle English), when ever (Middle English); equivalent to when + -ever (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wher, from Old English hwǣr (“where”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwār, from Proto-Germanic *hwar (“where”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷ-.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From where + as (English); first attested in the meaning of "where" in the 14th century. Compare thereas (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From where + -ever (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whether, whather (Middle English), from Old English hweþer, hwæþer (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *hwaþar, from Proto-Germanic *hwaþeraz, comparative form of *hwaz (Proto-Germanic “who”). Cognate with weđer (North Frisian “if, whether”), weder (German “neither”), var (Swedish “each, every”), hvor (Icelandic “each of two, which of two”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English which, hwic (Middle English), wilche (Middle English), hwilch (Middle English), whilk (Middle English), hwilc (Middle English), from Old English hwelċ (“which”), from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz (“what kind”), derived from *hwaz (Proto-Germanic).

Cognates include whilk (Scots “which”), hokker (Western Frisian “which”), welk (Dutch “which”), welk (Low German “which”), welcher (German “which”), hvilken (Danish “which”), vilken (Swedish “which”), hvilken (Norwegian “which”), hvílíkur (Icelandic “which”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From whiche ever (Middle English), whiche evere (Middle English), which ever (Middle English), which evere (Middle English); equivalent to which + -ever (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English whyle, from Old English hwīl, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu, from Proto-Germanic *hwīlō (compare wijl (Dutch), Wiel (Low German), Weile (German), hvile (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “rest”), kvila (Norwegian Nynorsk “rest”), vila (Swedish “rest”), hvíla (Faroese / Icelandic “rest”)) from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”). Cognate with sillë (Albanian “breakfast”), tranquillus (Latin), चिर (Sanskrit), شاد (Persian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Variant of usque (English), abbreviation of usquebaugh (English) (compare obsolete whiskybae (English)), from Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha (“water of life”), calque of Medieval Latin aqua vitae. Compare akvavit (English), aquavit (English), aqua vitae (English), eau de vie (English), and water of life (English) from the same source.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Affix: whisk + -y

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English whisperen, from Old English hwisprian (“to mutter, murmur, whisper”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwisprōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwisprōną (“to hiss, whistle, whisper”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweys-, *ḱwey- (Proto-Indo-European “to hiss, whistle, whisper”).

Cognate with wisperen (Dutch “to whisper”), wispern (German “to mumble, whisper”). Related also to hviske (Danish “to whisper”), hvískra (Icelandic “to whisper”), hviske (Norwegian Bokmål), kviskre (Norwegian Bokmål “to whisper”), kviskre (Norwegian Nynorsk), kviskra (Norwegian Nynorsk “to whisper”), viska (Swedish “to whisper”). More at whistle (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English whistel, whistil (Middle English), whistle (Middle English), from Old English hwistle, from the verb (see below).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English whistlen, from Old English hwistlan, hwistlian (Old English “to whistle”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwistlōn, from Proto-Germanic *hwistlōną (“to make a hissing sound”). Cognate with vissla (Swedish “to whistle”), hvísla (Icelandic “to whisper”), свистеть (Russian “to whistle”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English whit, hwit (Middle English), from Old English hwīt, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweydós, a byform of *ḱweytós (Proto-Indo-European “bright; shine”).

* wyt (Western Frisian)
* wit (Dutch)
* weiß (German)
* weiss (German)
* hvit (Norwegian Bokmål)
* kvit (Norwegian Nynorsk)
* vit (Swedish)
* hvid (Danish)
* šviẽsti (Lithuanian “to gleam”), šviesa (Lithuanian “light”)
* свѣтъ (Church Slavonic “light”), свѣтьлъ (Church Slavonic “clear, bright”)
* سفید (Persian “white”), سپید (Persian “white”)
* 𐬯𐬞𐬀𐬉𐬙𐬀 (ae “white”)
* श्वेत (Sanskrit “white, bright”)

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English who, hwo (Middle English), huo (Middle English), wha (Middle English), hwoa (Middle English), hwa (Middle English), from Old English hwā (dative hwām (Old English), genitive hwæs (Old English)), from Proto-West Germanic *hwaʀ, from Proto-Germanic *hwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos, *kʷís (Proto-Indo-European).

The sound change > (without a corresponding change in spelling) was due to wh-cluster reduction after an irregular change of to in Middle English (instead of the expected ) and further to regularly in Early Modern English. A similar change occurred in two (English). Compare how (English), which underwent wh-reduction earlier (in Old English), and thus is spelt with h.

Compare wha (Scots), wa (Western Frisian), wie (Dutch), we (Low German), wer (German), vem (Swedish), hvem (Danish), hvem (Norwegian Bokmål), kven (Norwegian Nynorsk), hver (Icelandic).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whoever. .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whom, wham (Middle English), from Old English hwām, hwǣm (Old English), from Proto-Germanic *hwammai, dative case of *hwaz (Proto-Germanic “who, what”). Cognate with wham (Scots “whom”), wem (German “whom, to whom”), hvem (Danish “who, whom”), vem (Swedish “who, whom”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English whos, from Old English hwæs, from Proto-Germanic *hwes, genitive case of *hwaz (Proto-Germanic “who”) *hwat (Proto-Germanic “what”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English why, from Old English hwȳ (“why”), from Proto-Germanic *hwī (“by what, how”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey, instrumental case of *kʷís (Proto-Indo-European “who”), *kʷid (Proto-Indo-European “what”).

Cognate with hwī (Old Saxon “why”), hwiu (Old Saxon “how; why”), wiu (Middle High German “how, why”), archaic - (Danish) and - (Norwegian Bokmål) hvi (Danish “why”), kvi (Norwegian Nynorsk “why”), vi (Swedish “why”), - (Faroese) and - (Icelandic) hví (Faroese “why”), quī (Latin “why”), πεῖ (Doric Greek “where”), чи (Ukrainian “if”), czy (Polish), či (Czech “or”), či (Serbo-Croatian “if”). Compare þȳ (Old English “because, since, on that account, therefore, then”). See thy (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: A variant of quey (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wid, wyd (Middle English), from Old English wīd (“wide, vast, broad, long; distant, far”), from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weydʰh₁- (“to divide, separate”), a dissimilated univerbation from *dwi- + *dʰeh₁- (Proto-Indo-European).

Cognate with widj (North Frisian “wide”), wied (Saterland Frisian “wide”), wiid (Western Frisian “broad; wide”), weck (Central Franconian), weit (Central Franconian), wick (Central Franconian), wiet (Central Franconian “distant, far, wide”), wijd (Dutch “wide; large; broad”), weit (German “far; wide; broad”), weit (lb “wide”), wäit (lb “far”), ווײַט (Yiddish “distant, far”), vid (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “wide”), víður (Faroese / Icelandic “wide”); also gwez (Breton “trees”), gwedh (Cornish), gwëdh (Cornish), gwydh (Cornish), gwÿdh (Cornish “trees”), fiodh (Irish / Scottish Gaelic “timber, wood”), fuygh (Manx “timber, wood”), gwŷdd (Welsh “trees”), dīvidō (Latin “to divide, separate”), vyds (ltg “middle”), vidus (Latvian “center, middle”), vidùs (Lithuanian “interior, inside; inward”), wätk- (xto,txb “to distinguish, separate”). Related to widow (English).

chain.meaning: wide, vast, broad, long; distant, far

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wijdly, equivalent to wide + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From wide + en (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English widwe, from Old English widuwe (“widow”), from Proto-West Germanic *widuwā (“widow”), from Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ (“widow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (“widow”), possibly from *h₁weydʰh₁- (Proto-Indo-European), *weydʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “*widʰ-”), whence also wood (English) from widu (Old English), wudu (Old English).

Cognate with weedae (Scots), wedow (Scots), widdow (Scots “widow”), bittaba (Cimbric “widow”), weduwe (Dutch), weeuw (Dutch “widow”), Witwe (German “widow”), wytwa (Ripuarian “widow”), 𐍅𐌹𐌳𐌿𐍅𐍉 (Gothic “widow”), fedb (Old Irish “widow”), gweddw (Welsh “widow”), - (Asturian) and viuda (Spanish “widow”), - (Aragonese) and vidua (Latin “widow”), vídua (Catalan “widow”), veuve (French “widow”), - (Galician) and viúva (Portuguese “widow”), vedova (Italian “widow”), văduvă (Romanian “widow”), ἠΐθεος (Ancient Greek “bachelor”), ve (Albanian “widow, widower”), удава́ (Belarusian “widow”), - (Czech), - (Slovak), and vdova (Slovenian “widow”), gdowa (Polish), wdowa (Polish “widow”), - (Russian) and вдова́ (Ukrainian “widow”), udova (Serbo-Croatian), у̀дова (Serbo-Croatian “widow”), بێوە (Central Kurdish “widow”), идӕдз (Ossetic “widowed”), بیوه (Persian “widow”), विधवा (Sanskrit “widow”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From , possibly by analogy with vídd (Old Norse “width”), though this is unlikely, as the word is not attested before the end of the 16th century and was historically unknown in Scots and the traditional dialect of Northern England, where one would expect Old Norse influence to be the strongest (these varieties traditionally employed wideness (English) instead). Replaced wide (Middle English), wyde (Middle English “width”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English weilde, wield (Middle English), wielde (Middle English), wijlde (Middle English), wild (Middle English), wilde (Middle English), wyld (Middle English), wylde (Middle English), wyled (Middle English), wyyld (Middle English), from Old English wilde, from Proto-West Germanic *wilþī, from Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz (“wild”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“hair; wool”).

Cognate with wil (North Frisian “wild”), wíeld (Saterland Frisian), wüüld (Saterland Frisian “wild”), wyld (Western Frisian “wild”), wüd (Bavarian “wild”), weld (Central Franconian “wild”), bill (Cimbric “crazy, mad; wild; stupid”), wild (Dutch / German / Low German “wild”), wëll (lb “wild; savage”), wyłd (Ripuarian “wild”), ווילד (Yiddish “wild; savage”), vild (Danish / Swedish “wild”), villur (Faroese “wild”), villtur (Icelandic “wild; lost; barbaric, savage; uncultivated; untamed”), vill (Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk “wild”), vill (Swedish “lost”), 𐍅𐌹𐌻𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍃 (Gothic “wild”); also gwlan (Cornish “wool”), olann (Irish / Scottish Gaelic “wool”), ollan (Manx “wool”), gwlân (Welsh “wool”), vellus (Latin “fleece, wool”), villus (Latin “hair, shaggy hair”), λάχνη (Ancient Greek “woolly hair; thin hair; soft nap or pile on cloth; quills hedgehog; leafage”), valai (Lithuanian “hair of the horse tail”), во́лас (Belarusian “single hair”), vlas (Czech / Slovak “single hair”), влас (Macedonian “fluff; thread (of hair)”), włos (Polish “single hair”), во́лос (Russian / Ukrainian “single hair”), вла̑с (Serbo-Croatian), vlȃs (Serbo-Croatian “single hair”), las (Slovenian “hair on top of head; nap, pile”), գեղմ (Armenian “fleece, wool”), پرچ (Central Kurdish “fax, headhair”), hirî (Kurmanji Kurdish “wool”), گرس (Persian “curl, ringlet; braid”), 𒋠𒀸 (Hittite “wool”), urṇ (xto “the circles of white hair between the brows of the Buddha or other deity”), *ūrṇ (txb “the circles of white hair between the brows of the Buddha or other deity”), वल्श (Sanskrit “branch, shoot, twig”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: wild + life

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wildely, wijldeli (Middle English), wildeliche (Middle English), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English willen, wullen (Middle English), wollen (Middle English), from Old English willan (“to want”), from Proto-West Germanic *willjan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”).

Cognate with ill (Yola), weel (Yola), well (Yola), will (Yola), woul (Yola), wull (Yola “will”), wale (North Frisian), wel (North Frisian “to want”), wolle (Saterland Frisian / Western Frisian “to want”), welle (Alemannic / Central Franconian “to want”), béllan (Cimbric), bölln (Cimbric “to want”), willen (Dutch “to want”), wollen (German “to want”), wüllen (Low German “to want; will”), wëllen (lb “to want”), וועלן (Yiddish “to want”), ville (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to want”), vilja (Faroese / Icelandic / Swedish “to want”), vili (gmq-jmk “to want; wish”), vilja (Norwegian Nynorsk), vilje (Norwegian Nynorsk “want; will”), 𐍅𐌹𐌻𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to want”); also velle (Latin “wish”), voleō (Latin), volo (Latin “to please, to wish; to want”), vouloir (French “to want”), volere (Italian “to want”), fleá (Irish), fleadh (Irish “feast”), fleadh (Scottish Gaelic “feast”), gwledd (Welsh “banquet, feast”), viltis (Lithuanian “to hope; to rely; to expect”), velet (Czech “to command”), volit (Czech “to choose; to elect”), woleć (Polish “to prefer”), во́ля (Russian “freedom”), во́льный (Russian “free”), веле́ть (Russian “to command, to enjoin, to order”), воля (Ukrainian “freedom, liberty, will”), вільний (Ukrainian “free”), веліти (Ukrainian “to will, to order, to command”), воліти (Ukrainian “to will, to prefer”), գեղձ (Classical Armenian “desire, wish”), वृणीते (Sanskrit), वृणोति (Sanskrit “to choose”). The verb is not always distinguishable from Etymology 3, below.

Compare typologically ще (Bulgarian), ќе (Macedonian), хтети (Serbo-Croatian) (< *xotěti (Proto-Slavic)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wille, from Old English willa (compare verb willian (Old English)), from Proto-Germanic *wiljô (“desire, will”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”). Cognate with wil (Dutch), Wille (German), vilja (Swedish), vilje (Norwegian).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle English willen, from Old English willian (“to will”), from Proto-West Germanic *willjōn (“to will”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”). Cognate with willen (Low German (Germany)), willen (German). The verb is not always distinguishable from Etymology 1, above.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English willyngly, wyllyngly (Middle English “intentionally, deliverately; freely, gladly”), from Old English willendlīċe (“diligently”), equivalent to willing + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: willing + -ness

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English winnen, from Old English winnan (“to labour, swink, toil,”) (compare ġewinnan (Old English “conquer, obtain, gain; endure, bear, suffer; be ill”)), from Proto-West Germanic *winnan, from Proto-Germanic *winnaną (“to swink, labour, win, gain, fight”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”).

Cognate with wan (North Frisian), wane (North Frisian), wen (North Frisian), wine (North Frisian), wune (North Frisian “to win”), winne (Saterland Frisian / Western Frisian “to win”), gabènnan (Cimbric “to win”), winnen (Dutch / Low German “to win”), gewinnen (German “to win”), gewannen (lb “to win”), vinde (Danish “to win”), vinna (Faroese / Icelandic “to win”), vinne (Norwegian Bokmål “to win”), vinna (Norwegian Nynorsk), vinne (Norwegian Nynorsk “to win”), vinna (Swedish “to win”), 𐍅𐌹𐌽𐌽𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to suffer”); also venus (Latin “beauty, charm, elegance, grace; beloved, love”), vuaj (Albanian), vuj (Albanian “to suffer; to endure”), वनोति (Sanskrit “to desire, like, love, wish; to gain, procure; to win; to prepare; to hurt, injure”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English winn, winne (Middle English), from Old English winn (“toil, labor, trouble, hardship; profit, gain; conflict, strife, war”), from Proto-Germanic *winną (“labour, struggle, fight”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, desire, wish, love”). Cognate with Gewinn (German “profit, gain”), gewin (Dutch “profit, gain”).

chain.meaning: toil, labor, trouble, hardship; profit, gain; conflict, strife, war

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wynne, winne (Middle English), wunne (Middle English), from Old English wynn (“joy, rapture, pleasure, delight, gladness”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunnju, from Proto-Germanic *wunjō (“joy, delight, pleasure, lust”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”).

Cognate with Wonne (German “bliss, joy, delight”), archaic wonne (Dutch “joy”), ynde (Danish “grace”), yndi (Icelandic “delight”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From wind (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
The noun is derived from Middle English winding, windinge (Middle English), wyndynge (Middle English “act of exposing something to the wind, airing, ventilating; act of winnowing (?)”), from winden (Middle English), wynden (Middle English “to expose (something) to the air or wind, ventilate; to cause (someone) to be out of breath; to winnow (wheat); of an animal: to catch the scent of (someone or something)”) + -ing (Middle English), -inge (Middle English).

The adjective is derived from the verb.

The English word is analysable as wind + ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
thumb|A winding (etymology 2, adjective ) road#Noun|road leading down a [[hillside from a dam in Gwynedd, Wales, United Kingdom.]]

The noun is derived from Middle English winding, windinge (Middle English), wyndynge (Middle English “directional change, curve, turn; bend of the leg at the knee; meandering course of a river; act of turning and twisting; twisting of things (especially thread) together; wrapping of a cloth around something; wattling of a structure; wattle(s); ornamentation with interwoven patterns; hoisting of something”), and then partly:

* from winden (Middle English), wynden (Middle English “to go, move; to move forcefully or suddenly; to direct, guide, lead; to go along a meandering or twisting course; to move in a circular pattern, revolve, turn; to move restlessly, toss and turn; to wriggle free; to move with a turning or twisting motion, bend, turn, twist; to form or mould (something) in one’s hands; to mix together; to cover; to clothe, dress; to wrap (a baby, a corpse, etc.); to encircle, surround; to bind; to interlace; to winch; (figurative) to conceal, disguise; to embroil, involve”) + -ing (Middle English), -inge (Middle English).; and
* from Old English windung (“woven object”), from windan (Old English “to twist, wind; to circle, curl, eddy, spiral”) (from Proto-Germanic *windaną (“to wind; to wrap”), from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn; to wind”)) + -ung (Old English).

The adjective is derived from the verb.

The English word is analysable as wind + ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wyndowe, wyndown (Middle English), from Old Norse vindauga (“window”), equivalent to . Cognate with windae (Scots) and windock (Scots), vindeyga (Faroese), vindu (Norwegian Bokmål), vindauge (Norwegian Nynorsk), vindue (Danish), archaic vindöga (Swedish), windog (Elfdalian). Displaced native ēagþȳrel (Old English) (the rare direct descendant is eyethurl (English “window, pupil, etc.”)). The “windows” among early Germanic peoples were just unglazed holes (eyes) in the wall or roof that permitted wind to pass through .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From wind + screen (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: wind + surfing

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English winge, wenge (Middle English), from Old Norse vængr , from Proto-Germanic *wēingijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”), thus related to wind (English).

Cognate with vinge (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Swedish “wing”), waingg (Elfdalian “wing”), vongur (Faroese “wing”), vængur (Icelandic “wing”), veng (Norwegian Nynorsk “wing”).

Replaced native fither (Middle English) (from fiþre (Old English), from *fiþriją (Proto-Germanic)), which merged with fether (Middle English) (from feþer (Old English), from *feþrō (Proto-Germanic)). More at feather (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English wipen, from Old English wīpian (“to wipe, rub, cleanse”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīpōn (“to wipe”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyp- (“to twist, wind around”). Cognate with wippen (German “to bob”), veva (Swedish “to turn, wind, crank”), 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐍀𐌰𐌽 (Gothic “to wreathe, crown”), swīfan (Old English “to revolve, sweep, wend, intervene”), वेपते (Sanskrit “to tremble”). More at swivel (English), swift (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compare vipa (Swedish), vibe (Danish “lapwing”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From wipe out (English) (verb) and wipeout (English) (noun) by shortening.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wir, wyr (Middle English), from Old English wīr (“wire, metal thread, wire-ornament”), from Proto-Germanic *wīraz (“wire”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁iros (“a twist, thread, cord, wire”), from *weh₁y- (Proto-Indo-European “to turn, twist, weave, plait”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wisdom, from Old English wīsdōm (“wisdom”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīsadōm, from Proto-Germanic *wīsadōmaz (“wisdom”), corresponding to . Cognate with wisdom, wysdom (Scots “wisdom”), wiisdom (Western Frisian “wisdom”), wijsdom (Dutch “wisdom”), Weistum (German “legal sentence”), Danish/Norwegian/Swedish visdom (Swedish “wisdom”), vísdómur (Icelandic “wisdom”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wys, wyse (Middle English), from Old English wīs (“wise”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“knowledgeable, wise”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing; knowledge”), from *weyd- (Proto-Indo-European “to see”).

Cognate with wiis (Western Frisian “wise”), wijs (Dutch “wise”), weis (German), weise (German “wise”), wies (Low German “wise; clever”), vis (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “wise”), vís (Icelandic “wise; certain”), *𐍅𐌴𐌹𐍃 (Gothic “wise”); also fios (Irish “knowledge; information”), fys (Manx “knowledge; information”), fhios (Scottish Gaelic), fios (Scottish Gaelic “knowledge; information”), gwys (Welsh), gwŷs (Welsh “citation, summons”), videō (Latin “to look, perceive, see; to note, observe; to comprehend, understand”), είδος (Greek (Modern) “form, kind, type”), vizë (Albanian “line, stripe, track; dash”), veids (Latvian “form, kind, mode, type”), veidas (Lithuanian “face; appearance, aspect, look”), ве́даць (Belarusian “to know”), вям (Bulgarian “to know”), vědět (Czech “to know”), wiedzieć (Polish “to know”), ве́дать (Russian “to know”), vedeti (Serbo-Croatian), viedieti (Serbo-Croatian “to know”), vedieť (Slovak “to know”), vedeti (Slovenian “to know”), ві́дати (Ukrainian “to know”), գիտեմ (Armenian “I know”), գիտենալ (Armenian), գիտնալ (Armenian “to know”), 𐬬𐬀𐬉𐬛 (ae “find”), 𐬬𐬌𐬛 (ae “to know”), نوید (Persian “invitation; annunciation; good news”), ime (xto “awareness, consciousness, memory, thought”), īme (txb “awareness, consciousness, memory, thought”), ūwe (txb “educated, learned, knowledgeable”), वेदस् (Sanskrit “knowledge, science; property, wealth”). Compare wit (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wise, from Old English wīse, from Proto-Germanic *wīsō. Cognate with wijze (Dutch), Weise (German), vis (Norwegian), visa (Swedish), vis (Swedish), guisa (Italian), guisa (Spanish). Compare -wise (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wisen (“to advise, direct”), from Old English wisian (“to show the way, guide, direct”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīsōn, from Proto-Germanic *wīsōną (“to show the way, dispense knowledge”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know”).

Compare wijzen (Dutch “to indicate, point out”), weisen (German “to show, indicate”), - (Danish) and vise (Norwegian Bokmål “to show”), visa (Norwegian Nynorsk “to show”).

chain.meaning: to show the way, guide, direct

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wisshen, wischen (Middle English), wuschen (Middle English “wüschen”), from Old English wȳsċan (“to wish”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunskijan, from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).

Cognate with wis (Scots “to wish”), wonskje (Saterland Frisian “to wish”), winskje (Western Frisian “to wish”), wensen (Dutch “to wish”), wünschen (German “to wish”), wënschen (lb “to wish”), ווינטשן (Yiddish “to wish”), ønske (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål “to wish”), ynskja (Faroese “to wish, to desire”), æskja (Icelandic), óska (Icelandic “to wish”), ønskja (Norwegian Nynorsk), ønskje (Norwegian Nynorsk), ønska (Norwegian Nynorsk), ønske (Norwegian Nynorsk), ynskja (Norwegian Nynorsk), ynskje (Norwegian Nynorsk “to wish, to desire”), önska (Swedish “to wish”). Via PIE cognate with Venus (Latin), veneror (Latin “venerate, honour, love”), wonder (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English with, from Old English wiþ (“against, opposite, toward, with”), from Proto-West Germanic *wiþi, a shortened form of Proto-Germanic *wiþrą (“against”).

In Middle English, the word shifted to denote association rather than opposition, displacing mid (Middle English “with”), from mid (Old English “with”), from *midi (Proto-Germanic); an earlier model of this meaning shift exists in cognate Old Norse við; elsewhere, the converse meaning shift is exemplified by - (sem-srb) 𐩨𐩺𐩬 (inm “between, amid”) spawning - (sem-srb) 𐩨𐩬 (inm “against”) and even likewise frequent reverse meaning 𐩨𐩬 (inm “from”). The adverb sense is probably a semantic loan from various other Germanic languages, such as German mit, Norwegian med, and Swedish med.

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English withe, wiþþe (Middle English), from Old English wiþþe. More at withe (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English withinne, withinnen (Middle English), from Old English wiþinnan; equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English witnesse, from Old English ġewitnes, equivalent to wit + -ness (English). Cognate with wetenisse (Middle Dutch “witness, testimony”), gewiznessi (Old High German “testimony”), vitni (Icelandic “witness”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English witty, witti (Middle English), from Old English wittiġ, witiġ (Old English), ġewittiġ (Old English “clever, wise”), from Proto-West Germanic *witīg, *witag (Proto-West Germanic), from Proto-Germanic *witagaz, *wītagaz (Proto-Germanic “knowing, wise, clever”), equivalent to wit + -y (English). Cognate with wittich (Middle Low German), gewittich (Middle Low German “knowing, clever, wise, understanding”), witzig (German “funny, witty”), vettig (Norwegian Bokmål), vittig (Norwegian Nynorsk “witty”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Middle English wolf, from Old English wulf, ƿulf (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *wulf, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos. .

Cognate with wouf (Scots), wulew (North Frisian), Wulf (Saterland Frisian / Low German (Germany)), wolf (Western Frisian / Alemannic / Dutch), bolf (Bavarian), bölf (Bavarian), Woif (Bavarian), bolf (cim,mhn), Wolf (German), Wollef (lb), wuf (Ripuarian), וואָלף (Yiddish), ulv (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk), úlvur (Faroese), úlfur (Icelandic), ulf (Swedish), ulv (Swedish), 𐍅𐌿𐌻𐍆𐍃 (Gothic); also olc (Irish / Scottish Gaelic “bad, evil”), 𐌖𐌋𐌊𐌏𐌔 (xlp), olk (Manx “bad”), वृक (Sanskrit), گرگ (Persian), vylks (ltg), vìlks (Latvian), vilkas (Lithuanian), воўк (Belarusian), вълк (Bulgarian), vlk (Czech / Slovak), волк (Macedonian / Russian), wilk (Polish), вук (Serbo-Croatian), vuk (Serbo-Croatian), volk (Slovenian), вовк (Ukrainian), ujk (Albanian), ulk (Albanian), lupus (Latin), λύκος (Greek (Modern)), 𒉿𒀠𒆪𒉿𒀸 (Hittite), 𐤥𐤠𐤩𐤥𐤤 (xld “lion”), walkwe (txb).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wonder, wunder (Middle English), from Old English wundor (“wonder, miracle, marvel”), from Proto-West Germanic *wundr, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą.

Cognate with wunner (Scots “wonder”), wonder (Western Frisian), wûnder (Western Frisian “wonder, miracle”), wonder (Dutch “miracle, wonder”), wunner (Low German), wunder (Low German “wonder”), Wunder (German “miracle, wonder”), under (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “wonder, miracle”), undur (Faroese / Icelandic “wonder”).

The verb is from Middle English wondren, from Old English wundrian, which is from Proto-Germanic *wundrōną. Cognate with wunnerje (Saterland Frisian), wûnderje (Western Frisian), wonderen (Dutch), wunnern (Low German (Germany)), wundern (German), undra (Swedish), undra (Icelandic).

Via PIE cognate with wish (English) (see more).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English work, werk (Middle English), from Old English weorc, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to make”).

Cognate with wark (Scots “work”), werk (North Frisian “work”), Wierk (Saterland Frisian “work”), wurk (Western Frisian “work”), werk (Dutch “work”), Werk (German “work”), Wark (Low German (Germany) “work”), Wierk (lb “work”), værk (Danish “work”), verk (Faroese / Icelandic / Norwegian Bokmål / Norwegian Nynorsk / Swedish “work”); also ober (Breton “to do, make”), gul (Cornish), gwul (Cornish “to do, make”), fearg (Irish / Scottish Gaelic “anger”), ferg (Manx “anger”), ᚒᚏᚏᚐᚉᚈ (xpi “he made”), gwneud (Welsh), neud (Welsh “to do, make”), έργο (Greek (Modern) “work”), argëtim (Albanian “entertainment; fun, pleasure”), argëtoj (Albanian “to amuse, entertain”), váržas (Lithuanian “fish snaring net”), врша (Macedonian “fish-trap”), wiersza (Polish “fish-trap”), ве́рша (Russian / Ukrainian “fish-trap”), вр̑ша (Serbo-Croatian), vȓša (Serbo-Croatian “fish-trap”), vrša (Slovak / Slovenian “fish-trap”), 𐔱𐕒𐕙𐔵 (xag “labour, work”), գործ (Armenian “work”), werz (Kurmanji Kurdish “bed, field, patch; season”), 𐬬𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬰 (ae “to do, work”), ورز (Persian “art, craft, trade”), ورزه (Persian “art, profession, trade”), ورزیدن (Persian “to exercise; to train; to work”), warkṣäl (txb “energy, power, strength”). English cognates include bulwark (English), boulevard (English), energy (English), erg (English), georgic (English), liturgy (English), metallurgy (English), organ (English), surgeon (English), wright (English). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English werken and worchen (Middle English), from Old English wyrċan and wircan (Old English) (Mercian), from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥ǵyéti (“to be working, to be at work”), from the root *werǵ- (Proto-Indo-European). Cognate with werka (Old Frisian), wirka (Old Frisian), wirkian (Old Saxon), warken (Low German), werken (Dutch), wurken (Old High German) (wirken (German), werken (German) and werkeln (German)), yrkja (Old Norse) and orka (Old Norse), (yrka (Swedish) and orka (Swedish)), 𐍅𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌺𐌾𐌰𐌽 (Gothic).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English werking, werkynge (Middle English), warkynge (Middle English), worchinge (Middle English), from Old English wyrċing (“working”), verbal noun of wyrċan (Old English “to work”), equivalent to work + ing (English). Cognate with wirking (Scots), warking (Scots), werking (Dutch), Wirkung (German).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English workyng, wirkynge (Middle English), worchinge (Middle English), werchinge (Middle English), workinde (Middle English), wirkand (Middle English), worchende (Middle English), wurchende (Middle English), from Old English wyrċende, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), equivalent to work + ing (English). Compare wirkand (Scots), werkand (Scots), warkand (Scots “working”), werkend (Dutch “working, acting”), wirkend (German “acting, working”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Deverbal: work out

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English world, from Old English weorold (“world”), from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz (“lifetime, human existence, world”), equivalent to . Eclipsed non-native mounde (Middle English “world”), from monde (Old French), munde (Old French “world”).

Cognate with warld (Scots “world”), Wārel (North Frisian), wäält (North Frisian), wråål (North Frisian “world”), Waareld (Saterland Frisian “world”), wrâld (Western Frisian “world”), wêreld (Afrikaans “world”), Wöd (Bavarian “world”), wereld (Dutch “world”), - (German), Welt (lb “world”), Wereld (Low German (Germany)), Werld (Low German “world”), wełt (Ripuarian “world”), וועלט (Yiddish “world”), verden (Danish “world”), wärd (Elfdalian “world”), verð (Faroese), verøld (Faroese “world”), veröld (Icelandic “world”), vrildan (Norn “the earth”), verd (Norwegian Bokmål), verden (Norwegian Bokmål “(the) world”), verd (Norwegian Nynorsk “world”), värld (Swedish “world”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Affix: world + -wide

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English werm,wirm,worm,worme,wrim,wurm,wyrm,wyrme, from Old English weorm, wurm (Old English), wyrm (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *wurmi, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz (“worm; snake”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis (“worm; larva”), possibly from *wer- (Proto-Indo-European “to turn”). , the latter of which is a fairly recent borrowing directly from the Old English.

First computer usage by John Brunner in his 1975 book '.

Germanic cognates include wörem (North Frisian), wörm (North Frisian), Würem (North Frisian “worm”), Wurm (Saterland Frisian), Wúurm (Saterland Frisian “worm”), wjirm (Western Frisian “worm”), Wüüre (Alemannic “worm”), bórm (Cimbric “worm”), burm (Cimbric “snake”), worm (Dutch), wurm (Dutch “worm”), Gewürm (German “vermin”), Wurm (German “worm”), Worm (Low German “worm”), Wuerm (lb “worm”), burm (mhn “snake”), vūəm (Ripuarian), wüm (Ripuarian “worm”), וואָרעם (Yiddish “worm”), orm (Danish / Norwegian Bokmål / Swedish “worm”), ormur (Faroese / Icelandic “worm”), orm (Norwegian Nynorsk “worm”), yrme (Norwegian Nynorsk), yrmle (Norwegian Nynorsk “female snake with offspring”), 𐍅𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌼𐍃 (Gothic “snake”), уррьм (sjd “gadfly larva”), uʹrmm (sms “gadfly larva”).

Indo-European cognates include vermis (Latin “worm”), ῥόμοξ (Ancient Greek), ῥόμος (Ancient Greek “woodworm”), rrime (Albanian “rainworm”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English worien (“to choke, strangle”), from Old English wyrġan, from Proto-West Germanic *wurgijan, from Proto-Germanic *wurgijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”).

Cognate with worgen (Dutch), wurgen (Dutch), würgen (German). Compare urgeo (Latin “to press, push”), वृहति (Sanskrit “to tear out, pluck”), ver̃žti (Lithuanian “to string; squeeze”), Russian (poetic) отверза́ть (Russian “to open”). Related to wring (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Affix: worry + -ing

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English werying, equivalent to worry + ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English worse, werse (Middle English), from Old English wiersa, from Proto-West Germanic *wirsiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *wirsizô. Cognate with wers (Dutch “worse”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English worste, wurste (Middle English), warste (Middle English), werste (Middle English), wirste (Middle English), from Old English wierrest, from Proto-Germanic *wirsistaz, superlative form of *ubilaz (Proto-Germanic “bad, evil”); compare worse (English).

Cognate with wirsista (Old Saxon), wirrista (Old Saxon “worst”), wirst (Old High German), wirsesto (Old High German), wirsisto (Old High German “worst”), værst (Danish “worst”), värst (Swedish “worst”), verstur (Icelandic “worst”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From worth + while (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old English wolde, past tense of willan (Old English), predecessor of will (English).

The loss of in this word is probably due to weak stress, as in should (English) and could (English) (though in the latter, the was due to the analogy of the former two).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Noun from Middle English wund, from Old English wund, from Proto-West Germanic *wundu, from Proto-Germanic *wundō (“wound”), from Proto-Indo-European *wen- (“to strive, toil, win”).

Cognate with Wuunde (Saterland Frisian “wound”), bunta (Cimbric “wound”), wond (Dutch), wonde (Dutch “wound”), Wunde (German “wonde”), Wonn (lb “wound”), וווּנד (Yiddish “wound”), und (Icelandic “wound”), *𐍅𐌿𐌽𐌳𐌰 (Gothic “wound”) (whence 𐍅𐌿𐌽𐌳𐌿𐍆𐌽𐌹 (Gothic “disease, plague”)); also վանդեմ (Classical Armenian “to destroy; to catch a disease”).

Verb from Middle English wunden, from Old English wundian, from Proto-Germanic *wundōną (“to wound”).

Cognate with buntan (Cimbric “to wound”), wonden (Dutch “to wound”), 𐌲𐌰𐍅𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍉𐌽 (Gothic “to wound”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: See wind (Etymology 2)

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English wrappen (“to wrap, fold”), of origin. Perhaps related to wrappe (North Frisian “to press into; stop up”), dialectal vrappe (Danish “to stuff, cram”), rincworpen (Middle Low German “to envelop, wrap”), wrempen (Middle Low German “to wrinkle, scrunch the face”), all perhaps tied to Proto-Indo-European *werp-, *werb- (Proto-Indo-European “to turn, twist, bend”).

Compare also similar-sounding and similar-meaning wlappen (Middle English “to wrap, lap, envelop, fold”), lappen (Middle Dutch “to wrap up”), goluppare (Old Italian “to wrap”) (from Germanic). ; related to envelop (English), develop (English). Also compare verber (Latin “whip, lash”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English wrappe, from the verb (see above).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wrist, from Old English wrist, from Proto-West Germanic *wristu, from Proto-Germanic *wristuz (compare wrist (Old Frisian), Wrist (Low German), Rist (German “back of hand, instep, withers”), vrist (Swedish)), from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną (“to twist, turn”). More at writhe (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle English writen, from Old English wrītan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrītan, from Proto-Germanic *wrītaną (“to carve, write”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey- (“to rip, tear”).

Cognate with write (Western Frisian “to wear by rubbing, rip, tear”), wrijten (Dutch “to argue, quarrel”), wrîten (Middle Low German “to scratch, draw, write”) (> wrieten (Low German), rieten (Low German “to tear, split”)), reißen (German “to tear, rip”), rita (Norwegian “to rough-sketch, carve, write”), rita (Swedish “to draw, design, delineate, model”), rita (Icelandic “to inscribe, sketch, write”), ritzen (German “to carve, scratch”), *ryti (Proto-Slavic “to carve, engrave, dig”), ryć (Polish “to engrave, dig”), rýt (Czech “to engrave, dig”). See also rit (English) and rat (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English writer, writere (Middle English), from Old English wrītere (“draughtsman; painter; writer; scribe; copyist”) and ġewritere (Old English “writer; composer”), equivalent to . Cognate with ritari (Icelandic “clerk, secretary”), ritari (Faroese “clerk, secretary”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English writing, writyng (Middle English), wryting (Middle English), wrytyng (Middle English), from Old English wrīting (“writing”), equivalent to .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English writinge, wrytynge (Middle English), writende (Middle English), writand (Middle English), from Old English wrītende, present participle of Old English wrītan (“to scratch, carve, write”), equivalent to write + -ing (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Morphologically write + en (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wrong, from Old English wrang (“wrong, twisted, uneven”), from Old Norse rangr, vrangr (Old Norse “crooked, wrong”), from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz (“crooked, twisted, turned awry”), from Proto-Indo-European *werḱ-, *wrengʰ- (Proto-Indo-European “to twist, weave, tie together”), from *wer- (Proto-Indo-European “to turn, bend”). Cognate with wrang (Scots “wrong”), vrang (Danish “wrong, crooked”), vrång (Swedish “perverse, distorted”), rangur (Icelandic “wrong”), rang (Norwegian Nynorsk “wrong”), wrang (Dutch “bitter, sour”) and the first element in the mythic - (Old Frisian) city of Rungholt (Old Frisian “crooked wood”). More at wring (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English wrongly, wrongliche (Middle English), equivalent to wrong + -ly (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Circa 1557; variant of yaught (English), earlier yeaghe (Middle English “light, fast-sailing ship”), from Dutch jacht (“yacht; hunt”), in older spelling jaghte (Dutch “jaght(e)”), short for jaghtschip (Dutch “light sailing vessel, fast pirate ship”), compound of jacht (Dutch) and schip (Dutch “ship”).

In the 16th century the Dutch built light, fast ships to chase the ships of pirates and smugglers from the coast. The ship was introduced to England in 1660 when the Dutch East India Company presented one to King Charles II, who used it as a pleasure boat, after which it was copied by British shipbuilders as a pleasure craft for wealthy gentlemen.

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle English yerd, yard (Middle English), ȝerd (Middle English), ȝeard (Middle English), from Old English ġeard (“yard, garden, fence, enclosure”), from Proto-West Germanic *gard, from Proto-Germanic *gardaz (“enclosure, yard”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ- (“to enclose”).

See also guard (North Frisian), Guart (North Frisian “garden, yard”), gaard (Dutch), gaarde (Dutch “garden, yard”), Garten (German “garden, yard”), - (Danish), gård (Swedish “farm, estate, land; court, yard”), - (Faroese), garður (Icelandic “garden; fence”), gart (Norn “farm”), - (Norwegian Bokmål), gard (Norwegian Nynorsk), gård (Norwegian Nynorsk “farm; townhouse”), 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌳𐍃 (Gothic “court, yard; house”), gardas (Lithuanian “pen, enclosure”), го́род (Russian “town”), grad (Serbo-Croatian “town”), grad (Slovenian “castle”), gardh (Albanian “fence”), gard (Romanian “fence”), 𐬔𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬛𐬵𐬀 (ae “dev's cave”), गृह (Sanskrit “house, habitation, home, dwelling”)), gardinus (Medieval Latin), jardinus (Latin “garden, yard”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle English yerde, yerd (Middle English), ȝerde (Middle English), from Old English ġierd (“branch; rod, staff; measuring stick; yardland”), from Proto-West Germanic *gaʀd, from Proto-Germanic *gazdaz. Cognate with gard (Dutch “twig”), Gerte (German) and probably related to Latin hasta (Latin “spear”).

chain.meaning: branch; rod, staff; measuring stick; yardland

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Clipping: milliard

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Partly from Middle English yanen, yonen (Middle English), yenen (Middle English “to yawn”), from Old English ġinian (“ġeonian”), ġinian (Old English “to yawn, gape”), from Proto-West Germanic *ginōn, from Proto-Germanic *ginōną (“to yawn”); and partly from Middle English gonen (“to gape, yawn”), from Old English gānian (“to yawn, gape”), from Proto-West Germanic *gainōn, from Proto-Germanic *gainōną (“to yawn, gape”); both from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi-, *ǵʰeyh₁- (Proto-Indo-European “to yawn, gape”).

Cognate with jåne (North Frisian “to yawn”), jaanje (Saterland Frisian), joanje (Saterland Frisian “to yawn”), genen (Middle Dutch), ghenen (Middle Dutch “to yawn”), jahnen (Low German (Germany) “to yawn”), gähnen (German “to yawn, gape”), dialectal gana (Swedish “to gape, gawk”), dialectal gina (Norwegian “to gape”).

Compare also зѣѭ (Church Slavonic) (зи́нуть (Russian), зия́ть (Russian)), Greek χαίνω (Ancient Greek)), Latin hiō (Latin), śew (xto), kāy- (txb), žioti (Lithuanian), Sanskrit जेह् (Sanskrit)

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English ȝellen, yellen (Middle English), from Old English ġiellan, from Proto-Germanic *gellaną. Cognate with gälje (Saterland Frisian “to yell”), gillen (Dutch “to yell”), gellen (Low German (Germany) “to yell”), gellen (German “to yell”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Scots yeld (“ceasing to give milk”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Middle English yet, yit (Middle English), from Old English ġīet, gȳta (Old English), from Proto-West Germanic *jūta, from Proto-Germanic *juta (compare jit (Western Frisian), jitte (Western Frisian “yet”), ooit (Dutch “ever”), jetzt (German “now”)), compound of (1) *ju (Proto-Germanic “already”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-, accusative of *h₂óyu (Proto-Indo-European “long time”) and (2) the Proto-Germanic *ta (“to, towards”), from Proto-Indo-European *do. More at aye (English) and -th#Etymology 2 (English “-th”).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Middle English yeten, from Old English ġēotan (“to flow, pour”), from Proto-West Germanic *geutan, from Proto-Germanic *geutaną (“to flow, pour”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”). Cognate with yat (Scots “to pour, yet”), jitte (Western Frisian “to scatter, shed, pour”), gieten (Dutch “to pour, cast, mould”), gießen (German “to pour, cast, mould”), gjuta (Swedish “to pour, cast”). .

etymologies.label: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Middle English yeten, ȝeten (Middle English), from Old English ġietan, from Proto-Germanic *getaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-. More at get (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Sanskrit योग (“yoking, union”), from Proto-Indic *yáwgas, from iir-pro *yáwgas, from Proto-Indo-European —, from *yewg- (Proto-Indo-European “to join”) (whence also yoke (English)).

etymologies.label: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Chamorro yoga

etymologies.label: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle English your, youre (Middle English), ȝour (Middle English), ȝoure (Middle English), from Old English ēower, īower (Old English “your”), from Proto-West Germanic *iuwar, from Proto-Germanic *izweraz. Cognate with jou (Saterland Frisian “your”), jouw (Dutch “your”), jo (Low German (Germany)), jos (Low German (Germany) “your”), euer (German “your”), jeres (Danish “your”).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English yourself, equivalent to your + -self (English).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle English youthe, youghte (Middle English), ȝouþe (Middle English), from Old English ġeoguþ (“the state of being young; youth”), from Proto-West Germanic *juwunþa, from Proto-Germanic *jugunþō, *jugunþiz (Proto-Germanic “youth”), corresponding to young + -th (English). Cognate with Juugd (Saterland Frisian), jeugd (Western Frisian), jeugd (Dutch), Jöögd (Low German (Germany)), Jugend (German).

chain.meaning: the state of being young; youth

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text:
. Borrowed from Italian zebra, from Portuguese zebra, zebro (Portuguese “zebra”), from Old Galician-Portuguese enzebro, ezebra (Old Galician-Portuguese), azebra (Old Galician-Portuguese “wild ass”), from earlier cebrario (Old Galician-Portuguese) (882), ezebrario (Old Galician-Portuguese) (897), from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus (“wild horse”) (Pliny), from equus (Latin “horse”) + ferus (Latin “wild”).

While the word was traditionally pronounced with a long vowel in the first syllable in standard English, during the twentieth century a vowel shift occurred in regions of England, with the shortening of the first vowel. This pronunciation is now used throughout the UK and most Commonwealth nations. The long-vowel pronunciation remains standard in Canadian and American English and is used in the UK only by some older, conservative RP speakers.

Originates in the advice often given to medical students, "when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras".

In reference to the black and white striped shirts they wear.

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: Collectively borrowed from Early Modern Spanish zero, Middle French zero, and (their etymon) Old Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zēphirum, from Arabic صِفْر (“nothing; cipher”), itself calqued from Sanskrit शून्य (“void; nothingness”). . Cognate with cero (Spanish) and zéro (French).

etymologies.label: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (“girdle, belt”). .
